title: Hinge is Absolute Garbage
text:
Zagg sent me the Slim Book as a replacement for the Rugged Book. I was on 3rd broken rugged book case and was fed up with replacements. The hinge on the rugged book would simply explode at the seam on the keyboard part of the case. Zagg customer recommended the Slim Book as a good replacement, said it would hold up better. We'll... 1 month and 3 days later I'm requesting a warranty replacement for the Slim Book. The back part of the hinge mechanism - the "lip" of the channel the iPad sits in - is cracked. That means the iPad simply flops around and pops right out when trying to lift it open. Honestly Zagg, I'm completely disgusted but the lousy quality off your Rugged Book and Slim Book cases. I'll NEVER buy one of your products again. Instead of sending warranty replacements, you should just refund the purchase and I'll buy a keyboard case from someone else.

Update Feb 2017: I'm now on my 3rd Slim Book case and Zagg is sending me the 4th replacement. It's the same problem every time. The lip where the iPad sits cracks. The frustrating thing is that it is such an obvious design flaw that should be simple to fix. Either use a better plastic (a glass reinforced nylon comes to mind) or make the entire channel out of aluminum and beef it up a bit. To their credit, Zagg sends out the replacements without question but I've had to pay another $40-50 in return shipping charges. I would have GLADLY paid an extra $40 at the beginning for a case with a sturdy hinge mechanism.

title: Nice emergency radio.
text:
I purchased this radio on May 1st, 2015 and I'm happy with its performance. I wish it came with an AC power supply to charge/power it at home. As much as these little radios cost, you'd think the manufacturer would include one instead of making it an optional accessory.
The hand crank dynamo and solar panel are nice options for charging. If not in direct sunlight the solar panel won't power the radio, but it does an acceptable job in direct sunlight. The dynamo works very well and I can fully charge the radio in a minute or two. I haven't powered the radio with alkaline batteries, only with the internal rechargeable battery and the solar panel so I can't comment on the play time of alkaline batteries.
In my region of the U.S. the radio's reception is acceptable but not great. The mountains and hills tend to block a lot of signal from analog radios. This isn't a problem for digital tuners or larger radios with better antennas. I wish the optional antenna was included with the radio but it is perfectly acceptable without it. One thing I have noticed is that you have to be very careful tuning the stations in or when you step away from the radio the reception worsens and you have to readjust the tuning knob. Most times it takes me 2 or 3 tries to get the station to come in clearly.
The LED reading light is great. It lights up a fairly large area and doesn't consume much power. I have used it camping a few times and during 3 power outages. The single LED flashlight isn't as useful as the reading light, but it does put out enough light to walk around in the dark. I see no use for the blinking red LED so I don't use it.
All in all I recommend this radio for those who want an emergency radio that is fairly cheap and is of decent quality. You could spend a lot more money and get a better radio, but I'm happy with this one with the few caveats mentioned.

title: Good as it Gets
text:
I bought one of these over a year ago for my truck and it still works as intended. Recently, I wanted to install Garmin GPS units on the vehicles that my wife and son drive. Since they both have (relatively) newer cars, there is not a flat spot anywhere on either vehicle that will take a standard GPS mount. (except maybe the hood or the roof, and those wouldn't work too well as a location for a GPS). These are the only mounts that work. They seem a little pricey for a piece of plastic, but it's the only game in town. I highly recommend this mount to anyone having trouble figuring out where to put a Garmin Nuvi. A heads up on installation--mount it on a smooth (not pebbled or grained) flat surface. Wipe the surface with an alcohol pad or alcohol soaked rag and let it dry. Press the unit onto where you want it HARD and then LEAVE IT ALONE for 24 hours. Don't try to rearrange it and don't put your GPS on it until it has just sat there undisturbed for a full 24 hour day, I don't know anything about the chemistry of this super tape, but I do know if you follow these instructions your mount will stay on as long as you have the car,

title: Absolutely superb camera.
text:
I LOVE THIS CAMERA! I've had and still use many Nikons including an 800 and a D4. The D4 did what it was supposed to, but had a number of shortcomings. The D5 is simply better everywhere. Superb noise and image quality. Great sensitivity. Super fast shutter and frame rate for action. Lots of customization to make it work the way you want. Buttons in the right places with the right customization capability. Great movie capability as well as stills. Incredible control on images as well as mechanics. Better autofocus on moving subjects than I have had before. Intuitive display. Touchscreen is nice. Feels great in your hand.

I just wish it had a built in GPS - but it works fine with several external GPS units, they just add unwanted bulk. And 24MP would have been nice. The 800 is great but more than I need many times. 20MP is right at the edge for great wildlife with sometimes shaky framing. But I think Nikon did the right trade offs on capture rate and image size for this generation.

An hour playing with the menus, tweaking the customization and practice shooting and the D5 felt like home. The menus and options follow the standard Nikon formats, with additional possibilities around things like time-lapse, movie settings, controls and notably shutterless photography - using the electronics of the sensor for very quiet and fast operation.

I have been using this camera in far more settings than I ever used the D4. It is great for many purposes. Sports. Wildlife. Portraits. News. While I recommend against handheld panos for stitching, the leveling display in the viewfinder has given me great results for landscapes and scenics. It is quickly becoming the first camera I reach for.

title: Works well, but there are better, less expensive products available.
text:
I bought my Pan/Tilt Mechanism Kit for Pixy (CMUcam5) along with my Pixy (CMUcam5), which I’ll refer to as the Pixy. It's mounted to a small mobile robot I built to follow colored objects. Here are some pros and cons of this pan/tilt mechanism:

First the Pros:
1. Because the mechanism is specifically designed for the Pixy, it fits like a glove. It looks like it's meant to work with the Pixy because it is!
2. It does not come with printed instructions, which may sound like a con, but the Pixy web site always has the most current detailed instructions (with lots of great pictures!) that make assembly easy. The link is even printed right on the outside of the Pixy and Pan/Tilt boxes. If you don’t have a lot of experience with this sort of thing, don't worry, just go slowly.
3. You’ll need 3 simple tools, which are shown in the instructions, but ALL the parts required are included, and in fact there are some extras just in case you make a mistake and need to cut and replace a ty-wrap or two.
4. If you follow the assembly instructions, it will work with the demo pan/tilt demo program (again, well explained details are on the web site), without additional tuning and tweaking, as you would hope and expect.
5. The 2-piece laser-cut, black acrylic base looks really slick, and it’s wide enough to support the Pixy Cam without tipping…when it’s sitting still.

The Cons.
1. The primary problem with the unit is an artifact of the design. The pan mechanism has to move the mass of the Pixy, PLUS all of the pan/tilt hardware including both servos, their wires, and a USB cable. Because the servos are fairly responsive, the entire unit has a strong tendency to move around on the table top when it’s being used, even though it has rubber feet. It’s kind of like the tail is trying to wag the entire dog. You will have to tape the base down to the table surface you want it to stay. (The Pixy web site even says this.) With that addition it works well, though it is still a little wobbly because the pan servo horn is not really meant to stabilize that much off-axis torque.
2. The other con is the price. For about half the price you can purchase a more stable pan/tilt mechanism from companies such as Adafruit. (Their unit uses the plastic components from the PT or ZITRADES pan/tilt kits available on Amazon, but it comes pre-assembled with servos.) However, it does not have a wide base intended to support the Pixy on a table top. It needs to be mounted to something, e.g. your robot. But once mounted it is much more stable than this unit, even though it has a similar design. It was not specifically designed to use the Pixy, so it requires some customization to mount it to the mechanism. But those instructions are pretty straight forward, and they are available on the Adafruit web site under the Pixy Pet, a small mobile robot that uses the Pixy. (Another fun project, by the way!)

All in all this is a very good unit to learn and demonstrate some of the incredible features of the Pixy. But it almost certainly won’t be the final pan/tilt mount you use if you incorporate it into a robot. Good luck and enjoy your Pixy!

title: Works great to speed up an old HP netbook
text:
This dongle thing plugged in and worked perfectly, not requiring any additional driver installations, on this 6-year old HP Mini 210 netbook (upgraded to Windows 10 Home, 32 bit) with a dead wifi card. The 5 GHz band on this dongle would not work until I had uninstalled the driver for the old internal Wifi card. After I did that, this thing worked great and speeded up all the internet activities with this netbook.

The netbook only has USB 2.0, so download speeds were somewhat limited to only around 20Mbps in this setup (my other laptops at home can do 60Mbps on wifi - my desktop, with a USB 3.0 connection, can do up to 66Mbps on the 5Ghz channel, but only 32 Mbps on the 2.4GHz channel ). The 5.0 Ghz home wifi channel registered a higher signal strength than the 2.4 GHz channel which was surely different and better than the other laptops.

The dongle is a bit bulky and will jam up the adjacent USB ports, so I also got these to use with it:
https://www.amazon.com/UCEC-USB-Extension-Data-Cable/dp/B0142BEEHW/ref=cm_rdp_product
https://www.amazon.com/Kitchenhoney-Female-Extension-Macbook-Computer/dp/B01HG39M1Q/ref=cm_rdp_product

The right angle extension cords also make it less likely that you will accidentally bang into this dongle and damage the USB port.

Now, a few words about why I had to go this route. The HP Mini 210 had become slower and slower for all things to do with the internet, and eventually the wifi completely died. It is actually really easy to take this particular netbook apart from the back plate, and replacing the wifi card would have been a snap. So I spent some time looking into getting an upgraded internal mini PCIe card with 1200 Mbps capability that would be compatible with this netbook. While there were several such products that would physically fit into that half height mini PCIe slot, it turned out that NONE of them were likely to be compatible. HP, you see, has this nasty "whitelist" policy embedded within the BIOS of this netbook, like many of its other laptops. This whitelist prevents you from installing any electronic part into their laptops, unless that part has a matching code built in. Which meant that even if I had chosen to replace the wifi card with the exact same model, but not purchased from HP with that internal matching code burned in, the replacement card would not work. Apparently Lenovo does something similar.

Ugh, so I got this dongle, and so far it works great. I'll post back if anything bad happens.

text:
[[VIDEOID:b9452a4ecbbd4b75e7488810a35ead2d]] I received this iPhone attachment not expecting too much. I am a photographer and own several really nice cameras. I just thought this might be fun to have and less burdensome than lugging around a camera bag constantly. I love to take impromptu photos on my phone and sometimes its fun to play with the pictures. If you like that, this is your product.
First, this kit includes a macro 10X lens. It make absolutely stunning close up photos. As with any macro you do have to be very close to your subject but this lens softly blurs the background and deeply focuses on your subject. Next is the fish-eye lens. This attaches to the macro lens and can't be used without that. It creates breathtaking true fish-eye pictures. I've never been a fan of the fish-eye photo but this has totally changed my opinion. The lens are clipped on with a heavy duty clip that easily and securing holds the lens in place without being over-burdensome when trying to use the camera.
The lens itself is multicoated, very clear, and appears to be excellent quality. They are made from aluminum and easily screw onto the clip and to each other (if you are using the fish-eye). Please note they are not manual adjustable focus, your phone does this for you. And if you are using the macro you have to play with the proper distance until it comes into focus, as with ANY macro lens or setting.
I am VERY impressed with the quality of the lens and the quality of the photos it produces. I'll be playing with set up quite a bit. It comes with a self-adhesive cord to attach the clip to your phone and a soft carry bag for your lens.
I highly recommend this product if you want something a little different and more advanced for your phone photos.

title: Does Not support Multi Room Music, has latency & the sound quality is well below the echo.
text:
I bought this as a a mobile option for the Echo. However, this product falls short for three reasons.

1. Currently does not support Multi-Room music.
2. Sound quality is far below the Echo and is on par with $20 range Bluetooth speakers.
3. There is latency between saying the wake word Alexa and the command. You have to say Alexa, and then pause around half a second before speaking the command. This means you can't talk to it the same way you can other Alexa enabled devices.

While I will admit its nice to have an Alexa enabled device that’s mobile, a few small improvements would make this a far better device. It needs to have the option to automatically enable the hands free mode when connected to the charging dock. It needs to support multi-room music and the latency for voice recognition needs to be addressed. However, even with these changes, the sound quality at this price point is somewhat unacceptable so I don't see this device ever deserving a 5 star rating..

If you are looking for a wireless Echo, consider using a dot paired with One of the speakers. It will support Multi-room music, offer higher fidelity sound and come in at nearly half the price.

title: Now if you just want it to watch your dog or cat during the day it will probably work just fine. I know the reason I purchased t
text:
Caution...Do not purchase this product if you are getting it for a security monitor. I just got off the phone with Nest support for the Nest Cam/Dropcam products and Nest has removed the option to enable and disable the camera when you leave or arrive with your phone (Geo Fencing). Their solution is to use the home/away feature of the Nest thermostat or log in manually to the Nest Cam site and enable / disable every time you need to turn on the camera. This means either you allow the Nest thermostat to turn off the camera when an intruder enters the house because it just triggers on motion and not identity or you forget to turn it on when you leave, which of course defeats the purpose of having a security camera in the first place.

Now if you just want it to watch your dog or cat during the day it will probably work just fine. I know the reason I purchased the Dropcam was as a security device and the ability for it to arm itself automatically when I left home and turned off when I arrived back was essential. I'm going to see if I can get my money back since they (Nest) has changed, to what I believe is, an indispensable and critical feature.

Up until the time Nest broke what was a very good product, I would have given 5 stars. I genuinely liked the Dropcam Pro product. Now that they have broken a common sense feature there really isn't any point in purchasing this product for the price since so many do the exact same thing with similar feature sets.

title: Fast powerful router, upgradable to RT-AC68U via firmware
text:
This is an excellent dual band router, very fast and very reliable. I've been using a regular Asus RT AC68P for over 1yr with no downtime or other issues. I wanted to get this to replace an existing 2.4Ghz router that I was using to extend my network to cover a deadspot.

First, the refurb unit I received looks like new. It was in perfect condition and came with the manual, an ethernet cable and a charger in a plain box. The only difference I could see from my AC68P was the T-Mobile branding on the front.

The first thing I did after unpacking was to swap over the firmware to Asus stock following instructions from bayareatechpros (search for ac1900-to-ac68u).

I then upgraded to the latest Merlin WRT firmware, first by upgrading to Asus stock 378.xxx, then to Merlin 380.xxx. The intermediate step is necessary because of a change in how Asus has structured the internal partition tables.

I now have the router running on the latest Merlin firmware as a Asus RT AC68U. The last thing was to put it into Access Point mode so that I could connect it to my existing network as an extender.

The whole process was somewhat time consuming but saved around $100 so was worth it. Another thing to keep in mind that Asus is currently beta testing its new AiMesh tech on a few of their models which will be rolled out to these ones in the near future. When that happens, these T-Mobile refurbs will be the absolute cheapest way to get a proper wifi mesh network with the next cheapest that I could find being more than $100 per node. On top of that you get all the powerful router tech that's already available.

Bottom line - I think this is the best deal out there for a dual band router at the moment bar none. To get a more powerful device, you'd need to spend more than 2x the money and would likely see no improvement in your network speeds.

4y Edit: I bought an additional one of these and am using both with the newer AIMesh firmware (MerlinWRT) as nodes with my RT-AC68P as the main router. Neither of the T-Mobile units has given me any trouble other than needing to slightly change the firmware upgrade process due to Asus attempting to lock them out. The new process - updated on the same page I reference above - still works to get these onto the latest firmware. Note that this only needs to be done once. After that the internals will register as a stock Asus router and you can use their firmware or aftermarket like Merlin according to your preference.

AIMesh works great and makes the nodes extremely easy to deploy and upgrade. Still highly recommended!

title: Has some very basic limitation
text:
So, I want to give a good review on this product because I think the product engineers need to fix some of these issues. And I would love to discuss these things with the Milo team. So, let's start.

First and foremost. The configuration app has some major limitations. So I have a new Android phone with the capability to see several WiFi networks without any issues. But I could not see the Milo SSID. Called tech. support, and to their credit, I was sent out a new unit very fast. After I received the new unit, the same issue. For the new unit, I used my laptop and saw the SSID, but with no app or program embedded on the device, I could not configure the device. Then I used my Fire Tablet and was able to configure the device. So, the limitation is if you don't have an IOS/Android device that works, you can not configure this product.

Second: I'm placing this in an office building with several WiFi signals. This internal radio must be drowned out, because it is not strong enough to work in an environment with several WiFI networks, even when the products says it can provide a coverage of 4,000 square feet. This office space is one floor and is not good.

Third: You have to log into an online account to configure the device. Why is that? Then when you want to have the Milo device join another WiFi network to expand the original network, you can not use the "+" in the joining SSID's password. This is very disturbing. No other devices has this limitation.

Forth: This device should have the ability to setup multiple SSID's. No advanced features for network performance at all.

Lastly: One of the other reviewers made a statement which is very true. You have to place the devices in "the right spot" to work.

I hope to hear from the Milo team, because I hope I can get a better product upgrade, but if this doesn't work out, I will have to return this device and get an established product brand like Netgear/Cisco/ etc...

title: Great machine
text:
The Good:
1 - The ssd version is fast (out of the box) and the price makes it a great deal, with up to date hardware and gaming capabilities;
2 - The overall usability is great, good ergonomics and the trackpad, while not centered, is good enough (above average after the necessary tweaks) and, since using a wireless mouse is kinda a standard these days, I don't think it could became a deal breaker;
3 - The keyboard is good, shure it is not a mechanical keyboard, but if it had a little more feedback, it would be one of the best keyboards i would have used in a notebook (and I have used a few) and is backlit;
4 - Screen quality is good and brightness is ok;
5 - Speaker are audible;
6 - It looks great with a style that does not scream "I'M A GAMER MACHINE";
7 - Great and easy access to the main (and updatable) components;
8 - Good battery life;
9 - I recommend the ram upgrade to 16Gb and adding the second hd (another ssd), it is a not so expensive upgrade and can make this notebook last the next 2, maybe 3 years with no regrets;
10 - The machine will handle everything you toss at it and if your brain begin to ask for some time alone, you can go play a little. :D

The not so good (for the half empty glass kind of people this is the bad section), in order of annoyance (for me):
1 - Update drivers / update bios / correct drives - you really need to do that, all the problems related to trackpad misbehavior, sound popping and wifi issues will be gone;
2 - Update Windows;
3 - Create a recovery image;
4 - The sound is average and the subwoofer do not make a big difference (and I really do not liked the Waves program, I disabled it and appreciate any inputs if you know how to used it);
5 - Heavy (sort of, if you had a desktop replacement before, you know what I'm talking about);
6 - A little light bleeding at bottom of the screen;
7 - Case is plastic (does not bother me).

title: A wireless Bluetooth speaker that makes you go WOW!
text:
Even so I usually start my review with a description of the packaging, I wanted to mention how much I was impressed with the actual shipping box and thick pieces of styrofoam used inside to make sure packaging box would arrive undamaged. Packaging box itself was made out of high quality thick carton and had a detailed description of key features, included accessories, technical spec, and even a picture of their Ground Control app. The list of key features really sets a tone to make you realize about dealing with a serious audio product. Of course, the focal point of the exterior packaging is a picture of the speaker on the front and the view of inner design on the back. You can clearly see how much pride RIVA takes in their product by showcasing their design, inside out! With a top of the packaging box off, you'll find a small rectangular speaker sitting on a pedestal of inner base, including more protection inside to prevent RIVA Turbo X from any damage. I do have to admit, it's not a lightweight product, and I was impressed with the amount of thought that went into packaging of it to make sure Turbo X arrives at your doorstep intact.

After removing a speaker from the box, you gain access to all the included accessories stored in the base underneath. Here you will find AC power supply, 70" 3.5mm to RCA connector (to connect Turbo X to your external audio source with RCA output port), 48" 3.5mm male-to-male audio cable (to connect Turbo X to any non-bluetooth 3.5mm audio port), and a very comprehensive manual. There is also a special Phono Mode you can activate by holding "+" and "-" buttons together so you can use Turbo X with a turntable that has a low audio output. Although not being able to use a common micro-usb cable for charging, I completely understand why RIVA went with AC power supply (impressive 19V/3.42A output) for a faster charging of its internal massive battery. Even so I didn't see anywhere mentioning of the actual mAh capacity, a mere fact of 26+ hours of battery life (with Surround and Turbo off, and at 75dB of volume level) and capability to charge other devices makes you realize you are dealing with a high capacity rechargeable battery.

Another included accessory is I/O splash cover - a very clever way to cover the exposed usb, audio, and power ports on the back. What makes it unique is how you can store this I/O cover plugged on the bottom of the speaker so you don't loose it. When in need to cover up open ports - it goes right in with a secure fit, and still providing an access to power button.

So how does Turbo X looks once out of the box? There is nothing "cute" or "colorful" about it, instead you are looking at a very elegant design in a shape of a straight forward brick. Surrounded by a mesh grill around front/back and sides, it doesn't scream "look at me", and as I later found out - it grabs your attention with its sound rather than flashy looks. The bottom of the speaker has two rubber feet for an excellent non-slip grip with a surface as well as some dampening of the weight pressure. That is something you will feel right away with a weight of over 3lbs and dimensions of 9" x 4" x 3.5". Unlike other audio products, when it comes to speakers - having "extra" weight is actually a good thing knowing you're dealing with quality drivers and amp inside of it.

Moving on to the top, you have a plethora of illuminated capacitive touch buttons with a proximity sensor that triggers all buttons to lit up as you hover your hand over it - excellent idea when you are in the dark. You can also lock these keys by pressing Mute and "-" buttons together. Of course, all the functionality is duplicated on the remote app for your phone, but more about it later. Here we have a Power, Bluetooth pair-up, Volume up/down/mute (3 separate buttons), and S (to activate Trillium Surround) and T (to activate TURBO) buttons. One thing I wish would have been included or somehow implemented is a transport control in order to play/pause and skip songs from within a speaker, though this functionality is already mirrored in a remote app. Plus, it’s understandable that every button (or combination of buttons) has multiple functionality, so it's a challenge to add more controls.

Also, at the top you have a dual noise and echo canceling mics for Speakerphone functionality. This speakerphone functionality is a great bonus, but to be honest I never really used it with any of my wireless speakers, and consider it to be just a nice "bonus", no more or less. For a speakerphone functionality, you can Accept or Reject the call right from the speaker by using T and S buttons. Last, but not least, the top of the speaker is plastic with a glossy piano finish which somewhat a fingerprint magnet.

At the bottom on the back of the speaker you have a selection of different ports, which as I mentioned before can also be protected with removable I/O cover. In there you will find 3.5mm auxiliary input, a micro-usb data input for a future firmware upgrades (a very important feature), a physical power button (another brilliant idea to make sure touch buttons on the top are disabled and battery is not wasted when not in use), USB charge out port (though labeled as iPad/iPhone it designed to charge any device), 19V DC Power adapter input (to connect AC/DC power supply), and a battery capacity indicator (depending on the color you can determine 0-30, 30-60, and 60-100 remaining capacity). Battery indicator is very important, and you can access the actual battery reading from Ground Control app, down to 1% accuracy.

Pair up with audio source was effortless, and I had no issues with either my Note 4 phone or AK120ii DAP. At first I thought that NFC would have been a good option, but later after discussion with RIVA I realized that due to a small footprint and proximity sensor on the top - NFC implementation wouldn't have been feasible. Once paired up, I had no issues with wireless connection across an open space of 40+ feet. Sound quality was very impressive and deserves a separate section in my review since we are talking about a true audiophile quality performance. And it's not just because it supports some of the popular SBC, AAC, and aptX audio wireless codecs, but actually because of its top notch audio hardware design. Since I'm Android based, aptX codec support is very important to me, but a transparency of the transmitted digital audio is meaningless without a quality amplifier and drivers to deliver their audio interpretation to your ears.

Before I go into a deeper audio analysis, let me talk a little bit about RIVA's remote control app which they call "Ground Control" app.

There are a few other premium speakers that come with their companion setup apps, but those are usually limited to mostly "setup" functionality.
Here, you are dealing with a control app that covers everything! Usually I prefer to leave my phone/source alone and control music directly from a speaker's transport controls (if it's available). Part of it has to do with me using more rugged speakers outside while keeping my phone out of sight. Since I found RIVA Turbo X to be more appropriate for indoor use, the roles reversed and now I was looking for any opportunity to fire up that Ground Control app. You get everything from a precise battery reading to every touch button “access”, including a large volume wheel and even a playback control with play/pause and track skip (though only when using native audio playback app, no 3rd party support yet). And if you want more customization, you can go into settings to change speaker "name", app background control, and my favorite - switch audio prompts between voice and tones. The only thing that can make it better is to add a "no sound" audio prompt option.

Finally, I’m getting to the actual sound! I have reviewed a lot of different wireless speakers, including a number of those which I consider to be smartphone accessories. With an exception of a few, a more detailed audio analysis was simply not necessary for those other speakers since there was nothing special about their sound. With RIVA Turbo X, even before getting to sound analysis, you have to look closer into the actual internal design to appreciate how much this speaker has to offer.

Unlike other speakers that use off-the-shelf generic or headphone drivers, RIVA packs 7 ADX speakers! Starting with three ADX 60mm full range proprietary drivers, it looks like they cleverly placed one in the front middle and two on the sides. Complimenting that, you also have four ADX custom dual piston bass radiators, with two facing front and two facing back. Pretty much, you have speakers and bass radiators all the way around RIVA’s compact footprint. But speakers itself is only a part of this equation. Driving power to these speakers is proprietary ADX 3-channel amplifier with 45 watts of RMS power under control of advanced DSP. This amount of power is higher than I have ever seen from any other Bluetooth wireless speaker in the same category. Keep in mind, more power doesn't necessary mean a louder sound, but actually corresponds to having enough juice to drive speakers to their full “undistorted” potential.

And if that wasn't enough, RIVA includes two "override" modes with Trillium Surround which enhances separation of the sound with 3D imaging and TURBO with EQ mode boost of up to 100dB in loudness level. Surround enhancement is very noticeable and sounds rather natural, not a gimmicky DSP effect. This mode is perfect for watching movies or playing video games, though I also enjoyed it while playing music where a lot of the sound details got a new 3D placement in space. TURBO takes a sound into overdrive. It definitely is useful when you are at the max of the volume and need to squeeze out a few more dBs. RIVA does that with an extra 9dB kick without any distortion (thanks to its smart compressor). This Turbo effect might not be necessary at lower volume, especially since it drains battery quite significantly, but when you want to fill a bigger room with a more powerful sound – activate this TURBO overdrive for uninterrupted 6+ hours of sound bliss!!! Unfortunately, you will take a hefty battery penalty, so if possible – keep it plugged in.

Sound analysis.

I found RIVA Turbo X to have an impressive audiophile quality performance with a full body smooth balanced sound. Just like with any pro speaker, sound quality benefits greatly from a speaker placement to take advantage of the natural acoustics of the room. As a matter of fact, RIVA even includes suggestions with a speaker placement to maximize its performance.

After a closer listening, I found Turbo X to have an articulate low end with a fast mid-bass punch and a deep sub-bass texture. Bass is clear and detailed, well controlled with just a minimum spillage into lower mids. Mids are overall warm and clear. They are thicker in sound, especially lower mids, and it helps in building a foundation for a full body sound. Upper mids are clear and detailed, but not too bright or analytical. Vocals have a very powerful and organic delivery. Treble is smooth, warm, doesn't extend too far, but still captures enough details.

Soundstage is good, and with Surround Trillium mode you expand staging to a new 3D width/depth dimension. Layering and separation is typical for a speaker, which is not necessary the best and even a bit congested when you are standing too close. But once you take a few steps back - sound opens up and fills the room with a more detailed presentation. I think it's a very important factor in order to appreciate this speaker – the quality of its sound perception goes up as you take a few steps back, just like with a regular full size wired speaker.

Another interesting thing about RIVA Audio, they actually encourage you to compare Turbo X speaker against their competition. You know, such encouragement can only come when you have confidence in your product. And to tell the truth – they have every right to brag about it. I have tested a number of other HD speakers, and I feel that when it comes to sound quality and features – RIVA Turbo X stands ahead of its competition.

For example, Braven 855s HD sound is more colored, with a muddy bass, also loud and powerful but not the same level of clarity; heavier in weight, less battery endurance, but with an advantage of a more rugged design. UE Boom is still among my favorites, but it’s not in the same “power” class and when it comes to a sound it has a nice mid-bass punch but no sub-bass support, and sound is thinner where it can’t fill the whole room; battery with only 15hr (though a crazy standby when powered off, lasting months), limited app, though a better splash proof design. B&W T7 impressed me with a build quality, but sound was more colored with a greater level of distortion, and you have to be facing the speaker, otherwise sound gets muffled – not even a matter of which corner in the room you place it, but rather at what height level. Bose SoundLink III is another good candidate for comparison, though I find its bass to be deeper and more on a muddy side, not to mention more spillage into lower mids; in comparison it sounds warmer and lacks the same level of detail retrieval. Didn’t have a chance to test BeoPlay A2 yet, so that one will be an interesting comparison as well.

Summary.

Overall, I was very impressed with a performance of RIVA Turbo X and an audiophile quality design behind it. 7 speakers (3 active and 4 passive) inside of one compact enclosure, 45W 3-channel amp with DSP processing, Surround sound mode, TURBO boost mode, 26+ hours of battery life, aptX support, firmware upgradeable, charge out port to charge other devices, touch control buttons with proximity sensing LED indicators, and a very polished Ground Control remote app – that is a mouthful for a Bluetooth wireless speaker under $350. Is this an absolute perfection? Maybe if the exterior design would have been a little more rugged and there was a way to implement transport controls from a speaker itself. Aside from that, this speaker could be considered a perfection as long as you keep it indoors and careful in handling it. Actually, lack of transport controls no longer bothers me because Ground Control app is truly a fun to use! But the most important thing, once you pair it up with your source and hit Play – you’re no longer hearing the music, but actually feeling it! I don’t think I can say the same about any other Bluetooth wireless speaker I have tested so far.

title: Very pleased with this binocular
text:
I purchased these binoculars to replace a similarly-sized 10x25 pair, from another maker, which I had owned for many years. I am very impressed by the clarity and brightness of the image in the Pentax, which is far superior to my older pair. Part of the reason for that is the older pair once had moisture intrude into the body, and even after drying them out the image was never the same. Of course, I have not tested out the waterproofness of the new Pentax yet, but I am hopeful that they will never have the same problem. I am also impressed with the lack of any chromatic aberration in the Pentax, which I feel is impressive for a binocular in this price range.

I like the extendable eyepieces and the lockable diopter adjustment, which are both nice features to have on a small binocular. I hope that these mechanical devices will be durable enough to last for many years, but I cannot say at this point. The focus adjustment seems to behave well, with just about the right level of fineness in its control.

The pair I bought was factory-refurbished, and I see nothing that would indicate that they are anything but brand new.

The only negative point I have is that I would prefer if they were just a small amount smaller in size, as they don't quite fit into what I usually use to carry optics when away from home (the pair came with a typical strap and carrying case, but I usually don't use individual cases for such things.) They do fit in my hands well, however, and are only a few grams heavier than the pair they replace, which is nice.

title: Not one of five HDMI adapters worked.
text:
NO HDMI VIDEO. So far, only the touch input works. We have tried FIVE different HDMI to display port adapters, including the brands that Wacom themselves recommends: Kanex and Startech. NOTE: THEY CANT EVEN POINT YOU TO A SPECIFIC ADAPTER, only BRANDS that MIGHT work.

Here are the ones we tried for anyone else who dares attempt this:

Kanex iAdapt Mini DisplayPort / Thunderbolt to HDMI Adapter with Audio Support for Apple
StarTech.com Mini DisplayPort to HDMI Adapter - Black - 1920 x 1200 (1080p)
Bosejet [DP 1.2 Version] Super 4K*2K Primium
Sabrent Mini DisplayPort (Thunderbolt 2) to HDMI Adapter [4K Support Gold Plated]
AmazonBasics Mini DisplayPort (Thunderbolt) to HDMI Adapter

NONE OF THEM WORK. You can see them all in the photo.

Bought this for my daughter for Christmas as joint gift between myself, my parents, and grandparent. My daughters laptop, (a gamer laptop by the way, 2 years old, dedicated video card) only has an HDMI out. Confirmed her HDMI port works on other monitors. Tested multiple cables on the Cintiq and on other monitors to confirm they are good. Still cannot get any video to show up on it. Running Windows 10, fully up to date, all drivers up to date.

Ordered from amazon because Wacom can't get their stuff together with their own websites purchasing system. Had to wait 2 months after Christmas just for it to be available on Amazon and skip the hassle of trying to buy it direct from Wacoms website (I even called them as recommended, and because their website ordering was down, they couldn't take my order and told me to call back 2-3 days later). Plus, Wacom takes forever to respond to email / tech support queries, you must call them. Even then good luck getting any resolution.

It could be their Display Link adapter that comes with it, but they want $70 for another one of these and I have no guarantee its going to to work. Screw that, I'd rather return your $1000 product. Ridiculous.

Why the heck would you not support HDMI out?! Instead you jam TWO USB-C ports into this thing. Ridiculous. Its still relatively rare spec at the moment and wont see wide adoption for another 2 years likely. Especially on one of your lower end products like a Cintiq Pro 13. Do I sound like the kind of person ready to drop thousands on a mac with USB-C and Display Port native? NO. Support HDMI out, its that freakin simple. Despite the ridiculous amounts of cables now required, You could have even INCLUDED an HDMI to display port adapter that you KNOW works for so much less money and saved us all the hassle. Instead you are going to lose out on a $1000 purchase.

title: Worth the buy, depending on your needs
text:
This is a decent budget laptop. The keyboard is nice, but not backlit. It does have a full keyboard with number pad. I was surprised how light this machine is. I think this laptop is good for moderate to light gaming.

The Nvidia GT 820 will play older and non demanding games well, but if you looking to play newer games at high settings you will want to spend more money for GTX 850 or higher. Its better than the intel 4400, but about the same as the Iris 5500. I pretty much just play the sims, and it's great on this machine.

I upgraded the laptop myself, I added a ssd drive, which really increased the speed. It has 2 ram slots, only one of them is in use. So you could buy one 8gb ram stick and upgrade if necessary. This pc is super easy to upgrade. The back has three screws, and then you have direct access to the hard drive, and the RAM, and the network card. So I would recommend buying this model with the processor and graphics card you want and upgrading the rest later.

The worst thing about this laptop so far is the screen. This is why it gets 4 stars instead of 5, but at this price you are lucky to find full HD 1080p at all. There are no viewing angles here. It's old school. However, when looking at it dead on its very nice.

Second worst thing is the sound, out of the box it's quiet as a mouse. I'm not sure if there are settings I need to change or what, but for a media laptop it's way too quiet. I use a Bluetooth speaker with it.

Overal, the build quality is solid, it's thin, has a comfortable keyboard, and is easy to upgrade. I use this for school, programming and light games. I haven't had any problems with it at all, not even after I tinkered with it.

***Update** 8/12/16
I have had this laptop for over a year and a half. I have killed the battery. I keep it plugged in all the time, which the laptop keeps begging me not to do. Right now after my complete lack of care for the battery, I am down from 6hrs to about 3. It's great with Windows 10, and still runs like it did when I first bought it. I thought I would update the review since a few people read it. I've been doing some video and photo editing on it, and with the SSD upgrade it's not too bad at all. It works much quicker than I would have imagined. My keyboard is clean still. Typically my keyboards are gross after a year, but the design of this keyboard does not keep dirt and crumbs underneath or between keys.

I hook this laptop up to two monitors using the vga port and hdmi port, and I run 3 extended displays including the laptop screen. This worked easily with windows 8, but is buggy with windows 10, will have to figure that out. I haven't put antivirus or anything on this pc, and I mostly just abuse it daily. I keep the usb ports full, I have a million tabs open in chrome, I run a whole bunch of programs in the background for long periods of time. I have left photoshop open for a month while working on other things without restarting and had no issues with performance. I still say it's a good cheap work horse computer that you can carry with you from time to time. Thinking about upgrading the ram now, just because I can.

If I was buying again, I would probably spend more money for something with the same specs, but lighter and smaller. It's not super heavy, but it is not a delight to carry around all day either.

title: The Good: The little alienware logo draws attention and my ...
text:
I needed a laptop with serious graphics power for my business (3D/Gaming). Alienware has always had a reputation for being an outstanding option for high-end gaming. This laptop had the top of the line graphics card at the time and a decent set of specs. I compared it to the competition, but was sold on the Alienware because of the longer battery life.

The last laptop I bought was a Toshiba 17". I paid about $800 in 2007. That laptop still works. I put Linux on it last year and gave it to my wife.

This laptop is a 17". I paid $2000 for it in 2015. Obviously, if I'm paying more than twice the price, I expect more than twice the computer. Did I get that? I honestly can't say I did.

The Good:
The little alienware logo draws attention and my kids like it. The screen seems pretty good. And the battery life is pretty good. Of all the things I like so far, the battery life is it. The only other thing that I like is the fact that you can purchase an external housing for a full-sized graphics card. That gives a lot of potential upgrade options and makes this a fairly good machine.

The Bad:
For starters, it wasn't until after I bought this that I read all about the issues with the power supply not being strong enough to drive the graphics card to its full potential. The long and short of it is that you have to call Dell and demand a replacement. I did. It took about 3 days to get here and I had to argue with them to get it.

Second, and this is the one that really steams me. There are two graphics cards in this. The first is the built-in Intel chip which the laptop uses for practically everything. The second is the Nvidia. There is no way to force the computer to disable the Intel chip and just use the Nvidia. Oh, sure, you can tell the Nvidia control panel to use the Nvidia as the main card, but in my experience running Unreal Engine 4.8, it was still using the Intel chip. I tried running the Oculus Rift and it was being pushed entirely through the Intel chip. I bought this for the Nvidia graphics card. The fact that I can't force the Nvidia card to be used is absolutely unacceptable.

Third, while there are two hard drives in here, the C: drive is really small. I put on 3DS Max, Maya, Photoshop and Unreal 4.8. Then decided to put on Unreal 4.7 and it failed because I had run out of space. That's nuts.

Fourth, the keyboard layout leaves a lot to be desired. I'm very picky about how the keyboard layout. I want my fingers to naturally fall on the keys. But there are special function keys on the left which require your hands to shift over, resulting in an unnatural feel. I constantly find myself mistyping and having to correct myself.

Fifth, this thing gets crazy hot. It's definitely not something you will want to put on your lap and use for any length of time.

Sixth, the battery life, while very good, is a little misleading. At the higher charges, it holds out very well. But when it got to about 20%, it told me I had about another 45 minutes left. Then in about 3 minutes it powered itself down. I'm used to my Android phone or iPad. When they say they've got 10% battery left, there's still a good hour left. So it was a bit of a disappointment to see the battery go into a sucking vortex.

Seventh, the design. I know some people love it. I think it's clunky and awkward. We had a friend come visit us and she saw the laptop and said, "Wow, that must be an old laptop." I didn't have the heart to tell her that it was brand new and that I'd paid $2000 for it.

Summary
I've had this laptop for about a month now. It's far too heavy to lug around. It's too hot to use while sitting on the couch. It doesn't have the hard drive space to put all the software I need. And the software I do have apparently doesn't work at full capacity, first because the power cord that ships with the unit isn't strong enough and second because the computer defaults to using the vastly inferior Intel chip for most activities. My $800 Toshiba with its 17" screen cost far less and apparently operates just as well. Do I regret this purchase. Absolutely. I'll use this laptop because I don't have much of a choice. But if someone had laid things out for me like I'm doing here, I would have saved my money. Hopefully you can do the same.

title: No longer a portable device
text:
Let me start by saying I have been an IPad fan for years. Every new release I've stayed up until midnight to be the first to purchase. I have an IPad, my wife has and IPad and both of my kids have IPads. So when I tell you that I don't care for Apple's latest IPad Pro, it's not because I'm anti Apple products.
Bottom line is the IPad pro is to big. I heard once that Steve Jobs was against larger IPads because he felt they were ergonomically incorrect. Well Steve was right. My Air2 felt perfect in my hands and fit easily the into any bag. The Pro does not. It feels even more conspicuous in public. Because of its size, it is not easy to handle and I've even found my left arm has developed muscle pain from tying to hold it like a previous IPad. I know that sound reticulous us but I'm telling ya...
However the improvement in sound is unbelievable. The four improved speakers actually makes watching a movie plausible unlike previous IPads which required headphones to hear anything. That's the only positive I can give though. I know reports say the processor and graphics are twice as fast, but I don't notice any difference. The Air2 was already pretty fast.
The only way I can see the IPad Pro being justified is as a laptop, but even that falls short. Mostly because for $1,000 you can get a super computer of a laptop. The pro doesn't even come with a keyboard for that price.
Bottom line is the IPad Pro is no longer a mobile device. And if it's going to be a laptop type device, why not just get a laptop for less money and more performance. I will sell my IPad Pro to the first buyer and go back to the Air2 ASAP.

I then purchased a Yamaha A-S301 from Amazon and was immediately wowed by its sound. It does not have the same tactile feel and luxe features of the Marantz, though it does have a couple of nice ones such as the well-implemented loudness control and a decent built-in DAC. I'm comparing these two models because they are the lowest-priced integrated amps from these two manufacturers.

My neighbor, an audio engineer, came over to help me A/B the units. He agreed that they both sound good, but the Yamaha was more detailed and vibrant; he pointed out that the Marantz is probably more accurate, even though it sounds a bit muddier. Ultimately, I've decided to keep the Yamaha and return the Marantz.

I'm listening through the Pioneer SP-BS22-LR Andrew Jones bookshelf speakers, so maybe I've simply found a good combo. Your mileage may vary.

title: Basic feature evaluation is, on balance, very good to excellent.
text:
On balance this TV is very good or excellent depending on your needs. We use this soley for off-air tv, Directv, Netflix, Amazon, blue ray DVD, but not for games. Since I have direct line-of-sight, unobstructed view of the source (across the bay, Sutro Tower, SF) , and have basically a perfect signal, it is not fair to evaluate this feature.

These features stand out.

Pros:
-very good to excellent picture ++++++ even blu ray DVD was exceptional (Sting Live Berlin), noticably better than on regular HD
-value +++++
-easy to connect to various apps++
-nice clean appearance, even though the edges are silver instead of black.+++
-easy and strong uninterrupted wifi connection (802.1 AC Asus router.) If your signal is weak try moving the router's antenna (if they exist externally) or physically change it's orientation and/or location to possibly provide a more acessable signal to the tv.++++

Cons:
-sound - frequency response (bad) --- useable volume levels are limited. With a simple adapter, I added amplified speakers powered by the tv's usb and use them instead of the built-in, or listen through the home theater (via optical cable)
-angle of view is characteristically narrow for this type of TV . One solution: I purchased an articulating arm that allows us to change the direction of the tv to point/tilt wherever you situate yourelf in the room. The arm 1) spanned studs for easier installation (location) 2) was such that the knobs to tighten the tilt were easily accessable
-rudimentary remote, but it gets the job done. It is a dated interface. The basic Vizio remote has remained the same for a number of years (although some features may vary). Some will find it cumbersome and difficult to navigate and input data on it's opposite side "keyboard".
-no internet browser, even though the tv connects with numerous internet addresses.

The vizio M43 provides most people everything you might need out of a UHD unit. Giving weight to the above pro's and con's will tell you whether to buy this or not. If this TV had a web browser, and a more advanced remote, it would be nearly perfect and would easily earn a "5". For the average person watching off-air tv or other sources, the Vizio M43 is worth serious consideration for an uhd TV.

title: A Great Multimedia Device at a Great Price!!
text:
This is a major improvement over the AIRMM03F while retaining the Android underpinnings. Beyond having a wonderful "space age" retro look, the horizontal screen makes it perfect for viewing videos from YouTube and other sources. The touch-screen tiles on the main screen are changeable so you can customize it anyway you want. I set one of mine up for Voice Help. That option mimics to some degree the functionality of Google Home. I can give it a command such as "Play Abbott and Costello Videos". It will launch YouTube and after the obligatory ad, will play the first video in the play list. The only thing you have to do is change the screen to full size. You can also launch TuneIn stations with the same type of command. You can toggle to a second screen which looks like an Android phone desktop. The sound of the radio is better than the 03F despite not having the subwoofer on the bottom. The larger size makes executing touchscreen commands much easier than on the 03F. I noticed on TuneIn that you get many more options on the homescreen. I like listening to hockey games and when TuneIn launches it will show all of the evening's games just waiting for me to touch play for my selection. The top of the radio has three buttons, power, volume up and volume down. Using the power button on the 03F was problematic, this power button works as one would expect. As with the 03F, this unit has an onboard battery. Some owners had complained about the 03F randomly losing internet connectivity. I've used this unit for several weeks now and have had no problems with staying connected to the internet. The back of the unit features connections for a headphone, micro-sd card and micro-sd plug (the same type used with cell phone chargers). The latter two inputs are less than ideal as most people shoot photos with a regular sd card. Thumb drives and cellphones output to a male USB plug not a micro-sd. I've ordered an adapter cable from Newegg that will change the micro-sd plug to a female USB jack. I'll update the review when that part arrives.

I've owned several internet radios and this is the best one yet. It is visually appealing and the video functionality just is icing on the cake. It is truly a "media player" as opposed to an "internet radio". I'm enjoying it thoroughly and I'm sure that you will too. Any questions, please feel free to ask.

title: NAXA NAB-4003: Infiniti G non-navigation drivers rejoice!  Best ~$10 I EVER spent!!!
text:
I own a 2013 Infiniti G37x Coupe without navigation (I can't vouch for any other Infiniti year/model) and a Samsung Galaxy S7 running the Android Nougat OS. I paired them together the first day for phone calls. (iPhone users get lucky with these Infinitis, as they don't need the following music streaming solution, since the internal, original USB port can just be connected to their phone via a Lightning(?) USB cable). My free trial XM subscription was nice, but 90 days later it was done and I didn't want to continue by purchasing a subscription. Thus, began my hunt for a streaming music solution that would use my phone's music apps and play them through my car's speakers. It's taken months of searching. Those with similar non-navi Infinitis unfortunately (or eventually) understand that the car's internal BT ONLY allows BT phone calls. After extensive research, I found the [[ASIN:B00J4YU7II NAXA Electronics NAB-4003 Wireless Audio Adapter with Bluetooth for USB Connectors (Black)]] referenced in a forum. I ordered it the day after I ordered the [[ASIN:B079FYG5TC Roav VIVA, by Anker, Alexa-Enabled 2-Port USB Car Charger for In-Car Navigation, Hands-Free Calling and Music Streaming. iPhone Users: Update to the latest iOS (11.3)]]. This Alexa unit worked fine (separate review directly under the Alexa product forthcoming), but only played back through my phone. The next day, my NAXA NAB-4003 arrived. Love that PRIME!

You don't need to do everything I'm about to describe, but it's made my drive more pleasurable and automatic. When pairing the NAXA, I initially made the mistake of plugging it into one of my spare USB connectors. My phone didn't see it. However, once I plugged the NAXA into the original USB port located inside the center console, it was easily recognized and paired (the ignition must be on). The BT in my Infiniti turns on automatically when the car is started, but I initially had to also open the phone's BT Settings and click on the NAXA to connect to the NAXA manually as a 2nd connection. Wonderful! Now, after starting the car I just had to press the AUX button below the Infiniti's non-navigation screen and either ask Alexa to play music or manually open my streaming music app and get on my way. That can take a minute or five to get it all going. Since then, I discovered on another forum an app named Bluetooth Auto Connect. In the app I configured My Car (Infiniti BT default name) as top priority, followed by the NAXA and finally, the Alexa device. Now, all my BT devices automatically inter-connected. But then, I realized I also owned the Tasker app. I'm in the process of writing a Tasker script that once everything's connected will launch my music app (Tune-In Pro in Car Mode which automatically plays the last station) and launches Google Maps for my navigation to/from work/home, but just on working weekdays. I also use the IFTTT app to automatically turn off my wi-fi when I leave home and on when arriving home; as well as turning off my BT when I arrive at work.

Many reviewers have mentioned "skipping" or a long delay before they hear any audio. I don't believe this is the fault of the adapter itself, which may have minimal, if any, internal memory (or cache). These delays are actually what is known as buffering. All streaming stations use it and you might find your music/audio app allows you to set the amount of time to "build" the memory buffer's size. Buffering is intended to be helpful by downloading your streaming audio into your smartphone's local memory in advance, in an attempt to eliminate further delays or "skips". However, there are many factors that determine whether your personal buffering experience will be brief or longer or whether it continues to occur as you drive. Among the factors: When you're driving, you're no longer connected to your home's high-speed internet. You are using mobile data instead. So, now it depends upon how close you are to any given mobile tower, signal strength, topography (hills/valleys, etc.), your phone's RAM/processor speed, operating system, weather, cell provider coverage "dead zones", etc. So, those of us who live in good/excellent cell coverage areas are less likely to experience these delays.

Oh, BTW: the audio quality may not match the finest audio units out there, but it plays through ALL of my speakers (stereo; front and rear) and sounds very good. Finally!!! My commutes are so much more enjoyable now and I can ask Alexa questions as I wish. The streaming music automatically either mutes or reduces volume when receiving navigation instructions, making/receiving calls or talking with Alexa.

Best ~$10 I EVER spent!!!

title: A small, effective switch for multi-device users
text:
My household has 4 different gaming systems, and my TV has only two HDMI ports, so switching back and forth constantly was obviously a hassle. I found this product recommended and bought it when it was on sale but after about a year of constant, daily use, I can safely say it's worth full price. The automatic switching capability is great-- even though it comes with a remote, we never have to use it, as the device can detect which system has been powered on and automatically switches over to it. That said, having the remote is handy, as sometimes we might be adding updates to one system while playing on another, and can use the remote to switch from the system being updated to the system actually in use (Note that we have literally never done this, but we COULD if necessary, and that's nice to know.). The switch is small and unobtrusive, it fits easily tucked beneath my TV and isn't distracting in anyway.

We have had no issues, as some users have, with sound not working when switching between devices. In our household, the auto switching is also a boon and not a negative, as we don't use DVR and therefore don't have to worry about being switched out of a movie we're watching if the DVR turns on to record. I can see how this would be annoying, but as I said, in my home, we only use it for gaming systems, so that situation has never come up for us. It also works fine for systems (such as the PS4) that we bring out of sleep, rather than powering on, no problems with auto switching there.

If/when this little thing finally gives up the ghost, I'll replace it with the same. The Kinivo switch has all the things I needed in an HDMI switch: low power use, unobtrusive design, auto switching, reliable. And it's inexpensive, too. A bonus.

title: HP "had" a real winner.
text:
I love this Chromebook. After trying several, in stores and in-person, I must say this model is the best for me.

First of all, I find the screen to be superior to the others. It is glossy, which I prefer, and the brightness and colors are spot-on. I found the screens on Asus, Toshiba and even latest HP Chromebooks to be dull and somewhat "washed out" by comparison. The overall build of the HP models is much sturdier and more solid-feeling than the others in my opinion. The Toshiba and Asus felt like toys while this HP feels well-made like my wife's Mac.

The keyboard is great, also better than the others. It has an excellent, large trackpad

The speakers are amazing, pumping out much better and deeper sound than expected. Although I thought the processor and RAM specs were the same as the other Intel models I tried, this model seems faster than those and even better than the nVidia-powered unit I tried.

I love the look, with the overall white finish and silver trim- reminds me of the older iMacs and iBooks.

The closest thing I can say to a negative is that this is the only Chromebook I have tried with a fan- and after seeing (hearing?) how mice a fanless laptop is, it's a bummer to once again have a fan. But the fan is relatively quiet.

Since HP has apparently decided to get rid of the nice, glossy screens in all their Chromebooks, I'm tempted to get another "last year's model" HP14 as a spare! The screen is that much better.

Be well.

NOTE: I thought I should post the following, regarding my impression that this Chromebook seemed a little faster than the others I tried. After writing this review, I ran the Peacekeeper benchmark on the machine. It scored nearly twice as high as the other Chromeooks I had benchmarked! In other words, it was apparently not just my impression but this model does run a little smoother. FYI.

title: Unless you enjoy reprocessing your photos to meet the idiosyncrasies of this frame, don't buy this product.
text:
At first blush, this appeared to be an ideal replacement for a ten year old frame of identical size and native resolution. Regrettably, it was not to be.

The product is an attractive design and initial setup was straightforward. Thereafter, however, things rapidly deteriorated. The frame recognised the USB stick but, rather than simply loading each file in sequence as my prior frame had done, initiated a laborious, extended and seemingly redundant process of preloading all files (there were 5600).

Once this process completed, pressing "Play" had no effect whatsoever although, after an extended pause, the preloading process restarted. Although there is no indication online or in the documentation, the frame severely limits the resolution of input files (mine are 5760x3840) instead of simply auto-formatting to the native frame resolution. NIX recommends converting files to 800x600 (1366x768 is apparently the maximum) and 72dpi which, imo, is a preposterous and onerous requirement. No decent camera is taking 800x600 photos these days. Moreover, it transpires that a very restrictive naming convention must be followed and standard characters such as underscores, which are commonplace with many cameras, are apparently prohibited. Needless to say, I am not going to rename 5600 files.

None of these deficiencies are documented in the skimpy manual nor, as far as I could tell, in the online knowledge base. They should be emblazoned on all documentation and promotional materials. There were also no error or warning messages which strikes me both as a serious omission and one which, if rectified, would prove helpful to the bemused user.

My now defunct frame, which this unit was intended to replace, could handle all my files as is in terms of resolution, dpi,file-naming and character handling. I simply converted from Camera RAW files to JPEG and reduced quality and was then ready to go. I would have expected the technology to significantly improve after ten years and not to actively regress.

The sole area in which NIX lived up to its reputation was in support which swiftly confirmed my suspicions of the product's limitations.

Unless you're into resizing your files, limiting their dpi and confining yourself to restrictive file-namingsimply to accommodate the vagaries of this frame, I would stay well away from this product. For my requirements at least, it is not fit for purpose. Unsurprisingly, I have returned the unit and will be researching possible alternatives with an unusual degree of care.

title: Great picture, absolutely the WORST operating system I have ever encountered on a consumer product.
text:
Extremely disappointed with the "operating system". The HDMI CEC control function can not be disabled. In other words, whenever the TV is turned on, any associated A/V receiver will be turned on as well - EVEN IF THE CEC FUNCTION IN THE RECEIVER IS DISABLED!

I just replaced our 32" Sharp Aquos TV with this Sony XBR 43" 800E TV. It's beginning to look like a HUGE mistake.

First, the user has no control over how the CEC function is implemented on this TV. I'm using it with a Marantz A/V receiver with CEC function. We like to set the receiver so that when it is not on the signal from our cable STB is "passed through" the receiver to the TV. It worked perfectly with the Sharp TV, but will not work with the Sony TV UNLESS the CEC "power on" function is also enabled on the receiver. Since we only use the AV receiver when watching movies, we don't want it on when merely watching TV, but it comes on anyway! Google software engineers are idiots.

Second .. today when my wife returned from lunch she turned on the TV only to be greeted by some inexplicable display of God only knows what. I eventually figured out that the TV was running the YouTube app, DEMANDING that the user select a movie to watch OR ELSE, and would NOT let us exit the YouTube app or even change inputs. I eventually had to select a movie to watch, then "stop" playback, then press the TV key to get back to normal TV operation, then switch the input back to HDMI2 so we could watch TV through the cable STB. All my wife had done was turn on the TV using the Pioneer Motorola universal remote ... she didn't even have the Sony TV remote in her hand - it was put away.

The last thing we need is a TV with a mind of its own that can not be controlled by the user. I'm going to give Sony one chance to fix this or I'm returning the TV to Amazon.

title: These things are for some stupid reason designed to be able to fold inwards and ...
text:
Piece of s***.
People review these so highly why? I can barely tell the difference in sound quality compared to my $20 headphones.
My main reason for making this review is an issue I came across only after a day or two after owning these headphones.
See the picture attached.
I put my headphones down, went for a break then came back and the ear clamp was on the wrong side, it was facing outwards instead of inwards. I rotated it back to normal but it didn't seem to fit right. I rotated it back around the other way twice and it still didn't seem to fit right. Next thing I know I can't get the headphones to sit properly no matter what I do. I rotate the speaker around the opposite way, nothing. I rotate around the way way a few times, nothing. After half an hour of trying to get the things to fit properly I gave up and started this review.
These things are for some stupid reason designed to be able to fold inwards and rotate 360 degrees. If you take them off normally they may rotate 180 degrees and you may just rotate them back in the incorrect manner and NEVER BE ABLE TO ROTATE THEM IN THE CORRECT MANNER,.
See my picture, that's what happens after normal usage after only a very short time. It clearly doesn't fit at all. How am I supposed to use them?
My $20 Sennheiser headphones never gave me this much grief.
I wore them, put them down, picked them up and put them on and now they don't sit properly.
Again, look at the picture, do you want your headphones to sit like that?
These are poorly built and poorly designed.
Aside from the drastic issue I faced, wearing the headphones normally blocks an unneeded amount of sound. I couldn't hear my mouse click, someone knocking at my door, a bird cawing outside, or even my desk fan. you go completely deaf when you put these on.
Worse than that, if you eat while wearing these you hear in high detail the food sloshing, mushing, and crunching in your mouth. It's all amplified like you wouldn't believe.
Wearing these things not only can I not hear ANYTHING in my surroundings but I can hear my actual breath, and my heart beat. It is very uncomfortable to be conscious of your own breath.

Overall, these headphones are s*** even at normal usage. For me after 2 days they broke physically. Only buy these if you like the idea of complete silence with your heatbeat in your ears whenever you have these on. Take them off and put them on again and they won't fit on. That's the reality. I am very angry and will have to chase this up with warranty.
I'd recommend a semi-open headphone or just anything else but these pieces of s***..
I didn't even put the box away before these f***ers broke on me.

title: Can't go wrong with the RHA MA750
text:
I did a lot of research before buying these, as I tend to do with every purchase of this nature. I could find nothing but praise for the RHA MA750, and now that I own them I can confirm those reviews. Fantastic sound, premier build quality, very comfortable to wear, reasonable price. There's just nothing negative to say about this product. Well, if I'm nitpicking I guess I wish the cord were about a foot shorter. I could easily put my iPhone in my sock for how long the cord is, but I suppose they need to accommodate users of all heights (I'm 5'11").

I worried I would not like the over-ear cable design. I once had a set of Shures that required an over-ear wrap. Those had a thicker cable and were quite a hassle putting on and taking off. Not so with the RHAs. The cord is quite slender and the "pre-bent" shape really helps. Sure, they take a couple seconds longer to put on than your standard set, but these are more secure. No problem with glasses either. They're also very comfortable to wear. My V-Modas had sharp metal edges that would dig into my ears. Horrible design. No such problem with the RHAs.

I love that RHA includes a full variety of tips so you can find your perfect fit. The double-flanged tips work best for me - they don't fall out during exercise. The foam tips seem worthless though - they don't squish down and re-expand like the foam tips I've used in the past. I can't get them to compress enough to get into my ear canal before they expand.

In a perfect world I would have purchased the 750i model, which includes the on-cable remote for the iPhone. But I worried about the longevity of that weak stress point on the cable. One inadvertent tug at unplanned strength in the wrong direction might mean the end of them. I would guess most failures on the 750i happen at that junction. So I guess I'll have to reach into my pocket more often in exchange for what I hope to be increased durability/reliability.

Just a brilliant design from this audio newcomer, RHA. My hat (Scottish beret?) is off to them. Overall highly recommended!

title: Thoughts and comparisons with the Sennheiser Momentum On-Ear
text:
I was looking for a pair of on ear headphones that looked decent, had above average durability and most of all, good sound quality! After a good deal of research I eventually decided on the Phiaton Fusion MS 430. When they arrived, I was immediately impressed by the downright stupendous packaging of these headphones, you can definitely tell that some thought was put into the unboxing experience. Inside, you'll find the headphones themselves, a very sturdy feeling detachable cable with a microphone and volume controls (worked on my Nexus 5, can't vouch for iOS), and a carrying bag, that while not as good as a hard case, is very thick and will keep your headphones safe from most anything they'll come across. In terms of build quality, these things are built like a freakin man! The earpads are made of what appear to be a faux leather with aluminum rings around them, the headband is made of a mixture of heavy duty plastic on the sides and a rubber based top with 2 aluminum posts that keeps the top and sides of the headband separate, and the actual adjustable band itself is remarkably durable and is made of aluminum as well. You have the option to put the 3.5mm cable into either earcup and that allows you to be able to share music with your friends by daisy chaining another pair of headphones into the other earcup, a very nice touch. Now on the category of comfort, I'm not gonna lie, these are rather uncomfortable headphones (even for a pair of on-ears) and I think that lies in the fact that the MS 430 isn't really sure whether or not it wants to be an on-ear or over-ear pair of headphones, now I have larger ears than most and the rubber headband just isn't very comfortable, so maybe I'm a special case, but even after I've broken them in, they still get quite uncomfortable after about an hour to an hour and a half. I also forgot to mention that the MS 430's do fold nicely into a smaller size for easy transportation. Now onto the main category for my purchase, SOUND QUALITY! To put things on a scale, I'm using a pair of Sennheiser HD 380 Pro's as my reference headphones, and I gotta say, when I first put these on, I was blown away with the mids and highs (especially with the Lord of the Rings: Fellowship of the Ring soundtrack), which made male and female vocalists jump to life (and let it be noted, these headphones do not see any major benefits from amplification). With that said, when I listened to "Homecoming" by Kanye West I couldn't help but notice that the sound signature was rather bass anemic, thinking it might have been a coincidence, I turned on "Bonfire" by Childish Gambino and the results were the same, and so on and so forth with every bass heavy song I played, that's not to say that there's no bass response whatsoever, it just doesn't give that same attention to the low end that it gave to the mids and highs.

Now over Christmas I got the Sennheiser Momentum On-Ear which is a completely different animal, with the main 2 differences between them being comfort and sound. But the Momentum's come with a semi hard case (that is better than the bag from Phiaton, but not by a lot), 2 proprietary cables (one of which comes with a microphone and iOS controls, and neither feels as premium as the MS 430 cable, but they're acceptable), and the headphones themselves. The Momentum's are made of stainless steel, with plastic earcups and an Alcantara earpad, overall the build quality is fantastic, but the MS 430 feels much more durable. Now in the category of comfort, they felt very similar on how they hurt my ears, but once I broke them in, the Momentum's are clearly more comfortable, due to their lighter weight and smaller earpad which feels like a legitimate on-ear. In the category of sound, the Momentum's take more of a V-shaped sound, which means there is more emphasis on the lows and highs with somewhat recessed mids, And in all honesty, when comparing the sound of the Phiaton Fusion MS 430 and the Sennheiser Momentum On-Ear, neither sound left me particularly thrilled like my HD 380 Pro's do, because I have a very wide music taste, when I switch headphones I find myself missing out on the lows or mids, however as my daily drivers, I chose the Momentum On-Ear because of it's much better comfort. If you have any questions about either, please don't hesitate to ask. :)
