title: Simple, straightforward, solid performance
text:
Update, Aug 2016: It's been 5 months since I installed this router and it has the distinction of never needing to be rebooted yet! That's a record for me, since some of my past routers needed a reboot every week or two (or even every day or two). I continue to be impressed with the rock-solid performance of this TP-LINK. It's not fancy and lacks some high-end features, but I'll take solid, dependable performance over flash any day.

Original review:
While this router won’t satisfy the needs of those who have complex networking requirements or those who like to tinker and tweak, it offers solid performance, AC speeds and good coverage at a very reasonable price point. If you’re looking to go to AC speed but don’t want all the bells and whistles, this offers a lot for the money.

The footprint is very small compared with other routers I have, which is a nice change. The overall build quality seems very good, and the two antennae are firmly attached (another problem I’ve had with lower-end routers). It has an off switch which is handy if you need to do a reboot. It runs warm but not hot.

Setup is very straightforward if you want to keep the default settings. Basically just plug it into a PC, access the router menu with your browser, set the network name and password, and you’re done. You can access more advanced features if needed, but for a basic setup the time required is less than 5 minutes.

Performance has been impressive. I also have AC routers from D-Link and Linksys that are far more costly than this, but this little guy holds his own when it comes to coverage and throughput. For example, I get Internet connection speeds of about 62mBps with my D-Link DIR-880L. This router, with the same PC and network card, gives me 50mBps. Wireless coverage is a little more spotty with this router on fringe areas (e.g., for a PC located a floor above and at the opposite end of the house from the router) but it still maintains a connection, albeit at lower speeds.

This does lack some features that could be helpful for some situations. It has a USB port, but only has one, and it’s a 2.0 USB port. It lacks a gigabit port as well. But again, for the price, it offers a lot of performance. So far I’ve had zero problems or glitches.

This router won’t excite a power user or satisfy complex networking requirements/demands, but for the basics, it gets the job done with solid speed and performance. Well worth considering if you’re looking for an inexpensive router.

Based on the price and the quality of the Domke F-10, I'm definitely going to be trying their other bags without hesitation.

In conclusion, awesome headphones for the price BUT the build quality is absolute garbage. 2 stars because they were good for what they were until that stupid left earbud detached. I will not be buying these again.

OK... had all sorts of problem with a Targus dock, even after a driver update. I thought I would give Plugable UD-3900 dock a try.
First: It took 5 min. to plug it all in.
Second... there was no second. It recognized the Display Link drivers already on my system and everything started working.
I mean, c'mon. How many times can ANYTHING take 5 minutes. It takes me longer to brush my teeth.
(If I did have to load drivers, maybe another 10 minutes?)

The unit is well built. There was no struggle with connections or attaching the power cord. The plug-ins are all well labeled, and I confess... and am not suggesting, but I did not read the instructions until everything was plugged in. Sound system, 24 inch monitor, USB devices all worked immediately. I really like that you have USB 3.0 for items like smart phones or external drives right on the front (really sensible - that is what will get plugged and unplugged most often). I went from only having 3 USB connections with the old dock to six with Pluggable.
I am in heaven.

title: A joy to use!
text:
What a great little camera! Rich in features, amazing zoom, and with all the different settings to choose from, a real joy to use and play with.

The flash is somewhat whimpy and easily covered up if you don't watch where you place your fingers when holding the camera. The viewfinder registers automatically and the LCD darkens when moving the camera up to the eye, a nice feature. Last night I played around with the different nighttime settings and took pictures of the full moon. The results were all really nice, but the 30 second shutter was a bit too much for such a bright object. 15 seconds was perfect. Needless to say, tripod is a must for such shots.

The only thing I wish was a bit better is lag time between shots. I use a high speed Ultra card and still find it a bit slow with processing before it is ready for the next shot. Thankfully it has burst mode, a necessity for my wildlife pictures.

The hight speed movie mode is very interesting but does not work well in a regular lit room. You need very bright light for it to really pop. But it produces smooth slow motion video.

This camera lacks a GPS function, but I don't find that a negative. GPS is a battery eater, and I would keep it off anyway.

Highly recommended. You can't go wrong with this camera.

title: Great motherboard!
text:
Due to outgrowing my HP desktop, I decided that I wanted to build a new system but stick a budget while using some components from my older system such as my RAM, power supply, SSD, HDD's, and video. I already had a case, so all I needed was to choose the processor and motherboard.

I read a ton of reviews on Amazon, Newegg, and everywhere else online. A lot of people really like the Asus boards. Don't get me wrong, Asus makes some great products, but sometimes I get the impression that you are paying more for the name (like the ROG series) than for the motherboard.

I've already been using MSI products before, starting with my GTX 750 ti TF OC. Since I was happy with that, I went with this motherboard. I am really happy with it.

It has a ton of USB 3.0 connectors and headers for your front panels on your case. OC Genie is cool too, although I can't comment as I haven't yet decided to overclock my system since I'm happy with the i7 4790k's stock speed of 4Ghz.

The UEFI bios is pretty straight forward and it was easy to install Windows 7 from a USB flash drive by pressing F11 to get into boot options and selecting my flash drive. Updating the bios was easy did that the conventional way using a usb flash drive.

As for drivers, MSI does a pretty good job of making it easier to install and update drivers. I prefer to download the latest drivers than to use what came on the DVD, so I did that. I also decided that I didn't want the Killer Network App and decided to install the stand alone Killer Network driver instead.

I put this motherboard into a Cooler Master HAF 922 case with two Cooler Master MegaFlow 200 fans, + 3 Corsair Air Series SP120 Quiet Edition fans connected to my NZXT Sentry Mesh Fan Controller to keep everything cool and quiet.

I've had my system built for the last two weeks and everything runs really well. I'm very satisifed with this MSI motherboard and I can see using this system for the 4+ years without any problems. I'll update as needed should anything change. Otherwise at this time I would like to say that I highly recommend this motherboard.

title: Improves speech and greatly improves music; easy to set up; good value
text:
Like many flat screen TVs, ours has terrible speakers. Music sounds muddy and dialogue can be hard to understand. Our style is modern/minimalist so one of those gigantic racks of audio components plus large floorstanding speakers were out of the question. A sound bar seemed like a good compromise. However, our TV stand is also minimalist, so the standard bars of 30"+ wide would have to sit on the floor and I wasn't too wild about that. We have an extensive Sonos system but between the width of the Sonos Soundbar and the high price, I wasn't too excited to go that route. I was excited to find the Boost and gave it a try. It noticeably improved speech and dramatically improved music.

You will probably need to have the JBL learn codes from your existing remote control. This was quite fast and painless for me to do with our setup. I much prefer this over the reverse of having to add another component and set of codes to the multi-remote. The Boost included analog (RCA) cables and an optical cable. Connecting the Boost to our TV via optical was quick and easy.

Overall this is a solid product for $200 and I'm quite pleased. Don't let the 4 stars make you think this isn't worth buying -- I simply reserve 5 stars for truly amazing products.

title: Do not use to power devices with a common ground
text:
This POE splitter has killed a Roku 2, an Onkyo AV receiver, and a Raspberry Pi. The "ground" voltage output by the splitter is at -48v, which when used to power my Roku shorted with the HDMI's ground and killed everything that was connected over HDMI. Thankfully my TV survived.
Buyer beware. This does NOT comply with the POE standard.

text:

Yes, they connect a computer to an external Hard drive. Yes, you can view your files for a short time. Yes, you will then see a warning window telling you your drive is DAMAGED. Yes, your pictures, files, and your life's work will be DELETED.

Yes, that is Hard Drives (Plural). Using the cable to connect to the hard drive loads the external hard drive in Windows then transmission errors occur that will damage or delete Hard drive Master File Tables. ENTIRE FOLDERS WERE DELETED. THOUSANDS OF FILES DAMAGED OR DELETED. The cables are DEFECTIVE, and they damaged the file system on not one but two new hard drives (and an almost a third one).

Using these Cables to run hash checksums (file verification) results in RANDOM ERRORS generated (ie files checked twice results in two different checksums. ie transmission corruption). Certain files transferred over cables results in corrupted transfers.

Once cords were replaced with another brand, all file checks using check sum hashes resulted in zero errors. However, when using the cable, random errors generated. Experimenting. I tested this on a another drive, on another computer. Again Hard drive damaged window popped up.

You have been warned. If you value your data, buy another brand.

title: Frustrating at times...but awesome shots make it worth it!
text:
(BOUGHT FROM BESTBUY -- REVIEWING HERE) *DISCLAIMER* I am NO professional photographer, professional video/picture editor, or camera aficionado. What I am is a person who loves to be active, go on adventures, and documents those experiences. I DO, however, like to video edit with Adobe Premiere Pro, and edit pics with Photoshop. Im definitely not a pro, but I would consider myself above average in terms of how I use and handle video equipment and how I deal with footage and pictures. My goal is to write this review from the perspective of the "average" user, but with the experience of an above average one. I went on a month-long trip to Hawaii to visit my sister who lives there. I used this heavily every single day in multiple conditions/environments. Here is my in-depth review.

Starting off with the pros, then cons, then criticisms (things not necessarily cons, but depending on who you are/how you use the GPH6, it is important to know).
PROS:
+ Design. The new gopro hero line (plus, 5, 6) are all waterproof up to 10m by themselves. No case needed. Assuming you have the battery and plug doors all closed correctly, the gopro does just fine under shallow water, in rain, or near the occasional wave or pool splash. The removable/interchangeable/REPLACEABLE default lens on this camera is also a great feature. If you crack or damage the lens, its an easy $15 replacement for a pack of 3 on amazon. This also allows you to use different lens with different filters for underwater/lowlight/etc. The touchscreen is no iphone screen, but it is responsive enough and works well. The battery and plug doors can be removed as well to use external batteries/microphones during recording, but obviously the waterproofing goes away. Overall, the design looks sleek and has great functionality. I do wish the LOOK was different per camera. Dare someone to be able to tell the 5 and 6 apart from each other from its face. They wont be able to. I wish there was some noticeable indicator that the 6 is the best and biggest brother in the line.
+ Features. If you are planning to buy the best action cam on the market, there are only two products that come remotely close. Yi and Sony. The Yi 4k+ and the Sony FDR X3000R are the top of the line models of the competitive brand. Picture quality aside, the features of the gopro are nearly unparalleled. Protune. HDR. 4k30fps stabilized, 2.7k60fps stabilized (my favorite mode), 1080p240fps, 4k60 (unstabilized), wide view, linear, zoom, looping video, burst, nightvision, etc. This camera has it all. But the one thing none of the others have including the hero 5 is.....
+ EIS. Say it with me. E. I. S. Electronic image stabilization for those who dont know. Everyone, including YOU, (even if you dont realize it) prefers OIS (optical). But the way GoPro was able to achieve EIS on a camera of this size and maintain its quality picture is an amazing feat in itself. There is absolutely no other camera on the market that does EIS better than the GPH6. And for an action cam, you cant ask for it to get any better. Attached to a self stick and walking around, youd think the camera was on a gimbal. If you have the GPH5 and are looking to upgrade but arent really sure, then just do it already. Its everything great about the 5 with EIS and that is EVERYTHING. Smooth footage = happy footage.
+ Accessories. This category doesnt exactly only apply to the 6. All gopros really. Gopro is the Apple of action camera accessories. All the best accessories and mounts are made for and work best with the gopro line. As good as Sony or Yi maybe, there are times when the camera just doesnt fit with certain accessories you may have.
+ Video quality. I dont wanna dive too deep into this right now, because I'll get into it later. In short, however, the video quality is great. Better than the hero 5.
+ Picture quality. Also great. I will address a thing about it later. But still, it gets you GREAT shots when youre doing "action"-type things. Cliff jumping, skydiving, drone footage, jetskiing, snorkeling. I did it all during my trip. And I got some amazing pictures.
+ ***THIS BULLET POINT ONLY APPLIES TO BESTBUY*** If you're gonna by the GPH6, get it from Bestbuy. Unless you find a better price somehow, get it here (but they price match anyway so might as well get it here). The warranty and protection plan is $50 and with that, you can bring back your gopro for any reason and get it replaced, no questions ask. That is something that is just so invaluable. Obviously getting lost or stolen is NOT covered. But any sort of damage/problem you have? Take it right back, and get a new one just like that. Thank you BestBuy.

Okay on to the cons:
CONS
- So why is my title "Frustrating at times"? Because thats exactly what it is. Frustrating at times. In the 28-day trip, I was putting this thing under HEAVY usage. turning on and off multiple times a day, thousands of pictures (literally), hundreds of videos, timelapses, different modes, mobile charging, car charging, underwater, in the air, running, hiking, you name it. Through all of that, the Gopro froze on me 3 separate times. That sounds like a large problem that happens often. But take my word for it, it did not happen as often as it seems and Im pretty sure one freeze was my fault. I accidentally pressed multiple buttons at once to do different things and it tried doing all of them and just froze and reset. The other two times however, just froze on its own. One time was at an unimportant time while I was walking, and had plenty of time to reset it myself and get it back up and working quickly. The second time was mid-snorkel session, and I missed a lot of cool fish and a turtle. Had to swim all the way back to shore to reset it. I updated it to the most recent firmware. It hasnt happened since that snorkel freeze. But just know....it definitely can happen. For the amount of times I was on this thing, 2 freezes is not so bad. Not great. But not bad. Does put a small frown on my face for $400. (I can forgize the 1 freeze cuz it was my fault)
- "Sliced" video. This happened twice. To describe it, during recording, half the screen froze on a freeze frame of the video, while the other half continued recording. I thought this was just a screen issue, but when I looked back at the footage on my computer (plugged in microSD card), it actually recorded like that. Half the video was perfectly fine while the other half was a still image. It was really strange. Happened twice within 5 days of each other. Hasnt happened since. Thats an annoying thing. Not game-breaking. But annoying enough to mention it.
- Battery life. Battery life on this thing is not great. I dont use GPS or wifi, and I set my brightness to around 40%. Filming at 2.7k60fps, I could get through a whole day at the beach and finish with around 25-30%. But this comes with turning it off when not in use. I would hope other users do this as well. If you plan to leave it on the whole time, you will get significantly worse battery life. I never left it on and recording for an entire time to see how long my battery life was, and I would often charge it in the car when driving place to place, but the longest I went without charging filming at the resolution I said before, was about 7 hours. For me, thats pretty nice. Pictures here. Videos there. Turn off. Turn on 20 mins later, repeat. But when doing a ton of video only, I could drop down to 60% in as easily as 30 minutes when leaving it on. So point is, dont leave it on or in direct sun. Keep a spare battery on hand (I got a free one as a bundle, thanks again Bestbuy!!!!) and an external battery pack. I never actually had to use my spare in an emergency. But it was always nice to have.
- Price. It is expensive. Thats up to you whether you wanna spend it.
**these final 2 cons are objectively bad, but subjectively useless to me**
- Audio. If youre buying a gopro expecting good audio, or buying a gopro wanting to use it as a vlogging or interview tool. Please look somewhere else. This video is for ACTION. Awesome video and cool pictures. Not how those sound. Yes sound is important for great cinematic videos. But if youre expecting to hear the beautiful sound of nature and mountain breeze, youre looking in the wrong place. I dont mind it because when I make videos, I vlog with my phone, and put music over gopro footage. (ya know...like a SANE person). Audio sucks. But you shouldnt be looking for audio out of an action cam.
- Lowlight. Lowlight performance isnt good. Similar with audio, using a gopro for lowlight situations is less an ideal. Maybe for that occasional concert or night event, but overall, if youre looking to use this thing mostly at night or in dark environments, also look elsewhere. I never snorkeled at night and Iwont ever cliff jump in the dark. Know your intended uses before buying anything. You wouldnt buy a Prius to drag race. Dont buy a gopro to film at night. I'll admit the footage is usable if you really want to use it! Its just not very good. Nothing like day time.

CRITICISMS. Like I said, not necessarily pros or cons. But things you should know.

1) Ease of use. Would I say this thing is user friendly? In a sense, yes it is. Anyone can pick it up immediately out of the box and start recording and be happy with it. However, because I am somewhat more experienced and analytical of my footage and pictures, default settings are often not what I settle for. I use protune and go through a lot of trial and error on what works and doesnt work depending on the situation. I love the option of having protune. But the fact that, if I were an average user, that I'd have to go in and understand what iso, exposure, white balance is, and which color profile works best for what Im doing is a little farfetched. The average user DOESNT know those things. So its hard for me to call this user friendly. Most people will be okay with the default settings and how things look. But the untrained eye often settles for what doesnt disturb it. Trained eyes see much more in the details. To get the perfect shot, you will have to do some tinkering. Again this is not a con. And maybe it serves the "Pro" in Gopro. But Im disappointed in how ugly the default settings are when you compare it to those who edit pics and videos. Video quality is very serviceable right out of the box. But if you want really GREAT video quality, you gotta know what youre doing a little bit. Go on youtube or read some articles on protune to get the MOST out of your gopro. I highly highly recommend doing this if you want the best.
2) Purple hue/highlights. **SEE PICTURES** Like with video, protune allows you to adjust things to get the best out of your gopro. However, no amount of adjusting gets rid of the strange purple hue/highlight that shows up in bright. In the pictures I attached, if I hadn't pointed it out to you, would you have noticed? Some maybe yes, others maybe not. The pictures are unquestionably great pictures. And some of my favorite shots. However, in the dog picture, look closely at the highlights around the edge of the rocks. In the sunset picture, look at the reflection in the sand on the right. Do you see that purple hue? I have seen very few (definitely a couple) people talk about this. But one youtube video, I cant remember who, did point it out and say it wasnt a big deal. And frankly, I actually agree. When I showed these pictures to all my friends and family, they all said how great the pictures look and nothing else. I didnt point out the purple, so maybe someone noticed and decided not to say anything, but otherwise, no one mentioned it. I dont think its a big deal. It doesnt ruin the shot. And it can be taken away with some postediting in photoshop. However I uploaded these in its unedited fashion. I tried getting rid of it with protune on the gopro, but it would still be there. I do want to point out that this does not happen often. Sometimes its there. Sometimes its not. Sometimes its very noticeable. Sometimes its subtle. Its a toss up really. If you think this is deal-breaking, then thats up to you. I am fine with it. Im not sure if its a software issue or hardware lens issue. Im leaning toward hardward. I hope GoPro addresses this in the hero 7.
3) The final criticism I have of this great action camera is this. Inconsistency. Like with the purple hue, protune, freezing. All combined together. Sometimes the gopro will mess up and do weird and pretty frustrating things. But when it isnt doing that, its getting great video, great pictures, and is a ton of fun to use. For me personally, Im okay with it. Because like my review title states, the times you do get those awesome shots makes it all worth it. If it was frustrating ALL the time and only got good pics/videos a few times, I'd probably say otherwise. But for right now, the awesome shots outweigh the frustrating times and I have had a blast using this. I go out of my way to try and participate in things where I can use it more and record more. Since buying this camera, Ive done more things even AFTER my Hawaii visit. Im not saying this gopro will change you as a person. But if you let the purpose of the camera shine through the frustrating mishaps, it definitely is a great buy.

Buy it from BestBuy if you can. They'll match any lowest Amazon price and you can do the protection plan. And you can probably get it faster. You probably live near a bestbuy so you can do instore pickup. Thats what I did! If not, buy it from wherever you please. I do recommend it. Have fun and thanks for reading my essay! And that is my fear that it may become slower by installing all those Windows applications. Over the years, I have always been choosy in installing Windows 10 programs because a lot of them modify the registry and startup with Windows, which slows down the computer.

But as of now, I really love this Windows 10 tablet!

title: Entire weight supported by 1/8" nut which failed, but otherwise a good design.
text: I really liked the flexible design of this switch which is why I was willing to pay a premium price for it. The flexibility in mounting options and the power cord were key features since I am a bit OCD about messy tangles of cables. But after being installed for 2 weeks, today I found a design problem with the mount. Initially I had mounted the switch with the wider edge to the mount and had no issues. But today when trying to neaten things up a bit, I decided to see if using the narrow edge mount position would work better. It was in this position for just a minute or two before I determined it wasn't an improvement and decided to go back to the wide face mounting position. Unfortunately, although it appeared the catch on the end had released, the switch would not come away from the mount more than about 1/4 inch. Closer inspection showed the metal plate holding the catch had come loose from the plastic mount. After fully removing the mount, I found the cause to be poor design. The entire weight of the switch is held to the mount by a single screw going into a small nut press fit into the plastic. The nut had pulled out of the plastic by the extra weight of the switch in this orientation that sticks just a bit further out from the mount. I checked the other intact end and it was a similar poor design, but at least it had two screws on either side to distribute the weight better. I am going to try super glue to see if that will secure the nut in the plastic better. If not, a screw through the empty hole all the way into the wall stud should do the trick. But I shouldn't be having to do this on an otherwise premium product. The rest of the design was done so well it is unfortunate that the physical security of a $130 switch all hangs on a 1/8" nut press fit into plastic. It couldn't have cost much more for an actual through bolt.

title: Cool concept, execution has some issues
text:
I've been slowly getting into Home Automation and wanted to add some exterior security cameras that I could integrate with SmartThings. I didn't want to have to run new electrical lines or have extension cords draped all over, so I was looking at battery powered cameras, specifically Blink and Arlo. I wound up deciding to go with Blink because (a) it's cheaper and (b) I read far fewer reports about delayed recording starts with Blink.

Currently, I have two of the Blink interior (white) cameras mounted on the exterior of my house in well protected areas (covered front porch, screened-in back porch) as well as an XT/exterior (black) camera mounted where it is subject to the elements.

On the plus side, set up of the cameras was easy and straightforward, and both the audio and video quality are, in my opinion, quite good. I can't comment on battery life except to say that after slightly under a month of use the cameras are still reporting their battery status as "OK"

On the minus side, I do experience significant delays in recording start times with all of these cameras. For example, when a neighbor kid recently was watching our dogs while we were out of town, the porch camera didn't start recording until she had walked up the walk to the house, traversed the porch, and had started unlocking the door, at which point she was barely visible on camera. I finally decided to try an experiment with the exterior camera; I armed it, went outside, walked to about the edge of its field of view, and then ran to the camera, jumped up, and touched it. It did record, but it actually didn't start until after I was underneath it and hidden from view. If somebody wanted, they could actually steal my security camera by running up to it like I did, jumping up and grabbing it, and removing the batteries. The solution, I suppose, would be mounting enough cameras that a stealth approach to one camera would be picked up by another, but that's a lot of cameras and expense.

I'm also disappointed with the SmartThings integration. That's my fault, as I did insufficient research to determine that while there is a custom device handler which supports Blink, the author charges for it. Arlo integration with SmartThings can be accomplished free of charge.

I'm still tinkering with placement and sensitivity settings to see if I can get the cameras to work better, and not having used the Arlo cameras, I can't say if they work better or worse, but I am somewhat dissatisfied with my Blink cameras. On the other hand, in my mind one of the primary benefits of having the security cameras is simply to deter would-be thieves or vandals; why take the chance of being caught on one of my cameras when they can just go to a neighbor's house and have no such concerns.

I have some interest in buying an Arlo camera to compare the performance, but at least for now the interest isn't strong enough to compel me to actually do it. On the whole, I think my take with the Blink cameras is that they're a pretty neat idea but don't work sufficiently well that I'd want to rely on them in a situation in which timely recording was critical.

title: Great value
text:
I was a little skeptical about this alarm clock as I have been using the same Sony Dream machine for the past 15 years until it threw in the towel.
The Magnasonic so far has been a great addition and a very good value.
The clock was easy to set as it does have an automated feature, you pick your timezone and it does the rest.
Dual alarms was a must have and works well. You have the option of setting the alarm for every day (1-7) just week days (1-5) or weekends (6-7).
The alarm wakes me instantly on the first beep and gets louder and more frequent as it goes. The snooze is activated simply by waving your hand over the clock, this could be dangerous for some folks I suspect.

Many people have complained that the display is too bright even when set on low, while I might agree with that Magnasonic has provided a solution, you can set the display to auto off, it will stay on for a few seconds then shut the front display off while the projection stays on. If you want to see the clock just wave your hand above it and the front display shows for a few seconds. Perfect for me.
The projection display is fantastic, very easy to see in a dark room, during the day it is a bit difficult but still can be seen. You can rotate the projection to shine behind the unit all the way around to the front where it can shine on the wall across the room.
Radio on the unit leaves a bit to be desired, it shows digital tuning but you do it with a manual wheel which can be a bit tricky, not a problem for me since I do not use this feature.

Over all a solid product at a good price!

Great sound quality with some manufacturing and quality control issues.
This is a follow up review:
I don't pretend to be an audiophile and I know head phones are also about personal taste but I must say I still like my old HD 600's better. With an inexpensive amp/dac the HD's just "sound" better. They are also more comfortable overall.
The build quality and ear pads are better on the HD 600's. Don't get me wrong. For $299.00 these Hifiman's are a great buy but for $349.00 (on Amazon) I purchased a new set of HD 600's and they just "sound" better to me.
I listen to all types of music for an "old guy". Classical, metal, jazz, blues, techno, and yes even rap are part of my daily listening habits. Currently I am also trying to get through the latest iteration of DOOM.
All the files have been converted from CD or LP to FLAC and sit on my local Server with my ripped Blu-Ray movies.
I still like the Hifiman's but for $50 more the Sennheiser HD 600's driven at 300 Ohms just sound better. The tonal neutrality is really what works for me when it comes to a good set of cans. Thanks.

title: NUVIS 2689 and 2699: KEY FEATURES, ADVICE and TIPS
text:
Nuvi 2689 and 2699 - KEY FEATURES, ADVICE and TIPS

This review has a very unusual perspective, which addresses only a bit about "What's New" and Great on the Nuvi 2689. Instead, my focus is on its generally wonderful performance as the latest Nuvi, primarily because it operates A BIT BETTER IN MANY RESPECTS than my predecessor 3590 (now over 3 years old).

I actually own the Nuvi 2699, which is NOT offered by Amazon. However, since it is virtually identical to the 2689 sold by Amazon, I am posting this report here; my perspective also directly concerns the "sister" models 2599 and 2639 (and virtually all other recent Nuvis with Voice Command in the 24xx and 25xx lines). Thus, I am hopeful that Amazon will recognize the value of this review, and allow it to display here [My 2699 has a Traffic Alert cable that supposedly updates slightly more often than the 2689, but that's the only difference.]

I have used 3 Nuvis extensively for the past 6 years and love them, and also enjoy spreading the good word about them. I offer this unusual perspective for the Nuvi 2599, and the 2689 and 2699 (the latter both are 6" models).

[Please notify me in "Comments" about errors anywhere in this review, and I will respond in kind, and correct this report.]

MOST NOTABLE NEW FEATURES
The 2699's best improvement for me, over my 3 year model 3590 is (1) the Bigger 6" screen, which is THE main reason I bought: It makes a crucial difference for my eyes, eliminating the sometimes blurry text.

Another major difference is (2) "Real Directions," but not quite the way Garmin promotes it. Although Real Directions does occasionally use "business landmarks" to call attention to city street turns, I estimate that occurs no more than 10%: My wife and I find those instances interesting, but not truly valuable. Instead, we really like the turn guidance improvement that simply says "Turn at the traffic light:" That announcement is always made with just one traffic signal DIRECTLY ahead; combined with the enlarging white arrow on the magenta map route, it removes all doubt that THIS is where we are supposed to turn. Our previous Nuvis (855 and 3590) would instead name an upcoming street turn, but often we were uncertain which of two upcoming streets it really was (unless there was an overhead sign in large enough print). Whether or not this is "Real Directions...as spoken by a friend," we greatly appreciate the improvement.

The third (3) major improvement is the ability to customize up to 4 "Data Fields," and display them in what I term a "stacked-trio box," of "Trip Data," at the Right side of the map. [The 3590 had a similar ability to display a lesser amount of "Trip Data," in a format titled "Dashboard."] I discuss this feature later in the review.

There are multiple other slight improvements (over the 3590), but I consider them making the Nuvi only a bit better, i.e., slightly faster or more helpful. This includes the Up Ahead feature for POIs such as gas, food, and rest areas. [The 3590 had a similar feature, but it only worked on freeways; Up Ahead functions everywhere.]. This new feature is also discussed later in the review.

Another slight improvements include guidance on freeways with multiple lanes, such as "be in the second lane from the left (or right) on freeways AND at occasional traffic signals, thus preparing you to make a second (quick) subsequent turn; and directing you while inside large malls and parking lots (and guidance L/R when exiting back out to the street): Previous Nuvis offered no direction off streets; however the 2689/2699 will direct you right to the door of a single business in a giant shopping mall (Garmin titles this new function "Direct Access)."

A useful new feature is that this Nuvi always shows the street name just below the map, plus the screen is much brighter and easier to view than my 3590, and the "pinch-to-zoom" map scale adjustment is far easier to use than the older unit. Other features that SEEM to work at least a bit better or faster are Voice Command, Search, initial satellite connection, quick route recalculation after my errors, and the map identifying most small towns (and small rivers) on highways that we drive through.

I am a bit of a "stick-in-the-mud" guy, when it comes to adding the latest technology onto my Nuvi 2699. Thus, I have NOT used Bluetooth to connect a smartphone, nor downloaded Garmin's Foursquare online link: My wife has her smartphone on when we drive, but we have no need of Foursquare's trendy POI reviews, nor "ecoRoute;" and we can certainly get weather reports and gas prices via her cell connection while driving. Thus, I have no comment on those Nuvi related features.

I am still undecided whether the added "Foursquare" database of POIs (built directly inside the Nuvi, versus the Smartphone connected version) is a significant improvement; similarly, I don't have enough experience with Traffic Alerts on this device to judge that feature. I can only hope that each proves worthwhile in time.

My only major dislike with the 2699 is that the cable connection is on the device itself (rather than on the mount, like the 3590), requiring constantly disconnecting it upon every time we leave the car: I worry about theft. I strongly preferred leaving the cable permanently connected. It is also frustrating reconnecting the back of the Nuvi to my air vent mount with each re-entry. [NOTE: Owners of the very similar, but two years older Nuvi 3597, are enthusiastic over their Magnetic mount, which easily "click-connects" and disconnects the Nuvi!]. I also dislike the very limited internal battery life of just one hour, but this is not a biggie. Otherwise, I just love this unit!

-------------

My Advice to Help Learn and Enjoy Your Nuvi:
I will offer 3 EXAMPLES of crucial Nuvi features, and explain how Voice Command, Trip Planner, and the "onboard" Help App can work for you.

This is followed by 2 TIPS for customizing and using the features Up Ahead and Trip Data (you won't find that info in the manual, or "Help").

Just in case that's not enough in your quest for knowledge, I also offer "My 6 Most Important Features of the Nuvi."

Further personal opinions are: It Isn't Perfect....followed by.... My Best Advice

Related Nuvi Considerations...and...Final Comments

THREE EXAMPLES OF IMPORTANT NUVI FEATURES
Most of the remainder of this perspective really applies to all Voice Command Nuvi models produced during the past the past three years. These comments and advice are the result of having read many hundreds of Amazon user complaints, many of which indicate misunderstandings or complete ignorance of how some features work. I think it sad that so many users post their frustrations on various Nuvi operations, and the great majority never receive any feedback Comments. While some claim they are returning their units, my guess is that the rest use their Nuvis inefficiently, or never realize how much they don't know...and simply "miss out" on some features.

1st EXAMPLE - We were driving on a Palm Desert, California, three lane residential highway, and suddenly remembered that we wanted to buy a grocery item. [This city was totally unknown to us.] Using Voice Command, we said "Find Category"...and then said "Grocery." The Nuvi offered a list of the nearest groceries in just a few seconds. While pondering out loud IF we wanted to choose #2 on the list, it heard us and immediately responded and offered to navigate us to "Ralph's." We said Yes, and agreed with the offer to add Ralph's to our existing route back to our resort. This was a very quick interaction with the Nuvi, while traveling at 50 mph, and choosing a grocery only .9 miles away: We arrived within about 3 minutes, bought our item, and the Nuvi immediately routed us back to the street and our destination.

While on our 2,000 mile road trip (so far), we made similar Searches to "Add to Existing Route" dozens of times (often several each day), to reach McDonalds, Costco for gas, Starbucks, Denny's, Rest Areas, etc., receiving excellent instructions to and back to the highway or street. The Voice Command works wonderfully to conduct the Search, as directed by myself or my wife, as "co-pilot."

2nd EXAMPLE - I used the built-in App called "Trip Planner" to create 10 driving routes, for our major daily trips. [Any GPS will take you from Point A to Point B, but this (and several other Nuvis) include Trip Planner, to go from A to B, and then set a custom route to C, and then D, and end up at a motel at Point E.] Each route is thus pre-programmed and SAVED as long as you want, until you start your trip. I use a road atlas while in my living room to visualize all the highways I want to travel each day, and then program each route on the Nuvi, basically "shaping" them to go exactly where I want. I use a feature within T.P. to "Browse Map" and place a finger directly on the screen to "build" each waypoint and day's interim destinations. When done, I review each route by "zooming in" on the map to insure all highways and points are as intended.

A simple day's Route may be nothing more than the starting point motel in the AM and that night's motel at the end. NOTE: I search for and SAVE each motel before I begin any of the routes, and use those as Start/End points for each Route: Everything else--highways, towns, scenic national parks, or whatever--is just added in between, and the Nuvi then creates the full day's Route. I might add a diner into the route for the AM, but leave lunch and gas to be searched for later each day.

3rd EXAMPLE - All recent Nuvis contain a built-in HELP feature; the 2689/2699 store HELP inside "Apps," which is on the Main menu screen. Press HELP and you have access to the main elements of the Nuvi online manual. Although I consider both HELP and the manual far too brief, and virtually without any accompanying images or examples, they are still very useful to new users. The App HELP is especially handy where ever the Nuvi is, to recall the meaning and use of most basic operations. The HELP feature contains 12 broad categories, each filled with sub-menus and brief explanations. You will also often find a blue Question Mark at the top Right of some menu screens: Press the "?" and you will get some instruction for that specific screen. [As crucial as HELP can be, I believe this may be the first ever mention of this feature in any Amazon Nuvi Reviews!]

TWO TIPS FOR (1) TRIP DATA...and...(2) UP AHEAD
TIP #1 - Modify your Screen to Display Key "TRIP DATA"
You can greatly enhance your screen display, by creating Custom Information Fields, to show travel data such as Arrival Time or Distance, VIA Point Arrival Time or Distance, Direction, Time of Day, and Elevation. Thus, in addition to the gray data box at the bottom Right of the map (commonly "Arrival Time"), you can create a "stacked-trio box" to display any 3 of 9 data elements. To do so, while the Nuvi has an active route (and you are PARKED!), tap the gray Right data box, and a scrollable screen will appear, offering 9 data categories: Tap your choices of any 3 to form your first three-tier box. Note that you can ALSO change what is displayed in the existing, gray square box at the bottom Right; different choices are offered for either while on a route, OR not on a route. The four total boxes are the equivalent of what used to be titled on other recent Nuvis as a "Dashboard."

You can "fiddle" with this list AND the bottom Right box to avoid having a duplicate category; with some effort you can end up with a total of 4 different data fields (instead of your original, single box). For active, long trip vacationers like ourselves, the ability to custom build a range of data fields is a tremendous improvement over the previous 4 fixed fields (termed Dashboard by Garmin).

NOTE 1 for above: You must first go to Settings > Map and Vehicle > Map Tools and tap the chosen Trip Data item to place a "check mark" by it; then tap Save and return to the main menu screen. Now experiment with your possible choices. [This Tip is NOT explained in the Nuvi online manual, although there is a tiny reference to it on page 6.]

NOTE 2: All 9 categories can be VIEWED AT ONCE, by tapping the gray Speed box at bottom LEFT; this brings up a black Trip Data screen, which is scrollable; it contains the same data categories you use to create the three-tiered box at Right.

NOTE 3: The above modification also works on several older Nuvis (units since at least 2013). I choose to have the following in the stacked-trio: Arrive In (=time until reach an interim Via point), Via Distance (in miles), and Arrival Time (at Final Destination). Complementing these in MY gray square at Right bottom is Distance (=miles to Final Destination). I know this appears confusing and complicated, but these settings make long trip routes easier to enjoy the passage of time.

[Please notify me in "Comments" if I am in error anywhere in this review, and I will respond in kind, and correct this document.]

TIP #2 - Use "UP AHEAD" to Search while On A Route
Much like Trip Data, you can also customize a list of popular categories for a quick (manual) Search while driving, to display 3 items (out of about 7 choices). The neat part of Up Ahead is you can flip back-and-forth with Trip Data, by tapping the three black bars, OR leave one of those features on the screen as long as desired.

NOTE: A list of 3 Up Ahead items is offered by default, but you can switch them with other categories as desired; tap on the deployed UA list (such as Gas, or Rest Areas, or Food), and the Nuvi will automatically display the closest places to your location as you are moving. Change the categories by tapping any one; at the next screen, tap the "Wrench" symbol at upper Left, and "scroll" the screen choices to view all 7 items; tap one to replace an existing category.

NOTE: The 3 Bars require manual manipulation and is most safely done by a passenger; however, depending on the Nuvi placement, a driver may have a short reach and do it him/herself. My air vent mount makes this easily reachable. [The safer alternative is for a driver to use Voice Command, and perform Searches via the full menu listings, such as Find Place and Find Category.]

SIX MOST IMPORTANT FEATURES OF THE 2689/2699
Voice Command - To search hands-free Named Places, Categories (especially food, gas, and rest areas), Recently Found, Saved Locations, Cities, etc.

Trip Planner - As described earlier

Get You There, Under Any Conditions - It is awesome when you are on an unknown highway, road or street, or in an unfamiliar city, and you have Total Confidence that you will reach your destination with exact and efficient directions. I might sometimes be confused, BUT I'm never lost! I have read tons of complaints about poor and/or ridiculous routing, but very rarely experienced same (although some have been my own "user error"). On the other hand, consider this: Just imagine driving in the dark and/or behind a rainy windshield, trying to fold and hold a paper map, where you are uncertain about the road or intersection or know that you made some mistake "back there:" This (and any Nuvi) Will Get You There. Remember that you can make decisions with the Nuvi all day long, and with Voice Command, never have to stop along the road.

Detailed Turn Directions and Large Map Screen - The combination of Turn Arrows, Lane Assistance Arrows, Freeway Exit ramp graphics, precise spoken instructions several times before each turn, an obvious white arrow on the magenta route line, the enlarged intersection view as you get closer, the new spoken "Real Directions" at the end telling you to "turn at the traffic light" (or a Real Directions landmark) is just terrific. Real Directions will often (but not always!) place you in the best lane to be in if there is a quick second turn about to follow. I enthusiastically endorse the 6" screen for making it noticeably easier to read (especially the tiny lettering used for street names on the Trip Data and Up Ahead screens).

Easy To Use Search Functions - Some persons may not find Search easy to LEARN, but with practice it is Easy To USE. Repeated practice with Search, both manually and with Voice, will make use efficient and frequently stun you with its accuracy. But it does require much practice to avoid frustration. You cannot expect much if you just plug it in and go. Learn to Search in a specific city (identified in the black box at upper Right); THEN, many placename Searches CAN produce correct results without having to go through Find Place or narrowing down a specific Find Category: Try it yourself, especially for major brand names! It is up to each user to practice and experiment. My wife and I are constantly delighted by quick and accurate Search results; we also laugh at some results, shrug them off, and love to keep re-entering Searches with different methods until we are successful (if Voice fails, she will manually Search).

Preview of Route ALTERNATVES Before Selecting GO - EVERY time that you Search and receive a list of possible destinations (and when you choose a POI from Saved, or Recently Found, or Categories), the Nuvi displays a three-part line beneath your choice: Thus, it offers "Routes - i - Go!" (the small I inside the white circle stands for "information"). Press "Routes" and it will quickly calculate and show up to 3 possible routes, color coded and showing distance/travel time. Press the small i and it displays brief info about the POI, including address and phone #, plus travel time/distance (based on its favored route). It's up to you to select Route preference, and then press "Go!"

Recent Nuvis in the 24xx, 25xx, and 35xx lines will operate with mostly the same 6 features as above, but I don't know how smoothly and quickly they operate. I do know that the three 26xx models, and the 2599, are the latest evolutions (versus the other 2-3 year older ones), and that my unit is better in most respects than my three year old 3590.

IT ISN'T PERFECT
This is my 3rd Nuvi in 6 years, and each new one improved significantly enough to warrant the upgrade. I have read thousands of Amazon Nuvi reviews, reflecting many seemingly valid complaints...and many ridiculous ones. I, too, have encountered some major glitches (frozen screen, erratic satellite reception), to the extent that I exchanged faulty units with both Amazon and Garmin, and the 3 replacements have worked great (including one "refurb"). Yes, Nuvis will make frequent mistakes in pronunciation, you will suffer some frustrations with Voice Command recognition and Search responses (but fewer with the new 2689/2699), spoken turn directions will sometimes come late (and some TOO late), a store might actually be on the opposite side of the street, screen glare will frequently hinder you a bit, and you might suffer a rare screen "freeze." BUT all of the foregoing mishaps are easily survivable, and many can be overcome with simple patience: repeating a command, searching manually, glancing at the map to know where a turn is imminent, tilting the Nuvi to cut glare, "rebooting" to reset the unit, etc.

I am always amazed at new user complaints like "it doesn't take the best route to my house...so how can I trust it when I'm somewhere unknown?" Conversely, everyone already knows how to get home, but it's precisely when I'm "away" that I need guidance...and CONSTANTLY, mile after mile! I trust the Nuvi to take the right highway for hours, switch onto another one when necessary, find any desired POI along the route, get us to the nearest grocery in city X, and return us directly back to our motel...EVERY TIME.

In our experience, the bigger the Nuvi mistake, the more we laugh in amazement at how it goofed; some glitches become "teaching moments," and we learn from them. We have NEVER actually failed to reach any interim or final destination. For all of the many shortcomings, our Nuvis have been overwhelmingly wonderful in "getting us there." They have been 90% great for us, and the 2699 deserves a 5-Star rating so far. We revel in the confidence of driving ANYWHERE UNKNOWN, and knowing we will arrive as intended, regardless of freeway complications, dark and rainy nights, temporary unit malfunction, or our own mistakes. Nuvis no longer speak "recalculating:" they just silently re-route you. I initially hated not hearing "Recalculating," because I liked knowing I had goofed, but really, the end result is always a successful arrival. However, there are still a few cues to alert me about a recalculation: One may notice the white map arrow and magenta line suddenly radically shifting (redrawing) to correct your route; also, since I have "U-turns" enabled (= UNchecked!) in the Navigation > Avoidances settings, some turn errors will generate a spoken command to "make a U-turn when possible." That is a great alert about a driving boo-boo.

MY BEST ADVICE
Buy from a vendor that will let you drive the Nuvi long enough to try many situations, and to take a long trip for experimentation. Practice with all the functions, and try not to let any frustrations become a "showstopper." Be receptive and try your best to learn all its features, realizing that the great majority of positive Amazon ratings (4.2 stars, currently) mean that it works well for "them," and it should also be great for you. Be willing to exchange it if it has a major glitch: Amazon, Costco, and Garmin have all provided me great customer service. Amazon is currently selling only the 2639 (no Voice Command) and 2689; Costco is selling only the 2699, as of this April.

Download the online manual directly from Garmin and read it to get a good overview of the main features. Review it again after driving a lot, and you will probably absorb a lot that you didn't realize at first. NOTE: You should also take advantage of the extensive HELP feature, found in APPS on the Main screen; get used to using it...until you don't need it anymore.

PRACTICE...Practice...Practice with main Menu Settings and features, as recommended below. The more you use the many features, the more confident and efficient you will become; if your passenger learns as well, driving will be safer than letting the driver sometimes becoming too distracted from the road. Go through all the Menus, and their sub-menus, but BE CAREFUL adjusting the settings: You may want to make one change at a time, and review the effect before finalizing each choice. Be especially careful about selecting/changing Voice Language ("Samantha" is best, for Real Directions), and Navigation settings (most users will want to chose "Faster Time;" many will also leave most "Avoidances" UNCHECKED, except for "Unpaved Roads").

Because the Garmin manual is so brief and inadequate with explanations, it is mostly up to YOU to experiment with tapping everything you see on the screen...and you will be surprised with lots of discoveries! TAP While You Are Driving (or have a passenger do it). Again, TAP everything!

For instance, tap the turn arrow at top Left. Press the green Navigation Bar at the screen top to help you review ALL upcoming turns, and remaining distances while driving. Press the 3 black Bars at bottom Right, and explore the various options, but especially Up Ahead, Trip Data, and Traffic alerts. Tap the Speed box and the other bottom gray box at Left, both on a route and also with NO destination. Press the + and - symbols at the left side to Zoom in and out for map scale. [HINT - count your Zoom taps, so that you can go right back the exact same number, and be at the original map scale. The Nuvi will automatically reset to a default map scale, as needed, at all turns.]

Explore the APPS category, shown on the Main Screen. The HELP app is VERY useful to new users, as it provides info about a wide range of operations. Since I never have used the Smartphone Link, Phone, ecoRoute, Where I've Been, or Last Spot, you're on your own to explore those Apps.

RELATED NUVI CONSIDERATIONS
I encourage owners of the Nuvi 2639/89/99 (and the virtually identical 2599, a 5" model), to consider buying the following three accessories that I rely on:

Arkon Vent Mount or a "beanbag mount" (rests on the dashboard): both place the Nuvi closer to the driver, making it easier to read and manipulate by hand; I think they make for safer use than windshield placement. My vent mount puts the Nuvi about One Hand Length Away from my steering wheel.

Soft or Hardshell Case: Both help protect the Nuvi against drops. I prefer the Garmin branded Soft "sleeve" case (= about $20) for its minimal protection, because it fits inside all my pants pockets; a hard case will be bulkier, but stronger. Will it fit in all your pockets? I take the Nuvi and case with me every time I leave the car: GUYS...think about it: Would you want to HOLD a thick, Hardshell case throughout your visit to the restroom? Or worry about leaving it behind on a table after dining?

Wall Charger: is certainly not crucial, but for the $6 I spent, it is really handy to practice with the Nuvi in your home when it's new, and to enter many "Trip Plans" while in your easy chair (and not exhaust the limited 1 hour battery life). Another benefit is that while on the wall charger, the Nuvi operates as if on car battery, so you can view live Traffic Alerts in your area..

Every prospective buyer of a Nuvi model 26xx (and 2599) should take advantage of all the Amazon Nuvi reviews categorized as "Most Helpful," to understand their features and pros/cons. Collectively, I believe they are the Best (and most honest) source of information BEFORE You Buy. They also address most everything else about these models that I have omitted.

Conversely, the best sources AFTER You Buy, are two GPS user forums: You will have to do a simple Internet search for "Gpsreview" forum, and "POI-factory" forum, to find them. [Amazon might delete the full, specific addresses.]. Both have the largest Garmin user followings on the Internet, and are filled with experienced owners who love to help others solve their Nuvi issues. Ask away, and you will feel welcome at both sites. Most of what I know about Nuvis came from them!

FINAL COMMENTS
I still have about 1,500 miles to go on this current "test drive," but am confident in this review's accuracy to date. I have not had any unit "freeze" yet (although I did reset it once), nor suffered any major glitches. My wife and I have enjoyed encountering and puzzling over various little "mysteries," which usually give us something to chat about...and continue to "learn as we go." I expect to edit and add to this report by mid-May. I look forward to any comments or questions from readers, and will reply as necessary.

title: Fit my large hands perfectly. Extremely well designed mouse
text: Im an estimator for an extremely large construction company and I basically live at my desk. I work on average +/- 70 hrs a week. Prior to getting this mouse, I began feeling carpal tunnel in my right hand. Since using this mouse for over a year now, those symptoms have subsided tremendously. The mouse itself takes a little getting use to. But after about a month I used it for every computer task. I'm 6'3" and with large hands, the large sized mouse is the 1st mouse I've ever owned that fits my hand great. I use the wheel all day taking blue prints off online and the feel of the mouse is great. I also work from home quite a bit and I'm about to buy a 2nd one. I also bought the mouse that needs to be charged. Using the mouse for 8-10 hours a day, I can use the mouse for at least 10-14 solid days before I need to plug it in. And when it's plugged in , I'll continue to use it. I would say it takes no longer than 90-120 min to fully charge. Best mouse I've ever owned. I've been a full time estimator for 8 years utilizing the wheel and this mouse doesn't disappoint.

title: 3.5 Stars.  Excellent sound quality in this well-made and handsome unit but over-priced
text:
I am perhaps a smart-speaker/Bluetooth speaker addict. I love to set them up and listen to different sounds and I enjoy figuring out which have the highest value-ratio. Also, I am generally a fan of Bose products, in particular their Soundsport and Noise Cancelling headphones.

Summary of this item:
This is a standalone unit with front and rear-firing speakers that connects to your home Wi-Fi to create a Network of Connected speakers if you have more of this same unit or either of their new Soundbars. What this means is that you can use pretty much any music service you are a member of (Amazon, Apple, Spotify, Pandora, etc) and through the Bose app, connect to those accounts and toggle easily between those services and your playlists or content on any of them. These 500 speakers can then be placed in different rooms so you can play the same music in all rooms at the same time or different music in different rooms. All controlled through the Bose app. If you are aware of what Sonos is, this is what they do. This speaker can also go in to Bluetooth mode so you can connect it directly to your device such as iPhone, iPad etc. It also has an Auxiliary port for even more connect ability.

Positives:
-Handsome and well made.
-Screen is nice which shows song and artist as well as album or song art work. I am not sure how necessary this is, but it does look good.
-The sound is very good and "Room Filling" Think of their Wave Radio from back in the day and you thought "How could this much sound come from this small device?" That is a Bose hallmark and not missed on this device.
-Connection options: I love that you can go in to Bluetooth mode or have the Aux cable. This is something Sonos does not do.

Neutral:
-There are two soundbars that can be networked to this or other 500 speakers.
-Size. See photo with pen for perspective.
-Sound: True to Bose, it does sound overall well, but specializes in nothing. Bose does a good job representing the sound exactly as it is and not being bass-heavy or treble heavy. The sound is good and at times spectacular. At high volumes it isn't at it's best but at medium volumes it is.
-There are two subwoofers that are compatible with this unit and those would probably sound great, but one is $400 and the other is $700.
Negatives:
-Price. At $400 you can purchase two of the newest version of the Sonos One. I have one of those pictured in size comparison to the Bose 500. Those Sonos One also have Alexa and be separated for true stereo. In my test with both a single Sonos One and Stereo Sonos One, I preferred the Sonos One in both. With just one of them, it was close, but with the pair it was no contest. Sonos. Not only that, but you can separate the Sonos One to be in different rooms and then combine easily for stereo when needed. (Note: I have nothing to do with Sonos, but feel they have excellent products.)
-The App lost my speaker numerous times over several days and I had to touch the speaker like turn volume up or down on the actual speaker in order for the App to re-find my speaker. If it couldn't find it, I couldn't do anything with the music unless using voice control. This was annoying! The app should just work and find the speaker right away.
-With front and rear firing speakers, the sound can fill a good sized room, but becase they are front and rear, what that means is that your display would need to be sideways in order to have the sound travel throughout well. Look at my photo of the Bose 500 against a window. In this position, the speaker will fire against the window and forward. If you can position the speaker truly in the center of a room, that would be ideal to maximize it's range and effectiveness but how realistic is that?

Summary If you listen to this in a demo at Bose or as a standalone you will be impressed with the sound coming out of this small package. And you should be. It's excellent. You will also like the screen and you should. It's great. But be aware that I don't feel the networking is ready for prime time in my experience compared to Sonos. I just don't know why my app couldn't find the speaker numerous times and then all of a sudden could? It's has great connection options with Bluetooth and Aux and looks great and upscale. For sound, there are better options of networked speakers at this same price point that will provide a more robust audio experience although not quite as versatile.

title: Perfect size and features for carrying a mirrorless body and 2 or 3 lenses
text:
I own many Think Tank products and had high expectations for this bag. No worries, it lives up to all of them.

The quality is fantastic, as expected from Think Tank. The stitching is strong and neat. The materials are rugged and durable. And the design is very functional. The shoulder strap seems a bit lightweight, but this is a lightweight bag. The strap is more than up to the task.

The space inside the bag is more than enough for a mirrorless camera and 2 or 3 lenses. In my bag, I have a Sony A6000 with the 16-55mm kit lens attached, a Sony 55-210mm lens (with hood reversed), and a Tokina 11-16mm without hood but with a Neewer Nikon F-to-Sony NEX adapter. Also in the main compartment are a small 3rd-party battery charger and two spare batteries. There's a pocket inside the compartment which is advertised as big enough to accommodate an iPad Mini. It's also big enough to fit a letter- or A4-sized sheet of paper "tri-folded" so as to fit in a #10 business envelope.

The dividers are pretty standard - 3 thin, very lightly padded. velcro-attachable. One of the dividers has an internal slot for a cell phone or similar-sized device. Another of the dividers also has a strip to accept the velcro of an additional divider. That additional divider is designed to span from one end of the compartment to the middle of the divider with the strip, so you get 2 square spaces instead of 1 larger, rectangular space.

On the outside, there's a double-zippered front pocket that's very close to the full size of the bag. The zippers go the full width across the top and about 2/3 of the way down each side. This allows full access, but keeps the front of the pocket from flopping open when the zippers are fully unzipped. Inside, there's space for spare memory cards, papers, a passport maybe. There are 2 small pockets inside. One of them is occupied by the included rain cover. You'd better be confident in your map folding abilities if you ever have to pull it out -- it's folded really tight and fits very snugly in its pocket.

Inside the top is a flat rectangular pouch with a zippered closure and a transparent front. The transparent panel isn't clear plastic that will wind up separating or cracking or yellowing, it's some sort of woven material. A nice feature.

The top of the bag is a nice design. As with the front pocket, it's a double-zipper opening. In addition to the zippered part, which is the rectangular-shaped opening of the top of the bag, there's a flap that extends beyond and hangs down over most of the front of the bag. This doesn't just flop around - there are two magnets inside the flap that will hold it flat against the bag. They *will not* hold the top shut if there's gear in the bag and you pick it up by the top handle. They're just there to hold the flap against the bag. This is a good setup, I think. If you don't want the bag to open, you can zip it fully, or just zip one or both sides and leave the front of the zip unzipped. No problem, the bag will stay shut. If you're going to be in and out of the bag while you're wearing it (cross-shoulder looks to be the ideal way), you can leave it unzipped and just rely on the magnets in the flap to keep the lid shut. It won't take much to open it up, but the location of the shoulder strap mount points (metal hardware, by the way - no plastic parts involved in attaching the strap to the bag) means that the bag won't "tip over" and allow your gear to fall out unless you're doing something that turns the bag upside down.

On each side of the bag is a pocket. The one on the right side (as viewed while wearing the bag) is non-elasticized and partially lined with what feels like nylon. On the left is a fully elasticized pocket made of stretchy material. Each pocket is about 3", or 7.5cm, square.

Finally, the back of the bag (closest to your body) includes a flat sleeve that will allow you to mount the bag on your belt if you'd rather do that than use the shoulder strap.

Top marks for all of the above. If you're familiar with Think Tank's Speed series of waist packs, you might expect more external pockets and storage space. It's clearly a design trade-off to keep this a small and lightweight bag, in keeping with the small, lightweight gear it's designed to carry. I have more than enough room to carry all the items that correspond to the ones I normally carry in my Speed Freak bag in support of my DSLR -- body, lenses, memory cards, spare batteries, charger, data cable, small documents.

There are cheaper bags that aim to do the same job, but nothing is designed or made as well as Think Tank. In my opinion, this bag is well worth the money.

title: Either I got a lemon or the fit of this product is not working for me.
text:
According to the reviews, this little company that cannot even put a good one sheet manual, somehow managed to make the world's most amazing headphones comparable to those big companies with deep pockets for research and development. Reviewers said: "fantastic in the lows with rich bass", "have incredible bass", "deep but tight bass", "packaging is easy to open", "Very good noise cancelling", "Good fit", "Comfortable to wear", "solid quality",
Let's walk through these properties

Physical Build & Packaging:
It has a solid build, Pair of headphones with the smallest ear inserts weigh 6.8 grams (0.23 ounces). It is missing some of the fine details, for example left and right ear markers are not etched on the headphone, instead it is on the inside of the silicone insert.
The cable resists tangling but I wouldn't characterize it as "anti-tangle". If I compare it to standard Apple issues headphones, yes it is more resistant to tangling.
Packaging is just OK. There is a sticker outside indicating that one must pull hard to open the box in broken English. If you don't have long fingernails, you'll need some sort of a prying tool to dislodge the box's top.

Fit:
The fit is average for my anatomy. It does not come off when running or training, but it does not position the speaker deep enough in ear canal to produce good sound. Unlike those earbuds that cover your ear channel with suction to isolate noise, this actually sits comfortable without covering your ear channel. Downside to that is you don't get noise isolation (if that's what you are looking for)

Sound quality:
Please note that the fit has a big play in perceived sound quality.
I disagree with almost all the reviewers before me. It does not have "deep bass" or "great bass", it sounds like a tin can. It has no bass at all. Let me put it this way, if you don't like the standard Apple iPhone's headphones for bass generation, you will hate this headphones. It has nowhere near the same quality of bass production of iPhone's headphones. Hence, there is no point to compare it to a $99 or higher priced premium headphone.
Overall it is just average. it does not produce rich sound, it produces hallow metallic sound.
Noise cancellation: They don't claim to noise cancel anyway but some reviews claimed that it did noise cancel. Well, it doesn't, which is fine since they don't claim to do that.

Would I recommend this to anyone:
No, because it is not a sure bet like some of the other brands that I used.

title: Good replacements for my Razer Deathadder 2013
text:
Switches work well and the solder job was fairly straightforward on my older Razer Deathadder 2013. If you are considering fixing a double clicking mouse by soldering instead of replacing the internals, here are some tips (I learned basic soldering doing this):

You will need a soldering iron, rosin core solder, a soldering wick or a desoldering pump, a damp sponge and 00 iron wool.

Watch some soldering tutorials for through hole components / keeping the solder tips clean, and...

Make sure to tin the solder tips and keep them free of oxidization! This is very important. The solder won't remove easily, and new solder joints won't form easily if this is not done. I nearly bricked a board learning these things. Learn from my mistakes and be prepared!

title: So much negativity ...for not
text:
Plenty of people have reviewed this laptop and for those who didn't do their homework and are giving negative reviews...well good luck to you. I am not an HP promoter or fanatic or would I claim that their product is better than any other manufacturer, but you need to read and see what others are saying. I for one read a lot of negativity about this laptop and praises as well, not only here but reputable online reviews and blogs.
But for me it was a simple choice, I just needed a well made light laptop with a great screen, keyboard and had to have a stylus. Portability was my concern. Needed to take on the road for email, typing and the occasional video chat and that's it...Oh and coloring, that was the purpose of the stylus.

I was also considering the Dell XPS 13 and the Razer Blade Stealth 13, but HP won over the others due to value and I was also willing to make a compromise over its "flaws".

For one this laptop will get hot and I will admit that. If you are heavy into streaming, such as watching YouTube videos or you thought you could play World of Warcraft for hours on end "Yep it gets hot". If you are a "Lapper" like me, you use this device on your lap, do the smart thing get a laptop cooler or a lap desk of some kind preferably with a fan. Don't use a towel or cloth to protect you legs you will just block the vent intake ports and cause the laptop to overheat that much faster.

For those having glare problems, I recommend getting an anti-glare screen protector, which is what I did works great for me with no issues with the touchscreen. As far as the touchpad well... it's not Apple "What can I say" and trust me no one is near Apple when it comes to touchpads. So you have a choice, you learn its quirks or get a mouse, I for one hate touchpads and got the matching mouse from HP.

This is my laptop and I knew very well what I was getting into and I am very pleased with the choice I made.

title: Excellent Quality High-Res Monitor for MacBook Pro
text:
Having been spoilt by Apple's 27-inch Thunderbolt displays, I was looking for a worthy replacement which comes at least a bit close to Apple's quality, to use with my mid-2014 MacBook Pro (with 15" Retina Display).

I first got an LG Monitor: [[ASIN:B01BMES072 LG 34UM68-P 34-Inch 21:9 UltraWide IPS Monitor with FreeSync]] thinking a 34-inch size and a 21:9 aspect ratio would make the monitor even better than an Apple monitor. Boy was I disappointed. The display was pretty blurry and I couldn't get a high enough resolution to match the resolution on my laptop. So windows would look really large and stretched when dragged from my laptop screen to my external monitor.

I exchanged that one and got this Dell monitor instead: [[ASIN:B073VYVX5S Dell U Series 27-Inch Screen LED-lit Monitor (U2718Q)]]. I couldn't be happier. The default resolution is so high that I have to reduce it to match my (now-seemingly-old) MacBookPro. The default out-of-the-box settings are perfect and I have excellent natural picture quality without needing to tweak anything. The fact that this monitor works with macOS' HiDPI settings (under Display Preferences) is icing on the cake.

I'd now say this monitor is even better than Apple's Thunderbolt displays and I didn't think I'd say this of a monitor going into my research. Plus this Dell monitor rotates! I'm a happy camper.

Now I'm hoping this monitor lasts as long as Apple's.

P.S.: I primarily use this monitor for software development and occasionally watching movies. Your mileage may very.

My only issue is, because it did not come with even an inexpensive, thick vinyl sleeve to keep it in, I have to wrap it in a scarf or buy one somewhere so that it does not get damaged or scratch something else in my backpack or purse. title: Great CPU + Cost
text:
Pros:
-----
*Hexacore for a reasonable price
*Very good performance, especially if you use it for more than gaming (e.g. streaming, multimedia)
*Decent overclocker

Cons:
-----
*Getting the overclock just right can be tricky and with uncore tossed into the mix, you really need to read up on the subject before attempting it. It's definitely not for newbies.

The reason I say this is because most games will not use 6 cores and you will end up with extra heat and less OC vs a devil's canyon processor that has 4 cores and can OC higher. Also be aware this CPU has limited PCI-e lanes so if you plan to add more than two GPUs, you'll need the 5930K or 5960X.

title: Used for computers that don't have stereo inputs, only a mono mic input.
text:
Used for computers that don't have stereo inputs, only a mono mic - if your computer has a stereo input or the mic has a software driver that will record in stereo using that mic input you don't need this capture card. You can connect directly the the source using the 3.5mm patch cord or a Y adapter with 3.5mm on one end and RCA red & white plugs on the other.

I bought this to transfer LPs and tapes into the digital world [my computer only had a mic in]. My computer recognized the USB device - no problem. You can connect the RCA red & white plugs to an amp, stereo receiver or tape deck using the standard output wires from any of those sources. The third connector fits any 3.5mm output including headphone jacks. I didn't use the included free audio capture/converting software ( Audacity) because I prefer another program to record analog music. The good news from that is other software recognizes the device too. My purchase was sold by FlyKan Shopping Mall and Fulfilled by Amazon Prime. I received it as expected and even got a follow-up Email from FlyKan asking if I was satisfied and requesting I fill out a questionnaire.

Under the product description, the last feature - "Recording From Microphone/Line In/Auxiliary Input" puzzles me, I can't figure out how or why this can even be possible. Plugging this capture device into any of these inputs means the source would have to be the USB connected device. The only USB device I can connect to is the computer, which is the input - connecting any of the other end wires to inputs of any other device might possibly send the signal to those devices but frankly I don't think it can. And even if it could be possible the only digital recording device would be another computer - everything else would be analog inputs. In that case you would be better off just loading the music on a flash drive and transfer it to the other computer. The same goes for digital music players to copy the files. Don't base your purchase on this feature alone, I think it is an error.
