title: Point and shoot remote works out of the box, simple and sweet, no frills
text:
I read several reviews which stated these do not work or only work from very short distances and aren't like an OEM Roku remote. The simple fact is they are not, Roku remotes in many cases use WiFi or Bluetooth frequencies and have a pairing button under the battery door (some not all). These remotes are RF only using infrared (old school simplicity) and also unlike the OEM units use 2 AAA batteries not 2 AA batteries so they are smaller in size and weight. The short version, I plopped in a couple of AAA batteries, pointed it at my Roku 4 and the TV and Roku powered up to the main screen. FYI if you don't have your Roku unit programmed to turn on your TV via the HDMI cable, you should, makes like so much easier than having to turn on the TV then find the Roku remote. Still need the 2nd remote for the TV volume but if you don't change it too often what does it matter.

Onto the devices, construction is the same as any OEM unit, they are not flimsy, they are fine, maybe a 10cent part where OEM might have used 15cent parts but honestly for the price and the fact that I can get 4 of these for the price of 1 Roku remote, worth every penny.

These have 6 buttons on the top menu and no voice search button, something I never used so no issue there. These don't have volume buttons either, that's a feature of a connected remote like the OEM, if you want then then spend the 29 dollars for the OEM units from Roku and don't bother reading any more of this review because these units are not for you.

The reports that these units only work at 3 or 4 feet, greatly exaggerated and disproved, again these are RF remotes you need to point them at the unit but I was 15 feet away from my TV and they worked perfectly. Each of the pre-programmed buttons worked flawlessly, I don't have a couple of the apps but the ones that I use all came right up so programming was fine. I didn't find that I needed to push extra hard, I didn't find that I had to get up close and personal, I knew going in that I wasn't going to need to pair the unit via pairing button and wasn't going to expect headphones on the remote because it's a simple remote.

If you have a lower end Roku unit (non IR remote) then this will be plug & play.

It completely eliminated the high-pitched whine coming out of my monitors. The power-conditioning feature of this unit works in spades.

Things to know:
If you're trying to remove noise from your audio, make sure that EVERYTHING in your audio system that has a plug goes into a power conditioner . . . you never know where those annoying hisses, hums, whines, etc. could be coming from.

Someone else mentioned that, if the unit is going to sit on a desktop, you need to put felt pads on the bottom. THIS IS VERY VERY TRUE. It put a huge scratch on my very nice oak desk. But I blame myself for this... I should have checked this out before sliding it across my desk. For desktop use, I'd actually recommend putting it on a softer more forgiving surface, like maybe a couple of mouse pads.

The rack-mount ears are NOT removable. But if you are concerned about width or fitting the unit into a tight space, don't be. The total width of the unit is 19 inches... that includes the rack ears (anyone mounting devices into racks would likely know this, but, for me, I wasn't exactly sure).

title: Absurd amount of chromatic aberration. Completely useless to me. Update 11/17/15 W/ info on CA sensitivity & comparo to ED II's
text:
I so, so much wanted to like these binoculars. I read review after review after review. The OVERWHELMING majority of reviews said they are the bees knees. And a small minority complained about chromatic aberration. Well, put me in the latter camp. For those of you that don't know what CA is, here's a description copied from elsewhere...

"Chromatic Aberration - Chromatic aberration is the inability to bring different wavelengths of light (colors) into focus, usually producing a relatively faint halo of color around an object. It may depend on the brightness of the image and may not treat all images alike as to the color of the halo. Also, the halos may be one color on one side and another color on the opposite side. You can test for chromatic aberration by looking at a high contrast item such as an overhead wire against the bright sky. Chromatic aberration will often show up as green, yellow, or violet fringes of light along the edges of the object."

Whew! That's a mouthful! But it sums it up nicely. Here's another explanation in my words.

When I look through these binoculars at, say, the edge of a roof, or the tops of a copse of trees, with the sky in the background, I see a distinct halo of purple or green, depending upon if I'm staring through the top or the bottom of the lenses. This isn't a subtle, slightly there aura. It's unmistakable. It's as if you took a prism and shined a light through it, then used another prism to change the rainbow back to white light, and it missed a color or two. Make sense? And it's not just there for high contrast, straight lines. I saw an amazing purple cormorant on the Puget Sound today. Almost thought I'd made an important discovery, until I double checked with my 25 year old Nikon Action binoculars. Nope, just a regular old cormorant. So sad.

Seeing as there are so many positive reviews,on Amazon and elsewhere, I suspect it may be a quality control issue. And when you consider the price ($220 when I bought them, plus a $25 rebate), it's tempting to mess around with Vanguard doing a warranty exchange. But if they're all like this, I will have missed the return window and have, quite literally, thrown my money away ('cause I'd just chuck them, they're useless to me).

It's too bad, because I like them in every other respect. They are bright, light, and compact. Comfortable to hold. They appear to be very well built. And the warranty is awesome! But living in a laser show just won't do.

BTW, I'm still giving Vanguard a shot. I've ordered their Endeavor ED II, their top of the line bins. Made with premium Hoya glass. Also well reviewed. Unfortunately, they are a couple of hundred dollars more (hope my wife doesn't read this review!). I will report back here whether or not they're an improvement.

Update 11/17/15.

I did, indeed, try out the ED II's. They are a MAJOR improvement. I still found some CA, but it's much less obvious. Additionally, the overall view through the ED II's is clearer from edge to edge. I won't write more about them, as I'll review them separately, but if you are sensitive to CA they are a much better bet.

As to chromatic aberration and whether or not it matters, I've come to find that evidently some people see it, and some people don't. It's a demonstrable phenomenon, easily photographed through binocular lenses, BUT... Some people see it, some don't. I'm guessing some people see it more than others, as well, as I seem to see it everywhere. Or at least through roof prism binos.

I have tried the Endeavor's, the Endeavor ED II's, Zen Ray Prime HD's, and Maven B2's (all of these got progressively more expensive, of course). It's been evident in all of them. The Zen Ray's and the Maven's are are superior to both of the Vanguard's, but roughly equivalent to each other. I kept the ZR's ($600 cheaper than the Maven's).

I also went to Cabela's and checked out the top ranging models from Leupold, Nikon, Swarovski, and Vortex. Yup, still there, even in the $2700 Swaro's. Guess I'm ultra, ultra sensitive. Good to know, money doesn't solve everything.

title: Possibly the worst mouse I've ever used
text:
I really wanted to like this mouse. I love the gesture functionality, but I was shocked by the lack of pointer precision -- particularly at low speeds -- which made the Magic Mouse nearly unusable for me. A good test here is to open a paint program and repeatedly try to draw small circles -- on the two other mice I tried I was able to easily draw something resembling a circle, but on the Magic Mouse my circles would just collapse into diagonal lines. I went to my local Apple Store and tried another mouse to verify that mine wasn't defective -- the other Magic Mouse I tried exhibited the same behavior. It's bad enough that I'm really amazed Apple could ship such a product.

I think part of the problem is that, for some bizarre reason, the sensor is placed near the front edge of the mouse instead of at the center. This means if you twist your wrist and rotate the mouse slightly, the pointer will swing in a wide arc. Since I primarily mouse using my wrist, this was a big problem for me. But even when I deliberately held the mouse completely straight, without rotating it at all, the poor precision prevented me from easily clicking on small objects.

I ended up buying a Logitech MX Master instead.

title: Remarkable clarity and soundstage, true neutral signature
text:
When I got my pair of [[ASIN:B0016MNAAI beyerdynamic DT 770 Pro 80 ohm]], I fell in love with them. Phenomenal clarity, deep booming bass and that great sounding V curve.

When I got my [[ASIN:B0024NK35S Beyerdynamic DT 880 Premium 600 ohm]], I also fell in love with them. Similar, slightly better clarity compared to the 770-80s, but with more natural bass and a better soundstage. I assured myself that audiophile gear was a land of steeply diminishing returns: it couldn't get significantly better than this.

Then I got the DT-1770. My love of the 770s had me salivating at the 1770s, wanting to hear the amazing successors to bring that heritage to the Tesla drivers. And, amazingly, I found the returns did not dimish.

Closed-back headphones with stunning clarity -- in many cases they aren't noticeably better in clarity than the 880s, but then you find that one song that just completely blows your mind. This first happened to me with the opening for [[ASIN:B013GYEZBQ Outlander - The Skye Boat Song (Extended)]], which sounds markedly better on the 1770s than any other properly EQed headphone I owned.

They come with a remarkably neutral signature, one I have not felt the need to EQ. I can't say I've ever encountered this before! This means bass can feel very muted if you're used to the common V signature. That isn't to say they aren't capable, though: if the source asks for bass, there is plenty there to give and it doesn't muddle up the rest of the frequencies.

Soundstage not quite equal to that of the open 880s, but closer than I thought possible with closed headphones.

One unexpected thing I've found is that they are easy to drive despite being 250ohm drivers. Taking them out of my O2/ODAC, I curiously plugged them into my [[ASIN:B017V4OEYA Lumia 950]] and was able to drive them to acceptable volume and bass response. Their clarity does tend to point out flaws in your source -- I did hear noise pretty easily, but that's hardly a fault of the cans.

So, lets talk about cons. Weight and clamping force is a thing. These are significantly heavier and clamp significantly harder than the 880s, and you definitely feel it -- I've not made it more than two hours without having to take a break. Most of the time, I don't make it much past an hour. The mini-XLR cable also sticks out pretty far from the cans, and depending on how you're sitting can hit your neck or shoulder when you tilt your head.

Overall, I think these were worth the money. I feel dirty saying that, knowing that being an audiophile is mildly comparable to a placebo disease, but against all odds they brought new understanding of music I was already familiar with, making me excited in ways I thought I was done with.

title: What can I say that hasn't been said; Its Great.
text:
I bought the Aiwa Exos-9 speaker in September of 2016. (its the end of May '17 at the time of this writing). I wanted to give this thing a few months of service before i came back on here to review. I was skeptical of all the 5 star reviews, the lower ratings are what looked to be faulty units, naturally a 5 star product on amazon is questionable... So i waited, after ordering the thing i was excited. consider what you are buying here, a wireless speaker that runs 8-10 hours and you can take pretty much anywhere besides the water. I have and own smaller devices, wired as in no battery/portable devices and some that are AC only... which works well in the house but i wound up selling those off and keeping my sound systems of bookshelf units (one oddly enough is a 90's Aiwa system still kicking today). So after 8 months here i gotta say i absolutely love this. Its not all rainbows, surely you've read the reviews on here about the faults of the speaker - bluetooth hijacking (fixed, well kinda), Lack of song skipping/next song on the device (both of which is fixed with the remote sold separately but worth it). The sound on this thing is great, absolutely surprising for a Bluetooth battery operated speaker. I have yet to find a speaker that sounds remotely close to this without needing to be plugged in. The sound is loud and rocking, the bass pumps and with the on-board EQ allows you to tweak settings to your liking. of course your phone/tv/device also has an EQ, making it possible to get the sound perfect to any music, movie or hockey game. I was a huge fan of Aiwa before, and they just disappeared... like a phoenix to rise from some metaphoric ash to create something special....

I'd like to see some housing improvements as well as a splash proof if at all possible in the future. But im nitpicking to find flaws with the Exos-9. As a home only device, its elegant and fits in with my other electronics. As a portable device, it surely steals the show of any party, my neighbors have more reason to hate me, this being the first summer shes getting let loose. I am considering buying another, for no reason because my uses one is more than enough. I just want to see how loud it can get. I use this every single day, and its the best investment someone like me who spends time outside and loves music could ever make. Welcome back aiwa... I hope you create more music pumping devices for many years to come!

I am the type of person that likes to try a product a couple times before writing a review. Day 1 I loved this bag, Day 11 and after taking it out on four photo walks, I STILL LOVE IT! This bag is well worth the money. Now I can change lenses and camera on the go. There’s no need to put my camera or lenses down on tables since I can use the comfort of my bag... I’m 62 inches 129lbs and this bag is much bigger than I expected. Not that big is a bad thing. The setup in the photos is a Canon 60D w/ 18-135mm lens attached, Canon 5D Mark IV w/ a 24-70mm f4 attached, 16-35mm f4 and 85mm 1.8 in the bag, 55inch tripod on the outside, lens case, 2 extra batteries, pelican card case, iPad Pro with keyboard... NOT BAD HUH? This is a fairly large setup as I was out for a while but I typically travel lighter... Another setup I did is my trinity: Canon 5D Mark IV 24-70mm attached, 70-200 2.8 IS II, 16-35 f4, and 85 1.8, all in the bag. The bag is exceptional. Satchels hurt my shoulders and backpacks have to be taken off often.

CON: There is only two and that is the strap is fairly uncomfortable. It could use some padding for comfortability. Secondly, because of my small frame the bag doesn’t fit quite right. Sure I could downgrade to the smaller size but this bag for me has the ideal room I am looking for.

title: Garmin Astro 320 T5 Mini
text: I purchased the Astro 320 T5 Mini Bundle for my 20 pound Treeing Feist squirrel dog.  I was very concerned about such a small dog carrying this "large" collar, but she handled it without any trouble.  What a great tool this is.  It takes all of the worry out of hunting with a wandering dog.  You know exactly where your dog is and what it is doing.  For example, my dog trees squirrels.  If she gets out of earshot and trees a squirrel I can look at the handheld GPS and see that she is staying in one place, and if I'm not monitoring the screen the GPS will even beep to tell me she has treed.  What a great feature.  I removed the topo map micro chip from my other Garmin GPS and put it in the Astro 320.  Now, at a glance I can see the best route to get to my dog based on the terrain.  This unit completely changed my hunting experience.  Worrying about a lost dog is a thing of the past.  What a great tool!

title: Best activity tracker on the market - Updated 6/28/16
text:
I've been using it for almost 2 weeks now, I got lucky and got one really early. So far, I love it. Between weight training, elliptical running, biking (outdoor with ant+ sensors connected) and a huge amount of yard work, I am extremely impressed. Unlike previous wrist based trackers I've had, this one actually tracks movement when I cut the lawn or push a shopping cart. I use the GPS for yard work (turn on the walk activity), and it's really cool to see the movement map when I'm done.

For anyone thinking about this, keep in mind that this is an activity tracker with some smart watch functionality. If you're thinking about this or something along the lines of a Gear S2 or Apple Watch, you are comparing the wrong products. If you want something to count steps, go with a Jawbone or FitBit, no need to spend $250 for a pedometer. This also isn't small. My wrists aren't large, but it looks fine on me and the size isn't an issue. If you wear dress shirts a lot (with sleeves down and buttoned), you might have a bit of an issue. I had to wear a suit last week, and it was tough to get the shirt cuff over the watch. Doing that daily would be a problem for me.

The watch faces are good, fairly limited, but good. Actiface is my favorite, it shows time, steps, battery life, date, sunrise/sunset time, calories burned, distance moved, max steps and cal for the week and it also has a graph showing calories and steps over the last 7 days. Great face to see a bevy of stats at a glance.

This was money well spent for me, I'm very active and this can keep up with everything I do and then some. The apps are limited, but again, this isn't a smart watch, it's a smart tracker for more athletic types of people. I love it, it was worth the 2+ months of waiting. I debated getting the Fenix 3 HR, but I'm not at that level of outdoor activity, so this was a perfect choice for me. The fact that it can go in the shower/pool/ocean without turning into a dead device makes this a no brainer in the price range.

5/16/16 Update:
I found out yesterday that, on a long trip, it will count steps in my car. I didn't have that problem with my wife's car. My UP24 did the same thing, so as with that, I will just take it off in the car.

HR tracking while lifting weights is not perfect, it's basically flipped: When lifting, HR goes down because blood flow is restricted, when I drop the weight, it goes up when normal flow returns. As with all wrist based, it's not perfect. For really detailed HR tracking, a chest strap is the best approach. I'm ok with how this works, but I will be getting a chest strap to get a more exact measure for weight training.

I have seen complaints about the size. Get a tape measure and you can easily see how big it will be on your wrist. Negative reviews based on size make no sense to me, it's clear how big it is. Cut a piece of paper or something to the size stated to see how big it will be on your wrist. It's not small, but it's also not as big as the Fenix 3. GPS, HR, touch screen, battery, all of these things need space for components. If you want something small, you'll need to sacrifice features. It can't be much smaller and still make sense to have a touch screen.

After 3 weeks, I'm totally sold on this still.

title: Not bad
text:
I just bt it from HP after some searching. My old HP laptop lasted 5 years without any problems!! Then the keyboard suddenly wouldn't talk to the motherboard and then it all went dead, dead, dead, So I like HPs. I stay away from Dells. My old one was a Pavilion I think.

This computer worked out of the box and was a snap to set up. The reason I only gave it 3 stars was that it appeared to be designed by the engineering staff without any marketing department input.

1. It has only 2 USB ports. Thats bad. It has an additional smaller lightening type USB-C but frankly for the average working person it is useless.Bottom line is that the computer only has 2 ports. Not enough.

2. The back lit keys are hard to see. The keys are silver on silver so to see the keys you have to turn off the back light and turn on your lamp. If you have it back lit with a lamp they wash out and you can't see anything. Bad design.

3. No CD-R or DVD player. HP fell into the trap of taking out the CD player to save weight. They forgot that weight is not important since laptops are no longer used as "on-the go" devices since we all use phones and tablets for that but instead are used for occasional portability. So HP makes you buy an external CD-drive which is quite large and adds more wires etc. My old laptop had a nice CD drive that caused no problems and did not affect the portability.

4. The 12 gb Ram is nice. A bit overkill for document work which is what this is used for. You would not play games or do graphics on this computer. Instead you should buy an Omen for that. So 12gb is overkill. I had 8 gb on my old one and it worked great.

5. The 1 TB hard drive is ok. No one needs that much really so its sort of useless. I found portable Hard drives to work just fine when I wanted to off load pictures or other things. A much better design would have been a 500 GB at 7200 rpm vs this 1 TB at a low 5400 rpm.That is what I had on my old one.

6. This has an i5 not an i7 chip. Now some i5s are faster than i7s and some i7s are faster than i5s. It's complicated. I7 is for graphic/games so for document work I was fine with the i5 here.

7. Cost is 699 plus 47 for an external CD player plus 47 in tax.

So my final score is a B. The question is longevity. Because the design seems to have been done without any marketing/customer input I fear bean counters also may have gotten involved. This could mean I will be lucky if I get 3 years out of this. 3 years is fine for a consumer product but this is for business. If it fails, then I'll just build my own desk top which is very easy with quality parts and have a cheap rarely used laptop for portability. I think we are all headed that way anyway.

title: Great sound and surround reproduction, BUT no HDR support
text: Okay, lets address the elephant in the room first: While all HDMI  2.0 ports pass through 4K at 60hz, they do NOT pass HDR metadata per the HDMI 2.0a spec, and Yamaha has admitted ( begrudgingly) that because of the chipset used for HDMI in this model, the firmware in the YSP-5600 will not and cannot be updated to accept 2.0a, which means this Yamaha model will never pass through HDR. Pretty disappointing for sure, since pretty much all 4K displays( the exception being computer displays) are now capable of HRD, and it DOES improve the picture.  That being said, while I would not purchase this model now in 2017 ( I have owned it for a year), you can always feed the audio signal to the 5600 through one of two optical ports, or the analog sound inputs as well.  The sound quality of this sound projector is amazing!  You WILL need a sub, btw.  The DSP capabilities are nearly endless, and with a conventionally shaped room, the reflective sound will amaze and confound you as to how Yamaha pulls it off. As always a separate Receiver/suround speakers/sub setup will always give you better quality surround.  Most of the purchasers of the 5600 are aware of this, however the pluses of this particular piece of equipment far outweigh the negatives for us.  I just would PASS on this model now, knowing  that it is not, and never will be capable of passing HDMI 2.0a metadata for HDR.  And while there are workarounds for this shortcoming for current owners, there is no reason now to forgo HDR capability, since it is not simply a trivial video improvement, but a major one, along with 4K reproduction.

title: Great SSD, but here's what I had to do on my laptop
text:
I gave this a five-star review when I installed it on my desktop PC, because installation was easy and the supplied Acronis software worked fine. This three-star review is for the same SSD that I installed in my five-year-old ThinkPad X200s notebook. The hardware was fine, but the Acronis software refused to clone the disk, whether I tried migrating from the original hard drive to the SSD on a USB-to-SATA cable or vice versa. So I'd say that, for at least some notebook users, the MX200 is likely to be "5 stars" for hardware and "1 star" for software and installation.

I finally got the SSD working via a two-step process:

1) I used Paragon's inexpensive "Migrate OS to SSD 4.0" software to clone my hard drive to the SSD (which was on a SATA cable). The SSD still wouldn't boot after I installed it in my notebook, so I went on to the next step:

2) I downloaded the Paragon Recovery Media Builder add-on (free to registered Migrate OS to SSD 4.0 users), installed it, created a Windows PE bootable USB drive, booted from the USB drive, and ran the utilities for fixing boot issues and the master boot record. The MBR Repair utility did the trick: It instantly fixed the problem, and the Crucial SSD drive booted perfectly after that. (I should warn that Paragon's Recovery media Builder add-on is poorly documented, and it took me a couple of tries to figure out that I needed to download and install the Windows Assessment Kit or Windows ADK from Microsoft so the Media Builder could create the bootable Windows PE environment on my USB drive.)

title: Good idea, but I returned mine because the HDD portion was ridiculously slow
text:
It is a simple and good idea to put an HDD and an SSD into the same 2.5-inch package, esp. for laptops and such that only have room for the one drive. This is the only product (so far) that I've seen doing this, so I thought it would be a great solution for me -- increasing my overall storage and increasing most performance. Unfortunately, there are a few problems that blocked this from becoming a reality.

The Acronis True Image 2013 software that WD bundles (you must download it) requires that the drive be present in order to activate its features, which is fine I suppose, but just getting it to activate properly required numerous reboots, uninstalling and reinstalling, and generally a lot more hassle than it should have required. I'm not sure what went wrong. I did perform a couple of seemingly-unrelated steps in a different order than what they said on their video, so perhaps it was my own fault, but it's hard to imagine how that could have had any impact. The enabled features are reasonable, but I still needed to use a live gparted CD (free -- look it up) to rearrange and resize some partitions once I had transferred everything from the old disk to the new. Arranging things so that you have a reasonable split between what goes onto the SSD and what goes onto the HDD is not a trivial exercise, even for someone very experienced with such things. And moving from drive to drive had some difficulties for me with respect to my user profile (home directory) since I keep it on its own partition and mount it into the right place -- if you ever log in without the right drive letter or mount point for such a thing, then WIndows (XP, at least) will recreate a whole new home directory, which then requires logging in as another administrator and deleting the unwanted directory and ... blah blah blah ... most people would never run into that particular issue. :-)

You can only see one of the two halves (or the other -- can't remember which) unless you are using Windows and initialize the hardware with the downloaded drivers.

Most importantly, my unit proved to have horrendous performance problems in the HDD portion. Applications that used to work just fine, including just plain ol' Windows Explorer, would sometimes hang for half a minute or so after switching to this drive, for no discernible reason. Playing back a sound file, there would be occasional nasty glitches that would last for several seconds, under "normal" circumstances that weren't taxing the system nearly as much as I used to without any glitches at all. Doing large transfers was also very, very slow. But given how much I work with media, and the infuriating "hangs" that were happening quite often, I decided to contact WD support just in case there was truly a hardware fault or maybe even a quick fix they could advise. I filed a case, looked for and downloaded their SMART analysis tool, used it, and it told me that everything about the drive was just fine. Yeah, right. Apparently, it didn't care about the performance problems.

WD Support did respond, but after a short exchange, they left one of my emails unanswered for over a week. I was getting concerned about limitations on being able to return it. So I went ahead and started the return for refund with Amazon. Amazon is amazingly good about that -- even to the point where I could see how some folks might purposely abuse it. I sent WD a note to let them know, and for whatever reason, they couldn't even read my email message. Overall, I think WD has some good and some mediocre products, and I've never really needed to use their support channels before, so this was very disappointing.

I'm not going to replace that unit with another, for fear that the same problem might exist in more than just that original unit. Your mileage may vary. And one last thing: I could not really notice any particular speed-up of anything by using the SSD portion (almost everything was there, including the OS itself). Maybe it was faster, maybe it was about the same, but it was not a noticeable change for me (perhaps my old laptop's interface could not take full advantage of the SSD's speed, so again, this may not reflect what others would experience). With the very noticeable performance problems that arose whenever dealing with the HDD portion, this unit was simply unacceptable. I sent it back.

title: Fantastic Amp, plagued by poor software.
text:
I’ve been using the Heos ecosystem since late 2014. Over time, I’ve purchased several of these Denon products and now own: three Heos 3’s, a Heos 5, and a Heos Amp. In January 2015, I reviewed the Heos 3 in an Amazon review after about a month of ownership, and as I read through that review my impressions have not changed. Over time this platform has grown to include more streaming services and a new soundbar as well as some equipment for professional installation of the Heos in a four-room amp configuration. Denon has also created functionality for some home control systems and most recently updated their app with more robust graphics and a new streaming service, Amazon Music.

As per my prior review, these products excel in sound reproduction and the Heos Amp is fantastic and similar to its Heos relatives in this regard. I’ve used it to drive a set of Paradigm speakers as well as some more modest in-wall speakers in my living space. The sound produced by this 100-Watt-per-channel unit is excellent and consistent with my dedicated Denon Amplifier my living room.

Sadly, this unit, and the Heos ecosystem in general, remain plagued by poor streaming consistency, dropped wifi connections, poor app syncing, and dysfunctional playlists. Denon has excelled in design of the sound production from this amp, but at the same time burdened the actual use of the product with an inconsistent software and streaming ecosystem. My wife is constantly upset with these devices as the Heos system drops her playlists in the kids room. I get very frustrated when we are entertaining family or friends and the music begins to cut-out or drop off all-together. These concerns are very well published in numerous reviews on Amazon and the in various app-store reviews on hand-held devices, including dated and recent reviews.

Shame on me for buying so many of these devices. Shame on Denon for failing to get their software right over the year of my ownership of these products. I keep hoping that somehow the next firmware release or app update with produce a consistent product. Denon Heos service has done nothing to help remedy these concerns. I have invested in a very high-end dedicated wifi router, excellent high-speed internet, and have excellent wireless distribution in my house…as measured independently and by Denon’s own Heos app. I use all of these products on the same wifi band and have been careful to follow setup directions and tips from the internet and Denon support. These products could easily out-perform many other competing products, but underperform so heavily on the software and streaming side that frustration abounds. These are five-star sound products with a one-star software and firmware ecosystem. I don’t have experience with other products to make an educated recommendation for another brand, but I am in envy of those who have positive things to say about competing products and I wish that I had not been so swayed by the Denon sound quality and the local sales representative when I had initially listened to this product line in my local store.

title: UNIT FAILED BIG TIME  --- See Update --- (Original) Install was Quick and Operation is (WAS) Painless
text:
UPDATE #2 --
After this unit failed (see below), I contacted Winegard Tech Support (Thank you Nikki H.). They confirmed that the E3 Error was present and offered to ship me a new (actually refurbished) unit at no cost to me. I received that unit in 8 days, swapped out the antenna dome on the roof and the control panel inside my Coach and proceeded to verify the newly shipped unit was working properly. I packed the old (defective) unit up and sent it back to Winegard along with the RMA label they provided and the shipping label for return shipping to Winegard. Check back for some more updates as I get back on the road and figure out how long this exchange unit keeps working.

UPDATE ---
After my first road trip, the unit failed after briefly working for a mere 2 days. It consistently now reads the dreaded E3 Error when trying to locate any OTA stations. My research indicates the E3 Error exhibits when the unit draws excess current/voltage at the dome motor when rotating in an attempt to locate stations. There is also discussion that this can be caused by a faulty "wire wrap". Since this motor must rotate to allow the antenna locate the stations of desire, it is critical that the unit rotate freely, the motor works and the motor does not draw excessive current/voltage.

The unit is slightly past the deadline (even though it has been used on one trip) to return to AMAZON so that's a DEAD END trying to get help from them. I will update after contacting the Winegard Technical Support. Of course, that should have never been necessary but the price you seem to pay for new technology. Disappointed owner of a Winegard Antenna right now....

**************ORIGINAL REVIEW FOLLOWS HERE******************
Installed this in just under an hour for the outside portion and about 30 minutes for the inside parts. This was ordered to replace an Antenna Craft HD 360 unit that comes as the factory option from Tiffin Motorhomes on new 2015 models. I opted to try out the Rayzar for two reasons: first, the HD 360 unit sticks up almost another 8 inches higher (taller) than the Winegard and second, the HD 360 is about the most cumbersome device I have ever had the dis-pleasure of using.

I am an electronic engineer by training with almost 40 years in the industry. My opinion of the HD 360 model from Antenna Craft is only my opinion but if you've ever seen or used one, I'm sure you too, will agree. That unit requires prior knowledge of where the antenna towers are located and then you must rotate the antenna to that location all the while never being able to see the antenna rotate or never knowing quite where the antenna elements are pointed with relation to the orientation of your rig and the antennas. By the way, the operation manuals for the HD 360 unit are of little help. I finally disassembled the unit to see where the unit points when you see the numbers 1 - 16 display of the control unit. In my case, the unit pints straight forward when the number 6 is displayed on the control unit. I have no idea the logic of that reasoning when they designed it. And by the way - there goes your warranty once you open the unit! OK, enough bashing that unit - on to the Winegard!

I have operated a number of Winegard products over the years on a number of RVs I have owned, or used. I have never been let down by Winegard and they are made here in the USA which makes me feel even batter about supporting them.

The biggest pain in the install was the take-down of the old unit - even though the rig was only 6 months old. The removal of the HD 360 and scraping, cleaning and reattachment on the roof for the Winegard took about an hour all said. Install was simple - place in the center of the roof, away from any obstructions, apply the appropriate sealant for your roof type (rubber, metal, or fiberglass - the most popular) and drill the three holes for each of the three antenna feet and tighten the gold anodized hardware provided and reseal. Screw on the coax cable from your previous install and you are pretty much finished up there.

For some installations, you will need to place covers on the existing holes (external and internal - and yes, they are provided as part of the kit) if you had a bat-wing or screw type antenna mast - mine did not have those so those steps were not necessary. I do have some extra parts (coax, plates and screws).

The inside equipment install required connecting the coax (existing) from the old roof antenna into the Winegard control panel and the output coax going to the TV and festening the control panel to a convenient location for use. Mine ended up in the same location as the unit I removed. An additional coax connector on the control panel is provided for connecting the external wire that feeds an outside SAT dish or park cable if used in your rig. I tapped into the existing +12 volt DC power (and ground) feeding the rooftop Winegard In-Motion SAT and fired up the unit.

Search process took about 45 seconds, finding the stations in my area. After that a simple channel scan of the TVs and the HD channels were up and running. The Winegard unit is 100% AUTOMATIC - no fussing with where you are, where are the towers, how are you orientated with relation to this all. Just power up, hit the scan button, scan your TV and your ready to watch.

Clarity is good and the unit installed (outside and inside) is attractive.

Nice job and Kudo's to Winegard!.. Thanks guys...

text:
OK, the Garmin InreachSE+ was purchased with a bit of trepidation because I wasn’t sure it would work for me. This was because of some negative reviews that sounded a bit nasty. So, I purchased it and then used Garmin’s website to pay for a “Freedom Plan”, the lowest cost. I had every intention of returning the unit the minute their website started flaking out on me. But… perhaps they have improved the website. It worked quite seamlessly. I was able to register the device and I signed up for the cheapest Freedom plan with every intention of canceling the service and returning the SE+ should any trouble arise.
I then set up the SE+ and signed into the Garmin website called https://earthmate.garmin.com/ and added my SE+ to the list of devices. The SE+ comes with a cable that allows it to plug into a USB port. This is a good thing to do as the SE+ likes to have its firmware (software) updated right after purchasing. The above website directs one to an installer that will install an app on your PC that does this syncing job for you. It also syncs various items, contacts, tracking points, etc., with the PC data and with the MapShare website data.
OK about MapShare. This is Garmin’s approach to allowing you to be tracked by your loved one(s). Instructions for setting up the MapShare account are included in the “earthmate” website listed above. One must select share to MapShare and choose different options. I chose to use a simple password that my wife could remember so that she could always come to the same place to see where I was. This works from an Iphone equally well.
Also on the Iphone, you can install an App called “Earthmate”. This App communicates via Bluetooth with the phone and also, after you input your Garmin Login and Password into the app, will sync key items from the phone to the Mapshare website.
About the tracking points on the MapShare website vs inside the device, what is up with 1 minute interval fine points vs 10 minute interval coarse points? The answer is that only the 10 minute interval points are transmitted to the Iridium Satellites. The fine tracking points at 1 minute intervals are saved until the Earthmate application has an opportunity to “sync” them. Once they are synced, the Mapshare website shows the fine points as well as the coarse points. So, fine points via Bluetooth, coarse points via satellites.
I have used the SE+ now on about 8 – 10 separate hikes and the battery has gone from 100% down to 75%. So, for my day hiking, the battery life is great. I have included several screen captures from the websites and app showing the details of what I'm talking about.
I would buy the exact same thing again and am very happy with the purchase.

title: Reddit Fan Favorite; I Approve!
text:
Whether you are after your first or your fifth mechanical keyboard, and a Pok3r is not already in your collection... I politely ask: What are you doing with your life?

I deduce that you arrived at the Cherry MX Blue variant because you do a lot of typing. Personally, I spend 8.5 hours a day at my desktop for work and then several hours more playing games and so on. I am an avid computer nerd. This was purchased as a backup to my KUL ES-87 w/ Clears, which is currently in the process of getting an overhaul. I needed to fill the void while I underwent my Ergo-Clear project, finding the perfect springs, lubing all 87 switches, clipping stabilizers and so on.

Fun fact: At my best, I can type 115 words per minute. With MX blues, I set my highest score ever on tenfastfingers 2 days ago: 125 wpm / 100% accuracy. The proof is in the pudding ;)

If you are a fan of reddit like myself, the Pok3r is a household name... and found on the front page of r/mechanicalkeyboards at nearly all times. The programming functionality, form factor, build quality and so on are all fantastic. I can very comfortably recommend this keyboard to anyone. I was personally worried that Blues would be too light for me and while they do take some getting used to, the definitive click and tactile feel really help w/ that fact. I will most likely throw some stronger springs in the future, but for the meantime, this is a great back-up. It may very well end up my main keyboard for work. Not having dedicated arrow keys, PgUp/Dn, Del. and so on is really weird. I'll admit it. However, I am taking the time today to program this board to perform commonly used functions... and it will end up being easier to do them than ever before. Your imagination is the limit. For example, I will be programming some FN+Letter to execute my usual arrow key + ctrl + shift function, which highlights 1 word at a time.

Do yourself a favor and buy a sure thing: Vortex Pok3r in a switch that sound appealing to you. I can highly recommend MX Clears & Blues while swearing MX Reds off completely. I hated Reds but to each their own =]

Oh also. The ABS keys on this model are really really nice compared to other stock ABS keycaps I've used before. They have a very nice texture, and grip your fingertips.

title: POOR quality control, UNSAFE.  See pictures.
text:
Just received one of these in the mail. Upon inspecting the romex wire that comes with it, I found:

- Several of the conductors are nicked, the result of a poor job stripping the wire. Ask any electrician why a nicked conductor is bad. Makes it VERY easy for the stripped part of the conductor to break off.
- One of the conductors (the HOT lead) has a nick in the insulation where it shouldn't. This is also a hazard; you don't want any of the conductors exposed except for where they're SUPPOSED to be (at the ends).

Buying a solution like this which is supposed to be "code compliant" doesn't do a whole lot of good if it's shipping with compromised wiring. Yes, I can cut the ends off and re-strip my own portion of wire (and I will) which is all well and good, but, that only works for people like me who are handy enough to do something like that, and who have enough know-how to spot stuff like this. This is a product that claims to be "the perfect solution for any skill level, without the need for an electrician." The average consumer with "skill levels" lower then mine would have probably installed this as-is without noticing the faulty workmanship, leaving something potentially unsafe behind their walls.

title: Lots of Potential, but...
text:
This thing has a ton of potential, but know that by purchasing this, you are really just volunteering to be a beta tester. Securifi's tech support is awesome and extremely helpful, but they are learning and constantly addressing functionality issues from the bugs reported by customers. This product is maybe a six months to a year away from being really ready for the market.

There are still very basic bugs being worked out, and there is only a small handful of home automation devices on the market that this product will fully support. Securifi is working hard to add new home automation support, but, again, this really is not a product ready to compete with its competitors.

The router portion functions fine, but the software is still being tweaked. It is basically just OpenWRT that you can install on any router yourself and the company is tweaking firmware revisions to address various issues as customers report them. Having a router integrated with home automation is a great concept, but you may want to think about two separate and more polished products on the market if your intent is serious control of your home while you are away. This item is just too buggy and unfinished to trust with your home's safekeeping.

I love the concept and the company has one of the best tech support teams I have ever seen, but the product is just not ready for prime time. If Securifi keeps moving forward with this, they will definitely be the company that's leads this market.

**Update**
This product had so much potential. It is a shame that after all the hype and all the money it it ended up being a bit of a flop. No one is even managing their forums anymore.

Samsung purchased SmartThings and is releasing a new version that will surely be the nail in the coffin for this product. I feel like spending $250 for a product in Alpha was a huge mistake--lesson learned.

title: Great mid-range 4K monitor with HDR support
text:
I'll start by saying I would give this monitor 4.5 stars if possible due to excessive backlight bleed with the first monitor I received.

Also, note that this monitor is currently available for significantly less than on Amazon, selling for $550 from Dell and $500 from Microcenter (as of late Aug 2017).

I've had the monitor for a few weeks now and use it primarily as an external display for a 2017 Macbook Pro but also with a PS4 Pro and with a secondary PC.

Pros:

--Works well out of the box with my 2017 Macbook pro using a USB-C to DisplayPort cable. HiDPI scaling in OSX works well and offers a noticeable improvement in sharpness/ picture quality over my previous Dell 1440p monitor.
--The U2718Q is one of the first "affordable" monitors to offer HDR10 support. HDR automatically kicks in when connected to a PS4 Pro and offers a very noticeable improvement in both color depth as well as contrast. The monitor also displayed HDR from my Samsung 4K Bluray player without any issues.
--Every monitor is factory color calibrated. The U2718Q supports 99.9% sRGB coverage making it a great choice for photo/ video editing.
--The monitor offers many connectivity options including: HDMI 2.0, DisplayPort 1.2, mini DisplayPort, 4 x USB 3.0 ports and an audio out.
--The stand is height, tilt, swivel, and pivot adjustable
--The monitor is really beautifully designed with ultra thin bezels and a premium fit/ finish
--Comes with a 3 year warranty/ advance exchange service/ premium panel guarantee (substantially better than most other manufacturers at this price point)

Cons:

--Quality control issues. My first monitor had some of the worst back light bleed that I've ever seen. My second monitor is substantially better, although still has a bit of bleed along the bottom of the panel. This is not really noticeable unless viewing dark material at night.
--Many people would not call this a "true" HDR monitor as the panel tops out at around 350 nits of brightness (reference HDR requires around 1000 nits). Truth be told, I'm still really impressed with the HDR performance of the U2718Q connected to a PS4 Pro: Uncharted Lost Legacy looks absolutely spectacular in 4K HDR on this monitor.
--Lack of support of full DCI-P3 wide color gamut for Apple users or professionals. Can't really hold that against the monitor given its price point. The only monitors that I'm aware currently supporting it cost well over $1,000.
--Lack of support for Nvidia G-Sync or AMD FreeSync.

In summary, I'm really pleased with the monitor so far. At the $500-600 price range, I feel that it represents an exceptional value and is a great choice for photo/ video editing, mac users, and people looking for a 4K HDR monitor for a PS4 Pro or other 4K content.

title: ++++++THE RIGHT SPEAKER STAND FOR VIRTUALLY ANY HOME THEATRE SPEAKER SYTEM IN THE UNIVERSE ++++++++
text:
I wanted to write this review because I had wasted a lot of time and effort in finding the right speaker stands (cheap but still comparable to the Bose stands) for my home theatre system. IF YOU DON’T HAVE TIME TO READ THE FULL REVIEW, JUST KNOW THAT WHATEEVER YOUR SPEAKER SYSTEM IS, THIS SPEAKER SYSTEM WILL BE THE RIGHT FIT FOR IT because these stands some with a variety of attachment options and they will surely fit your speakers. BUY WITHOUT HESITATION AND YOU WONT REGRET.

I recently bought Bose Sountdtouch 520 home theater system and wanted to buy speaker stands for front and rear speakers. After spending about 1600 dollars for the home theatre system, I was not very keen on spending another approx. $300 for four speaker stands. That’s when I turned to tried and trusted Amazon to search for an economical yet a comparable alternative to the “original” Bose speaker stands!!!

I came across many of them and was not sure which one will fit best. Tried to get answers/suggestions from previous users and the sellers/manufacturer on Amazon but didn’t get any definitive answers. Then I decided to take advantage of Amazon’s awesome return policy and thought of getting one pair of speaker stands and try them out myself. Finally after 4 weeks of contemplation, I decided to get the “Atlantic Satellite 77305018 2 Speaker Stands”. Thanks to Amazon Prime, they arrived within two days.

I would like to list the pros and cons below:

1. As soon as I lifted the package from front door, I knew its quality stuff because the package was very heavy.
2. The rods and the base of the stands were made of cast iron of very good quality.
3. The best thing I like about these stands is that they come with a huge variety of screws/supports/washers and other accessories (see attached images), which make it possible to use them virtually with any home theater system in the market.
4. They have two iron rods with an adjusting hinge/screw that allows to adjust you the height of your speaker depending on the height and placement of your sofa/furniture in the room.
5. The base is triangular in shape and pretty heavy. This prevents the stands from tipping if someone slightly nudges them while passing by.
6. For 17 dollars per stand, I would say these are comparable to the ones Bose sells for 65 dollars apiece ( I saw and felt the original stands in Bose store before buying these).
7. Bose sells a different type of “short” speaker stands for front speakers. But I would suggest to get these stands because that gives you freedom to adjust them as far as from the TV and you will not be limited by the size of your TV stand/table to place them. Also, you would be able to adjust height of the front speakers.
8. The stand come with a detailed packaging list and pictorial instructions which explains use of these stands with varying type of speakers offered by different manufacturers.
9. The black color has a matt finish and they look elegant in a room.

Cons:
1. The inner hollow space of the iron rods is very narrow and the ends are even narrower. I could not pass the proprietary Bose wires with connecters for speakers through this rod. But this is not a deal breaker as you can use Velcro or scotch tape to tie the wire with the stand rod.
2. I cannot point out any other flaw in these stands so I would just write that they come only in two colors (black and white). Would have been great if they were available in red, magenta, yellow and pink ;)

+++++Specific comments for Bose Sountdtouch 520 home theater system+++++

If you have a Bose Soundtouch 520, use the stands as I did and you wont complain about it and would be glad to have saved $250 by not buying the Bose stands (these instructions may sound confusing but trust me that you will be fitting the stand effortlessly after you have them in front of you):

1. Attach the iron rod to the base and tighten them with hand (if you use a plier, wrap some cloth around the rid before clamping the plier or you will scratch the rod).
2. Put on the square base on top of the rod and tighten it with the provided screws (two screws labeled I-a).
3. Before tightening the screws insert components labeled “E” and also put the components D1 trough “E”.
4. Pass the Bose wire connector through the gap in component D1 (do not connect the speaker yet). I used D1 because the speakers a bit long. One can use D2 if the speakers are short.
5. Now tighten the screws using a screw driver
6. Peel of the cover from one side of the provided two-way adhesive tape and put it on the square base only on three sides (not including the rear side).
7. Connect the wire to the speaker.
8. Peel off the cover form other side of the tape.
9. Carefully place the speaker on the tape, adjusting it in such a way that the component D1 touches the back of the speaker
10. Use the fourth remaining two way tape to attach the back of the speaker to component D1 (do not peel off the other side of the tape, see photo).
11. Use Velcro or invisible tape to keep the wires close to the stand.

It is a reason to be skeptical about pasting your speakers on the tape because it will stay permanently. Even I was worried about that but then decided to use it on one speaker and see hoe it goes. I kept it for a week and then I did it for the second speakers also. Three weeks later I ordered another set for my front speakers also.

GET THESE STANDS AND YOU WONT REGRET HAVING THEM!!!!!!

title: Very nice for the price
text:
I was looking for an inexpensive tablet that could perform a few tasks. Here is what I wanted and how this tablet performs:

1. Office applications - This tablet does a great job of allowing me to open and edit Excel spreadsheets and Microsoft Word documents. I also am able to use PowerPoint presentations on this tablet in front of customers. It works well for my needs.

2. Email - It handles my Outlook (exchange) account as well as my personal GMail account. A simple task, handles easily.

3. Movies/Video - I use it a good bit for Netflix and videos on planes. The picture is HD quality and works wonderfully.

4. Web browsing - works very well even with multiple tabs open.

5. GPS - I use this tablet in my Jeep on offroad trails. I use the Gaia GPS app to navigate on trails. It is able to receive GPS signals without the need for cell signals/wi-fi. It gives me a nice large map and is very accurate for my backcountry travels.

6. Remote desktop - This is one of my favorite things to use this tablet for. I have a computer at my corporate office that is logged into our internal system. I am able to use the remote desktop app to access that computer from anywhere. It actually works better on the tablet than my laptop.

Now, let's talk about looks. It is a very attractive looking tablet. The screen is vibrant and works well. I have no idea if the back is metal or plastic, but it is high quality and looks great.

Cameras - They are ok, but my iPhone 7+ is far superior so I have not used them much. I do use the camera to take pictures of receipts when I ma traveling. I would say the cameras suffer in comparison to most high end cell phone cameras.

The screen is really odd in that it picks up a lot of fingerprints. I thought that it was just the nature of the beast, until I put a tempered glass screen protector on it. Suddenly, the fingerprint issue went away. Now the screen stays relatively clean and clear. I would recommend this one:
https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01FJ5DFOS/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

My other accessory purchase was a small bluetooth tablet keyboard. A great accessory if you are doing work on it.

Overall, I'm really happy with this inexpensive tablet. Is it the best for "power users"? No, but for me it is good enough that I can leave my laptop home on some business trips. My only regret is waiting so long to buy one.

Edit: After owning this tablet for a month, I love it. It actually has me considering replacing my iPhone 7+ with a Samsung Note the next time I upgrade. The only reason that I chose this tablet over an iPad was the better GPS capability and being cheaper was a bonus. I don't think the iPad would have been that much different in daily use.

title: Type-C, Backlight Bleed, Average Build Quality
text:
Because HP doesn't make it entirely clear, I want to confirm that the Type-C port does act as a video input in addition to carrying USB. So that's 3 digital video inputs in total (and one VGA). HP doesn't include a Type-C to Type-C cable, however, just a Type-C to Type-A cable, which can't carry video.

Incidentally, the Type-C cable that HP included with my unit appears to be faulty. Connecting the monitor's hub to a PC with that cable results in hung POSTs and "device descriptor request failed" errors in Windows Device Manager. Using my Type-C to Type-C (Apple) cable, I've not seen a single issue.

This monitor has what should be totally unacceptable levels of backlight bleed, but this is the new norm. Wasn't expecting anything other than appalling black screen uniformity, but no pleasant surprises here.

AG coating is MINIMAL.

The casing is all plastic. My lower bezel has a ripple in it, and a gap between it and the screen. The foot is also plastic, however, the vertical part of the stand is finished aluminium, reminiscent of the stands Dell put on their U2711-era monitors. This is nice, when even Dell has moved to plastic clad uprights.

Sitting beside the Elitebook x360 1030 G2 with it's full aluminium casing and impossibly perfect fit and finish, the E273q is a little underwhelming.

title: Works well! But there are a few things that you need to keep in mind...
text:
These surprisingly work well with the carpet I have. I think I have looped-pile carpet, and according to other reviews I read prior to making my purchase, it works perfectly well on my floors. While it was pricey for me as well ($50, because I bought two of them), I didn't know how much I realistically needed, so be aware of the cost -- this should be considered an investment.

The material is strong and sturdy, but it can be easily cut with a sharp pair of scissors. When application starts, I would recommend having a partner because they can precisely put down the cable cover as you apply pressure (SLOWLY) on each section as you evenly distribute the tension to cover your cables. I ended up covering 16 gauge speaker wire, and I used one to cover two cables and another to cover six. The one I covered six pieces of speaker wire had to be carefully twist-tied together to ensure the tension could be distributed evenly. Also, with the six-covered cables, it's considered a high-traffic zone because leads from the living room to the kitchen, so I ended up duct-taping the ends a little bit to keep it covered, but overall, the Velcro holds well and you don't have to get it an a gaudy trip-hazard yellow (unless you need to warn people of the covers).

The color I ended up going with was black, and it fits the earthly tones well of my sound system. Just remember: 1.) Have a partner, 2.) Use twist-ties/zip-ties in addition, 3.) Be aware of the cost, 4.) Have loop-pile carpet. This isn't a miracle cable cover unless you're literally covering one cord at a time. Like every DIY solution, think about it logically and you should be fine. Also, my cats run across the covers all the time without anything happening to them, so with bipedal humans, everything seems to stay sturdy.

title: and overall am pleased with the picture quality and sound
text:
I've had this TV for a couple of weeks now, and overall am pleased with the picture quality and sound.

This TV replaced an old 32" I've used in the living room for the better part of a decade. When I started the shopping process I was all set for a 55-60" 4K set with all the bells and whistles, but realized that size wouldn't look right on top of our credenza (and I wanted to avoid a wall-mount). Once I started comparing sets below 50", the 4K seemed to be less of a priority. Although 4K would be nice, I didn't want to risk buying a rock-bottom 4K set with a name I couldn't pronounce, so settled on a decent Vizio set to use until 4K finally becomes the norm (at which point I suspect prices will fall on name brands as well). Overall, due to the this bezel on this set (to be fair, most set have equally thin-- or thinner-- bezels), it doesn't take up much more room than my old 32", and fits on the credenza perfectly.

The picture quality on this set is good, but it's worth going online to google the model and find what the "experts" recommend you adjust the settings to for this model (I used this as a rough guide, but didn't follow their suggestions exactly). As for the sound, it seems to be adequate and I can't complain about it (it's fine for weeknight TV and sports). If I was a movie buff or gamer I'd likely add a sound-bar, etc... but then again, if you're a movie buff you're probably buying a larger set with more features to begin with.

The TV has some smart apps on it, but the interface and offerings seem a bit clumsy, and I prefer to just use the Fire TV box I have hooked to it. That said, I'd recommend this set for anyone looking for a decent quality "basic" TV and isn't quite ready to buy into the whole 4K thing.

title: Incredible headphones but you need the right amp!
text:
I have had these headphones for about 9 months. I didn't want to review them until They had settled in and I was used to them. I have used several headphones in the past and currently own several. I have owned Grado SR325, Denon AH-D5000, PSB M4U-2, AKG K845, Audeze LCD2, and currently own Oppo PM2, AKG K712, B&W P3 and the HD800. The HD800 is my favorite headphone so far. It can be difficult to find the right amp for it. I have tried it with the Oppo HA-1 (balanced), Schiit Valhalla 2, and Marantz HA1. They were excellent with both but didn't really shine until I got my Luxman integrated amp. It is a pure class A amp and the headphone out uses it's speaker amp with a resistor in line to reduce the output. These headphones absolutely shine with this amp. They finally have deep, impactful bass. They were never really lacking in bass. The bass was beautifully detailed with great presence but didn't have the punch that it has now. I'm not sure what headphone amp would be similar to my Luxman but this is the ideal paring for me. Coincidentally my AKG and Oppo headphones do not sound as good with the Luxman as they do with my Oppo HA-1.
With the right amp pairing these headphones are absolutely amazing. They have an incredibly wide sound stage and "audio microscope" detail. They are the best "speaker replacement" headphone that I have found. No headphone is as good as a nice set of loudspeakers but these are as close as I have found. They will show any weakness in your system or the recording you are listening to. Beware, you will be looking for the best recorded/mastered versions of your favorite music and that can get expensive. They are also the most comfortable headphones that I have ever used. Most people don't think enough about comfort when they buy headphones but it is a huge consideration for me. If your headphones sound amazing but you can only listen to them for a half hour before they hurt the amazing sound quality does not really matter.
These are not portable or utility headphones. If you buy these plan on using different headphones for portable or un-amplified use. These are best used for just sitting by your stereo and listening. If you can amp these properly buy them. They are amazing.
Protip: When you get your headphones register your serial number on Sennheiser's web site and they will email you a frequency graph. They make measurements for each set of these that they build so the graph is for your headphones. Some of the early models have a small treble spike that gave these headphones a reputation for being bright. My graph is flat with no spike. I have compared it to other people that have posted their graphs on a thread at Head-Fi.

title: Powerhouse of a Computer!
text:
As a game programmer, Steam user, website creator, musician, and professional writer, I need a computer that brings the power. This Dell does just that for a low price. One thousand dollars may seem like a great deal of money, but in comparison to other computers with similar specs, this is actually a few hundred dollars cheaper.

Generally, at any given time, my computer is doing the following things: hosting a Plex media server, running multiple tabs of Google Chrome, running Steam, running an Antivirus Agent, running Tonido (a personal computer server), handling three monitors (two 1080p and one 1440p), handling a printer, and running game creation software. On top of that, I may be watching TV or a movie and playing a game such as Civ V at the same time. Normally, this would require an immense amount of RAM and CPU, but this computer handles it with finesse. I have never reached the RAM or CPU limit in the 8 months I've had this computer.

If that isn't enough, this computer is built with expansion in mind. Below the CD drive, there is what appears to be another CD drive. However, there is actually nothing in there. It is empty space, space where another hard drive, a blu-ray player, SSD drive, or other peripheral can be added internally. In addition, the computer can handle up to 32GB of ram. The processor and video cards can be upgraded as well. This computer was designed with future-proofing in mind.

This computer does come with Windows 8.1, which is something that many people may not like. However, I was able to "circumvent" this by installing a program that mimics the older Start Menu. With that alone, you can use this computer almost as if it were Windows 7. This computer also has a free upgrade to Windows 10, which should provide relief to those who are normally against using Windows 8.1.

I find the high number of peripheral inputs to be highly useful. I have connected to the computer a USB 3.0 hard drive, Xbox 360 Wireless Adapter, printer, 3 monitors, two cables for charging phones and other devices, sound system, surge protector and battery information input, keyboard and mouse input, webcam input, and USB 2.0 hub input (assuming that I am not forgetting anything). The only reason I have the hub is to open up extra input ports for occasional thumb drive or miscellaneous use. The computer handles everything like a charm.

Overall, I would definitely recommend this computer to anyone looking for a power-house. I was surprised with how easy it is to set up and use, and believe that you would be as well.

The form on their website has a spot for the review text, the star rating given, and some instructions include the following lines of text:

"The star rating of your review has no impact on your extended warranty."

but then

"7) Complimentary extended warranties will only be given for reviews that are deemed helpful and constructive. Any reviewer that meets all standards will receive an email notification with the Extended Warranty Confirmation."

which is leading. Now, granted nowhere do they actually say leave them a good review or a review of a certain number of stars. title: Better than OEM, but not impressive. Go component instead
text:
Installed these highly rated Kicker 43DSC6704 D-Series speakers into Toyota Sienna van (instead of OEM front door speakers). Upgraded stock radio to Pioneer as well. Speakers sound better than OEM, but I'm not impressed.
I prefer a natural sound, not a boomy and not a bright. I don't like to use equaliser/effects as well and prefer to keep flat settings. I don't use a separate subwoofer in my home stereo system and satisfied.
The first concern with Kicker 43DSC6704 was almost no bass. I would be happy to avoid a separate sub in the car, but not with these speakers. To resolve bass issue I got an amplifier (Alpine MRP-F300) and a kicker 10 inch subwoofer box. I put subwoofer into van trunk and connected these speakers to the amplifier as well. The bass issue was resolved (subwoofer helped) and sound improved.
But I felt that something still missing. I pulled JBL/Infinity mid-range speaker from another car component system and installed it into left door + connected the stock van tweeter to it. I kept these kickers in the right door. So I could compare sound using left-right balance setting.
And finally I figured out what was wrong. These kickers has a very small mids bass and loud highs. When I compared vocal to midrange speakers, these kickers produces sound like singer has a rainy nose. So my main concern is almost no mids. Second - weak bass (sub eliminated second issue).
By the way, while I kept midrange speaker in the left door, and kicker in the right, sound was pretty good.
As for me I decided to return these kickers and Installed midrange speakers into both doors and keep stock tweeters for now.
After I replaced these kickers by midrange speakers I noticed that actually there is no need in the subwoofer. It improves sound and for noe I keep it, but for me the difference is not huge (it was a huge difference kickers+sub vs kickers and no sub).
So, my wrong selection costed me several days of work, buying sub/amp and headache with their installation + speaker return fees.
My sound project is still ongoing, but these kickers are not a part of it anymore. I keep 3-star rating because they sound better than Toyota stock speakers and based on other reviews there are people that love them. Probably they might be okay for some kind of music. But I would prefer a good component speakers instead.

text:

DeepCool makes some well-reviewed reasonably priced cooler mats with adjustable speed fans -- for some reason most of this product line is not available on Amazon as of May 2015

title: Decent wallet for the price with some design flaws
text:
In summary, this is a decent "change purse/wallet", made of attractive and soft leather, that can hold cards & an ID too. I think calling it "slim/thin," "minimalist," or a "money clip," is inaccurate (for which I docked it a star) and some of the design elements make it annoying to use (for which I docked it another star). The brass snap is maybe the nicest feature of this item.

First the pros:
-The leather looks and feels nice. It has an attractive texture and it is soft to the touch.
-The brass snap looks and feels like it is good quality. It snaps solidly and holds nicely, with just the right amount of release tension to open the wallet.The brass color is also very attractive against the black leather.
- The construction and quality seem pretty decent. The stitching looked pretty well done. I did find two thread tails sticking out and some of the seams are visible and don't line up, but I didn't count those things against the wallet since they don't seem to affect anything and you can probably just cut the thread ends off and never notice them again. I've posted a picture just so you can see and make your own judgement.
-There's an extra slot behind the ID slot for storing cards or whatever that you don't access often.

The cons:
-This wallet is quite a bigger (length, width, and depth) than the description makes it seem. It covers my hand almost completely and it is quite thick. I would not call it minimalist or slim by any means and I think you'll understand why I say that when you look at my photos. If you're not looking for a slim, minimalist wallet, then this won't be a con for you, but I'm listing it as such because I did purchase it for that purpose, the description does say it is, and it does not meet my standards for such.
-Going along with the above, the description states it will fit comfortably in your front pocket. I'll disagree with that. It is too big and thick to fit comfortably in any of my pockets. My intent was to carry it in my purse, so I was not affected directly by this, but I think this is worth mentioning due to the description.
- The clear portion of the ID slot is too small and it covers a large portion of the edges of my driver license. My license also does not fit all the way in, it sticks out the side of the slot (kind of the way the credit card tops stick up out of their slots). I think the ID sticking out gives a messy look and I didn't like the obstructed view of my DL.
-The credit card slots don't quite line up properly. I expected the tops of the cards to stick up out of each slot evenly and neatly, but really, the lower one almost completely covers the middle one. Again, this looks messy and it makes removing the middle one more difficult. The card in the top slot sinks all the way in and does not stick up at all, also making it harder to remove.
- The money pocket is a nice feature and I thought it would hold my cash nicely and stay relatively flat, only expanding if needed (like if stuffed with stuff). But it does neither. The wallet pretty much stays in the expanded position at all times. Cash, folded in half, reaches the bottom of the pocket and fits nicely, except then it gets all crunched up by the expandable portion. So to carry the cash properly, it has to be kept above the expandable piece. In that position, the cash sticks up, out of the pocket and then the wallet doesn't want to close properly because the cash is sticking up into the area that folds.

I was offered a discount on this wallet in exchange for my unbiased review, but I actually bought this because I needed it. I got a Hauberk wallet instead and it met and exceeded all of my expectations. You can see my review of that wallet on my profile if you're interested. I gave this one to my toddlers to play with and, to its credit, it has held up to their scrutiny thus far!

With some design changes, description changes, and cleaning up of the thread ends, this could easily be a higher-priced, 5-star item. But If you're looking for a reasonably priced, change purse-type wallet that looks nice, this will definitely get the job done.

title: Micro USB charging at a cost of cradle charging.
text:
This isn't my first Motorola radio, I've been using them for years. Its the first that I've used that doesn't include a cradle charger, even though the case has the contacts to support such charging. Motorola should have taken the time to make both effective to use for charging, not sacrificing cradles -1 star. The micro USB charging is welcome, but its soon to be a legacy connection standard as USB charging is already moved to the directionless C connector. Sure there's not a lot of them out there right now, but it will be even more prolific than micro USB in a year or two, time to get on the bandwagon Motorola... new cell phones use USB-C.

The case is much larger and less pocket friendly than a standard talkabout. You will need to use the belt clip to carry one of these , unless you are stuffing it somewhere else than your pocket. The clip is removable and needs to be so for the batter compartment to be accessible. This phone can run on its rechargeable battery pack or by 3xAA batteries in a pinch. Since AA rechargeable are everywhere in my house, it makes an emergency use as simple as a gathering exercise to harvest toy batteries.

With a weather alert radio and a FM radio built in, this is definitively a great emergency handset. The LED light added into the mix provides a beacon to find the radio in the dark in a power outage and a useful tool when needing emergency light. The two-way radio performed fine in Ohio suburban world... maybe 1.5 miles, maybe 2 enough distance for comms when you cant see each other, especially if you are making rounds on a property to verify everything is closed up for the evening or secured for a storm.

Color? Why the scarlet and grey? I'm the biggest OSU Buckeyes fan, but I don't get this color scheme for an emergency radio. I would have preferred something more neon (Orange, Yellow, Green) that really stands out to make it easy to find.
