title: Excellent battery life, very fast boot up, almost no bloatware. Good basic laptop
text:
In comparison to my Toshiba Satellite 15" with similar specs, this ASUS is about equal - there are definitely some things I like better about the ASUS for everyday use and a couple of small quibbles that bother me. First off the computer itself is about the same weight as my Toshiba so carrying it around is exactly the same and it fits in my existing laptop sleeves and bags. It does have a DVD tray so you can play movies & music and burn discs as needed (as does my Toshiba), but a lot of laptops don't offer this anymore, so this is a definite plus.

I do really like that the ASUS comes a lot cleaner out of the box than my Toshiba - almost no bloatware pre-installed. The basic Windows 10 and you can don't have to spend 30 minutes messing around with a bunch of garbage you don't want and won't use anyway. Additionally, the ASUS boots up about 20 seconds faster from off than my Toshiba and again from the sign in screen, the ASUS is still faster. The screen is very pretty and clear with a variety of images and video - keep in mind that it's NOT a touchscreen. I've been averaging about 6 hours of use with the battery before it hits the 30% mark - that is net surfing, watching some random videos, and mostly word processing. Leaving it on in sleep mode with no use - it went almost 4 full days before needing a charge. The wifi connects immediately and I've had zero issues with it dropping out either inside or out on the back deck.

I really like the keyboard and the overall shape of the frame on this particular laptop. My Toshiba has the keyboard just open and exposed and what happens is that the heels of my hands tend to slip upwards as I type or bump the space bar. Or my thumbs slide into the mousepad area and now my cursor has bounced someplace new & I'm typing in the wrong spot. The ASUS keyboard is slightly lowered and has a border around it - for me anyway, this design is MUCH easier to type with. (See the photo.) The shape of the overall frame is better on the ASUS than the Toshiba as well. The rounded corners and edges on the ASUS don't poke into your wrists after an hour of writing or research.

My quibbles seem small on the surface, but after almost three weeks of use, they are aggravating me. First - the ASUS doesn't keep time as well as the Toshiba. It's off by 2 full minutes. (See the photos) I've checked both a couple of times and set them manually at the same moment and within 24 hours, the ASUS has lost 2 minutes - it never loses more than that though. Second - The charger is smaller than every other one I have for the other two laptops and the Chromebook in this house. The other three are standard size, but the one on the ASUS is a tiny bit smaller and thus you can't use another charger for this laptop in an emergency. Third - the speakers on the ASUS don't sound quite as full as the ones on my Toshiba. Of course... no built in speakers on a laptop are really meant for full music enjoyment.

My bottom line is that at this price point, this is a nice machine and will do almost anything you can want with regard to basic internet surfing, movie watching, office work and the like. This is not a gamer's computer and it's not meant to be. But as a regular, go to every day laptop, it's a pretty good one. I want to give it 4 1/2 stars.

title: Solid Gaming Workhorse @ 1600x900
text:
I was seeking a display adapter for a budget DIY gaming desktop computer. It had to conform to the PCIe 2.0x16 standard (paired with Asus M5A78 LM-E USB 3.0 motherboard) and Amazon had the most extensive selection of GPUs with that feature. I had never heard of ViewMax before - most of my computer building experience was with manufacturers such as MSI, EVGA, and ASUS. This device was reasonably priced and the memory capacity of 4GB - albeit DDR3 instead of DDR5 - made it an attractive option so I took the plunge.

At first I tried running a game at 1920x1200 resolution over the HDMI connection. Image quality was smooth but play was slightly choppy at the graphics settings selected by NVIDIA's GeForce Experience optimizer. I manually disabled vertical synchronization and my screen went dark and my system froze. I was aware that I was probably expecting too much at 1920x1200 and I wasn't disappointed with the card.

I throttled back to a 1600x900 monitor, and I am most satisfied with this card's gaming performance at that resolution. Gameplay is smooth and color is good at medium settings over the DVI connection. I have ordered a Sceptre E205W-1600 1600x900 monitor to take advantage of this GT730's HDMI output - another attractive feature of this GPU.

GeForce Experience optimal settings with this card for the action-RPG "Path of Exile" are:
- Anti-aliasing: Off
-Display Mode: Full-Screen
-Post Processing: Off
-Resolution: 1600x900
-Shadow Quality: Off
-Texture Filtering: Trilinear Filtering
-Texture Quality: Medium

The game runs quite well at these settings, but just as test I manually adjusted the anti-aliasing level to 'Medium' and the GPU responded without a hitch or stutter.

title: I've got no strings on me!
text:
I love running with over-ear headphones, and lately my Crossfade M-100s have been my go-to cans for that. The one thing that I've always hated while running with any headphones is dealing with the cords - pulling earbuds out of my ears, rubbing and getting in the way of arm movement with on-ear or over-ear, etc. I can tuck them in my shirt or whatever, but then they're annoying and pull when I turn my head. And let's be honest - most cordless headphones sound like garbage. Been there, done that, returned it. Yeah, first world problems but why not shoot for perfection? The only reason I even gave these a shot is because they're V-MODA and I'm not just surprised, I'm blown away.

V-MODA claims that these sound equivalent to wired headphones. I'm going to disagree for my most common use case - connected directly to my iPhone 6S. In this case, they sound a bit better. The integrated amplified delivers more and cleaner bass presence than my iPhone can. Not as good as with a standalone DAC/amp, but I'd say about 30% better than the iPhone alone - which is not a subtle improvement, and without the distortions introduced by the iPhone's electronic equalizer. You can practically see the strings on a bass guitar vibrating in your mind, and the bass drums have a beautiful kick. Highs and mids still feature V-MODA's trademark clarity and nice, even frequency response. So yes, the sound is wonderful, which is what everyone really cares about. I've seen some complaints in forums, but as far as I can tell these have been narrowed down to devices that just can't send good quality audio over Bluetooth. I haven't personally had any issues yet, but I've only tested with my iPhone and MacBook Pro. Charging is accomplished with a standard micro-USB cable, so most people won't have to worry about carrying extra cords or chargers to keep the Crossfade Wireless topped up while traveling. Battery life hasn't yet been an issue. They come with a typically excellent V-MODA travel case, the sort that puts every other brand to shame but V-MODA buyers have become pleasantly used to.

Minor quibbles:
* No cliq-fold hinges like the M-100s and XS. Sorry, V-MODA, you spoiled us and it's hard to go back.
* A single button for pause / resume / track-forward / track-back. I suck at pressing these fast enough, so I always wind up just pausing it.

I'm pretty nit-picky about things, so that's a pretty short list. I'm loving these so far!

title: USB 2.0 speed on USB-C cables that fail at data transfer
text:
There are no warnings or notes on the product page that these USB C cables are only USB 2 standard. If your phone assumes that the USB-C cable is of the current USB 3.0 specifications, then data transfer will fail anytime it tries to go past the throughput speeds of USB 2.0. Your computer may recognize your device and you may be able to start a transfer, but anywhere between 5 seconds to 2 minutes into the transfer, your transfer will fail on any of these cables.

Charging works fine, but data transfer is unreliable.

However, the packaging clearly says in its product title "Sync & Charging Cable". It does not sync properly on most devices.

However, if you want to use any of the other functionality, that is where it gets a bit frustrating.

Pros --
Relatively easy setup -- read Amazon reviewers feedback first.
If you are looking for a static camera, it is great; picture is clear, microphone, audio all great.
Night vision crystal clear.
Customer support is great, called and spoke with Bob. Resolved all initial questions/issues that were resolvable. ** note: not everything is fixable!!

Cons --
Documentation does not exist. For someone who just needs basic information to get things setup on their own -- does not exist.
--what is a dither? region setting how does that work? is blacked out area to detect motion or not? turns out functions one way on mobile
device and another way on PC setup!
Cameras cannot be managed exclusively with mobile device (phone/tablet), you must setup the PC application to get full functionality.
--example, camera date/time can only be setup on PC
Amazon reviewers provided more details / better documentation than Amcrest
--example, Amcrest cameras need 2.4Ghz wifi network, cannot use 5Ghz. Which Amcrest states, however they do not elaborate or explain.
What it means is that you must change the network your mobile device is connected to for setup to your 2.4g network, once setup is complete

title: No regrets!
text:
After my husband commandeered my old Wacom Intuos 3, I needed a new tablet that would work with Windows 10, PhotoShop CS2, and Krita. I'm very happy to report that my new Huion does the job just fine for less money than a used Wacom 3 on eBay. It's every bit as good as my old Wacom and perfect for light illustration, digital painting, and photo retouching.

I thought charging the pen would be a drag, but it's not that bad. I understand that Wacom has a patent on the wireless/battery-less stylus, and that's why you pay a lot for them. I'll save $300 and deal with it. For the price you pay for this tablet, you could buy a couple extra pens to have on standby if you use it that much. (One criticism: the pen holder would be nicer if it had some weight to it. It's too light and the pen falls off it all time, particularly while it's charging and the cord pulls it off. I use my old Wacom pen stand and store the Huiron with the extra nibs in my desk for safe keeping. Minor thing, but just a thought.)

The buttons on the side are only moderately helpful. I haven't programmed all of them, and I probably won't because there's no way to identify them without pulling up the driver menu if you forget what they do (besides just blindly mashing them). I feel that many are just unnecessary. But it doesn't affect the drawing surface at all by having them there.

Overall, I'm super happy with my choice. If you must be a Wacom snob, then obviously no review will suede you. But for those who want a product that's very affordable and every bit as good as the lower Intuos models, the Huion gets my vote.

title: Worse than a smoke alarm if the battery runs down mid-listen; otherwise pretty cool
text:
These things are neat. They are very compact and light, with a generous battery life and a pretty good range. They also come with a USB cable for charging and a double-ended audio cable for physically connecting them in transmit-mode. Initial pairing with devices involves a bit of jiggery-pokery (pro-tip: make sure all your receivers are active and sniffing for Bluetooth before you power up the transmitter), but once that's done, they work pretty darn well. I own two of them (one to transmit, one to receive) and have no regrets.
However, I do have two complaints:
1) They add their own noises to the signal to tell you stuff like "I am active", "I am connected", "battery is low". These noises are, to put it mildly, obnoxiously loud. My mom complained about it when we were using them to stream audio to her headphones, and now that I have them hooked into my sound system, I see why - I just about had a heart attack the first time the receiver blared out the "I am connected" beep, and whenever it runs low on battery, it gently notifies me by emitting the loudest g**d**n sound that can physically exist in our universe, and it keeps doing that every five seconds until you either turn it off or your speakers blow out. Don't try plugging it in to silence it - it will keep on complaining the whole time it is recharging, despite the fact that it will happily run off a DC adapter at all other times. This is an audio relay, guys, not a smoke alarm or a nuclear reactor safety sensor - the deafening, repetitive tones are bit excessive.
2) I cannot get them to pair with my phone. I bought two, hoping one could connect to the phone in Rx mode. If that'd worked, I'd have used the double-ended cable to hook it to the other unit, that one set in Tx mode. Then I'd have been able to send my phone's audio signal wirelessly to two Bluetooth headphone sets, which is what I wanted. That way, me and my mom could listen to the phone without disturbing others. No joy - set the phone and device in seek-mode several times but could not get them to acknowledge each other. This probably won't affect you, unless you a) have an older phone like mine where the physical audio port is all jacked up from years of being janked when the wire caught on something, or b) got suckered into buying some sort of weird, hypothetical phone that, say, has no headphone jack because its makers hate their customers...hypothetically ;)

title: Very good clock with lousy instructions
text:
I like this clock for its simplicity -- from the look of the case to setting the time to handling DST (Daylight Savings Time), this clock is well designed. The projector is way cool. It's like having an invisible secret clock built into the ceiling that can't be seen during the day. The biggest problem with digital clocks is DST. Congress has changed the dates that DST takes effect. Clocks bake the date into the internals. I have several clocks that are one hour wrong for a few weeks twice a year. This clock's solution is genius. When DST changes, press and hold the DST button for 3 seconds. Presto! the time is perfect. It even has a DST light so you know which mode the clock is in. Most of the other digital clocks I have owned have a dimmer for the display, but they don't dim the display nearly as much as I would like. This clock has 3 brightness settings. The third setting is perfect. I also like the AAA battery backup. I don't know why some clocks use expensive and hard to find button cells. I always have a couple of AAAs around. Some reviewers have stated that it's hard to set the time. Setting time is actually easy. The problem is the lousy instruction sheet. Here's how to set the time:

Start by setting DST. Check the DST light on the display. If it isn't correct, press and hold the DST button for 3 seconds. If the display brightness changes, you didn't hold the button long enough. Try again.

To set the time, many clocks require you to hold the "Time" button with one finger while pressing the "Hour" or "Minute" button with another finger. This clock is different, and that difference makes setting the time much easier. Press and release the "Time" button. The clock will go into the time set mode, which is indicated by a flashing display. While the display is flashing, press the hour or minute button until the time is set. When you are done, leave the clock alone and don't press any buttons for 5 seconds. The clock will exit the time set mode and the display will stop flashing. That's it. You're done. And you only need one finger. Setting the alarm or the radio station works the same way.

The manufacturer says the clock can store 10 AM and 10 FM radio stations. I don't know about that. I set one AM and one FM station. It's easy to turn the radio on to either station. That's enough for me. After all, it's a clock, not a boom box.

title: I Really Liked This Speaker
text:
I would describe myself as an older guy who has been into audio most of my life. I'm retired and have a dj hobby-business (Traktor software/hardware, QSC and Yamaha PA spkrs/subs, Mackie mic-mixer, etc.). At home I've got a semi-audiophile-wannabe-on-a-budget setup: B&W 684s (first generation) with matching middle speaker, Mirage sub/surrounds and a mid-range Denon AV receiver that replaced an expensive Marantz that crapped out early. Over the last 50 years or so I've owned a lot of different audio equipment, mostly good and some bad. On the portable, non-bluetooth audio side I have a Bose SoundDock Portable 30-Pin iPod Speaker Dock and Kicker iK501. I have the following bluetooth speakers: JBL Flip 2, Sony HT-CT780 soundbar and the JBL Charge 2+ being reviewed. My musical tastes run mostly from classic to modern pop/rock/singer-songwriter and blues (mostly vocals), edm, some rap, jazz piano and a hodgepodge of other stuff. Sorry if this seems boring or worse, pretentious. I simply want to convey my frame of reference for this review.

I read a ton of reviews on the UE Boom, Boom 2 and MegaBoom; the Bose Soundlink Mini and Mini 2; and the JBls. In the end, the JBL Charge 2+ seemed to fit what I was looking for: a portable, reliable, not overpriced, great-sounding-for-the-money bluetooth speaker. I was persuaded by some of the reviews that pointed out, while perhaps not an acoustically flat/neutral speaker, it has solid bass for it size, good (not overblown) highs and mid-range clarity/presence. All of these things are true. I hate speakers that over- or under-emphasize a particular part of the audio spectrum to the point of being annoying. I was worried that all the comments about the bass might mean it was boomy. Not so. It's got a pleasing balance (but isn't flat/dry sounding) and the emphasized vocal presence sounds just about right to me. Btw, I can't think of too many things that are more subjective and subject to more variables than audio (particularly speaker) reviews.

The bottom line: given my taste in music, my experience with a wide variety of audio equipment, my aging ears, the price of the Charge 2+ compared to its competitors, the fact that it just sounds"right" to me, JBL's long history as a quality speaker manufacturer (particularly vs. a tech company like UE (Logitech)) and the fact I find the Charge 2+ very listenable for extended periods, I felt this deserved a 5 star rating (unfortunately, no one offered me a free product). EDITED 1/25/16: One caveat (shared in so many words by others): This is a $130, 7.25" long bluetooth speaker (not an array of 1000w PA mains/subs that can collapse your chest). It will certainly play loud enough in a medium-sized room to interfere with conversation, but it is not really loud enough to drive a semi-noisy party in a larger room. With those expectations in mind, this is a great little speaker.

title: linear taper--bad for audio
text:
The main problem with this is the potentiometer (thing that does the work to control the volume) is linear (that is, it changes the same amount for each degree of rotation). This is wrong for audio applications because ears are kind of weird about sound. The result is your get most of the volume change in the first third of rotation and then nothing else much happens.

It should have a logarithmic (also called "log" or "audio) taper which would provide much more control through the range of the knob.

title: Great kit. Everything you need to get started.
text:
Great little computer. You can't go wrong with this thing, and for the price, you just can't beat it. It's fun, to say the least, and the things you can do with it are endless. And for such a little computer I'm shocked at the responsiveness. I'd buy one again, and in fact, I did yesterday, though the kit without the card, card reader and cable.

As for the kit itself, for someone just starting off it's the way to go. Everything you could need. The heat sinks, though probably not necessary for regular use, are a great little addition, especially if you're going to stress the Pi a bit. The card reader is really handy if you want to load a different OS on the card. The case is basic, but adequate, and neat looking. I like it better than the solid black one. The HDMI cable is a basic HDMI cable, but it's adequate. The memory card is enough for many things, though if you plan on adding a lot of info you'd probably be better off getting a 32GB card, or even the kit with such. All in all, I couldn't be happier with this kit.

title: my guilty audio pleasure - and great for PSVR
text:
These sound great. Who cares that audiophiles say you need a flat response. Sometimes you just want to have some fun, and these are fun (though I do certainly appreciate a flat response). These have great bass and sub bass. The low frequencies do not bleed into vocals so those still sound natural, etc. Everything is nicely detailed and sounds wonderful. For the price, it is a no brainer. I paid less than fifty, again, a no-brainer. I lowered the bass also to see how they (really) sound, and the clarity and detail is there. The clarity and detail exists normally, but getting the bass down to normal levels will reveal a bit more. I like these better than my Ultrasone HFI-780 for music. I also have Hifiman 400i which I love - and also a variety of IEMs . I just bought a Loki mini to bring the bass up a little bit (or alot depending on my mood) on the 400i. So whenever possible, I prefer the 400i, but when I want or need a closed back, these are my new go to. I have no regrets. I hope they last, the build quality seems very good, but the cord is fairly inexpensive feeling. But it is replaceable which is great and I will do that if or when I need. (I also had the Focal Spirit One S which I liked the sound of but had to return as they were like wearing a torture device and were on-ear and not over-ear). These JBLs are very comfy.

The DSP on this is very hit or miss. I have used it on some music and it has sounded good, but sometimes it sounds bad. I'm not sure if it depends on the mix or what. When it works, it gives the music alot of air and space. It's definitely not for critical listening, but at times, I really like it. I've also used it during some TV/movie playback. Again, it is hit or miss on this. But again, when it works well, it gives a great amount of air between dialogue, background, music, instruments, etc. Don't buy it for the DSP, but don't hate it because of the DSP as these are very good headphones without turning that feature on. I am enjoying these very much for both music and movies/TV.

Fwiw, I have been running these at home through a Fiio K5 amp and sometimes through my Yamaha AVR. The AVR gives it a bit of a muddy sound as I believe the headphone out jack on it has too high of an impedance whereas the Fiio is near zero. I've tried it out of my phone for Spotify and it works well, plenty of volume, etc, but I will use my IEMs for phone/mobile audio use.

**small update 1/9/18**
I received the Playstation Virtual Reality for Christmas, I love pairing these headphones with the PSVR, they sound great. Other headphones may result in lack of bass when plugged directly into the PSVR, but these do not fail. Also, when plugged in, they sound nice and open, thanks to the 3d audio processing from the PSVR I believe. These are my go-to headphones for PSVR, whether for playing games or streaming Netflix, etc. They fit great with the PSVR also, at least on my head.

title: Good price for a very nicely equipped and very quiet 4k gaming PC
text:
First Impression: How do I open the retail box (i.e. the "pretty" box inside the plain corsair box inside the amazon box)? The pictures on the plastic things on the side were not very helpful in telling me how to "unlock" (press in on the tabs, then pull them outward), and even then did not realize that I needed to pull those black plastic things out from the box itself to free up the box to open.

Second impression: HEAVY and bigger than the picture led me to believe, but solid steel construction.

Third Impression: tunk-tunk-tunk from the fan once I turned it on. I was able to "pull" at the top metal grate over the fan, and was able to get it to stop interfering with the fan's operation. I've had to do that a few times early on, especially after moving the PC, but so far I have not had to take it apart to fix it.

It installed Windows 10 1709 right away (after asking if I wanted to update now), but this took a very long time (about 3-1/2 hours) and disk utilization was pegged around 100% during that time. I also tried my mouse via the built-in Bluetooth, and it did not respond well and alternated between laggy and not responding. Between these two things, I was worried something was seriously wrong with the machine. After the updates were applied, I tried my USB "universal" wireless adapter for my mouse, and the poor mouse response was fixed. I also saw little to no issues with installing or running any software or games, including a video benchmark app (for the one game that did run long on installing, I'm going to blame on the installer).

In the past week or so, I've been running games flawlessly in 4k resolution and even at full load for hours at a time, I've not heard the fan get noticeably louder (a sharp contrast to the gaming laptop this is replacing). Despite being pretty heavy (almost 25 pounds), the footprint size is very reasonable, and there is a nice selection of ports on the back. Heat from the machine does vent straight up, so I would not recommend putting it directly under your house's thermostat, but otherwise that should be fine and I never found it to get much more than "warm".

After the initial rocky start and concerns, everything has been smooth sailing with this Corsair ONE, and I'm very pleased with my purchase.

title: Good for constellation-viewing

On a night when only Vega of the five bright stars in Lyra is visible without optical aid, these glasses let me see the other bright stars. Smaller constellations like Delphinus benefit from the slight magnification, but large ones aren't too magnified to be seen as a whole.

They are quite light compared to standard binoculars. If they came with earpieces, you could wear them as glasses.

On the other hand, because they are so small, it is harder to grasp them firmly. In the dark, it is hard to be careful to not touch the very large front lenses with your fingers.

title: Good solution but a bit pricey.
text: Installed with new Nuvi 65LMT with latest firmware update, powered from backup light. Worked pretty much as advertised unless the engine was running, at which point it might work once, briefly before connection was lost and not again until after engine was shut down and whole thing restarted. Display is grainy but usable, camera mount needed some adaptation to work with my car. After talking to Garmin, I tried running the camera from a constant 12V power supply (extended from an accessory socket). Connection issue went away, so a faulty transmitter was ruled out. Apparently a peculiarity with the backup light operation (2012 BMW) was interfering with the switching system in the transmitter when the car was running. I installed a relay triggered by the backup light as the recommended work around for the lighting system issues. Now it works fine. A buyer should be prepared for a little more installation hassle and cost than indicated in the Garmin videos, particularly on cars with recent higher tech auto lighting systems :).

title: Fast and cheap card ($0.41/GB for 32GB) that has a lifetime warranty. It's a win win!
text:
Whether you are transferring files or taking pictures, the Silicon Power Elite 32GB is a cheap but effective microSD card for your needs. Details inside, including a full TLDR.

▶ Package Contents
• Silicon Power Micro SD Card
• Silicon Power SD Card

▶ Specifications
• Form factor: microSDHC (32 GB) / SDXC (64 GB)
• Card dimension: 15 mm x 11 mm x 1 mm
• Operating temperature: 0ºC to 70 ºC
• Storage temperature: -40ºC to 85ºC
• Compatible with microSDHC UHS-1 enabled host devices.
• Combined with a SDHC adapter can be used as standard SDHC memory card
• Lifetime Warranty

▶ Hardware
When it comes to form factor, the Silicon Power Elite microSD card very much follows the same size as any other microSD/Tf Card.

The differences between cards are the following: speed, price, and durability. The SP Elite can match benchmarks of 85MB/s Read and 20MB/s write, which should handle video at 1080p, and transfer files adequately – if you’re seeking a faster read/write speed, then purchase the SP Superior instead, which should match much higher speeds.

The current price of the 32GB Elite is $12.99 ($0.41/GB), and the 64GB Elite is $22.99 ($0.36/GB). Both really cheap in terms of storage.

I’ve purchased and owned several different SD Cards and USB Flash drives, and have yet to find a drive fail on me, and with the SP Elite’s Lifetime warranty, this shouldn’t be a problem.

▶ Testing
For initial testing I used an app called CrystalDiskMark, a program used to measure the sequential read and write speeds of storage memory. The following results were from transferring 1GB (1000MB) of random data.

Read: 93.12 MB/s
Write: 21.62 MB/s

These speeds match some of the fastest microSD/TF cards from last year, which are very fast speeds.

I then tested the micro SD card w/SD Card adapter in my [[ASIN:B005OGQXJW Nikon J1]], a camera that takes really high quality 1080p digital images and video. I’m able to take several burst shots, without lag.

▶ Final Thoughts
It’s not the fastest microSD card, but it matches the speed of several cards of yesteryear. This paired with the price and lifetime warranty makes this a very compelling card to add to any SD card slot.

5 Stars
Recommended

+ Fast speeds

I have no cons for this product

title: Great rig. Great price. Plug in and go - not so much
text:
I'd been keeping an eye out for Nvidia 1060 class "gaming" computers ever since Nvidia announced the 1080 back in May 2016. The idea of the Pascal engine seemed exciting to me and I was looking forward to putting together a replacement for my kobbled together a bunch of upgrades and re-doos. When I saw the SkyTech Shadow on Amazon, I decided to get it as an early Christmas present for myself. Just so you know where I'm coming from, even though I've been assembling computers since the early 1980s, I don't really keep up much any more with the trends. Nowadays, if I want to upgrade something, I do a lot of googling and try to get a little informed before I make a purchase. The SkyTech seemed to fit the bill on paper in almost every way. I put dream systems together on PCPartPicker.com so I had a good idea of the performance price value of the SkyTech when I decided to buy it. It's priced very reasonably all things considered.

I really only play one game so this review will be pretty limited for folks looking for a more general sense of how the system performs. I play Second Life and now with the GTX1060, I can move in world with 30 FPS and ultra graphics. That's with no tweaking. I'll get to tweaking the card and CPU later on in the year. I've capped the Second Life settings at 30 FPS because that's my maximum requirements for now. I've made videos for YouTube with the older card with very low graphic settings and the goal for my rig is to get 30 FPS 1080p YouTube game captures. So far so good.

I like the system overall but there's a few things that don't sit well.

First up is the case. It looks cheap. the back panel seems paper thin and easily bends. Fortunately, I'm not back there that much.

Second up was the horrible noise from the CPU fan. Just ridiculous. So I went out and bought a DeepCool Captain 120EX liquid cooler to replace the CPU fan. It's advertised as being very quiet. I put that in recently and it is indeed whisper quiet. I'm much happier with the unit now. During installation, I discovered that the exhaust fan (which I completely replaced) was plugged in incorrectly. The exhaust fan wasn't even on the whole time before I replaced the CPU fan.

Third up is the silly USB 2.0 wireless adapter. Although it performed adequately, I needed something with a bit more umph - Second Life downloads textures on demand so the WiFi needs to be really good. So I bought a great little PCI express board but Surprise! - The GTX1060 blocks the PCI socket completely rendering it useless. So I spent a little more money and got a USB 3.0 NET-DYN 867Mbps/300Mbps adapter. Given these three annoying issues with the unit, I'm still rating it 4/5. My preferences/requirements/experience may be different so there's no need to downgrade it below that because it still is an excellent value system.

No software whatsoever - Just Windows 10. Woo hoo! I'd happily pay an extra 50 USD for that feature.

title: This is an excellent little light
text:
This is an excellent little light. Even on the lower power setting it is bright enough to read my Kindle in bed at night. It is quite light weight and trim, so it effectively adds almost no weight to my Kindle or even a book. Additionally, the battery lasts quite a long time, especially with the lower brightness setting.

The "clip" does have a certain range or thickness it can work with. I have a folding cover over my Kindle. I found this item worked best when my Kindle cover was folded open and I attached the clip over both the front and back covers, but just behind (or above) my device itself. This did mean that I had to detach it each time I shutdown my Kindle in order to close the front cover, but it has worked well.

As the device requires a minimum of about 1 cm or 5/16 inch of thickness to hold it in place, it was a little harder to find a good way to attach it to a hard cover book (I did not try a paperback), but I was able to carefully attach it over the back cover and a thickness of unread pages adjacent to the back cover. When I reached the last parts of the book and needed to read the pages, I simply moved the light over to the front cover with a portion of the adjacent and already read pages to make the thickness needed to hold the light in place. So, not a big problem as a work around.

Overall, I really love this little light. It is better than a previous type I owned as this light does, indeed, illuminate the entire page and has a longer arcing neck to position the light where you desire. I have owned this for a few months, use it every night for a hour or so, and so far so good and no battery change yet needed.

title: Great Headphones but Broken After 3 Weeks
text:
The earbuds are actually very good and of high quality. I don't really care too much about the ANC as the earbuds already go into your ear so it offers passive noise "reduction" by design; however, the noise cancelling for the mic could do better. Nowhere near the Plantronics 5200 series but the benefit to this is that your voice on the receiving end sounds more natural. I've noticed that with some of the Plantronics devices, they offer excellent noise cancelling on the mics but the voice just sounds very low quality, as if audio is highly compressed or the sample rate is low.

However, the noise cancellation is not the biggest flaw of the earbuds, the biggest flaw is actually how they're built, and this seems to be true for the other lower-end Jabras that share the same design paradigm. That is, something happens at a hardware level and whenever the chords are moved or positioned in a certain way, it induces static in one of the buds, in my case it was the right earbud. I was able to reproduce the issue simply by physically moving one of the wires.

It's a shame because they're otherwise a great sounding product and would've loved to keep them, but I had returned them due to this issue.

title: Too buggy, very disappointed in quality for the money
text:
I've had this watch a little over a year, and honestly for $300+ I expected way better. Sure, the running functions and customizable screens work fine, when they're working. And it's not like I'm going to switch to Polar or somebody else at this point, I bought into garmin and have been using their watches for years and wouldn't want to go through the hassle of exporting and reimporting all my data someplace else.

Almost as if on cue, a month after my 1 year warranty would've been done, the little belt loop thing for the strap broke off and now I use a hair tie to keep the excess band from flapping around.

At least once a month it gets confused about what time and day it is (like weirdly goes a few days and random number of hours into the past), or it freezes up from a push notification, and when I restart it any of the day's data is lost if it hadn't already been synced with my phone. The whole reason I switched to this watch over using my fitbit and older forerunner just for runs was so I could consolidate devices, so the fact that the key features like sleep tracking, step tracking, and push notifications are all buggy is really off putting.

While I was still under my 1 year warranty, I called customer service/technical support to try and resolve one of the times it had gone randomly a few days into the past, hoping maybe Garmin had some knowledge I didn't about how to restart it without losing my data. Nope, in fact I knew more than the tech. He said he had never heard of my issue before and that it was "weird" that it went back in time days, not just hours. After some troubleshooting, he told me that the .Trashes folder was a "corrupt file" and to delete it. A .trashes folder is a common OSX file on computers and usb devices that just retains info about files you've deleted. He didn't know how to delete it, so I told him the terminal command to do so in case he wanted to tell any other mac users to do the same thing. I humored him and deleted the file, but it didn't do anything, and obviously every time I plug it into a mac, it's going to recreate that file if it doesn't exist. He also tried to blame me by saying it happened because it had been a while since I went on a run with the watch, and it just needed to get the correct time from the satellites. This may have been the case at some point with some older Garmin watches, but it's literally a setting on the watch to choose to sync with your phone instead, and I have that enabled. So several times a day this thing knows what time it is and should never have an issue with that.

So, it seems the two ways I've successfully gotten it back to the correct date and time were to either turn the watch off, then plug it into the computer. It'll boot in order to charge, and the time is then correct. Or, just leave it on, plug it in to charge and when it gets to 100% power then it rectifies itself.

This isn't a low battery issue, I've had this happen at 75% battery.
This isn't an outdated firmware issue, I've updated each time a new firmware version has been released.
I've also completely set it back to factory settings, and it still happens.

So this is either an issue with my individual watch, or others have this same problem (and in that case I'd surmise it's a problem with their firmware) but I couldn't find anyone with this same issue when looking online.

I really wish you could customize push notifications, or that they'd at least mimic the customization on your phone. For example, I have it set up so the text of a message doesn't go to my lock screen, but the text of a message will show up on my watch face.

One last gripe, it's still really bulky, and I feel like at this point in technology abilities, it really doesn't need to be. I have a small (female) wrist, and I can't do any workouts involving my hands. Push ups, bench press, etc. The sides of the watch dig into my arm and back of my hand, inevitably push the run button and then it starts trying to connect to GPS. Usually to remedy this I strap it to my bra strap.

title: Nice try Fuji but such a disappointment anyway
text:
This is is my first Fujifilm camera and frankly speaking I am disappointed. My last film camera was Zeiss Ikon, after it I moved to Sony A7 with Zeiss branded lenses (35mm and 55mm), so you can consider me a spoiled :) and I do not like any compromises in optics. It must be sharp wide open - period. At some point I were looking for travel camera and I discovered Ricoh GR II. I were sceptical about it but it turned out to be a true gem. But gem with 16MP sensor :) so I were looking for upgrade. Few weeks ago Fujifilm started sales of XF10 in Hong Kong, I saw it and grabbed one, heading for short trip in Singapore. Here my observations, comparing with Ricoh GR II.

1. Lens. Fujifilm lens is pure disappointment. Compare to Ricoh GR II, where lens is sharp, really sharp. I never had to use unsharp mask or anything else. Ricoh - Macro mode, normal mode, 2.8, 3.2 anything - it is sharp, XF10 it is so soft, like cheap zoom lens wide open. Even considering 24M vs 16M it is still way too soft for my taste. Of course, if you never use proper primes, most likely you would not notice for me it is critical deal breaker.

2. Ergonomics/Build - it's little bit heavier and bulkier compared to Ricoh GR but not to degree what I would complain, still - GR is sleak. I would give XF10 a credit it is build very well, solid brick. My respect to Fujifilm.

3. I do not care about tilting screen or hot shoe, actually I am happy what Fujifilm dropped all these elements, never needed on GR, not missing on XF10.

4. Controls. OMG! Such an awful design on XF10. You can customize couple buttons but only they functions, not values (!). In GR I simple select values, modes and assign to MY1 or MY2. For example, for HDR, Let's put AE+/-2, ISO 100, 2Sec Timer, wide area AF, it will be MY1, so when I would like take HDR shots, on GR it's just a turn of dial to MY1, on XF10 - I have to do all these steps again and again. Thanks God, they allowed to disable touchscreen another useless gimmick (at least for me).

5. Lens cover. I have a questions to Fujifilm designers - do you ever use your own product? Cap which attached by strap to strap and hanging down when you taking picture - or you put it in your pocket? Common folks, again look on GR. Lens is covered, press a button - magic happens :) lens barrel extends, protective cover is removed and most important - Ricoh's front element is located almost 10mm inside lens assembly which creates a simplistic but effective hood. I do have fanky but super cool Ricoh's hood but even without it I never encountered flares. With XF10, no hood, lens is popping up - ghosts, flares - you name it. In addition to all of it, you can NOT attach external hood (!).

6. AF - XF10 is clear winner, I did missed quite a few shots in using GR in situations when I where needed an unexpected shots or candid ones. But I do mostly landscapes and static things, so I do not care much nevertheless I noticed AF on XF10 is faster, much faster and using of focus joystick is very convenient.

7. High ISO performance, again XF10 is clear winner, on Ricoh I prefered to stay under 800, very rarely using 1600 and nothing above. XF10 - 3200 is good as 800 on Ricoh.

8. Software. Even I have Capture One and Corel After Shot Pro (btw both do not support XF10 yet) I always prefer vendor supplied Raw converters. Because it is my first Fujifilm product, so actual usage of film simulation modes was kind of surprise for me and I like it. At the same time Ricoh's software not bad as well.

9. Geo tagging, with Fuji App on smartphone geotagging is not perfect but still possible which I appreciate could be done more effectively but I am Ok with Fuji approach.

10 Electronic level. OMG - Fuji folks, really?! You call it 'Level'?

Bottom line. If you owns Ricoh GR II, do not even think to move to XF10 without actually trying it, otherwise you are risking to be disappointed. If you have smartphone and almost happy with it - stick with smartphone :) I see no reason for you to spend few hundred dollars. Frankly, I see no target audience for this camera. I know - sharpness is not most important part of picture and human can adapt to any user interface (or lack of it) but photography is my hobby and I would like to enjoy to use my gear, Fujifilm with XF10 missed so badly.

PS Fuji, please, please buy few Ricoh GR hand it over to your design department which is responsible for XF10, send them for weekend trip somewhere.

*Ignore below if you wish, the is the most recent up date is above*
It was this or the cooler master 180mm cooling fan and I decided this because of simple math. 4 medium fans vs. one large fan. Simple right? Sure. This does the job. Buuuuut it is not THAT efficient. My laptop runs in the 80C though 95C range of temperatures while under load. It gets HOT. To add on top of this there is a docking station that I use that covers half the two top fans. (Not an issue with this product in particular but was hoping that the two top fans could be wide enough to get passed this gap, but to no avail.) I just feel that this does not push enough air that I need. The main reason I am writing this review is frankly more due to the noise than the airflow. When the bottom fans are turned on, it is LOUD. Not in the "airflow being moved" kind of way but more of a "errrRRRRR" way. It sounds like a motor, not like a fan. The two top fans are super silent when working alone though, but then I get less airflow to a much needed computer. So in conclusion, it works, it is mid-range, no drastic temp change, mine makes "errrRRRRR" sound when bottom fans are on. In the end I noticed no difference in temps.. Make your decision. I would return but it would cost too much so I will keep it.

*Update*
Still a no from me.
After owning this for a while I finally came to understand it's designs. The problem for me is this pad does not provide "Massive airflow" as it states in the description. This is one step up above a passive cooler. The airflow cools the metal mesh, so contact to contact is needed in your hot zones. For me, this is bad as I have a docking station that elevates the back portion of the deck and I needed the air to push up to the computer. I could put my face right up to the thing and would feel almost nothing. I would get a temperature probe and put it right in front of a fan and the temp would not change. But as soon as I made contact with the metal the temperature dissipates through the metal cooling the probe.

The rating I give is not because of performance, and this thing is still far from silent, but I give it 3 stars because I feel I was misled. Yeah, there is "Massive airflow". But not going out of the fans, but into the metal instead. Same story with my other laptop pad, it seems to be a trend. Try and find 3 laptop coolers that don't use wire mesh.

I took the mesh off my last pad and salvaged the fans, which, actually have decent CFM or cubic feet per minute, once the mesh is removed but it seems all these fans on the market lack static pressure, or the ability to fight resistance placed in front of them.

I would have maybe rated this 4 stars if I was able to take the wire mesh off but sadly in order to do that you have to remove the rubber pads on the bottem and that I really don't want to mess with because I want to keep the pad because it is a nice looking pad.

If your laptop sits flat, great, this might work. But if it's elevated like mine, forget about it. The difference will be minimal.

title: Excellent entry level analyzer and decoder for use with a PC (Linux/Windows/Mac)
text:
I bought the red Logic 8 as a hobby tool to work on coding and robotics projects with my kids and sometimes small things around the house. The current Logic series can handle the many types of signals available in most electronic projects. The ability to handle analog and digital signals and decode many of them is a huge help. The current release of software now allows for real time display during capture and this is a huge help for those of us with less expertise in electronics. The Saleae interface is very clean and polished and the hardware is a tiny but gorgeous piece of engineering. While the hardware is a great piece of engineering, what you are really buying is the software. This is continuing to be upgraded and improved over time. The recent software changes are great to see and make this a better product now than when I purchased it.

In this day of overseas suppliers with zero tech support and little or no knowledge of their products it is fantastic to work with a company where they really care about customer service one-on-one. I was in a longish chat session several weeks ago when the fellow I was chatting off and on with needed to leave. Someone else took over while he was gone and later when I noticed the name it was Mark Garrison (one of the founder/owners). I was just asking some technical decode questions about the product and he pitched in while his employee took a break. That was fantastic to see they care for their employees and they would spend the time to answer what were pretty basic questions from someone who had yet to buy their products.

Pros
Excellent hardware build quality
Amazingly attentive tech support and live chat available on their web site!
Moderate cost
Very Wide range of software decodes included
Realtime Display Addition (great new feature)
Analog and Digital support
Higher voltage support for RS-232 protocols
You can download the software and see it work with the simulator to get a better feel for it
Money-back guarantee and warranty are excellent (3 Years and 180 day return policy check their web site)

Cons
Can't decode/handle differential signals
Realtime display is still in beta (but has worked pretty well so far for me with a couple of hours of testing)
Can't save directly to disk yet while capturing, so a capture needs to fit into the PC RAM (64 bit native app so it can generally use all you have)
Screen print/export needs a white background/inverted colors option instead of just black so it prints easier (minor)

title: Great quality, high-speed USB-C hub with plush velvet sleeve
text:
[[VIDEOID:db2dd909b9d29c76dc824bac6def28c]] This hub is fast, beautiful, and really high quality with a really nice gray velvet sleeve to protect it and keep it looking good. I've had my hub for a week and did some testing with it and used it for a few work presentations. It works great with my 1080i protector. Since it advertises 4k too, I hooked it up to my 75" TV and it looks stunning. I know I could just use AirPlay, but I wanted to make sure this was compatible, since I had some trouble with my other Mac with the built-in HDMI not working with some projectors or TVs. So far this has worked GREAT!. Also, the USB 3.1 ports are faster than my Mac's. It was also faster than the ports on my other USB-C hub that doesn't have an Ethernet port, but does have SD card slots that I infrequently use with my Sony point & shoot digital camera.

I did a test with the FIO utility on the same disk with the same parameters and returned the following results on the USB 3.1 ports using the same retractible 128 GB Lexar High-Speed USB thumb drive (bought at Costco):
MacBook Pro Mid 2014 15" (4 core) USB 3 ports: Read 1172kB/s & 286 IOPS | Write 391kB/s & 95 IOPS
MacBook Pro 2017 13" (2 core) with older high-quality USB-C hub: Read 1381kB/s & 337 IOPS | Write 461kB/s & 112 IOPS
MacBook Pro 2017 13" (2 core) with CharJen Prime USB-C Hub: Read 1834kB/s & 447 IOPS | Write 613kB/s & 149 IOPS

So this USB-C hub is has 56% faster for read & write throughput and IOPS compared to the older MacBook Pro ports (that I used to think were fast!) and 33% faster than my other USB-C hub! I didn't think it would make that big of a difference. Note that I made multiple test runs and the results were consistent.

Here is an example of the command I used for the tests:
fio --randrepeat=1 --ioengine=posixaio --direct=1 --gtod_reduce=1 --name=test --filename=/Volumes/SteveUSB/test --bs=4k --iodepth=64 --size=1G --readwrite=randrw --rwmixread=75 >> new-secondpass.txt

Now the only time I'm going to break out the other USB-C hub is when I need to read from an SD card.

Note that I also tested the Ethernet port, which I use for network troubleshooting or other times when I need a consistent wired connection. I have a fast Wi-Fi system that tests at almost 160 Mbps for downloads, but I'm able to get almost 180 Mbps. I'm not sure what my maximum theoretical speed is, since I'm supposed to only get about 80 Mbps. And it connected without fuss.

I HIGHLY recommend this quality hub.

This work well. The Bravura Easy Sync software that's included with the cable is better than the Windows Easy Transfer program: First, it works more consistently, and second, it lets you be the boss (which those familiar with MS will appreciate.)
Here are a few tips for using the Bravura program: Contrary to conventional wisdom, the connection is detected faster if you plug in the cable before starting the program. Just don't allow the Windows program to run if it starts automatically.
Always select the drag and drop method for transferring files. This lets you transfer program files and other executable files like downloaded installation files, which will be skipped if you put the software in charge of decision making.
Drag and drop folders unless you want to select individual files.
If the program says it can't find a certain file, or a file has been blocked by an antivirus program, click "continue." Do not click "cancel" if you are transferring a folder.

title: The Pinnacle of AMD Graphics Cards
text:
I've had this card for 5 months now. Upgraded from a 280x, and have used it exclusively for gaming. Mainly, I upgraded to a monitor with a resolution of 3440x1440, and also started playing Tom Clancy: Ghost Recon Wildlands. The old 280x couldn't take it. Neither could a crossfired pair of them.
Enter the Vega: FE, Liquid Cooled Edition.
This card makes short work of the games I throw at it. I'm pretty sure I'm bottlenecked by my CPU now (i5-2500k). On the benchmark of Tom Clancy, I get at least 34 FPS at 3440x1440 on Ultra preset, usually more like 45 AVG. I'm happy with that, personally, as I grew up on the original Halo: Combat Evolved (30 FPS on the original xbox). Everything else I play is just laughably simple for this card.
True to the memes about AMD graphics cards, this card ages like fine wine. On release, it traded blows with the Nvidia 1080 (consumer flagship), and in October of 2018, it now trades blows with the 2070 RTX. Sure, it doesn't have the Nvidia-specific RTX cores, but no games use them anyway at the time of writing.
If you're into hard numbers, this card will do 13.7 TFlops (single precision). That's better than a 2080ti, which posts 13.4 TFlops (and that card is $200 more expensive, without liquid cooling). This card also comes equipped with a nearly-indecent 16GB of graphics memory. You'll have the choice to run gaming drivers or professional drivers, easily toggled from within the driver menus. Also, as all recent AMD graphics cards do, this card supports Freesync.
The only aspect of this card worthy of any hand-wringing would be its power consumption. It is a toaster oven. Fortunately, I live in the grand old US of A, and if I ran it balls-extended for 8 hours every day, my power bill would go up by $10/month (including overhead of the rest of the computer and a lamp). If you can afford Netflix, you can afford the power consumption of this card.
TL;DR: If you like AMD better than Nvidia, or you want professional drivers for less-than-professional prices, just buy this.

title: Great Router
text:
Bought this router to replace the CellSpot ASUS router that we had in our house. Wanted something with better throughput and range. This router isn't necessarily cheap, but you DO get what you pay for....and for what you get, it's well worth the price.
1) Easy Setup. Out of the box to completely set up took less than 15 minutes.
2) Second 5GHz channel. LOVE this. Allows me to have a separate network I use just for my wife and my devices and 1 for the kids/other devices.
3) Great throughput. The old CellSpot is still a great router, made by ASUS, but it did get overly congested when we connected multiple devices. The AC3200 has no such problems whatsoever.
4) Easy sharing of Network drive/printer.
5) Range is excellent. Not that the CellSpot was a slouch, but this thing is equal or better in every regard.
CONs:
1) It's pretty huge. This isn't the kind of thing I would want sitting on a desk, as it takes up a lot of space. Also not going to be something that most people will agree works with their decor...there are more stylish routers out there....though I would be willing to bet this is much better than those options

Overall a great router

title: A decent dash cam if you can catch it on sale.
text:
Before purchasing this item, I had tried a cheaper mirror dash cam ($35) that didn't meet my expectations.

The MiVue 420 is a considerable step up. Video is very sharp, and this unit references GPS satellites to pin-point your location/speed.

You can customize the menu settings for an array of features such as lane departure warning, following to close alerts, etc.

You can mark the location of speed cameras, and it will warn you the next time you approach one.

The recording of sound may be turned off, which is a good idea if you commonly carry passengers who may not realize your conversations are being recorded. You can also customize the timestamp to include just the information you want it to include.

Here is why video resolution is so important. I had an occasion to test the quality of the video recently when someone passed me illegally on a double-yellow line. It was daytime, but raining and overcast. I imported the video file into a video editing program and was able to save screen shots that clearly showed the offender's license plate number as they went by. On the cheaper mirror dash cam I tried earlier, this would not have been possible.

Video may be set to save in 1, 3, or 5 minute segments, which brings up my only complaint about this unit. When I stop and turn off the switch on my car, the MiVue immediately turns off as well. When I took the micro SD card out of the unit and copied video files to my computer, I discovered that any file written just before the car was turned off would not play. There are files saved in MP4 format, and some of them will play...just not the ones saved on that last bit of my journey. For that reason, I changed the setting to 1-minute, so I'd still have all the video except the last minute or less before I reached my destination. I'm not sure if this is a design issue, or if it's unique to the one I purchased. It does concern me that if I was ever in a wreck severe enough to cause the power supply to the unit to be disconnected, I might not have the footage to prove who was at fault.

Otherwise, I have been happy with the MiVue 420. I purchased it through a Woot.com deal for approximately $69 including shipping.

title: Decent unit, though not without its quirks.
text:
It's not bad for the price, but in regular use it has some irritating little quirks.

Pros:
- Price. You get a lot of features for less than $200.
- The GPS is better than it has any right to be.
- Screen is nice and bright, glare doesn't seem to be an issue.
- Quick and reasonably responsive.
- The ability to add a back up camera is nice.

Cons:
- Wonky user interface. The touch screen interface on mine looks nothing like the one in the picture. Navigating through menus is less than intuitive. The back button doesn't actually go back to the previous menu, it just takes you to the home screen, which makes navigating the settings frustrating.
- There's some strange behavior with the physical buttons. Sometimes pressing a button will give you unexpected results. For instance: if you accidentally press the middle of the volume button, it brings up the GPS.
- You have to hold down the button to lower the screen. So, you have to keep your finger on a button on the bezel while it's moving. Weird.
- It'd be nice if it remembered what you were doing when you turned the car off. Example: on other units, if you're listening to something via Bluetooth, it will pause it when you turn it off and resume when you turn it back on. This unit always defaults back to terrestrial radio.
- That remote is....not great. Lots and lots of buttons that all look and feel exactly the same, so using it in a dark car is nearly impossible.

All in all, not a terrible stereo. Pyle is a value brand, so temper your expectations accordingly.

title: So far so good, better than the CREATE
text:
Coming from the Logitech CREATE – which crapped out 100% in only 11 months daily use – there are certainly some pros & cons between the two. I love that this one makes my iPad Pro feel more like a laptop, the screen is sturdy & adjustable, I can control additional devices with a super fastNeasy tap of a button, you can remove the screen for easier reading/drawing, & the device as a whole feels more solid – my iPad actually fell out of the CREATE on more than one occasion from it’s flimsier design.

What I don’t like is that it has to be charged, the user manual is lacking sufficient details or even a url to get a more in depth guide to the unit, & the lower region of the screen is a little more difficult to tap because of the screen mount. I also found pairing to be more difficult than other bluetooth devices I’ve used in the past. When I could even get the device to show as available to connect, there were many errors trying to connect, or it would connect and say connected but not work; and again, the instructions were not the best on how to address these issues. It is working fine as I type this now though, so we’ll give it a pass on that for now.

I really feel that many do not understand the true power of the iPad Pro, and when critics mock it for being too large they are missing the LARGER, haha, point! With my iPad Pro I can work nearly anywhere; and on top of that, not only am I able to work on a mobile device that is encased in iOS so I can use those apps, but with a data connection and remote desktop, I am able to use my iPad as well as any laptop. Because I do not rely on usb, card readers, or working on a subway, my experience is no different, if not better, than with a true laptop. I have my macOS computer, my home & work Win10 systems, unix, servers, you name it. The IT industry has changed, and that is where I feel the iPad Pro is above the Surface. It is a good system, but it will never be able to run iOS; and these days, if you’re using usb drives to store your data you’re doing it wrong.

title: Read the reviews before purchasing
text:
I tried the AmScope NDPL-1(2x) adapter with two microscopes: an AmScope SE30SR-P-LED dissecting microscope (10 - 30 x) and an AmScope B120B compound microscope (40x-400x) with a Nikon D3000 dSLR camera. Setting up was straightforward but the results disappointing. Previously, I used the afocal approach (holding or supporting the camera with its own lens next to the eyepiece). Using a simple point-and-shoot camera through the eyepiece produced better results than the NDPL-1(2x) adapter with the Nikon dSLR. The image of a standard graticule using the adapter was not as sharp, particularly away from the center of the field (see image). I used a remote release to avoid vibrations and tried shutter speeds from 1/8 to 1/200 with ISO 100 to 1600 settings but it made little difference. Other reviewers have also commented on this problem, included those using the same adapter with a Canon mount. The problem seems in part due to the fact that the eyepieces of microscopes are often designed to compensate for aberrations in the objective lenses, and therefore a single NDPL-1(2x) cannot be optimal for all microscopes.
On the positive side, the adapter was a good fit to both microscopes and dSLR camera and the combined systems were not top heavy. Also 5 stars to Amazon/Amscope for a quick refund.

title: A Lot of Machine for the Money
text: Unlike some of the reviewers on this page my initial impressions of this cd player are all positive. To be on the safe side I did purchase the extended warrantee but hopefully it won't be necessary. My unit might well be a newer model than those of the negative reviews, having a 'B' designation added to the model #. Not only does this unit perform beautifully, with great clear tone, dynamic range, stereo separation, etc., but also it's carousel mechanism is very smooth and quiet. On top of all this, the Onkyo seems to cure a problem I've had since moving to FL from NYC. In NY, I could play any of my cd's, on any of my machines, anywhere. Even those self-burned cd's that have been put through an undue number of drafts on cdrw's. However, down here I've experienced some form of EM interference that prevent the proper tracking of too many of my discs. I could surmise that part of the problem may be that now the cd player is in close proximity to the cable/video systems. Lead foil around the bx wire and junction has been ineffective. Besides, the problem is in the car too. But the good news is that I've been able to play discs on this new Onkyo that I haven't been able to listen to for years. The shielding must be fantastic! So I'm very happy with this purchase. If I could change anything it would be my wish for display controls on the remote. Also, I could do without that big blob of green LED staring me in the face. Little things. I certainly would recommend this unit, but I'd keep my fingers crossed you don't get a lemon.

The enclosure itself was well packaged, came with all the screws and a small screw driver along with the USB type A to B cable which is about 1ft long. Install was easy and once assembled seems very sturdy and well made.

It does have a small indicator light on the end with the USB port, which is white in color and blinks on activity.

I am very happy with it as I was able to take a SSD I had no other use for and turn it into a very fast, reasonably small external drive that wouldnt be a burden to carry around with the laptop while traveling.

I primarily use it for KVM VM images/files that I do not use frequently. It worked perfectly for this letting me install Windows 10 within a VM in about 5 mins.

title: This Was My Endgame.
text:
So these are my first impressions on this keyboard, and I just have to say: I'm totally over-the-moon about this one. I've spent so much money on various keyboards - testing case material, switch types, etc. Never had I actually lifted a keyboard out of its packaging and immediately felt like it would be perfect. But this NiZ Plum - yeah. To me, it's perfect.

While I'm impartial to heavier switches (my daily driver used to be with MX Blacks and I thoroughly enjoyed the stronger "rebound"), I find lighter switches to better in the long term. Also, I'm not very heavy handed, although I bottom out keys as a habit. 35g seems pretty intimidating when the general consensus for light linear switches belong to Cherry MX Reds at 45g, but honestly? If you're the sort of person who has a lighter touch and feel that you type faster on lighter keyswitches, these electro-capacitive ones will feel awesome. I can't really articulate the difference between Cherry MX Reds and these plum electro-capacitive switches despite having them right next to each other - the NiZ domes definitely feel lighter but they're also more...responsive. I guess similar to how a Topre slightly "snaps" to the bottom after initially pressing it down, whereas Cherry MX linear switches feel consistent from top to bottom.

This keyboard looks like it has the standard tenkeyless layout, but there's plenty of media functions to be had. Volume controls, windows lock, and even swapping left Ctrl/caps lock can all be done on the function layer. Unfortunately, the manual is completely in Chinese, although a google search on the keyboard turns up some clues. It would still be much better if it just came with an English manual though.

The aesthetics are nice. I'm sure that an option for black would be a good alternative for people who would prefer that over white/grey. I personally love the keycaps (Cherry profile by the way!) and the round, plastic look of the keyboard. It's charming in a simplistic and elegant way that complements my HHKB Pro2 nicely. Also comes with keycaps for Mac to swap out the Windows key with, as well as some 10g springs if you prefer having some more resistance on keys like the spacebar or Esc.

Overall, I really really really hope this keyboard lasts. It's awesome and I love it.

title: Great headphones for active users.
text:
I am a headphone junkie so I have tested or purchased every one of LG's Tone series headphones. These are the ones I use the most. I walk my dogs every day and these allow me to listen to podcasts or audiobooks without having anything in my ear. This is a fantastic feature but I don't often use it for music. The external speakers, while good, are not going to blow you away with their sound- they're just too small. Perfect for podcasts and audiobooks (like I said) and anything else where you're trying to listen to information rather than music. Once you switch to the earbuds (by putting them in your ears and switching a button on the neck strap) the sound is about as good as any of the tone series.

Like all the LG Tone headsets, this one has the microphones on the neckband which is fine if they are unobstructed with no wind blowing on them but problematic for telephone voice quality in other conditions. Thus, I only rarely use them for telephone conversations- especially if I am running or outside in the wind. If you want to use it for phone calls, make sure you don’t have anything obstructing the microphones (one is on the top left of the neckband toward the front and the other is below it on the side- both must be unobstructed) like a shirt or hoodie collar (or neck fat) and don’t even think about it if it’s windy out.

In my opinion, LG should come up with completely different names for their various products. The Tone Infinum for example, has had 2 completely different iterations yet you can still buy both at various online retailers and they are very different in looks and sound yet LG did not differentiate the name in any way. That is important if you are considering this model because there is an LG Tone Active and an LG Tone Active+ (this model). The differences are significant. For example, the original Tone Active has a higher waterproof rating IPX5 as opposed to the + model which has IPX4 (probably due to the external speakers). The talk time and time listening to music on the + is better by 1-3 hours over the original Active. Most importantly, the original Active does not have external speakers. There are other differences and you can see them on the LG site. (The comparison there is not as good as looking at the product pages for each version)

I am dubious of the retractable earbuds. The Infinum and Platinum have a button on the side that retracts the cords into the neckband while these on the Active + (and regular Active) act like retractable shades or the cord on a blow dryer at a hotel. You pull it out a little more first and then they roll in to the neckband. I have not broken mine but if you pull too hard too often, I see it happening. It happened to my first Tone Infinum headset but they replaced them at the Verizon store.

One recommendation- read the manual. I tend not to and did not realize I was missing out on features as a result. It’s also good to learn the dual functions of some the buttons since you can’t see them when the device is around your neck.

I will also make a recommendation for any of the Tone headsets: They all come with the rubber or silicone style ear gels (like most headsets). I don’t like these for two reasons: They seal your ear (which I find uncomfortable) and thus there is pressure with every impact motion (foot hitting the ground- running, walking, etc.) which translates to a thudding sound in your head. I used to use Bose earbuds for this very reason as they don’t seal the ear. This can be resolved with Comply foam ear tips. They aren’t super cheap but they are made of a slightly moldable foam that keeps the sound of the street out but allows air to move in and out. You don’t need them but it will make the experience of using these headsets (and almost any ear sealing headset) MUCH better. I promise neither I, nor anyone I know works for them. They just make a huge difference.

As a result of this feature, regularly I have to switch the watch face back to my chosen screen and I need all sorts of back up alarms because my sleep pattern dismisses the alarm. There is an auto-lock feature for the watch, which I may try soon to avoid these minor annoyances. I have been hesitating to use this feature because I am not sure how it will feel to unlock the watch any time I need a feature. (Unlocking is just pressing and holding the side button for a brief moment.) I will update this review when I have tried this feature.

Other than that, this is a -wonderful- device. I love that I can easily switch the watch band to any style that I want. I love the round face which makes it look more like a traditional watch. It looks professional with my work wardrobe and doesn't scream fitness tracker to everyone who sees it. My wife has the Fenix 5S, but she does mud runs and cross fit. Both of us have decided we have the right device for our purposes.

It works great as a GPS tracker for my bicycling, which is my preferred mode of travel. It does NOT pick up the vibrations from my motorcycle as exercise (which was an issue with another brand of tracker I owned.)

I love that it is independent of my cell phone. It syncs well with my iPhone, with no issues there that I have seen.

I have only had one instance of battery confusion, which was last night when my watch was suddenly off and I couldn't turn it on. I think it was updating the system though, cause once I plugged it in it still had more than 50% battery life. Speaking of battery, it charges quickly, and while I know I could wear it in the shower, it has a full charge by the time I am done with my 10 minute average shower.

Edit May 10, 2018: Locking the touchscreen keeps it from being annoying. The silent alarms do not wake me up. Not sure if it is a software problem or a hardware problem. Only snoozes once when it does randomly work even though it gives the option to continue snoozing. Also, Garmin Pay only works for Visa or MasterCard, and I use discover. :/

June 5, 2018: Added photo of a map. The black line represents a segment of my bike ride yesterday that the watch deleted when my wet rash guard swiped the screen. 😭 locking the screen to make the alarms work better, but I think I now need to use it when I am actively working out too. I've probably used dozens of different keyboards over 30 years, but the K750 is the most comfortable, productive, responsive and practical keyboard I've ever used. I know keyboard preference varies greatly from user to user, but everyone I've recommended this keyboard to loves it. Besides usability, not having to change the battery EVER is icing on the cake. It just feels right when you type on it from the key height to the tactile feedback to key spacing to the key layout. It fits nicely in a laptop bag and has an easily accessible on/off switch so you can clean it without random keystrokes being sent to your computer.

Are there additional features I wish it had? Yes!

title: *UPDATED* Excellent product! Very happy with this little guy
text:
*UPDATED late November 2022* - I originally purchased this in January 2018, and nearly 5 years later (five!!) this is still going strong. This remains my single favorite purchase on Amazon and maybe my favorite purchase ever, particularly when factoring in the price and OUTSTANDING value. For its size, price, build quality, sound, and (I can now say) sheer longevity, this is a product that has lived up to its cost many times over. I've brought it on everything from ski-trips to my friends Bachelor party, and daily I use it as a small (but mighty) speaker to plug into my computer monitor for whenever I'm not using my headphones. I can't say enough good things about this product. Pick one up if you haven't already. These are still an absolute steal--especially these days when inflation has made the price of just about everything else go sky-high. You won't regret the purchase, that much I can promise!

Original Review:
For what you pay and how compact this awesome little speaker is, the sound and value are amazing.

I bought this to replace my portable iHome speakers that finally bit the dust. It's worth noting that those died in part because of on/off switches that would often accidentally slip on in luggage, ruining the battery; they also had rather cumbersome wires.

These address those issues and more, including adding a number of great little touches:
-Rubberized buttons that are water resistant
-The speaker automatically shuts off if no sound is coming through them to preserve battery--unless it's already plugged in; great design feature!
-Great battery life, partly because of the above point, and partly because it's just a high quality, high capacity battery
-Did I mention that the sound is amazing for its size and price?! Brought this to my friend's bachelor party in Mexico and it was plenty loud for the big house we rented out. No, the speaker is not a Bose 7.1 Dolby Surround home theater set up, but it shouldn't be. It's only about 5 inches wide and costs the same as a trip to the convenience store.
-Bluetooth reduces the need for cords, but also works with a standard headphone jack (and comes with the cord!), which you can use to plug into a computer, for example

Altogether it's one of the best purchases I've made in a long time.
