title: A Software Developer's Review
text:
Edit: 10/22/2016
I now use the trackpad on the right, but on the left is a cheap no brand mouse. I love the trackpad but I have hand pain when I use it too much. So when I start getting hand pain, I switch to the mouse (it took me a few days to get used to using the mouse with my left hand). And I still have easy access to my beloved gestures. It's been working out wonderfully in reducing my hand pain. If anyone is in a similar situation as me, then I highly recommend this setup.

Original review below
------------------------------------
I didn't understand why anyone would use a trackpad if they didn't have to. Then I purchased my first Macbook Pro back in 2008. Since then I've become so accustomed to the multi-touch trackpad that I feel handicapped without it. My setup for years has been an external monitor connected to my Macbook Pro, using its trackpad along with a mouse. I recently purchased another large monitor and my desk no longer has space for the laptop, so I've been using it in clamshell mode and with the mouse only. After a couple days, I was getting frustrated at not having access to all the gestures.

At first, I thought to myself, "Hey, why don't I get the Magic Mouse instead so that I can have the best of both worlds!" Then I went to the Apple Store and tried the gestures on the mouse. It just didn't feel the same or as comfortable -- actually a bit awkward. The price has increased significantly so it gave me pause, but after using it for the past 3 days, I am already very attached to it.

Bluetooth:
You can use it via Bluetooth or connected to the lightning cable. If using it over Bluetooth, I would suggest that you check to see that your computer is compatible with the version of Bluetooth required (search the web for "Magic Trackpad 2 Bluetooth Version"). I am on a mid 2012 15" Macbook Pro and it's compatible. No problems with pairing.

Battery:
I was actually considering picking up the previous generation of the Magic Trackpad because it is significantly cheaper. However, research taught me that it was a battery hog. I charged it up to 100% a few days ago. I am in front of my computer ALL day, and I'm still at 82% as of this moment. Pretty good!

Force touch:
This thing is great! No matter where I press, it clicks with the same pressure! I'm normally a tapper, but since purchasing the Magic Trackpad 2, I've been clicking a lot more.

It's been great to use while coding. The bigger size really works out well for me due to the extra real estate on my external monitors. Also, if you are a BetterTouchTool user, it works but not without some issues. If you use it on your laptop, you have to either have the lid open or disable the laptop's trackpad (in accessibility) if you're using it clamshell mode, else the tool won't work. Also had some quirks -- like gestures would actually register but sometimes it would also move the mouse pointer. Just a FYI.

title: Excellence in design!
text:
I'd like to state up front that I did, in fact, receive this item for review purposes from Sabrent. I was asked that I provide critical feedback of the item and pass this information on to potential buyers. I am not in any way required nor rewarded for providing a positive or even a 5-star review. I was asked to provide my honest feedback, and this review is just that.

That being said, I honestly believe this is a 5-star item. I am very impressed with its quality and design, the same way I am with all Sabrent USB hubs. I had never thought of such a design that included an RJ45 adapter right in a hub, but this is brilliance in design.

The reason being, most people want to use their USB hubs on devices with limited USB ports. These are often ultrabooks. Many of the ultrabooks on the market lack both USB ports and often even dedicated wired networking ports (RJ45). It is highly desirable in this case to have a USB hub that provides more USB ports as well as an RJ45 wired network connector!

Sabrent takes this a step further and ensures that the RJ45 in the hub is GIGABIT, and this has been tested for my review - The unit is in fact capable (and recognizable) as G/bit speeds. Highly impressive for such an affordable unit.

Please take note when buying this, that any USB to RJ45 connector (like the one included in this hub) is an EXTERNAL NETWORK INTERFACE CARD. That is, it does not work with the card in your laptop or desktop - it, in essence, adds a network card to your system. A new network adapter interface will actually be added to your computer when using this device and you will see its driver installation in the device manager. This is only important to note that when connecting to networks on this item, they will appear 'new', and your system will have a different MAC address due to the address of the card. Just something to be aware of for the very few people that this will matter to.

Overall a great product. Fast USB 3.0 speeds, reliable, excellent build quality, with the addition of being able to plug a network cord in your system that does not have an existing port.

title: Good sound quality, terrible cable design. Skip these and wait for more traditional ones, or look elsewhere.
text:
I got bored of Apple's earbuds one day so I did a little research and decided to order these Sennheiser CX 300 II earbuds from Amazon for about $35.

I have a very keen sense of sound quality, and these put out a pretty good sound for their size and price. The bass is underwhelming, as should be expected from earbuds in this range, but highs and mids are crystal-clear and satisfactory. These earphones are great for classical and acoustic audio, but don't quite deliver when it comes to rap/hip-hop/EDM/anything bass-heavy.

But my biggest complaint is the cabling that comes with the earbuds. The right earbud has about 1.5x longer wiring than the left one. Now, I'm sure this looked great on paper - after all, with this system, the junction of the two earbuds' wires is no longer in the center of your chest, and is off to the left, which is supposed to stop the wires from getting in the way of athletics or other activities.

Does this work? Nope. The genius behind commonplace earbud wiring is that the load is evenly distributed between each earbud, so that if something (say, gravity, a falling phone, or a stray hand) accidentally tugs downward on the wiring, it tugs on both ears. This means that the pair of earbuds is less likely to fall out if tugged. This is NOT the case with these Sennheisers - even a TINY tug on the cable will cause the left earbud to pop out instantly, with the right-hand one following close behind. The entire force behind any wire-tug is sent to the left earbud because the right earbud's wiring is slack (it's too long).

I'd skip these earbuds. They have good sound quality, and would work great if all you plan to do is sit still while you listen to your tunes, but the moment you start to move around, they'll fall out. I've tried using all three of the included earbud attachments and none of them fit my ear well enough to keep the earbuds secured for more than a song or two while I'm moving around.

title: No significant difference in image quality vs. telephoto "L" glass for APS-C camera bodies
text:
Pixel peepers may disagree, but I would argue that there is no significant difference between the image quality output of this sub-300 dollar lens and a "professional grade" lens priced at or north of 1000 dollars when mounted on an APS-C body with apertures set equivalent.

I think people who own APS-C bodies (Canon Rebels, 70D, 7D, etc) often assume a common fallacy when they begin to covet expensive lenses such as the Canon 70-200 f2.8L IS II: that "professional" glass will consistently yield significantly sharper images. I know I did until I did some testing and found that for the majority of use cases this is simply not true. Most of your pictures will be viewed by others at a resolution and size where the human eye simply cannot objectively discern a difference in sharpness between pictures taken with this lens vs. a professional lens (stopped down to the same aperture and mounted on the same camera body).

So please APS-C camera body owners, do not go down the gear acquisition rabbit hole of buying expensive lenses without truly assessing where the value resides. Understand that what this lens does not provide is the ability to shoot at low apertures. That is the primary gain of mounting a more expensive EF professional lens on your crop body. Low apertures are beneficial for low light situations and subject isolation (fyi. even f5.6 produces really good shallow depth of field at 200+ mm that would satisfy most non-commercial applications which the Canon 55-250mm IS STM can do). But if low light photography and fancy super blurry backgrounds is really your thing, then instead spend those big bucks towards a full frame camera. Your APS-C body with that expensive lens is the wrong combination for that application.

Of course others will praise the build quality/ruggedness and weather sealing as other values of a more expensive, professional lens.... whatever... I feel a lot less nervous taking this cheap lens on rugged adventures, knowing at most I'm out a few hundred bucks vs. thousands in the unlikely event that I damage my gear.

So if you have a legitimate need to shoot 70-200mm at f2.8 or even at f4 then by all means pay the extra thousand bucks for a fancier lens than this one. Please understand that it's not a significant image quality gain, but instead it is actually a gain in versatility. Otherwise know that the Canon 55-250 IS STM lens will give you brilliant, sharp images within its very reasonable aperture limitations at a price that is affordable.

The tablet itself is VERY light. I am slightly worried that I see scratches when I use it, but then they wipe off. I don't know if that's the nib wearing down on it or not. Or if eventually, the scratches will stop wiping off? I don't know...Thought I'd just mention it :)

title: Just what I'd hoped for!
text:
In short, if you're looking for a 4k 27" monitor, this is a great choice.

I don't normally order high-priced items that have absolutely no reviews anywhere on the internet, but I had seen excellent reviews for the (now-discontinued) Lenovo ThinkVision X1 and there was speculation on various sites that this model was the same display without the built-in webcam and speakers. I can't say for certain if this is the same panel as the X1, but it is definitely a nice, color-accurate, near-retina display.

The "u" in the model number indicates that this display has a USB-C port that works with 2016 and later MacBook Pros. I tested this configuration and the monitor can charge the MacBook and receive a 4k 60Hz video signal on the same cable.

The monitor also works great with 2014/2015 MacBook Pros. In order to get 4k at 60Hz you will need to use a Mini-DisplayPort to DisplayPort cable which is not included in the box. The HDMI connection on the older MacBooks will work, but I sometimes had issues with scaling and the HDMI port on the Mac won't support going above 30 Hz at 4k. Just buy a cable.

On Windows 10, I spent days working to figure out why blacks were terribly washed out until I figured out that Windows and/or the NVIDIA display driver assume that any HDMI connection should be run at the video 16-235 color range instead of 0-255. Forcing "Output dynamic range" = "Full" in the NVIDIA Control Panel under Display->Change Resolution->"Apply the following settings" and putting the monitor in the factory-calibrated sRGB 6500k mode fixes the issue and makes a fantastic setup! I do color-sensitive work and this display is really well-suited for photo editing.

The monitor came with a Color Calibration Factory Report that showed my particular display had a delta E of less than 1 in all but one test (Red3) for both sRGB and Adobe RGB color space modes (and for that one test the delta E was less than 2). When set up properly as described above, the monitor really looks spot-on.

Some more notes:
* The monitor's native resolution is 3840x2160, 166 PPI.
* The anti-glare is effective and there is no disturbing sparkling effect.
* Both HDMI ports are HDMI 2.0 spec.
* The USB-C port also drives the built-in 3-port USB-3 hub. The fourth USB port is for charging only.
* The BT.709 and DCI-P3 color modes do not appear to be calibrated or even to spec.
* Custom color modes only allow independent adjustment of the R, G, and B white point. There is no manual color adjustment for blacks.
* On Mac, the default scaling made text/menus appear one scaling size larger than on a standard 27" Apple Thunderbolt Display. In the Display System Preferences I had to manually adjust it one more notch towards "More Space" to match Apple's display.
* The monitor has a pass-through audio connector that works with the DisplayPort or HDMI connections. On a Mac laptop, the device gets used by default even if you don't have any speakers plugged in, so it mutes your laptop. In the System Preferences Sound panel on the Output tab I had to manually switch the output device back to the Internal Speakers in order to hear audio with the display attached to the Mac.
* Oh, yeah... it's a great gaming monitor too. Just make sure you have a powerful GPU. Note that at this dot pitch you can turn off FSAA and just let your eye do the anti-aliasing, so you get a little speed back from that.

title: Not awful.
text:
I gave these a three because they're fine as far as working together wirelessly, sound is what you'd expect from a tiny speaker like are in these (e.g. not awful, you know), but there's a few annoyances that prevent me from recommending them to anyone.

Pros
* Cost is very reasonable for this type of device.
* Build quality is very good.
* Form factor is simple, interesting and functional.
* Pairing, starting and stopping, and controlling volume are painless.
* Shutting down one, shuts down both - a nice touch.

Cons
* Not comfortable. The larger round plastic area presumably housing the driver is hard plastic, and presses uncomfortably against my ears. I have medium sized ears. My wife cannot fit them in her ears. If I wear them for more than an hour my ears are sore.
* LED lights. For me, and call me crazy, but would not beeps or voice messages be much more intuitive and useful for telling me status and whatnot, rather than throbbing lights I cant see - SINCE THEY ARE OUT OF MY SIGHT IN MY EARS! But no, they /really/ like their LED lights, and they allow it to be different colors for different notifications. But, here's where it gets **extremely** annoying: Continuously while being used they are both throbbing a quite bright white light that, if you happen to wear glasses, reflects off the inside edge and will not turn off! It's enough to want to just /stomp on them/ truthfully. I had to cover mine with electrical tape or I was going to go insane. When it's dark it's even worse, reflecting off the phone, and lighting up your environment - they are ridiculously big and bright!
* Bluetooth mostly sucks, and should really go away in my opinion anyway. The switch away from music to answer a call shuts down the right earbud (you have to switch, they can't work together). That's not just these though, that's pretty much all BT headphones IIRC.

TL;DR
Meh, they work, sound is reasonable, I'm not sending them back, but you'll need electrical tape to cover the battery-sucking-completely-pointless-LEDs, and have bigger ears than me to really enjoy using them.

title: US GPS works in Europe exactly as hoped
text:
We used the City Navigator Europe SD map in a US-purchased Garmin Nuvi 2555 LMT GPS unit (purchased in 2013).

The SD care ended up being super simple to install -- just pop the micro SD card into the appropriate slot on your GPS. There were no instructions, but it was easy. A youtube video showed me how to do.

The product comes with the maps on a micro SD card and full size SD card adapter into which the micro SD card can be put (if needed).

The City Navigator NT Europe card (purchased in 2017) seemed to include maps and points of interest for "All of Europe" (see vendor's description of exactly where). We had no map issues in France, Germany, Austria, or Italy.

Our rental cars ended up having installed GPS with much bigger screens. However, familiarity with how to make my own GPS function made me happy to have this. (and i didn't reserve cars with GPS, we just ended up with it).

The point of interest searching seemed a little slower than in the US. While it might have not have even been real, the slightly longer lag may be because it was installed in the microSD card memory, rather than internal system memory.

I think the description makes it clear, but this is a one time map/POI database purchase -- there are no Europe map upgrades included, even if you have "lifetime maps" feature on your GPS (that is only for native maps). So if you plan on using this over 10 years or more, the maps might get a little out of date...

(As a side note, traffic worked in Germany and Austria, but did not seem to work in France -- traffic features have NOTHING TO DO THIS THIS PRODUCT which is a MAP and POI database).

CONS:

* sSATA CPM speed is 35MB/sec (vs 46MB/sec on others).

Basically, if you just need to plug up two drives, this is fine.
If you need to use the port multiplier support, it's better to go with:
* Any SIL3124/3132 based card, even though they are not super fast
* ASM1061 based card, if you can find a decent one
* 88SE9235 or 88SE9230 or 88SE9220 based card (newer chip).

I have gone through probably 10-15 different SATA cards, and am still trying to find something that will push over 122MB/sec. title: The ultimate botanical, butterfly and backpacking binoculars!
text:
We learned about these from Betty Gatewood during a class she gave at the 2018 Shenandoah Wildflower Weekend. Betty does exquisite flower illustrations ranging from simple journaling to rigorous botanical illustration. She needs to see what she is drawing VERY clearly. She is used to critical viewing, and can tell when a tool is above average.

There are three big advantages to these: 1) crisp, clear, undistorted image and colors; 2) small, light, easily packed size; 3) ability to focus just about at the end of ones fingertips!

Without #1 the other two really don't matter. But the image IS right up there. Pentax used a "porro" prism setup instead of the more popular "roof" prism design. This means the glass has more joints that moisture can seep into. Pretty sure Pentax thought of that... it feels VERY well sealed! But this also means that the light has a less tortured path through the glass, which help the clarity and color correctness. This also means that the far end of the glass (the "objective" end) can have lenses closer together, which allows a closer focus without the feeling of going cross-eyed.

How important is the close focus? A butterfly won't settle at all if you get very close. But if you are three or four feet away a settled butterfly will stay put until the reason it landed goes away. An eight times magnification of a butterfly at four feet is a sight to behold! You can see details of wing patterns, antenae, legs, etc. that you would normally have to use a magnifying glass for on one that was dead.

Folks who love looking at flowers in national parks and gardens know there is a "do not pick" policy. With the close focus you can see such flowers BETTER than if you held them in your hand... without having to bend over!

And all this comes in a small light package. No, ultralight backpackers need not apply. This isn't THAT light. But it DOES pack easily in the brain or outer pocket of a pack, and weighs less than a lot of other FAR less capable glasses.

This has to be the the ultimate botanical, butterfly, and backpacking binocular!

title: So much money...and so much awesome!
text:
I admit that I don't know enough about the technical side of monitors to provide one of those awesome, thorough, detailed reviews, but I can tell you this: as much as I wanted to hate this monitor so I could return it and save some money with a lesser unit, I absolutely love it. From the moment I plugged it in I was blown away. The colors right out of the box were great for me, and there is not a single dead or stuck pixel. Moreover, the IPS glow and back-light-bleed is practically non-existent. Having purchased my share of monitors over the years, and having read a number of horror stories about this model in particular, I was thrilled and pleasantly surprised with this one.

All I had around the house was an old 1080p Acer (the Olympic edition, for those who know it) and a 1200p ASUS ProArt. Both were great monitors for what they were, and the ProArt was a solid IPS. I recently built my first Windows PC in nearly 15 years and needed something for gaming and fun. I tried the Dell S2716DGR (I think that's what it is) which is fairly highly reviewed and regarded, and while I could see why, it *did* have an annoying bright green pixel right in the middle of the screen. More than that, I could not get it to look anywhere near as good as my old ProArt. It was official: I was an IPS guy. This was frustrating because I picked up that Dell for $479 at BestBuy and a week later it shot back up to over $600. :) I really wanted to save the money. But I decided to *try* the ASUS and while I wish I didn't have to spend an extra few hundred dollars, the quality of my particular unit is undeniable and I'm very happy.

All the bells and whistles work as intended. The 1440P and 144+hz are noticeable to me and awesome. The bezel is nice and thin, and while the stand is not too "gamery," I have it mounted on an arm on my desk and it just looks great. title: I didn't return it because of a few redeeming qualities
text:
Reasons I kept it:
-The large white display numbers are easy to see and easy on the eyes.
- The alarm doesn't wake you up with a loud, startling noise. Instead it coaxes you up with an awkward frequency at a quieter tone.
- If the alarm is snoozing, the alarm icon blinks. I like that I can tell if I hit the buttons correctly in my grogginess.
- Someday I may use the USB to plug in my iPhone...

Reasons I thought about returning it:
-The alarms do not function independently. I was hoping to create a 3 or 4 minute alarm cycle by having one go off and then the other, but once alarm 2 goes off, alarm 1 cancels. (I just kept my old alarm and now have to use both.)
- Alarm is not easy to turn on and off. You have to hold the alarm 1 button down, then cycle through several function before OFF finally comes around.
- Alarm can be set for a single week day, all week days, weekends, or all days. This is not good if you have an off schedule. Or if you have a Monday off for a holiday, because then you have to turn the entire alarm off, and like I said above, its sort of annoying to try to turn it off.
- Alarm is not easy to set. I was skeptical to believe others who were saying this. But after trying it out, I have to say I agree. I can figure out how to change things on the system, but I have to re-learn it each time. First you have to hold down the button for the alarm you want to set until it blinks, then if you want to change the hour, push a right arrow button going up or down, for the minutes choose left or right. Then to set the days, push the middle button and cycle through until you get the correct ones highlighted. To change the volume you have push the left button while it's blinking to cycle through until the Volume is blinking and then push the right buttons to change it. The blinking only lasts for a few seconds, so if you think for too long you have to start over.
- The snooze button is not easy enough to push. You have to push it exactly in the middle. I prefer ones that I can just slap down with my entire hand and it will shut off.

title: No timers? Really? I can get weather but no timers?
text:
Cool idea. Too bad that's where the coolness ends.

Here's a question: where would you likely store this device? The kitchen, right? It even has a magnet that sticks securely to my fridge. So, of course, the Dash Wand supports reminders, alarms, and timers, right? WRONG! Are you kidding me? This device would be perfect for those functions but nooooooo. Amazing.

Scanning? Not so much. If it works, which is rare, it ends up in your Amazon.com shopping cart. But wait, there's more! The item isn't there--you still have to manually select what you want. And that's IF the scanning works. Most time it doesn't.

Say it? Hold the phone. If you say "hand soap", just like that, it's supposed to add hand soap to your Alexa shopping list. HA! No. I don't know where those words go, but they sure don't go anywhere useful. You have to say, "Add hand soap to my shopping list." But you can do that from any Echo or Tap, so nothing special there.

"Buy hand soap" will start you on a path of unrelenting questions about which hand soap you want to buy. I did it with toilet paper because I happen to need toilet paper. The Dash Wand offered me Angel Soft, and I said "no". Then it offered me "Scott Tissue" and I said "no". Then it told me something like, "Sorry, that's all the offers I have for you!" Huh? Amazon has only two types of toilet paper I can buy on the Dash Wand? Seriously?

Did I mention the think sucks as a scanner? I did? Well, it bears repeating. I scanned a can of brand name beans and got a scope mount for some rifle. When I saw that in my cart, I thought someone had hacked my account. I guess you could say the Dash Wand hacked my account, and put something in my cart I don't want and can't use.

When I think about all the things this device could be, I get excited. When I use it and see what it is, I'm horribly disappointed.

At least it was free with the promotion. If it wasn't, it surely would be going back.

title: The Best Earbuds, and a Great value.
text:
These really are excellent earbuds (or "In Ear Monitors" ). I read up on them on a review site called "Wirecutters" and these were in the Under $100 category. I listen to a lot of music, and I have many headphones. I'm not a fanatic aobut headphones but that is just the way it works out in my house because I like to keep the peace and normal speakers just don't work out.
I normally listen with over-the -ear headphones.
I like the idea of earbuds, but until now i avoided them for because they don't sound very good for the money you pay, or they just dont fit well. So, as a comparison, I have had Sennheiser CX 3.0; Etymotic ER-4S; an old pair of Shures where the plastic tips degenerated into a gooey mess so I don't remember the model number; Bose (where the cord failed in 6 mos so I don't remember that model number);and many iterations of the buds that come with Apple devices.
Hands down, these are the BEST overall earbuds I have ever had.
First, they fit perfectly and do not take more than a second to press into place.
Second, out of the box they sound great. They sound very clear, with good definition of most instruments and are mildly bass heavy. They sound great for modern jazz and rock. For classical I think the Etymotics are better.
But Etymotics are really are difficult to use. They require a whole ritual taking about 60 seconds to fit into the ear canal. If you have to talk to someone, you have to take them off, not just shut the player, because they shut out outside noise. Then you have to refit them all over again. AND after about 2 hours they begin to hurt my ears because of the very tight fit needed.
The "1More" fit like a dream and I have worn them for much more than 2 hours without distress. They come with an entire tray of different sized eartips so they should fit most people. I never knew I had two different size ear canals, 0.5mm apart, and this kit let me get a perfect fit for each side.
I do not know how well they will hold up. I have had them a week. The Shure and Bose I have had both failed pretty quickly. But so far these have a huge plus in terms of comfort and out of the box sound. Plus they are packaged like they cost way more than 99.

title: You put them on and it sounds like you're in a tin can
text:
Where do I start. You put them on and it sounds like you're in a tin can. But you end up not taking them off, that is the odd thing about these things.

It seems the engineers said, "Limit upper frequencies and make a nice, but gritty center, handle bass as much as necessary. Make sure both sides are equal so the listener gets good stereo image. Make them comfortable."

Done. You put them on, they sound like s***, you leave them on, you say: good Lord somebody is playing some game with me because I like this.

They remind me of a couple times where I went somewhere and someone was blasting some old Yamaha 15" woofers with those odd horn tweeters they had. And they were running it through this bi-amped situation, and those speakers were farting and strutting their stuff, handling the whole thing with aplomb. And you were like Holy Crap I didn't know that could sound so good.

So that's what these things remind me of, they're very musical, as in-- they, you forget they're there and you pay ALOT of attention to the music. Really, really nice. A bit pricey at $130 but then again we wouldn't learn to respect the sound of these if they were too much less. $89 would be okay but only in light of a new and superior successor.

After I bought these, I was originally so disappointed that I bought the Sony headphone studio monitors that ar about the same price, they read "Professional" on the side or whatever.

They have different and less bass, yet far more treble. Once burned in, they are acceptable and work-worthy, no doubt.

You would never use these headphones to do equalization. They simply are not about that, they are not monitors. They bill themselves as neutral, but you cannot mix EQ accurately in these, nor can you in the Sonys. Apple's $35 in-ear phones are the best for that. Great bass and highs, acceptable midrange, very balanced and show deficiencies in mixes that aren't up to snuff. So if you want cheap good phones for mixing, get those. If you want phones to lay back and enjoy the music and forget about the speakers, get these.

title: Best Value in IP Cameras
text:
The best of the Foscam models so far, in my opinion. Great video quality, good night performance (with and without IR illumination), reasonably stable firmware, and good pan/tilt performance.

Setting the camera up on your network will require some effort. Particularly if you want to access the camera when you are away from home, you will need to understand IP addresses, DHCP reservations or static assignments, DDNS, and port forwarding. If you don't know what those things are, enlist help from a knowledgeable friend or family member, or consider Foscam's paid setup support.

I have seven of these in my house, facing out windows. All have been running at least 6 months, 24 hours x 7 days. All still function perfectly, including video, audio, and pan/tilt.

Beware that when located inside a window you cannot use the IR illumination at night. If you do, it will simply reflect off the window directly into the lens. Fortunately, the IR can be disabled. And even more fortunately, this camera has very good low-light performance -- so if you have an outdoor floodlight or street lamp nearby, the view is surprisingly good at night.

Video can be set to 960P, 720P, 640x480, 640x360, 320x240, or 320x180. Frame rates up to 30fps are supported. A "main stream" and "substream" with separate settings allow simultaneous access to streams appropriate for high-bandwidth or low-bandwidth (such as mobile) locations.

I have added a couple photos -- one day, one night -- from the same camera. The illumination in the night photo is from a [[ASIN:B004QXRU6O Lithonia 2-LED Floodlight]], equivalent to two standard 100w incandescent floods. The green vertical line is an aberration from the window it looks through.

The camera supports a variety of advanced features, including video recording/playback to onboard SD card, and emailing or FTP of motion alerts. Again, setting up email or FTP requires some technical expertise so plan to enlist some help if you aren't a computer nerd.

If you have multiple cameras, especially different brands/models, then I highly recommend abandoning the camera's web interface and purchasing the [[ASIN:B008YD80KC BlueIris Professional]] software. (NOTE: As of this writing, Amazon has only version3 -- but version4 is available). It is a fantastic program, and very well supported by the author. BlueIris supports just about every IP camera made, thus integrating multiple brands/models into a single interface. title: Very good sound. No big cons to report.
text:
I previously owned the Sony Xb90ex earbuds with 16mm drivers. They cost $200 less but had the most bass I have ever heard in earbuds. Especially when hooked up to the Fiio E18 headphone amp. Well, when I went looking for an IEM upgrade, I was looking for something that had the same, if not more bass than my Xb90s but with added clarity in the mids and highs. The Xb90s has so much bass with the bass booster on and equalizer set on phone, that you could feel it vibrating in your ears. It was like sitting next to a 12" woofer. So, Sony's hybrid IEMs were the first earbuds that I considered. I looked at the XBA-H3, A2 and A3 before settling for the XBA-A3. And I have to say, they are pretty awesome.

First off, I'll review the comfort:
Now, like many other reviewers will state, not everyone will agree that one pair of headphones is comfy and the other hurts. For me, they are comfortable. Most Bluetooth headsets and devices that hang on my ear have started to hurt over time. These IEMs have surprisingly soft over ear supports and can be molded into almost any shape as long as it isn't a sharp angle bend. I watched 2 movies in a row with these earbuds on and I was conscious of them being on my ears but they never started to hurt or get uncomfortable. I just felt them there, probably cause they are rather heavy for earbuds. Overall, I think Sony did a good job on here.

Convenience factor:
When it comes to portability and such, well, I knew I was buying over ear IEMs when I clicked "purchase" and they ain't going to be as portable as in ear jobs. But they are slightly easier to transport around than full size headphones. It can be slightly difficult to fit these in the tight zipper case you are given but it allows you to carry them around in your pocket without getting the cable all tangled up. When setting em up, it can be a small bit frustrating at first to fit these things over and into your ears. With regular earbuds you can be like, "I want to listen to music right now and... Oh, they are already in my ears. Thanks hands!" Well, with these, you are more like, "Ok, step 1, remove from case. Step 2, start molding ear rests. Step 3....." When you have done it 15 times, you do get a lot faster though. For the convenience factor, it's fine but it will require you to stop what you are doing and focus on adjusting your personal sound system before continuing work.

Durability:
I've owned these earbuds for a few weeks now and haven't had any durability problems with them yet. I know from some other reviews that the cable detachment point can become loose over time if you remove the cable from the earbuds a lot. So I haven't separated them at all since I got em and they haven't jiggled or felt lose at all. I'd recommend not detaching the cables if you don't have to.

Cool factor:
Cool is subjective but what will the average person probably think of these? Well, I went on a trip to Natural Bridge in VA recently and wore my new XBA-A3 IEMs while walking about other humans. I got a lot of stares. I did. It was slightly awkward but they sounded too good to take em off lol. Because they are big and stick out of your ear a lot, people will probably wonder what they are. I don't know exactly what they are thinking but I do know from looking in a mirror that I look a little like Frankenstein from the front. When looking at my head at an angle (only 1 earbud visible) it looks more like some high tech device in your ear and less like Frankenstein. That explains why most of Sony's model shots of people wearing these are at an angle or from the side. Go buy some Beats by Dre if you want better looks. These IEMs are for people who care more about sound than style.

Sound:
One of the biggest aspects, is the quality of the drivers and the sound they can produce. I find these triple driver hybrid earbuds to work very well. I use them with my Xperia z3v as the source and the Fiio E17k as the amp and DAC. The Z3v is very DAC friendly so I didn't have any problems hooking it up to my previous E18 or my current E17k headphone amps via Micro usb. I also used Tidal with the lossless music for my review. When compared to my Xb90s that I mentioned earlier, the bass is much tighter and the mids and highs are much more crisp and clear. When I turn on the bass booster on my Fiio E18 (for comparison to Xb90) there is in fact slightly less bass than the Xb90s. But the bass sounds so much less bloated and I can hear so many more hidden sounds in my music that I wouldn't want to go back. When listening to music with my Xb90s, the piano would sound distorted or irritating to the ears at certain keys. With the A3s, classical music is a joy to listen to. I do have to say though, that you can be tempted to turn up the volume at times. Everything sounds so smooth that you can find yourself turning up the volume higher and higher. One way I found my music was too loud is when I would pause the track, and then play. And boy did that hurt sometimes with the sudden stop in the music and suddenly playing again with the same volume. When it comes to noise isolation, I found that they work very well depending on the volume level you are listening to. I couldn't tell if my lawnmower was running or not when music was playing sometimes. It does a fairly good job at shutting out the world around you. It is interesting not being able to hear yourself talking when you turn the volume up a bit. When it comes to sound leak, they aren't the best at keeping your music to yourself. When sitting in the passenger seat in the car, the driver and people directly behind me could tell when my music was playing or not.
And that was with the white noise produced by the car like the AC and engine. They ain't Bose quiet comfort headphones when it comes to noise isolation or preventing sound leak but they do a pretty good job for earbuds. I haven't had the wind problem with them in my ears though.

In conclusion, these IEMs are great if you want lots of bass (16mm dynamic), while maintaining trebble and mids (twin armatures) and slightly more portability than headphones but with a headphone like sound stage. If looks and the interesting fit don't sound like they would bother you, then these are a very good deal. I would, in fact, recommend these to a friend, and complete strangers who ask me what are in my ears. I hope this review helps! I plan on updating if anything comes up.

title: BEWARE WHEN SETTING UP WITH MULTIPLE DRIVES
text: I'm sure when this product works as designed it is great, but I had a very bad experience with the setup of the NAS.  Following the instructions I backed up data on two drives I wanted to initially install, to then allow me to backup data to those drives and install additional drives.  The two drives I installed into the enclosure were different drives, one 2TB and one 3TB drive.  Unfortunately, there is no warning about this in the install guide, but the NAS automatically tried to assign the drives to a RAID 1 array upon install.  The problem was that they were two different sizes and that seemed to cause all sorts of issues, including the volumes not being accessible.  I did not want to use RAID, and I wish the install would have asked me the question instead of deciding for me.  To make matters worse, upon trying to reformat the drives so I could start over with one drive, and then turn off RAID, one of the drives will no longer work.  I get an I/O error at best, or completely unrecognized at worst even when trying to run Seagate's DOS drive utility.  So now I'm down one drive simply because of bad installation instructions, lack of a warning, the NAS choosing the drive set up, and/or a combination of all of those things.

title: Great picture and extremely bright, the Epson VS345 is pretty darned awesome.
text:
[[VIDEOID:c4f17f1cb916ea645855361f314e6123]] The Epson VS345 3LCD projector has basically exceeded the expectations I had for it. It's rated at 3000 lumens, but it really seems brighter than that and is perfectly suitable for use in standard lighting conditions (although we generally use it in the dark). Color quality is good and the WXGA resolution (1280x800) offers HD (if not full HD) resolutions. There are also plenty of inputs, as you can basically connect just about any video surce to this projector. It offers standard RCA (composite, the yellow, red, white SD video cables you've been connecting for years), along with S-Video, standard VGA (D-Sub) and HDMI, so you can connect just about anything. From old gaming consoles and DVD players to PC's, tablets, you name it, with this you can throw it up on a screen (or in my case, the wall).

The menu and included remote are pretty standard, but also easy to navigate. I've purchased Epson projectors in the past and didn't notice anything out of the ordinary here. If you've ever used a projector before and tweaked the settings before, you'll be up and running in a couple of minutes (I didn't have to crack open the manual). It's all fairly intuitive, once you get the button functions and locations down.

On our first use, my daughter and I connected this to my laptop (Lenovo Twist) via HDMI for some on-the-wall Steam gaming, and the results were more than satisfactory. Brightness and clarity were both good, with minimal tweaking needed (mostly to the keystone to get the screen dimensions right on the wall). The VS345 also has a built-in-speaker, and while the sound quality isn't going to win any awards, it was more than loud enough a medium volume levels, at least for our needs. I've uploaded a video of a bit of that, and while it's really kind of impossible to get an idea of the image quality from a relatively low-resolution video, it will give you an idea of how bright this projector is.

After that we hit it up for some Netflix (via the Windows 10 app in full-screen), and again, everything was very nice and crisp, almost impressively so thanks to the brightness (which at night, will light up a room pretty well; my daughter continually remarked that it was "like a movie theater"). Video quality also has a lot to do with the video source, but you can assume that if your source is up to it, the VS345 is up to the task of displaying it. I purchase projectors for business applications, though generally at a slightly lower price-point. The VS345 is significantly better than lower-end projectors that I've purchased, more than enough to satisfy the meager price difference. This is still an inexpensive projector, but it performs as significantly more.

title: Buyer beware, mine leaked.
text: Do not trust your priceless vacation photos with this case.  We took all the precautions as instructed, by testing the case empty in a bowl of water submerged for 30 minutes and the test was a success.  However, after installing the case to the phone, it leaked.  The claim is that the case is submersible for 60 minutes in about 6 feet of water.  The phone was in my swim suit pocket in a swimming pool in waste deep water for less than a minute and it got completely soaked.  Yes, I made sure the charging port trap door was latched and the earphone bezel was screwed in tight.  When I opened the case the gasket fell out on the ground.  We had taken pictures all morning at various attractions in Niagra Falls and the pictures are gone.  Furthermore this happened half way through our trip and my wife and I had no way of communicating with one another if we were to get separated in an unfamiliar city with our two children.  Now we are out a phone, and pictures that can not be replaced.  I will never trust a so called water proof phone case again.  I am not writing this to be vindictive, but rather hoping to save another person from experiencing a loss like this.  We go to the lake a lot and love to swim, so I was really disappointed in this failure.  I haven't reached out to the company yet, but plan to soon.  I hope I can write a follow up review about a great customer service experience, but we will see.

title: Works almost perfect in Linux, with JACK2 and 10.3 ms latency!!
text:
This is a review of the "StarTech.com 7.1 USB Audio Adapter External Sound Card with SPDIF Digital Audio Sound Cards ICUSBAUDIO7D" card.

I bought this card to do one thing -- take the input from my PS4 from TOSLINK and output it to my speakers and headphones. I figured I could use this to not only replace my laptops horrible onboard audio but also get input from the PS4 to my laptop.

I am running Arch Linux, and using jack2-bus with very low latencies (10.3 ms) with this card from my Lenovo Thinkpad T520. Realtime kernel, with pulseaudio-jack running in the background.

I do get about 1 xrun every 10-15 minutes, but that is most likely due to my laptop having shared IRQs all over the place. No matter what I do I can't get 0 xruns.

Considering I bought this card September 16th, 2016, and it is now July 25th, 2018 as of this updated review, the card still performs without issues. For around a $30 USB card that works out of the box with no configuration this has been some real bang for the buck.

title: Very impressed
text:
Thanks to Amazon's lighting deal, the decision between 730 or 750 was made for me. Why Phaiser would position 2 very excellent headphones together this was is puzzling however hearing is believing when it comes to the 750. Saying that I'm impressed is an understatement as below is a breakdown of what impressed me coming from owning a Jaybird X2 which was okay but had trouble with the size of the thing as it kept popping out till it popped out and was crushed accidentally.

Audio Quality - On par with the X2 with richer bass tones and treble. The earpiece is angled allowed the headphone to fit naturally and comfortable. I found that I have to twist it in a little for that seal...it isolates so well that I have not used the comply tips that comes with it or crank the volume up so high. For me, the sound far exceeds what i would expect from an 8mm speaker.

Battery - On par with the X2 but seems to standby longer as I forgot to unpair my iPhone and it stayed connected all weekend with juice left. As as as playtime, it does not last all day at work however in between meetings I was able to plug it in for about 30 mins and it cranked non stop all day. I also appreciate the micro-USB charge port being on the in-line control/mic. The mic sent over good audio during phone calls and no issues were noted by those I was talking to.

Pairing - As easy as it gets. Hold the power button and find it on your phone to connect to. Multiport pairing is a must for me as I have it paired to my pic for skype calls simultaneously. Music plays until a call comes in and answer button pauses the music and switches me to the pc.

The 750 is a solid 5 stars headphones simply because it sounds amazing, has good battery life, solidly built and comes with more accessories than you'll need including pretty sweet carrying case. You get all that and more for less than $50 bucks.

title: Cable does not conform to DisplayPort spec.  Connects pin 20.  May damage your electronics.
text:
I got power surge warnings from Asus anti surge on my brand new computer and eventually isolated this cable as the source. After doing some research, I learned that many non VESA-certified DisplayPort cables connect pin 20 (the one closest to the angled part of the plug). This pin, when connected, carries power. It is not supposed to be connected. I tested this cable with a multimeter and indeed pin 20 is connected. This can easily damage your electronics. DO NOT USE THIS CABLE.

Also, what the heck, Amazon? I trusted you.

Look for VESA CERTIFIED DisplayPort cables.

title: Near Perfect Companion for the Traveling Photographer (and Most Everyone Else!)
text:
I love to take photos when we travel. However, I've always been graphically limited when it comes to travel photography. I carry a Nikon DSLR, a FujiFilm FinePix S1 and the ageing but still amazing Canon S90 point-and-shoot–sometimes using two or more of the cameras at a time. So capturing the images isn't a problem. What to do with them afterwards has been. They need to be minimally processed at least and backed up.

At first glance, my iPad Air would seem to be a logical photo travel companion as it has 128 GB of memory, can display RAW images and has a terrific screen. However, Apple's lock-it-down policy and the limits of iOS make it next to impossible postprocess images or even get them on or off of the device. I've looked at using various Android tablets as an alternative. However, while Android has much more open system than the iPad, it really hasn't got what I need to handle many large images. I suppose that I could haul my HP Envy notebook along as I travel. It has Lightroom and Photoshop installed, but I really dislike taking a laptop with me. It's size and form factor make it hard to keep the laptop protected in a hotel room or cruise ship stateroom.

Then there is the Microsoft Surface Pro (2017) Tablet. The Surface Pro uses a version of Windows 10 Pro so it can run full desktop versions of Lightroom and Photoshop. It's a pen-based tablet with a great screen, so I can post process images on it. It also has a MicroSD card reader, but, alas, none of my cameras use MicroSD cards. That will mean that I have to use an adapter for SD and CF cards, but there is a USB 3 port on the side of the tablet, so that's hardly an insurmountable issue. I'll simply bring along my USB 3 card reader.

A word of caution here--not about the Surface Pro, but about me. I've never given much attention to the Surface product line as I'm really not a big Microsoft fan. I cut my teeth on the original Apple iPad (Generation 1)--in fact, I owned the first iPad sold at Best Buy in San Francisco. (Yes, I waited in line for hours to get it!) I now use an iPad Air and recently started using various Android version tablets. So the world of tablet computing on a Microsoft product is entirely new to me. Therefore, for better or for worse, I am writing this review as a novice user of Microsoft tablet products.

I am using the middle of the line, the Microsoft Surface Pro with the Intel Core i5 processor, 8GB RAM, and 256GB SSD. There is a version below it that uses an Intel Core M processor with 4 GB RAM, 128GB SSD. Despite the lower cost, I would hesitate recommending this model as, for many needs, it is simply too underpowered. There is also the top of the line model sporting an Intel Core i7 processor with 16GB RAM and a 1TB SSD. Honestly, that is more than most of use are likely to need. Plus, the advantage of the Core i5 model is that, unlike the Core i7, it has no fan. Thus I am sacrificing speed and power for a modicum of weight loss and absolutely quiet operation.

Unlike previous models, the 2017 Microsoft Surface Pro Tablet (this should be the Surface Pro 5, but version numbers have been dropped by Microsoft) comes without a case, without a keyboard and without a pen. These are now extra cost and rather pricey items. Shame on Microsoft for failing to bundle these essentials with the Surface Pro! They want to position the Surface Pro as a laptop replacement, so, at the very least, a keyboard should be included. After all, no one buys a car sold without a steering wheel or a house without a roof.

Microsoft apparently doesn’t get this, so I had to find ways to cope with the omissions. (As for the pen, I am reminded of the famous comment made by the late Steve Jobs. "Who wants a stylus?" Jobs once said. "You have to get 'em, put 'em away, you lose 'em. Yuck! Nobody wants a stylus. So let's not use a stylus." Well, times sure have changed. Even Apple now sells a pen for their iPad Pro.)

Cheapskate that I am, I bought a less expensive pen with the strange Chinese sounding moniker of YOTTAFUN Active Stylus. It is said to be compatible with the new Microsoft Surface Pro. However, it has 1024 pressure levels of sensitivity as opposed to the three times more expensive Microsoft New Surface Pen with its 4,096 pressure point levels. I also went cheap on the keyboard opting to use an existing Satchi Bluetooth keyboard that I already own instead of the fancy Microsoft Surface Pro Signature Type Cover with Alcantara® material. I did buy a ProCase Premium Folio Cover Case as I am very uncomfortable using a tablet (or even a smartphone) without a protective case. Experience counts!

To be honest, besides trying to save some dollars with an already free review product, I wanted to see just how well the Surface Pro would perform with an older style pen and a standard Bluetooth keyboard. It's a worthy test despite the "new wine in old wine skins" metaphor. (A metaphor with some merit in this case, I might add.) Besides, I take some exception to Microsoft's premium slant on these peripherals. Whatever happened to "computing for the masses?” The bottom line is that the keyboard, the pen and even the case all worked flawlessly.

Cortana (Microsoft's version of Siri, Alexa, etc.) talked me through the initial phases of installing and configuring Windows 10 on the Surface Pro. Of course, in typical Microsoft fashion, during installation I was greeted with a "Please wait" message and spinning dots that seemed to be never ending. Actually, they were never ending as the installation had hung. I had to do a forced shutdown and reboot. That took me back to the beginning of the installation process with all my previous configuration settings thrown away. Sigh!

The problem appeared to be that installation was locked up with some issue with my Microsoft account. Once I rebooted, I bypassed the Microsoft account log in and the configuration finished without further delay. The only other glitch that I encountered was a lock up with Google Chrome while I was writing this review. Whether this was a Microsoft issue, a Google issue, or just a passing hiccup is hard to say.

Now it was time to hammer the Surface Pro. No kid gloves here. I simultaneously installed a number of large applications (Photoshop, Lightroom, WordPerfect Office) while listening to a FLAC encoded music played through a Schiit Fulla 2 DAC running from the USB 3 port on the Surface Pro. Got all of that? I did this while running entirely on battery power. After several hours of intense use the case was warm but not hot to the touch, the battery was still 75% full and there was not a stammer or stutter anywhere. In short, the Surface Pro performed every bit as well as a modest Windows desktop would and just as good as most every laptop that I’ve used on Windows 10. Given its size and form factor, that’s saying something!

Finally I watched HD videos on the Surface Pro. They played flawlessly and without any discernible frame loss. The image quality was every bit as good–and perhaps even a notch better than running the same videos viewed on my iPad Air. I couldn’t help but be impressed.

In short, my only gripe is the lack of bundling especially at the premium price that Microsoft has set for the new Surface Pro. Even so, there is no question that the Microsoft Surface Pro (2017) will be my regular traveling companion during my next photo shoot or vacation. The iPad Air is definitely staying home!

title: Not Canon quality but not Canon price, either.
text:
I've been wanting a vertical grip for my MkIV since October. I have a Canon OEM grip on my 7D MkII, but this grip (Pixel Vertax) on my 5D MkIV and another third-party grip (Phottix) on my 5D MkIII. I included the three attached images to illustrate the difference between OEM and third-party grips. As you can see by the images, the Canon OEM grip on my 7D MkII is built to much more exacting tolerances than either of the third-party grips, as evinced by the noticeable gap that exists where the battery tray meets the body of the grip. The Phottix is marginally tighter than the Vertax, but neither compares very well to the build tolerance of the Canon. That's not to suggest the third-party grips don't work. They do, but I've already gone through one Phottix grip on my 5D MkIII in less than two years after buying it owing, in part, to the less than robust build. Still, I would have to buy one more grip for my MkIII to match the price of the Canon grip, so I'm ahead of that cost game. So far.

Yes, the Canon grips are more than three times as costly as the Pixel Vertax grip, but they are built to last a lifetime, which is not something I can say about any moderately-priced third-party grip. The old adage that "you get what you pay for" definitely applies.

Now, having noted all of that, this grip does work as advertised (though I wouldn't trust it to be weather sealed in a downpour), and - for the price - works well for the budget-concious photographer. I use grips on all my cameras because I have large hands and these grips just make the cameras feel more secure when holding them. Time will tell if this grip will hold up to the rigors of shooting wildlife and portraits but, for now, it seems like it will do the job. Will post updates as needed.

title: Great Product-Great Price.
text:
The box arrived on a rainy day and I was terrified that there might be some damage, but it was double-boxed so everything arrived in great condition. No broken light bulbs, all parts included but no instructions, although it wasn't difficult to figure out.
The softboxes open up easily and it's a little tricky getting them attached to the light head, you will want to do this FIRST and THEN install the light bulbs. Be SURE to keep the boxes and packing materials for the individual light bulbs in case you ever want to break down and travel-you'll thank me for that piece of advice. Trust me, opening the softboxes is the ONLY part that "assembled" in 3 seconds.
Once you put the softlight covers on the front the light is wonderful to photograph with and it barely leaves a shadow, even on the white background.

I assembled the backdrop frame easily and had to leave out a cross-beam on the top because it was so large. Even with three pieces it was about 8ft across with one more cross-beam unused.

The backdrop needs to be ironed of course and it didn't extend all the way to the floor, as it only covered a little more than half of the entire backdrop area. I extended it up almost to the ceding and had to stand on a chair to put the clamps in place-I'm 5'9, so this backdrop frame is about as tall as you'd need it to be. I suppose you could get larger backdrop cloths if you needed them, but I DEFINITELY recommend the 6 backdrop clamps Amazon recommends as the ones that come with the set just aren't as easy to use as the larger clamps. You might want to purchase an additional set of 6 just in case.

The photo of the ugly guy is me with just TWO of these lights on and the third one packed away in the carrying case for those jobs we might need to bring a long a little extra light. The backdrop comes with a carrying case, too so this set packs up easily and doesn't weigh a ton. Folding down the softboxes will take a little getting use to, they have straps to hold them closed and come with their own padded protection sleeves that zip right up for safe, easy storage. Never try to attach or detach the softboxes from the light head with the bulbs in it and ONLY use cool-burning florescent lights.

The power cords are a little shorter than I expected and that WILL come into play when you use the overhead light. If you choose to use sand as a counter-weight, make sure it is in a THICK, WELL-SEALED storage bag. DO NOT put loose sand in the counter-weight bag as it only has a draw-string closure. I used decorative river-rocks bought at a hobby store that work just fine, but counter-weighting WILL BE an issue if you use the overhead light as it is shown in the product photos, so be careful.

The light stands themselves are amazingly adjustable and the legs can be adjusted to a wide or narrow stance for cramped quarters. If you use these lights outdoors, you will probably want a sandbag or two to keep a gust of wind from pushing them over as they are pretty lightweight and once they are set up, they're naturally top-heavy.

I'm a relative newcomer to the world of professional photography, so I want quality gear to be able to take those great shots, but I don't have a fortune to spend, either. This is a rather nice set-up for the money and I'm been both surprised and pleased with the price I paid, the quality of the equipment and the features it offers. This isn't "rugged" equipment for regular, outdoor use but if you have a home studio or even a professional studio, I think you'll be rather pleased with this purchase.

title: Not too small, not too big.  Just right.
text:
Reviewers with the technical ability to do so say sharpness and other image qualities are very good indeed. So what! I doubt there has been a single poor lens offered by the major camera companies for quite a few years.

Someone, knocked my Fuji's 60mm off a table. The cost to repair was about the same as replacing it with a slightly used or open box 60mm. Since I rately used the 60mm for true macro - close up more often -I decided to try something different. While I make an occasional people photo, I'm not really in to portraits. Thus the size weight and price of the 56mm were not compensated by its prime virtues.

What all that came to was a decision to try the 50mm. It has filled all the non-specialized niches of the two lenses above while being a lot more user friendly. User friendly to me means not being a burden to lug around having quick accurate auto focus. For photographing people in public it's not "in your face" like the 18/23/35mm lens. It is not as intimidating/annoying to the subject as any of the tele-zooms This helps even with people you know. 50mm encourages you to compose by narrowing you view from the whole scene before you. The focal length is not so long as to be super dpecialized so you can leave it on all day if you like.

Although this lens will not replace the 60mm's macro capability, it works well with Fuji's auto-extension tubes (which can slip into a shirt pocket) to provide some worthwhile closeup capability.

You can certainly do portraits with the 50mm. No doubt the 56mm produces better out of focus regions but I have long suspected that non-photographers can't tell and don't care. Depth of field at f/2 is narrow enough to to separate the subject from the background in nearly all cases though the 56mm will work better in certain situations.

In short the 50mm is easy to use and carry about and for me anyway, more versatile. Note I never said "good enough" because it is too good to be just "good enough".

Oh yes! I and some others felt that with the earlier Fuji lenses the lens hoods, and front & rear lens caps were a nuisance. Easy to accidentally fall off, hard to put back on. Hood were hard to put on reversed for storage. Some lens hood just seemed too monsterouly huge to be practical. Someone must have been paying attention because none of that applies to the 50mm f/2. They all work just fine

title: Doesn't Compare to the Origami Cover for the HDX 8.9
text:
My previous tablet - Amazon's best ever, the HDX 8.9 - had a leather origami cover on it that I absolutely loved.

This cover SUCKS. First off, the "cobalt purple" is pretty distinctly blue. Still pretty, but not what I was hoping for. The real problem, though, is that the kickstand style is not nearly as stable as the origami cover was. In portrait mode, it lists and will NOT stay up if you touch it. So probably okay if you're using to read or look at a recipe hands-free, but still annoying because of the obvious list to one side.

In landscape mode, it's reasonable stable (not likely to out and out collapse on you), but it shifts a little with moderate tapping on the screen. And over time, as the kickstand seam breaks in, the angle is going to tilt the tablet back even more from an already non-optimal angle.

The kickstand style is also not helpful for holding the tablet in one hand, while tapping with the other. The origami case gave the hand something to hold on to, but this one does not. So you have to flatten it out and hold it by the edge, which is fatiguing.

This cover is cheaper than the leather origami cover, but not enough cheaper to make up for its shortcomings. The fact that it's fabric is reason enough for it to be cheaper, but there's no excuse for the downgrade in functionality!

title: Triplett CamView IP Pro+ can be a great product, but not yet
text:
The Triplett CamView IP Pro+ has the potential to be a great product. (Note, I am reviewing the Pro+ which as the maximum number of features that you may not need.) The biggest problem of the unit will naturally resolve itself but at the moment, May 1016, the product is version 1.0 which means that users will be living on the bleeding edge of technology with the product. Documentation is sparse and many items must be 'figured out' with not everything being intuitive.

There are distinct items that were not well thought out in this initial release but some, perhaps many, may well be resolved in future versions of the firmware. I worked with the tech group at Triplett for multiple hours and they were extremely interested in what I had found about the unit and they sincerely seemed committed to making improvements where needed.

An example of something that is evidence of the first release is the extremely awkward use of the QWERTY keyboard that is not even obvious when first viewing the device online. The front panel of buttons swings open to reveal a fully QWERTY keyboard to allow for the input of the required numbers and letters for many inputs and tests. When you try to enter an IP address though, things quickly become un-fun. The 'period' is accomplished by Shift-D! (The shifting is accomplished by pressing a 'SYMBOL' key to get to the 'special' keystrokes like !@#$%:() and others. But what were they thinking??? Who wants to press '1-9-2-SYMBOL-D-SYMBOL-1-6-8-SYMBOL-D-SYMBOL-0-SYMBOL-D-SYMBOL-1 instead of 1-9-2-.-1-6-8-.-0-.-1 Fortunately there are ways to fix this via a firmware update. One suggestion I offered was an autocomplete such that after the user types '1-9' the unit auto types the '192.168.' series that will essentially always be next. This and many other items need to be rethought. The typical subnet for IP cameras is the 192 subnet but unfortunately, the current default is the 10 subnet and the unit does not make use of the 'last used' subnet so there is a constant need to edit the subnet that you are wanting to work on. Being smart about the next release of the firmware will show their true intent on allowing this product to be a useful tool or an expensive toy.

Other inconsistencies in the minimal documentation also need to be corrected as the product has many features and learning them should not be the difficulty that it currently is. Sometimes the documentation will show a button at '+', other times as IRIS +, and other times as a colored checkmark. Figuring out what they mean each time should not be the difficulty that it is. Then too, there is a SET button that doesn't 'set' anything but instead cancels all of the entries you've made and moves you back one level in the menu losing all of your work. Heck, didn't you really think that 'SET' would set something?

I love where the product might end up but whether Triplett decides to really take it there, only time will show. Until then, I do have an expensive toy that is a bit of a pain to use and it needn't be that way. :-(

title: A little disappointed with this device
text:
A little disappointed with this device. We purchased one for our datacenter collocation and it's working well at that location. We purchased a second one to replace a Cisco RV082v3 at another facility and unfortunately there is a known issue that makes it unusable to us.

If you have a static IP block assignment, and the assigned addresses are not contiguous with the WAN IP, the 1-to-1 NAT assignments won't work. Ironically, this was not a problem with the RV082v3, which is somewhat of a previous version of this device. After contacting Cisco Support, they notified us that this is a known issue with no work-around which would not be addressed by a future firmware update.Unfortunately, our only options were to have our IP block assignment changed or search for a new device.

For our one location, we opted to look for a new device. However, this suits our needs and works flawlessly at our datacenter collocation.

title: The Best 4K Monitor in this Price Range -- Plug and Play with 2015 Macbook Series Computers -- Retina Quality Display
text:
Image Quality: 10/10
Ease of Set Up: 10/10
Value for Money: 10/10

I recently purchased a 2015 Macbook Pro 13 w/ Retina Display and was so overwhelmed by the color and text quality that I decided I needed to upgrade my desktop monitor as well. I wanted something that was plug-and-play using a display-port cable, and ultimately I chose this monitor for these reasons:

1 - the 24" has the highest pixel density for the resolution -- if you go up to 27 or 28" you will get excellent resolution but not as crisp text
2 - the color testing by Dell provides 99% accuracy -- my side by side photos enclosed show the color accuracy
3 - I wanted expansion capabilities in the back of the monitor -- the 4 x USB SuperSpeed (3.0) ports come in handy on my desktop
4 - the base is extremely stable -- no wobble
5 - the monitor does not crash/fail to wake up when the laptop goes to sleep -- *Note* -- I find that if it is slow to wake up after being asleep for a long time simply pressing the menu button above the power button on the face of the display wakes up the monitor immediately
6 - the colors are the SAME as my Macbook side by side, and the text is the same degree of sharpness side by side as well
7 - I am able to use the Dell supplied display-port cable out of the box and plug it into my Thunderbolt port and it auto detects every time. *Note* -- do not use a Thunderbolt cable to your Mac -- it will not detect the monitor. Use the cable supplied by Dell.
8 - The display-port cable provides audio output support, so you can plug your desktop speakers into the Dell Monitor rather than your Macbook and it works perfectly fine. *Note* -- the display-port audio out port disables the audio control on your MAC so you need to use speakers with volume control built in or plug your audio system into your Mac to retain the volume control functionality.
9 - Antiglare is easier on the eyes -- this monitor does not come with the glossy image you see in the Macbook Retina Display which I thought would bother me, but side by side, it is actually EASIER to work in Photoshop without the glossy image than with it.

I don't know how else to describe it except to say once you buy this monitor you will throw your Apple Cinema Display in the garbage. Plug and play out of the box with my Macbook Pro 13, no support issues, no video card issues,

title: Died after 3 months; "Irreparable" to Panasonic support
text:
I bought this camera for travel and through my first couple trips I was really excited about the images. I'm not much of a photographer yet and this let me take better quality photos at the point and shoot level and got me excited about learning more and more about my camera without shelling out for a dslr and with having the ease of a smaller camera that can fit into any purse and most jacket pockets.
I bought the camera June 23, 2015 and I currently (Oct 10,2015) have a lovely little brick that does nothing. After repeatedly poorer and poorer sensitivity, the power button quit working on me. I could turn the camera on by taking out the battery and the putting it back in (yes, the battery is fully charged), but the power button will not turn on the camera. I sent it in to Panasonic support and found out today that the camera was water-damaged. WHAT!? There were a few extremely humid times that we used it and once in a very light drizzle, but water damage is not something that ever ever ever remotely crossed my mind. So my only options after 3 months of using a $350 camera is to pay $280 for a replacement. Nothing they can do to fix it. Nothing. It's apparently a brick now. Super disappointed in apparently the fragility of this camera and Panasonic support. I would never recommend them.
As mentioned in other reviews, the ink on my mode dial also completely wiped off after the few months of use. Not a huge problem because you can use the screen to see which setting you are on, but still... a small indicator of the lack of thought that was put into this camera.

title: Well worth the money!
text:
I've likely tuned hundreds of antennas SWR over my year using the old method of checking each end of a band and adjusting a bit to center the dip. I looked long and hard at the cheap $30 and $40 meters and I've had so much bad luck with them I thought about getting something better ... and ended up getting WAY BETTER!

The meter is so simple to use. You select the correct output 2M and above or 2M and below and connect the antenna up to the meter. Twist one knob to select the band and the other to pick the frequency inside that band and the cross needles indicate the SWR and the impedance of the antenna.

Press a button and the meter will sweep the band displaying the slope on the small color screen. With HF bands this is very handy to see just what the SWR is across a wide number of frequencies. Tuning dual and tri-band VHF/UHF antennas on my Jeep was simple.

The only thing missing is a USB port to off load screen captures of the SWR plots.

title: Seasonic has just made the competition look irrelevant.
text:
As a high end user in the medical industry I choose components that offer me the best performance and reliability. For the the past 7 years I have almost exclusively used Seasonic Power supply units in all my custom workstations. I have never had a Seasonic unit fail or require RMA. During the same period I have had to RMA several units from other sources such as Coolermaster and Corsair. Lesson learned, stick with what works.

For that reason I was not surprised when I heard that Seasonic increased their factory warranty on all Seasonic PRIME series power supplies to 12 years. They stand behind their products and have backed their claims with the longest warranty in the industry.

These new units have the best voltage regulation I have ever seen, have excellent ripple control, and even when I load them to 100% capacity the power draw from the wall shows them performing at Platinum efficiency levels. I literally have no complaints with this unit. The same can probably be expected from the whole line all the way up to 850W (which I plan on using in an upcoming Ryzen build).

There you have it, if you need a power supply. This is it, they have literally just made the competition look irrelevant.

text:
I went with the Ring Video Doorbell 2 because it went on sale and I got 20% off that price. If I could do it over, I'd probably spend a bit more and go with the Nest Hello. My reason is because the Nest records 24/7 whereas the Ring 2 records based on motion detection. The issue is that the Ring 2 sometimes starts its recording a bit late and ends too early.

Otherwise, it's a good enough product. It's nice to be able to live view what's going on at my front door whenever I want.

UPDATE (Aug 22, 2018): After owning this for barely 2 months, I'll say it's not worth it. I received an email from Ring yesterday that I should charge my battery soon. The thing is, it's hardwired so why is the battery draining? I removed the battery, checked the connections. Even the app confirms it's hardwired. I even tried reversing the wires. Oh well, I guess I'll just have to charge the battery every month or so (and wow does it take hours to charge).

title: A Solid Product for Laptop Protection
text:
I received this cover set a few days before the XPS 13, and when I first took it out of the package I was surprised at how pink it looked - I was nervous it was going to look a bit too pink when placed on the laptop. It's touted as being "red" after all, not pink.

When my XPS 13 arrived, I easily snapped the top and bottom pieces into place and the colour is most definitely red. I'd prefer a slightly darker red hue (heck, I'd love to see a completely opaque option), but thankfully it doesn't look pink. In some light, it looks orange. The bottom though has so many holes for heat venting it looks quite garish and over the top. I'm not entirely convinced they're all required for thermal reasons, but given how infrequently the bottom is seen, it's not a big deal. The bottom also gives you small pop-out legs that angle the laptop upwards a bit, also creating extra space for cooling. It's a nice touch.

This product was created to fit the XPS 13 *perfectly* - there isn't a wasted millimeter anywhere, which is great. The plastic is thick, strong, and of a very high quality. It does add slightly to the thickness of the laptop, especially the pop-out legs, but only by a few mm. I've used it for a bit over a week now, and some small scratches are visible - so I think it's a bit soft. I'm OK with that though, I'd rather replace a shell every six months than have my laptop be damaged.

Overall, especially for the price, this is a good way to protect my laptop and I'm happy with the purchase.
