title: Great Sound, But Not Easy To Handle
text: I will start by stating this is a well-engineered product, and sounds superb. The sound has a clarity I don't usually expect from a portable unit, and which rivals the DACs in my Integra DHC 80.3 home pre/pro. But I returned the product for a refund. This was largely due to form factor. I had purchased the unit to pair with a Samsung S5 to improve audio playback when on the go. Note to Samsung owners: some Samsung mobile phones do not match well with the Oppo and produce glitches and crackle sounds due to USB driver issues (the noises sound like the pops and snaps of old vinyl records). Streaming audio from Pandora was similarly affected. I had tried different software players like VLC, foobar2000 and others. None of my other devices exhibit this phenomenon and play cleanly. Correspondence with Oppo reveals they know of this and are working to correct the issue. Until then, they recommend using a specific audio software player (purchased, not free) which apparently provides its own USB drivers. I used the free trial version of the player, and it did indeed work, and the sound was stellar. However, I felt let down that a specific (paid for) audio software player was necessary to make the Oppo work right. Note:  I am a current owner of an Oppo Blu-Ray player and am well-pleased with its performance. I do believe Oppo makes a good product. The real issue prompting the return was the clunky nature of mating the mobile phone and the Oppo via the supplied USB-b to USB-b cable. My purchase was supposed to be for portable and travelling situations in which I still wanted some quality music available; but the clunky way the two devices were cobbled together certainly prevented placement in any pocket, nor was it even easy to carry about. I did not try the elastic straps Oppo provided to tie them together, but they would have covered the mobile phone screen a fair bit anyway.  I reasoned that if I had to travel with an additional product roughly the size of an audio DAP, why not have such a device that does fit in a pocket, or is at least a bit less clunky to handle? And would still keep the phone handy and available for its intended use? So to sum, great sound and quality, but clumsy in handling and not a convenient form factor. ( I did inquire of Oppo if they might slap on some storage and audio player software to make a variant of the HA2 into a true DAP, but they indicated it would be a bit costly and likely only appeal to a niche market). While disappointed with this product, I do support Oppo and their quality products in general, and look forward to future products they may offer.

title: Unimpressive write performance
text:
Like so many SD cards I have tried, this card has dreadful performance on small writes. Unlike so many other SD cards I have tested, its performance on larger but randomly placed writes is merely poor, and I do not see long stalls when the load includes a mix of reads and writes. Naturally, the read performance is where the maker clearly concentrated.

For linear reads, I saw over 75MB/s, for large random reads, over 55MB/s. For write performance, it cleared 13MB/s linear and 3MB/s large random (most cards I have tested can't hold 1MB/s for large random writes). The small random reads were over 6MB/s. The <1MB/s small random writes were a bit disappointing, though, and the just better than zero transfer rate with multiple outstanding writes says the card can't deal with multiple streams at once. Copying a set of files that ranged up to 100MB per file (with an average over 1MB per file) achieved around 4MB/s.

Overall, it could be tolerable as a file storage card, and it looks like it might make a useable camera card if your camera has a reasonable write buffer.

The 32GB version of this card has clearly better write performance and does not choke on multiple streams; I would recommend it instead, unless your device can not handle it.

I have had no issues with corruption or data loss so far, but I have not had this card a long time.

title: This is an excellent webcam. It provides full HD quality as well ...
text:
This is an excellent webcam. It provides full HD quality as well as a wide view, allowing the webcam to pick up a wide area. This is perfect for home use as well as for classroom settings, office settings, and conferencing settings, especially those where many people are involved and all need to be visible at once. In my experience, the webcam has always rendered in high quality and has never given me any problems.

This webcam can capture light coming in from 120 degrees. This means that the device will be able to pick up more area than the average webcam can. In other words, the webcam can "see" more of the room. In my opinion, this gives the video picked up a more professional look. It also gives you space to move around the room while still remaining in the field of view.

The 12 megapixel sensor ensures that the video will be taken in the full HD definition with excellent quality. Cheaper webcams advertise having full HD capabilities, which they very well may, but if the quality is not good, the resolution can be HD and still look bad. That is not a problem with this webcam in the least.

This webcam also comes with a built-in microphone. In my experience with this device, the microphone quality is very good. It will not give you professional quality recordings or a band rehearsal (or something similar) as it is not that kind of microphone, but it should be good enough to make a professional or near-professional quality Youtube video, visually and aurally.

The device comes with a sort of clip. However, all of my monitors seem to be too "deep" for the clip to hold. To compensate, I simply took a small amount of mounting tape, put it on top of my monitor, and pushed the device into it. No real force is needed; a small press should do the trick.

Overall, I would recommend this webcam to anyone who is looking for an HD webcam with good quality and large viewing area.

title: So close to perfect - BIOS (UEFI) fixes would make this AMAZING
text:
Some major setbacks make this almost the best laptop on the market. Some problems have easy fixes, but we'll see if ASUS actually makes these changes.

First - Audio is a major, major problem. The speakers REQUIRE the two audio software packages to be run (ICEpower audio and the standard ASUS audio) and not just the drivers - otherwise the audio is garbage. These will not be installed automatically on a clean install; you need to d/ these yourself off ASUS website and run them.

Second - the keyboard has for me a MAJOR flaw: there are no media buttons, and there is no way to lock the fn key. So simple! Easy to do! Not available. ASUS needs to make media buttons (play, pause, stop, skip forward, skip back) standard on their keyboards. ASUS also needs to make the fn button lockable so that these keys work all the time. DELL, TOSHIBA, everyone else has this! For some reason this is not possible.

UPDATE - #3 HAS BEEN FIXED WITH LATEST UEFI [[Third - the backlighting on the keyboard comes on AFTER logging into windows. I need the backlight in the dark to log INTO windows!]] Backlight for keyboard now comes on at start and stays on for logging in. Way to go Asus!

Fourth - these three things above should all be options within the new UEFI: this is what's taking over BIOS in every single computer. UEFI look amazing in every other laptop, and even ASUS has amazing UEFI interface. Not here. I actually thought it was still BIOS but no - their UEFI has minimal options and looks like crap, so that it looks like BIOS. Backlight on after POST, locking fn key, overclocking: None of these are here.

Fifth- there is NO MIDDLE MOUSE CLICK on the ASUS Smart Gesture! Ridiculous. Had to get it off of a programmer's website. ASUS it's 2016! How can you not have three-finger tap = middle click?! Dell has had for at least ten years! Thankfully there's a fix online, but it's not elegant. UPDATE: Here is the webpage with the middle mouse click: ceezblog (dot) info and look for the middle mouse fix

Sixth (minor) - the "end" key is the power button. I use "end" and had to re-learn the keyboard. No problems though.

Ultimately - you'll notice these are small-medium size issues, depending if you're a heavy media (google play, etc) user. Overall, this is still one of the best available laptops on the market. Amazing keyboard, great video card, unbelievably quiet, reduced heat, amazing display, low cost, component expansion (note the M.2 uses SATA! Buy the correct M.2! DVD drive = another slot for another HDD with a caddy.) and even a decent webcam and microphone round this out to be a great laptop for a great price. But honestly if these simple but essential situations are not fixed, I'll likely be selling this laptop within 2 months or so.

UPDATE: 7 Sep 16 - Decided to keep the laptop, and so far zero major issues. Everything working great, updated to win 10 anniversary without problems. My only concerns are again, the speakers are barely passable (but I use headphones and external speakers anyways), the lack of media keys still sucks, and I do miss my "end" key. But for under $1k, this thing is awesome, and light.

UPDATE 2: 7 Nov 16 - So Asus has released an updated UEFI/BIOS which has the keyboard backlight come on at start! Unreal! Good work and maybe having media keys is still a possibility. Great support from Asus so far.

title: Great Little Chromebook That Acutally Has Personality
text:
Surprisingly good for the price. This is my second Flip; the first arrived with an erratically behaving touchscreen and Amazon was fast in getting it replaced, so kudos to Amazon.

So is this little gizmo a MacBook killer, or even a Google Pixel killer? No, far from it. If you are considering buying one of these thinking you'll get the build quality found in those machines you'll be sorely disappointed.

What the Flip does is reveal the potential of the Chromebook form factor, and from that perspective it does a great job.

First things first - don't even bother with the 2 GB version. Go straight for the 4 GB model.

For years I thought the concept of a laptop (either Chrome or Windows) with a touchscreen was an answer in search of a question, but after using this little gem for a few weeks I've become a big supporter of the concept. I actually flip this thing into tent mode and use it for PowerPoint presentations at work. The touch interface isn't 100%, but that is as much a factor of the screen size and the interface's difficulty interpreting just where you are touching on a cramped screen. Clearly a larger screen would help here, but it is what it is. It is somewhat awkward to use in the tablet mode because of the shape of the case and the fact that the keys are exposed on the back, but it works.

Overall system performance is actually pretty good, and the screen, while small, is very sharp with great color and contrast.The keyboard is a bit cramped but still quite usable. The mini-HDMI port works well as long as you don't want to do hi-def presentations. It only comes with USB 2.0 ports, but most Chromebook users won't find themselves using the USB ports anyway.

One negative - it takes a proprietary charging connector. It looks a bit like the new USB Type C connector, but it's not. This means you can't use any of the 20 or so micro-USB cables and chargers you have laying around. But you won't be charging it all that often. This thing sips electrons!

Overall I like this little Chromebook. It's more of a technology demonstration platform for me as I try to get my workforce more and more interested in cloud services. ASUS and Google need to take the lessons learned from this first trial and come out with an ASUS Flip 2 with a larger screen and keyboard, a non-proprietary charging connector and a beefier hinge.

That said, I like and can recommend this little gem!

title: Great for Push/Pull Setup!
text:
This is a great low-profile heatsink with a decent fan.

The problem was that I have a 95W CPU, and this heatsink is only rated to 65W. Here's the scenario:

I had one of those slim tower cases from SilverStone - the ML08B (although all the Raven models have the same dimensions). The cooler height needed to be below 60mm. This heat sink tops off at 40mm. So what could I do to improve it? Well first, I replaced the Scythe fan with this one, rated quieter and more powerful with the same dimensions:

http://amzn.com/B00HWGZT3I

Next, I measured the cooler height and found I could get in a 25mm tall fan on top of the heat sink. So I purchased a Noctua 3k rpm fan to go with the AKASA 3k rpm 80mm one:

http://amzn.com/B00KFCRATC

Finally I purchased a PWM y-splitter to make sure my push-pull cooler ran out of the same 4-pin connection on my motherboard so both would work with my heat sensor:

http://amzn.com/B00OZ10FI2

title: Big Case, little value for $85
text:
Firstly, this isn't my first case I've built a PC in, and definitely not the last.
To start, the size of the case is huge which is what I was looking for. I wanted to put three 120 mm fans in the front. I asked ahead of time if it could fit three, they all said yes. But when I tried to install three, a third fan wouldn't fit. So to get the max efficiency from the front fan mounts, use two 140mm fans. CORRECTION: This case does fit 3 front 120mm fans, but you have to remove the dual 5 inch drive bays.
My biggest and most disappointing complaint about this case is the top isn't big enough to fit a 240mm radiator. My plan was to mount the radiator to the top with the fans pushing air out of the build. The top mount isn't big enough to attach the radiator in this configuration as the radiator is just slightly too long. Therefore I had to install the fans to the top mount instead, which put me in a config to which the fans suck air into the build instead of out. Technically, this is better as the fan suck in fresh air from the outside. But I really wanted to have the fan inwards so my white fans could be seen and look cool for my LED lights. And there's not enough space for a push pull config. I guess this mainly due to the case having 5 inch drive bays for DVD drives. It takes away room for the radiator. But there's plenty of room in the front for a 240mm radiator.
Cable management in this case was a big plus. I had no problem fitting on the back cover. There are included Velcro straps and little slip that can be used to wrap zip ties around. Very useful.
The four USB ports on the front were a big selling point and are very useful.
The handles at the top are more than sturdy for my build the weighs a hefty 40-50 LBs.
Another big selling point for this case is the tempered glass. The glass on this case looks great. No complaints.
Plenty of SSD mounts. Extensive room for HDD mounting. Although contrary to the pictures here on Amazon, the case only come with one mount case for two hard drives. Which is okay for me, but maybe not for others.
The bottom plate the secludes the PSU from the rest of the build is fantastic, and hides some of my bad cable management skills. Dust filter included for PSU fan.
Finally, this case is not half bad for cooler master, though I've seen better and wish I could of bought better. The only thing that make this case worth $85 is the glass panel. But from the outside looking in to my monster build, this case is pretty good looking.

title: Great stills, good HD video, but make sure you buy extra batteries.
text: Very good camera. Lightweight and very full-featured. You can record full-HD video with the push of a button on the back of the camera. The best thing about it is the optical zoom while shooting video. Other cameras I've used that record video do a digital zoom, which pixelates the image and makes it look fuzzy. It's not the smoothest, but if you want higher end video with smooth zooming, I'd use a video camera and not a still camera with video capabilities. The focal length and image stabilization are excellent. If you want a lightweight camera that does good double-duty as a still and video camera, and fits in your pocket, I highly recommend this camera, But make sure you get at least 3 or 4 extra batteries. title: Good Value for those who need portable amplification
text:
I read the above review. And while I agree with 90+% of it. Comparing the C5 to anything other than the Fiio E12 is Apples to Oranges. I own the E11, 12 and the C5. I have roughly 40 pairs of earphones of varying costs. The difference between the E12 and C5 is minimal. I need amplification as I do not hear well. I am using 75-100 % of the output of both of these amps. This makes finding earphones a bit challenging but, I have found quite a few actually. Mainly due to the clean power being put through them. Both amps bring out the detail and soundstage in any music. I usually listen to .flacs on a rockboxed iPod. I also have a Fiio X3. I pair the Fiio's and then the iPod and C5. I have swapped back and forth. The X3 and E12 just fit better together.
The C5 is an excellent product as is the Fiio E12. Fiio has been at this a long time. Playback time is about the same, my players need charging before the amps.
Packaging doesn't mean anything to me at all. It could come in a plastic bag and if it was not damaged it is good to go. I am concentrating totally on the sound.
You NEED to use a line out with either amp. You are taking sound from a mediocre amp and putting it into clean power. You will not get the full benefit of the amps that way. You also can't turn it up very much as any distortion would fry the earphones.
If your music is not of top quality, you won't get the best sound from either amp.
Just my $.02.

I use the large pocket to hold my laptop and I added some padding around the bottom and sides as there is no padding whatsoever in this bag. That being said, the bag is what I expected.

My only concern is with the fumes that emanate from this bag. I knew this bag was made in China - and that is the only way a bag of this quality could be offered so cheaply, but the trade-off is that they use a lot of potentially dangerous formaldehyde to treat the leather. I had the bag next to me for a couple of hours when I first got it and I got asthma-like symptoms that lasted the rest of the day. These are the short-term effects of formaldehyde. You will need to air this bag out for several days for the fumes to subside.

There are more expensive bags made elsewhere that may not have this problem - but you just don't know.

title: I have been SO happy with this body and my lens's that I have ...
text:
So, last year, almost to this date, I purchased my K1. I have been SO happy with this body and my lens's that I have used for it. This is not the be all end all of bodies (there will never be, but the Nikon D850 is trying it's best, but I don't want to spend three thousand dollars on a camera body when i am an enthusiast and not a professional). This was an upgrade over a K50 which was an admirable crop sensor camera that took very good photos for a sub five hundred dollar kit. I had bought a 35mm 2.8 for it but I was itching to have something a little better. Enter in the K1.

I was not actually trying to enter the full frame market per say. I wanted a camera with more options, and better features than the K50. Pentax was coming out with the K70 I knew, and I had known that Pentax had the K1 out for over half a year when I was looking at cameras. I could have bought used Nikon or Canon bodies for less than I spent on the Pentax, BUT WHEN I TRIED OUT THE K1 I FELL IN LOVE WITH IT'S SIMPLE USE, EASY FEATURES, AND INTUITIVE DESIGN.

Since we are talking purely about the body here, let me reiterate that. If you are a user of another brand, and you get a K1, you will indeed feel like things are simpler. If you already are a Pentax user, you will love the design and it will be easy to learn.

The color and detail on this 36 MP sensor are incredible. The modern lens autofocus with the body work great. The ISO is about the best ISO for the price point I've seen. Wow.

The K1 has useful options too. I've used Astrotracer a few times now and it really work well. This camera is a dream for landscape, still portraits, and astrophotography. I have a 14mm Roki and it's exposures are amazing. Even on a full-moon night, the galaxies bleed through.

Another useful feature, though very limited and takes a little bit of cross software to utilize, is PixelShift, created huge files but awesome images to blow up on canvas, etc. You can thank me now, but when the K1 first came out, users were frustrated that in stills taken with slight wind or movement, the Pixelshift (4 images taken in sequence) image would have distortions in it. Lightroom did not support a correction for this.

But, RawTherapies now supports this feature. The native software that comes with the K1 does too, but its' a mess and buggy. RT is easy to use and then you can export as a TIFF file to then be edited in LightRoom.

I am so pleased with the image results of this body paired with my 77mm Limited, 35mm 2.8 cheapy-but-goodie, 14mm Roki, and Tamy 90mm macro. That 90mm macro produces INSANE detail.

If you are not shooting fast moving objects, the K1 will be a dream. There are now more FF modern lens than before, so it is indeed a good purchase to make. Support Pentax. They are really a camera-man-woman's camera maker.

Video is 'ok'. If I were anyone who wanted 4K video and all the bells and whistles, I'd tell you get a real Video Camera then.

Less than two thousand spent on this camera allowed me to get a line up of lens to use immediately with the K1 and I am more than happy so far.

title: DOES NOT WORK WITH PS4!!! Works as expected for extracting Dolby Digital 5.1 from HDMI for SONOS Play Bar.
text:
NOTE: After extensive testing, does not work with PS4. Since the Jtech device says it supports DTS audio, the PS4, when set to Bitstream(Dolby) will always output DTS. If you have a SONOS Soundbar like I do, then you NEED Dolby Digital 5.1(DD5.1) and so this box will NOT work with a PS4.

I bought a SONOS PLAY Bar and realized it could only take Dolby Digital 5.1, and the new Apple TV does not have digital out.

Setup of the extractor was easy and as expected. I plugged it into the wall, then the HDMI in from my HDMI switch and then from the extractor to the TV.

I then took an optical cable and plugged it from the extractor into the SONOS PLAY Bar. On the extractor, I set the mode to 5.1, and in the Apple TV, select Dolby surround as my sound output. It worked like a charm. Movies sound great
.

I also setup a Xbox 360 and PS3. Whatever devices you connect, make sure the output is set to "Dolby Digital 5.1". Note: The PS3 IS capable of encoding DTS-HD and other audio formats to Dolby Digital. Simply select to only output stereo PCM and Dolby Digital 5.1. When you have a DTDS audio only movie, the PS3 will still output the correct Dolby Digital 5.1 mix of DTS.

title: Excellent for my Ipad Pro
text:
I was a little nervous about buying a glass protector for my Ipad Pro. I've never used Tech Armor for starters, but I know from applying glass protectors on smartphones that it is very difficult.

Having bought glass screen protectors for my smartphones in the past, I was a little concerned about how it would ship. The smartphone ones are packaged in a slim cardboard box. Not very safe. What keeps them safe for delievery is the box they are shipped in. However I was really impressed. Tech Armor has it in a nice secure box, on top of the box Amazon used to ship it in.

Needless to say, it was BIG. But so is the Ipad Pro. I'm not going to lie, it was difficult to put on. I made sure my work area was clean and dust free. I cleaned the screen with the supplied cleaner and removed all the dust. (This was the hardest part. I'm a perfectionist and I want ZERO dust spots under my screen protector.) To get around placing the screen on the Ipad Tech Armor supplied to small suction cups. I actually loved that, made aligning the cover and placement a breeze.

In the end I am 100% happy with the screen protector. It probably took about 10 minutes to put on, (but again that's because I am a perfectionist and probably took longer than really needed.) It was difficult to put on, but that's the nature of glass protectors and applying them to something this big.

text: [[VIDEOID:f7adcf660ccb20d6273a8a329cc6981c]] We've been using this for a month now, and so far everything has worked as advertised.  Setup was easy with the QR code.  I opted for the 7 day storage option, and so far that's been plenty.  We've already caught one of the kids sneaking a boyfriend into the house while we were at work.  Actually saw a little more than I wanted to when reviewing the clips.  Our camera is hidden in a fake plant and if you don't know it's there you'll never notice it.  I would say that if you pan or zoom the camera remotely someone in the room will likely hear it moving.  A better online user interface and more intuitive controls would get this 5 stars from me.  As it is right now, the Amcrestview option to view live is a convoluted mess in all the browsers I've tried, but it gets the job done to just view live.  The Amcrest Cloud viewer runs better in the browser, but doesn't have as many tweaks during live viewing.  I've been able to download clips and save them off to Google Drive.  The Amcrestview app for Android works fine, but is slow to load.  The Amcrest Cloud app is actually a little faster, in my opinion, for viewing activity after the fact.  Takes a bit to figure out the menus to set up notifications and such, but once I got familiar with it adjusting those was pretty simple.  All in all I'd say it it was well worth the price, I feel it's a good value.  I'd be comfortable adding a second one of these for more coverage.  It appears the viewing apps are set up pretty well for using multiple cameras.  I've attached a video so you can get an idea of what you can when viewing on a PC.

title: Fantastic beast!
text:
I purchase this beast for my husband to replace his 6-year old Acer and another one for work. I have to say this is the top of the line gaming laptop for only $1499!

PROS:
+ Top specs (128GB SSD + 1TB HDD, 3GB NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970M, i7-6700HQ, 16GB DDR4 RAM) at affordable price
+ Sleek and cool design
+ Red and blue backlit keyboard (the logo on the back of the laptop also lit up)
+ Loud speakers with subwoofer (I don't even need to buy external speakers for this laptop)
+ Sturdy built
+ Extra third fan (frost core) that you can swap with the DVD drive to enhance performance
+ Full HD screen
+ Impressive battery life for a gaming laptop (It lasts about 4-4.5 hours for me while streaming movie on medium brightness)
+ Macro keys (My games all have built-in macros so I don't use these)
+ Self-cleaning fans software (the software will reverse the fan so it will push out the dust inside)
+ Easy personal upgrade components (1TB HDD, M.2. SSD and RAM)
+ Stays relatively quiet and cool (others say this laptop can be loud but not to me and if you have the volume on, you won't notice a thing)

CONS:
- Heavy (9lbs for the 17inch model), since it has a study built
- Limited backlit keyboard colors (red and blue)
- No touchscreen (I wish this is an option in the future, but not a necessity because I use mouse most of the time)

I would definitely recommend this laptop for those who wants something with superb desktop specs but can still be easily carried around when need to. If you are looking for something for medium everyday use and portability, I would suggest looking elsewhere. Again, I am very happy with my both of my purchases and I can't wait to see what Acer has for the next Predator generation.

title: Quick Delivery, Works as Stated, Using for an interface to make HDMI conferencing cams work as webcam.
text:
This product works great! My company is using this to utilize the Cisco Precision HD Cameras (from Cisco C20 system) as webcams for Skype and GotoMeeting. We decided to go with this product instead of the BackMagic Design Intensity Shuttle due to the large number of reviews stating compatibility issues. This was also less expensive and was a Prime product so I was able to get it faster. I also contacted each of the products support with questions and StarTech was also very happy to help whereas BlackMagic was far less helpful and treated me as if I were bothering them..

Pros:
Fantastic picture, great quality and the cameras maintain their PTZ functions with the remote. You will likely need a separate 12V 2A power supply as ours was originally powered by the C20 unit via Ethernet. I tried to power it with a power injector and would not function that way..

Another reviewer stated that they were using ManyCam (manycam.com) as a virtual camera driver for Skype and that DOES work at a drastically reduced quality (1280x1024 max) unless you purchase the license at $49.95 for a single license or $149.95 for enterprise up to 5 devices.

The included SteamCatcher software provides the driver to make it work without the need to do that. I HIGHLY recommend downloading the latest driver from startech for the USB3HDCAP device.

I am using it on both Dell and HP desktops and have tested on Dell and HP laptops as well. For those that are not aware, USB 3.0 will either be blue in color or be indicated with an SS on your PC or laptop. It will NOT work with USB 2.0 with the setup I have.

Our setup: Dell 9010 or HP 4300 SFF PC with ASUS HD 5450 Graphics cards (for HDMI video and sound to our displays) Cisco Precision HD PTZ cameras (http://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collaboration-endpoints/telepresence-precisionhd-cameras/index.html) connected with this product to a USB3 port with StarTech USB 3.0 HD Video Capture Device. We are utilizing separate microphone inputs; in our case the built in room microphones that was built into the original VTC system.

We are happy with the initial purchase and have purchased more for the remaining rooms.

Cons:
The only complaint I have is that I purchased it for $168 on 3/20/2015 and purchased the rest from the same place from the same ad for $178 on 2/25/2015. I am not sure why the price increased 5 days later but for what we want to do with them, they are saving us thousands of dollars in conferencing equipment to make the current system work as we wish. Feel free to reach out to me with any questions on our setup as I had to dig around to figure it out.

title: This dongle works for me. Oh joy!
text:
After trying/ buying 3 other products, which did not work at all, this one worked very well. I'm connecting a Gateway 20 inch VGA monitor to a Dell Inspiron 15L, which only has one HDMI ports for adding a monitor. This dongle fits snugly in the HDMI port, though I'd be careful not to bump it too much for fear of damaging the dongle, or the port. I plugged everything with power on all devices "OFF." Then booted up as normal with monitor turned "ON." Within 5 or 10 seconds, the monitor came to life! I made a few adjustment within "DISPLAY" in Windows 8.1 and all is well. I am delighted as this will save me $ 200+ on a new decent monitor with HDMI adaptability. All else was fine... Packaging/ instructions/ delivery was prompt.

* Quick update: As this is an HDMI output, the sound on my system is trying to play through the monitor, which has no speakers. Basically, I've lost sound through the laptop speakers. I'm sure that there are some adjustments that I can make to rectify this. If I can't, I'll just plug in some external speakers through the 3.5mm jack port.

** Follow up: I fixed this (above) by going to device manager > sound and then right clicked my laptop sound device to "disable" and then immediately did the same thing again and selected "enable." I then disabled the device that showed the monitor speaker... I left that disabled. I now have sound again through the speakers on the laptop.

title: Highly versatile and useful media device
text:
This little Tenker unit is a pleasant surprise, with lots of great features, including a Remote Control! I've only had it a couple (busy) weeks, thus have been unable to test the DivX file replay functionality, but I will update when I do. Other than that, it has worked very well to play standard DVDs, and MP3s (music) from a tested USB flash drive-- but get this->it ALSO has an SD slot AND A/V input/output!! ("What does that mean?", you ask?)
That means:
• SD card slot - Save MP3's and DivX video files to an SD card, and leave it loaded (in the slot) to have Music and Videos ready to play at any time, without worrying about damaging the card or player, like a USB possibly could by sticking out and snagging/breaking during storage/travel. Super Travel-friendly, and less likely to be tampered with by younger children.

• A/V Input (analog/RCA) - Gives the ability to use this Tenker DVD Player SCREEN for ANYTHING!! This means Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo, Arduino, Roku, TV tuner... Any other device that has an RCA audio/video output (just like connections to a regular TV) can be used, giving this little unit an extra point for versatility. (Note: The use of an 'HDMI to RCA convertor' could render a Chromecast and/or Amazon Fire player possible as well. If I get a convertor, I will update with a brief how-to.)

•• A/V Output - this allows the Tenker player to be connected to any other RCA-input device, such as a larger TV screen, projector, etc. Up-size!

•Built-in Battery - Lithium-polymer battery is claimed to last 4-5hrs, which is decent, all things considered.

• 12v AUTO/Marine power adapter (via Cig Lighter/ Power port) - Take your media to Go! Never without a way to play and charge, for ultimate convenience.

The Tenker media device played the DVD without a hitch and use of the Remote Control really makes it a comfortable experience. Have reasonable expectations with regards to overall build quality, and you won't be disappointed. This is a budget priced unit with lots of features, keep that in mind. The sound isn't going to astound you with fidelity, but it will be plenty loud enough to hear very quiet dialogue scenes, and the Headphone Output gives the option to use a full range setup, like a home stereo or Car AUX port, should that be desired.

Bottom line: This Tenker DVD/Media Player is a highly versatile and useful device to have for travel entertainment and/or study, at a reasonable price.

title: So uncomfortable it's patented?
text:
To start, I should state that I am not an experienced audio reviewer. These follow a short list of cheaper earbuds and are by far the best.

Pro's:
Visually pleasing
Refined sound (The bass is strong, but not unnaturally so. I am however a bass enthusiast, so to some ears it could come across as too much)

Cons:
Very uncomfortable (I read the reviews warning of this issue, and brushed them aside assuming these reviewers had abnormal ear canal shapes, or something. I have very average ear canal size and shape, and had previously never been physically pained by earbuds. The problem somehow lies in the ear tips, they have a tendency to dig into the ear as they are very slowly pulled from the ear over time.)
Sound quality drops massively if the earbuds aren't situated just right, which will happen frequently if moving around while using. This problem is greatly reduced by employing the use of the included earbud clip, which I have made a part of music listening routine.

Over all impression/suggestion: After around two months of use, the discomfort of use has ever so slightly decreased, and I have decided to keep my pair. However, I would suggest moving along to a different pair. I think its a joke that they advertise these earbuds as being comfortable, and I feel the consumer am the butt of that joke. I am a huge fan of Klipsch and am a proud owner of a kmc-3 but I feel let down.

I waited awhile to leave my review to make sure I really liked this Echo.  I went to a big box store and listened to some other bluetooth speakers and this Echo blows all of them away (even two Bose speakers that I tried but maybe the floor models were abused).  The walnut grain is really nice and looks rich.  It goes with my room decor really well.  One of my most used features on the Echo is the nature sounds for sleeping.  There are some great rain sounds that you can put on loop while you sleep!  I also hook up the Echo to my tablet so the sound comes out of the Echo instead of the tablets dinky speakers.  Watching youtube with the Echo as my speaker has been great!  I will be buying another one eventually.  I have two Echo dots also.  One of the dots is hooked up to Klipsch speakers on a stereo system and the sound is obviously much better but for the size of this Echo you really can't beat the sound.  Bottome line: don't let the bad reviews sway you away from this thing.  Amazon's return policy is the best so at least give it a try and see what you think. title: Needs firmware fixes to boost reliability; may work for your particular situation but be prepared to return if not.
text:
Did not work for any of the office's Windows+Mac switching set ups. Got it to work for a solitary Mac+Mac switching setup so it's not a completely dead unit but consistency is apparently still in Beta as of Spring 2016. Firmware is upgradeable so hopefully they can fix it.

Unfortunately even with reliable firmware fixes, I couldn't go past 3 stars because the square form factor is poorly thought out for all the generic office arrangements I tried. If you are going to mount this puck to a desk or the wall, or otherwise can route attachment cables through the desk and just dump the resulting tangle behind/under the desk into the existing rat's nest, then it could be fine. But thick Display Port 1.2 cables plus USB A-B trunks assure that you're turning this 3"x3" puck into at an unwieldy 7"x7" octopus. It's so light that it's going to twist around to odd sitting arrangements in all 3 axes without mounting the puck or zip-tying the cables to anchors.

But if they can fix the firmware, and your situation is not going to be impacted by the cabling problems, this isn't a bad solution until the kvm market catches up to the influx of 4K displays.

I got this for my son's turntable and now I am jealous. This thing not only handles turntables but also line level and S/PDIF inputs. It outputs to USB, line out, and S/PDIF. For recording Vinyl records it was truly plug and play. Windows found the drivers and automatically installed them. I then brought up Audacity (open source, costs nothing) and began immediately digitizing my LPs. All of those inputs plus the ease of setup made me jealous.

Pros: Many inputs including S/PDIF.
Adjustable pre-amp level for turntable.
Ground for turntable
Adjustable output for headphone monitoring
Standard 1/8" headphone jack.
Powers from USB.

Cons: Does not include a wall wart for powering if you are not near a computer with a USB jack. I am sure one of the electrical plug to USB devices I have from my last 4 cell phones would work but come on! At this price you should not have to hunt an adapter.

Update 17 May 2015. My recommendation now is to just buy the ART PreDJ preamp without the USB. ART claims that Win7 has an issue which causes the USB input to be way too loud and gives steps on their web site to fix it. Two points: (1) the steps do NOT fix the issue. (2) Replacing the USB part of this device with a cheap $15 USB audio capture device and a $150 focusrite 2i2 shows that neither of the replacements have the same issue. title: UNRELIABLE! (A complete downgrade of my initial review)
text:
My initial review (Left in place at the end of this one, if you're interested) stated that this was a pretty good value "for what it was" (inexpensive and small).

I withdraw that assessment and substitute the POOREST EVALUATION POSSIBLE for the following reasons:
1) an alarm clock MUST be reliable beyond all else -- never mind ease of setting and sound -- and this one ISN'T;
2) almost one year (to the day!) after I bought this, the LED lighting behind the dial FAILED.

Initial review follows:

-------------------------------------------

A PRETTY GOOD DEAL FOR WHAT IT IS

"For what it is" means that product ratings submitted as part of this review are "pro-rated" in consideration of the price and size of this item.

By that I mean the following:
=> The sound quality is just fine, if you consider that this item is relatively inexpensive and small -- but it cannot compete for fidelity (or bass) against larger and more expensive competitive items -- relatively tinny, and you can hear the box rattle a bit when the volume is turned-up.

=> Setting the time, channel, and alarm is fairly easy (did most of that without having to read the manual); but the small form factor for this alarm clock means that the lettering is "a bit too small" on the various (yep, small) buttons -- especially when you consider that this alarm is the last thing you'll probably have to manipulate before bed -- tired and impatient; and the first thing you'll probably have to manipulate when you wake up -- disoriented and "dull."

=> I would hasten to add that the instructions for this device are clearly written and easy to understand!

=> And finally, as referenced earlier, the light weight is also implicit in the (tiny, easily moved and packed) form factor. Clever of the manufacturer to also cut weight and lower the likelihood of failure by substituting (3) triple-A batteries for the classic nine-volt backup source in so many other alarms. (Have you ever noticed that old-fashioned battery connectors ALWAYS FAIL OR DESTROY THE BATTERY TERMINALS? I have!)

Overall, I'd buy it again -- a good value, and seems to get the job done well so far.

title: Decent for the price.
text:
*Edit 5/9/2016

After 2 rides this system stopped working. Seems pretty poor quality in my own experience and reading the reviews of others. My advise would be to find a higher quality unit. I removed mine and will be returning for a refund. Not sure if i will replace it at all at this point. I've wasted a lot of time already.

Going from a full fairing bike (2003 HD Ultra Classic) to a bike without a fairing (2005 Victory Kingpin) has been tough. I missed my tunes the most. I have a windshield so I was hoping these speakers would be "ok" but I knew they wouldn't be as good as a four speaker system on a full fairing bike. First I want to address the claimed wattage, the 800w claim is a lot misleading. This amp has a 10 amp fuse, so at 12 volts you're talking 120 watts before the fuse goes. I'm guessing the true RMS wattage is about 25w per channel max. The amp is nice and small, I was able to mount it under my seat. The wired remote is not what I expected, I assumed since it's made for a motorcycle it might mount on the handlebar. Nope, it's flat on the back and doesn't fit any place well. I have it zip tied to the center of my bars between the risers. The harness for this thing is not laid out well either. I had to cut it up and make some modification to get it to work. I added some black wire loom to the power wires as they come unprotected. The fuse is on the wrong place too. Needs to be closer to the battery. I installed the speakers using the provided bar clamps, nothing special there. Removed my fuel tank and seat and concealed all the wires with the factory wires and cables. Pairing with my iPhone was simple. The speakers sound ok, I've played with the EQ settings in my phone and the less bass you have the louder the speaker will play. With my Vance and Hines exhaust I can hear the music clearly up to about 55mph, past that it gets blow away by the wind noise. All in all, this is probably worth the money, it is cheap and fairly well put together if you don't mind modifying it. One of my speakers has a crackle noise in it right out of the box. Long term, we will see how well it holds up.

title: Works, Better Products Available
text:
This product works, I did notice an improvement to wifi on the far end of my house based on the support provided by the Powerline Adaptor. However, the improved quality of my wifi signal was negligible compared to other NETGEAR products I have tested. In short, consider the Wifi Range Extender or a newer router like the Nighthawk.

The set up was a little trickier than the Wifi Range Extender offered by NETGEAR, in that this product sends out a much weaker Wifi signal than I expected and required moving the relay to a few different power outlets in my house until I settled upon using the closest outlet to my desk. Less than ideal because I would prefer hiding the transmitter (relay) in the adjacent guest bedroom. Still, the wifi was no better than what little signal I could reach with my vanilla Xfinity router/modem.

Hardwiring the Ethernet cable I saw an improvement, but again this is simply adding wires and clutter when I would prefer to not have any at all.

The set up took less than ten minutes and was really easy, though took a few tries and had a less-than-ideal but still successful install.

If it sounds like I am being harsh on the product it is because I have been exposed to the full suite of products available for extending Wifi capabilities through NETGEAR. The NETGEAR Nighthawk router is quite a bit more expensive but comes with such a great boost to speed and reach I could hardly imagine spending any money on the Powerline when the Nighthawk is a more elegant solution. Furthermore, NETGEAR's "Genie" software that came with the router (at least for me) frequently troubleshoot any internet issues on my computer whenever I am out and about: changing settings and fixing problems on the fly to meet my needs.

The Powerline works, but for anyone on the fence I say "splurge on a better router".

I was provided this product for free as a part of Netgear's Family and Friends Program.

title: Cloud Storage is the way to go for some applications
text:
I have the original Dropcam Pro as well as 4 Nest Cams. Although I like the original better the Nest Cams have so far performed fine. Camera is not as wide angle and 1080p is not supported but 720 is fine and reduces the network load. Eventually you'll be charged for how much data you transfer on your network (some already are) so the reduced picture quality so far is acceptable for me.

I like the cloud storage, yes a bit costly but I use (2) of these camera for security at work and (2) others to monitor elderly parents. I especially like being able to playback earlier day events to make sure caregivers are treating my parents properly. I also have (3) higher end Panasonic camera's for monitoring vacation property. Their picture quality is far worse and the cameras cost more. The setup of the Panasonic was difficult as well and not for the average person. Nest setup was only a couple of minutes for the first and maybe 30 seconds for the others after you get use to it. Am using the standard Verizon Actiontec wireless router and it works fine with that, have not tried any others yet.

The Panasonic cameras are better with motion detection and emailing pictures, Nest great with streaming and playback. Depends on your needs but this camera is far easier to setup than any others I've seen, including Foscam.

Edit: Just dropped it a star. Got another camera and could not set it up on the Verizon Fios network that I use the Dropcam on. Had to use my iPhone to do the setup. Now working fine but could not set it up using my laptop. Thankfully iPhone setup worked on the same network.

title: It's a nice little radio. It would be 5 star if user could select signal strength threshold on scan
text:
The radio is small light-weight, and it's nice design. It has an easy way of discovering all available stations; just press and hold the M button for 2 seconds and it searches the entire band width and saves up to 20 stations strong enough to break the established signal strenght threshold. Then you just press the M+ or M- to move up / down to the next available station. It displays a little number in the upper lefthand corner to identify the memory location 0-19.

Using a cell phone 4 bar signal stength icon for this analogy for received Radio Station's Signal Strength (RS3):
1 bar - is mostly static (25/75)
2 bar(s) - the music/voices are discernable above the static (60/40).
3 bar(s) - listening is easy (75/25)
with all 4 bars are lit the sound is crisp and clear. (95/5)

When scanning for available stations the radio stores RS3 from 1 - 4.bars which is fine if you're trying to pull a weak RS3.
It can be a bit annoying if you're looking for crisp and clear RS3's. I would give this radio would be a 5 star rating if it gave the user the option to select how sensitive a search scan is. IE: 1 for the hard to get Stations through 4 for just the strong stations.

title: Great Choice as a Linux User (and for Others)
text:
Bought this laptop to run Manjaro KDE (Linux) and act as my primary "everyday use" computer at home. Ill break the review down into 2 parts. Ill start first with the hardware which should be helpful to anyone reading this and then the second part will specifically be about using Linux on it. Model is Dell i5379-5893GRY-PUS (Dell Inspiron 13" 2-in-1 touchscreen)

Hardware:

The build quality is nice. Despite being a plastic shell (instead of metal like the Inspiron 7000) it feels of good quality to the point of questioning if it is plastic. The finish is nice and doesn't appear to attract finger prints as much as glossier finishes. Its a good balance of enough weight to not feel cheap but not too much that its "heavy" for its size.

Specs:
* Intel i5-8250U (8th gen i5 with 4c/8t @ 15watt TDP)
* Intel UHD Graphics 620 (integrated graphics, no dedicated GPU)
* 8GB DDR4 2400mhz RAM (I think 1x8GB, will have to verify)
* 256GB SATA SSD (Samsung PM871 from what I can tell, seems to be 2.5" 7mm not m.2)
* 13" 1920x1080 IPS touchscreen (glossy, but not terrible)
* Webcam supports Windows Hello

Ports:
2x USB 3.1 type-A
1x USB 2.0 type-A
1x HDMI (listed as 1.4)
1x SD card reader
1x Headphone/mic combo jack

The monitor has, in my opinion, pretty large bezels. At first I was disappointed by this but considering its ability to take a tablet form, this likely was done to give something to hold onto in tablet mode without touching the screen by accident. Otherwise its sharp and bright with decent viewing angles.

The rear of the base has a short, somewhat wide vent to exhaust hot air out and does have an active fan however at its loudest it was negligible. I would have to focus on trying to hear it to notice. The upside is it should allow longer boost times on the CPU before throttling sets in.

I found it a bit strange at first that the power and volume rocker are on the right side towards the front of the machine, but have since gotten used to it and figure it is also likely purposeful due to being able to use it like a tablet.

The hinge between the base and monitor is sturdy and feels like it should last if treated well. I dont notice any wobbling while typing on a hard flat surface. The keyboard is ok but not great. I like the look of it and the backlighting can be plenty bright but the feel leaves a bit to be desired. The key presses seem to allow for pressure un-evenly on a key allowing one side to press further than the others which gives the sense that its not that sturdy. I would expect for the press to evenly push the key down but on this keyboard its a bit "mushy". For what its worth it appears to be the exact same keyboard as the Inspiron 13" 7000 series. On the flip side, the touch pad is pretty nice and I typically hate touchpads. This one is pretty large and the buttons (bottom right and left of the touchpad itself) are clicky.

It doesnt look like there are any bay doors on the bottom to access the SSD or RAM and the batter is a built in job, not easily replaceable (if at all). It is unclear if the laptop has the 8GB included soldered in or in 1 of 2 ram slots. Its also unclear, but I expect that there is an empty 2nd ram slot (as most documentation seems to indicate it can be upgraded to 16GB by the user, just not how). I would imagine this would require removing the 8 or so screws on the bottom and maybe even using a pry tool to unsnap some plastic fasteners are the edges.

For the price I was unable to find a laptop with everything I was looking to compete with this. I wanted a 13" or smaller 1080 touchscreen with an 8th gen CPU, 250GB+ SSD, 8GB+ DDR4 RAM. This was the best deal I could find at the time including that ($709). There are tradeoffs with that. Some of what you dont get are:

* USB type-c
* Thunderbolt 3
* NVMe PCIe SSD
* Metal body
* Higher resolution screen

I would say this is a great machine for anyone who wants something small and portable with decent specs and that doesnt require a ton of storage or super demanding tasks (CAD, 3d rendering, advanced photoshop, extrmely large databases/spreadsheets, etc.) or gaming.

Linux:

I am now using Linux at work alot and learn best by giving myself a practical purpose to do something. I wanted to entrench myself in Linux at home while having something that was modern, aesthetically pleasing, functional, practical and portable.

Prior to getting this laptop I tried about about 10+ distros and decided that; a) I liked KDE Plasma as a desktop environment best and b) I like Manjaro Linux as a distro the most.

I didnt get this to do development type work from or anything like that. This is meant to be my "daily driver", its what I will use every day to browse the web, check email, work on documents, watch media, do some minor photo/video editing, occasionally run a VM, etc.

I downloaded the 17.0.6 Manjaro KDE ISO and setup an USB3 drive to install from. Booted from the drive and ran installer which took about 5-10 mins which is on par or maybe slightly faster than I would expect for a Win 10 install using the same hardware/specs.

Out of the box all of the drivers where recognized and working. Here are a couple things I was worried about and can confirm all working:

* Qualcomm AC Wifi (will add model later, not handy right now).
* Qualcomm Bluetooth
* Touchscreen
* Keyboard Backlight
* Webcam (both standard and infrared lol)
* GPU drivers for Intel
* Screen Brightness
* Sound

I have not yet found any part of the hardware not working as intended.

Battery life appears to land me at about 6+ hours of steady use so I am very happy with it.

Software wise, most things just work. I have had to, as with any linux distro, troubleshoot and work out some kinks but nothing I can even recall as worth mentioning.

At the end of the day, this is the first time I have felt like I really own the computer. KDE especially allows a level of customization I could only dream of in Windows. This is coming from someone who not only likes Windows 10, but previously worked for a company for 6 years with MS partnership in which we provided remote and on site support for many of their products including Windows and Office. I've developed professional course material and classes on Windows and taught the classes. I have defended Windows 10 fiercely at times. I have Windows Server 2016 Essentials at home and 3 other Windows 10 Pro computers on the domain with it.

Why say all this about Windows? If someone like me can escape MS's strangle hold so can you. If you have considered moving to Linux this laptop is a great choice. However, dont take my word for it. Do your research, decide what distro and make sure it will work with whatever you install it on.

EDIT (11/20/2017): So it appears the RAM and SSD can be upgraded. To do so requires removing the bottom of the laptop (roughly 8-10 screws and using a pry tool to unhinge the plastic tabs). Crucial shows upto 32GB (2x 16GB) RAM and guarantees compatibility. The SSD is a 2.5" SATA SSD 7mm height, so m.2 drives will NOT work and especially not PCIe/NVMe drives. I havent upgraded myself as I have no need to now.

EDIT (01/02/2018): For anyone concerned with firmware/BIOS updates while using Linux I have done a Intel ME Firmware update and a BIOS update (1.3.2).

For the Intel SA-00086 advisory and update Dell has a page listing all model affected with links to their updates (a link to it is posted on Intel's official page for the advisory). In this case I used a Windows to Go drive to boot to Windows 10 without altering the installed setup on my machine. I had to install drivers to Intels ME and reboot. I then ran the update from Windows to Go and then shutdown and booted back to Manjaro KDE to verify the results via the script Intel provides and it returned that the issue was patched. Be aware booting from Windows to Go wouldnt be needed if running Windows already.

The BIOS is actually easier. You just put the BIOS update exe on a thumb drive and plug it in, boot and press F12 to get the boot menu, select BIOS update. Browse to the update file on the thumb drive and run the update. I havent seen any other firmware udpates related to the laptop but if there are others I will likely use a Windows to go drive to do so unless its specifically a BIOS update.

**Upgraded machine!!!

I have since purchase changed the wifi card and upgraded the RAM. I did this as the QCA6174 wifi card made by Qualcomm isnt exactly Linux friendly. It worked, but had 2 major issues. Slow SMB xfer and it would report wifi connecting at 6 MiB/s (incorrectly). I bought an Intel 8265 which is officially supported for use in Linux brand new for $20 and works perfectly.

I figured while I had it open to add another stick of RAM so I bought an 8GB stick of crucial RAM [[ASIN:B019FREJOQ Crucial 8GB Single DDR4 2400 MT/s (PC4-19200) DR x8 Unbuffered SODIMM 260-Pin Memory - CT8G4SFD824A]] and it worked perfectly. To be honest the RAM upgrade wasnt even needed, but didnt want to break it open just to change the wifi card out. I considered an SSD upgrade as well, but I have like 200GB free of the 256GB so I am not exactly hurting for space.

Also using this bluetooth mouse [[ASIN:B01M1F98YR Logitech MX Anywhere 2 Wireless Mobile Mouse, Long Range Wireless Mouse with Hyper Scroll and Easy-Switch up to 3 Devices - Navy]] which plays very nicely connected via bluetooth. Latest stable Manjaro update even adds its battery status to the battery notification area! Really like this mouse.

Would still highly recommend this laptop as I am sure it will serve me for years to come.

EDIT (9/7/2018):

Switched from Manjaro to Fedora. Love Manjaro but I use CentOS/RHEL frequently at work and wanted something in the same family, plus Fedora supports secure boot and SELinux.

I am actually not a fan of the Fedora KDE spin (very bloated), so I did a minimal install of Fedora from the Everything DVD (not sure how its different from netinstall DVD) and then after minimal install added only the packages I needed for KDE desktop and a select few KDE apps I actually wanted. I have since configured it and added all the software I wanted.

The install and setup all "just" worked. All hardware was recognized and working, havent had any issues. Ive got Grub themed, Secure boot enabled, LUKs encryption on the whole SSD, SELinux enabled and Firewalld. Bootup is roughly 20-30second including 5sec Grub menu and 2x logins (LUKs then KDE), so not bad at all.

I am amazed by the CPU in this, especially when you consider the cost. I can do all my normal day-to-day stuff with no issue while running 1-2 VM's in Virt-Manager/KVM (Win10 and CentOS). The Additional RAM turned out to help now that I have some VM's I run on this. I have an external USB3 enclosure with a 256GB m.2 SSD that I keep the VM's on and just connect it whenever I need them so I dont take up my laptops storage with them.

I think the price has also dropped since I got this laptop, down to ~ $650. At that price, I would highly recommend it.

EDIT (3/11/2019):
I am still using this laptop as my daily driver with Fedora 29 and KDE as the DE. Its running flawlessly. The only negative comment I can make at this time is that the battery life seems to have degraded overall since I first got it.

To preface the battery life comments I am going to make, I honestly do not use it off the charger often as I am generally sitting at a desk with it plugged in. I also think its perfectly reasonable for the overall battery life to decline as the laptop/battery age.

Having said that, when I initially used the laptop and reviewed it, battery life was around the 6 hour mark for mixed usage (not properly tested, just my experience using it over multiple charge cycles). I would say that now, with relatively the same usage, I am seeing more in the 3-4 hour range. Again, I think this is normal considering it was a $700 (at the time) laptop and is now about 1.5 years old. It could be my fault for keeping it on the charger for extended periods, not going through full charge cycles, etc.

The only worrying part of the whole thing is the battery is not removable or at least not meant to be user serviceable. So if the battery is degraded, replacing it would not be for the faint of heart. I would have to open it up again and while it may not be too difficult to switch out, it could be more difficult than I anticipate. Hopefully it does not come to needing to do this before its ran its course and I am ready to replace it.

Dell does have a method of testing all the hardware from the boot menu/in the BIOS. A few months back I did this and the battery health was under 70% which was a little concerning. However I looked again a few weeks ago and it was above 90%. This leaves me to believe that the battery health reading is either inaccurate or contrary to my understanding of it a dynamic measurement instead of a falling value comparing specd capacity vs current capacity.

Otherwise, this seems to be priced at ~$650 right now which is a steal to me, not having recently compared it to whats available. As per my initial list of things this model is missing that one may want (like thunderbolt, usb-c, NVMe slot, etc) it may now be possible to find those features along with what this model has for around the same price.

Last comment, I have been impressed with Dell's releasing BIOS and firmware updates for this model. Usually cheaper machines get 1 or 2 firmware updates and then nothing. This model has had about half a dozen BIOS updates (however the last being 8/2018) and a few patches related to Intel ME firmware which are important for security.

title: Mind the hinge
text:
I was convinced that I needed a combination of laptop and tablet with extra-long battery life. That's how I ended up with a Lenovo IdeaPad Yoga13. After the left hinge broke and I was forced to pay $187 to repair it because it wasn't covered under warranty, I was ready to swear off Lenovo entirely. But then the Flex 4 came along and here we go again.

So let's start with the hinge. It's clear the hinges have been reinforced on this latest version. There's no telling how it will hold up, but comparing the hinges between the two laptops shows that the Flex is definitely sturdier. The solid state drive makes the laptop heavier too, which can affect using the "tent" form of the Flex (a combination of tablet and laptop forms), but that's the trade off for a faster computer.

There's several other physical changes too. There's no longer a physical sound control, which is now managed by the F2 and F3 keys. The power cord is a downgrade; instead of a yellow connection it's more along the lines of an AC adapter with a hole for the thin plug on the left (rather than the Yoga's right) side.

Speaking of side changes, the power button moved from the Yoga's left front to the right side. This is an improvement, because my fitbit would accidentally shut the Yoga off while typing. The touch pad is also an improvement -- the Yoga was too sensitive but the Flex seems a little more tolerant. There's one USB on the left, and two USBs on the right. The video port was also moved to the right.

By far the most important part of the laptop's functionality is the gyroscope that gauges when the Flex is in laptop mode and when it's in tablet mode. The Flex seems a little less finicky in that regard, but this is just one additional component that is likely to degrade over time from heavy use.

In most other respects (processing speed, hard drive storage, screen size) the laptops are surprisingly similar. What I don't end up using is 1) the tablet mode, and 2) the fingerprint recognition which is totally unnecessary. Only time will tell if the Lenovo Flex learned from the Yoga's mistakes, but I'm cautiously optimistic.

title: Capture good images/vids, with a minimum of fuss, with my cellphone camera mounted on binoculars or a simple telescope
text:
[[VIDEOID:6e456aedeb6bfddc1779568f15e5a90]] I used the Snapzoom adapter to work directly with a pair of Fujinon 14x40 image stabilized binoculars, and also with a simple Astroscan reflecting telescope with 28 mm eyepiece lens. I am taking photos using my cellphone camera (iPhone 6 plus) and have been extremely pleased with the resulting photographs and videos. Being able to capture great looking images/vids, with a minimum of fuss, with my cellphone camera mounted on binoculars or a simple telescope is surprisingly useful, and allows me to record higher quality images that I previously tried to obtain in hit-and-usually-miss fashion with hand alignment.

I particularly appreciate being able to make double use of my binoculars+cellphone outside, rather than having to carry an SLR camera with large zoom lens. The binoculars also typically deliver more zoom than one can comfortably carry in an SLR. Obviously the binocular+cellphone will likely have a less sharp image/lower light collection than an SLR, but I found the quality of image achievable was really very impressive. I include a few examples of the original cellphone image and then one taken through the binoculars+snapzoom+cellphone. In regular daylight the image of birds at the top of a tree works extremely well. Even at sundown the images of the lighthouse and video of flying birds worked extremely well. I also shot an image of the moon through the Astroscan. There was minimum setup involved and the results were quite acceptable.

The Snapzoom is roughly 5” x 5” x 1.5” and weighs only 4 oz. It can be carried in a coat pocket. It is very well built and appears to be made from extremely durable plastics and metal. (Caveat: I have only had mine for about a week, but no signs of any weakness.) It can be adjusted in the field to hold the cellphone camera directly behind an eyepiece. The adjustability of the Snapzoom was well able to to accommodate the 3" width of my phone. The Snapzoom mounting jaw opens up to a maximum width of 3.5". The eye piece clamp opens up to accommodate a 2" diameter, and is designed for either a monocular mount or a binocular mount. In the latter case the phone uses just one of the eye pieces, but clamps to both for stability.

When mounted to the binocular the mechanical design of the Snapzoom makes it a rock solid attachment - no unwanted wiggle. The first screw adjust works well to tighten the grip around the two eye pieces. The second screw adjust firmly clamps the phone. If one wants to use the binoculars in conventional mode it is quick and easy to take the Snapzoom off, and then slip it on and tighten again for a photo. Once the adjustments are made for a given cellphone you don’t appear to need to make any further adjustments other than simply opening and closing the screw clamps to insert the cellphone and mount on the binocular. The process of getting good optical alignment initially requires a little bit of finesse. One does appear to need to use a little digital zoom to remove the vignette (dark circle) around the edge of the photo, but this is only around 1.2x in my case. It really just amounts to cropping the image slightly.

With mounting on a telescope one find that the Snapzoom will tend to rotate the single eye piece. The company provides an adjustable balance weight to even the rotational load on the eye piece. This operation a little more fiddly, but still works easily enough to make one keen to capture new astronomical images.

I intend to continue to use the Snapzoom when at sporting events with my binoculars, or ready in my coat pocket when walking in the field. It will also work when looking to record a quick image from a telescope in the field. It is very quick to mount, feels solid and allows one to capture surprisingly good quality images.

Photographs/video taken with iPhone 6+ with and without snapzoom+binoculars:
Tree (middle of photo) with birds at top - regular iPhone 6+ field of view
Just top of tree using binoculars 14x + snap zoom + camera phone
Lighthouse (middle of photo) at cloudy sunset - regular iPhone 6+ field of view
Lighthouse (middle of photo) at cloudy sunset - using binoculars 14x + snap zoom + same camera phone
Snapzoom mounted on binoculars from two different angles
Video of Lighthouse (middle of photo) at cloudy sunset using binoculars 14x + snap zoom + same camera phone

( I bought the previous Snapzoom that worked with smaller cellphones. This new model Snapzoom was provided to me free as a review item. )

CON's

title: Great Little Record and Cassette Audio Capture Device
text:
For the cost, this is just simply amazing. First, at least on Windows 7, there is no driver to install. When I plugged it into my Windows 7 x64 machine, Windows recognized it and installed its own driver. Second there is a newer version of the free Audacity software that comes with it that you can download from the internet. If you are coming from vinyl to the computer, you will need a preamp between the turntable and this device UNLESS the turntable has a built-in preamp. Some do. Then open Audacity, select the "USB microphone" input. Yes, Windows call it a microphone but that does not affect anything. You will also want to turn on play through so you can listen while you record (Edit->Preferences->Recording then check "Software Playthrough."). The process becomes four steps: (1) Capture, (2) Click Removal (3) Normalize (4) Label Tracks and (5) Export to MP3, WAV, FLAC, AIFF, etc.

For converting cassettes, things are easier. Just connect the cassette player to the device, record, label and export. You do not need any kind of amplifier between the cassette player and this device.

title: Best of the current crop of streaming boxes.
text:
I've uesd a ton of streaming boxes over the years. Dozens of them. The new Fire TV is quite possibly the best of the latest crop. It's got a powerful CPU and a GPU good enough to play even some of the most demanding games. It has 802.11ac wireless built in. Setup couldn't have been more painless. It even knew who I was and asked if I wanted to use my amazon account right out of the box (I assume they register that on the box before shipping. It'll do 4K UHD video, has a micro-sd slot and comes with a 32GB card to get started, and has a usb port for hooking up external media. It does only support 30fps 4K video but that is acceptable as 4K media is still in short supply anyway, let alone 60fps media. It will definitely be needed in the next version of the hardware though.

The game controller makes an acceptable remote control, but I ordered the voice remote along with it and actually used that right out of the box. The game controller, interestingly enough, did not pair up immediately and I had to pull the batteries and the power to the firetv in order for it to find the controller. Once it was paired though I never had another issue with it.

I had been using Plex on my Xbox One, but that version of the software is so incredibly flaky that merely adding files to the plex libraries required me to kill the app on the XB1 and restart it in order for it to see the changes. Plex on the Fire TV has been perfect. No hiccups, no random disconnects from the server, always detects changes to libraries and updates them...

All around amazing piece of kit.

I took the step of cloning the device's MAC (hardware) address with that of my PC that was configuring the device (it will see that automatically in the "clone this MAC" page.
At the hotel I powered up, plugged into wall data port ( it seems my hotel did not have an authentication login page).
Within a few secs, the green blinking light went to green and all my devices were live on Internet wifi.
As for the throughput.....amazing, it lives up to it's rated speed, my son's XBOX game showed no lag whatsoever, and my web browsing was instant.
I ran a VPN back to my office, my wife was watching live shows on web based Directv, and no lag anywhere.
This device is a steal for under $30.

Update Oct-2017: I wanted to provide an update to my initial review. I have used this battery heavily over the last 10 months, running down and recharging the battery at least a few times every week. According to BatteryCare the wear level is at 27% and total capacity is down to 58 Wh. Not bad considering the heavy usage it has been under! It has held up better over time than other (higher priced) batteries I have purchased, many which failed me around the 6 month mark. At this price, I would definitely recommend this battery to other shoppers.
