title: How to determine if this Arlo camera will work for you
text:
I am writing this review in hopes of clarifying for potential buyers what the Arlo wireless video monitoring system is and what it is not. I read a lot of reviews before I purchased mine. They were mostly positive reviews that talked about what the Arlo can do, and rarely did they talk about what the Arlo does not do. It seems many of these people were testing the system to rate it, but not really using it for any specific, intended purpose. I think the Arlo system can be a great system for a subset of people, but I think for many others (myself included), the deficiencies negate the benefits.
The reason I bought the Arlo was that my wife wanted to monitor a couple corners of our yard where there are gaps between fencing or hedges. We have a Dropcam, which we like, but it is an indoor-only camera. And they charge $10/mo to store 7 days history in the cloud. I looked at normal video monitoring systems, but they all required cables of some sort, either for power or to connect to the base. I am a lazy installer. I don’t mind setting up the technical parts, but I prefer not to have to drill holes and string cable. When I found the Arlo wireless system, it sounded perfect. It is waterproof, so it is indoor/outdoor. It is battery powered, so it doesn’t need to be plugged in. It is wireless, so it doesn’t need to connect to the base unit. The base unit plugs into power and to my home wifi router, but that is all inside the house, so that’s fine. And Arlo provides 7 day history in the cloud for free. The Arlo gets good reviews. In general, it seemed like a wire-free, outdoor version of the Dropcam. It seemed quality-wise, maybe it’s not quite as good, but considering the extras (wirefree, outdoor, free history) and that is cost about the same as the Dropcam, it seemed like a good choice. And so I bought the 2-camera system.
The system itself was easy to set up, both the base unit as well as the cameras. There is a mobile app and a website. Both were also easy to set up. And as expected, the cameras mounted outside without any wires or cables. So far so good…
However, one of the cameras got false alerts almost every minute. It seems the leaves blowing in the wind caused it to go off. I changed the level from 80% down to 10% and it seemed to help. The other camera rarely triggered an alert. Even with a cat clearing on the path where the camera was pointed, the system never noticed. I started doing more research online and that’s when I found out the biggest difference between this Arlo system and others.
Most other systems, like the Dropcam, videotape 24/7. They notify you when there is movement anywhere in the video (or you can create a zone to limit the area where it looks). You can set the monitoring to certain times (so you don’t get blasted with alerts) or you can turn the camera off, but otherwise they are constantly recording. And you can go back and look at these recordings later.
The Arlo camera actually consists of two parts: the camera and the motion detector. This is an important difference because of the way Arlo is designed. Since it is powered by batteries, it needs to conserve power. It does this by turning off the camera. So about 99% of the time, the camera is in standby mode and it is not recording any video and not sending anything to the cloud. The second part is the motion detector and that stays on all the time. The only time the camera turns on is when motion is detected. One problem with this is lag time. If someone is walking quickly, the may be gone by the time the camera starts recording. The Arlo tip is to use two cameras: one to detect the motion and a different one to take the video. Kind of an expensive workaround, but could be effective.
The bigger problem, at least for me, is that the motion detector is different from the motion detectors for other cameras. Most systems look for motion within the video they are recording. Since the Arlo camera isn’t even turned on, this is impossible. Instead, Arlo uses a heat-based motion detector. This would be ok (I don’t care how it detects motion as long as it detects it), but its heat sensor only works for a very small area. They claim it works up to 20 feet. I think it’s about 15 feet. But it is definitely NOT the same as the area that is in the video. It is much, much smaller. Also they say it detects cross traffic well, but has difficulty detecting motion coming towards it. Huh? That’s not good…
I have one camera pointed to one corner of my yard, past the driveway and the other pointed to a different corner following a path. Although the leaves near the camera can blow in the wind and set off the alerts, I can jump up and down in the driveway and nothing happens. This is because I am 15 or 20 feet away. The corner that I want to monitor is about 40 feet, so no chance of that triggering. The other camera is pointed at a path. Only when I walk directly in front of the camera (the middle of the path) will it detect me. I want it to detect movement all along the path, not just a small portion of it.
The other problem is with the 7 day history. With the Dropcam, they save 7 days of history, meaning there are recordings for every hour, every minute. They have markers where there was activity, but even if there is no activity you can still view the history. With the Arlo, it saves video clips that were triggered during the last 7 days. Video clips are 10 seconds by default (or up to 120 seconds if you change the setting) but you only record a clip if the heat-sensor detects motion. If not, there is no video. Thus, you could check the 7 day history, and you might not have anything to view. You cannot go back and look at the previous night, for instance, if there were no alerts.
Although this system does not work for my intended purposes, it should have value for some people. It is truly wire-free and it’s easy to set up. The night vision works well and it takes decent videos. It probably works well indoors, although I would recommend a Dropcam over Arlo for indoor monitoring as it has a lot more features and wires shouldn’t be an issue indoors. It would also work well for a small, well-defined space, like a front porch or doorway. But it definitely does not work for larger spaces, like yards and paths and even the driveway.
I buy mostly from Amazon prime, but I was being cheap and stupid when I bought this. In order to avoid $30 tax, I bought from a different retailer. That was a mistake. Now, if I return this, they charge $45 for restocking and I have to pay my own shipping $10. So I may just keep it and find another use for it. title: AWESOME new version. A must have to cut down on cable costs.
text:
We have been using The Roku products for YEARS. This is by far the best yet. The voice search option is great addition. The wifi connection faster, browsing easier. All around A+ for this model.
* It is very easy to skip the credit card request when creating your account online via a tablet. One little blue Button under the all the credit card info that says SKIP. It will tell you to rent a movie you will be required to enter a credit card/debit card, click ok and off you go.
*The remote has changed a bit, still has the headphone jack, lost the wrist strap, added direct buttons for Netflix and three others, and the back loop button was replaced with a search button.
*The Roku remote app still works and with voice search. (I.E. iPod, tablets, smartphones etc.). I LOVE this app since it had a drop down touch screen keyboard. Easier than arrowing around clicking ok on each letter) So there is no need to buy additional remotes.
*The sound quality through the remote jack seems to be smoother than the older version Roku 3 remote. (Ours stopped working on the older version of the Roku 3, had to buy a new remote)
*The loss of the wrist strap wasn't an issue for us, we don't play games on it, or use it for anything other than to reach it off the table lol
*We would not upgrade to this model just for the few added items, unless we got a TV in another room. The Roku sticks are nice, but SLOW, buffering often.
*My review is not as technical as some others. I just reviewed it as a normal everyday user.
*This was purchased for my parents who are in their early 60's. I set it up for them, since we all know can take some time activating/authorizing new devices for applications. Once that was done, I ran through the basics of how it works, streaming channels etc. They were able to breeze through it.
*The voice search option is great for them. Patience and eye sight is not a something some older folks have when introduced to new stuff. Cable costs have gotten so out of control, this product helps with a budget.

title: Sound is fine. Mounting is a nightmare.
text:
I'm pleased with the sound but I must give 3 stars at best purely for the ridiculous installation. The original reviewer complaining about the 'size of the screw' left us hanging as to what exactly the problem was. I will expand on what he said.

I don't think they make screws with the outer diameter of the heads small enough to actually work with the stupid-small mount tabs they provide. When you screw the screw in all the way, the top 2 screw holes (there are 3 holes in a triangular shape) are positioned so close to the tab/flange that they mash it towards the wall, making it impossible to set the speaker mounting notch onto it. You have to back the screw out to let the tab/flange relax back to a decent distance from the wall.
You are then left with a wobbly mount.

And forget wall anchors. The screw holes are so close on the mounting bracket that you can't put the wall anchors in the drywall without chewing up all the 'grip' area.

Harmon Kardon wall mount geniuses -- please include the screws to mount these things because I will probably have to get a machine shop to build me what I need.. Gheez.

title: Prepare to be frustrated, and your bedmate will hate you.
text:
It's hard to recall ever being this frustrated with the controls on a piece of hardware. I've had this thing for almost *two years* and STILL hit the wrong buttons when trying to set my alarm at night — the buttons for which are in various positions on the rounded edge of the device (some on the left around 10 o'clock, some around 2 o'clock and a few others nearby), often causing the sleep timer, the button for which is about an inch away from the alarm B activation button, to turn on which quickly ramps the light up to full brightness before you can easily find the button on the *opposite side* of the clock to turn back off. If you really mess up, the radio will come on too. Next up, the buttons on the front you use to adjust the clock settings CLICK pretty loudly, even when holding a +/- button to change the minutes. Alarm set for 9:00 and you want 9:30? Prepare to make 30 rapid, loud clicking sounds. My workaround is to keep alarm A set to an even hour number like 9:00 and alarm B set to 9:30 (opposite side, deal with it) so I only have to set one of the two and adjust the hour by hopefully a click or two versus having to click through 30 minutes. Want 9:15? 15 clicks, deal with it. Share a bed with someone who is a light sleeper that might be awakened by any of this nonsense? Tough.

Original review was rejected for profanity.

text:
Picked up a pair of Sennheiser CX 880's shortly after my original CX 300's had a wire failure as a result of a good 7 years of use (oddly enough the same month that a driver died in my PC350's after 5+ years), and I got exactly what I expected.

Sound quality does not disappoint. The low-range response is nice and punchy with minimal distortion. Mid-range is clean as well, but the high-end has a touch of flatness to it. Obviously geared for the quality low to mid-range. Volume control is more of a design element than a technical feature... sound distortion is distinct when making adjustments which is disappointing knowing Sennheiser has inline volume controls which work cleanly. Cord noise is minimal during normal "sitting" use. When more active, it's noticeable like any ear canal headphone I've experienced but definitely minimized compared to my old 300's.

Carrying case (with magnetic closure) and accessories are nice and usual high quality from Sennheiser. Standard set of 3 earbud sizes included for customized fit. Design of these has been improved since the earlier model I've been used to. Newer inserts have a more rigid plastic base and more pliable externals allowing a more snug but comfortable fit inside the ear canal with less play.

title: I'm taking control of my telephone with this
text:
I like my CPR Callblocker. It has definitely quieted things down at this house.
First, I manually entered about 30 numbers that had been bothering us for awhile. I have just a simple one-phone line on a cable modem, but I keep the callblocker next to the modem where I sit at the computer a lot, and the phone is in another room. Serial or parallel wiring both work, but I keep it in serial mode so I can manually block numbers if necessary.
The phone service does not like the double-star codes, but pound-star works fine.
I have blocked four more numbers with the "Block Now" button. If I don't recognize the number I block first and look up the number later. I like how easy it is to unblock a number you blocked by mistake. There is room for so many numbers in the callblocker, I'll never fill it up.

title: If you are caught between buying the JBL Xtreme and the UE Megaboom, this review is for you!
text:
I purchased a UE Megaboom, not from amazon, but from best buy because i'm super impatient.

Initially i was caught between buying the JBL Xtreme and the UE Megaboom because they were both rugged speakers designed for the outdoors. Primary usage for this speaker would be around bodies of water so it needed to have some form of water resistance. In this review im going to use the Harman Kardon Onyx as a benchmark for some aspects of comparison.

SOUND QUALITY:

The UE Megaboom has a very balanced sound, it is not super bass heavy like the JBL Xtreme, but it can definitely hold its own. One thing i should mention is that the JBL Xtreme is only water RESISTANT, it is not waterproof and submersable like the UE Megaboom. This aspect will definitely affect sound quality because as we know, bass is created by air movement. When you have a watertight space, it makes releasing air difficult. The Megaboom has 4 passive radiators to remedy this issue. The JBL Xtreme only requires 2 because it is only water resistant and is designed with the radiators on the end of the device. It is impossible to get a waterproof speaker to sound like, say, a Harman Kardon Onyx because the Onyx cant even go near moisture, it has a radiator and absolutely no water protection so it can move the most air and create the most bass tones. That being said, the UE Megaboom has a very solid sound that can keep up well with many different styles of music.

I put the UE Megaboom through a series of tests with different styles of music from the Amazon Music streaming service, here are my findings

Hip-Hop: Hold On, Were Going Home - Drake
This song's tight, punchy bass comes through super bright on the UE Megaboom. Vocals are also clean and bright. it struggles slightly with the deep sub-bass tones, but that is to be expected from two 2 inch drivers. The most important aspects of the song come through.

Pop: Get Lucky - Daft Punk
This is a song i have heard on a multitude of different speakers so i would say that i know how this song should sound. On the UE Megaboom, this song's rich, warm tone comes through beautifully! The speaker has no problem clearly differentiating the guitar from the bass guitar. Pharrell's vocal tone also comes through nicely also. When the robot's start to sing towards the end, the treble tones are incredible and come through loud and clear, but not enough to drown out the rest of the tones.

Classic Rock: Panama - Van Halen
Rock music is really where the UE Megaboom shines. This song sounds good on just about any speaker, but on the UE megaboom, it makes it sound like youre hearing them live. The guitars come through very nicely and compliments the bass tones from the drum kit. Guitar solos come through incredibly since they consist of treble tones, which the Megaboom is able to replicate clearly.

Reggae: One Love - Bob Marley
Reggae music is not a bad option for this speaker. On a remastered version of Bob Marley's One Love, each instrument comes through the clearest of all the genres i have played so far. It is super bright and clear, that is all i can say. Buy one and listen for yourself.

EDM: Be Right There - Diplo & Sleepy Tom
EDM is a genre that is rather hit or miss on the UE Megaboom. Some songs can sound good and some not so much. Be Right There by Diplo and Sleepy Tom is a great example of EDM that sounds fantastic on the Megaboom. Bass tones come through with a nice rumble. Between bass and the majority of the treble tones, the Megaboom has no issues differentiating them. By the time the first drop comes around, the Megaboom handles the bassline fairly well. We do not get very much of the super deep sub-bass, but we get the bass tones that matter.

Country: Brad Paisley - Water
It is at this point that i am starting to see a pattern between the UE Megaboom's clear tones and organic instruments, and Brad Paisley's Water is no exception. Brad's vocals come through very strong and the guitar tones benefit as they are complimentary. Like in the rock genre, guitar solos come through very clear and clean.

VOLUME:
I usually listened to the Megaboom at around 40-50% volume. Playing an hour of music at 75% volume got me a nice note from my neighbors on my door (I live in a college dorm with thin walls). So trust me when i say, volume is not an issue with the Megaboom, its got a ton of oomph behind it!

Now lets compare features and weigh out the Pros and Cons.

BATTERY LIFE:
The JBL Xtreme only gets a 15 hour battery life while the Megaboom keeps the party going for an additional 5 hours.
You are able to charge your phone on the JBL Xtreme while you cant on the megaboom, but with the money you save buying the Megaboom, you can buy yourself one of those power banks to charge your phone from. One other advantage is that if you have a Power Bank, you can charge the Megaboom off of that since it charges via USB instead of a proprietary plug that reminds me alot of the one that came with my Harman Kardon Onyx.

EASE OF USE:
The Megaboom and the JBL Xtreme rival in their ease of use. Both have a complimentary app and they both have some form of social mode. They both are able to pair a second speaker to create stereo sound. Do i have the budget for that? Heck no, but it would sure be cool to see them work in tandem! Once you get the Megaboom charged (It requires at least 6 hours for the initial charge, the charging light will stop flashing when it is fully charged), turn it on, and you can get it paired to your device within 30 seconds initially. Once its paired to a device it will pair almost instantly once turned on.

SIZE:
The UE Megaboom is about the size of a 40oz HydroFlask. It is skinnier by about 1/4 inch which makes toting it considerably easier. Its weight is about half of the JBL Xtreme which also makes portability a win for the Megaboom. The JBL Xtreme is heavy, weighing in at almost 5 pounds. JBL knows its heavy too because it comes with a shoulder strap. The Megaboom can be easily tossed into a backpack while the Xtreme requires you to carry it off body which could limit the places you could take it.

CARE:
Both the JBL Xtreme and the UE Megaboom can be cleaned under a running faucet. However, i believe the UE Megaboom can handle water better since it is IPX7 waterproof and can be submerged for up to 30 minutes in 3 feet of water. I would honestly be wary about a device that can be cleaned under a faucet, but you cant submerge it (JBL, im looking at you). Both the JBL and the UE have the same woven skin over the speaker which gives it a really unique look. Ive heard that the fabric is plasma coated which gives it its water resistance.

SUPPORT:
The UE Megaboom has a 2 year warranty and a battery replacement service (yes, the battery is replaceable!). For 49 bucks you send your Megaboom to Logitech and they replace your battery. The JBL Xtreme is a sealed unit and the battery is not replaceable, or it is and they dont advertise it like Logitech does, its kind of a mystery.

CONCLUSION:
While yes, the JBL Xtreme may sound better, it has some limiting factors that affects intended usage. When i think "rugged speaker", i want to be able to take it everywhere without worrying about damage. Since the UE Megaboom is not only waterproof but also shockproof, i believe that it is a superior rugged speaker in terms of the amount of abuse it could be able to handle. The only speaker that may surpass it in ruggedness is the Braven BRV-PRO which is designed to go wherever a go-pro can go because of its mount but you are sacrificing sound quality at an even greater level for ruggedness. The UE megaboom is a great compromise between ruggedness and sound quality and i would recommend it to anyone heading out on adventures and wants a great sounding speaker to take with them!

title: Solid predecessor to the KEF LS50W
text:
I've seen some reviews on here saying these are thinner and lacking bass compared to comparably priced systems. I want to say that this couldn't be farther from the truth.

These speakers are all about placement and room selection. If you want to fill a larger room, get larger speakers. I wouldn't use these in a room over 200 square feet and make sure they're somewhat close, but not too close so the bass ports can breathe, to a wall and these are are impossible to beat for under $1000. They'll play just as loud and have just as much bass as my Pioneer SA-7500II with JBL 4408 setup but are a much finer in detail and broader in soundstage.

Also, don't get these unless you're willing to shell out a bit more for higher quality digital files. They sound great with Spotify Premium and will sound even better with FLAC files. Don't use anything less than 320kbps on these because they'll expose the flaws in the audio file...which is what I suspect is the problem with a lot of the negative reviews on here.

The build quality on these is amazing, the setup is completely effortless, and the sound--lows, highs, mids--are all impeccable. These give my Yamaha A-S801 with JBL 4410A setup a real run for their money. Forget the negative reviews, you can't beat these for the price, especially when they KEF puts them on sale.

title: A great price on a good MP3 player.
text:
I wanted an MP3 player to replace my aging Sansa Clips. Two things I wanted: a long lasting battery and the ability to use cards bigger than 32Gb.

This player exceeded my expectations on those two points. Battery life is great. I tested a Lexar 32Gb card, a SanDisk 32Gb card, and a SanDisk 64Gb card. All worked perfectly. And after I read some reviews I tested a PNY 128GB card and it works as well. I imagine a 200GB card might even work.

Now for the problems. I use this exclusively for podcasts so take that into account. First problem is the directory structure. It lists files by date copied and not by file name. Second problem is the fast forward. It is fine for a 4 minute song but if you want to get to hour 2 of a 4 hour podcast, you'll be pressing the button for a while. Third problem is the fact that it doesn't save your place (it has bookmarks but I don't like having to set a bookmark every time I turn the player off). So when you turn the player back on you have to start the file from scratch. All annoying issues but not deal breakers.

If you want a Clip replacement, this is probably the best you'll get for the price.

title: These are version 2.  They're better than version 1, and  better than the PolarPro filters
text:
I chose these over the PolarPro filters because the ND/CPLs offered by PolarPro have a plastic base with an aluminum/glass lens element. These FStop Labs CPLs have no plastic on them. Both the base of the CPL element and the glass mount are made of annodized Aluminum, and the rotation of the element is smooth. Both the FStop Labs and the PolarPro's ND-only filters are aluminum.

All 6 of the FStop Labs filters engage and disengage with the appropriate amount of resistance, and all remain reliably attached without any noise/rattle/jiggle when attached, just like the factory UV filter

These filters (like any good M2P filter) has small steel inserts where the camera's ball-detent engages to keep the filter secure. This prevents wear to the aluminum.

For me, quality is everything, and I have bought the best filters I could find.

I did initially wish for a filter removal tool, similar to the one that PolarPro includes for free, because I think it would definitely help a novice with the tricky business installing/removing filters from the M2P camera. Ultimately, after you learn the trick, the microfiber cloth is more useful than the tool, keeping your dirty paws off the filter glass, and conveniently giving you a way to clean the errant smudge now and again.

Finally, about the gimbal covers:
Both the FStop Labs and the PolarPro filters claim not to interfere with the gimbal cover placement. I can vouch for these being 100 perfect in that regard. PolarPro claims the same, but I wonder if the larger diameter of the PP CPLs makes the process *slightly* more fiddly than it is compared to the FStop filters.

title: Superb Mouse, A Bit Heavy For FPS
text:
The Basics

121-ish grams WITHOUT optional weights installed. 3366 sensor. 20M omrons. RGB lighting. Went to a Best Buy to pick up the G903. Tried G903, did not like shape. Tried G502, liked. Left store, meditated upon previous dislike for ugly G502 “spaceship design.” Meditated upon adopting a mouse that seems to weight twice as much as my truck. Bought G502 online next day. Proceeded to enjoy.

Why do a G502 review when the mouse has been around forever? Because it is still a relevant choice on the market, because I like going Nit-Noid on mice, because this mouse deserves the attention it gets, and because pleas need to be made to properly update a winning formula. Testing time prior to review was 19 days.

The Good

Very good for fingertip, that style feels good even with the heavy weight taken into consideration.

Good materials. Quality rubber flanks with some nice patterning action going on.

Excellent 3366 sensor, low LOD. Surface tuning option did seem to make a positive difference.

Good clicks everywhere. Primary clicks are medium stiffness and manage to have excellent feedback without being terribly loud.

Excellent thumb buttons, no travel or rattle issues. They are labeled, (nice little touch) and all have light actuation with good tactility. All buttons on the mouse are good, but I do think they would be better with a textured finish as found on the G203.

Logitech has excellent software. Reliable, intuitive, functional albeit limited in the total number of bells and whistles available compared to a growing portion of the competition.

The software enables use of the G-Shift option. Basically you can map your mouse to act as a “shift key” so that virtually all the other buttons on the mouse perform an additional function when pressed with the said shift key.

Good sniper/extra buttons, I think they are conveniently placed for medium hands and work well. I immediately missed the extra functions when I swapped away from this mouse.

Infinite scroll is a nice option. I didn’t know how much I would use it...until I ended up using it a lot. Another thing easily missed switching away from the mouse…

Apparently durable scroll design. I have no intention of opening this mouse up, part of the reason for that is because there are a number of good teardown videos out there. One thing I learned from a teardown vid is that the regular scroll mode gets its tactility from a plastic arm in contact with the inside of the scroll wheel. That arrangement seems like it would be more durable than what you typically see in most mice.

A tilt scroll option is not only present, it is easy to use with mercifully light actuation.

Between the infinite scroll, extra buttons and tilt function, I found the G502 superb for word processing. I had backspace set to one side of the tilt scroll, and the “end” key mapped to the other. The additional index finger keys were mapped to copy and paste, just for fun. Between the G-Shift and switching profiles on the fly, you can quickly run into more options than you can quickly memorize.

The Middling

Decent looks in my opinion, but it took a while to get there. If you don’t like the looks, all you need to do is think of its functionality, you can stab someone or club them with this mouse. Many uses, such versatile.

The Bad

Scroll wheel is metal and not rubberized – it feels cold, often a little slick. Rubber should have been an update on the Spectrum model.

The braided cord is what I would call moderate-stiff, definitely room for improvement.

Scroll tactility is quite good, but rather clunky. Also, there is enough mass to the scroll wheel that you can overscroll easily in some situations.

Scroll rattles, sometimes even in game. Not a huge distraction, minor gripe compared to the convenience of having infinite scroll available.

Heavy weight means a lot more inertia for fast-paced FPS. This is an area where this really good all-rounder isn’t so well rounded. The weight means that picking it up is not completely transparent to your mind in-game, even after a week of use. It did go away eventually for me. This mouse is probably unusable for FPS for players who operate below 1000 DPI, even then it is not ideal.

Okay for small palm and medium fingertip, but larger hands (18.5cm+) that try to palm will probably drag their pinky or feel annoyed trying to keep it off the mousepad.

There is space for a passable claw grip, but the 502’s weight means you have to squeeze that much more with limited thumb surface area. This seems a good recipe for hand fatigue/discomfort over time.

Scroll toggle button is useful, but would be better as the rearmost of the two buttons behind the scroll. Sure it makes a harder engineering problem, but that is why Logitech employs engineers.

Rather narrow grip width caused some ring finger fatigue. I always thought of the G502 as a larger mouse, it actually isn’t as big as it looks. Making the mouse slightly wider with slight modifications would make it much more comfy and easier to pick up at the same time since more of fingers 4 and 5 would end up in contact with the side of the mouse. The right-side grip surface should flare out slightly more to right with same basic curvature. It would also be good to raise the height of the right side grip section by 2mm to be just slightly more similar to the G403. Forward of the scroll wheel on the right side (where the ring finger goes), the lip section should be flattened slightly to give more options to ring fingers.

The primary click button was loose in the upward direction. On my copy, if the index finger is not perfectly dry, the mouse button adheres to it and gets pulled upward with the finger and results in a distracting rattle when the two go their separate ways. This was one of the most annoying issues with the mouse. Thankfully it was easily fixed. I put a piece of tape along the front seam of LMB, preventing it from traveling upward out of position.

Failure to update and missed opportunities. The Proteus core was released some 3 years ago. The Spectrum is still on store shelves some two years after Logitech updated their G logo. Kinda advertises that it is an “old” mouse. Logitech isn’t putting 50m omrons on the mouse. Redundantly...no rubber scroll and no attempt at weight reduction with the Spectrum release. Makes me sad. Worse, the G900 weights 15 grams less and it is wireless. For the Spectrum update, Logitech simply added RGB to the logo and deleted some teal from the thumb rest. If it had been my company doing such a minor change, I would have simply updated the mouse and let people notice the fact there was a nice little production update.

Conclusion

Despite the fact this is an older design, the Proteus Spectrum is still a good design that holds up well in many areas. One of the best compliments I can give the G502 is that I’m not terribly tempted to go back to my G403, probably my fave mouse of all time - and that is coming from someone who, until recently, was looking for a 70 gram gaming mouse. Is the 502 ideal for FPS? Nope. But, it is still probably the best all-round mouse I’ve used. This mouse’s “honeymoon phase” lasted almost two weeks, an eternity for me. That’s part of why I kept using this mouse as long as I did – I didn’t want to move on. It’s not perfect, and there are several legitimate gripes. This mouse’s shortcoming are all the more painful because without them this mouse could have been A+ material so easily. That said, I look forward to using it a lot more. I hope we see a “G503” come out in a wired and wireless version. The wired version should retain the basic shape with all the buttons and be no more than 100g with adjustable weights, 110g for starters with the wireless version. I can dream.

title: Great camera... EXCEPT it doesn't save your WiFi password or Facebook login info!
text: I did a lot of reading and research before deciding to purchase this camera. It gets terrific customer reviews and it got positive reviews by various places on the Internet when it came out. It has a nice solid feel and user-friendly design, and it's packed with terrific features. I received it this afternoon and was happily exploring the various features and getting to know the camera, when I came across one deal-breaking stumbling block for me. Unfortunately, the one thing that I didn't read about in any of those reviews before I purchased it (and it was certainly NOT mentioned in the product description) is going to be the main reason I return it: It does NOT save your WiFi password or your Facebook login info (or presumably the login info for any of the other services you might want to use, such as Picasa). This means that after you turn off the camera and some time has passed, it loses that info and you have to re-enter it all if you want to quickly post a photo of Facebook. Good grief, doesn't that defeat the purpose of a WiFi camera?? Since I decided to buy a WiFi digital camera just for ease of sharing with other people (whether by e-mail, posting on a website, etc), this is a HUGE disappointment and a big design flaw! Even low-end smartphones can save that kind of information, so it really boggles my mind that Samsung put this camera on the market without including this functionality. AND I'm surprised that I didn't run across references to this issue in the reviews I read. I'll be sorry to send this camera back, because there's so much I liked about it. But having to enter a complex 16-digit WiFi key and then manually logging in anytime you want to post a photo? No thanks. By the way, I did go to the Samsung website and chatted with a Customer Service rep there who was very pleasant and did some digging and confirmed that this is indeed the case with this camera. Such a disappointment. He did say that the Samsung Galaxy Camera 2 will save that information, so I guess I'll start doing some reading up on that one and also see what else is out there in other brands. :( I'm so disappointed!

title: Nice Light-weight, compact tripod for travel or backpacking.
text:
I've had this for about two months, now, so I can't speak to the long-term durability. In the short-term, it's been working very nicely. I like the compact size and light weight. It fits nicely into my photo backpack (I have an Amazons essentials photo back pack, which I will have to review elsewhere), and would fit into any other backpack, small duffle bag, or any rolling luggage. It also comes with a small over-the-shoulder bag of its own, if you want to carry it that way. There are multiple locking stops for how wide you want to splay the legs, and three folding locks for the tripod legs as you telescope them out. You can also slide the middle support up a bit, as well. I actually did full extend the legs and raise the center support to max, to shoot over a railing. Long, nighttime exposures, with a super wide angle lens. The results were quite nice, but, again, this was with a super wide angle lens.

I don't know how they calculate the maximum payload weight. It might be that they know the leg supports would telescope back in if you over load it? I haven't come anywhere close to that point. The legs are definitely spindly if fully extended. The heaviest load I shot with was with a Sigma 100-400mm C lens, which is only supposed to weigh about 2.5 pounds (though it seems heavier!). I shot a Nikon D3400, so that's also pretty light. However, because there is no collar mount for the Sigma lens, you've got the 2.5 pounds of lens leaning out in front of the camera. That's enough torque to make adjusting the tripod a little tricky. You need to tighten the ball head lock with the lens pointing a bit above target, as it will still sag a bit after tightening. Especially noticeable when you're shooting telephoto. On the other hand, when I was shooting super wide angle, everything moved smoothly and locked down tightly. If you can keep your payload balanced, that's how things should be. In other words, I think the camera movement upon tightening is more a function of the lens design than the tripod design.

On a more general note, these ball head mounts are just wonderful for shooting dslr. In contrast to the old pan-and-tilt mounts, these are much quicker and easier to get level for either panorama or portrait mode, especially for lighter and well-balanced loads. As noted above, with the long and unbalanced telephoto lens, it was a little tougher, but still easier than with a pan-and-tilt. However, if you do want to pan, there is the built-in bubble level. I may add a few shots taken while using the tripod, just to demonstrate the stability.

title: Tuning, mounting, and more to be considered before purchasing.
text: This thing looks like the Pixar lamp.  The Cloud Cam security camera comes with a swivel-head camera, mounting bracket, screws/mounting inserts, a fairly long power cord, and instructions.  Once plugged in and Cloud Cam App is downloaded, I needed to connect the camera to my WiFi.  After that, you just need to get accustomed to the settings.  There are not as many options as I had imagined.  The more useful options come with monthly payments is called the “Cloud Cam Plan” (sold here on Amazon; it is a plan that allows extra features and additional perks), but I detest monthly rip-offs so I will not be purchasing this plan, especially since I already paid for something expensive like a high definition camera.  At first the motion sensor would trip routinely from a big Monstera leaf blowing in my yard and notifications were spam messaging my phone via the Cloud Cam App.  Luckily there is an option to control how many and when notifications are to be sent out.  The options allowed me to lower the sensitivity to the medium setting with “human-sized” objects at ten feet, so, I think I got it to a more reasonable setting for my home.  Had it been the upgraded plan, I believe you could schedule specific zones and detect persons, so, not enough to justify an annual fee.  The camera is stationary and does not move on it’s own, but it does have night vision so you can see facial features of people in the dark.  The camera also allows you to use a two-way microphone through your phone via the Cloud Cam app so you can talk directly to whoever is near the camera and hear what they have to say.  Kind of creepy, and possibly shockingly so for burglars (especially at night).  One option available (without the plan) is the ability to turn the camera off automatically when you are at home.  More accurately, it is what your phone’s location settings show that you are at the same location as your camera.  I prefer to leave the camera on at all times, so I will also not be using this option so I can record intruders breaking into my home if, say, I am asleep.  This may not be for those who are too paranoid of government spying or hackers waiting to get you.  All purchasers must accept the possibility of hackers finding a way to hack this camera, but for me, I doubt it they will get any useful information out of me even if they do hack mines.  I am more afraid of my computer being hacked than a stationary security camera that is watching a doorway.  I also would prefer that there is some way to record thieves breaking into my house when I am not there, and having something to show the authorities if my house was robbed.  But hey, that is just my opinion.  If you do not like the camera on, there are some settings allowing you to turn the camera off completely whenever you want in the app.

title: UBP-X800 w/second HDMI for Audio only ROCKS!
text:

What impressed me about this 4P player is that Sony put a second HDMI outputs on this player. There is 1 HDMI output for the Projector/TV (High Speed) and the second HDMI output for audio (no video content, just Dolby 7.1) which plugs into our Non-4K yamaha reciever. Eventually we will upgrade the receiver to one that supports ATMOS and 4K HDR, but for now we can still get 7.1 Audio (Lossless). You can use the TOSLINK, but the sound seems to get stepped on pretty hard. The Audio only HDMI shows that Sony is watching out for what new customer are going to need as they move to 4K.

One last note: Of the half dozen 4K movies we picked up none have HD audio, they all have Dolby 7.1 and Atmos. I'm guessing the Dolby HD and DTS Audio Master are being replaced by Atmos and Dolby-X.

title: A Beast of a laptop, future proof as well
text:
So I've had my MSI GTVR for a little over a week now and let me say it is an absolute beast. I previously owned a MSI GS70 stealth which did me well for the last 3 years but it was time for an upgrade, I use these gaming laptops as a desktop & for the 1st time I have full desktop lvl performance out of a laptop. Something that should be noted is I use a 48' Vizio 4k 60hz HDMI setup and have my laptop hooked to it. I game & work off my 4K TV and everything works flawlessly. Many people are uninformed and think you need a Computer Monitor that runs 4k with either displayport 1.2 or HDMI 2.0, but this isn't the case at all. Thank to Nvidia HDMI 1.4 which can allow 60hz on 4K as long as your TV supports it and all 4K televisions should.

Gaming: My frame rates in games range from 50-60 normally. And I play all triple A rated FPS (titain fall 2, BF1, CSGO, Diablo III, Borderlands2, GTA 4&5 etc. Using Msi after burner I have my base speeds of the GTX1070 OverClocked at 1631mhz Boost at 1833mhz & memory at 2151mhz (Base settings are 1443 Boost 1645 and 2002) . The Nvidia 1070 is a smart chip going down to 100-200mhz when I'm not doing anything but surfing the web working in excel. CPU temps gettings as low as 36-55c on average. While gaming max I get up to is 74c with over clock speeds. Because the laptop comes with an button to turn on the CoolerBoost solution to max It immediately drops my temps to around 62c I am shocked how well it cools when running my new OC on default. (I also have a cooler pad under my laptop with 3 fans blowing air so that helps as well)

All in all I did research and I was planning on 4K gaming. For the price this is the best deal you can get around also since the GPU model is an MXM & memoery support up to 64GB and a free SSD bay this is as future proof as it gets.

title: The case of my dreams is here!
text:
NZXT has knocked it out of the park with this case and I could not be any happier! Perfection in every corner of the case and one of the most rewarding builds I've ever done!

+PROS+
+Nice sleek matte black and blue case paint job fits PERFECTLY in my build.
+Captive thumbscrews on the side panels keep you from losing them when you're taking the panels off for whatever reason
+Front panel comes off easily and provides simple access to the dust filter and fans for installation and cleaning.
+Top side USB/Headphone/Mic/Power button access is nice, especially with the flat top on the case.
+Shroud over the power supply makes it dead simple to stuff excess cabling underneath and not worry about cable management
+Dead simple installation of the power supply thanks to a bracket that is installed prior to case installation.
+Included case fans are 3-pin and spin perfectly quiet and move a good bit of air.
+Plenty of tie-downs for cable management on the backside of the case
+Plenty of room for bulky cables on the backside thanks to the bulge on the other side that acts as a shroud/cable channel, leaving the rest of the cables to sit nice and clean behind the mainboard.

-CONS-
-Touching on the power supply once again, I would have been fine without thumb screws for the securing of the power supply bracket to the unit itself. I don't see myself pulling the power supply out any time soon after initial installation and they might be removed for standard screws.

~OTHER THOUGHTS~
-The PCI covers don't have any kind of cover for themselves, leaving a gaping hole in the back of the case for dust to drift inside.
-The thumbscrews feel a little janky or gummed up from painting and initial install, sometimes what feels like the right amount of unscrewing will free them from the case instead of just the slot they're in.
-Finding this specific case (matte black and blue) on sale for a reasonable price was quite difficult and took some good timing to land it. Keep your eyes pealed for sales.

title: The Garmin RV 760LMT GPS is an amazing GPS for RV'ing..
text:
I have used at least a half a dozen different models of Garmin GPS's and several different brands of GPS's and the Garmin RV 760LMT is one of the best and easiest to use. It is one of the better ones for RV'ing because you can input different criteria about your RV, which is taken into account when routing you through areas that may have conditions that would make taking an RV difficult, awkward or even illegal. You can input the length, wide, height and weight of your RV, which allows you to avoid those routes or roads that will not accommodate your RV. It can even help you avoid tunnels that do not allow vehicles carrying propane tanks. The split screen feature is really helpful when approaching turnoffs and route changes. It tells you what lane to be in and looks identical to what you see in real life as far as signs, number of lanes and terrain. If you pull a travel trailer, this unit also allows you to create and easily change your profile to accommodate just your vehicle, which routes you accordingly, to normal roads that a regular vehicles will fit on.

The screen is large (3 3/8" x 6 1/8") and the touch screen feature makes it easy to use and navigate through the different options. It is Bluetooth capable allowing you to make and receive phone calls and the speaker volume is loud enough to hear during noisy driving conditions. We have used this GPS on several long trips from coast to coast and it especially came in handy in the different states on the east coast that have a lot more bridges, older and lower overhead passes, restricted tunnels, narrow roads with tight turns, etc. This GPS also allows you to connect up a compatible, wireless backup camera (to your RV), giving you a large, clear picture of what's behind you when you want to backup your RV. Overall, I would highly recommend the Garmin RV 760LMT GPS to anyone who drives a motor home or tows a travel trailer.

title: A sub that's good enough that you can't 'hear' it.
text:
Very impressive performance for the price. In my classroom at school I have a pair of Audioengine A5+ speakers with the A8 subwoofer which fill a large room full of students very nicely. For a small (12ft x 12ft) room at home I decided that a pair of the A5+ speakers would do the job on their own. They are good (and go down to around 50 Hz), but I really felt they needed some filling in at the bottom end. I couldn't justify an expensive unit like the A8 for such a small space but I didn't want to ruin good music with something 'cheap' (boomy or mushy). Based on reviews I got the Dayton Sub-800, and I'm glad I did.

On the minus side it didn't come with any connecting cables. I have a bag of spare cables left over from other systems but for some users this might be a frustration, which is why I've given it 4 instead of 5 stars.

On the plus side: I plugged everything in, set crossover to 80 Hz and gain to halfway, powered up, started a liquid dubstep mix..... Huh? Couldn't hear the sub! Confusion for a second or two until I tried turning the gain up and things got boomy, turned the gain down and the bass disappeared. I hadn't expected this level of quality - when properly set it merges with the regular speakers so nicely you can't hear it as a separate unit but you get a richer sound down to a much lower frequency. Simply outstanding at the price.

ps: two things you might want to note:
1) Don't pass judgement until you've played it for a few hours. It seemed to me that like high end systems it took a little while to loosen up.
2) Even though it is very impressive at the price, don't expect it to do everything that high end systems will do. It's only rated down to 40 Hz so you'll miss out a bit on those bone-tingling infra-frequencies.

title: Nice DAC/amp with one flaw
text:
I got this DAC/amp today and have listening it for 3 hours. As a summary, this is a good desktop DAC/amp with one flaw. Sound-wise, it is soft and clean. It provides wider stage than my other headphone amp, which is Audioengine D1. I can't say it is a tube-sound, but definitely it is warmer than my other gears, and still crisp at high.

Here is one flaw. When you connect it to a PC through USB (meaning that you use its DAC function), clipping happens. It makes the sound very muddy. That's why my first impression was "what a crap!!" In order to fix this, you need to reduce sound of a music player, such as iTunes or foobar2000 at the PC. Since it is all digital, you don't lose in the sound when you turn the volume down. It makes clipping away. I heard that HIFIman knows this limitation. I don't understand how they let this problem stay. For me, it is not a big deal. However, if you don't know the workaround, no one will like its sound. I am sure they fix this problem in the future.

Update: I raised rating of this amp to 5 stars. As I spend more time, I liked it more. I have to reduce the volume out of foobar2000, but it is not a problem since the amp still has enough power to drive HD650. I switched the tubes to GE JAN5654W, and the sound is even better.

title: Unbeatable at this price for home use
text:
I have generally used quite a few headphones in the$200 -$400 range in the past, or what is known as mid-fi (though for the un-initiated, even $300 can seem like crazy money for headphones). For home use, you will be hard pressed to find a better value at this price range. It is basically a great all-rounder which handles all genres of music with panache and verve; supremely comfortable despite its size, and solidly built. It creates a wide out of head soundscape - with diurnal recordings I sometimes find myself instinctively turning right and left towards the apparent source of the instrument! It has a sound signature with slightly emphasized base and gradual fall off at the higher frequencies which would please the average listener stepping up from sub $100 headphones. Despite being quite consistent across the frequency range it has FUN and exciting sound signature which is non-fatiguing.

Let me elaborate on some of the main points one looks at, while choosing a headphone, in the paragraphs below:

Comfort
In terms of comfort, especially for extended hearings, THIS CAN'T BE BEAT! The huuge velour ear-muffs are like soft pillows cradling your noggin and it never gets too hot unlike memory foam+(p)leather combos like Sennheiser Momentum 2 (just sold) and B&W P7 (tried and returned).

Sound signature
Open and airy as expected with an open back but with more bass presence than expected of such headphones. This is a great balance that Philips has achieved. There is no need to get into more technicalities - this will suit most music genres. I listen to wide range, but mainly acoustic and vocal heavy genres like folk, country, blues, soft rock, and despite the slight V-signature, it handles vocals like a pro. This is also excellent for late night movie watching - the provided 10 feet long cable is perfect in this regard, and open backed nature of the headphones really help create the surround like atmosphere for the movie sounds and score (even though, technically, only stereo). Generally speaking, sound signature can be described as warmish and (only) slightly laid back. anyone who does not have a very specific set of preferences (such a very heavy bass leaning or completely flat signature) should be happy with the sound signature.
The sound profile is also non-fatiguing to my ears which, together with the physical comfort features, makes this my go to headphones for long listening sessions

Match-ability
To be honest, these turned out to be harder to drive than the 30 Ohms impedance and 100db @ mW specs suggest. I could drive them, just about, from my phone (LG G4) but I need to put the volume to atleast 85-90% to get a decent output and the SQ was not great, slightly muted, especially in the lower frequencies and without the detail and spaciousness which I know the cans are capable of. The ipad air (and a friend's iphone) do a much better job at driving the cans so maybe the LG g4 has a weak amp. Similarly, my Desktop (Asus 87-pro motherboard based, no extra soundcard) struggles to do justice, but I have better luck with my Dell Latitude work laptop, which is able to drive these satisfactorily at about 65-70% volume (your volume preferences may vary). Therefore, I conclude that these headphones are near the limits of what can be driven without external Amp-ing, and hence an amp (or DAC/Amp if you are so inclined) is recommended. Success will vary with source - a dedicated DAP will probably not require an amp. However, almost any portable amp should work - at least in terms of sufficient power. Since I use this almost exclusively with a Chord Mojo (with which it positively sings!) this is not an issue for me - but it is worth considering if you are planning to drive these straight from a mobile/computer.

Build Quality
Built like a tank. There's a lot of metal and a high quality hard plastic to go with the leather headband. It'll take a beating. the earmuffs can attract lot of lint and hair, but nothing a bit of lint remover cant fix.

Price-performance ratio
I got this "Used-Like New" at $194. At this price it is a no brainier. I would argue that even at $100 more than that - it justifies the price. It compares favorably with the more portability friendly can priced at $400 and above, without the portability and pretty frills, ofcourse. Which brings me to.

Portability/ travel use
None. Zilch. Nada. It stays at home (or if you have your own cabin, office). It leaks sound (nothing drastic but its there), lets in ambient sound, and more importantly, its huge and doesn't fold any.

Cable/ connections:

10 feet long and with both 3.5mm and 1/4 th connector options. Again, the thought is home use.

I like that it has the standard 3.5 inputs on both ends. This lets me change the huge-ass icluded cable for one of the many shorter aux-cables lying around when sitting at the computer. More importantly, when doing small chores around the house, I can connect a bluetooth receiver with a short 3.5 mm cable clipped to my shirt/tee (I use the aventree clipper pro for now which has apt-x). This flexibility is a game changer for me and often can be a factor that tilts buying choice (other factors remaining constant).

Conclusion
In short, if your budget is less than 250 bucks and you want a set of cans for marathon listening sessions at home, you need to get this. You will have to get to the $600 range and above to find an open-back appreciably better at SQ. I have the $999 focal Elear for home as well; which is subtly better in almost all respects (especially clarity and that sparkle in the highs, but NOT sound-stage possibly) but still I use this almost as often.

title: Works with very limited capabilities on a Mac
text:
Here is my unbiased review. I am not a "vine' member. Just bought this tablet based on what I read here and I guess many that bought it may have missed some key points. FYI, I am on an iMac running El Capitan (OSX 10.11.2) with dual monitors. My primary use for this tablet was to touch up portraits and landscape photos. I was also replacing my old Wacom tablet that was too small and did not work on the latest OSX. So here is my quick take.

Unboxing and installation was just fine. I did not find anything missing and I could download the drivers from the Huion website (although, it seems that all the drivers for various renditions of the 610 are the same and so are the manuals. I am not sure why they had to create a separate category for each. Regardless, the install went fine. Upon connecting the graphics pad, OSX could not recognize the "keyboard" and kept asking for pressing a key. After a while, this guide (to install the new keyboard) disappeared and I could actually play with the driver options as well as the "PenPressure Test" utility. Using it on actual applications was another story! The tablet behaved erratically and the keyboard shortcuts on the left of the tablet worked only at times. The day after I put it together, I noticed that the lamination started coming off on it's own! So, buyers beware of the build quality.

Pros
- Inexpensive as compared to a Wacom or equivalent tablets
- Nice looking
- Did I mention inexpensive? :)

Cons
- As you can see from the image, the build quality is not great.
- Keyboard "express keys" and "soft keys" work only occasionally
- Pressure sensitivity is definitely not in the thousands. More like 5 - 10 levels

My final take:
Would I recommend it? If you want a graphics pen that makes it easier to touch up photographs (or draw) this tablet can do it. However, I had to struggle a lot to get it to this point by disabling all keyboard input from the device and remembering to click with the pen on the photoshop window when going between applications. Else, I noticed that photoshop would freeze and not take input even from my keyboard or mouse.

Hope these tips help another Mac user out there that is on the fence or struggling after purchase.

title: Right away I loved having one monitor in front of me instead of ...
text:
I bought this to replace my 2 27" monitor setup. My 27's were the 2560 resolution so you can tell what I was coming from. Those were powered by a dedicated tower and killer video card setup. (This is my work system, I work from home full time). Right away I loved having one monitor in front of me instead of having to move my head compared to the dual setup I had. The curved display will mess with you a bit at first, but then you do not notice it. I am running this from my Surface Pro 3, so I was able to get rid of a large dedicated PC with 2 27's that ran at 105 def each, plus the heat of the PC... this monitor runs at 89 deg, much cooler! The surface is cooler as well running at 106 deg. So I was able to get rid of 3 huge heat sources. (Granted my dual 30's and PC on the other side are still putting out lots of BTU's), but it has made a noticeable difference in the room. I lose some screen space going with this single 34", but I don't care or miss it. It is enough to have things going on each side with no change in productivity, in fact it is easier since you no longer have to click in the other monitor to "activate" that app. The Surface is OK for driving it, but a better video card would make it way more better. Runs at 50 Hz full native resolution. Speaker suck, they suck more than the Surface docking station speakers, so I don't bother with the audio. I love how there are no buttons on the bezel, it is under it as a joystick and you can tell if to have the ON light off or not. Easy to use menu, pretty right on with color after calibration with a puck. Runs very cool for the size. Great software also for it to run 2 PC's off the same monitor and use the same mouse and keyboard. I use a Ergotron mount for it and all my monitors. The base is pretty big, too big for my taste, taking up lots of desk room. PIP is awesome as well. I was worried, but I am so glad I made the jump. I get no light leak either.
I am now thinking about getting another one to consolidate my dual 30's, or run 2 of them. I also like that the transformer is external, so if it dies, you can get a new one and not open up the monitor. Also saves some heat from above.

The only bit of "bad" I do not like about it (this is personal taste)...
I wish the bottom bezel was made to mimic the rest so it was the same all around.
Speakers could be better (I know they are built in so I was not expecting amazing, but they are HORRID).

Just go for it, you will love it. Ditch the dual setup, this is easier.

title: Really wanted to like this TV
text:
Really wanted to like this TV...Purchased this from another retailer... I would periodically get screen tearing... best way I can describe it is that about 5 times an hour randomly the image on the screen would look like the video signal was going to cut out...whitish flashing pixelation that would travel sideways. This would happen on all HDMI inputs with different cables and different devices streaming... it would also happen with the built in apps. Returned the first TV.. got a second. Both were sealed new TV's. Second TV had the same problem. Returned the second and got my money back. Also this TV seriously LAGS. If you use it to play games and for example there is a cursor on the screen.... you push the joystick to move the cursor and there is a lag between the time you push the button and anything actually happens on the screen... and when you take your finger off the joystick to stop the cursor from moving... it still moves for a little bit.. so if you are trying to accurately pinpoint something on the screen with that cursor it is extremely frustrating. I have WII U which has a built in screen on the game controller which made this extremely obvious. Also when watching movies the sound output lags... the people on screen will be talking and the sound from their voices is slower than their lips are moving. There was no difference if connected thru an optical cable to my receiver or using the built in speakers... which are terrible and tinny. Also on either side of the screen you can see that the back lighting and colors look off.. about 1 1/2 inches on either side of the screen from top to bottom. It almost looks like an edge lit LCD where both sides are brighter but this supposed to be direct lit. I did some research and found a forum where others who have this TV took pictures of the screen with the same issues... It's a normal thing for these TV's... which if you research are outsourced by Panasonic and made by the same manufacturer in china that makes cheaper brands like Westinghouse...

Really the only thing this set has going for it is that when you power it up (which takes forever) it says "PANASONIC" in big letters which is extremely satisfying. Also the bottom of the screen on the black plastic bezel is says "PANASONIC"... and on the remote as well. :)

title: Worked perfectly for my Westinghouse EW39T6MZ 39" TV.  Highly recommended!
text:
I have a Westinghouse 39" TV model number EW39T6MZ and it recently stopped working. The problem was weird because it just refused to turn on almost as if it was unplugged. I troubleshot it with a voltage tester and found that the power brick was getting power from the wall while the output to the TV was showing no current. Clearly, the brick was dead and I was hopeful that a replacement would bring the TV back to life.

After much research, I decided on this unit. While it does not state that it matches my model number exactly, I found another listing for the same power supply ([[ASIN:B00AI15J7A T-Power® AC Adapter For Westinghouse LD-4655VX, LD-4680 LD-4695, EW39T6MZ Widescreen 46" LED HDTV Power Supply Cord]]) that said that it did. (I chose this one because I wanted Prime.)

Anyway, it arrived with the usual Prime speed. I tested it with a voltage tester to ensure that the current aligned with what I (and the TV) expected and that the polarity matched. After testing it, I decided to take the plunge and plugged it in and....

IT WORKED!

That's right, my TV is now 100% back to normal. Amazingly this $15 item has literally save me $300+ for a new TV. Awesome!

The oddity is that this unit includes a three pronged plug while the one it replaces was only two pronged. I am not sure why that matters, but the TV works and that is all that I care about.

If you have similar symptoms with your TV, this item is a worthwhile investment. A little voltage testing can help too!

title: Excellent, just know what you're getting into.
text:
I love Youtube 360 videos. They're so immersive, and I have to believe that very soon the technology is going to be everywhere. However, it's still a new technology, and so the really high-quality videos you can find out there aren't really possible for consumers. Instead, you need some cumbersome system, like mounting six Go-Pros into some huge rig.

The LG Cam 360 is really well-designed for what it is - a 360 camera that is easy to use and take with you. It's very simple, I found myself able to take pictures and video right away, using my camera as a view screen. Then I shared the videos with my youtube app, and pretty soon I was looking at my videos in Google Cardboard. There's only a couple of buttons on the camera, the product seems solid, it has a case which slips off easy and can be used to hold the camera up just a tiny bit higher. You don't *need* to use your cellphone (and I have a Samsung, not an LG), even if you probably want to.

So if the actual operation and product design is great, the results are not. It's very, very clearly pixelated. However, the results are about the same as the other consumer 360 videos I saw. I don't know, maybe the Ricoh Thetah S is slightly better, but neither of them is all that good, and this version is smaller and about half the price. Look at what's available on Youtube and see what you think.

In a year or two I imagine something will come out which fits in a pocket and has much better quality output than this or any other consumer camera. In the meantime, this is a fun toy.

title: A beautiful laptop with a lot of quirks.
text:
So between balancing work and school I was in the market for a powerful ultrabook. After doing quite a bit of research the Razer Blade Stealth made a lot of sense for what I was needing. The dual core I7 processor while not a powerhouse would give me more than enough power to do some photoshop work and cad. The SSD is lighting quick when loading up my applications and the Intel HD 540 IGPU really surprised when it came to performance in older video games. I can’t say enough good things about the screen. With a 3840 x 2160 resolution and 100 percent adobe RGB rating I wish my 4k TV looked this good. Lastly for the chassis you’re getting a CNC aluminum body that weighs only 2.6 pounds and you will find one two USB 3.0 ports, one USB type C connector for the power which is thunder bolt 3 compliant and a HDMI 1.4 port
On paper I couldn’t find another windows laptop that seemed so nice. Then came the downsides that I found out within two weeks of ownership. My number one complaint is the battery life. In class to take notes I would use Onenote 2016, make sure I no other applications running and I would turn down screen brightness to 25%. I was lucky to get three hours of use. Then the screen, while beautiful for content consumption and great for media editing the high gloss screen loves to show finger prints and with how often I was seeing my reflection I felt like I’m always taking a selfie while using the stealth.

Now for quirks I ran into with the stealth. If I let the battery die, then go to plug it in I would have plug and unplug the type C connect from the provided power brick multiple times to get the laptop to recognize the charger. Then there were issues waking up from sleep. While this is more of an annoyance than anything but whenever I wake up my stealth from sleep mode the fans will ramp up to the point where they audibly loud for about 10 to 15 seconds. In a class of 40 people this is pretty embarrassing.

The Razer Blade stealth is a laptop that looks great on a showroom floor. It will turn heads with its RGB keyboard, razer thing profile and beautiful screen but I cannot recommend this laptop with the 4k screen. Other reviews say the 1440P model fixes my issue with battery life but with the other issues I have had with this laptop I will be returning it.

title: Garmin Fail!
text:
I've been a Garmin customer since their very early days in the GPS market. The RV770 does not measure up to my expectations of a Garmin product. When selecting the shortest time, it routes you around major roads, even when in "automobile" mode. For example. While driving from Salt Lake City to Tucson AZ, it tries to route you through Las Vegas which according to all other mapping software solutions is incorrect. The shortest route is I-15 to UT20, to US89, to I-17, to !-10. Even after turning onto UT20, it attempted to have us do a U-turn where it was not possible. Finally, after driving for 10 miles on UT20, the GPS realized it was a shorter route and the ETA was cut by over 40 minutes. This is just one of many, many poor routing selections the GPS provided during 7,000 miles of driving since the purchase. If you purchase this unit, make sure you check other mapping software and map books to make sure it's not sending you on a ridiculous route.

Additional Note: So I see the Garmin has answered with their canned response. The maps and software are up to date which I do before every major trip. UT20 has existed for over 50 years, so it's not an out of date map. I know how to use a GPS, and previous Garmin units worked well. This unit is a POS, and I highly recommend perspective buyers look at alternative GPS solutions. Garmin = FAIL

title: Very good PC, a real power pack.
text:
Didn't buy from Amazon, bought from Micro Center, an authorized ASUS warranty service center as well, which works nicely.
Started having some problems with it about 3 weeks after bringing it home. Some blue screens, freeze-ups. I could hear the cooling fan inside starting to run really hard, and I got the idea it was overheating. Without going into a long description of trying to verify an overheat, I took it back after a couple of months to MicroCenter and they couldn't reproduce the problem, but added some thermal paste under the CPU and graphics chips which sounded like a good strategy. It didn't fix anything. About a week later they offered me a new one as a replacement even outside their 30 day replacement window. They treated me fairly, imo, which these days you always appreciate.

My new one is running very reliably, no problems so far. I'm a month or so into the second one.

It seems to stay pretty cool. I'm trying to not leave it on all the time 24/7 because of the tv news about lithium batteries in PCs exploding. I always use the correct charger so maybe I'm ok, but it is also to avoid the unit overheating from vent blockage, etc.

There were a few device drivers that were out of date and they were fairly easy to update. Surprisingly there are a bewildering number of device drivers that go with these laptops, it can take awhile to go all the way down the list in the device manager, checking each for updates.

I find nothing inferior about the screen not being full HD. On a 15.6" computer who could really use full HD, imo.

I find nothing cheesy about the plastic case. I don't think it feels like a bad build quality at all. Those seem like esoteric complaints.

The only reason I bought an Asus was because Toshiba stopped selling laptops in the US. I've owned a lot of them. They weren't getting very good ratings there the last few years, but I was happy enough. I'll know in a couple of years whether Asus is my lifetime "go to" brand. I've already eliminated HP, Sony from bad past experiences. Its looking fine so far.

title: Not ideal for portable use
text:
I replaced the $1700 Audeze LCD-X with the $180 NAD Viso HP50, so I'm clearly a believer in Paul Barton's "RoomFeel" headphone tuning philosophy. Naturally I was curious to see how that sound translated to in-ears, but unfortunately these didn't sound much more spacious or open than the [[ASIN:B004PO10E2 Shure SE215-CL Sound Isolating Earphones with Single Dynamic MicroDriver]]. I've been using in-ears for many years, so I understand the importance of getting a proper seal. As is so often true, none of the included silicone tips fit, but fortunately the [[ASIN:B01EH0MKGU SpinFit CP100-L - Patented Silicone Eartips for Replacement (2 Pairs, Large size) (3.8mm Nozzle Dia.)]] I had on hand fit perfectly. Unfortunately, I can't say the same about the overall housing and wire design. The non-moldable ear loops are fiddly and annoying, and the multi-driver design results in a housing that's too big to rest comfortably against the concha and a massive nozzle that can't be inserted deeply into the ear canal.

So what about the sound quality? I was prepared to forgive all weaknesses in fit and finish if the sound was spectacular, but it wasn't, at least not played straight out of a phone. I found these earphones to be extremely recording-dependent: on some recordings, they blew the Shures straight out of the water (treble micro-detail and bass impact are both very impressive), while on others the Shures actually sounded better. Played directly from my phone's headphone jack, the PSBs struggled to get loud enough across all frequencies, leading to an unpleasantly recessed midrange, which made vocal and instrumental music sound cold and strange.

My suspicion is that these require an amp to really sound their best, but I didn't bother to try that because I'm not going to commute with a headphone amp in my pocket. If you're in the market for earphones for desktop listening with an amp, I'd say these are worth checking out, but for commuting, the Shure SE215 is still the gold standard: they get loud easily and evenly, they're great for all genres of music, they're light, comfortable, and durable, and they isolate from outside noise exceptionally well.
