title: Perfect hybrid device!  My first Chromebook and I am loving it so far
text:
Best hybrid device if you want to replace a portable laptop and an Android tablet at the same time...

I have been struggling with finding the perfect device for my needs over the last few months. I needed a replacement for my Android tablet because it was too small (or my eyesight was just getting to bad for close-up viewing), and so I looked at 2-in-1 laptop designs. At first I only looked at Windows devices because I didn't realize how far Chromebooks had come since their inception, and frankly I was a bit of a snob thinking they couldn't offer what I needed. So I tried 4 different types of Windows devices: two "tablet" types (HP Envy X2 and Acer Switch Alpha 12) - I won't go into details, but neither suited my needs. Then I tried a few 2-in-1 "flip" style laptops: Lenovo Yoga 720 and Asus UX360CA. Again, both devices had their problems, especially when it came to dual booting Android (Remix OS - the Lenovo flat out can't do it, and the Asus just couldn't handle it and keep cool - although it came the closest to being usable).
By this time I was getting pretty frustrated...until I just decided, on a whim, to look at Chromebooks, since nothing else was fitting the bill. And that is where I discovered the Asus Flip (and also looked at the Samsung Chromebook Plus and Pro). Torn between Samsung and the Asus, it came down to Android functionality for me. The Samsung Pro still has a few quirks, and while it has a better screen, the keyboard suffers from a poor design. So I decided to purchase the Asus Flip, and so far it has met every one of my nitpicky demanding needs, more so than any other device (Windows, Android or otherwise).

Sorry for the long intro, so here is my review of this Chromebook so far:
Build quality is very good, nearing the "excellent" mark, especially for the price. Aluminum construction, no creaking or significant flexing, and still thin and light enough to be a serviceable tablet and an awesome laptop. This is built better than the Asus UX360CA Windows 2-in-1, and that thing costs several hundred dollars more and doesn't have a backlit keyboard :P The display is superb, with decent color range (not as nice as the Samsung Pro, but that is Samsung's bread and butter, and I would rather have a better keyboard from them, TBH). I am liking the 16:9 screen ratio, as it is "normal" for laptop use, and also "normal" for older Android tablet formats. I don't use tablets in portrait mode very often.

Sound has been fine, except for a few issues with an Android app, and that can easily be software related as Android is still in infant stages (or at least toddler) on Chromebooks, and I expect those quirks will smooth out over time as Chromebook software is updated on a very regular basis.

I love the USB C charging, and especially the fact that I can charge from either side so if I am using it in tablet mode or laptop mode, it can be plugged in on the side closest to the outlet. Small thing, I know, but with traditional laptops sometimes you have the cord wrapped around your head or something weird because of where you are sitting :P Also quick charging is great, super quick to charge up to full. I have been taxing the battery pretty hard, but it has been showing decent numbers on time left. Not a lot of experience with it so far, but I anticipate it will be just fine especially compared to similar Windows devices.

The keyboard is very nice for me. It is very similar to a normal Windows keyboard on a similarly sized laptop, and the keys feel good. The keyboard itself is very solid, almost no flex, especially comparing it to the Asus UX360CX... I wish that unit had had this keyboard, especially with the backlight. Some people may say a backlight is no big deal, and they are probably right, but it is very handy at night or low light, and also just adds a little bit of class to the device. Key travel feels good. Overall very good compared to other devices like the Acer switch Alpha 12 and Lenovo Yoga 720.

Software. Chromebooks are up and coming, and there isn't much you can't do on these things anymore. Sure, you are limited to one browser, but Chrome is well suited for most websites these days, and the apps and plugins are beyond compare. While it isn't my favorite browser on a Windows machine (it is pretty resource intensive), it seems to operate just fine on the Chromebook. And if I really want to view a website in another browser and not switch devices, the remote function to my Windows desktop works like a charm with almost no lag, so it will serve in a pinch.
Android is running flawlessly so far, barring one minor incident with sound on Clash of Clans (which went away on reboot). I also just got an update to non-Beta channel for the OS, although Play Store still says (Beta) next to it, I think Android is now running on this machine in the stable build. I could be wrong, but for my experience, I didn't have to do anything special to enable the Play Store and it is working with no issues.
Best of all, with Android, the laptop features work seemlessly with Android apps. For example, screen rotation, disabling the keyboard and touchpad when in tablet mode, etc. Those were not available options when dual booting into Remix OS on a Windows device (if you get it to work at all). So even if you have a 2-in-1, there really wasnt a tablet experience available for them. But this device goes from Android tablet to a pseudo-Windows laptop in a flip, and with no hiccups or other quirks.

Performance: so far I have mainly run a few Android games and browsing. I have noticed a little bit of heat on the graphic intensive games, but otherwise the machine stays calm, cool, and collected. No issues there, and I don't anticipate any since the Intel M3 processor is really overpowered for Chromebook functionality, and seems to be suited well to run Android so far (although that will depend on your app usage, or so I have heard).

TLDR version: perfect hybrid device if you want a light-weight laptop to browse, email, watch movies, etc, and also flip into Android tablet mode with a bigger screen than the normal Android tablet fare. Quality is excellent so far, and the software/hardware combination works like they were made for each other (which is what you want :))

text:

Nicely the QFX plays loud enough to be heard in the garage and in the driveway in front of the garage. The other main feature that I wanted in the unit was USB playback, I live in a low spot with a ridge between me and the nearest city which keeps me from picking up FM radio stations reliably. The QFX plays USB well and also plays from the same file it last played when restarted. This another place where the Naxa failed, it always started playing back at the beginning of the file list.
Back to the radio, I picks up local FM stations well, even the nearby city. As a bonus the radio also has two short wave bands. I can't say how well they work but they do work, I've heard the atomic clock from Colorado and I live in North Carolina. Tuning on the short wave seems to very picky and it may be hard to return to the same stations but that isn't what I bought this unit for. I agree with other reports on this unit in that its radio is not calibrated very well and stations are tuned in not close to where they should be on the dial. At least the dial is big and it is easy to return to stations on the FM band, I did not test the AM band.
Other bonus's are three tone controls which work, but not very dramatically. The only real failing of the unit is the X-bass. With the tone controls you may be able to get some bass response but not much, but the sound is still ok. The cassette works and sounds ok, I will try recording off the cassette to USB in the future. AC power was necessary, I didn't want the rechargeable battery like some other units have. I'll finish by saying that I would highly recommend this unit, for the price it is remarkable.

title: Very, very impressed
text:
I was a bit cautious buying these. I know B&W enjoys a famous reputation for great speakers, recently some killer automotive audio, but that doesn't always translate across to a defensible premium "lifestyle" product. The aesthetic also isn't really my cup of tea - neither the colors nor the rounded square cans. But, I bought them through a rewards program quite a bit less expensively than MSRP. Nevertheless, I'll write this review in the frame of mind of paying $399 for them.

I've been spinning through and testing a number of headphones, from $18 pairs to $550 pairs. Over the last few years I've started using over-ear bluetooth headphones for hours every day, in the office, cooking dinner (active noise canceling especially helpful here with four small kids), working in the yard, working on the cars, watching TV after the kids are in bed and so on. For me it's very clearly worth it to me to find the units that sound spectacular, but at the same time, do not produce fatigue - neither in listening nor comfort. I can absolutely appreciate and enjoy some good, solid, entry-level offerings and at the same time find it very much worthwhile to pay what it costs for the best of the best, when on business trips and so on.

In the "preimum" area, to date I've tried the Sony MDR-1000X (now replaced by WH-1000XM2), Bose QC35, Sennheiser HD1, Bang & Olufsen H9, Bluedio Vinyl and Victory, Plantronics BackBeat Pro 2, and these, Bowers & Wilkins P7.

I can say, although I consider the B&O H9 still my #1 favorite-sounding set, these are a close 2nd, followed by Plantronics. These are so good it really comes down to trivial personal preferences. The bass is a bit richer and more resonant on the H9 but it's also richer and more resonant on these than just about anything else (esp. Sony, Bose, Sennheiser). That much perfectly-controlled bass has to be mixed with, obviously, good vocal mids and sparkling, crisp highs, all delivered with absolutely no distortion at any listening level - from almost whisper-quiet to blaring loud - and that, these can do, with aplomb.

I'll also point out that seeing them in person, they are extremely solid and well-made. The ear pads are very soft and comfortable - again, the 'win' goes to the B&O H9 but these are so good, near-as-makes-no-difference are superbly comfortable and well-made. There's also a machined polished aluminum bevel around the oval inset in the ear cup, as well as an embossed "Bowers & Wilkins", that looks very nice in person, understated but elegant. That detail creates an aesthetic of quality and precision in person that doesn't really come through in the ad photos. All of which to say, that alone doesn't make these worth more than a really nice-sounding $100-200 pair of headphones, but it adds to the overall experience, which is also something the B&O does superbly.

These do not have active noise canceling, which may be a detractor for frequent business travelers / public transport commuters. They are solid enough and the ear cups soft and form-fitting enough to call them "noise isolating" but when you have a loud drone like an airplane engine or lawnmower engine, ANC really does make a difference. From my perspective, ANC is only moderately important because I use wireless headphones in so many other applications where it isn't necessary or even welcome. Notably, the B&O H9 have good-but-not-great ANC, which you can obtain in any of a raft of good $50-70 headsets - 1/10th the price. I obviously value sound quality more than ANC. The Sony and Bose are the reigning champions of active noise cancellation, but suffer some penalties to outright sound performance to accomplish that.

These also do not have touch controls, which are becoming more common on premium headsets. They're pretty basic: on/off, multifunction button, volume up/down.

Finally, the Bluetooth reception is excellent, including outdoor applications. I have repeatedly, emphatically, whined and moaned about how the single primary use case for a Bluetooth (wireless) headset is wearing/listening with your phone in your pocket. And a plurality - majority - of that occurs outdoors. Many units, including high-end ones, just struggle to maintain their connection outdoors, even in some cases when you are sure to place your phone in your pocket on the same side of your body as the ear cup containing the bluetooth transmitter. If you don't, you get skipping; the headphone can't buffer enough data to handle disruptions in the connection between the BT transmitter and receiver. I have had no such problem with these (nor with the Sony, Bluedio, B&O or Plantronics).

Summing up: I was hesitant, but listening to these for a few hours made me a believer. I am totally pleased with these. I did not have nearly as good of an impression of the B&W T7 bluetooth speaker - see my review there - so this is not just brand name reflected glory. This is about the sound these produce and the quality of the packaging in which they do it. Excellent in every respect, and highly recommended.

title: The Sennheiser HD 598 Cs's are beautiful head piece but don't expect to listen to these on a PC or using an AMP or DAC.
text:
The HD 598cs - Is it what you would expect from Sennheiser? No, but I would say to expected the unexpected.

Preface: Tested on a gaming pc with a dedicated Creative SoundBlaster Z-Series sound card and on a Nexus 6 with and without the Fiio's A3 portal amp (https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00MFMW29I/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1)

The Design:

The Sennheiser HD 598 Cs's are beautiful, the construction quality is on par with my Sennheiser Game Zero's ($250 gaming cans). The head band is well padded as are the ear cups. The ear cups are a thick leatherette that blocks out the vast majority of outside sources and keep the audio contained with some sound leakage; not enough to be an issue in an office environment and acceptable in a library.

The Audio:

The lows were found to similar to the ATH-M50s; however, I found that the ATH-M50's won out compared to these cans in the clarity of the bass and the amount of punch it could give. The HD 598Cs were noticeably muddled and not as crisp or clean as compared to the ATH-M50's. The mids are actually surprisingly well rounded and clean with an ever so slight ting on the lower mid range. I feel that these headphones excel within this audio range.The highs sadly are similar to the lows in which they start to muddle up at the higher spectrum and I feel that the ATH-M50's win here as well. While listening to the various songs I could start to feel ear fatigue after just a few songs while on the PC.

I found that with the amp on my Nexus 6 to have similar results with the PC and given the fact that these headphones have a lower impedance I expected this. However, without the amp the Nexus 6 and the headphones were better with the 'muddiness' being less noticeable.

The long and short of it is this: These are beautiful headphones to look good in and they feel great on the head (being bald I can tell). However; the sound quality isn't what I had expected and carrying the HD 598 name (See the HD 598SE open-backs for those reviews and why it's the darling of the 200 dollar price range). I feel that these headphones are attempting to target the crowd of people that use headphones as an accessory and much less a tool to visit an audioscape like the Beats series. They are okay for those that want something to listen to at work, traveling, or just general usage but not for the asking price off $150... not even for the Black Friday's sale of $100 (maybe $79.99) and will be returning mine.

title: Third version of this, and I still love it
text:
This is the third incarnation of this type of Radio Recorder, from Crane.

The first one, I think from the 90s, was a big bulky radio-style box. It recorded on cassettes. I had 2 of them for years, and they never stopped working. I forgot the name of it, but it wasn't called a CC Witness.

When the first CC Witness became available, I jumped to that, because of the size convenience. One inconvenience with this first version, was the non-standard USB cable. The unit itself faithfully recorded several of my radio programs during the week, and acted as a decent mp3 player, and I used that for years, as well.

The thing about the CC Witness that always appealed to me, was how solid it feels. Many modern digital recorders have a flimsy planned-obsolescence feel to them, in contrast to this unit.

The one annoying problem, that I just accepted and worked around, was that the connection between the PC and the Unit often broke without warning, while trying to copy MP3 files. I ordered a second cable, but that didn't solve the problem.

However, this new unit with the Mini USB connector, doesn't have that problem at all. To set it up, I moved the old microsd card from the previous CC Witness to this one, and set up the date and time on the new unit. I then converted some Youtube videos to mp3, copied to folders on the Witness microsd card (with no connection interruption), and then sat listening for hours at a restaurant booth, while my wife entertained herself nearby. Just like old times.

Thanks, Crane. If there's ever another version, I hope you don't make it smaller, to conform to modern expectations of a proper digital recorder. This is the perfect fit, for an average hand.

I should note that I also used one of the accessory kits for the Witness. No doubt the rubberish cover was a factor in the lifespan of the first CC Witness. However, I don't see that cover available anymore. I rarely used the docking station, and the AC Adapter was too heavy and bulky.

10/19/2018 Note: If you have the CC Witness, make sure you upgrade the Firmware, to at least 1.4. Much cleaner interface.

title: Get one of these.  If you can afford it, get the Pro.
text:
Spoiler alert: I'm gonna gush about how much I like it, tell you that I took a star off because now that I have it I wish I had the pro model with the extra buttons, then maybe gush some more.

So the actual hardware review: It's SOLID. And by that, I mean the unit weighs a hair less than a pound. It doesn't want to move in any direction on the desk. The cap is coated in a slightly rubberized compound that isn't too bad on the skin. I do have a couple hardware gripes: The USB cable feels thin and flimsy, it's permanently attached, and has no strain relief at the base. so if it gets pinched, it's all over. The other is more minor, the serial number for the device is printed on a paper tag attached to the cord, not on the device. The 3Dconnexion logo is cermarked to the bottom of the device, the serial number should be there as well. There are two buttons on the base of the device. It took me a minute to realize exactly how these work; they click horizontally, as if squeezing inward. When you first use the device, your instinct is to press them straight down.

It is a little awkward to find a comfortable grip. The perfectly round cap doesn't fit the hand very well, but when you stop thinking about it and just start using it in CAD, it just sort of happens. Spend a little time with it and you start to wonder how you ever survived without one. Moving around in a 3D environment with the mouse and (maybe) keyboard becomes a total chore. I've only had the thing a couple days and I do NOT want to do with out it. I want to drive my car and brush my teeth with the thing.

I do regret buying this model, however. I want the Pro model with all the extra buttons. Heck, if I could have four buttons on this model I think I'd be okay. Enough for two modifiers and two functions. Like, Control, Alt, delete and fit would be my choices. Though with it close to the left edge of the keyboard, you can reach shift and control with your thumb. I am thinking hard about returning it for the Pro model.

title: Awesome except for one misfeature
text:
Very impressed with this device. Particularly pleased with the integration with other home devices; I can tell Alexa to turn off the garage lights, and the garage lights duly shut off (this does require setup, of course - like putting the garage lights on a controllable switch - but that only needs to be done once). Plays music without difficulty, from a variety of sources (Amazon, of course, but also Pandora, Spotify, several others). Voice recognition works remarkably well, all things considered; I've only been able to confuse it when there have been several people speaking at once. (Including a loud 3 year old standing right next to it. That's a challenge most humans couldn't beat). Currently there are only 3 "wake words" (words which tell the device to listen up; they are "Alexa", "Echo" and "Amazon", and can be set in a menu via the app); I would prefer to have that be a settable parameter (and if people choose to abuse that, well, so be it; adolescence is not a phase you can bypass. I promise you the kid won't call his Echo "b*tch" or equivalent once he has a girlfriend, or for that matter a boyfriend, regardless of gender; one wants to make a better impression than that, usually).

So why the 4 star review, you ask? One word: search. At present, Alexa uses the incredibly lamerpants Bing search engine, by apparently unalterable default (if they meant for it to be changed, I rather expect that feature would be prominent. It is not in evidence; Moreover, the internet (based on searched using a real search engine, to wit: Google) has been unable to find this feature either. I thus assume it does not exist). I suspect that Amazon has taken money from Redmond to implement this. My advice if so: give it back, and implement real search, using the customer's choice of engines. You'll make up the money in units sold. Trust me.

text:
I have only had this headphone for two days, so I will update with more information later. I hate to give this superb headphone four stars but there are just a few kinks that I feel I need to address before writing a full review in the future.

First, is a static noise. I only hear it when I listening on my phone, and it's most noticeable when I'm watching Netflix. It's probably just that Netflix has poor audio quality, but the highs of this headphone seem to accentuate the effect, and in some cases it can be a little annoying. It's nothing too bad though.

The second thing is the earcup. Naturally a head is curved. There's an incline between the top of the side of your head and the bottom of that side. Thankfully, HiFiMan gave you the option to rotate the earcup up and down, however, the pad interferes with that. To make an adjustment I need to press the earpad down and push the arch that holds the earcup through. Once it's on your head it's completely fine and comfortable for several hours, but getting it there takes a good 7 seconds of configuration for maximum comfort. Not a big deal, but a strange design choice.

Again, I will be updating this review with more information in the future, but I don't think I've spent enough time with them to judge them well. However, I will say that I'm very happy with them.

These headphones are really great with at home use. Comfortable for hours, and genuinely great audio quality. But they broke. The part that connects the metal arch that holds the sides of the earcup and the headphone split. Honestly sucks, I loved these guys.

Now the major issue: The rechargeable battery is not meant to be user-replaced.

After a few years any rechargeable battery will not take a charge anymore. We all know that. Logitech surely knows that. But still they decided to bury the battery inside the keyboard under the sealed orange rubber backing (and 19 screws).

(If you want, you CAN replace the battery, just YouTube it. Let's put it this way... It requires a hair dryer to warm the glue, slowly peeling off the orange rubber backing and taking out all the screws. Some sellers have the battery here on Amazon if you are so inclined. I'm not. I'm buying a new keyboard.)

I have a premium bluetooth speaker by Logitech that has the same issue. The battery is built-in and not replaceable.

Come on Logitech, you know batteries don't last forever.

Two classic cases of design over function.

title: Great 144hz 1080p monitor if you can overlook a few minor shortcomings.
text:
Pretty good monitor. Low lag. Great color and uniformity for a TN panel.I'll never be able to go back to anything less than 144hz (so smooth!), and 1080p is great for scaler-less console gaming. Surprisingly better than awful speakers. 48-144hz Freesync range. Decent amount of height adjustment.

Negatives:

A 1996 CRT monitor has a better, more intuitive menu system than this thing. And there's no manual to explain what any of the myriad options actually means. A lot of the "game modes" have no explanations and have a curious impact on image quality. They also disable and grey out different features at random it looks like. Turning "SmartSync" (no explanation of what this is either) on causes weird over-sharpening artifacts on the screen for me. The buttons are illogically placed and cheap feeling, it takes what feels like 10 button presses just to change the volume, for whatever reason pressing the "2" button (the OK button) when not in a menu blacks out the screen. I wish the brightness of the light underneath the monitor was adjustable. The ports aren't easy to access without rotating the monitor.

Looks like they made a great panel and some decent hardware to run it, but rushed it to market and made the UI and menu system an afterthought.

But you're digging in those settings and dealing with the shortcomings for approximately .02% of the time you're actually using the monitor, so for this price I find all of those negatives livable.

title: Great while it lasted.
text:
For the time it lasted, the VSX-824 it was a great receiver. Set up was straight forward, LOTS of great features, fantastic signal processing, HTPC connectivity was a breeze, the automated speaker set up was indeed quite nice. It's got enough umph to rattle the windows and drive the neighbors crazy.
I've had everything running since the middle of December 2014 and have been VERY pleased with the performance, features, and sound from the VSX-824, then come Sunday Jan 18, 2015 the HDMI output and inputs stopped working. I swapped out cables, did direct connections to the TV from different sources and everything else worked -- just not the HDMI inputs or output from the VSX-824. Tuner works, Composite video works, analog audio works -- just no HDMI. The entire set up -- TV, HTPC, Receiver, etc are all on a 2500VA UPS - so it's only ever gotten clean, regulated power since day one. Everything else works perfectly, and the UPS registered no spikes or strange voltage levels. Sadly, I'm returning it and looking for a different unit that will last me more than a month. I really like the features of this unit, and the price isn't bad at all.
UPDATE 2015-02-05: Replaced the VSX-824 with a VSX-1024 and so far it's working very well. Got a great deal (via Amazon) - basically the same AV receiver but with 7.2 or 5.2 and "B" stereo output which will get wired out to the back porch this spring

I still gave the phones 4 stars however somewhere between 3-4 is more accurate. The bottom line is they work for what I was looking for. Price is way out of line compared to my Bose and my Beats. text:
I would have loved to keep this as it is a really well made wall mount with the exception of one MAJOR design flaw. The left side of the casing comes up too high on the PS4 Slim itself, specifically preventing the PS4 wireless headphones dongle from plugging in. As the PS4 Slim does not have a rear USB port, this makes it impossible to plug in the wireless headphones dongle using this mount. If you use the PS4 wireless headphones, unfortunately you‘ll want to look elsewhere for a wall mount as this one will be useless to you.

Other than that, it really is a nice mount. The lines are clean, the damper pieces are well-thought out, and the built-in level is a nice touch. And do note that I tried plugging in a couple “standard“ USB drives and they did fit. (But the PS wireless headphones dongle is a bit thicker.) If you don‘t ever intend to use PS‘s wireless headphones, it‘s a great purchase. Unfortunately, that‘s not the case for me, and I imagine many others.

title: Not for my 2017 iMac 27 (32Gb kit, 16x2)
text:
My 2017 iMac (27", 5K, Core i7), is brand new and came with the base, 8Gb RAM. Like others looking to save money from Apple's exorbitant prices, I thought I'd order some reputable, aftermarket, 2400mhz memory instead. My plan was to order 32Gb via a pair of 16Gb sticks and combine them with my stock 8Gb, giving me a grand total of 40Gb RAM.

My Kingston Hyper X 32Gb (16x2, 2400Mhz) kit arrived at the same time as my new iMac but I set up my computer first using its factory 8Gb. Once that was complete, I added the Kingston set but my Mac wouldn't boot at all, just the black screen. I then tried swapping the installation order (1-3, 2-4) and same no-boot result. Then I removed my stock 8Gb, leaving only the Kingston set installed and still, no-boot, black screen.

Finally, I removed all memory and then installed each Kingston stick one at a time. The first one finally allowed the computer to boot but reported a total of 8Gb which was half of its capacity. I removed that stick and installed the second Kingston stick and just like before, the computer wouldn't even boot at all.

Finally, I removed both Kingston sticks, installed the original 8Gb from Apple and my Mac booted and functioned perfectly. Yes, I completely powered down, unplugged and held the power button in for 10+ seconds each time I added or removed any RAM. I really had high hopes for the Kinston kit and simply wanted to open my Mac once, stick in the added RAM and be done with it but hours of frustration later, I'm back where I started.

Shipping was very fast, thank you. This expensive RAM came in a thinly padded envelope instead of a box if that makes any difference. I read someone here with the same new iMac bought four of these for a total of 64Gb and they seemed to work fine so perhaps mine were somehow damaged from automated postal machines. I don't know but I'm returning these.

title: EXCELLENT Large Capacity SSD
text:
**Pros**
Capacity (2 TB of solid state storage!!)
Price (Paid about $0.10/GB [$208.99] total during an Amazon flash sale on Cyber Monday)
Speed (Plenty fast for a SATA based SSD)
Longevity (Not one of the new quad-level cell [QLC NAND] SSDs so it should handle more write cycles)
Management software (Firmware updates/extra features/etc…)

**Cons**
None

**Other Thoughts**
I've been looking at options for getting mass storage in my ITX build and I was hopeful that a good deal on a multi terabyte capacity SSD would show up around the Black Friday/Cyber Monday season. Sure enough, Amazon put this one on sale. It was very hard to resist at that price. I looked at several 1TB options around the $120-$140 range but I wanted something with a bit more capacity without having to pay over double the cost of some 1TB options available. Even though the speed would be excellent, I also didn't want to run a RAID array of 1TB SSDs. Not only for less complexity but also for lesser cables to manage in my compact ITX build. This SSD fit the bill perfectly!

I owned a 1TB Crucial SATA SSD in the past but parted with it due to switching platforms so I had no problem going with Crucial again. I'm using this for mass storage of Google Drive files, video game files and Hyper-V Virtual Machines. This works perfectly for all of those purposes. My personal rig is all solid state storage with a 1TB M.2 NVMe SSD and now this 2TB SATA SSD. Everything is speedy and it's kind of sad to say that now this SATA SSD is the bottleneck in my system when I'm transferring files (as if 500+ Megabytes per second isn't fast enough).

There's not much else to comment on about this SSD. I got it for what I believe to be a reasonable price and without having to make any compromises!

title: Works exactly how I need it to.
text:
I received this yesterday and the only purpose it has for me is to stream HD videos from my desktop over LAN. I was pleasantly surprised with everything about it so far.

Here are the pros and cons:

Pros
- Setup is as easy as plugging in the stick, plugging the USB into the stick and TV, then pressing the power button on the stick. It took 5 minutes to complete setup and get into Windows 10. My old Vizio e601i-a3 has a USB port which DOES provide enough power to not have to use the power brick.

- Strong Wifi signal (I have an original Logitech K400 keyboard/mouse so I have't tried Bluetooth and Wifi at the same time).

- I'm able to stream 1080p MKV videos over LAN from another Windows 10 PC with ease.

Cons

- I really don't have any yet. I'll update my post, probably with a little rage, if something comes up. I imagine the only issues I'll have moving forward are Windows Updates affecting drivers. I'm thinking about disabling Windows Update completely to avoid it.

UPDATE:

This little device is still chugging along with zero issues even with all of the latest Windows 10 updates.

In response to the comment regarding disabling Windows Update - You CAN disable Windows Update by setting the network that the device is connected to as a 'Metered' connection even if it's your regular home network. Another option is to upgrade to Windows 10 pro and it can be disabled using group polyicy editor (gpedit.msc) - http://www.howtogeek.com/224471/how-to-prevent-windows-10-from-automatically-downloading-updates/

title: Disappointing, unreliable, and now dead
text: This thing was horrible. I say "was" because I just had it for a little over a year and it's already dead. The remote and the menus were just as confusing as other reviewers mentioned. The use of buttons changed depending on which screen you were in. I bought it for the recoding capabilities and there were several times when it just decided not to record for no apparent reason. Everything was set correctly. One day it would record. The next day it wouldn't for the exact same program. It only used military time and doesn't adjust for Daylight Saving Time, so that made setting it to record the correct program nice and tricky. The on-screen guide was supposed to let you easily set up a recording, but most of the time, it only showed me programs that were coming up within the next few hours, so if I wanted to record something the next day, I was out of luck and had to set it manually. It doesn't have a hard drive, so you need to use a USB drive with it. The problem with that is that the unit sometimes gets hot and I think that damages the USB drives. Before this thing died, it took out 4 different USB drives - none of which I was able to reformat and use for anything else. It also records is a non-standard format, so if you are hoping to take the recordings and play them on a Mac, you're out of luck. They need to be converted to an MPG or MOV first. Reception was also spotty. I got 3 channels on one side of the room and about 15 on the other with the same antenna. The quality was also shaky. Some channels came in clear and crisp, but others would blink out on a regular basis. If it's windy outside, forget it. You're not watching TV. Congress promised this whole switch to digital television would be better for the consumer, but that was a costly, bold-faced lie. I'm pretty sure this move was meant to make watching TV so irritating that people would be forced to throw money at the cable companies who supported this move. I'm very disappointed.

title: Freedom of Movement with Good Sound
text:
I did not know that I could get such good headphones for the low price I paid! I have been using these every day, and the sound quality has been very good. I finally have freedom to do housework while listening to XM or Pandora, and I am able to answer the phone from the headset.

They are a bit heavy, but not too heavy. They are obviously not for sport or athletic activities.

They clamp onto the head firmly, but not too firmly, which is good for me because I use them while cleaning house. I bluetooth-connect to my smartphone, playing music while vacuuming, I hear the music well, and they stay on my head without slipping off, the way some headphone will do.

When my smartphone has a call (or text) while connected via bluetooth to the headphones, I can answer (I have talking text on my phone) from the headphones by tapping the power button. The microphone works well. Whenever I would ask a person on the other end how I sound, they would say good.

All controls, indicators and the microphone are on the right headset, positioned well for managing without looking.

I can listen to just the headphones, or I can listen to the headphones with the external speakers on (to share what I am hearing), or I can take off the headphones and listen to the external speakers, just like a little set of stereo speakers. The quality and volume of both the internal speakers and the external speakers is very good.

The products looks, feels and sounds like good quality.

The range of the signal is good. I have been able to have my smartphone on one side of the house while I am on the other side (75ft) I also have been able to have the phone upstairs while I am downstairs. In such cases, I have not experienced any breaking-up or other audio artifacts.

Interesting thing, and this might be something that happens with just my phone: If I briefly tap the volume-up button or the volume-down button while listening to XM, it changes channels. I found that I must hold the volume buttons for a longer moment, in order to change the volume. It took some practice to get it.

title: A reliable router with good connection range and the necessary security features.
text: I currently use the Linksys model just prior to this one and have now added the AC1900 for a second residence.  While working with computer hardware and software since before the first personal computers came out, my primary interest is in a product for residential use that provides superior, if not the best overall security and protection.  I have used a number of wireless routers over the years including Linksys and found many of their models meet my requirements.  While some people want to login as admin and make changes to their routers through a wireless connection, it is important that if this feature is available that it can be [and is] disabled.  Many routers also have an option to easily authorize computers and other equipment to access the router [your network] with an "automatic" procedure that utilizes a single button.  It is also important that this shortcut process that bypasses most of your security can at least be disabled in your admin settings [and can be in these models].  This wireless router also has one of the strongest signals of current home models.  There are a number of other security options that also should be considered and are available on this model and many other brands.  Bottom line for me is that this meets my needs and is reliable, I've had few problems with the Linksys routers in the past and don't expect to have problems with this one and their customer support is as good as most.

title: Was waiting for this for a long time
text:
I have used the likes of Riva turbo x and philips fidelio bluetooth speakers in the past. These are by far the most beautiful sounding portable speakers to date. A lot has been said about them by other reviewers so I'll try to say a few things which add to, rather than repeat what has already been said.
1) Break in period. Give it at least 50 hours of continuous play to let the drivers settle in. Off the bat they are very point source and flabby in the bass region. With time the bass tightens up and they slowly become 'invisible'
2) These speakers are very sensitive to the quality of music being fed to them. Use low quality bit rates, and you get just that. Use hi res Dsd or 24/192 pcm recordings and they will reward you with a rich and full sound. i love the way vinyl rips in hi res sound through them.
3) GET A GOOD QUALITY AUDIO CABLE. Again, these are sensitive speakers. Use junk and you get degraded sound.
4) Probably the most effective tweak is to attach small felt/rubber feet to the bottom. Its Amazing how this 'liberates' the sound from the speakers.

I have been enjoying these speakers so much that at times when I dont want to wait around waiting for my tube amp to warm up (in my main rig) I just use these instead. I am seriously considering getting a second one and then run them together in left and right configuration. (still working out what kind of cable I'll need for that, probably have to make one myself. Here's a note to Benq. Make it possible to run two of them in stereo configuration)
So why only 4 stars? Heck, you could always improve upon it. Make the electrostatic panels detachable, for example!

Edit 14 July 2016:
I am updating my review to five stars from four.
I have been using TWO speakers since a while linked together with a custom made cable to form a stereo pair. Each speaker outputting left and right channel respectively. With respect to this, I would suggest that Benq make provision for setting up two speakers in stereo format in future iterations of the product.

They are now atop 4' high stands and linked to the aries mini streamer directly using two 3.5 mm to 3.5 mm ugreen silver plated cables https://www.amazon.com/dp/B00WHUTR8W/ref=twister_B00WHWEY6A?_encoding=UTF8&psc=1 . The end which connects to the streamer first goes into a mono male RCa to female 3.5mm stereo adapter, https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01ERTK59K/ref=ox_sc_act_title_13?ie=UTF8&psc=1&smid=ALZYDHGPLQNLD which effectively outputs one single channel into both the channels of one speaker.

The results are simply mind blowing. I've got a full blown electrostatic system for under 500$.
I've had to do some tweaks to reduce vibrations from the main cabinets. Seems that in reality the bass is quite boosted, which can over the long term cause the passive radiator grilles to rattle a bit. I wont go into details how I removed the vibrations, but the tweak is quite simple and now there are no vibrations,and the boosted bass has been tamed.
I've got my listening chair dead centre and 6 feet away, the stands are placed 16 inches from the back wall with a slight toe in.

Simply heaven. if you're a bass head, add a mini subwoofer (PSB audio has a really good one) and you've got a fantastic hi end system for not much $$.
I'll be adding a passive pre amp between the benq's and the aries mini soon for better control.

text: The shipping was very fast and the charger was in a very nice box, but one corner of it was crushed in. All contents inside were fine, with no damage. First off, the issues I seen with the instruction manual. In the manual, it says non-recharging battery detection, but it did not detect non-charging batteries when I inserted them. The manual also says it has capability to charge Li-ion, LiFePO4, NiMH and NiCd batteries, but under cautions it says, only charge Ni-MH/NiCd batteries, charging any other types “my” (should be may) cause personal injury or damage to the charger. Now for battery testing, first I tried an AA alkaline non-recharging battery and when inserted, it never detected bad or non-rechargeable, it showed NiMH. When inserting an AAA alkaline battery no detection of bad or non-rechargeable, but showed as Li-ion. I tried to charge 2 different Li-ion 18640 batteries with the switch set to Li-ion and got the following results. Both 18650 batteries would make the charger display and blue backlighting cut off and on, as if, it were being plugged in and unplugged constantly. I tested 6 different rechargeable NiMH AA batteries and found the following. The AA batteries charged, after a couple of them were detected as bad. When one detected as bad, I moved to a different slot until it would detect as charging and it showed the correct type of battery for all. After they finished charging, I put the batteries in a device and let them discharge and recharged in a different charger. When finished charging in a different charger and they were fully charged by verifying with a volt meter, I inserted them into the Tenergy charger and all the batteries were detected as bad, no matter which slot they were in. I would give the charger a 2 out of 5 stars. title: Schott Glass: Might Not be All it's Cracked Up to Be
text:
I bought three sets of these Ritz Gear MC Super Slim Lens filters for two different brands of camera I own. This is a preliminary review and I will update if I should find that I simply got a bad copy. However, thus far the results I am seeing are puzzling.* The 52mm UV filter has entirely eliminated the ability for my camera to produce a focused image, whether in autofocus or manual focus modes.

I have gone through a couple of off-brand UV filters for my lenses and, realizing that they diminish image quality or flare to some extent, I decided to research my options. Ritz is a trusted brand, whereas Schott optical glass is used in filter brands costing $80+ for a single filter. This set seemed like a no-brainer — a store brand alternative to the costly brand-name counterparts. Unfortunately, the filters I have unpackaged thus far have been marked up (dirty) right out of the wrapper, and there are no instructions indicating if the coating is adversely impacted by any particular type of cleaner. (Some multi-coated lens filters don't allow for anything but dry microfiber cleaning.)

I was trying to improve upon my current off-brand lens filterers but ended up putting the old UV filter back on my Nikon lens because the 52mm filter included in this set produced such overtly soft and unfocused images that it is entirely unusable. Upon closer inspection, the entire surface of the glass is marred with micro-size pits. It's no exaggeration to say that using the same lens I've shot through window glass in my home (birds at the feeder) and through my car's windshield with far less ill effect. Perhaps I just got a defective one or perhaps the entire product is a counterfeit. (Interestingly, I did a search and found one Chinese company advertising, somewhat comically, filters "made with Schott glass or home-made glass". If Ritz made use of the manufacturer I stumbled across, it could very well be a toss-up!)

Notably, too, I expected there to be some type of guarantee or warranty with these filters. Even no-name filters have a five-year warranty and many a lifetime warranty. However, I could find no warranty card or instructions in the box (which was sealed). Moreover, one of the three sets I received was already opened. To open these boxes you have to physically cut a seal on either end of the package. So it looks like Amazon is doing their usual thing of reselling customer returns, too. Don't get me wrong: I've been an Amazon shopper more or less since this company got started, And yet I am reminded, in this case, why I ought to be shopping for this sort of thing locally. (Internet shopping is hugely convenient until you have to send stuff back!)

If I get better results with any of the other filters in the kit(s) — assuming I want to risk that Amazon won't take these back if I open the remainder of the packaging to test all of them one-by-one — I will update my review. Until then, please view the attached with Ritz Gear UV filter image (1st) and without (2nd), and judge for yourself the impact this lens filter had on both color and image clarity.

###

*OCT 1 UPDATE: As stated, I bought three of these sets so I have 12 separate filter evaluations I need to make; however, preliminary tests seem to indicate that the UV filters on my two micro 4/3 lenses are not doing any notable harm to image quality, whereas the 52mm UV filter is unusable on the Nikon 55-200mm zoom. Having tried three other brands for this particular 52mm lens, this is by far the absolute worst of the UV filters I've tried. As a result, I will most likely return the 52mm set. If I run into any problems with the 37mm or 58mm filters, I'll update again, and if I find that the other filters are problem-free I'll add a star, too.

title: Okay, but I'll probably go Pioneer next time.
text:
I have owned this headunit for a few days now, but I wanted to write a review so shoppers can make an informed decision, since nobody has written one as of yet. I have never owned an aftermarket headunit before, but I have played around with a Pioneer one, so by comparison, here are the pros and cons:

Pros:
It only takes a few seconds to boot
You can use your rear-view camera as soon as you turn on the car, without waiting for the headunit to start up
Has quite a bit of audio options (13 band EQ, distance between listener(s) and speakers, etc.)
Android Auto and Apple Carplay
Capacitive screen is smooth
Charged my Android phone pretty quickly
Pretty quick and responsive in general

Cons:
Haven't had the chance to play around too much yet, but once tried plugging in my Android phone as soon as the car started, and the headunit failed to recognize the Android device. Had to disconnect and reconnect.
Annoying warning message (be safe while driving) that must be manually dismissed every single time you boot up (unlike Pioneer's new headunits)
Android Auto does not start automatically (unlike Pioneer's new headunits)
Attracts fingerprints very easily
No light sensor for adaptive brightness

I have not had a chance to try Apple Carplay; only Android Auto. It's okay, but could use improvements. These are some gripes with Android Auto itself, and not the headunit, though it can be improved later with a software update (hopefully). It's annoying that you can't do much (such as typing or seeing your music playlists) with Android Auto. Though I'm sure it's for safety reasons, it's worse that you have to do it from your phone using a workaround (press the multitasking button to switch out of the Android Auto app since it doesn't allow you to do anything on your phone while in that app). Fortunately you can manually use Google Maps and Google Play Music this way, and it will still work on the headunit. As of this writing, album artwork also does not display on the headunit, whether you use bluetooth, or connect it with Android Auto. I do wish that you could use Android Auto without plugging it in though.

I have not had a chance to use the CD/DVD player, so I can not comment on that.

Overall, it is an okay headunit that is a bit behind modern technology that you're used to (with modern smartphones). Think of it like a mid-end smartphone. Would I recommend it? Well, yes and no, depending on your situation. It is definitely better than most manufacturer headunits, but it is pretty hefty for $800 or even $700. If your headunit isn't that bad, I recommend waiting a few years for them to advance their technology or user interface, unless a software update is pushed with improvements.

Not a bad unit, but a better one would (hopefully) be released in a couple years.

7/16/2016 Update

I had the chance to try out the USB connection by plugging in a flash drive. You can change the background, with what seems like any sized picture, even though the instructions say 800x480 resolution is required.

Album artwork does work with a flash drive. However, the user interface is AWFUL. Just TERRIBLE. You browse through your folders with a left and right arrow, with no name of the folders. If you really want to use USB for music playback, I recommend putting all your files in one folder, so you can scroll through the whole list. Otherwise you have to press the left and right arrows blindly to find the folder you want. Also during video playback, you can fast forward by holding down the next button (as usual), but there is no slider. You CAN NOT seek and jump to a location in a video. If you have titles in your video you may (not sure, but wouldn't be surprised if you couldn't) be able to.

DVD playback is okay. Not sure when I will use this feature but it's there. Same issues as video playback via USB: you can not seek, but you can select titles (chapters) if you go to the DVD top menu. If your headunit is attached to the parking brake, you can't watch a video or play a DVD unless the parking brake is activated. The audio will play, and the video will display when the brake is activated.

The brightness okay most of the time during the day on max brightness. However, if the sun hits the screen directly, forget about seeing anything on the screen.

8/17/2016 Update

I have had some issues regarding Android Auto itself. For example, Google Maps takes a while before it figures out I'm going a different direction and rerouting is needed. When I first start navigation, it can be difficult sometimes to determine if it thinks you're even going the right direction or not. Furthermore, there is no compass, so you can't figure out which direction it thinks you're facing.

Also, connecting my phone to initiate Android Auto has been more problematic more often now. During the past few days, I have had to disconnect and reconnect for it to recognize my phone, as it would say "Device Not Recognized". This has been very annoying, and I hope that it stops soon.

If you have any questions, leave a comment and I'll try to answer what I can.

9/24/2016 Android Auto Update
Android Auto is now worse. I'm not sure if it's the firmware update or the app update, but now you can no longer use the multitasking button workaround. When Android Auto is connected, only the back and home buttons appear. I have a Nexus 6P; I'm not sure if physical buttons from some Android phones may continue to work with the multitasking feature. It will, however, still let you scroll down your notifications and select the music app though.

1/29/2017 Update

Android Auto allows the workaround to switch apps again so that's good. You can even go to the press the home button from the multitasking menu to go to the home screen.

The compass on the home screen is now functional. I believe it was corrected with the last firmware update.

I am downgrading my review from 3 stars to 2 stars due to the fact that Android Auto on the headunit has ceased to function after only using it for approximately 6 months. I have tried it with 2 Android different Android phones and different cables. When I plug in my phone, there is no response on the headunit (not even a warning message). I know the connection is good because my phones will still charge when plugged in and show Android Auto as activated (though it doesn't lock up the phone like it usually does when connected and in use with Android Auto). I know it is not an issue with my phone or the Android Auto app on my phone because I went to a Best Buy store and connected it to a Pioneer demo unit with Android Auto and had no issues whatsoever. Next time I'm in the market for a new headunit, I'm going Pioneer.

2/5/2017 Update

The Android Auto issue has been resolved. I had to take it to the audio shop for them to reset a microprocessor from the back of the unit. According to the tech, it can not be done through the software (factory reset) or through the front, which some other headunits are able to. If you ask me, something is wrong with that picture. I am not too familiar with hardware, but I'm pretty sure manufacturers aren't supposed to require you to take out the headunit to reset the microprocessor after only using it for a few months.

4/28/2017 Update

I haven't been having much problems recently regarding my device not being recognized so I changed it back to 3 stars. Just upgraded to a Galaxy s8 and this phone does not show the multitasking button when Android Auto is connected. This is an Android annoyance, not a headunit issue so that doesn't affect my rating. However, the following cons still stand:
Annoying warning message (be safe while driving) that must be manually dismissed every single time you boot up (unlike Pioneer's new headunits)
Android Auto does not start automatically (unlike Pioneer's new headunits)
Attracts fingerprints very easily (I seem to have gotten used to this though)
No light sensor for adaptive brightness

title: Didnt suit my needs.
text:
I used this filter on a 10" Dobsonian with a 24mm and 10mm eyepiece, in Huntington beach on a clear night. There was very little to no difference in image for me. The light pollution in my area is really bad, almost as bad as LA, so I was hoping that this filter would allow me to finally see galaxies and faint nebulae. When looking at the Orion nebula (the only nebula I can ever see from my backyard) I switched back and forth from filter to no filter several times, and concluded that I could 'kind of' see a little more of the outer cloud, but I had to switch back and forth like 5 times before I could confirm that, so it obviously is not a big difference. I then decided to try and find a Galaxy, which from my backyard is almost impossible. they look like very tiny smudges that are like 1% brighter than the rest of space. After an hour I finally found one, and switched back and forth from filter to no filter, and it was clear really fast that the filter was making no notable difference for me.

I'm returning the product, because it was purchased for home use, and Its clearly not going to help me much with these light polluted skies, but it seemed like a high quality product in general, and might be of more use to folks wanting to use it out in darker skies, or with photography applications. If your in an area with a lot of light pollution, I don't think its going to fix any problems though.

title: Tech support will not be there for you
text:
Regret having to write this, but it may help you be a more informed buyer. I purchased the Drobo Mini for two purposes, to be my back drive and to archive my photographs. Whether it is truly a RAID device, not as fast as other devices, etc. was irrelevant. All I wanted, all I expected, all I paid for was complete reliability. Didn't happen.

What did happen was that the unit began to unmount itself and then become unavailable to the desktop. The actual details don't matter. I could not access my data. I could not back up my main drive. I opened seven, yes seven support tickets with Drobo; not a particularly seamless process by the way. I sent three diagnostic dumps. I wrote detailed accounts and carefully followed the few tech support suggestions. One of which was "your disk is corrupted. Clean it up with Disk Warrior." Now how a disk can become corrupted in a RAID-like system is beyond me. I thought that is what they are designed to avoid. But I dutifully spent $125 on Disk Warrior which promptly crashed upon encountering the Drobo. Then I was instructed to reset the Drobo, which of course promptly removed all the data from the drives. Finally was bounced up to "senior tech support" who agreed with what I'd been saying all along. The unit was defective. Having known that would have saved the data. So after 60 days without a back up, Drobo has shipped a replacement. And BTW not shipped against a credit card pending return of the defective unit, but only after I shipped the unit back to them. More backup days lost. I understand units fail. The one star is for the non-listening, ill-informed, slow tech support that cost me the loss of a huge archive (which fortunately still exists, but must be re-migrated) and exposed me to two months without back up

Think carefully before you purchase the Drobo Mini

title: Works great in Thinkpad T440p
text:
I got this for my Thinkpad T440p, upgrading from 12 GB of PC3-12800, in the form of an 8 GB Samsung stick and a 4 GB Hyundai. The old RAM had CL11 (11,11,11,28) timings. I measured the old RAM's transfer speed at 12530 MB/s in NovaBench, a little shy of its theoretical max of 12800 MB/s. I was skeptical whether the T440p would run this new RAM at full speed. All the public specs list it as taking up to DDR3 1600, and there was no mention of XMP support.

I decided to take the plunge, and CPU-Z shows this RAM running at the full rated 1866 (actual clock 933 MHz). The XMP 1.3 profile shows CL10 (10,10,10,30) timings with a 2T command rate. Oddly the system is running it with 10,10,10,32 timings and a faster 1T command rate. (As a guess, the faster command rate might be because they're running in a dual channel configuration.) Now I'm up to 14786 MB/s on NovaBench, closer to its max of 14900 than the old one was to its max.

This RAM has profiles for both 1.35V and 1.5V, so it will work in laptops that use plain DDR3 as well as those requiring DDR3L.

I haven't done a battery life comparison, but I would expect faster RAM to cause a small reduction. I can't say I've noticed any difference in how warm the laptop is when doing normal tasks.

From the product pictures, I assumed there would be a heat spreader. Turns out this is just a sticker. This RAM neither has nor needs a heat spreader.

As a side note, 8 GB should be enough for gaming, and I probably wouldn't bother with 16 at the moment. I got this because I do a bunch of stuff involving virtual machines and a bit of RAM-bound data processing. The 12 GB I had was technically enough, but I had to watch my memory use when doing RAM heavy things.

title: Good for adding 802.11-ac to an old laptop
text:
Disclosure: I received this USB wifi adapter from Netgear for free through their Friends and Family program, but I will give my honest unbiased review.

Likes:

The AC1200 Wifi adapter comes with a USB extension dock that allows you to move the adapter away from your laptop (since the adapter is quite large and will get in the way) or your desktop since it may sit on the ground and get bad reception.

I installed the AC1200 adapter in a laptop with built-in wifi 802.11n on 2.4ghz band. I connected the AC1200 on 5ghz and was able to get about a 30% increase in performance from the same spot, about 15 feet and 1 room over from my wifi router. I do have a 802.11-ac dual band router.

There is a antenna that is activated by swiveling it sideways on the adapter. This allows you to fine tune reception a bit compared to other adapters. I did notice that the position of the antenna does have a large effect on download speeds.

The range was improved as I moved my laptop around my house. I was getting a better, more stable connection as compared to my laptop's internal wifi.

I downloaded the drivers from the Netgear website and included in the package was a driver only install without all the additional Netgear programs.

I tried it on the external usb port of my Winbook TW802 and the adapter allowed me to stream HD content from my Silicondust HD Homerun Prime, whereas before the internal tablet wifi caused the picture to stutter badly and I had to SD resolution to get a watchable picture.

Dislikes:

The adapter itself is wide. On my laptop, it blocked the two neighboring ports on either side. Not totally blocked, but enough to render the neighboring ports inaccessible.

Verdict:

The adapter worked very well for me, it kept a good stable connection. If you are looking for an USB 802.11-ac adapter, this is a good one.

title: Amazing monitor is a vast understatement.
text:
If you're a gamer and you're looking for a monitor, don't look any further; from one gamer to another: buy this, you will not regret it. Don't gimp your high performance setup and expensive hardware with a 60Hz monitor. If you're running current top-end GPUs and pushing frame rates over 60 FPS, if your refresh rate doesn't match your frame rate, you're going to have issues. The biggest thing I'd like to push is the fact this monitor is not only built for gamers, it also looks amazing, do not in any way be dissuaded by reviews stating this monitor looks horrible, or has bad color. The capability for adding 3D and Nvidia G-Sync is also a great option to have. I've seen some reviews on various websites that state this monitor looks ''washed out'' and other such cons, but I've seen no such issues. Out of the box stock settings admittedly look bad; however these are just OEM default settings. A few minutes spent in the menu tweaking contrast, brightness, color correction etc., gets this monitor looking absolutely gorgeous. Some people recommend downloading ICC color profiles and jumping through hoops to ''try and make this look good.'' Bottom line: it isn't necessary. If you want to follow one of those guides, download a color profile and do all that, it's your choice. But honestly, in less than 5 minutes you can have this monitor adjusted to your liking and looking great on your own just by adjusting some menu options. I used a Envy 17-3D gaming laptop for years with HP's LCD-LED display,and this Asus blows it out of the water by a country mile.

I can't understand why some people write bad reviews for an item without fully testing it out first, and at the very least adjusting menu options. I paid $250 for this, and for a monitor under 300 dollars, I couldn't be more impressed with the features, and the visual quality. This is a gaming monitor built with gamers in mind. The vast majority of bad reviews stating this is a monitor with bad visuals are from people wanting to compare a $250 TN panel meant for gaming with monitors not built for gaming and 3 times the price. This monitor boasts a 144Hz refresh, 1ms GTG lag, amazing contrast ratio, availability for G-Sync & 3D upgrades, Gameplus features built in and other gamer-centric features. Comparing this to IPS monitors with only 60 Hz refresh rates, 10+ms GTG, input lag and cost anywhere from $500 dollars to well over $1,000, is far from correct. On top of being an amazing gaming monitor that will show no ghosting, artifacting or screen tearing and built in features for gamers, for a TN panel monitor this looks amazing. In my opinion during routine everyday PC use, and for gaming, you'll see no noticeable difference in color and visual performance with this TN panel than you will higher priced lower performance IPS monitors.

Finding a monitor that does gaming well, as well as have great visuals is a hard find, but this does it and it does it for a great price. The 24'' monitor is large enough that you get a great view, yet not so large you have to constantly move your head side to side to see everything, or have to sit far away from the monitor just to get it all in your field of view. It has a good solid base, and a bracket for cable management on the back of monitor. The monitor swivels, it tilts, it pivots, it has height adjustment and you can flip the monitor for either a page orientation of 16:9 widescreen or a portrait orientation. So no matter your setup or how you sit at your PC, this monitor can be set for maximum comfort and best viewing.

** IMPORTANT: First, be sure your GPU has a DisplayPort I/O so you are able to use a DP cable to connect this to your GPU if you want the full range of performance this monitor offers. *DO NOT USE* HDMI or DVI with this monitor! If you use HDMI or DVI with this screen, you will not be getting or seeing the performance you paid for. Neither HDMI nor DIV/DVI-D are capable of full HD at more than 60 FPS (60Hz). The majority of the reason for going with this monitor is the superior 144Hz refresh, 1ms GTG, and no discernible input lag. Thus allowing high FPS with no graphical issues. If you want to be able to use your monitor at 144Hz, if you want to be able to run 100+ FPS and not suffer blurring, ghosting, artifacting, or screen tearing, and you want the best viewing experience and performance, DisplayPort MUST be used. This monitor only comes packaged with a DVI-D cable and audio cable, and does not come packaged with a DisplayPort cable; so be sure to pick up a VESA certified DisplayPort along with this monitor.

title: I researched the Dell as much as I could and most people concluded that the new Dell S2716DG is just another washed out TN with
text:
I've been waiting for the Asus PG279Q to release for months but, after hearing of the quality control issues, I decided to go with the Dell S2716DG instead. The Dell has everything I want in a monitor ( 1440p, g-sync, 144hz ) but is a TN panel. I've owned Everything from a regular ole TN to a 4K TN ( Acer XB280HK) to a 5k iMac and did not want to go the TN route. I researched the Dell as much as I could and most people concluded that the new Dell S2716DG is just another washed out TN with terrible colors and horrific viewing angles because it shares the panel from the old Asus PG278Q. However, I decided to try it anyways.

As soon as I turned on the monitor I was surprised by the color. It looked good to me. Not mind blowing but it looked really good. I turned down the brightness from the default 75 to 30 and the contrast to 65. I then used the nVidia control panel to change the gamma from 1.0 to around .88 and the color vibrancy from 50% to 62% and now I feel the picture looks amazing... I am VERY happy with how everything looks; from the desktop to games.

I'm a little confused by how good the viewing angles are. I had an Acer XB280HK (4K, G-Sync, TN) and I could see an obvious shift in gamma from the top of the screen to the bottom. If you moved your head from side to side the image would almost disappear. I thought this was just what TN panels did and I was willing to accept that with this Dell. However, when sitting in front of it, the image looks perfect. No obvious shift in gamma or change in color from the top of the screen to the bottom. Also, I can look at the screen from the sides ( 178 degree viewing angle) ...and I can see the picture fine. It actually barely changes color at all. Same from a straight view from above. The only way I can tell the monitor is using a TN panel is if I look at it from the bottom, like... If I get down on the floor.

Pros:
-The monitor if in perfect condition. No dead pixels, no pixel inversion, no defects at all.
-144hz and G-synce feel VERY smooth! I'm not one of the people that feels a drastic change from 60hz to 144hz but the difference is there and it does feel nice.
-G-Sync is great. I can't go back to a monitor without it. There is no screen tearing and no lag. A VRR monitor is a must have of you enjoy great visuals.
-Viewing angles are amazing for a TN panel.
-Colors look very nice with nVidia vibrancy set to 62%.
-Build quality is top notch. Leaps and bounds better than my last Acer this price (XB280HK).
-No IPS glow (because it's a TN)

Cons:
-The only real con I can come up with is maybe the AG coating (anti-glare coating) used. It is very heavy. Some users may prefer this but I would rather have a semi gloss finish. The AG coating is so heavy that some users (myself included) feel that you get a little "sparkle" effect on solid white backgrounds. Almost as if you feel you need to wipe a slight residue off the screen. It is by NO MEANS a deal breaker. It's not noticeable during general use or gaming. I would just like a semi gloss coating.

title: Not a good choice
text:
Bought this camera a few months ago and wanted to give it some time before I wright this review. If you want to just use this camera to LIVE view an area, then this camera is an excellent option as long as you mount is very high. However, if you want to use this camera for security, then I suggest you look for another camera vendor. The cameras zone detection for movement is terrible and difficult to use compared to other cameras I own. There are 4 windows you can drag and drop into the areas you want to monitor for motion and they are difficult to set up and not very reliable. Sensitivity of the detection zones is questionable. Also, many times after movement is detected, the action has already occurred and is partially recorded or missed completely. The alarm zone setup and functionality of this camera are not good enough to warrant purchasing this camera for security.

The other feature of this camera that is disappointing is the vertical up/down function. You will have to mount this camera very high to be able to look out far enough to utilize the zoom. My camera is mounted 9 feet up and it is still not high enough to zoom in fully utilizing the 4x zoom function. The photo of the camera on the amazon web page shows the camera in its highest 'up' position. Actually, it more down, not even level enough to look strait. The problem this creates is if I try to zoom in on something, I end up looking at a spot on the ground.(attached image is the highest possible vertical position of the area compared to the standard view.) Very disappointing.

The local web interface software is really bad. Many functions do not work even though they are shown on the screen. Also, during playback you can not fast forward or rewind. To watch an alarm detection video, you have to hunt through hundreds of 20 second videos one-by-one. They do not automatically flow from one to the other during play and again, you can not fast forward. This makes the security aspect of the camera useless. If you intend to download and save video, you can only download one 20 second video at a time as apposed to several videos within a specific time period. Not user friendly or productive.

The good points are its connectivity options are very good. The day and night image quality is very good. No complaints there except again, if you try and zoom, unless your camera is 15 feet in the air, you will be looking at the grass. I do not recommend this camera as there are many other brands with a better interface and functionality.

title: Beast of a mount, but it works great!
text:
Definitely a beast! I've got an Orion 10" x 1000mm Newtonian Astrograph attached to it, and it has no problems moving with multiple finderscopes and imaging devices attached. The mount itself is a little awkward to carry, but not too much trouble. Plan to order additional weights if you have a large instrument like mine, and be sure to get the right ones. It comes with a pair of 11Lb weights, and I ordered a pair of 17Lb weights to go with it. I currently have a 17 at the end, and an 11 about midway up the shaft.

This one was a bit pricey compared to the AVX mount I was looking at for $800. However, I got this to handle a variety of scopes I was looking at, as the AVX was a tad small when I started looking at the instrument weight capacity I needed. This handles up to 55Lbs, and my current instrument rig is about 40Lbs (too high for the AVX). The counter weights are not part of the weight calculation, as the capacity is the essentially the mass the drive can move. I recommend having a bit of headroom in the capacity, and I've heard people recommend not to exceed 50% of the rated capacity. However, I think, if you know how to balance it, you can run it up close to the limit without trouble, and Celestron has told people it will handle the full 55Lbs. I setup and balanced everything inside and I marked my weight shaft for where the weights need to go, which helps get it set up faster outside.

The scope sits a bit high when mounted. With my scope, I set it up with the tripod legs fully retracted so I can reach the eyepiece. If you're doing visual observing using a longer scope where the eyepiece is near the aperture, such as a Newtonian, you might look into right-angle adapters so you don't have to constantly reposition the scope to reach the eyepiece.

Tracking is solid. I don't notice any shake during imaging, and objects stay pretty much where I put them. I'm still getting used to proper alignment, so I have to make periodic corrections. They just recently released the polar axis scope for it. So, I'm hoping to get a more solid alignment as soon as I mine arrives. I also find it doesn't shift much when I adjust the position of the scope in its' rings.

Since I've never used a computerized mount before, it took a bit to set up. I recommend fiddling a bit before trying to use it for the first time. I have several other alignment, guiding, and control accessories for it that I haven't had a chance to try. So, I can't speak to them just yet. But I found it does pretty good right out of the box.

Definitely get the vibration dampening feet for the tripod if you're on any type of pavement or other rigid surface.

You'll need the 5A power supply, if you intend to use it where you have AC power. I use a big jump pack with a 12AH SLA battery to power it, even though I'm usually well within reach of AC. I've gone a couple of nights on that setup without recharging the pack. Unless you turn off tracking, the motors run continuously when the mount is on. So, take that into account with your power source.

I usually have an imager and computer attached and haven't had any issues keeping the cables from tangling. I think it helps that the wiring for the mount is internal, so I only have to deal with cables for the mount power, hand controller, and imager.

So far, I'm loving this! I'll try to remember to come back and post some pictures of my rig and images from the scope.

UPDATE 2018-06-29:
I've been having intermittent issues with the RA drive since my original post. It's not anything user adjustable. The RA drive just decides to rapidly move back and forth (I call it shoe shining, something anyone familiar with computer tape drives from the good 'ol days will recognize), or it will start moving until it hits the stop than reverse, and it keeps doing this regardless of input or power cycling. It recently became extremely consistent. Celestron support has been very quick to respond on this issue and wants me to send it in for repair. Unfortunately, that means shipping to California and being without a mount for several weeks. I probably won't have it back in time for the upcoming Mars Opposition, which sucks, because this is my only mount.

Also, in this update, I added a few pics of the various setups I've done. The one with 4 instruments was my eclipse viewing rig back in August 2017. The mount handled it with ease! The other two pics are my current solar rig and the 10" Newt (for reference, the gal looking into it is about 5' 3").
