As well, there's a sizable population of such vendors who engage in falsifying reviews, sometimes in mass quantities (I ran across a cellphone screen protector company that would mass create *thousands* of five star reviews, I'd report it to amazon, a week later there would be a thousand new ones replacing them).

So, why all the preface here? Because while this vendor has an oddball brand name, and the listing's descriptions are riddled with what is sometimes unpleasantly referred to as "chinglish" - all that said....these are excellent cables. Period. I use them to power my small "farm" of mad-scientist Raspberry Pi micro computers. I recently added a new one to the bunch, and had to press an older, very thin but 'braided' exterior (faux high quality) USB cable into service. Repeated crashes, all prefaced in the system logs with 'undervoltage warning' - a sure sign that the cable, in a word, sucks.

I've never had an undervoltage with these cables. Raspberry Pi's don't draw a huge amount of current, granted, but I sometimes push these little guys hard. Never a problem.

I've seen a small number of one star reviews, suggesting that the cable worked fine for a while than would no longer fast-charge xyz device. I can only imagine some sort of horrible abuse of the cables that would cause that - or, maybe on rare occasion there's been a defective one that slips through.

As for me, I'm buying another set of these, because even though there's other cables with 'more' reviews, nearly all five stars, at least in this instance, I know that regardless of the review stats, these are excellent quality cables, proven in use.

How's that for a review of a piece of wire?

title: Spectacular machine!
text:
Honestly, after living with it a week, I have to say that this is THE best computer I've ever owned. Every aspect and feature works perfectly, significantly exceeding my expectations. Where to begin? Okay:

I find I love the the cool RGB lighting with its near endless variety of colors, patterns, and animations controlled by the included remote, even though it wasn't even a factor in my computer hunt originally. Seen through the tempered glass side panel, it really is striking. The fans are nice and quiet, as well.

This is my first true gaming rig, not to mention my first PC with a solid state primary drive, and all I can say about its blazing speed is WOW. I'm mainly a gamer, but I bet this would be great for the home user wanting to do video editing and rendering. Speaking of games, the 2TB secondary drive has plenty of room to install all your favorite games. How do they run? Spectacularly! Looking at Steam's in-game FPS counter, when I disabled the framerate limiter in The Witcher 3 and set every graphical setting to on, maximum, or Ultra, I saw an astounding framerate of 188(!) FPS...needless to say, even with everything I could throw at it, the game still ran smooth as oiled silk, as it does for Far Cry 4 and others.

Remember, the RTX 2070 card's ray tracing ability hasn't been used in a published game yet, so you're relatively future-proofed. I expect to enjoy mine for quite a few years before needing any upgrade beyond minor improvement (increasing RAM at some point, for example) and very possibly without having to do a thing.

In summary, I think this machine is a complete thoroughbred in every respect. The GMA1394A has only been available for a few months but I'm glad I have mine...I believe as people realize what a terrific value it is, the demand for them could well drive prices upward.

***EDIT*** Eight months in, and I'm still loving it, this PC handles all the games I throw at it with aplomb. Also, I did notice a bit of fan noise at first when it warmed up, but after a bit of time the sound disappeared...I'm assuming it was molding flash on the ends of the blades that wore in over some time.

ALSO also- This has got to be the BEST PC case I've ever had. At eight months in, there's virtually no dust in the interior as can be clearly seen through the glass side panel. A swipe of the hand once in a while over the intake grilles on top clear beginning accumulations of dust debris. I think it's because the feet on the lower corners keeps the bottom of the machine above the surface, discouraging most dust accretion.

title: Nice
text: The antenna seems well-made and it works.  I tried it initially indoors on the first floor.  I wasn't expecting too much, as the TV stations are around 50 miles away.  I only got a few stations set up this way.  It makes a difference where in the room the antenna is located.  Sitting in a window that faces the direction of the TV stations is the place to start.  Or maybe in an attic.  This antenna is also designed for outdoor use.  I mounted it outside on an eave-mounted TV mast.  If you have a mounting mast, it is VERY easy to install.  Now all of my stations of interest come in well, with one notable exception.  All stations except CBS were UHF and came in fine.  CBS is VHF and I couldn't get it at all. (Most stations are UHF these days).  The antenna looks nice enough for indoor use, but has survived some good storms while outside. It comes with plenty of cable, so I didn't have to buy any or make an extension.  This model has no pre-amp.  For many people, this is a plus.  Some folks on the fringe may benefit from a pre-amp (this adds complexity and the need for power for the pre-amp).  All in all, I am quite satisfied with the antenna, although if I knew I would end up mounting it outside, I should probably have just purchased an outside antenna.

title: Comparison between Samsung 8500 and Sony 800
text: Great Blu Ray player. I also have a Sony UBP-X800. After extensive side by side comparisons between the two models I have concluded the following: Sony faster load times, Ability to play Hi Res Audio. Samsung is glitch free where switching between 3d and HD, Sony requires tweaking some of the auto settings. There are VERY slight differences in 4K pictures but only noticeable side by side, I couldn't choose which was better. I read many reviews about the Audio Quality difference...there are none and I was really listening for them through my $10 grand 7.2.4 ATMOS/DTS X setup and a dozen or so ATMOS recorded movies. Samsung has more Online Content, both perform well (IMHO most complaints I see are user, signal or content issues, not machine based), Sony has a much higher quality chassis. My Samsung has been in use(hard use ie KIDS) for about a year now with no problems, and in general I have pretty good luck with Samsung components. I have had many Sony players off the shelf at Walmart go bad, hopefully they put the same quality in the internal components as they did into the case on this one. I have chosen to keep the Sony with the my main system, but honestly, the only reason is the appearance, it looks nicer racked with other AV gear. I don't buy CDs I get just all my HiRes content from TIDAL and Spotify Premium. That reminds me, one other sale point for SONY is it does include SPOTIFY direct, which if you have an AV sound system that doesn't have it already  then you are in for a real treat, puts BT and IPODs to shame. This bag was actually my 2nd choice because my first choice had the "KomalC" stamped much more prevalent in larger letters on the front of the bag. The letters on this bag are small and on the back, so not too bad. My advice would be keep these letters small or put them in an inconspicuous spot like inside the bag or under a flap.

title: Fantastic remote!
text: I recently upgraded the audio receiver in my home entertainment system and began the process of learning how to use HDMI pass through  technology.  My system is relatively simple consisting of a 55 inch Sony Bravia television, a Yamaha TSR 5790 receiver, an Arris cable box and a Sony Blu-ray disc player.  I used an HDMI cable to connect the cable box to the receiver and used the ARC input on the receiver to connect to the television. The bd player was also connected to the receiver by  HDMI. I then found myself wanting to consolidate four separate remotes. Some research on Amazon led me to the Logitech remote which I ordered and received the same day. The remote connects to your computer through a supplied USB cable and the instructions are pretty intuitive.  I was able to set it up quickly and figured out my basic programming scenarios: watching tv, watching Blu-ray Discs and listening to music through various receiver options. There are spare buttons on the remote that can be programmed to mimic your specific cable box needs such as the DVR recording list and the settings menu.  I did need some help in setting up a scenario that turned on the TV without the surround sound of the stereo. My wife prefers a quieter output from the TV. I called logitech support and had a completely satisfactory session where the new scenario was programmed by the tech remotely. (There is a 90 day period of free tech-support so you can get most of your questions resolved.) This remote has tremendous capabilities and even people who are not technically savvy can find their way through the programming.

title: This is the cheap 35 to learn on
text:
*For the cost* (very important), this lens does everything you'd need a cheap, quick 35 f/2 to do. It's build quality and feel are surprisingly nice. The focus ring is satisfyingly tactile - smooth and large enough for my fingers to grasp easily and well, unlike my nikkor D lenses.
It's not the widest aperture for a 35, but for less than 100 dollars, you get functionality and value. We use this lens to film vlogs indoors with inexpensive studio lighting and it works well enough for our needs. It is soft at f2 well into the edges and is difficult to nail focus with. The AF is quite slow, but seems accurate enough.

I intend to try this lens for astrophotography, but do not have high hopes due to that lack of sharpness at f2, but I'll remain open minded until I test that out. Stopped down to f/2.8 though, clarity and sharpness improve considerably. We shoot our indoor vlogs at f3.2 for that extra depth of field, but wouldn't have an issue going down to 2.8 if needed and the improved sharpness is nice at 3.2. I included two files - one full size image of a tree section unedited at f/2 (1/4000th of a second to rule out motion blur) and a cropped in version of that file to show poor sharpness right in the center of the image.

The lens is a nice size. Slightly bigger than my nikkor 50mm, but smaller than my Rokinon 85mm. It works well with my Nikon D500 and when focus is on where you need it, images do look good. It also focuses close enough for near-macro photography, so that's nice.

compared to other more expensive 35s out there, this is crap, but those lenses are hundreds and hundreds of dollars more in cost. That's why I give this a 4/5. It's a great lens to get the feel of a 35mm lens under your belt, but I would not recommend for pro use at all.

+
Good build
Good Value
Close Focus

-
Slow AF
Not sharp at f/2

text: [[VIDEOID:6244343799c625e03a03219a4204076d]] My next door neighbor's car got broken into overnight while parked in their driveway. After a lot of research, I decided on the Reolink Argus. Now a few months later, I still think I've made the right decision. It's great being completely wireless. Since I have flashlights using CR123 batteries, I've already got a small stock pile. I just have to remember to turn off the motion detection (PIR) while doing yard work. The night vision works better than I expected, so does motion detection, maybe a little too sensitive on the mid setting. It consistently picks up traffic across the cul-de-sac 50-75ft away from the camera (see video showing the UPS truck). It would be great if Cloud video backup is available, but a snapshot via email attachment is probably sufficient in most cases. Considering the price and the feature set, a solid 4.5 stars.

title: Great tracking & nice design but a couple issues to note
text:
Background: I'm a software developer and use a PC for several hours a day. Event though I'm not a gamer, I often using "gaming" stuff because it works well for general use, like this mouse.

This is a very nice mouse that has excellent tracking and the design makes it look pretty cool as well. The DPI button changes the DPI on the fly and works great. The scroll wheel feels good too and the middle click button is excellent.

I am a big fan of Logitech mice but they often end up having clicking problems where clicks are not registered correctly (usually as a double click). It's quite annoying. This mouse claims to have a 20 million click life-cycle. I imagine that should last me awhile if true.

Now for the downsides:

* While this mouse has a height-adjustable palm rest, I do not find the design quite as ergonomic as the Logitech mice I use (like the G502). That could be due to the ambidextrous design (which some people will like but some may not).

* The side buttons feel "mushy" as another reviewer stated. They have to travel a greater distance before registering a click than other mice I have used.

Overall though, there is a lot to like about this mouse so I am giving it 4.5 stars out of 5 and rounding it up to 5.

NOTE: I was sent a free product sample for review. I was not paid or told what to write.

title: Hi quality turntable at a reasonable price.
text: Pretty impressed with this turntable so far. .... IMO its probably the best turntable you can get for under $1500.00 (with Cartridge) in the US. The 9 inch composite arm is a good above average arm. The heavy aluminum damped plater is also above average ... The electronic controlled speed stability is very good The included RCA cables are of good quality and acceptable for most situations, although some improvement may be possible with a higher quality after market pair that has better shielding; if your system is prone to radio or electromagnetic interference.... The isolation plinth is acceptable (above average for this price range) some improvement in isolation may be obtained using an isolation platform of some kind, which is true for most turntables in or near this price range anyway ....  The weakest link is probably the Cartridge it comes with...The Ortofon 2M Silver...Its not a bad cartridge really somewhere between the performance of the Ortofon 2M Red and the Ortofon 2M Blue. In fact it can be upgraded to better than Ortofon 2M Blue performance (near 2M Bronze) by getting the 2M Blue stylus. and replacing the existing stylus; which is a direct fit and upgrade.. For a lot of people that is going to be good enough and satisfying.However the 2M Silver is not going to exceed the performance of the Ortofon 2M Bronze which is actually a different design and better cartridge....So that's the dilemma...I am pretty happy with this turntables performance so far and I like the cartridges sound quality.  This turntable benefits by replacing the felt mat with a cork mat and also using a light weight record clamp. (JA Michell type or similar etc.) Do not use too heavy of a clamp as it will interfere with motor stability.... Due to all the controversy over the Ortofon 2M Silver at some point you might want to replace it. Some recommendations for a higher performance replacement cartridge include but are not limited to: The Ortofon 2M Bronze or Black; Nagaoka MP-200 ; Goldring G-1042; Hana SL or Hana SH; Dynavector DV10x...

title: Fantastic Upgrade to my Arlo Security System
text:
I had previously purchased a three-Arlo camera kit including the Pro base station. I decided that I needed at least one more camera, so I purchased a single Arlo Pro camera with a Pro base station, removed the older base station, and connected my three original Arlo cameras to the new base station, along with the Pro Camera. I then stuck a 128 GB flash drive into the new base station after syncing the cameras and firing up the system.

My first observations are that the new camera, with its rechargeable battery is going to last a long time between recharges; not to mention that the siren, the audio features, and the video quality are pretty amazing. But what really surprised me was that the batteries in my older Arlo cameras seem to be having a greatly extended battery life relative to previously. I can only assume that the Pro base station connectivity is far more efficient regarding battery life. Additionally, the whole system seems to be much faster at picking up movement and recording it.

I would highly recommend the Arlo Pro to anyone desiring a wireless security system and encourage anyone with an old system to upgrade ASAP.

title: Worth it
text:
I have had this laptop for almost three years and not a single complaint, when I bought it in 2013, I could play most of the games released then on high settings. Three years later, I could still run the witcher3, mgsv, and dragon age: inquistion on high settings at 1080p. I got the sli version

To be clear, when I first got it I felt cheated because I got the cheapest version with sli (gt 750m) and then found out much later that a newer version was released with a slightly better gpu. To add insult to injury, I discovered much later that I had the version without the m.2 slot. However after I replaced the HDD with a 1tb ssd, I've had no complaints. Here is a site that benchmarks the 750 sli, (...)
In conclusion, here are the pros and cons

Cons
bad battery life (true with most gaming laptops anyway)
The charger is big and the laptop could be considered heavy
It gets a bit noisy (not obscenely so) and hot (get a cooling pad if you're concerned)
not really future proof
Trackpad is not great (use a mouse)

Pros
Works perfectly after three years
Keyboard still works well
The screen is perfect no complaints whatsoever
easily upgradeable (I.e ram, and storage device)
It also flies under the radar (doesn't look like a gaming laptop)

That's about it. I didn't say anything about the speakers because I barely use it. However, it's good (not mediocre, not great, just good!). If you're considering this laptop mainly for gaming then any laptop that doesn't have at least a gtx 860m or a thunderbolt 3 connector isn't worth it when compared to this.

After receiving this new one and comparing them both, the new case looks and feels a bit cheaper made than the old case. Last thing, the screen protector that came with the 9.7 case is flat out junk.

Overall, the new 9.7 case just doesn't look or feel as nice as the older cases Boriyuan made. I'll be shopping for a different iPad 9.7 case soon.

title: Great product, well engineered, allows amazing videos
text:
I get steady video results from this swivel mount. No vibration, just occasional flex. The aluminum cam lever is an excellent touch and much appreciated for quick mounting/release.

I mentioned elsewhere but this bears repeating:

Cameras have high power consumption whether recording or not. Better to leave camera OFF with its on-board Wifi ON until you want to record. Here are my suggestions for Hero 4/5/6 or Garmin.

Setup:
- pair camera with your smartphone or a wifi remote (I like GoPro's remote)
- place the camera in a waterproof protective shell to protect from debris and falls
- mount to tie-down eyelet
- adjust your camera's shot angle and preview with smartphone or camera's screen
- shut camera off, but **leave camera Wifi ON** (e.g. Hero's screen will be blank, but have a blinking blue light. Will refer to as "Wifi standby mode")
Usage:
- before something interesting: safely! use smartphone/remote to turn the camera on and start recording
- afterwards: stop recording and remotely power-off camera. It will remain in Wifi standby to record again.

This way you can stretch out your ~30min battery to cover a multi-hour flight.

title: Yep, very happy customer.
text:
Updated: I've been paying the $99 membership fee for recordings for 3 devices. The issues being felt right now are because there was a free tier.

For those of you upset that you can't get all of the features for free; what did you expect? Canary is in the business of making money! Yes, Switch to Nest, and go see what the cost of running Nest cams is for three devices.

If you are not interested in paying for the membership, consider a Foscam R2 or some other device that you have to pair with a NAS or some other means, I still believe that Canary is one of the best solutions out there.

Their measly $99 for up to 3 devices (2 if you are a new user) ensures that their developers get to eat, and I continue to get support.

/endrant

I love the new features in two-way chat. I can now speak to my family while at work.

As a longtime user of security systems and cameras, I am happy to say that Canary does an incredible job. At the time of this post the software and firmware has matured enough that the hardware is simple to use, with a few caveats.

While I did have problems with my wifi connection due to the complexity of my particular setup, I was able to connect my Canary directly to my wifi repeater and have had no issues since. Control from Amazon Echo, Wink, and the Canary app has been exceptionally simple.

The $49 per year for extended recording capabilities easily saves me money vs my other camera solutions, and the bonus alarms and auto away sensing plus incredible night vision and 1080P recording makes a big difference.

Because the subscription plan is per address, not per device (unlike Nest Cam), the costs are significantly lower the more Canary's I decide to buy (up to 4).

I really like that the camera can be set to privacy mode so that no recording takes place, as well as non-notification recording happens when in the standby mode. A quick look at the Canary tells me if it is armed, disarmed, or in privacy mode from across the room, but is generally not necessary since when my phone is home, the Canary disarms.

I can also say "Alexa, trigger Arm Canary." to manually arm the canary with the Amazon Echo when my phone is not in reach.

It also has sensors such as air quality and noise which connect and add additional features to my Wink hardware. Bonus!

All in all a great value under $170 per Canary and bonus points for renters and home owner's insurance discounts!

title: Lots of nice features for the price but not the most reliable receiver
text:
It was tough to give this receiver 2 stars because I really liked this receiver. Before I go any further, I would be considered somewhat of an audiophile. For the average person who is looking for an above average receiver for a home theater, Onkyo has made the setup and operation of this receiver incredibly easy. From unboxing the receiver to full operation, the process took only an hour (which includes calibrating the room with their AccuEQ and setup microphone). A little fine tuning and it was set to go. I'm running 5.1.2 with 4 in ceiling speakers, 2 floorstanding speakers and the center channel under my TV.

One major issue with this receiver is that the automatic calibration is very innacurate. you can run it several times, and the results will almost never be the same. The crossover is not set correctly, so I use that as a baseline starting point and then self calibrate the speakers. If you aren't familiar with crossover settings, and the working of a speaker, you're not going to be getting the best sound out of your system.

After 14 months, the Video Processor stopped working. Thankfully Onkyo has a 2 year warranty, however, instead of exchanging the unit out, you have to take it to an electronics repair shop which takes 2-3 weeks to repair.

I think Onkyo receivers have a lot of great things that make them easy to operate and enjoy, but hopefully they can fix some known issues.

title: BUYERS BEWARE OF "ALTERED" DRIVES (AND BAD SUPPORT FROM WESTERN DIGITAL)
text:
WARNING: DO NOT PURCHASE THIS DRIVE FROM A THIRD PARTY SELLER

If you do I recommend immediately checking the serial number on WD's website and confirming the model number. I purchased 4 of these drives, which came in the standard sealed envelopes, and one of them just failed. The drives have a two year warranty, but even though it has only been a year WD will not honor the warranty because the serial number of the drive comes back as being a 6TB My Book drive. (In fact, all four drives I purchased are listed as My Book drives on the WD serial number lookup, which I find odd).

It is also unfortunate that WD has awful support. They are very polite on the phone but their ability to actually help you is useless. I was given the runaround numerous times, told to call back, wait for emails, and finally a few days later was informed that they would not help me.

So this 1-star review is based on 1) my experience with WD being unsupportive in my case, 2) the actual purchase of the drives being apparently "altered" (WD's claim), and 3) one of the drives physically failing after 1 year of use.

I buy a lot of drives. I've never had such a headache replacing one that went bad. Never buying a WD drive again.

title: Amazing and only $29!
text:
I had read reviews for the full sized Velocifire keyboard and they were good so I figured THIS ten-keyless version should be equally as good. Well it IS! I am actually quite amazed that I got this for $29 bucks!!!
This thing is SOLID! It's got heft to it which is nice as mashing buttons while gaming will make a lightweight keyboard slide all over the place. Not this thing! The weight and the larger than typical rubber feet are wonderful! the rear 'feet' pop out and raise the back by about 1cm. Works well for me,
The Zorro brown mechanical switches feel smooth and even all across the keys. Unlike the mechanical blue switches, there is no clack clack sound to irk the whole house. A membrane keyboard may be slightly more quiet as you DO hear the key-caps bottoming out which is pretty standard on any mech keyboard. Some o'rings will fix that and also shorten the fully depressed distance of the keys.
The back lighting is a teal/blue. Pleasant. Not overly bright yet distinct. You can play with lighting movements but I find that distracting and I only use low-on and off, there is no need for me to use on-high. When the back lighting is off, the keys are difficult to read as I am not a touch typist and playing SWTOR, GW2 and many other games, I tend to have to rely upon feel and sight.(I use a dab of clear nail polish on the W and #2 keys and when it's nearly dry I swirl it with a tooth pick for touch sensitivity) The lighting helps amazingly! But without them, the clear lettering isn't as bright and easy to read as say a $10 keyboard with white, printed on lettering. On a good note, these key caps feel decent and far from cheap as does the rest of this keyboard! I am HIGHLY impressed and still amazed this was only $29! I would easily spend double now that I have had my hands upon it! If you're looking for a near silent keyboard, I'd suggest ordering o-rings for under the key caps for $6 here on Amazon. It's unreal how much a decent keyboard makes a difference over a spongy $10 one! I do not know how well it will hold up to the spilled beer, wine, coffee and water challenge but if Velocifire would like to send me a test subject, I'd be happy to test it out with lots of abuse! hehehe

title: Decent Router but bugs in firmware and poor documentation
text:
I have only had this router for a few days but the jury is still out on whether I will keep it or not.

POSITIVES:
Gigabit wired ports
Covers all the WIFI protocols including AC
Has good coverage with three different power levels

Broadcasts on the 2.5GHZ and 5 GHZ band simultaneously. You can also setup separate SSID's so you know which devices are using what band. Actually you can setup three separate SSIDs, (2.4GHZ, 5GHZ and Guest Network) Nice!

Has a separate guest network, which is really nice for allowing people network access but not on your private network.
Has USB3 and USB2 ports to connect printers and drives. I haven't tried it yet but they are there.
Has an actual ON/OFF switch - thank you.
Has a WIFI ON/OFF switch - thank you.
Directional antennas - thank you.
Has an embedded security pin to initially setup the unit via WIFI and gives you the ability to turn it off later.
The configuration GUI is nicely laid out and very logical to use.
Good price compared to competitive routers.
So far no drops in connections on G, N and AC clients.
Compatible with Open Source Firmware - but it voids your warranty.
2 Year warranty.
Nice looking unit which is white and has light blue status indicators.

CONS:
I don't mind the vertical configuration as it does help the unit with cooling, but the stand could have been better designed as it is fixed in place and causes issues with wires and accessing the buttons on the back of the unit.

Tightening the three antennas is difficult due to the plastic housing being in the way - this is just a nit - but could be improved.

I received Version 1 of the hardware. Some people claim they have version 2. It appears version 2 is coming out, (as noted by the recent price drops on this router) so you might want to wait a bit for the new hardware version. Others say there is very little difference. There is no information I have found as to what the differences are supposed to be.

I'm still not sure if I'm getting advertised download speeds, but I need to do further testing - transferring data to and from my NAS was has been really slow. (I also just purchased a WD Mycloud NAS) which transfers data fast across the wired gigabit ports but is really slow using AC WIFI adapters I just purchased. They were the Satechi USB AC adapters. I'm sending them back to Amazon as they clearly don't perform as advertised. I was getting around WIFI B speeds on an AC only network. I just ordered some Netgear WIFI AC adapters, so later this week I'll find out if the problem was with the adapters or is a problem with the Router.

5GHZ signal drops off fairly quickly at longer distances, (part of this is due to the physics of the frequency)

No hard-copy manual - only a CD and a startup guide.

Runs pretty hot - but no problems with overheating yet.

No automatic firmware updates - you need to do it manually - I hope they fix this in a future firmware update. Manual firmware updates should be a thing of the past. You can backup configuration files but it isn't clear to me if you upgrade to new firmware that the configuration backups will work. Even TP-Link can't tell me.

Bugs in firmware. I found that when reserving DHCP addresses, if you don't use a single word in the description it drops all of your devices - not good. The firmware has locked up on me multiple times and sometimes information seems to be lost for no reason. It sure doesn't give me a lot of confidence.

There is no information to tell you if you need to reboot or not after firmware changes. I contacted Tech support two times. The first time they got back to me via e-mail right away, however, they didn't answer any of my questions. I sent them a second e-mail asking them to be more specific and have not heard back. So far their tech support has been useless.

Overall I want to like this router. There are quite a few complaints about it not working well in unusual environments. I did have to update the firmware to a later version when I received it and I think quite a few improvements may have been made with the later firmware updates, but it still has a ways to go. So, some of the early reviews that had complaints seemed to have been resolved by later firmware updates, but other problems have cropped up.

I have a fairly complex network in my home and this router has handled everything pretty well. I have three Roku's - two support WIFI AC the other supports WIFI N. I have six other computers in the home, (Mix of WIFI N and AC) I also have multiple Android devices (WIFI N) and a Play Station 3 that only supports WIFI G. I setup a 2.4GHZ mixed SSID for WIFI G & N and a WIFI 5GHZ band to support mixed N & AC. I'm finding most of my N adapters don't support 5GHZ. I also have a guest SSID setup but turned off for now that I can use when company comes over. I also have a Western Digital 4TB NAS connected to the router and a Obihai 200 TCP/IP phone network box along with Kindles, etc.

I first had channel allocations set on Auto on both bands. I was surprised to see the router select a 2.4GHZ frequency right on top of my next door neighbor's router channel. Channel 11 was clear so I manually changed it to that. So much for auto allocations in firmware.

I think TP-Link could do a much better job of documentation and provide better functionality in their firmware releases. For instance, you can't copy and paste MAC or IP addresses to put in the reserved DHCP list. A real pain.

Are there better routers out there? Yes, and they cost more. However, I'm willing to pay for a better router as I need something that performs well and is reliable. I want to like this router, as the specs were competitive and the price was lower, but so far it doesn't seem to perform like it should on a WIFI AC, which I'll find out is caused by the router or not. I hope it's not. If it is, it's going back.

For now I can live with the firmware in hopes they clean up their act. I'm tempted to put DD-WRT firmware on this router, but I really don't want to void my warranty. I have used Tomato with great reliability on another router before.

So - the jury is still out for me on whether I'll be keeping this or buying something else. It appears this new router is having some "firmware" teething pains right now. I'll post an update once I get my new WIFI AC adapters.

Update Nov 11

I have contacted technical support twice now regarding the buggy firmware. The first reply told me nothing. The second reply told me to send the router back to Amazon. The service tech admitted to me that their firmware is buggy and that is just the way it is with all routers. NOT! I can tell you that DD-WRT or Tomato open source firmware's are not buggy. I ran Tomato on an ASUS router for six years and never once ran into a firmware bug.

For the money, this router works, but I have deducted two stars for buggy firmware and bad technical support. I sure hope TP-Link works on the firmware and gets their technical support act together.

Update Nov 12

Technical support finally answered some of my questions.

First, they offered a modified firmware to fix the DHCP reservation bug. Since I already have it working now, I decided not to mess with the firmware. If you do a backup of the configuration file of your current firmware settings you cannot restore those to a new firmware release. This is not good if you, like me, have lots of changes to the firmware. I certainly hope they fix this going forward.

I am upgrading my rating to a 4 as the router has been working well the last couple of days now that I have it configured the way I want.

One star is deducted for bugs in the firmware and poor documentation.

title: Oldie but goodie
text:
The E6400 I ordered from Blair Technology was listed "Used - Like New". The unit I received was refurbished (according to the tag on the underside) and had a few nicks on the speaker grilles (on either side of the keyboard) that were easily covered up with a Sharpie. There was also a 2"x2" L-shaped smudge inside the screen that disappeared completely when the backlight came on. I rate these as minor flaws considering the price.

I immediately installed a Crucial 250GB SSD and 4 GB of Crucial RAM (the E6400 will take 8GB but that seemed like overkill) and was impressed at how fast this seven-year-old laptop still is. I'm not a gamer but I watch streaming sports video from MLB.TV and ESPN and the E6400 handles this like a champ. I also really appreciate having a real keyboard again, instead of the chicklet type that seems to come on most inexpensive laptops. My unit came with a DVD drive, a nice surprise since I was expecting it to come with just a CD drive.

A novelty with this laptop that some may appreciate is the number of peripheral formats it supports. If you have any PCMCIA or ExpressCards lying around you can use them again with the E6400. There's also Firewire (IEEE 1394a) in addition to USB 2.0.

Another small problem cropped up with the power supply that came with the unit. When running the laptop plugged in my internet connection practically stopped. Turns out the power supply was picking up interference from my new Powerline (internet via electrical wire) network. Swapping the provided PS with an old Dell supply cleared up the problem instantly. The one they give you works OK in most situations but appears to be poorly shielded.

All things considered I'm happy with this purchase. Buying refurbished goods is always an adventure, but if you're willing to upgrade and do a little troubleshooting you can have a very serviceable laptop with a real keyboard, that's still quite fast for it's age.

title: Can be rewarding but it's a very difficult lens to use
text:
This lens is difficult to use, but is rewarding in the right circumstances. Certainly not for "action" photography. I also wouldn't recommend unless your camera has live view with good magnification as you need that for focusing.

The Good:
1. It's sharp. A bit soft wide open, it quickly sharpens up and works fine on my 36MP D810.
2. I find the tilt and shift controls work well enough, and the lens is much more flexible than the Nikkor. I don't have any problem with the small knobs or the knobs getting too tight to loosen.
3. The price is right. This lens is made by Samyang and also sold as Bower (which I bought), Rokinon, and I'm sure other brands. Bower was the least expensive when I purchased.

The Bad:
1. Lots of distortion. If you are considering this for architecture. you won't get straight lines when you shift. I'm afraid you need to buy the Nikkor. I bought the lens for landscapes. If I want to shift the lens while shooting up a tree or waterfall, the lines in nature aren't straight anyway!
2. Focus ring doesn't have long enough travel to easily manual focus. Also ring is very wide and easily hit by accident (such as when closing down the aperture.
3. Yes, I know it's a 100% manual lens, and I'm fine with that (used them for many years when I was starting out) but I wish it had the simple addition of the preset ring. A preset lens lets you set the aperture and the the preset ring makes it easy to open up for focusing and closing down to the set value for the exposure.
4. It doesn't come with a lens hood. It doesn't handle glare well so don't shoot into the sun and keep stray light off of the lens.

The Ugly:
Some people might get frustrated with the manual operation. This is not really a fault of the lens. But you might want to keep in mind before purchase:
1. Metering doesn't work well or at all (depending on the camera model) with the lens tilted or shifted. You need to set the exposure first and perhaps take a test shot. Since you want to open up the aperture to focus, you need to remember what the setting was so you can go back to it later.
2. Focusing doesn't work with the focusing aid provided by the autofocus sensors. You really need to use Live View and zoom in. You need to perform a juggling act checking near and distant focus while adjusting the focus ring and the tilt. You might HATE this.
3. As far as I'm concerned, don't even think about using this lens hand-held. You need a tripod.
4. Take notes -- the camera exif won't record aperture or your lens. With some cameras you can specify manual lenses which will record the focal length. Of course there is no exif recording of the tilt or shift.

title: Great no-frills mechanical tenkeyless!
text:
Typing on this now (plug-and-play for Windows 10). I purchased this to compare the Kailh Brown switches to the Cherry Browns on my Cooler Master tenkeyless. They both have the same signature feel: nonclicky with a tactile bump at around 60% of the press. These switches feel like they have a slightly higher starting actuation force. One pro is this prevents me from accidentally press surrounding keys, like on my Cooler Master because Cherry Browns are just too soft. A con though is that when I press backspace with my pinky, I need slightly more force than I'm used to. Quality of the switch joints looks good; all of them feel and are uniform. The margin of error between switches, if any, is unnoticeable. I cannot comment on the longevity or quality control of the switch so far so I may update my review in a year or so. Overall, there is little difference in feel between Cherry MX and Kailh; I'm happy typing on either.

The keyboard build quality is VERY solid. Screws attach the steel top to the PCB and some very heavy plastic. Plastic appears to be ABS all around. The stabilizers for the bigger keys are consistent with higher quality Costar boards (Cooler Master also a Costar board). Keycaps themselves appear to be ABS as well (didn't test this, but they're definitely solid). I didn't take apart the board but from what I can see this is a quality keyboard.

Aesthetics-wise, this BLOWS the MODA v1 out of the water. No funky bevels, no alien-like gamer keyboard designs. It's a sleek and slim two-tone minimalistic design brick. I love that it's frameless as I often clean out my keyboards and have to pull every keycap off when I want to clean my Cooler Master. Material textures are very fingerprint resistant. The key text design is simple, nothing to write home about. I don't particularly like the abbreviated print screen, scroll lock, and pause break keys. There's also some residue left behind on the insert key which came off easily. Also not a fan of logos plastered on boards, but this one was pretty nicely designed, so I didn't mind too much.

Keyboard's advertised features all work. I tested all the FN keys and the NK/6 key rollover and had no issues. It comes with command/alt keys for those of you with Macs. Cable is non-detachable plastic jacketed with 3 stress relief holes. I've had issues with detachable braided cable keyboards throughout the years (see Rosewill RK series), this was a plus to me.

Packaging was also simple. Box was attractive. Foam was supportive.

This was my first keyboard purchase in about 4 years, and I'm very happy with it. It compares favorably to Cherry keyboards from Filco and Topre, and compares VERY favorably to budget-minded Cherry keyboards from Leopold, Cooler Master, Corsair, Rosewill, etc.

title: Incredibly convenient and inexpensive. Convertible USB/OTG connector is finicky.
text:
Apple's iOS is wonderfully secure thanks to its "sandboxed app" design, but by shielding the user and apps from the file system and other apps, it makes it very difficult to work with external storage. While you can perform backups and copies when attached to your computer, it's very difficult or even impossible to perform these tasks on the go.
Every need creates a market, and there has been a cottage industry of external storage solutions, starting with the AirStash. They're either WiFi based like the AirStash, or Lightning/USB based. Until recently, the Lightning devices used built-in memory and were very expensive, but this new device uses standard microSD or SD storage, so you can benefit from the constantly decreasing price of flash cards.

The device has two connectors: USB on one end and Lightning on the other. When you plug the USB into a computer it behaves as an ordinary card reader; the USB plug is very special as it has an extendable OTG microUSB connector which lets you plug it into any Android and Windows phones and tablets that support OTG (most recent models).
When you plug the Lightning end into an iOS device for the first time, you will be automatically directed to download the corresponding app, "iDiskk Pro". Later on, it will just ask you if you want to launch it. The app allows you to backup/restore contacts, copy photos and videos to/from the phone, but it also contains its own PDF, music and video player that allows you to play even formats unsupported by iOS such as AVI, MP4 and MKV. In case a file is not handled to your liking (some of my MKVs did not play correctly) you can use the "open in..." feature and choose the app to open the file in -- but this will copy the file into the sandbox, using up space on the phone.

This is an incredibly versatile device that addresses the limitations of iOS very elegantly. It would deserve five stars if it weren't for the fact that the USB 3.0 + OTG connector is more trouble than it's worth; I'm having problems plugging it into my computer and I'm always afraid to ruin the USB socket. It would be very convenient if it worked well, but as it is, it just renders the USB connector useless; I'd much prefer a plain USB connector, and if I need the OTG functionality I can always stick one of those $1 adapters (the plug works fine in a USB 2.0 socket)

One more thing: the Lighning connector will not fit if your iOS device is in any sort of case. Even if it does, it will jut out of the phone or tablet in a way that guarantees it will snap off. I very strongly recommend the purchase of a Lightning extension cord to use with this device. If you want to also use the device as a USB reader, I strongly recommend using a USB extension cable instead of plugging the convertible connector directly into the USB 3.0 port of an expensive computer.

Recommended.

title: MAJOR Wi-Fi problems-am returning after 3 hours.
text:
So yes, its a budget tablet. I know quite a bit about computers and am very tech savvy. I knew what I was getting with paying $70. I just needed something to watch streaming movies, add my audio books, light web surfing--in other words, something on the bedside for those nights when I can't sleep, etc. I knew low RAM, was prepared for slow lag time, etc. But I really liked the idea of a windows 10 based tablet for the freedom it would give me vs. an Apple, Android, or Amazon operating system. DRM be damned.

Here's why the 1 star. Out of the box I noticed I couldn't connect to our home 5 ghx wifi channel (router was about 20 feet away). I thought, OK, budget tablet, that's cool, I'll roll with the 2.4 ghz. Connected but then quickly disconnected. Lather, rinse, repeat that step about 10 times and it kept bumping me. Searched for this on the internet and sure enough folks not only had this problem, but also where it would repeatedly disable the wifi adapter. While I was searching (obviously on laptop) I thought I'd reboot the tablet. When tablet restarted, it was like magic-but black magic. Wi-fi adapter was disabled and the only way to enable it again was to reboot...then within 2 minutes of restarting, it would boot me off my network, then disable wi-fi adapter again. I read something about maybe turning the firewall off and that may solve it. Tried it, didn't work for me. I'm a person who would 'find a way' to make it work through research or tinkering, but I thought...if this is happening in the first 5 minutes, what else am I in store for? As Danny Glover said in Leather Weapon..."I'm too old for this sh**"

I rarely (if at all) write reviews, but those of us who buy this aren't expecting top of the line, but we do expect it to perform as advertised. I'll keep searching.

title: I LOVE MY CLONER BOX PRO!
text:
I initially purchased the HDML Cloner Box (non Pro) because of the good Amazon reviews. I was looking for an HD DVR device and the HDML Cloner Box reviews said that it would record virtually anything across an HDMI connection with excellent video quality. I ran into the common issue of the “blank screen” after hooking up the Cloner Box and went the manufacturer web site (Cloner-Alliance) for help and found the “Pro” model with Remote Control, Timer Recordings, and Instant Playback. The Pro being a new product had no reviews on Amazon so I didn’t see it on first pass. After testing the Cloner Box and seeing for myself that recorded everything I tried (CATV, Blue Ray, PC Stream) with Excellent Quality, I instantly purchased the Pro Model and arranged to return the Box version. The blank screen on the Box version was resolved by pressing the 1080/720 button for 5 seconds (you do the same with the Input button on the Pro).

In addition to wanting an HD DVR, I also am in the process of moving my owned DVDs and Blue Rays to MP4 files for my Home Theater Server. I have another software solution for moving my Blue-Ray movies to MP4, but the Cloner Box can do that too. I have found using the Cloner Box for the “Extras” is nice because I have to view them to choose which one to copy and it is easier on the Cloner than the software solution.

I LOVE the HDML Cloner Box Pro. Similar to the non-Pro Box, it records EVERYTHING coming across the HDMI port with EXCELLENT Video quality. The Remote functionality is fantastic. I have yet to test the Timer recording, but understand how it works. The Pro also allows you to Record on the PC through a 2nd Mini-USB port using their HDML-Cloner Pro Helper Application. The PC recording functions worked perfectly, giving you a mirror image of the HDMI stream on the PC (with a slight delay) and full recording control (with the addition of a Pause that you do not get on the USB Drive recordings). The recordings on the PC were as perfect as the ones on the USB flash drive. I can see one advantage of the PC recording is that you can record without having an HD monitor handy. I’m going to test recording from my DSLR Camera where that functionality will come in handy. The Cloner Box Pro Also has a Mic AND Headphone Jack (Mic Jack also on the Box), adding a headphone monitoring capability I currently do not have on the DSLR. The PRO also allows you to control the volume of the HDMI stream and Mic to get a perfect mix. One thing I noticed is my initial recordings had low volume (the Box recordings were slightly louder than the original program). I had to adjust the HDMI volume higher (controlled via remote) to get my recorded volumes back to “normal.”

The file sizes on the recorded videos are very large. Cloner-Alliance obviously made a decision to provide the best possible MP4 video quality and did not try to over-compress the video. I’m seeing that the Pro files are about 2G per half hour of video. You can choose between 1080 or 720 recording quality, but the file size does not change a whole lot. The Pro also has a 2G file size limit so it creates a new file every 2G (or 30 minutes). Cloner-Alliance recently removed that restriction on the Box version and is promising new Pro firmware soon that removes that restriction. I had a problem trying to record baseball games where the recording stopped after 1 hour and it appeared the Pro had trouble creating that 3rd file after filling 2 2G files. Cloner-Alliance support was excellent and suggested a different USB flash drive. That appears to have been the problem. Since changing flash drives I have been able to record two 2 hour movies without issue. After the All-Star break I will try baseball again.

Cloner-Alliance also provides another software application “MP4-Cloner” which allows you to “Trim” “Combine” “Convert” and “Burn” (to Disk). The Trim and Combine function do not re-compress the video so they work very fast, and do not diminish the quality. “Trim” allows you to remove extra things that are recorded at the beginning or end of the file (lead-in and recordings after the program had ended). Trim on a 30 min 2G file only took a few minutes. Combine allows you to combine the 2G MP4 files together into one file. The last 1.5 hour movie that I combined only took about 10 minutes to complete. “Convert” allows you to convert the native MP4 streams into other formats, although what I used it for was to reduce the 6G movie file down to 3G by decreasing the BPS setting. “Convert” does re-compress the video so it takes a bit longer. The video quality of the 3G file was still very good.

The Pro also allows you to record from various other input types: VGA, RGB, and standard AV signals. This is accomplished by a provided cable with those various plugs that feed into a multi-purpose plug (reusing a 2nd HDMI-looking physical connector). Of course I purchased the Cloner-Box to get away from an older RGB recorder so I don’t see using anything other than HDMI.

If you’re looking for a device that will record Full HD Video from your Game Console, Cable TV Box, PC Streams, or Blu-Ray Player, the Cloner Box and Cloner Box Pro is the device you have been looking for.

title: So while this is a bit more expensive than a good APC or Tripp Light with the same power rating
text:
Most UPS units aren't worth paying for if you plan to use them to 'protect' your computer. Power supplies in computers these days are all 'Active PFC' types that are much more sensitive to surges and the standard UPS doesn't switch to battery back-up fast enough for these PFC power supplies. The CyberPower PFC series is designed to work with the modern PSU in your PC. It is remarkable how many power supplies from the big name manufacturers do not, including Tripp Light, APC and others. Even with CyberPower, you need to be sure you are buying this specific series or you will not have this 'Perfect Sinewave' technology which works on Active PFC power supplies.

And it does work! At my shop we have four PCs, most on standard APC UPS units, one on a newer Tripp Light unit and I put this CyberPower UPS on my PC. We have a lot of power surges and short duration black-outs during the spring and where every other computer shut off and had to be rebooted after a power blip, my PC never shuts down. In fact, I never see the slightest screen flicker even if all the lights go out.

So while this is a bit more expensive than a good APC or Tripp Light with the same power rating, if your PC was made in the last 3 years, skip the rest and buy the CyberPower PFC series that fits your power needs. You won't be sorry. (But do be careful - CyberPower makes other series that look almost identical but do not have the Active PFC Pure Sinewave technology! Be sure to select a model from this series!)

title: Adds bass but not much else (and you still need headphones that can deliver)
text:
The M-Audio Bass Traveler does what it says. It increases the bass with a three position switch and drives your headphones easier than the built in amp in your phone or most listening devices. It will *not* make bad recordings or bad phones suddenly sound amazing. Additionally, if you are still using a pair of $20 headphones to listen, you'll probably push the headphones over their limits.

I tested the M-Bass on three different in-ear buds: Ultimate Ears Super Fi 5 Pros, Shure earbuds, and a cheap set of Logitech buds.

Pros:
+ Adds bass just as described. If your music calls for it and you have headphones that can handle it you'll get the overage of bass that your booty desires. Some Skrillex, Bass Nectar and classic Beastie Boys were in their element. Beethoven? He wasn't so happy.
+ Battery Life: I got about 8 hours of consistent but not constant use. Basically, it got me through my commute and workday on a single charge. It was easy to charge up each night, ready for use again the next day.
+ Size: It is very compact and doesn't take up a lot of space when I use it on my desk or in my pocket during my commute. Speaking of pockets, the volume knob is not recessed into the case so sometimes the volume would change accidentally in my pocket. Be aware of that. I need to find a better solution.
- Price: I'll admit it. Although not even close to the high end very expensive amps that are out there, it is a good deal for the money.
- Two output jacks: This allows me and my wife to listen to the same thing with two sets of headphones. It's especially useful when we travel by air and want to watch a movie on a tablet or phone. We don't share music this way, but those explosions and car chases in the movies sure sound more exciting now.

Cons:
- Background Noise: This is one of the areas where a cheaper model like this shows its differences from a much more expensive model. With only the headphones plugged in and no source material playing, this amp adds a noticeable amount of background hiss to the sound. I notice it more with high end headphones (expected) but it's definitely there. I can forgive this because of the price, but if you're willing to spend more, be aware of the extra noise.

Final Thoughts:
Far from the best model available, but also far cheaper. In my opinion, the only thing it adds to the audio is MOAR BASS and didn't add enough to justify its use. If that's all you want (and that's a totally legit desire) then it is worth your consideration. Otherwise, spend more or skip it entirely. I'm giving it four stars because of its value, not its absolute capability.

title: It sure does sound great. I drive with my windows down in my ...
text:
It sure does sound great. I drive with my windows down in my old car. The engine is loud. I have high-powered speakers so I can hear the music with all the noise. This can drive it without an external amp, and that saves me room and wiring in my car.

This is honest to goodness 40w RMS at 0.2% THD per channel, and it sounds clean when turned up to the max.

The styling of these things is pretty awful - they look like the 90s - pretty much every car radio looks like this, so after years of waiting for something better looking, I just decided to deal with it. There are other weird options out there. Semi-truck radios look nicer but are usually a few years behind the curve technology wise. Some marine radios look okay, and then the very expensive retro audio radios are another option. I originally set the lighting to match my dashboard - a yellow-greenish color - but It doesn't match quite right. The brightness can't be adjusted, but you can use a custom color with everything turned down to the minimum levels to kind of reduce brightness - I find it's pretty bright at night depending on what color is selected. I ended up setting the buttons to red and the screen to white.

You do need dedicated power AND ground wiring to this - the stock power wire can't deal with the draw this thing can do. It'll blow your fuses and set your wiring on fire if you don't do this. I have an 8 gauge wire running from by battery to a small fuse panel under my center console. One fuse goes to this radio, and one goes to a very small 20w RMS powered sub in the trunk. I also have an 8 gauge ground cable going to a bolt near the firewall. The big megabass button does indeed make it boom - but my tiny sub can't really do anything with it all.

My Volkswagen was not originally wired to turn on the radio with the ignition, and doesn't even have an ACC position on the key. If you wanted the radio on, you just turned the thing on, and then off when you are done. This radio requires a long press on the power button to totally shut it off. You can also just remove the face to shut it off. I ended up wiring the red wire to the defroster circuit which is on when the ignition is on. This is really just a signal to the radio to turn on, so it won't blow the fuse when the radio and defroster are on. I connected the orange/white illumination wire to my parking lights which is a simple on/off signal to dim. Apparently some stereos have a true dimmer wire which is just orange, which can be connected to the dimmer wire to match the brightness of the dash lights. This one doesn't do that.

title: Too small! Amazon cut corners on this one.
text: I think the problem with this case is that the advertised measurements only work for laptops with rounded corners. I purchased this case for a very common Toshiba 17.3" laptop within the bag’s specs, and I can barely zip it closed. The back corners of my laptop are rounded and the front corners are square. The case will only close if I insert the laptop with the hinges last and toward the zippered opening. If I slip the hinged edge in first, instead, the front edges of my laptop are too square to get the zipper around them. With the two front corners of my laptop pressed so tightly against the bottom of the case and the two back corners rubbing against the zipper, I need to be very careful about carrying it. My laptop measures about 16 1/4" x 10 9/16" x 1 3/8”. The advertised dimensions are probably OK if your laptop has rounded corners. With squared corners, however I’d say the width and thickness are OK but 10 1/4” is the depth limit for a laptop to fit comfortably in this bag. Oh, and one of my exterior zipper pull tabs is oddly different than the other four. If your device fits and the zippers match, this bag is 5 stars. I’m usually very happy with AmazonBasics, but they literally cut corners on this one!

title: Clear.Crisp. Sharp. Bright. Pentax Par for the Course, These Are Binocular Worth Twice Their Price
text:
Edit: 2.5 years later in January 2021
Giving these that last star for the full 5. I have nothing bad to say about their optics or handling. Just superb.

Original Review:
Fantastic binocs. We've a couple good pairs in the family, one I used most was a much older Zeiss 10x50 from the 60s. I've only had, personally, a couple cheaper Bushnell pairs of 8x25. This puts them to shame. I went binocular shopping a while back after seeing several new - I'm no expert whatsover, but I am a photographer (film and digital) of two decades and experienced with good optics in general.

These have fantastic optics. I'm not certain I was even aware that Pentax made binoculars - surprising because at this point most of my favorite and best glass is Pentax for photography - that's why I looked closer when I saw a pair. It seems the same is true of their binoculars that is true for their camera lens offerings: fantastic performance from years in the industry, but for much less money than "popular" brands.

It's been written numerous times, in my brief research over Pentax binoculars, in reviews that Pentax are "just as good or better than binos double the price".... That was often what I found in the camera lens world, and it holds true here. These binoculars have a great FOV, they are very sharp, and they are ridiculously bright.... All for about half what I expected to pay for a pair this good. That's a win.

Only complaints, as many have stated, are that the included strap isn't that great and the objective lens caps are a poor and cheap design that pop off constantly. If these are the corner Pentax cuts to make these come in at this price point, fine by me. I always reserve a star for products I review early after receiving... but I was hesitant to do so this time.

title: Really poor sound quality, expected much much better for the price and name
text:
I was completely blown away by the HORRIBLE sound coming out of these headphones. Really. I read a review that stated they doubt whether these are a legitimate Sony product because they couldn't believe Sony would sell such a bad product. I thought - there's no way, that reviewer must be smoking something. Sony makes goooood stuff, right?! Well, not these headphones, that's for sure. Not even close. I don't write harsh reviews often, and I'm generally pretty forgiving of products, but for a $100 set of headphones made by a reputable company like Sony, I just can't forgive the poor sound quality.

So, what is one scenario in which you should go ahead and buy these? IF you literally have NO other options. If you NEED wireless you should get a decent set of bluetooth headphones and a little bluetooth adapter if your TV doesn't have bluetooth. Avoid these unless you have no choice.

These are (barely) an upgrade over most TV's built-in speakers, but that's it. A $20 bluetooth speaker sounds better. My son's $9 earbuds sound better. My $80 sound bar sounds better. For the SAME price, I have AKG bluetooth headphones that sound, oh, easily about 10x better than these. The sound curve on these has ZERO bass, and mids are so forward that you might as well just put a phone speaker inside a big paper cup - it would sound about the same. Actually, some phone speakers these days might sound better in a cup than these headphones do. And before anyone says anything, yes I know that you want more mids for speech when watching TV, but honestly these sound so...bleh...that you're likely to just want to take them off.

I would assume that most of the positive reviews on here are people who have only used built-in TV speakers their whole lives, because yes, these will sound better than most built-in TV speakers. They clearly have never used anything else though...

Unfortunately due to circumstances I missed my return window, so now I'm stuck with a $100 set of headphones that I literally never use. That's how bad they are. I'd rather NOT use them than use them.

For the record, I haven't had the connection or charging issues that some people complained about which is the one and only reason why these get two stars instead of one.

title: Female friendly, easy to use and great health features
text:
I bought this one for my wife and after 2 weeks, she loves it.
In a nutshell, here are the positives:
1) It's very comfortable to wear. She forgets she is wearing it which means it is a good watch to sleep with.
2) The size is great for female wrists. She is a tiny person (5 feet 1) and it looks good on her.
3) HR monitor seems to be good, very consistent. I read some other people have issues but so far it has been good for her.
4) Battery life is great. I goes a bit more than 25% per day so 4+ days may be a stretch but it is fantastic anyway.
5) Sleep tracking data is great.
6) The watch does a good job picking up activities automatically. I wish there were more activities but so far it has been good

The things that could be better
1) App selection is very limited but she was coming from an Android Wear device and in full honestly you don't use apps that much besides activity tracking. Who really calls an Uber from your watch?. I wish we could see more airlines, smart locks, hotels, car companies adding apps. And of course, the health ecosystem as well: blood pressure, glucose monitors, and so forth.
2) Software no so snappy at times but not a big deal.
3) As I said, the list of activities it tracks could improve a bit
4) I wish we get the same iWatch feature that the watch alerts you if your heart rate goes crazy. That would be cool and I believe it is just a software update.

Overall if you are looking for your first smartwatch, if you are on Android or a combination of both, this is the one you need to get.

This BDR-XD05 might have been a great product 4 years ago but has fallen from grace as of 2015 with Win 10, etc. There is almost no support from Pioneer (The support number on their website end up placing you into voice prompts which eventually give a different number to all and THAT number does the same thing, directing you to call the FIRST number you called! REALLY?) and they include software which is no longer compatible with modern OS. This means that in addition to buying what now appears to be a good price on the hardware, you must pay an additional $100+ for software to use it!

Without software, the BDR-XD05 on 12/03/2015 read from all CD's I wanted to use to read files and install software - although I do use a USB 3.0 hub with 3 power USB ports which the BDR-XD05 will not work when I plug the 2nd Y USB connection to the power USB port (so I have to plug a USB 3 into USB 3 port and the USB 2 half of the Y into another USB 3 port rather than a USB power port). If you don't plug the 2nd part of the Y into a USB 2/3 port, or connect the BDR-XD05 to an external power supply, the BDR-XD05 WILL NOT WORK CORRECTLY. It will function as though it's broken, what it "needs" is more power.

Without software, as far as I can determine so far, you will not be able to use the BDR-XD05 and write ANYTHING to the discs. Technically I'm attempting to write to DVD's rather than CDs but IMHO there should not be a difference. Even worse, the discs you place into the BDR-XD05 to write files to will no longer be usable, they are effectively "closed" once you write to them, which results in 0 data on the disc and 0 GB available to write onto the disc. I attempted this by manually copying a selection of files, and also running a backup. In the manual copy process, the files are properly set to be burnt to the disc but there is not an ability to actually burn them (and the disc is still closed). For the backup, I was prompted by the MS Windows 10 software to replace disc after disc for the backup process but it turned out each disc had 0 written to it.

title: Awesome Styling with Excellent Switch Feedback
text:
I was blown away when I saw this keyboard in person! The styling, the perfect tactile mechanical keyboard with quiet switches, and the bright lighting in all the right places was far superior to the loud and dimmer Razer keyboard I currently had.

While I loved the Razer Blackwidow keyboard feel, the software was the dealbreaker, and the noise of the clicky switches was a bit too loud for everyone else in the household. CLICK CLICK CLICK over and over could be heard throughout the house when slaying an army of orcs. And I had to use it without the Chroma and other customizable features, as the Synapse software kept disconnecting my keyboard and mouse randomly when installed, and customer service was far from helpful over weeks of troubleshooting.

Enter Alienware Pro. This beautiful piece of hardware seemed to be the answer to all of my woes. While not perfect, I'll break down the pros and cons from my point of view to see if it's worth it for you.

Pros:
- The styling is beautiful, it is heavy and durable, and the design is well thought out and the LEDs are not only brighter, but the lettering of the keys was much easier to see than on my Razer. The Blackwidow Chroma, while more muted, did have the edge when it came to the smoothless of the spectrum cycling. The change of colors across the keyboard was much smoother than on the Alienware, which seemed a bit stuttered. Not a dealbreaker, but hoping Alienware matures this in it in future products.

- The switches are AMAZING! It took me a while to get used to the less noisy switches, after using Razer for so long, but after a few hours of use, man I love these switches! Hats off here.

Cons:
- The Alienware software was odd, in that it didn't seamlessly integrate with the existing Alienware Command Center and lighting tools that are used in the laptop AlienFX. While the software was not as feature filled as the Razer, it did work and didn't cause any issues with my hardware, which plagued me on my Razer gear on all my systems. Again, if Alienware can integrate the software better, this will be a 5 star product.

- No TenKeyLess design. For you this may not be a dealbreaker, but this was an issue for me. I consistently bump my mouse hand against the side of the keyboard when gaming on full keyboards, and this Alienware is extra large as it is full keyboard, PLUS it has the extra set of macro keys added. I love the macro keys, but in addition to the keypad, makes this a behemoth of a keyboard. If it had the macro keys and lost the keypad... this keyboard would be pretty much perfect.

Conclusion:
Excellent and solidly built keyboard, sexy design, with macro keys, volume roller, and a bunch of extra features. So close to perfection. If this is too large for you, I found the Logitech Pro is an excellent TKL design, while not as sexy, the software is solid and offers a much reduced footprint.

title: Fast and Affordable
text:
Hi. I've been building gaming PCs for almost 20 years. I'm an old, salty, experienced tech, and I'd like to tell you about the ASUS VG278Q. This is a great display for any GAMER looking for a large, fast, 1080p, 144hz display. As you can see from my review photos, I also own the ASUS VG245H, so my review can apply to both displays. I purchased the VG245H to be my PS4 Pro/PC display. It has worked great for both the PS4 Pro and my PC for almost a year now, without issue.

After building a new gaming PC for myself, I decided to go with the VG245H's bigger brother. The difference between the two is the size of screen and most importantly, the refresh rate. The VG245H is a 24" display and features a 75hz refresh rate, while the VG278Q is a 27" display featuring a 144hz refresh rate. Both of these displays have a TN panel. If you are just a casual gamer and you like to do a lot of photo and video editing on the side, you might want to look at an IPS or VA panel. These TN panels don't have the greatest color or contrast, but they feature some of the fastest G2G response times available. So, if you're a gamer with a competitive nature, these are monitors that you should strongly consider. Try not to pay much too much attention to the reviews claiming that these displays are great for gaming but terrible for everything else. These displays can be tuned and calibrated for a great "all-around" computing experience; via the monitor's OSD, and your GPU's control panel. While they will never be as vivid as an IPS or VA panel, they can still be good for day to day computing. So take a little time to dial them in before giving in to the idea that these display are "washed out" with "poor color reproduction".

Pro tip: Make sure that the RGB range is set to FULL and not LIMITED in your GPU's control panel.

Both displays come with the same sturdy, ergonomic stand.

Who should buy these? Anyone looking for a fast, reliable, and affordable display. Serious gamers who value speed over contrast and color accuracy. Who shouldn't buy these? Anyone looking for rich, saturated colors and life-like reproduction of movies and photos. So it all boils down to what is most important to you. If fast and furious is what you are going for, this is the monitor for you. If eye candy and features are more important, then you should look elsewhere...and be prepared to spend more.

title: First Adapter Wiring Setup if Your Modem is Separate from your WiFi Router
text:
Our problem is pretty simple - we want to reliably stream HD movies via Roku in an area of the house hwere wifi signal quality is iffy. MoCA tech seemed the best and network speediest solution, and Actiontec appears to offer the only options currently in production. As with most tech purchases now, installation instructions are minimal which can be both a blessing and a curse. I am not an expert or a techie, but I manage to get by usually with some amount of googling and common sense. Installation for me took longer than necessary because the wiring diagram for the first adapter assumes the modem is combined with the router in one unit. It doesn't specify what to do in cases where a modem box such as mine (Motorola SB6141) is separate from the router box (ASUS RT N66). When I followed the directions as is, I successfully got all the lights lit on each MoCA unit, but when I tried to connect my Roku via the second adapter's ethernet cable (and subsequently tried with my laptop), there was no actual network available for the system to use. My frustration was doubled by the fact that my feeble google attempts yielded little in the way of assistance, which is why I am writing this post.

Here is what I finally ended up with in terms of wiring. Please keep in my mind my system has been in place for a couple hours now so things might change or fail, and if they do I will update. We do not have cable TV to worry about with the first adapter so no splitting was necessary.

WALL coax plug -----> MoCA (coax IN) using coax cable
MoCA (TV/STB out) ---> MODEM (coax IN) using coax cable
MODEM (ethernet jack) --> ROUTER (ethernet In) using ethernet cable
ROUTER (ethernet out) --> MoCA (Ethernet)

It's difficult to speak to the actual product quality as things have only been up for a few hours, but if it consistently performs as it has in its infancy, it will be a winner. Some folks here have mentioned doing firmware updates, and it's unclear to me how they are able to do this. I wrote to Actiontec inquiring about this as I am hopeful that they might add password protection in the future, as they have with the earlier versions of this device. In the meanwhile, I anxiously await delivery of my poe filter, while I stream Downton Abbey in its full HD non buffered glory.

title: A reasonable subcompact Bluetooth speaker, with some serious drawbacks
text:
I bought this from Target the other day on a whim to replace a dying TDK A33 Bluetooth speaker. I'd been using the TDK in the bathroom to play talk/entertainment podcasts while I shower and it worked well, but it was only splashproof so it couldn't go in the shower with me. This unit claims to be waterproof and submersible, and since it's so tiny, it can fit on the small ledge of the shower stall. The A33 is a much larger unit and has tons of bass and plays extremely loudly for its size. This Altec Lansing is much more limited and in my opinion not at all suited for music at "normal" volume levels due to bass distortion, but for speech? It's just fine. At top volume it's just adequate to hear the talk programming streamed from my phone over the sounds of showering, but in a bedroom or small office it's more than adequate.

The unit's super compact and has a nice rubber jacket surround over the buttons and all non-speaker surfaces. The power button doubles as a pause/play button, and holding down the volume buttons skips tracks forward and reverse, a nice feature on such a low end device. It comes with both an aux-in cable and a USB charging cable, but no AC adapter. A small caribiner is also included for latching to a backpack or what have ye.

The unit suffers from several drawbacks, unfortunately. The power on/off, pairing and connected to Bluetooth voice prompts play at top volume, with no way to lower them. It's super annoying. As mentioned before, the unit's so quick to distort at higher volumes that it's really unsuitable for most modern types of music. Another issue is I've found the unit itself can distort at any volume if the input volume via Bluetooth is too high. I've never experienced that on other Bluetooth devices. They usually work best at top volume from my Moto Droid Turbo, which has relatively low output to start with. Another odd design choice is the AUX input is on the bottom of the unit. So if you need to use that input, you can't set the speaker on its base. Bluetooth pairing is simple the first time around, but pairing additional devices requires waiting on the speaker to time out trying to connect and then it goes into pairing mode. There's no way to get there straight away. There's also no published limit that I could find in the number of devices that can be connected.

Overall, this might be worth snapping up if you can find it at a deep discount somewhere and need a really tiny, super portable speaker than built better than the cheap garbage that hangs on peg boards at the dollar store. Just don't expect quality sound, or the ability to fill even a modest bedroom with rich sound. If you buy this in a store, there are addition colors available besides the aqua blue pictured here.

One last note: Although the Altec Lansing, Amazon and Target websites only show this aqua blue version, Target sells red and off-white models as well.
