title: Very disappointed with both audio performance and build quality of these ...
text: Very disappointed with both audio performance and build quality of these headphones. They are made entirely of cheap plastic, the ear cushions are made of a material so thin I don't see how they will hold up to continued use without tearing. The fit was good and they seemed like they would be comfortable wearing for extended periods should you choose to keep them. I returned mine after two days. In my opinion based on build quality alone they are not worth $279. My intent for these headphones was going to be mainly for watching TV (optical out of TV to the transmitter optical input) and I thought it would be nice to not have to worry about the cord. I also didn't want to disturb my house-mates when watching TV. These headphones did seem to perform well when watching TV programming at moderate volume levels. Audio quality was good when listening to TV shows, Netflix, Amazon Prime, that were mostly dialog driven. Voices were clear and discernible, you could hear a lot of detail like things going on in the background, etc. However, when I listened to some more demanding soundtracks that were louder, or if I just turned up the volume then I lost the imaging and sound staging and the sound just gelled together. Listening to uncompressed FLAC music files is where these headphones really fell short in performance. There was no midrange warmth or bass extension, no pace, everything just sounded flat. My Audio-Technica ATH-M50 headphones (I think I paid around $140 for mine) being fed by an Audio Engine D1 USB headphone DAC outperformed the RS-175's in every possible way. The Surround modes were essentially useless, the LO setting did enhance voices (dialog) bringing it more forward in the head space while the Hi setting just produced an unrealistic reverberation and didn't really create an in-your-head surround sound experience. The bass boost really just overemphasized the bass response at higher volumes although at lower levels it did provide some needed bass much like the Loudness controls on AV receivers are intended to do. Also, as a closed back design these headphones leaked way to much sound out which negated my trying not to disturb others with my TV viewing. Some people might place more weight on the convenience of the wireless aspect of these cans and find the audio performance shortcomings an acceptable tradeoff but I just couldn't justify the cost of these headphones for the performance I was getting.

title: I like it!
text:
I bought this watch as kind of an impulse after wanting a Fitbit Alta for a while, but was in the fence because Fitbits are so ugly.
I stumbled across the Pebble display at Best Buy and decided to give the Time Round piece a try.
The styling of this watch is beautiful. It's light and thin and feels like a regular watch. I'm enjoying the face customization, the step tracking, and the notifications.
The interface is easy to use, and I love that there are actual buttons instead of a touch screen.

That being said, the major thing I'm not loving is the almost immediate deterioration of the watch band. The pictures attached are of the watch after only two full days of normal wear. I wasn't doing anything particularly laborsome and the band is already discolored and dirty. Major bummer.
I specifically chose the red band over the "sand" color to avoid this. I've already had to order another band from a third party seller, as I feel like this dirty band makes my $150 investment look cheap :(

I've also been having issues keeping the Bluetooth connected with iOS as well - well, seemingly. I get an alert for the Bluetooth being disconnected, but I still receive all my phone notifications so I'm not too worried about this. Some digging online shows I'm not the only one to have this problem, and a solution may be in the works with the new software update.
My only other qualm is that the buttons on the right of the face tend to get pushed in on accident when I bend my hand too far back. Not a major problem, but something to keep an eye out for.

All in all, I'm happy with my first smart watch purchase. This thing is a no-nonsense, pretty timepiece with basic phone notifications and fun customization - which is exactly what I was looking for.

Then the Archer C9 router utterly failed a few weeks later and it was kaput, per Tech Support. Finally got a replacement unit from TP-LINK after (merely) a couple of weeks of no wifi. Working fine thus far.

My next router will be a different brand.

title: Great Layer 2 / Layer 3 switch for the price!
text:
I have purchased 4 of the Cisco 300-28 switches to date for different projects. I must say that I was a bit skeptical about not having a full IOS command line at first, but after using the web interface for a while, I got used to its quirks and flow.

This switch has a lot going for it. Rich feature set, sturdiness, quiet operation (no fans!), performance and price are all things we love.

As with any product though, there are things we don't love (as much). I knocked off a star for a handful of reasons:

1. The firmware upgrade process. The main firmware image can be updated through the web interface but the boot loader must be done via TFTP. Certain versions of the firmware require specific boot loaders and Cisco's site does a poor job outlining the version dependencies. You have to read through the release notes to get this information (you probably should read these documents anyway). Thankfully, firmware upgrades aren't needed all that often.

2. Switching from Layer 2 to Layer 3 or back to Layer 2 requires a reboot of the switch and this of course means downtime. If you envision yourself ever using Layer 3 features and don't mind the slight performance degradation, enable this feature shortly after unboxing the switch. The firmware version my units shipped with happened to lose their VLAN configuration when switching between the two modes.

3. Power. These units only come with a single power supply configuration. We knew this from the start, so it's a gripe and not a product flaw. Do note that some of the units are shipping with the European-style power plug in the inner-box and a standard US plug (NEMA 5-15) in the outer box.

Having said all of this, these are solid switches for those that require gigabit connectivity for small branch offices and workgroups. I hope you found this information useful!

title: Gorgeous at a glance, solid performance, slightly underwhelming finish detail...
text: Pretty, clicky and functional.  Wish the finish detail was just a wee bit better.  I got this one (Classic white with copper) along with the regular MK Retro in the white with silver (it wasn't available in "Classic") so I got to compare them side by side.  They are both beautiful keyboards with a very comfortable key spread, convenient shortcuts and nice, clicky feel.  They both fired up and worked perfectly out of the box with no set up required. The ladies for whom they were purchased both love them and they both get lots of compliments from clients.  The only noticeable differences (to me) are the back lighting, leather face cover and metal plaque.  The back lighting is gorgeous and does provide noticeable improvement in visibility - if you need a little extra visual boost or type in dim light it's worth the extra hundred bucks. The other features are cool in theory but execution could have been better; the leather is not high quality, surrounds on the keys and feet are coated plastic, not metal, the plaque (which looks so sexy in the pic) was attached at a wonky angle. Oh, one of the key surrounds was floating in the box- I was able to pop it back on but it doesn't feel totally secure so I'll probably glue it. Having said that, the unit is heavy and has nice, tight contact points, the cable is braided, feet adjust smoothly and stay in position, keys have just the right amount of travel (same as with the MK retro).  Bottom line, it's nice, really nice, and the back lighting is FAB but if you don't care about that you'll probably be just as happy with the "plain" MK Retro for a lot less $$. title: File structure FTP generates on a server is far too complicated
text:
This review is my opinion and a review of my experience with it.

In my opinion, the flaws with this camera make it useless for my application. The flaws are with the user software and the camera firmware. The camera hardware is very good. My home security architecture is kindergarten simple. There are 4 cameras which FTP video and image files to an IIS FTP server on a Windows 10 computer. I access the Windows 10 computer remotely (copssh) using VNC to view the images and videos throughout the day to keep an eye on my home. Three of the cameras are EasyN's which I've used for years. The EasyN's are easy to configure and reliable. The fourth is this Amcrest. My issues with the Amcrest are:

1) The directory structure that the camera creates on the server is insanely complicated. It's virtually impossible to review a days worth of images and/or videos if you have many trips of the camera's motion sensor. Each trip of the motion sensor generates a new directory structure based on date and time. As such hundreds of directories are generated:

Key: YYYY = year, MM = Month, DD = Day, HH = Hour, mm = Minute, XXX is an incrementing index

Videos are saved in directories: \AMC00002_QB4Z4M\YYYY-MM-DD\XXX\dav\HH\videofilename.dav
Images are saved in directories: \AMC00002_QB4Z4M\YYYY-MM-DD\XXX\jpg\HH\mm\photofilename.jpg

The filenames are unintelligible. Examples:
Video: 19.07.18-19.08.15[M][0@0][0].dav
Image: 07[M][0@0][0].jpg

On the plus side, once you find the images and videos they are very high quality.

2) It is not possible to FTP video files to a server in a common video format. What is sent is are '.dav' files which require a proprietary player. An common '.MP4' format is offered only when saving video to the camera's local SD card.

3) Amcrest provides a free player for the proprietary '.dav' format. However it doesn't recognize mapped drives (network mounted). So, if I want to view the videos when at home I need to do a remote VNC over the internet to the Windows 10 computer to use the server's viewer even though I'm on my local subnet. It would be much easier to simply run the viewer from my laptop.

If I'm missing something let me know! Is that convoluted directory structure a protocol for something else? I just don't understand how the developers of this camera came up with this approach.

title: The perfect matching Barlow to the best zoom lenses currently available to amateur astronomers
text:
For many amateur astronomers, one of the first items they upgrade (or add to) is their set of lenses. And usually, around the same time, they typically add a Barlow lens to their collection, which is simply a unit that doubles (or triples, etc....) the magnification of any lens it is mated to. Until recently, no manufacturer really made a reasonably priced zoom lens that could hold its own against expensive fixed focal length units, like the Televue Ethos, Naglers, or Panoptics. Fortunately, as of 2010, Baader pushed the bar ahead again and has been making their Hyperion Mark III Click Stop Zoom lens 8-24 mm. This is a roughly $280 unit that equals the best fixed focal length units at the center of field. (It does not do as well at the edge of field or is as corrected for coma as some high end fixed focal length units). Until, 2012, the Mark III did not have a matching Barlow until Baader released this little baby. (btw, purchasing the Hyperion Barlow 2.25X does not include the Mark III zoom lenses)

The Baader Hyperion Zoom Barlow is just that, ... a 2.25X Barlow lenses that perfectly screws into the body of its twin, the Mark III Click Stop 8-24 mm Zoom lens. It actually can screw in by two different configurations, giving 2.25X or 2.35X. It is a great little unit and does not take up as much room or generate as much moment as a regular Barlow where you have an entire cylinder that the lens typically slides down into. Because it is so small, this Barlow only adds about 80 grams (I am guessing) to the Mark III. It is also extremely easy to screw in or out in complete darkness while observing.

How is the visual acuity through the Hyperion 2.25X Barlow? In my humble opinion, it works extremely well. I have now used the Mark III Zoom and this accompanying 2.25X Barlow at two star parties and compared them apples to apples to Televue Ethos and Nagler models that were kindly loaned to me. About 50% of the time, I felt the Televues were providing slightly more detail but about 50% of the time, I felt this Baader combination was. It was that difficult to decide who was better when looking at Jupiter's Great Red Spot, craters on the Moon, Andromeda, Orion, etc... At the center of the field of view, I could not usually tell much of a difference. At the edges of the field is where I noticed the more expensive Televues began to look better. I use an Orion XT10G GoTo Dobsonian and since it tracks targets for me, I am not as concerned about the edge of the field of view. All I can say is that the combination Mark III Zoom and accompanying Barlow 2.25X are really neck and neck with the best fixed focal length units, but with the added bonus of not needing to change lenses often. The only time I change lenses during an observation session is when I want a wide field low magnification view (as for some deep sky objects). With this unit and the 1200mm focal length of my Dob, I have been able to reach up to 337X in magnification and even at that high power, if the seeing is good, I am greeted with crystal clear views of craters on the Moon, the atmosphere of Jupiter and the rings of Saturn. This mated barlow really kicks in during high magnification planetary viewing.

For me, this Barlow along with its big brother, the Mark III Click Stop 8-24 mm Zoom lens is a godsend. I do not have to change lenses at all usually during the night and I can simply rotate the Zoom unit from low magnification to high. Which makes this easily a five star unit. The only possible thing I can think of which a veteran might want to add is a higher end wide field unit like a 31 mm Nagler or a 35 mm Panoptic to complete their lens collection.

Five stars!

title: Overall, a great Z-wave Plus motion sensor for SmartThings
text:
I have 17 of these motion sensors in a smart home setting with over 100 Z-wave devices working well with SmartThings; these are one of my favorite Z-wave Plus motion sensors. I like that I can change some of the settings (such as the red LED motion indicator, which I wanted to turn off) using the "Dome Motion Sensor" custom device handler, and I like that these use a CR123A battery, which is fairly easy to buy (on Amazon) and replace. The mounting system is also nice, as it allows you to fine-tune the positions of the sensors and easily take them down and put them back up without any special tools to replace the batteries. Setup has been a breeze with each unit, with no problems pairing with the SmartThings hub through network-wide Z-wave Plus inclusion at the actual installation location (don't seem to need to be within 10 feet of the hub to pair these successfully).

The light sensor doesn't seem to be super accurate, but I bought these only because they seemed to be good motion sensors; ideally, I would have preferred motion + temperature + humidity, as available in certain competing motion sensors, but the competitors don't seem to be as good for motion-sensing, so I'm sticking with these. I've eliminated the light reporting from my SmartThings setup by switching these over to the generic "Z-wave motion sensor" device handler after first updating the settings with the "Dome Motion Sensor" custom device handler (you can find this handler linked on the Dome Home Automation website by searching the internet).

One gripe is that I'm having trouble using the custom device handler to disable the LED light (or change the other settings, such as reducing the light-reporting interval to increase the battery life) on two of the 17 of these that I have. I've tried everything I can think of, and I just can't figure out why two of the 17 of these have been so much more difficult for me to change the settings through the custom device handler. Might be how these are routing through my Z-wave network, or might be a SmartThings issue, but I tend to think not, as the other ones have worked fine.

title: Easy Setup, Works With Vera, Not So Sensitive
text:
Setting this sensor up with my Vera Secure was painless -- I added it as a Generic Zwave device and it was paired with no troubles. It creates two devices, one for the motion sensing function, and one parent device with which you can set the device parameters.

The device is less sensitive than I expected. I'm using it in my kitchen as part of a motion controlled lights on/off setup, so I needed it to trigger no more than about 10 feet or so from where the sensor is. It didn't work reliably at all at the default sensitivity setting of 4, and I had to crank it up to the maximum value of 8 to get it to work for my case.

My only "mild complaint" was that the battery was tightly shrink-wrapped in plastic. This "old guy" thinks that it should be a requirement to be arthritic in order for one to be allowed to design packaging!

I really like the magnetic mount concept -- it's really flexible and easy to adjust. But in order to make it magnetic, the the sensor "ball" has a hemisphere of metal on the inside of the plastic cover. It makes me wonder if that affects the range of the Zwave signal or at least makes the antenna pattern very directional. I have not seen any signal reception problems though.

title: C'mon, Sony!
text:
Disappointing. After years of being a total Sony nerd these Bluetooth cans let me down. I have also reviewed at least 16 headphones, own 3 superior Sonys, so I have a lot for reference.

They do fold up nicely, and easily tuck into the included carrying bag. So much for “the pros” (No; one more but you have to hear me complain first)

I think my ears are of an odd variety, I have problems with most “on ear” cans- except my favorite Sennheiser's, and these were no exception. The cups were almost big enough to be over-ear, but not quite, and not all that comfortable without a lot of tucking and sliding. With glasses? Forget it.

Even though I knew better, I tried to pair them to my tablet without downloading the app. It sees them, but connection is not possible unless you do. In a slight defense, the app has some nice features and works well, but not everyone will want to add yet another memory pig just to listen. I wanted my wife to try them, she had the same problem and when I explained that he software is needed she just handed them back and said “forget it” and switched back to her corded Bose.

It operates as a separate entity from my iPad’s control panel and music system. I don’t get it, Sony has tried and failed to take over like this a few times in the past and it never ended well. It’s not like this iteration is complicated, just to me, unnecessary. So we have “Headphone Connect” which allows you to play with the EQ and a few other absurd frills, i.e. a setting that allows the user to choose between sound quality and “stable connection” . I have tested both, and while they boast an impressive 70 foot line of sight connection, degrading the sound for a few more feet- why?

The other app- “Music Center” reminds me of the software needed to run their original line of MD recorders and players (yes, I have two) In other words, unnecessary, irritating, and make me less inclined to want to use the H800’s. I have had no trouble managing my music over many, many years (too many) and this offers me nothing.

Obviously, the cord included with the ‘phones make use a little easier, though if you are of the unwired generation, it would be a drag. There is no control pad on the cord, all of this being run from the earpieces. I have not tried out the phone or mic capabilities while listening to tunes, since I would rarely, if ever, pause my music to take a call. And for on the go- is it legal anywhere to drive with both ears covered? Last time I checked, not, and this is the best place to try it out.

And ironically, this is where the Sony's shine. The connection is good and strong, voice in both directions is more clear than the corded type thing. And even though my phone volume was off, a not entirely unpleasant ringtone jangles in the cans. I can see this as being useful while driving (but I won't try it! ;-) and plugged into my iPod wile making and taking calls, but I'm not sure if wearing cans is enough to get one pulled over these days. Don't think I want to find out, a real shame, but they could be useful on the road otherwise.

Now the sound again, marginally disappointing. I have found my old in-ear MDR-WD8’s approach the quality of the H-800’s. (And if you can find a pair, can command a price almost of them). Decent enough for casual listening, and I must admit, the app seems to connect faster than a normal Bluetooth setup, but a trial through my usual test tracks showed me nothing above the ordinary. I found changing the EQ on my iPod to make what I would now call significant improvements, and my analog equipment, adjusting bass, treble and mit (remember? :-) also greatly improved things. But, changing settings for basically each tune is not a feature I appreciate. I would get used to this in time, but the difference is still hard to get over. And when it does sound dialed in, I notice how much the cups annoy my ears.

The Sony app EQ is fun to play with, but after hearing so many sets that did not require constant attention, I am at the point where I just want them to sound good out of the box and know it's possible. I expect the list price could be considered inexpensive or entry level these days, but even so- c’mon, Sony, we expect better.

However, less than two months after receiving the TV, it is broken.  We came downstairs one Saturday morning to find that it would not turn on, or do anything for that matter.  The primary reason I am writing the negative review is because of the customer service response from TCL following the TV breaking.  I have had to repeatedly call to badger them to get a tech out to my house to fix the TV, and each time they have told me that the tech would call the following day to schedule an appointment.  The last time this happened was just last night, and they said they spoke with the tech and he would come this weekend to repair the TV.  Well he finally called, and told me he would come during the day on Monday.  Bottom line, I have to take off work to be here to have this TV repaired, and after spending over a thousand bucks on it I am not happy with the overall experience.  I was hesitant at first to buy a TV from an unknown company like TCL, but decided to take the leap because the positive reviews.  I made a mistake.

title: Great way to add Nav and high end raio to a basic truck
text:
I bought this kit for my 2013 Ford F150 XLT Supercrew with the 4.2 inch screen with Sync. I had the basic radio that also included SiriusXM.

The Kit fits perfectly and is a straightforward installation with included instructions that are pretty good. There are a couple of screw size errors but they don't effect the overall outcome. The finish goes very well with my existing dash setup and looks great. As you can see from the Amazon picture it maintains the existing climate control buttons and knobs with one difference. Pressing either the fan or temperature button will cause a screen to appear on the new radio with all the controls as they are currently set. You can use the buttons or the touch screen to make changes.

Along with the kit you will need the Maestro ADS-MRR Factory Integration module for $122 that makes the connections between the Ford/Sync, new radio, and connections to the kit for climate control. The module will need to be programmed for your vehicle specifics and preferences from the manufacturers website. You connect the module to a computer using a USB cable for programming.

Before you place an order you will need to decide which double din radio you want. I selected the Kenwood DNX892 that includes navigation, is satellite ready, has HD radio, IPhone or Android integration, and is supported by the kit. Go to the website http://maestro.idatalink.com/ and follow the instructions for your vehicle (they support much more than the F150). You will be asked to verify some things about your vehicle setup and then select your radio. In the end they will tell you pretty much what you will need to get the job done and have links to installation manuals.

One reason I selected the Kenwood radio was because you will be able to make a direct connection to your truck diagnostic port and display data on 10 gauges across two pages. For instance you can monitor your exhaust manifold temperature (great for the Ecoboost turbocharged engine), coolant temperature, and many others. The Pioneer radios will not but there may be other makes that do. All of this will be shown when you have made your selection. You can actually run through a number of radios just to see what is supported. Very nifty.

You will be able to maintain your steering wheel controls and have the capability to change what the buttons do when you program the MRR module. Each button can be assigned two functions of your choice. One option is selected when you press a button and the second option is elected when you press and hold a button. You can print out a small card to help you remember what options you programmed.

Another plus is that if you have tire pressure monitoring and proximity sensors that can also be displayed. The tire pressure page on the radio will show the current pressure for each tire. When you put the vehicle in reverse a screen will appear when the proximity sensors sense an object giving you a visual idea of where and how close the object is. You will also hear the warning beeps.

The Kenwood supports two camera and are labeled as front and back. If you connect your current backup camera it will show in the screen only if you have turned the interrupt to ON. You cannot get both backup camera and proximity detectors on the screen at the same time. It is one or the other. There is a button you can press that will display the second camera. In my case I still use the rear camera in my mirror, the proximity detectors on the new radio, and, when I want, the second camera that is mounted on the back of my RV.

You will have many choices to consider when you configure the pieces but you are not locked in concrete and can modify things at anytime.

You will also need two antenna adapters, one for Satellite (SAT1) and one for your AM/FM radio antenna (Metra 40-EU10) for about $10 each. Because the Satellite receiver is embedded in the Ford factory radio you will also need the SiriusXM SXV300v1 receiver that costs about $35.00. The Sat1 allows you to connect your existing SiriusXM antenna to the SXV300 which will connect to your radio. By the way, the satellite radio integration in the Kenwood is really good.

For approximately $1300 I was able to make a big step up in features and capabilities that look factory installed. I now have a Garmin based navigation with INREX traffic and weather. My Android phone connects to the Bluetooth and I have Pandora and IHeart radio. Once I get the WIFI adapter that plugs into the radio I will be able to mirror my Android phone on the Kenwood display. The Kenwood supports two hands free phones, which is great. If you retain the hands free on the Ford Sync then you cannot also have hands free on the Kenwood

Now for the Maestro people. There web site is really good and everything is very clear and easy to understand. They have a technical support forum that I used before and during my installation that was top notch. They responded very quickly with clear and accurate information. Their tech support is probably the best I have ever experienced.

On review I really can't say what I would change about the whole setup without being a nitpick. When you consider the number of vehicle types and the varied options and then couple that with the huge selection of radios it almost boggles the mind. Everyone from Maestro to the radio manufacturers have done a credible job.

My setup isn't perfect because there was a limit to how much I was willing to spend on the radio, but, overall I am extremely pleased and am looking forward to RV trips with first rate navigation and great entertainment.... I didn't mention DVD capabilities that can be watched if you disable the parking brake connection. I did not do this but I am tempted but for safety it is best not to do this. However, if you add a second display you can feed the video to the kids in the back. My kids are grown now but it sure would have been nice all those times my uncle Sam sent me to a different place to live on the other side of the country!

I sure hope this helps you come to a good decision for you needs. There are cheaper in-dash navigation systems out there but they don't come close to doing all that this setup does.

title: Excellent phone case choice for iPhone 6
text:
This Red Pepper ImpactStrong Waterproof iPhone 6 case is wonderful. I just upgraded my phone so I was on the hunt for a "full meal deal" case since I didn't want to have to buy a case, then a screen protector. I also wanted something that I wouldn't have to worry about water spilling on since I frequently have my phone near me while washing dishes and stream music while in the shower.

I really like how this is a full enclosure case. When I first put it on I turned it over where the "Apple" logo shows through and thought it wasn't full enclosure--but that portion is a cut out and there's a clear plastic there. There is also a portion on the bottom were the charging cord and ear bud input is that looks like it doesn't enclose, but it does. Don't be alarmed if it appears as though it's not full enclosure. I highly recommend doing the waterproof test included in the instructions if you can feasibly see yourself having to utilize that feature.

There are several buttons and inputs on the iPhone 6 that need to be utilized so I went about testing them out. The input on the bottom for earbuds is a screw cap, works easily and quickly. The bottom input for charging clicks off and all of my charging cables work just fine with it. It has a slightly bigger opening than the provided cable that comes with your iPhone so it should work with most any cable you buy. I had a problem with a previous case not having sufficient room for non-Apple cables to fit. I was very pleased with the silent mode button design. This was a huge problem on a previous case, ended up breaking the case and couldn't utilize that feature because of that poor design. This one is a turn knob, turn one way to silent, other way to turn on. Works fantastically. The on/off button and volume control also works well through the case. And finger ID works as well! I was super pleased because part of the reason I got the iPhone 6 was because of the fingerprint feature. The whole of the touch screen area works great. I can see this case lasting a long time.

Overall, I'm very pleased with this case and I'd highly recommend it!

Key Points:
-full enclosure case
-thumbprint ID does work through the case--HUGE bonus for me
-fun color (pink)
-smart design for silent mode button

*Please note that I received this product at a discount in exchange for an hones and unbiased review. Should my experience with this product change at any time, I will plan to update this review.

title: Do NOT buy this if you want to cut to length and crimp on your own ends
text:
I ordered this to cut to length and make some custom cables since I didn't need enough to buy a 500' or 1000' spool of coax. It Is good quality cable and the pre-installed connectors are good quality too. If you plan to use this as is, you will be happy and I would recommend buying it.

However, I would NOT buy this cable again with the intent of cutting it up and putting my own ends on. The reason is that the dielectric insulation around the center wire is really well bonded to the center wire and very difficult to remove. It took several extra minutes to install each F connector because of this. You pretty much have to slice the dielectric off with a knife or razor blade and then use a needlenose pliers or knife blade to clean all the remaining insulation off the center wire. It is stuck on there REALLY good and cleaning it all off is a chore. If your intent is to chop this up and put your own ends on, get something else - you will regret trying to do that with this cable.

title: Unsigned Drivers Cause Windows Boot Problems
text:
This was my 4th Samsung SSD, the others being 840 Evo and an 840 Pro, but apparently Samsung didn't bother going through the Microsoft certification process to get their drivers signed, so now that Win8 & Win10 have cracked down on unsigned drivers my machine does a double fail at boot-time and then offers me 3 options (Lenovo laptop), one of which is to hit F8 at which point I get 9 options. Option 7 is "Don't check the boot-time driver signatures".

After putting up with this for a week I found a way to permanently disable that check, BUT, to do it I had to edit the BIOS and disable Secure Boot, because otherwise the BIOS will block the bit change needed to stop checking for unsigned drivers.

Comm'on Samsung. You're all grown up now and there's no excuse for this kind of BS. Get'er done!

title: Great radar detector
text:
I'll keep this review simple. If you're looking at this detector, you probably already did a lot of research on the brands and the options. I will give you a bit of advice that might help you make your decision. I debated on getting either this radar detector or the Valentine 1 for a very long time now. Both of them are great at what they do, however, I ended up choosing this one simply because I live in more of a suburban area. The 9500ix is great if you live or drive around densely packed areas [i.e. New Jersey]. The Valentine 1 would be great if you live more in rural areas or areas where there are lots of highways and not a lot of people [i.e. midwest or Pennsylvania].

You probably looked into all the options so I'm not going to tell you a whole lot in this next part. The detector itself is great. It picks up on a lot of signals and you can lock out signals that you know is not a cop [i.e. the automatic doors from shopping centers]. The detector does take some time to get use to - you will need to tweak the options a bit and lockout false signals near you. The detector does go crazy near shopping centers as I would assume the Valentine 1 does also. This is something you cannot avoid unless you turn off a lot of the signals. I keep my detector on highway mode all the time just so I can get the most out of this product.

It was a little more expensive than the Klarheit, which was why I didn't choose it first--but all I wanted from the start was a way to play MP3s from a USB flash drive in my car. I didn't want to mess with my phone or an MP3 player to do it, either. The Klarheit couldn't manage that simple task.

So, after looking over my options, and not wanting to spend too much, I settled on this. I've just installed it, and here's my preliminary review:

USB: While it lacks an easy search function, it does at least let me skip from one album (Directory) to the next, so if I have an idea of the general whereabouts of an album on the drive, I can track it down. It accesses the files in the order they were written to the drive. This means that if you copy your whole library at once, alphabetically, you'll have an easier time finding your stuff. If you add a new album, you have to go to the highest numbered files to find it. Having said that, I had no problem actually getting there (something I can't say for the Klarheit). I used the remote to type in the high track number (something like 1600), and quickly found what I was after. Unfortunately, if I don't happen to know where the song is on the flash drive, it's going to take a little hunting to find it. Still, at least navigation isn't awful, and yes, it does display MP3 info, which at least helps in figuring out what directory you're in.

Bluetooth Hands Free: I easily connected my phone to the BOSS, and tried a quick call to a friend to test it. She said the connection had a little static and was a bit quiet on her end, but she could hear me clearly enough, and I could hear her well once I turned up the volume on the unit. I placed the call with the phone, and hung up with the button on the BOSS. It worked fine, and I'm pleased to have this feature.

Sound Quality: For me, the sound quality seems fine, but I don't have the ear for music that some people do. As far as I can tell, the sound is clear, the volume capabilities are good, and I'm pleased with it.

Radio: I used an antenna converter, and hooked up the radio, but haven't found any stations yet. I don't listen to radio, so I actually don't really care, and I'm not sure if the reception problem is due to the converter, the fact I was sitting in my garage, the fact that I just didn't spend much time trying to find a station, or the unit itself (but I doubt the unit is the problem). If I figure it out, I'll let you know...but it's not actually a priority for me. I almost didn't bother hooking it up at all.

Display: Basic. Info scrolls across, and MP3 info includes track/artist/album. At night and in the shade, it's easy to read, but in my car at least, it gets a bad glare during the day that makes it very difficult to read unless I'm in the shade.

Clock: The clock does not display continually or alternately, as far as I can tell so far. You have to hit the Display button to check the time. A bit of a pain, but not the end of the world. When I have a chance, I'll see if there's a way to change that.

SD: I haven't tried it yet.

Removable face plate: Haven't tried it yet.

Overall impression: This is a very simple unit, with a clean design. It serves my purposes so far, although I do wish I could easily search my music library by artist or album. Since I had originally been looking for just the ability to play MP3s, the Bluetooth Hands Free feature is something I consider a bonus, and I'm glad I decided to return the Klarheit and spend a few extra dollars on the BOSS. Definitely worth the minor cost difference!

title: Good luck
text:
This camera system is at the very tippy top of the list of my all time worst purchases. I am an electronics engineer and a moderate techie, yet I have been fighting and struggling with this system for 3 months now. The product description makes it sound great, but please dont be fooled. What it says and what it does, with even an ounce of ease or reliability are totally different. I can't really say if it's the hardware or the software (android app) that makes it so bad, but believe, you WILL experience an exercise in unrenting frustration with this product.

It all starts with the setup and configuration......linking the cameras to your network and the app. After many hours of futszing, I realized my first mistake was trying to follow the generic instructions they provide. Another several hours later, I finally stumbled across enough work arounds for its idiosyncracies to actually get things to start connecting. I don't drink, but I was about ready to start. Holy crap. All together, I had 6 cameras that I wanted to set up, including a door bell camera. The only good thing I can say about the setup (initially) is that after you've connected them once, they will usually reconnect automatically after loosing power.....if you keep your fingers crossed in the process.

Once on operation, the problems never stopped. Also, in the time I've had them, Zmodo has pushed out no less than two or three app updates. Each update was like a roulette wheel as to what would be fixed and what other feature would then be broken. Before or after any update, I can't say thay ANY feature ever really worked as advertised.

Even though I had a good, reliable wireless router, in a bout of frustration, i decided to upgrade to one of the best, highest bandwidth (remember these will only work on 2.4 GHz so you can only go so high) router available. I also moved all wireless devices i could over to 5GHz to minimize activity on my 2.4, to offer the Zmodo cameras as much BW as possible. In the end, I had a nice router but still an extremely poor, frustrating wireless camera system.

The best help I found was through the FAQ section on their website. Trying to get something out of their customer service is a waist of time, especially if you want a response inside of several days.

Another thing is that I did not subscribe to their cloud service. For 6 cameras that would have been in the neighborhood of $50/month. Which is why I wanted the NVR. Perhaps subscribing would get someone a better product and service.

I think it would be fuitless to try detailing every issue I had over this short marriage. The mirade of problems kept evolving and shifting.

I am now cutting my losses and divorcing myself of this system. I'm moving to a more reputable brand of wireless camera.

oh....is that my new therapist calling.....?

The time between blinks and their duration was completely random but frequent enough to make the monitors completely unusable.

Some research revealed that most DisplayPort cables, especially mini DP cables are noncompliant with the DisplayPort standard and feature a 20th pin (DP_PWR) that has no purpose in direct PC to monitor connections save to cause interference and possibly damage the video card. More info can be found at the link below. I went back to using my original cables and everything is fine. I'll take a shorter length over non-functional cables any day. title: I just wish it were a little quieter
text:
The construction is unimpressive but not poor. The mesh cover for the fan compartment can be removed to clean the compartment and the mesh. It can not be collapsed or adjusted, but that much is pretty clear from the description and pictures.

This is big enough for my Lenovo P70 'laptop workstation', and manages to help keep that heating device cooler, and prevents it cooking my lap. It is comfortable enough to use for a long time, the fan runs off power it draws from a USB port (though the PC does not see it as a device, so you may need to make sure the port where it is plugged does not get switched off to save power).

Unhappily, the fan makes a low growling noise that drowns out the P70's onboard fans, except when they are running flat out, and even then I can still tell this thing is running under the machine. I was hoping for something where I heard mostly airflow, but this thing sounds like a miniature version of the cheap single-point-of-unbalance centrifugal bathroom fans, with its sort of low gurgling growl. I definitely can not hear the small amount of airflow it provides over the fan noise. It's not obnoxiously loud if I'm listening to music or something like that, but it would be far too loud in a quiet place.

I tend to prefer performance over silence, but my tolerance of fan noise is mostly toward the airflow noise. I don't really care for fan motor noise, which I consider gratuitous at this scale, and this thing provides what sounds like mostly motor noise. If it were a quiet fan and merely made wind noise, I might have rated it five stars.

Unplugged, it makes a reasonable platform for smaller and less power-hungry systems, but I would not advise using it that way with anything that really needs improved airflow (something that does well sitting on a normal hard surface should be fine). The wide lip around the edge prevents it being easily useable as a single workspace for an even smaller (tablet-sized) machine plus an external mouse.

title: The Three Most Important Words: "Wait 30 Seconds..."
text:
OK, this is a tale of repeated failure and ultimately success. I tried for three days to set my SkyBell HD up. Watched the videos. Followed the install instructions to the letter. Went to the website and read all the FAQ, installer notes, troubleshooting...all of it. Would connect to the SkyBell using my iPhone and try to get the app to recognize it. Nothing. Just a spinning grey wheel of death for three days. So I finally broke down and called Tech Support. After many hours (holiday rush, I'm guessing) they called back. He tried to go through all the usual tricks (speed test, correct home network, etc.) but I stopped him and said "we can't even get to a network--the app won't recognize the SkyBell at all." He said "OK, no problem, let's try it one more time, but this time, after you connect to the SkyBell's wi-fi signal with your phone, WAIT 30 SECONDS before going back to the app." So I waited 30 seconds, went back to the app, and it immediately recognized my SkyBell and my setup was complete about a minute later.

NOWHERE in the installation video, the packaging, or on the website does SkyBell say ANYTHING about waiting to go back to the app after connecting to the SkyBell for the first time. One more line of text on the app during the installation process would have saved me three days of frustration and a long Tech Support call. I suspect there are more out there like me, so SkyBell, please...PUT "WAIT 30 SECONDS" on your instructions! That snafu costs you a star on this review, but I have to say, now that it's up and running, SkyBell works like a dream. Notifications are instant, video is seamless, and the motion detector works as it should. We love our SkyBell HD!

title: Roomy, affordable and fast!
text:
I'd give it 5 stars if it was performing at the very apex of USB 3.0 speeds, but almost no products actually do anyway. I also always hesitate to give a perfect score. lol

I have large storage and backup needs for several of my businesses. I also have an IT background, so I don't suffer inferior tech products. These USB storage devices can be hit and miss. 4 years ago, every Seagate USB drive was a gamble and the drives inside often failed. It's not a matter of warranty or cost, as much as, how precious your data is. Seagate seems to have a good product line currently. Having used or installed over 30 plus of these very devices I am confident to recommend them.

So what are my write speeds and what are realistic expectations?

My write speeds, using benchmark tools and just my eyeball average 40 MB/s to 125 MB/s. Why such a large variance? There are many factors really, but the most common issue is file size. If the files are small...say under 500MB, you'll see faster transfer speeds but if they are larger...say 1.5GB or larger, you'll see slower speeds. This is normal. And yes, the Seagate Expansion drive speeds are right on PAR with other similar products. A transfer of 25.05GBs of data of 92 various sized files in 115 different folders took a total time of 11:03 minutes.

Another factor is that the internal HD is a Seagate drive designed for NAS devices and backup type work. It is also a mechanical type drive and not an SSD. Ergo - these are NOT performance drives. These are drives you 'dump' data to and mostly forget about it until you need it. I see some reviews of people complaining about the performance because they are trying to run programs directly from them or have removed the drive from the external casing and installed it directly into their PCs. THIS IS NOT WHAT THESE ARE MEANT FOR! You will not get reliable performance if you do that. If you want that, buy a proper internal hard drive that will also give you a nice long warranty.

This is just the expansion unit. There is no backup or imaging software that is including. That's fine because if you already have that stuff (which I do), you save money.

The truth is, any hard drive manufacturer can have a bad run. WD, Samsung, Hitachi...they have all had their problems. It's not a perfect world. That's why you must have numerous and redundant backup systems if your data has any value to you.

These units have proven to be reliable in my opinion. I do not hesitate to recommend them. Best of luck!

title: fixes HDCP handshake drop outs and issues between receiver and tv
text:
My use case scenario does not involve using this splitter to send a signal to two displays, rather I needed something to help address HDCP handshake issues between my Onkyo TXNR626 receiver and a Mitsubishi DLP tv.

My TV worked fine when I had my pc hooked up to it directly with a 6 ft HDMI cord; all locally stored video and HDCP protected content like netflix all worked fine. I finally upgraded to a proper receiver and that's when problems started with screen going to black but audio continuing. This happened quite often when watching netflix but less so with local content. I did change from a short 6' HDMI cable to a 30' HDMI cable as my room layout changed, so maybe that was the issue? Swapped out a different brand HDMI cable, things improved a bit but still happening. Maybe the HDMI board was going bad on the TV? Or maybe something with the HDCP handshake? Started researching and found that sometimes powered splitters and HDMI selectors can act as HDCP intermediaries; holding connection to both sending/receiving end to keep both devices happy.

Added this splitter in between the TV and receiver and have been able to watch local content and netflix with no flickering issues or black screens for about 2 weeks now.

Saved me from prematurely shopping for a new TV!

title: Great Receiver, Lacking Documentation
text:
Pleased all around. First off, bought as refurbished. Came in a boxes that were clearly not retail, but packed expertly, Device itself looks as though it just left the factory. All accessories were also in perfect condtion.

Upgraded from a 6 year old Yamaha 5.1 receiver, and I am stunned at the advancement in connectivity since then. The sound itself isn't an order of magnitudes better, but is better. Setting up the receiver and calibrating was simple. Looks flawless. Connection back panel is well organized and not as daunting as receivers past. I guess HDMI ports taking the place of RCA jacks will do that. This receiver really shows the difference (compared to my old Yamaha) in quality of recordings. The dynamic range seems to be much better than the older Yamaha and higher quality recordings sound much better than the yamaha. Feed your machine with high quality and/or lossless recordings, and you will get a better idea on how much better this unit is than receivers of yore. Poorly produced or low bit rate music sounds poor regardless of the unit you use. I bought this for the connectivity options, not the sound quality improvements as I didn't think there would be ANY. I was wrong.

The one thing that is specifically annoying, is the lack of instructions on how to connect your device to other devices, spefically the lack of assistance available even online on how the Spotify Connect option works, as they are NOT listed in the on screen menus if you have this hooked up to a monitor. I spent several hours online; researching how to connect Spotify on my pc to the Denon, forwarding ports on my router, examining settings, eg. Very frustrating.

I am still not sure how i DID get it working. Being exasperated, I decided to try to connect Spotify on my phone to the receiver, and it worked immediately, so, the issue wasn't my router. Or was it because my phone was connecting via bluetooth? I am still not sure. Right after successfully connecting my phone to the receiver, Spotify on my PC finally gave me the option to "Connect to Denon".

Long story short, there is no button, or option within the receiver itself for Spotify Connect, it simply accepts a spotify programs transmissions if you send it the receivers way. The "button" for spotify connect is on the device you are playing from, and is NOT a program within the receiver. Just set the input on the Denon to online music, then run spotify on your OTHER device, and cross your fingers you get the option on the OTHER device to connect to denon wirelessly. Denon, If you are going to tout this as a selling point, then add some clarification for this. All in all though, if you are familiar installing receivers into your system, you should have no install issues. I've never run a calibration program before, and found it just too easy.

I do think this is an excellent receiver, but find Denons documentation lacking, both out of the box and online. That's why it gets docked one star. For a good review on this unit, search: Wirecutter The best receiver 2015

Recommended.

>Comes with a SSD vs HDD (this is a very good thing). You are going to be trading the storage capacity of a HDD hard-drive for the lightning fast responsiveness of a SSD, you can always get a large capacity SD card or an external hard-drive if you need more space. This thing boots up very fast. If the laptop is completely off and you hit the power button, or if you lift the screen from its closed position, you are at the login screen in just a few seconds. The SSD also makes computing tasks quicker.
>The i5 processor is very quick, there are faster options (slower also) but I think you are getting more for your dollar with the i5, I don’t think the i7 is worth it unless you know for a fact you are going to be using processor intensive programs.
>The r7-371T came with Windows 8.1 and I was immediately able to update to Windows 10 for free. Windows 10 is much much better, IMO.
>The tablet mode is a fun feature, personally I don't think you will use it very much, don't buy it based on this capability. The positions in-between "laptop mode" and "tablet mode" are where it's at. Being able to move the screen a few inches closer without moving the base is awesome especially when working in a small space (see picture).
>The screen is very bright and the HD display is wonderful.
>The keyboard has a backlight which is awesome (see picture), you will not have a problem typing in the dark.
>The battery seems to last for a long time, I haven't tested or timed the battery but that is because the battery runtime has never been a problem for me. It says it is supposed to get 8 hours’ battery life, I couldn’t say if this is true or not.
>The touchscreen is very responsive and i have had no issues with it, I love it.
>Plenty of USB ports, two 3.0 on the left and one 2.0 on the right. It also has an HDMI port and SD card slot, if you have a micro SD card just buy an adapter for a full size port, it works great (see picture).
>Very light weight
>The fan is very quiet.

Cons: (sort of)

>(I have fixed this issue, read on) This is not a fault on the laptop but rather windows 10 in its early stages. I did have an issue with the trackpad after the update to Windows 10, the trackpad would freeze and make a beep noise when I moved the cursor to much and it drove me crazy. If you encounter this problem don't waste your time trying to fix it by updating drivers as that is not the issue. Search the acer forums, there is a thread there about this. I was able to fix the problem for myself and explained how I did on that forum. If you can't find the thread do a search for "R7-371T Windows 10 Synaptics Driver gives beeps" either in google or on the acer forums. If you plan on updating to windows 10 make sure to do so first and see if you are going to run into this problem. It’s not terrible if you do just a little annoying.
>The speakers on the laptop are not loud at all. BUT, there is a program on the laptop called Dolby Digital Plus (see picture), when you switch this on the speakers will get much much louder and then this is a non-issue. You will see the icon for this program in the system tray. If you don't need the sound very high keep it off and save some battery. I am guessing this is the purpose of the quiet speakers/sound boosting program.
>The back of the display (top of the laptop in its closed position) looks and feels like glass. This gives it a very premium feel/look but it is also a fingerprint magnet (See picture). Nothing a quick wipe won’t fix, but I like my things clean/looking clean and this is just a little annoying.

Conclusion:

I highly recommend the Acer r7-371T

title: Amazing Drive Performance, Got Bit By Bad Hardware, but Samsung RMA was Mostly a Breeze

title: Nice upgrade over previous models
text:
This is the third unit I've had in this line, having previously used the DDX372BT, then DDX573BH. I like this layout with the physical volume knob and useful physical buttons on the left hand side for use in an older vehicle that lacks steering wheel controls.

The older models were good, but had some problems, and there are a lot of fixes and upgrades here that I like. The biggest upgrade is that Spotify can now be controlled with an app interface rather than a generic Bluetooth stream where you could only control the current playlist. The unit also seems more responsive navigating through menus, and in particular, navigating through USB files. The screen is crisper, and a little bit better with glare, but it's still not good on bright days in direct sunlight. Qualcomm aptX was also added for higher quality Bluetooth audio streams, but source device support is not universal (many flagship phones, and Android O will natively support it).

I have found all these models to be sufficient with features like audio adjustments, the backup camera function, Bluetooth calling, and radio tuning. The Bluetooth call interface on this model is a bit nicer with larger buttons for the dialer in particular. I have found radio reception to be slightly worse than previous models though. I can't say anything about the integrated amp because I don't use it, but it should be noted that all integrated head unit amps are going to be at best barely sufficient with anything more than low power OE speakers.

The only drawbacks I have found is that the button below "Home" that used to always take you to the current source after making calls or settings adjustments now always take you to the camera. I don't really understand that, but at least the back button on the screen does now take you to the current source rather than back one screen. I have also had intermittent issues with the Bluetooth connection being lost, but Kenwood should address that with a firmware update (they have in the past). A lot of head units have this problem because they are built on ancient operating systems, and Bluetooth itself is an old protocol. Lastly, using the Pandora and Spotify apps can sometimes be buggy, but that always seems to be an issue with the source phone, and is is rectified by clearing the application data, or reinstalling the app on the phone.

Overall, nice unit that is definitely an upgrade over the previous models. With higher end models that have Android Auto and CarPlay coming down in price quite a bit, these more basic models may be in more of a gray area value wise though.

title: Fits in Fractal Design Core 500, even with Optical Drive

Sure enough, I stumbled across this fan, and I felt it would work, so I gave them a shot.

It was a tight squeeze, but 2 of them JUST fit right into the top slots, including right above the disk drive, if you shift everything around just right. Now I've got a nice positive pressure setup and my temps are nice and cool.

I assume this is how it is with most case fans (this was my first build) but the screws were a little tricky, since the holes in the fan weren't threaded, I nearly stripped a few of the screws trying to screw the fans in, then out to slide them around in the slots a tiny bit.

Sound wise, they aren't perfectly silent, but they are much quieter than the fans in my previous computer. Since as it turns out, this was basically my only choice for this task, I'm still pretty satisfied.

title: Good construction EXCEPT for backpack straps: extremely UNCOMFORTABLE!
text:
First and foremost, I need a convertible backpack which allows for transport - all materials needed for the long days on campus (grad student). In addition, I need the professional aspect to function as a briefcase. Solely on those points, this bag fits the bill. (BTW - no discount or freebie here for this review - I paid for this!)
PROS:
1. Material: feels and looks professional, good color, seems at the very least to be water repellent
2. Zippers: seem strong enough, especially when loaded - two of them house the briefcase handles
3. Padding: quality - on the backpack straps and particularly the section directly meant for the computer
4. Compartments: although the pictures do not necessarily show this, there are zippers on the outside, and inside, a pocket with divisions for pencils/pens/highlighters.

CONS:
1. Backpack adjustable straps: are on the lower part not allowing for easy adjustment while on your back
2. Lower connection backpack straps: hidden - cannot see whether sewn in well or not
3. Strap to hold computer in place: oddly long, which would allow for movement and sliding around, something you don't want your computer to do when inside
4. No compartment/pocket for a water bottle (my pet peeve)
5. PRIMARY (HUGE) ISSUE: Backpack straps which rest on upper trapezoids (left and right) are situated in a very uncomfortable position when fully loaded. I'm unsure if it's the angle or the placement, but the straps are too close to your neck and would cause pain. Primarily for this reason, I'm returning the backpack. Sad because even with the other cons (more annoyances than anything else) if it were not for this one, I would've kept the backpack because the pros outweigh the cons.

Pictures: It's important to see how a backpack will perform in my daily life. Therefore, the pictures provide a sense of how much stuff this can carry, with the contents both packed and unpacked.

Contents: Lenovo ThinkPad T460 in neoprene case, keys, 1 1/2" loose-leaf binder, yearly planner, scientific calculator, computer power cord, small cosmetic case, large cosmetic bag which houses pens/pencils/highlighters/usb drive/mouse/headphones and wallet.

Final thoughts: if only used as a briefcase/shoulder bag, this may be for you. However, if the primary purpose is to function as a backpack, good luck. I think another reviewer mentioned the oddly-placed backpack straps, but sadly, I ignored that advice.
In addition, cannot ascertain the strength of the shoulder strap as I didn't want to break the seal, but it is pictured.

The watch was in great condition when it arrived but after using it for a few workouts, I noticed that the hear rate monitor didn't have the same accuracy as my original Fenix 5 had.  When I complete a workout with the watch on my right wrist, the watch is spot on.  However, when I complete the same workout with the watch on my left wrist, the heart rate averages 30% less.  I contacted Garmin support and we went through the different possibilities (tattoos, grips, band tightness, left hand vs. right hand in watch settings, etc.) and none of this changed the inaccuracies on my left wrist.  Given that my original Fenix 5 performed flawlessly, my only guess is that the heart rate sensor isn't as accurate on this refurbished watch.

To raise it higher you can add a set of legs which raises the height by  just a little over 1.7 inches each. So in my case, I used only one set of legs which raised my monitor just a little under 2.75 inches. The maximum amount with all the leg options raises the monitor by 6 inches. title: It's an improvement.
text:
First off, setup takes only seconds if your router has WPS. Plug the device in, push two buttons and you are done. On the downside, this does not ship with the latest firmware installed so you will have to upgrade that immediately. The instructions say that if it shows a red ring instead of a blue, you are too far from the router. Well, the only way my unit stops showing a red ring is if it is in the same room as my router which isn't very useful (my router is a TP-LINK AC1750). Checking the repeaters setup page shows the 2.4 signal as good but the 5 as weak. So, I assume the 5 causes the red ring issue. Interestingly enough, the repeater seems to work just fine (I used InSSider to optimize channel and location) despite the red ring.

I purchased this because my current repeater did not support the latest WiFi standards and did not repeat the 5ghz. Like most people these days I wanted to stream a lot of stuff and really need both bands available everywhere. I chose this because it has received good reviews and was a match for my existing router. So far, this is doing exactly what I purchased it to do and it is performing to expectation.

UPDATE: This has been in continuous use for the past six months. No lost or dropped signals or any of the other problems reported in other negative reviews. Instead, it has solved every wi-fi poblem I was having and many people have commented on how good the wi-fi is now in my home. VERY pleased with this device.

title: Grab and Go!
text: Stylish, good design, easy to carry.  I immediately liked the look of the briefcase.  The case is Navy Blue on the outside with brown and black accents on the back, sides and front.  The Navy Blue portion of the bag gives the appearance of a woven fabric.  The fabric feels strong to the touch and should stand up well to regular use. The brown and black accents feel like they are made of naugahyde.  It does, at first glance, give the appearance of leather accents.  The interior of the bag is lined with a soft material and has a plaid/checkerboard appearance that is appealing. Of course the big question is, "Is It Functional?"  Simple answer, absolutely.  This bag could be comfortably used as a daily to and from work briefcase, or one to grab and go on a short notice business flight. It lends itself well to the regular traveler.  I was impressed with the space inside the bag.  I thought at first glance my 17 inch laptop would not fit in the interior.  However, I discovered the top is snapped on both sides.  Releasing those snaps really increases the size of what can fit inside.  My laptop at 16.5 inches wide easily slid into the interior, followed by an 11 inch X 7 inch Android Tablet and a 10 inch by 8 inch IPAD.  Both the tablet and IPAD were in cases.  The laptop and two tablets, just lying flat, come to almost four inches in height.  I still had room to easily insert an 11 X 17 legal pad.  The interior has three full length inserts and one smaller insert.  Two of the insert spaces have some additional padding.  I was glad to find the main zipper for access to the interior of the bag is metal and has a long pull tab for closure. The remaining zippers appear to be made of hard plastic with a metal closure head and long pull tabs.  There are two full width zippered pockets, one on the front and one on the back, of the briefcase.  They offer ample space for business note pads, books or other various and sundry items.  The two zippered pockets on the front of the bag offer quick access to small articles that in my case could be an additional phone, a food stache for packaged crackers or the like, needed medications, mints, etc.  There is a nine and one half inch wide by four and three quarters inch tall strap securely sewn into each side of the back of the briefcase which can slide over the handle of your wheeled carry-on.  The seams of the briefcase all appeared to be very securely sewn together. The briefcase includes a carrying strap.  I found it rested comfortably on my shoulder when filled with the items previously mentioned.  There are open pockets on both sides at the bottom of the briefcase.  I would not put anything in those I didn't want to lose but they could be used to hold a bottle of water.  Simply put, I think the bag is extremely well designed and one that I intend to use regularly.

title: Great stands, work perfectly with the Vive lighthouses!
text:
Previously, I'd been using two cheapy tripod stands for cameras. They weren't very tall, and so I had them mounted precariously on top of tables, cabinets, etc. Not a good long-term solution at all! But then I found these listed, and picked up a set - boy am I happy!

This set of telescoping stands with mounts on them are awesome! I have them set up in my basement, and they're not even extended as tall as they can go! The insides of the mounts appear to be spring-loaded, which is nice. This means that as you lower the mounts, if you slip and accidentally drop the tubing as you're retracting it, it won't slam into the bottom of the lower segment. There's a spring inside that will catch it, and protect it as you lower it.

These things are also SOLID! I don't have the legs as narrow as they can go. I've got them a bit wider, so that they have a bit larger footprint on them, to keep them from accidentally being bumped and toppled over. But with the slightly wider stance, and the mount extended almost fully, there's effectively zero wobble to them at all. The tracking is solid in the Vive, and there's zero movement to the sensors, even with my weight jumping around on the floor playing games!

The included adapter / ball mounts are great too. It makes it incredibly easy to attach the lighthouses to the mounts, and position them at whichever angle you'd like for the best coverage of the play area. In my case, I just mounted the lighthouses to the ball mounts, attached the ball mounts to the stands, and then extended the stands to the height I needed. In the end, I got a rock solid mounting system in place that prevented me from having to drill holes in my wall, with a very little footprint, and even the option to take my entire Vive setup with me wherever I want to go, thanks to the included storage bag as well! The bag isn't anything fancy, and is just a generic overall bag, but it makes a great product even better in the end.

I did have one minor issue with one of my stands initially. The spring latch system I mentioned previously, seemed to be a bit loose on one of the stands. When the lighthouses turned on, the vibration of the motors inside one of them was amplified through the stand / mount, and resulted in an annoying buzzing coming from one of the stands. I couldn't hear it when I was using the Vive with headphones in, but it was loud enough to be an annoyance to others around me if I was playing in a group. But, a simple email to support, and they rectified the problem for me immediately, and swapped it out with a replacement stand that worked perfectly. Now the entire setup is nice and quiet again!

Well worth the price. 5* product for sure!

text:
I have held off buying a security camera system for the outside of my house for nearly two years. I didn't want the hassle of wiring and the expense was just too great. title: Blood Vessel Bursting Frustration and Sleepless Nights
text:
It comes in a nice box... and that's really all it has going for itself. The Sabrent USB 3.0 SATA Hard Drive Flat Docking Station (Model EC-DFLT) is made of cheap, flimsy plastic and contains just one tiny set up manual with just one and a half 2.5" by 4" pages of documentation per language. Did I say documentation? I meant very basic technical specs and a picture guided setup instruction.

I tested this device on three different PCs. Two using Windows 10 and one using Windows 7. I tested three HDDs and two SSDs across all of those devices. While the drives were present in Disk Manager, they were not accessible for any type of process beyond looking at the amount of storage on the drive. I went to Sabrent's website and was disappointed to find that not only is there not a GUI based application to pair with this device, there are also no drivers and just one firmware update to theoretically support drives over 4TB.

I made a support ticket online with no response. I searched for drivers and firmware - nothing. Google search concerning the issue brought me to support topics on 3rd party websites full of people with the same issue - nothing worked. I called tech support FIVE TIMES and was handed over to an answering machine the first four times I called during business hours. Really? An answering machine for tech support?

There was a glimmer of hope when a real person's voice answered my fifth call to technical support. However after just a moment of speaking to the guy I realized I was not going to have my problem resolved. This guy was worthless. He had no idea where to start troubleshooting my issue. Our conversation was over in thirty seconds, and it went like this: "Is it plugged in?" "Is there a hard drive in the enclosure?" "Is the light on?" "Okay, send it back."

This hard drive enclosure is priced in the middle of the road among other enclosures. The lack of documentation online or in the box, absent driver support, uninhabited tech support wings online and over the phone, and the extraneous tech support experience I eventually received has officially made this the worst tech purchase I have ever made.

title: A great case held back by a bad screen protector.
text:
Hats off to Lifeproof for being the leader in waterproof phone cases and for slimming their FRE cases down to make them more useable and less obnoxiously bulky.

Having said that, for a 6/6s Plus - this case is still TOO BIG. I dropped my first phone in a pool and ruined it. $350 later, I decided that I'd lifeproof my second phone just to be on the safe side. After taking the case out of the box and fitting it on my phone I decided that FOR ME, the benefits of a waterproof case are not worth the trade-offs.

Firstly, the screen protector sucks. It's plastic, it feels plastic, and even with very careful install, I was still getting rainbow colored contact splotches on my screen wherever the plastic touched the glass. Part of the reason we pay so much money for these phones is for the high resolution, beautiful displays on them. I can't rationalize purchasing a phone for that feature and then covering it with a crappy piece of plastic. Sorry, it's probably really high-quality plastic, but plastic is plastic and it's just crappy looking, especially after you get a few scuffs and scratches on it.

To address this problem, Lifeproof offers the Nuud, a version of this case that seals around the phone's own glass screen so you can touch the screen directly. GREAT IDEA - but sadly, to make that seal work they have to put huge thick borders around the screen that are big enough to make an old school otter box feel like it fits in with it. Which leads me to point two of why I can't use it:

SIZE. For the iPhone 6/6s I think lifeproof made a FRE case that is just right. Perfect protection without adding too much bulk. For me, however, the formula doesn't translate over to the Plus model. The Plus is already just about as big as I can stand a phone to be, adding much of anything to the outside makes it more ungainly and awkward to hold. The FRE adds just enough to make it feel like instead of holding phone you're holding a block of slate tile.

Finally, SOUND. No one buys an iphone for the excellent sound quality, but passible sound quality is a must. In my experience, the sound quality was passable, but a marked downgrade from the naked phone. This makes sense. To waterproof the phone you have to cover the speakers with something that lets sound out and keeps water from getting in. In the case of the Lifeproof, sound comes out mostly from vibrating the plastic window on the back of the case. it's really strange at first. You can feel the case "pressurize" when sound is coming out of the speakers and it's mostly released around the Apple logo on the back of your phone. Does it sound muffled? A little, but it's not bad. The worst part is that it's quieter. Even with the sound all the way up you might have trouble hearing it in a loud environment.

To its credit it is waterproof and I'd assume shock resistant and dust proof - that's nothing to sneeze at. Would I put my phone it one? No. But that's because I prize the experience of using my phone over its own safety. You may find these trade-offs to be worth the protection the case affords you. If so, I don't think you can do better than a Lifeproof FRE or a lifeproof NUUD.

title: I liked the camera
text:
I am disappointing with this purchase. I am trying to be as objective as possible. At first, I liked the camera, but then I started taking points from it because of several issues:
1.- still pictures are blurry 50% of the time. It does not matter what settings you use, some times they look "OK" and sometimes they look terrible (look at example pictures). They look like pix-elated and the definition is bad.
2. As you can see in the pictures, the date stamped is wrong. You have to change the setting (which is not straightforward to do) every time you change the battery. There is no memory or anything that would save your previous settings. Because of this, some of the videos I took have a wrong date water mark that you cannot delete afterwards and some were recorded without sound because the setting change every time.
3. Video quality is ok, but only on 1080/60. 4 K quality is worse than 1080 / 60fps. I had read about this before, and did not think much of it, but the reality is that is misleading.
4. Remote works 80-90 percent of the time, which is not bad, but not perfect and it is hard to know if you are recording.
5. Battery lasts 30-40 min top, which is another thing that was misleading
Off all the above problems, I can survive most of them, except the blurry pictures. My cell phone takes better quality pictures, but I don't want to take my phone out in the snow or water.
The only pro I found is that the led that indicates that it is on and recording, is in the front of the camera instead that at the top. This is good when you have it on a helmet because you can flip it forward and look directly at it and know you are recording. Otherwise, it is just a guess because on most other cameras, you don't see a front display to indicate that it is recording.

Final verdict: planning on returning it.
