title: Low cost, functions as listed, just what I needed!
text: I had a DVD player in my motorhome that was ruined by a water leak, looking for a similar replacement, I came across this one.  I was looking for something that played DVD movies on a TV that was nearby. My previous unit  was a JVC with an AM/FM radio and USB port in addition to the DVD.  This one met the requirements and included Blutooth as well which was an added bonus.  I am always a bit leary of the no-name Chinese devices, but this one met all my expectations.  It performs all tasks great, playing DVDs on the TV in full screen mode (other reviewer had issues with this) plays mp3s from USB and CDs, and the Bluetooth works very well as well.  The only issue I had was locating the On/off button which turns out to be the Source button front and center.  All the buttons on the front (as well as the remote) have dual functions that active when you hold them for a brief time. The only real issue I had during the testing of all the functions was the fact that the DVD movie play seems to default with the close caption turned on, using the (long hold) button "Sub T" on the remote for this turned it off, but using the DVD menu to turn it off did not seem to make any difference. Anyway, I got it to turn off.  Also when playing a DVD movie if I selected a specific track number, it would play the track over and over, kind of unusual. If I went to the DVD menu, and selected play, it would often stop and I would have to press the play button on the remote. Other than these minor issues that can be worked around, it performed all functions fine and the sound quality of the music was excellent.

title: and I could easily remove the monitor from the mount if I chose ...
text:
I bought this camera system after much research into both wired and wireless systems. I have a 22 ft. enclosed car hauler that I needed to see behind when I was hauling it from place to place. Even with tow mirrors, I just wasn't able to get the safe views I needed to change lanes and see if anyone was following too close, etc. I chose this system above all the others because it was wired, had night vision, was expandable, has audio to help someone talk you through backing up if needed, and I could easily remove the monitor from the mount if I chose and store it away when not in use. So there are some things I wish to warn you about.

First of all, do not install anything until you have laid everything out first and looked at how you are going to route your wires. I should have started at the tongue of the trailer, and worked my way back to the rear, I did it backwards. By the time I realized it, I had already RTV'd the hole into the trailer and it would have been a huge mess. I did work from the rear bumper of the truck forward, which helped. As you can see, I mounted the camera and mount between the clearance lights at the top of the trailer. I aimed the camera up more to get a wider and farther view of objects and vehicles behind me. Once mounted and the included grommet was in place, I RTV'd the interior area where the wire came through just to make it even more waterproof. Please note, I used self-tapping screws instead of the screws included to I knew they would hold up over time. I highly recommend this. Once inside I ran the camera wire along the top of the trailer, and once I removed an interior metal trim piece, ran it down the corner of the trailer to the pre-existing hole where the trailer wires came in from the factory. I RTV'd the hole and ensured it was water-tight as well. I ran the remainder of the cable along the same route as the trailer wires, using existing mounting points to zip tie my video wire to the front. Once I was all the way to the tongue, I rolled the remainder of the 66' wire into a coil and zip-tied it securely to an area out of the way. I ran a bit for the connector through a gap in the ATP plate at the front of the trailer and mounted the connector on the middle I-beam on the tongue.

For the truck connections, I started at the rear bumper, and using a step drill bit, bore a hole the size of the diameter of the connector, I think it was 13/16, but don't hold me to it. I drilled out two smaller holes on the sides of the connector with a smaller bit for the two screws that secure it to the mount. I inserted the other end of the wire and fed it through, and I secured the connector to the bumper from the underside of the truck with the included screws and mount. I fished a wire through the frame of my 2015 F-150 and then followed with the video wire to keep the video wire free from any moving parts of the underside of the truck or any road debris I might accidentally pick up over time. I exited the wire from the inside of the frame near a factory entry point in the passenger floor area, through the grommet installed from the factory and into the interior of the truck.

Now, for the really fun stuff. Wiring everything up. I pulled all the interior trim pieces from the door plate, and kick panel and exposed the fuse panel and factory ground point on the passenger side. I grounded to the factory ground point. I connected the red power wire and the blue trigger wire together and connected those to a 16 gauge wire ran directly to the battery of the truck. I then connected the video wire that I just brought into the interior to camera 3 (as directed in the instructions). I took the ends and excess and coiled them up behind the glove box. I drilled a hole through the glove box in order to run the video connector into, and to be able to store when disconnected and not in use. Whew!! Now then, the video monitor... I bought a Panavise mount here on Amazon and installed it rear the factory sync system. I disassembled the mount provided from RVS and took the mount part (just look close at the pics) and clamped it to the panavise, drilled new holes to match the RVS mount and screwed everything down. Sounds simple, but it took a few minutes and a few choice words. Once I succeeded in getting that done. I mounted the video monitor to the panavise and zip tied some excess to the panavise. I connected the wires and turned the system on. Victory!! It works. And man is it just what I needed. I personally do not want to see the grid lines while I am driving, so I turned those off in the settings menu.

So to sum it up, would I buy this again? YES! Is it a pain the rear to install? Kinda, but if you have any basic skills and can read, this shouldn't be too big a task for you. If it is, I will say it would be money well spent to have it professionally installed. Any RV dealer, or the Geeks at BestBuy should be able to fix you right up.

If you are looking to buy this, you are making a wise choice. I hope this review helps and I will update as needed if there are any issues or I think of anything that I think you should know. Good luck!!

title: A comparison of Tone 700s, Infinim 900s, and Platinum 1100s.
text:
Fantastic upgrade from Tone Infinim 900s. These combine the flexibility of the original Tone 700s-series with the premium quality of materials and superior sound quality of the Infinim 900s. Where the 900s are rigid and inflexible, prone to snapping at the top in the neck band area—and the 700s are almost TOO flexible making them bend and contort in every which way, and the buds falling out all the time—these are the perfect balance of the two. The metal material is a nice upgrade from the cheap plastic of the 900s. The charge port is FINALLY on the outside of the device, where it should be for ease of plugging in. The LED light is 10xs brighter/bigger so you can more easily tell which state of charging it's at. The equalizer is built-in, although there are only 3 modes: Bass Boost, Tone Platinum, and Treble Boost. You can combine this equalizer with an in-app equalizer like the one found in Google Music to find the right sound. The retractable ear buds are back, as found in the 900s, but are far less likely to have ruined cables due to the slower speed of the retracting in these 1100s. The 700s, of course, use weak magnets to attempt to hold the buds in place, but never actually do for longer than 60 seconds. BEST of all I got these 1100s for $63 from a refurbished seller on Amazon; more on that below.

I would highly recommend seller 99Direct. These HBS1100s are supposedly "refurbished", but they look and function as brand-new. They came with ALL accessories (including the NFC tag these are supposed to come with), AND the price was around $63 when these are retailing for upwards of $150! No one has had trouble hearing me yet, but I've only had three calls.

I'll update this review as I test more call functionality throughout the months.

title: Failed after 60 days
text:
Bought 60 days ago specifically for backup of a NAS over USB. Copied over the data fine, and put the drive in a drive enclosure along with four other 3 TB drives, then put the enclosure in a safety deposit box at a bank. Last week, went to make another backup and the drive failed to write while connected to the NAS over USB. Thought it was a problem with the NAS, but it didn't work on my other NAS either.

I used Seatools from Seagate to see if the drive was bad, and got a green light, so I just erased it within seatools (took 2 days) then tried to copy data to it again. Again it failed after about an hour. Pulled it out and re-ran a long test from seatools on it, and now I finally get the error code AB716ASE, which is a bad sector or LBA. That's weird because most drives will silently remap a failed LBA in the background, but this failed and Seatools was unable to remap it. It told me to check the help file, which says 'bad LBA/Sector, Seatools can remap it and save from having to send it to Seagate for a replacement' but the help file refers to buttons that doesn't exist within seatools.

I am disappointed that the drive failed after 60 days and I have to pay $10 for Seagate to send me a replacement drive; especially when I am using it for the exact purpose it was built for: cold storage. Since I have to actually have a backup, I also ordered the same drive but in a USB enclosure a few days ago. That one is currently filling as a backup. It's also slightly cheaper than the bare drive for some reason.

I'll update this review with the results from the replacement. Besides being out $10 and spending way too much time on this, According to Seagate's site (current and when I purchased), the replacement will have a warranty of 90 days or the balance of the original warranty, whichever is later. So it should be in warranty for another 34 months (the balance of 3 years). That should be visible on their 'warranty lookup' page when the new serial number is entered. My guess is that the replacement will be a remanufactured drive, which is fine by me.

****
Update: I got a replacement drive today. The total time between sending back the broken drive and receiving the replacement was 17 days. With this being the fault of the manufacturer, and the fault was verified by their tools before RMA'ing it, there's no reason it should take that long. The replacement does not appear to be a re-certified drive, and I did look up the serial number to check the warranty, and it shows the correct 3 year period.

I am disappointed in how long the replacement process took. That time is perfectly fine for a business that probably has hundreds of these, but it's not okay for a regular consumer; especially one that only had the drive for 2 months. I'm not going to pay extra for seagate to pre-ship me a replacement drive; the true cost of that to seagate is absolutely nothing.

title: Dead in under a week
text:
tl;dr: I realize buying a $40 radio is a bit of a gamble as far as quality goes but this unit is pure junk.

I bought this unit to replace the factory AM/FM radio in my older Chevy Express work van. Since this isn't a hot rod my feature list consisted of : A) turns on, B) connects to my phone, and C) makes the phone noise come out of the vehicle speakers. After Installing everything worked as advertised and I had the unit installed and working within an hour. Success! I can finally listen to my music while in my work van. I drove around the rest of that day happily playing music from my phone via bluetooth. Audio wasn't great paired with the 8 ohm factory one-way speakers, it was tinny and the volume has to be bumped to max to get it to play at a moderate volume. That all improved once I installed decent quality 4 ohm two-way speakers. EQ is 2 band bass/treble so tuning is very limited and I found it tough to get a decent balance of sound.

It worked for about two or three days before a fairly quick descent into total failure. One night coming home the audio completely cut out. I tried adjusting the volume but nothing, silence. I switched sources in an attempt to debug the problem but it appears the radio amplifier had quit. I left the volume on low and waited to see if the audio would come back in the hope that unit overheated. After about 15-20 minutes the audio came back. Maybe it is overheating? The next day it worked on one commute for an hour but the next commute the audio started to crackle before cutting out after just five minutes. I shut it off for the rest of the day in frustration and left it alone. The next day I tried testing everything to make sure there wasn't a speaker problem but the display became corrupted and displayed random garbage while flickering. Then it completely died leaving me with only the lighting and no display or audio. Getting my money back for this lemon.

title: Great camera, great price, great images, no wires!
text:
A quick background on me. I am an IT professional of almost 20 years with expertise in networking, hardware and support. I provide managed IT services to my customers and have for over 10 years in my own business. There is a current trend for automation and security systems and I have recently done a ton of research on these items. With extensive research on security cameras. There are many many different manufacturers and systems out there so choose wisely.
Reolink - I applied to be a dealer with Reolink as I found their pricing very very competitive and their products looked well built and feature rich, comparable to higher priced manufacturers. I was contacted practically immediately by them and spoke with them over the phone. And was set up. But I digress a bit...even though I am a dealer at this time, I was not when I ordered this camera. On to the review.
As expected, this came within 2 days. All items were in the box as stated.and expected, not going to get into the contents but item was well packaged and shipped fast.
Instructions were clear and setup was simple and to the point. You will need to have a barcode scanner on you phone in order to establish a wifi connection but I didn't find that a big deal. If you follow the instructions as written you should have no problems.
First I tested PTZ functions on network, meaning I was on my local network at my house. All functions worked awesome. Pan, tilt and zoom were all excellent. I absolutely love the 2 way audio and video is fantastic. The range is very good too. I can say I set the unit approximately 75 feet from my router and the connection was still great. I really have nothing negative to say about this.
Externally, meaning I was at WalMart and decided to test the functionality of the camera. It literally worked as it did if I was standing inside my house. No issues, no problems connecting. This was not even on wifi, it was on my cell phones data. Very impressed.
So far I have not had to charge/change the batteries and I have had it running for about 2 weeks straight now.
If there was anything I could say about it is it would be nice if it had wifi 5G connectivity but this is definitely not a deal breaker.

title: Best ultra wide full frame E mount lens
text:
Extremely well made lens. The metal construction feels sturdy. The focus ring and aperture ring are very smooth and easy to operate. Click less aperture mode is easy to activate. The lens has an internal focus design.

The front glass element is convex forward so is at risk of getting damaged. I put on a 58mm filter to protect it. The metal lens hood is built in to the lens but wouldn't do a great job protecting the lens alone.

The greatest part of the lens is that all of the data is transmitted to my a7 camera in real time. The aperture is available to view when composing the shot in the viewfinder.

Immediately when I turn the focus ring, the camera goes into zoom mode to focus assist. There is no lag whatsoever. This option can be disabled in the camera body if desired.

The lens is sharp and appears to reproduce colors well. There are full tests of the lens online elsewhere, but for all my purposes this lens is absolutely fantastic.

For the price it would be hard to find a better wide angle lens that is this compact. I can literally disassemble the lens and camera and stick them in my pockets. Combined with an a7 type body, the Voigtlander 15mm Heliar iii must be one of the most compact and best ultra wide angle setups available.

title: Good aesthetics aren't enough
text:
I really, really wanted to like this item, but it is absolute crap.

I own a furniture rental business, and finding good looking, simple, readily available TV stands has become a bit of a struggle for us. Most people are mounting their TVs on the wall these days, so there just isn't much availability in the way of reliable, simple, and appealing to the masses TV stands. I saw this stand on Amazon, I thought it had good aesthetics, was a reasonable price, and had good reviews, I would order one and see if we liked it. Thank goodness I only ordered one.

My initial thought was that it was predictably made of pressboard with veneer, but this isn't even real veneer, it's foil veneer with a screen printed wood grain pattern. Basically the same as IKEA, only more expensive. Not a good sign. Then I started to put it together and the real nightmare began.

Bottom line, the hardware is absolute crap. Utter garbage. The cam bolts are clearly made of aluminum, and immediately when you attempt to screw them in (into holes that were drilled too small, just to make it extra difficult to get them straight and true) they strip out. It took my husband and I two hours to put 25 cam bolts in. We couldn't even screw them in with screwdrivers, we had to resort to using vise grips. And we know what we're doing; we assemble 10 pieces of furniture in the average week.

Then when you attempt to tighten the locking cams around the cam bolts, the cams pop up out of the holes and tear the holes all up, destroying any hope of a decent looking finish.

Final straw for us was realizing that the glorified cardboard that serves as the back panel literally provides structural stability to this piece. Please do not ever attempt to move this item. Do not scoot it. Do not pick it up (especially by the top lip!) Do not transport it. It will rattle apart and you will be back to square one with it. I'd take it apart and send it back, but at this point, my time is worth more than the $128 refund. It's literally going straight from Amazon to our donation pile. We won't bother putting this into inventory.

Just do yourself a favor and go get one from IKEA. It will be cheaper, better made, assemble more easily, and you can get matching bookcases and sliding door fronts, so it will look nicer too.

title: Great Device, Recommended
text:
On Windows 7 Professional, this reader is recognized immediately and adds four new drive letters, one for each card type. The bundled cable provides data and power to the device, is three feet in length, and appears proprietary to the device. When you insert a card, the Kingston logo lights up and blinks a few times. The SD slots are tight, and there is no "click" indication that you are done inserting, much like you might be accustomed to with other devices.

Seems like a great little device, but the quirky nature of the blinking logo loses a star for me. It is reasonable the blinking logo be used to indicate attempts to read or write, but it begins reading a bit too early in the insertion process. If you didn't insert it all the way by the time the light stopped blinking, you have to remove it and repeat the insertion. It's easy once you learn the slot depth, but make sure your user gets some supervised play time when they first open it. :)

For working with small volume (five or less) SD and microSD cards at home, this seems a bargain at $18. I enjoy having future options for working with Compact Flash and DUO media.

title: Acer is at the top of their game
text:
The Aspire R14 (14", 8GB RAM, Intel HD520, i7-6500U) has been a fantastic companion in the last year I've owned it. Build is solid, and the finish is very attractive. The screen is surprisingly crisp and vibrant. It is a gloss finish, which I am indifferent about. I use this laptop primarily as a productivity device (mostly xterm and a browser), which it handles excellently. It only had Windows 10 for about 15 minutes, during which everything seemed to work well as far as keyboard, tablet mode, touch screen gestures etc.

Once I was confident everything was working as it should, I reformatted and tried a variety of Linux operating systems. Ubuntu, Mint, CentOS, and Arch linux flavors worked somewhat well. With quite a bit of tweaking and probably rolling my own kernel, they could have been perfect. But nothing compares to Fedora 25, which handled this laptop's hardware with absolutely no issues. WiFi, Bluetooth, tablet mode, touch screen etc all work flawlessly. It even reliably wakes from S3, which is a rarity these days it seems.

Battery life is excellent, lasted well enough through a transatlantic flight, and gets me through most of the work day on WiFi and low screen brightness.

Steam also runs well under Fedora, and I've put quite a few hours into games like Factorio during my down time.

Overall a very worthwhile purchase. Acer appears to be on top of their game when it comes to laptop computing.

title: I rate it 5 Plus, read this Review for some real facts and information
text: While the instructions that came with this weren't very good, I did manage to get it all assembled and into the canvas carrying case in about an Hour & 20 minutes.  I had charged the battery overnight before starting the assembly. The charge had gone smoothly, and the battery was ready to go, so once I assembled the unit I turned it on & checked it out in simulation mode. Very Vivid screen. Weighing in at 9 lbs 3 oz fully assembled and with battery, it is slightly heavier than the Humminbird 100SX fishfinder I am replacing with it. I took it out for a few hours on my boat. It was easily carried down to the boat due to there being a handle around the unit, inside the canvas carrier, and there is a pocket in the canvass that allows you to grip the handle.  The unit was super easy to install on the boat, just wet the transducer cup, slap it on the transom, tie it down with a safty strap provided and it was ready to go.  I found both the map/gps function and the fishfinder function to be extremely vivid, and easy to read even in bright sunlight.  The menus were quite intuitive, at least they are in my opinion, but I do admit I have a lot of hours on fishfinders/gps units with several makes & models.  I bought this basically to use in rental boats in Alabama, Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Canada, just as I was using the 100SX for.  The GPS function works off of GPS satellites, so no cell towers or internet connections are needed.  It may be overkill, but I also bought a North American Navionics Gold Chip to make sure that I have access to all US and Canada Lake maps available.  The instructions indicated the unit had its own maps, but it also listed some compatible maps, and I have been using Navionics for several years and love it. Fishing is  my passion, so why not a great portable fishfinder augmented by what I know to be a superb lake mapping gps chip?  Having several years experience with Humminbird already, and a short trial run, I am quite confident that this unit is EXACTLY what I was looking for, that it will perform well for years to come, and I have no problem rating it a full five and recommending it to anyone that needs a great portable fishfinder/gps/chartplotter.  The price?  I think its a great buy too.

Obviously, don’t get it knowing this may be an issue having read this, only to return to complain about it). Mileage may vary for your setup.

Setting it up to work is mildly confusing if you carelessly click before reading.
The included print manual is mostly illegible. The setup page on the router (you’ll have to use anyway) is not. While the English is broken in some places, advanced technical expertise is not required and setup is straightforward. (Use common sense, context clues, and read.)

You cannot use auto select if your ISP isn’t Chinese. This is written under HELP, right next to ISP selection section.

title: Much better than what it is trying to be...
text:
This is a great laptop. I bought it a month ago and wanted to use it for a while to be able to write more than just my initial impressions. After a month, I can say that I like it better now than I did when I first opened the box.

I have the golden version, which I was worried would be too flashy but I needed the bigger drive. Fortunately, it is a nice gold with an excellent built quality, though I don't necessarily like the way it's trying to emulate a design of a different product that is inferior in every way, except one, the way it looks. It is definitely very similar to the Macbook but it is not better built. Even the lettering on the bottom is trying to imitate what is on an Apple laptop, just as if this were a cheap knock off, which it certainly isn't. Why then is Huawei trying to look like an Apple when in fact it's much better?

Matebook X is super fast, boots up in seconds and has a very accurate fingerprint reader. The screen is of very high quality with beautiful colors and a possibility to customize it many different ways. I personally like the auto-brightness sensor, and haven't had any problems with it so far.

The impressive sound signature is another feature worth pointing out. While it is not very loud it simply sounds premium, as if listening to a nice set of speakers, rather than a laptop. The sound is clean, well-balanced with a spacious stereo.

The keyboard is very good but, as mentioned in previous reviews, it is poorly, unevenly lit, which to some extent spoils the impression of otherwise great attention to detail.

The laptop has only two USB C ports. I'd rather not have to use a dongle but I understand it is the price paid for the super slim design. The laptop is actually smaller than my 11 inch Acer from a couple of years ago.

The trackpad is ok, just ok. It is responsive but I don't like the way it acts when pressed. It is too hard and there is a little gap between the upper glass layer and what's underneath. This would probably be the only element of the hardware I would like to see improved.

The screen ratio, taller but narrower, takes some getting used to but it is very practical for office work. The free subscription to Office 365 is a nice addition for those who need it for work.

Battery life is not great. 5 hours on average is not much but the device charges very quickly.

I also have a Huawei phone and was hoping to be able to benefit from that. Unfortunately, the Huawei ID, which enables file sharing between Huawei devices is not available in the U.S. version of the Matebook

Windows 10 is still far from a perfect OS and I've had a lot problems with the installation of updates. I am also using Linux, as a dual boot, which works fine, but obviously without the unique sound signature I mentioned earlier.

Overall, I can definitely recommended the laptop, but I would love to see Huawei developing their own style, which they have done with their phones, rather than pursuing the approach of copying a Mac and then trying to improve it.

title: 32 GB is really 32GB regardless of what your computer says...
text:
The Toshiba TransMemory ID USB 3.0 Flash Drive with 32GB Memory arrived on time and well packaged.

The flash drive offers a large amount of storage in a compact size to move documents, photos, music, videos, etc. from your computer to create more space on your computer. It is also a great tool for transferring information from one computer to another.

When I plugged the flash drive into my USB port, my laptop immediately recognized the flash drive and showed 29GB free, which really is 32GB of memory. Have you ever wondered why an external memory is different than what your computer will show? Let me tell you.

USB Flash Drives and other external memory is measured in bytes. The definition of a megabyte/gigabyte is different between computers and external memory manufactures, which is where the problem is.

A computer says a kilobyte is 1024 bytes and a megabyte is 1024 kilobytes. So one megabyte (one million bytes) is actually 1,048,576 bytes. To get to 32 gigabytes you have to multiply 1024 (bytes) x 1024 (kilobytes) x 1024 (megabytes) x 32 (gigabytes) which gives you 34,359,738,268 bytes of information.

However, external memory manufactures (including flash drives) had the idea that a gigabyte is defined as a “billion” bytes. So,, computers will see less space as measured in GB. You do get 32,000,000,000 bytes when you buy 32GB, but your PC isn’t counting the same way everyone else would! Dang computers!

Toshiba is a great brand and this is a good flash drive that will work as it should and hold 32GB of memory.

I received the Toshiba TransMemory USB 3.0 Flash Drive 32GB for a discount in exchange for my honest, unbiased review, which I have given to assist other buyers in making informed purchasing decisions.

title: Slipping issues in the past, but may have been fixed! ("Soft Genuine Leather" version)
text:
Notice: They will be making the loop holes smaller so that slipping is less likely (see in the comments). This change may have fixed the slipping issues. The unmodified past review is below:

I got this strap ("Soft Genuine Leather" version) not long ago and had the chance to test it with many types of cameras from the tiniest point-and-shoots to DSLRs and medium format cameras with various lenses. Let me set this straight early on:

This strap is NOT suitable for anything larger than a point-and-shoot.

The strap winds around the strap ring on the camera and inserts into a cutout in the leather (see photo). These are the only areas that hold the strap together. Only friction is holding this strap together. What do you get if you combine that with soft leather? You get slipping. I noticed that my strap would slip a millimeter or two every time I slung the strap over my shoulder. This was noticeable with heavier cameras like all DSLRs and most full-frame mirrorless cameras. I can see that this strap is fine if you use your gear very gently (like you hold your camera in your hand the whole time) and don't re-sling your strap often as you walk around. However, most users will find the strap creeping wider and wider. I would like to give this strap a good review because the quality is good and it is suitable for small and light cameras, but I have to get everyone's attention before their expensive camera comes crashing down onto the ground due to this strap. Their product description isn't very honest in saying that it can hold D/SLRs.

Otherwise, the leather quality is good for the price. The leather is thick and won't wear down and snap any time soon. The strap is basically one piece of leather so there isn't much to write about in terms of sewing and build quality.

Area of improvement for b.still:
Slipping a metal clamp latch or a tighter strap loop to hold the strap together will fix all of these problems and won't cost much.

title: If you want a clean, unadorned sound...
text:
Studio monitor headphones seem to often be treated with dismissal in our bass-heavy musical culture. However, Brainwavz HM5 continues the quality of this maker's line, and I am happy with these provided for testing. I've tried out various Brainwavz products, and the handsome case, two sets of cables, and spare pair of ear cups make this another reliable model from a quality maker.

It can be fun listening to well-loved songs on such a pair of studio monitor cans. The experience shifts as you may perceive a more dramatic absence of "sweetened" texture. Some note an arid sensation, but I found enough bass (as another reviewer put it, you hear it rather than feel it) to please. The difference is it's not pumped up or boosted, but remains likely on most recordings in the background. This also changes the soundstage. I hear less separation and more of a solid block, as if a "mono" feel, and this can be bracing on tracks with which I'm familiar.

You may also note a bit more hiss as these pick up the ambiance of the atmosphere. I also note halting in streaming some tracks on these, unlike other pairs--perhaps these are more sensitive to such nuances? They are a bit on the heavy side, so they may not (and probably should not) be worn continuously for long periods. I need to break these in longer for full appreciation, but so far, they meet the need for studio needs and audiophiles seeking a clean, unadorned profile.

Visit “Technical Product Specifications for Intel® NUC Products” at [...] for guidance on particular kit boards. Read “System Memory” and “Memory Configurations” sections to identify the recommended memory you need to get in duplicate. Two memory modules of the same size maximizes throughput, i.e. “Dual channel (Interleaved) mode.” Do not exceed the maximum memory capacity.

For storage read “Add-in Card Connectors” section to identify maximum bandwidth of SATA drives and M.2 SSD PCIe drives. Here is the relevant info about boards for two kit types:

Intel® NUC Board NUC6i5SYB and… NUC6i3SYB Technical Product Specification
The board supports M.2 2242 and 2280 (key type M) modules.
• Supports M.2 SSD SATA drives
― Maximum bandwidth is approximately 540 MB/s
• Supports M.2 SSD PCIe drives (PCIe x1, x2, and x4)
― Using PCIe x4 M.2 SSD maximum bandwidth is approximately 1600 MB/s
†NOTE: Stated elsewhere, “The board supports AHCI storage mode.” However, nowhere does it state that it supports NVMe mode. Many (admittedly old) troubleshooting threads online complain about trying to get NVMe modules to work with Intel NUC kits. For this kit AHCI is a safe bet and I got mine to work with considerable frustration, which you can avoid by disabling Legacy mode in BIOS (details below.)

Intel® NUC Kit NUC6i7KYK Technical Product Specification
The kit supports M.2 2242 and 2280 (key type M) modules.
• Supports M.2 SSD SATA-III drives
― Maximum bandwidth is approximately 540 MB/s
• Supports M.2 SSD Gen 3 PCIe AHCI, NVMe drives (PCIe x1, x2, and x4)
― Using PCIe x4 M.2 SSD maximum bandwidth is approximately 4000 MB/s
‡NOTE: The NUC6i7KYK spec specifically states that it supports NVMe drives.

For my [[ASIN:B018Q0GN60 Intel NUC Kit NUC6i5SYH BOXNUC6I5SYH Silver/Black]] PCIe x4 M.2 SSD has about 3 times the bandwidth of M.2 SSD SATA drives, which squander valuable bandwidth, so I recommend PCIe modules. I installed [[ASIN:B00VELDBJ6 Samsung SM951 512GB AHCI MZHPV512HDGL-00000 M.2 80mm PCIe 3.0 x4 SSD - OEM]]. (Benchmark screenshots below.) The [[ASIN:B01DJ9XS52 Intel NUC Kit NUC6i7KYK Mini PC BOXNUC6I7KYK1]] supports faster NVMe versions like [[ASIN:B01639694M Samsung 950 PRO Series - 512GB PCIe NVMe - M.2 Internal SSD (MZ-V5P512BW)]], which you might consider.

If you need a new monitor, then read “Mini DisplayPort” and “Multiple DisplayPort and HDMI Configurations” sections to identify the maximum resolution. I bought [[ASIN:B00OMEWQQQ gofanco® Gold Plated 3 Feet Mini DisplayPort to DVI Adapter Cable - Black Thunderbolt Compatible MALE to MALE for Apple MacBook, MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, Mac Mini, Microsoft Surface Pro / Pro 2 / Pro 3 & Surface 3, Google Chromebook Pixel, and Laptops with Mini DisplayPort Ports to Connect to DVI Displays]] to connect my old Gateway 1280x1024 anti-glare monitor. You could use a TV as a monitor with built in speakers via HDMI (which supports audio), but anti-glare TV screens are not common, so beware. I successfully connected an old set of desktop PC stereo speakers with a stereo audio jack into the Intel NUC combo jack.

• Front Panel Audio Jack Support:
― Speakers only (Stereo)
― Headphones only (Stereo)
― Microphone only (mono)
― Combo Headphone (Stereo)/Microphone (mono)

For keyboard & mouse I chose [[ASIN:B007PJ4PN2 Logitech Wireless Keyboard K360 - Glossy Black]] & [[ASIN:B0043T7FXE Logitech M570 Wireless Trackball]], but each device came with its own Unifying Receiver. During initial setup I plugged both Unifying Receivers into separate USB ports. After setup, I installed the Solaar applet through the Software Manager to pair the two devices to a single Unifying Receiver and was able to remove one and store it inside the device battery compartment. Solaar is a panel applet that pairs Logitech devices and displays battery status and warnings in Notifications (screenshots below). I personally prefer trackballs to mice. I feel no need to mimic cursor movement with arm movement, or pick up a mouse and move it when it runs out of real estate on a desktop. Rolling the trackball with your thumb is all it takes and the device remains stationary on your desktop. A troubleshooting thread complained about Linux USB 3.0 port drivers dropping keyboard input, which I have not experienced. Intel NUC kits have internal headers for USB 2.0 ports. I bought 2 [[ASIN:B000IV6S9S StarTech USB A to USB Motherboard 4-Pin Header F/F 2.0 Cable, 6" (USBMBADAPT)]] just in case, but never needed them.

The final device you'll need (other than an Ethernet cable) is a USB flash drive with a capacity of at least 4GB. First, update Intel NUC BIOS to latest version. On another computer, download latest Intel NUC BIOS. Go to “Downloads for Intel® NUC Kits” at [...] and make three selections: NUC kit name, “BIOS”, and “OS Independent.” The latest BIOS download should appear at the top of the list. Download it and copy the BIOS update file to the USB flash drive. Follow “F7 BIOS Update Instructions for Intel® NUC” at [...]. In my case I updated from version 28 (shipped) to 42 (latest). Reboot. Turn off unit and remove USB flash drive.

On another computer download the latest Linux Mint distribution (.iso file) and use it to make an EFI bootable USB drive. YouTube videos and blogs instruct how. Afterward, if you boot your Intel NUC directly from your USB drive with no changes and install Linux Mint then it will fail to boot from your PCIe SSD. Therefore, to avoid the frustration that many DIYers have experienced edit the Intel NUC BIOS before installing Linux Mint. To edit BIOS settings, press F2 on first startup and disable “Legacy” mode, enable “Boot USB Devices First”, “AHCI” should be selected not “RAID” (“NVMe” might be an option on NUC6i7KYK, I don't know) , and Intel recommends setting “Cooling” to “Cool” (screenshots below.) Press F10 to save and exit. You can now boot from the USB drive and double-click the “Install Linux Mint” icon on the desktop to run the installer (screenshots below.) As shown in the screen shot of the desktop there is no Internet connection. Therefore, connect your Ethernet cable between your Intel NUC and your Internet modem, and follow the installation instructions, including “Erase disk and install Linux Mint/Warning: This will delete any files on this disk.”, which sounds ominous. Remove the USB drive. Reboot.

The version of Linux Mint that I installed (17.3) did not have the proper Intel wireless driver. If you experience this problem, keep the Ethernet cable attached. Go to “[SOLVED]17.2 Mint Mate does not recognize Intel AC-3165 WiFi” at [...] and then copy (Control-C) and paste (Shift-Control-V) the commands of the solution one line at a time into a Linux terminal application. Some lines may prompt you for your password, which will not echo or otherwise give any feedback as you enter it. Have faith and persevere. This series of commands will download and compile a large number of plug-and-play wifi drivers, which will take a long time, but your effort will be rewarded. In time new updates to Linux Mint will make this step obsolete, but for now be forewarned. On next reboot, I edited BIOS to disable “Boot USB Devices First” while knowing full well how to enable it at some future date, if needed.

If you use Netflix, then you will need to use the Firefox browser to go directly to the Google Chrome website and download and install Google Chrome, which is the only Linux compatible browser that will stream Netflix videos. I connect my Intel NUC to a large panel TV via HDMI cable to stream Internet videos. An HDMI cable is another purchase you might consider, if you own a TV with an HDMI input port.

Just to be safe, I installed the free version of Sophos Antivirus for Linux. During installation, watch for the question that distinguishes between free or paid support. Default is paid support.

10 big surprises in a small package:
1. The AC power adapter is about the size of a deck of playing cards, slightly thicker but smaller in the other two dimensions. I was expecting a laptop brick.
2. Intel NUC footprint is smaller than a CD case, the diameter of a CD is wider than either side of the rectangular footprint. Chip miniaturization has made it possible to downsize into this small package power, speed & capacity far exceeding that of yesteryear's room size mainframes.
3. I never hear any fan noise. According to the specs it has a fan.
4. Boot time is roughly 10 second for my Linux Mint Intel i5 NUC with Samsung SM951 AHCI SSD. Boot times for Windows laptops with HDD storage are mind numbingly slow.
5. HDD technology should become extinct soon, even though laptop manufacturers still market it. This DIY Intel NUC kit gives us freedom to avoid HDD technology. Just say no to HDD.
6. I use the pre-installed Banshee application to stream internet radio (Classical KUSC FM & KING FM.) Close makes Banshee disappear from the desktop, but it keeps playing with song & composer titles appearing in Notifications. Close just hides the GUI. Quit completely ends it.
7. The Cinnamon desktop has crashed twice so far, displaying the option to restart which it does upon request. However, I am exploring new applets and applications right now to find the optimum working environment that suits me. Some applications that I install do not work as advertised or at all, so I uninstall them. Sometimes this creates a ripple effect and applets stop working that previously worked. So I remove them from the panel and re-add them, which seems an effective remedy for now.
8. I am a long time Ubuntu Linux user. Ubuntu gave new life to my old laptop that was burdened and crippled by Windows updates and anti-virus scans. I also dual booted Ubuntu and Windows on my old Gateway desktop, from which I scavenged the monitor for this system. Linux Mint now has video and audio editing applications to free any foreseeable need for Windows. We no longer need to pay the Microsoft tax to run Linux on an awesome Mini PC like this Intel NUC.
9. According to Friedrich Nietzsche, “That which does not kill us makes us stronger.” My experience troubleshooting the DIY nuances of Linux Mint & this Intel NUC kit have been frustrating at times but ultimately rewarding. I expect more great surprises from this small package.
10. I now have all the tools I need to produce Internet videos without having to pay a cent for the software.

*** UPDATE *** Linux Mint 18 resolves missing wifi driver issue *** 9/22/2016

I made a bootable USB drive of the latest Linux Mint 18 Cinnamon Long Term Release. It boots and has wifi access without any trouble. I upgraded to Linux Mint 18 and am currently running kernal 4.4.0-38. The Unigine Heaven Benchmark 4.0, a video game simulation benchmark, now runs over 22% faster on the same hardware. In Frames Per Second (FPS) Linux Mint 17.3 rated 12.1 FPS, whereas Linux Mint 18 rates 14.8 FPS. I installed the Intel CPU driver noted in the comment and achieved 15.0 FPS (screenshots below.) I also updated my BIOS to the latest version 51 released 8/10/2016. For my purposes this is fine, but if you are looking for a gaming platform with a minimum of 30 fps, then look elsewhere.

To follow the “verify your ISO” instructions on the Linux Mint downloads page you need to download the sha256sum.txt and sha256sum.txt.gpg files from a mirror site. The link to the .iso file is provided. Copy the mirror site link and paste it into your browser address bar, then delete the file name to open the directory where all the files are located. Save those two sha256sum files into the same directory as the .iso file on your computer (probably Downloads.) Then follow the directions.

Be sure to look at the release notes, which contain a link to a tutorial that explains how to install a windows version of FireFox that you can use to view DRM enabled videos, like those located on nbcolympics.com.

I am really impressed with this Intel NUC running Linux Mint. There is no fan noise, and I doubt the fan even runs it stays cool enough. I installed psensor from the Software Manager. The Psensor Temperature Monitor displays and graphs the temperature of the Intel CPU and Samsung SSD (screenshot below.) High temperatures were when it was updating to Linux Mint 18. Normal CPU temperature range is 85-95°F.

title: Clear highs but anemic sound; there are much better choices
text:
The Creative Labs Aurvana In-Ear 3 Plus in-ear headphones are not at all good enough to be especially worth considering at their price. They're balanced-armature in-ear phones, a technology that often produces excellent sound -- but compared both to top-notch competitors at lower prices, like the [[ASIN:B00264GYMG Klipsch Image S4i]] or [[ASIN:B00SLVB71Q MEElectronics M6 Pro]], and to higher-end balanced armature earphones like the [[ASIN:B006K556FI Sony XBA3s]], the [[ASIN:B00JB66VX4 UE 900]] (or my personal all-time favorite IEMs, the older [[ASIN:B0009Q4PH4 Ultimate Ears model SuperFi 5 Pro]]), the Aurvanas just can't compete.

The unboxing experience is poor: the In-Ear 3 Plus comes in a terribly hard-to-open and fiddly plastic box, with the headphones clipped into an awkward mount. Once inside the package, I found it easy to achieve a good seal and a comfy fit with the lightweight earphones (though I did have to change to a larger silicone tip before these light earphones, without ear-hooks and with a heavy cord, would stay put and sealed in my ears). The mic/remote is also minimal, strangely with a physical volume control rather than a digital one (perhaps so that it can be billed as both iOS and Android-compatible?), and calls are annoying to make with the sealed in-ear phones, but the set does the basic job. The fabric-covered cable is pleasantly tangle-free, and the right-angle plug feels solid. A nice basic fabric carrying case is also included. It's a reasonable package for a premium headphone, apart from the way it sounds.

The sound quality, though, is just mediocre, anemic, and thin. Where listening to a really good headphone (say, the UE900) can be like falling in love with your music again, listening to these had me wondering again and again, while testing, what I'd ever liked about a song in the first place. The treble and upper midrange are bright and clear, with the typical crispness of a balanced armature, but there is almost no bass and lower midrange at all. It's hard to believe there even is a "woofer" driver there at all. It's a terribly unbalanced, thin and hollow sound, even with volume turned up very high and a very solid in-ear seal. Not just bassy hip-hop music suffers, either (though it sounds horrible on these IEMs); I found the drums and bass disappearing into near-inaudibility in my jazz tracks, and the lower portions of classical orchestral recordings fading badly. Even the lower harmonics on vocals and guitar suffer, leaving almost any music sounding thin, sibilant, and hollow, like it's being heard from a great distance down a stone corridor. After spending a few hours listening to music on these next to several other, superior IEMs, I'd strongly recommend against them. The Aurvana In-Ear 3 Plus is just not an impressive headphone at this high a price (or really any price, considering how many good lower-end IEMs there now are from companies like MEE, Shure, and Klipsch), and I can't recommend it.

title: Tied into the amplifier it sends a good signal to all outlets in the house
text: I've been wanting to cut the cable TV for a while and with this antenna I will do that this week.  Installed and operating flawlessly.  I have the major networks and more.  About 40 channels and the unit is in the attic.  All sets in the house are picking up the signal.  I do live in east central Florida on the barrier island where the highest hill is called a causeway.  I hesitated for awhile because I did not wish to install on the exterior of the house or on a stand alone mast.  Finally resigned myself that I would push through no  matter how it was mounted.  Started with this antenna, and about 100 feet of cable.  I have a second  story and temporally installed it aiming at 325 degrees and searched on the TV in the kitchen.  It picked up all but the local NBC channel.  Next, I put it in the attic close to the distribution amplifier for the cable.  Tied into the amplifier it sends a good signal to all outlets in the house.  Thanks!!!  I have all the cable companies' digital tuners packed up and ready for return.  In six days the bill cycle for my account will reset, but this next bill will be without basic TV service.  Next is the internet connection.  I will be shopping for someone to give my business to and not the BIG names either.  Should've moved in this direction sooner, but can not go back  only forward.

title: From 5 stars to 3 stars in 3.0 days
text:
Previous to purchasing this amazing little machine, I had built my own NAS server using FreeNAS, an old Pentium 4 desktop and an assortment of USB hard disks. Well, due to FreeNAS being a little over my head, or the combination of misfit peripherals, I ended up losing all my 2TB of data I had stored on my NAS. Working from home and having a vast multimedia library (rather, ONCE having a vast library), I had grown dependent on my NAS, but would not risk ever losing it again.

I just received this item today, stuck in the red label WD disk, and I can happily say I am blown away by the features and ease of use. Its everything I've ever wanted in centralized storage, and best of all it has taken me a couple hours to fully configure just the way I want. One thing that I love, that I was never able to accomplish on FreeNAS (user error, I assure you) is access to the NAS while I'm out and about.

The ONE thing I will recommend to people considering purchasing this NAS server: If you are as enthusiastic as I am about NAS/Cloud/Centralized everything, get one of the higher prices Sinology servers with the increased CPU and RAM. While this model is working splendidly for me, I can already tell that I will be bumping up to the next highest model very soon.

*******UPDATE, Day 2 of using the device - I've been running this little guy pretty hard and have gotten a full realization of how slow it is. I've tried having it do a lot of things at once and its caused me to have to reboot the NAS, which then causes is it to freeze resulting in having to power cycle it to get it back online. Again, if you are a simpleton with simple needs, its a good machine...but if you are a power user, the increased CPU in the next model up may better suit you.

*******UPDATE, Day 3 of using the device - I've hit a turning point...This is the second day that I've woken up to find the DS214se in a crawl with all apps frozen. Its been indexing my photos non-stop, and while it does I am not able to view them in Photostation or DS Photo+ (sinology's web app and mobile app for photos). Those of us who are passionate about NAS servers know that the #1 attribute to a NAS should be uptime. 2 days of being non-responsive in the morning and I think its time to return it.

Final update - I am returning the unit due to lagginess and down time i incurred over 3 days of use. The beginning of the review is a great testament to the ease of setup, slick graphic interface, and feast of add-on apps...while the rest of the review reflects the overall functionality of the device. Synology is well-known for being the best interface in the game, and its evident to me that thats all they had in mind while designing this model. The 800MHz CPU and 256MB RAM is a joke, but a joke people will buy because, no other GUI can compete with Synology's DSM GUI. A joke that has me looking at their DS214play model even after my poor experience.

title: Very Padded, Strong, Secure, Comfortable, Perfect Fit Phantom 4 Backpack
text: IF YOUR LOOKING FOR A PHANTOM 4 BACKPACK, LOOK NO FURTHER! After searching for weeks through every single backpack that can possibly hold the Phantom 4, I decided not to cheap out and go with an established brand's backpack. I am SO happy I made that decision. I have owned over a half dozen film backpacks, and this one is by far the sturdiest, most padded backpack I have ever owned. It's so padded, you could probably drop this off a two story building with your drone inside and not damage it (on grass, of course:). As other people have reviewed, it is a tight fit, but as long as you remove a bunch of the dividers inside and rearrange it a little, it will fit the Phantom 4, two batteries, and whatever filters/smaller things you have in the bottom/middle compartment. The top holds the RC, and I use it to hold my charger/extra propellers/cords as well, and there's still a decent amount of room in the top. There's also an extremely padded laptop compartment, so you can fly and work on the go. Beware of the imitators of this backpack - I have seen two of them, they are not even half as padded as this one. If you actually want to protect your drone and carry it/hike long distances, this is the backpack to get. I will note one more thing: If you do get this backpack, make sure to get silicone motor caps for the motors on your drone. No matter what backpack you get, you will need to get these, and they are under $10 on Amazon. I couldn't recommend a backpack for the Phantom 4 more than this one, it is the creme de la creme of padded, supported drone backpacks.

title: First Impressions - Dell Inspiron i7559-763BLK
text:
Just received this laptop today, 10/27/2015.

***Summary***
Overall, I am very pleased with this laptop. I think it's a fantastic value for the parts you are getting. The overall look and feel of the laptop is great, the red trim is not overbearing. Using the laptop feels fast and snappy. Boots Windows 10 in less than 20 seconds! The weight and size keeps it portable, but it's no Ultrabook. The laptop doesn't have a touchscreen, if that's a deal-breaker for you.

More details are below, wanted to keep the summary at the top for the folks who don't care to read the whole review.

***Short review***
Build quality seems good to me. The unit is all plastic on the outside; however, I am okay with this. It is a very soft plastic that is nice to the touch. The unit does not feel flimsy and seems fairly durable. It also appears (at first glance) that access to the HDD and RAM won't be terrible, as opposed to some other new laptops on the market, there seems to be a removable plate/panel on the bottom of the laptop to access the bottom of the mainboard, picture attached.

Boot time is rather fast. From the time I hit the power button it takes about 17 seconds until I am at my Windows 10 desktop environment. This is exactly what I was looking for. You will not achieve this in laptops without an SSD hard drive.

Wireless internet signal is pretty strong. I am fully able to receive a signal in the very back room of my house (35+ feet w/ walls), on par with iPhone 6 Plus.

The main storage drive is an SSD, it is a SanDisk Z400s M.2 2280 256GB. Read/Write speeds are fairly strong, I have attached a picture from a CrystalDiskMark speed test I ran. The SSD drive from Dell has (4) partitions, you are left with approximately 200GB free of 225GB available when you receive it. The Dell backup image takes up about 12GB. The fact that your operating system is installed on the M.2 drive would mean that you can add an additional HDD or SSD in the spare 2.5" SATA bay for additional storage. I am not familiar with the spare bay yet.

Memory/RAM is pre-installed 8GB of DDR3, installed in 1 of 2 available slots, according to CPUZ. This leaves spare slot open for future expansion. The RAM is PC3-12800 (800mHz) (PC3 1600) Hyundai Electronics P/N - HMT41GS6BFR8A-PB, with a CAS Latency of 11, according to CPUZ.

Battery life is unknown at this point, I haven't had enough time to fully test this. While playing around with the laptop for the last 3-4 hours I still have about 87% left.

Keyboard is comfortable to use, even with large hands. The 10-key pad is a little undersized, but this keeps the primary keyboard area nice and roomy. The CapsLock key does have a light on the key to indicate whether or not CapsLock is on; although, NumLock does not. The backlit keyboard features (2) brighness levels and is a nice blueish white color light output. The backlit keyboard seems to provide adequate light.

Sound quality seems very good thus far. I watched a couple music videos online and the vocals were clear. The bass was lacking, but this is a laptop, this is to be expected.

I really like that the charger has an indication light on the cord, on the end that plug into the laptop port, that lets you know the charger is powered. The charger also features a built in strap to keep the cord neatly stowed while not using.

Not an overly amount of bloatware installed. Mainly Dell proprietary applications for updates and registration.

***For those who care...why I decided on this laptop.***
I had been shopping for a laptop for everyday use that could also handle heavier tasks such as multi-tasking with multiple browser windows open, music playing, light duty photo editing etc.. I did want a laptop that was portable, but I was not willing to trade off the "more affordable" power you get by not shopping for an Ultrabook. I was also not as concerned with a touchscreen (don't care for a smudgy screen).

My criteria was:
Sub $1000
256GB or greater SSD, I wanted something that would boot Windows fast!
8GB Ram Minimum
15" Screen Minimum
1920x1080 Resolution Minimum
Decent dedicated GPU.
Windows 10

text:
360 Electrical 36083A Compact Rotating Surge Protector Review

I used with with the [[ASIN:B00ATZJ606 Belkin SurgePlus 6-Outlet Wall Mount Surge Protector with Dual USB Ports (2.1 AMP / 10 Watt), BSV602tt]]. I have a glade plugin smelly thing and it doesn't work well sideways. So got this to turn it the right way. Works perfect.

title: Good, Not Great, Receiver for Average Use >>>>>>>UPDATED
text:
I am a pleased, long-time Onkyo receiver user. At this time I have three in my possession (one is heading for the recycle bin). Other than this newest model which I've had about a week, the others have been around and working for several years. The one I am replacing is losing sound in one channel after years of great service.

I'm going to be very basic and non-technical in this review...most people don't even read the specs for equipment the purchase.

I am using this in my home office, which is an average size bedroom in an average size two bed/two bath condo. I don't require great sound in my office, or much volume, which is one reason I went with this low-end model. I am using it with a pair of Polk bookshelf speakers and using it exclusively to with 2 Sony CD carousel players synced together, each holding 300 discs. (yes, dinosaurs...but great!)

Like most people, I play many types of music from varied decades and sources, thus the recording quality is all over the map. I've experimented over this past week and have come to one basic conclusion in regard to the sound with this unit: It is good sound - not great sound - not poor sound. If this were my only sound system in my home, I would never settle for this unit, which is why I have an older, but much better Onkyo running my other system which includes TV, DVD and music. This unit provides good sound and a reliably built unit (I hope - only time will tell). The sound, while good, doesn't have the all-around depth that my previous Onkyo provided on this set - the difference was obvious right away. (By depth, I don't mean 'bass'; perhaps ‘complexities’ would be a better term)

So, my basic thoughts are: I paid $149.95 for a brand new, low-end Onkyo receiver and I got what I paid for. Good sound and quality. I gave it four stars; if I could, I would give it 3 1/2 - somewhere between "It's OK and I like it. I'm not sorry I bought it. If you are particular about your sound system, move up to a better unit. If possible - listen before you buy. (Easier said than done in the shopping world of 2016)

Forgot to mention this: The remote control gives you adjustments for bass and treble....very handy when listening to many types of music. Saves you a lot of getting up and adjusting from the unit.
==============================
UPDATE: 10/11/2016 - Well, after using this for a bit, I realized that even though I am working in my small office, I'm still accustomed to better sound than this receiver can provide. So, I added a 9 band equalizer to my system I found it here on Amazon: [[ASIN:B000MJ406Y BEHRINGER MINIFBQ FBQ800]] It brought the system to life! With the wide range of music I listen to, each disc has its own "special needs" and this gives me all of the choices I need to bring out the best in each recording. Check out the equalizer. While shopping I couldn't find another one close to it for price and features.

Update 11/10/2016 - There is a vibration within the unit. It could happen right when I turn it on...or happen any time when the unit is on. First Onkyo I have ever needed service on. NOW, I am sorry I bought it. Wish I'd caught it in the first 30 days - but now I have to take it in for service. I envision my unit in the shop for a while.

title: Smart TV...still I use Roku
text:
I recently purchased a new 4K smart TV. The funny part happened when I had my first potential purchaser for my old smart TV came to look. The old TV needed a software update. "I have never used the smart features, preferring ROKU" was my answer to be unprepared for the demo. It is true. With a surround system, allowing HDMI passthrough/routing I prefer to have my smart features outside of the TV. As I read through reviews of new 4K TV's before purchasing, I realized that many operational issues that I observed on my sibling's TV (Sony with an android based OS) requiring periodic reboots are related to the OS and apps. Additionally, others were concerned about viewer monitoring via the google based OS. Personally I care less about voice and motion controls, and more about the only three smart apps I really use... Netflix, Amazon, and Plex.... (I also have DirectTV).... so another ROKU was part of the plan.

When I set up the new TV, I ignored messages to initialize via a google account, and went manual. I purchased a new 4K Roku the next day. It works as well as the prior ROKU. Set-up was a breeze with a wireless network. Most surprising was the upgraded app friendliness. As an example, Netflix detected a new 4K set-up and asked me if I wanted to upgrade my plan to 4K for a couple more dollars a month. Some people might find that unwanted, but for me, I had already planned on it anyway... so it was super convenient to hit "yes". In any case, navigation is the simple and the same for all ROKU's. And for me, I kept the old remote (which works just fine) because it has the Netflix and Amazon hot buttons (unlike the remote that came with the new unit).

ROKU provides an alternative op system for smart features that I appreciate and find simpler than navigating my TV's own smart features. ROKU can be pared down to the essentials, and for me reduces the number of remotes I need, along with making things less complex. For those reasons, ROKU can be great for current owners of smart TV's.

text:
I debated for a while what to buy... a schitt combo? a dragonfly (v1 or v2) or HRT? Not having tried any of those, I can't comment on their performance.

I do however have a 5K iMac, and the DAC used in most of the recent models is the same, and is generally regarded as not being terrible. From my testing I would rate the Mac DAC as being better than the fabled Behringer UCA-202, but I digress.

I do not own high impedance headphones. So there is that first of all. But for me (HPH-MT220) I'm sitting around 1/4 volume for comfortable listening volume, so I doubt that will be an issue!

Comparing the sound quality with the iMac, the difference is not light and day, both sound great for ordinary people who enjoy music! But while listening to the Meridian, I noticed, 'hey, those high hat hits sound so detailed; I wonder how it sounds on the iMac'. I played the same sample on the iMac and couldn't even pick the same sound out! I'm sure that there must be DACs out there that will be better, but the quality jump I experienced honestly makes this hard to believe. After playing a few more tracks, I am completely satisfied with this product, and at half price, I couldn't be happier.

If you are looking for headphones too - I can't recommend the HPH-MT220 highly enough too, transparent is the word I would use to describe them, having used for mixing live audio and enjoying playback.

title: Basic But Good Case For My Passport Drive And SD Cards- The SD Cards Fit Fine If I Don't Try To Press Them Down Too Far
text:
This is a basic portable case with a rigid exterior that feels like molded plastic and inner foam that provides ample protection for a My Passport external drive and SD cards. The outer canvas-type material (which looks a lot like nylon) has a tight weave and feels durable and easy to wipe clean with a damp (but not wet) cloth. The foam inside the case isn't removable and has cut out slots for 18 SD cards. There's nothing inside the case to secure the drive, but nothing seems necessary given the small size of the case.

I'm not having issues with the SD card fit. I think the depth of the cut outs falsely suggests the SD cards should be pushed down farther than necessary. Instead of applying a lot of pressure to push my cards way down into the slots, I gently press down the edges of my SD cards just enough so they're enveloped by the surrounding foam. The extra depth just makes it easier for me to remove my cards. My SD cards feel secure and don't fall out even if I turn the case upside down. This case may not have the best design for storing SD cards, but it works fine for me and they need to fit tight enough so they won't fall out of the slots. Overall, I think this is a relatively basic but good case.

title: DOES A NICE JOB
text:
Mounting 8 Element Bowtie HDTV Antenna 70 Mile Range DB8e

WHAT
After ‘cutting the cord’ from my ISP (Internet Service Provider) and installing Roku devices on our four TVs, in addition to Amazon Prime Video & Netflix, something was missing – local programming. Out of curiosity, I hung a 50-year-old, 8-inch, circle-type, UHF antenna on the kitchen TV and pointed it towards transmitters in Peoria, IL, about 25 miles away, and received 13 stations. Using a different, rabbit-ear antenna hung on a TV in the den, 18 channels came in clearly. Since a fair amount of work had been done concealing cable/wiring in the wall for these wall-mounted units, I wanted something that looked cleaner. Neither of the two TVs in the finished basement received local signals.

After reviewing multiple, attic-mount antenna products on Amazon & other venues, it came down to the 8-Element bowtie or a Channel Master CM-4228HD. Both units are somewhat pricey, but the (retired) design engineer in me was thinking about picking up stations 65 miles northwest (Galesburg area), and perhaps 82 miles southeast (Champaign area). Due to ignorance on my part (not understanding how the single, flat-panel Channel Master could be omni-directional), I opted for the 2-directional Bowtie.

HOW
Antenna research resulted in replacing existing RG-59 coax with tri-shielded RG-6 (quad-shielded for one run) and adding an AMP PCT-MA2-4PN amplifier. The longest run is 78 ft, the shortest, 42. Unfortunately, that required digging through 18 inches of attic insulation, to drill holes and fish cable. Original fishing holes couldn’t be used because the RG-59 was sourced from a different location.

As a point of interest, Amazon’s “Coax Cable Crimper, Coaxial Compression Tool Kit Wire Stripper with F RG6 RG59 Connectors”, which had the tools needed for making specific lengths of cable, was under $20 – a local big-box store was selling the crimping tool alone for over $30, pricey for a one-time use.

A comment needs to be made here: while YouTube videos depicting how to add connectors to unterminated coax is helpful, they failed to mention needing excellent gripping strength to mount the connector onto the coax far enough that the dielectric is adequately inserted. After many attempts using pliers to hold the connector while pushing/twisting the cable into it, it finally worked. A flaring tool may have been helpful.

The antenna was assembled and mounted onto an 1-1/4”x5 ft length of rigid PVC pipe (O.D. 1.66”) before going into the attic via a pull-down, ceiling ladder in the garage. Max. mounting pole size is 1-3/4”. Getting the mounted antenna through the 18x50” opening, unassisted, was awkward.

The antenna was mounted after lag-screwing a length of 1”x6” board spanning two roof trusses, then drilling holes into it for two U-bolts to clamp the PVC mounting pole. Using TVFool.com and a compass to orient the antennas, mounting was unremarkable.

To avoid compressing a large area of recently added insulation, I clambered around on the 1x4 cross-bracing of my trussed roof while holding/mounting the antenna. That turned out to be an uneventful adventure, other than digging through insulation to recover a dropped socket wrench. With attic temps easily over 120 degrees, it was a great way to lose weight.

RESULTS
- Kitchen (16-month-old Samsung SmartTV) - from 13 to 26 stations
- Den (2-yr-old Sony XBR Series, SmartTV – from 18 to 26 stations
- Basement office (6-yr-old Sony XBR series – from zero to 23 stations
- Basement media room – 10-month-old XBR series, SmartTV – from zero to 26 stations
- Clear signals were received from all stations including a few near Galesburg, 65 miles NW.
- None were received from stations near Champagne, 82 miles, SE.
- All received signals are excellent – no pixilation, ghosting, fading, etc

WRAP UP NOTES
I drilled a 3/16” hole through the PVC mounting pole, right above the top U-bolt clamp and put a 3” long ‘safety’ bolt thru it (with nuts on both side of the pole) to ‘catch’ the antenna if the clamping U-bolts loosened and the pole slid down.

There are probably other, less expensive antennas that would have provided the same results, but I wasn’t interested in pursuing antenna dynamics to figure out what was needed. I learned a long time ago, I can’t afford to buy ‘cheap’. Paying a little more for a product with good reviews and customer service, beats having to replace a cheap item that fails prematurely or performs poorly.

I used quad-shielded cable to the office TV because it ran down inside the wall next to a POE ethernet cable used for a security camera. I’m not sure that was needed but had read something about possible interference from the ethernet cable.

SOMETHING COMPLETELY UNRELATED TO THIS PRODUCT
There’s an, unrelated consideration for folks with multiple TVs who are thinking about cutting the cable. Initially, I eliminated everything but internet, but found I’d lost access to non-premium channels like Discovery, History, Science, PBS, MASH reruns, etc. – a subscription to a service was needed to get them. Some of those services, e.g. DirecTV Now, limit the number of TVs that can be streamed to, without paying extra. Customer satisfaction seems to be an issue too.

I did a cost breakdown to see how to get the most bang for my buck while streaming. With cable, I had 4 set-top boxes and was subscribed to 4 different Premium channels (HBO, Starz, ShowTime, Cinemax, which all seemed to show the same movies). My cable bill exceeded $220/month.

After comparing various services, I ended up going back to my ISP for a basic HD TV subscription to around 60 channels and one set-top box. Including fiber-optic internet, my cable bill has reduced from $227/month to around $110, plus $14(?) for Netflix Ultra (which seems to have recently increased in price). I’m not including the cost of Amazon Videos because it came as an extra to Prime, which I’ve had for years, but never used (video). The initial hardware cost of the Roku devices and antenna will be recovered in 4 months.

A perk of having the TV subscription is the free WATCHTVEVERYWHERE. Almost every channel I subscribe to through the set-top box, can also be watched on the other TVs via the SmartTV apps or Roku. One major exception is The Weather Channel (live). I still haven’t figured out how to get that.

title: Get the BD-209M instead
text:
After putting this drive through some use, I prefer my BDR-209M, aka the 2209/BDR-2209/BDR-209UBK to this drive, the 209D. I had problems with it right out of the box. I attempted to test it in an external enclosure, but that was no go. Discs would repeatedly fail to finish burning, dropping to 0.0x and never resuming. The drive would have to be powered off and back on to terminate ImgBurn. The 2209 I put in the same enclosure did not do this earlier in the year. However, that was on the old 1.34 firmware. I updated this 209D to 1.50 in the enclosure before testing it. So, it could be a firmware issue, but I doubt it.

The drive also leaves behind a funny ozone/chlorine smell to discs when ejected after burning.

BD-RE SL and DL,when Verified in ImgBurn, will begin Verifying at a higher rate then drop to 2x for a significant period of time before resuming at a higher rate of speed. The 2209 does not do it this way.

8x Ritek DVD+RW will fail to Verify sometimes even after it has just formatted the disc. Inserting these same discs that have just failed in the 2209 with the same image and burning software will then pass. So, the 209D apparently has some issues.

I can't say for sure if this is just a bad unit I got, because for everything else, it has worked fine. However, for all these issues I've mentioned that weren't present in the 209M, I would recommend forgoing this drive, the 209D, and going for the 209M. It costs more, but it also does more. It supports BD XL and TL media and M-Disc media, which the 209D does not. I've been using 209M's for years with relatively few issues. So, for my next drive, I won't be trying another 209D. I'll get another 209M, and I recommend you do the same thing.

EDIT 05-01-2018: I changed my review to I hate it. Eventually removed it and replaced it with a 2209 which I know works well. Got too many bad writes and ImgBurn Verify failures. Either I got a bad drive or this drive itself is just junk out of the box. Either way, I still don't recommend the 209 and would recommend you get the 2209 instead. Of course, it failed just 15 days after the window of returned had closed, so I'm stuck with a $70 piece of trash. Hence another reason I don't recommend you gamble on this drive.

EDIT 2018-06-10: My experience with the drive losing communication in the enclosure I am now blaming on the enclosure. On 2 different PC's, with 2 different optical drives, and on both BD-R and DVD+RW, I've had the enclosure lose communication with the software. So, it would seem the enclosure is to blame for that particular aspect of my review.
