title: Do This as a Precaution.
text:
Based on the specs and other clues, this hard drive is the Western Digital Red. So, you saved a hundred dollars by buying a "White Label" from GOHARDDRIVE - a 40% savings.
.
Reading the 1-star reviews on the WD Red, many users complained on this hard drive's short life due to the "load count problem." I examined my purchase's firmware, and it is free of this defect. Just in case if your's has this, here is an explanation of the problem and solution.
.
Since this hard drive's introduction, users have consistently reported premature failures and data corruption. These complaints were well warranted, for the manufacturer has shorten the life cycle of this computer component by design.
.
The source of the problem is Western Digital's attempt to make the device "more green" - use less electricity. One way to accomplish this goal is to park the heads on a plastic pad after eight seconds of no read/write requests instead of allowing them to float over the spinning platters of the hard drive. This adds up to 10,800 cycles each day. The numerous scrapings gradually wears out the heads. According to some literature, 250,000 to 1,250,000 cycles will result in damage that will lead to read/write errors. If you do the math, data corruption will begin within 23.148 to 115.741 days if you are employing the hard drive on a heavily used server. Regular consumers will not notice read/write problems until later. Some WD drives reported 3,000 to 5,000 cycles per day. At this rate, the first instances of data corruption will begin within 83.33 to 250 days.
.
From my experience, early data loss will not be noticed by the average user. There are no signs of trouble if work files are not accessed, edited, and save. With numerous usages, lost sectors on the hard drive appear and indexes become corrupted. Then, damages become apparent. During bootup, Windows OS will begin employing Check Disk (chkdsk/f) to repair errors. Chunks of bad information get deleted and corrupted indexes are re-corrected during the process. Eventually, 50%-to-60% drive gets wiped out before the user realizes the problem. He accesses a file, and there is none. Using a file manager, further examinations reveal other missing data. This degradation takes time - months to a year depending on computer usage.
.
Nevertheless, six years of complains have forced the manufacturer to do something - provided a firmware fix. WDIDLE3.EXE software is used to reset the parking cycle to as high as five minutes. For normal users, this change brings down the parking cycle to 133 per day. This is within the industrial average. Most drives experience 10 to 200 per day and are rated around 600,000. WDIDLE3.EXE can also turn off head parking. Unfortunately, this is not recommended. Users have reported that drive speed was reduced to a crawl or exhibited read/write problems.
.
This solution is a masterpiece in public relations. Instead of deactivating or eliminating the eight second head parking cycle on newly manufactured drives, WD forces the user to make the firmware change after the sale. The process is not easy, and the company's website does not explain or provide any information - it provides just the software. The procedure requires unplugging all other devices that are connected to SATA ports and numerous resets to the BIOS. The computer must boot in DOS via a CD or USB 2.0 thumb drive and typing the required codes. Just finding the necessary software to create the booting device is a pain.
.
As a result, non-technical consumers will not do anything and allow their hard drives to malfunction. For the "techkies," it will take hours of research, internet searches, and trial-and-error. Hopefully, they will also be discouraged. In one stroke, the company has placated the critics and still maintain high sales volume.
.
I have already done the necessary work. So, here is the easiest procedure using a booting USB 2.0 drive.
.
.
GO TO GOOGLE AND DOWNLOAD THE FOLLOWING PROGRAMS. . . . I can not provide links because the Amazon server automatically deletes their location.
. . . . . HP USB Disk Storage Format Tool
. . . . . Z-Zip
. . . . . wdidle3.exe
. . . . . FreeDOS (fd11src.iso)
.
DO THE FOLLOWING IN THIS ORDER TO CREATE A BOOTING USB 2.0 FLASH DRIVE.
. . . . . 1. Install Z-Zip
. . . . . 2. Use Z-Zip to extract HP USB Disk Storage Format Tool and FreeDOS iso.
. . . . . 3. Install the HP software.
. . . . . 4. Install a USB 2.0 flash drive on one of computer's USB 2.0 ports.
. . . . . . . Right-click the HP icon.
. . . . . . . Go to COMPATIBILITY/PRIVILEGE LEVEL.
. . . . . . . Check RUN THIS PROGRAM AS AN ADMINISTRATOR.
. . . . . . . Exit the program.
. . . . . 5. Activate the HP program by clicking its icon.
. . . . . . . Select FAT for FILE SYSTEM
. . . . . . . Place a check mark on CREATE DOS STARTUP DISK
. . . . . . . Go to USING DOS SYSTEM FILES LOCATED AT and point to the
. . . . . . . . . . subdirectory of the FreeDOS files. It is \FREEDOS\SETUP\ODIN
. . . . . 6. Format the USB 2.0 flash drive. Depending on the size, it will take time.
. . . . . 7. Use WINDOWS EXPLORER to copy WDIDLE3.EXE to your formatted USB 2.0 flash drive.
.
SHUT OFF YOUR COMPUTER.
. . . . . 1. Deactivate all devices connected to your SATA ports by pulling out their two cords. You do not want WDIDLE3.EXE to corrupt their firmware settings.
. . . . . 2. Connect your Western Digital Red Hard Drive.
.
RESTART YOUR COMPUTER.
. . . . . 1. Go into your PC's BIOS setting.
. . . . . 2. Turn AHCI off. This will enable your flash drive to be recognized.
. . . . . 3. Set the thumb drive as the first bootable drive.
. . . . . 4. Save your BIOS settings and exit.
.
RESTART YOUR COMPUTER. Your thumb drive should boot the computer and go into MS-DOS.
. . . . . 1. Type "wdidle3.exe" without the quotes and press ENTER. This will activate the program.
. . . . . 2. Type "wdidle3.exe /r" without the quotes and press ENTER. This will show the current timeout. The factory default is eight seconds.
. . . . . 3. Type "wdidle3.exe /s300" without the quotes and press ENTER. This changes the autopark timer to 300 seconds or five minutes - the maximum allowed.
. . . . . 4. Type "wdidle3.exe /r" without the quotes and press ENTER. This will check that the hard drive has accepted the change.
. . . . . 5. Shut off your PC.
.
IF YOU NEED TO PROCESS ANOTHER HARD DRIVE, pull out the two connecting cables, attach them to the next Western Digital Red drive, and repeat the above process.
.
ONCE FINISHED, TURN OFF YOUR COMPUTER AND PLUG YOUR SATA DEVICES BACK.
. . . . . 1. Turn on your PC
. . . . . 2. Go back into your PC BIOS setting.
. . . . . 3. Turn AHCI on.
. . . . . 4. Change your boot order.
. . . . . 5. Save your settings and exit.

title: Decent keyboard, great mouse, excellent combo for price.
text:
I purchased this keyboard a few months back, for my first gaming build. I was short of money after buying all of my components, and decided to get a cheap keyboard, as I could always upgrade in the future. The visual aesthetics look very nice with and along the blue lights in my build. Price in point, this is a good keyboard. A few keys tend to stick a little at times, but they still feel nice to game on overall. As for the mouse, I really like it. Good ergonomics, and a good size. Has worked very well to play Company of Heroes games with. As some of you may know, for those games you pretty much only use a mouse.

The only reason I'm rating this 4, instead of 5 stars, is because sometimes at random, when my computer is turned off, the keyboard will sometimes light up by itself, as if the computer were on. I've only noticed this a few times, especially when there have been storms nearby. It seems to be a problem with static electricity. The lights turn on if and when you hit any of the keys, and when you turn on your computer. My mobo has breathing lights even when its turned off, as long as the PSU has power as well. My solution to this has been to just unplug the keyboard when I'm not using my computer for long durations.

That said though, whenever you unplug the keyboard, it will go to its default Red setting. FN+SL will change it back to Blue or Purple though.

Everything said, my first reaction to this out of its box was, "Wow, this is good quality for the price." I still think so, as you get a mouse, keyboard, and a mousepad for around $40. That's tough to beat.

Mousepad though before I'm done. It's quite large in size, so I actually have it underneath a checkerboard mousepad that I adore. In case my mouse slips off of that, lol. It looks pretty cool, but it's just alright in quality. Not bad though. It's good to take along to LAN parties when need be.

Recommend especially if you're on a budget. Probably not quite as good as expensive mechanical keyboards, and high end gaming mouses. Although everything looks cool and seems to preform well, especially the mouse imo. Again, for around $40, how can one ever really complain?

title: Great choice for large screen entertainment tablet. Keyboard "issues" are fixable via Windows settings
text:
Update Sept. 19, 2015. Still works well overall, except:
- has power issues: would unexpectedly lock-up when off and charging, requiring a hard reset (press the power button for 15 seconds, then reboot). Almost daily.
- no upgrade support for Windows 10 as far as I could find. My other Lenovo had similar problems - no upgrade path to Windows 8. Older Acers I own and the Dell tablet have had much better driver and upgrade support.
- screen scratches somewhat easier than expected.
Lowering to 3 stars because of the above.

Great choice for large screen entertainment tablet ... if you get it at a discount. I bought directly from Lenovo outlet, refurbished model. Note their return policy includes restocking fee, so keep that in mind if not sure about the device.

First, about the "issues" pairing the keyboard. Lenovo should include instructions, as it is not at all obvious how to make it work properly! Pairing is easy - just standard Windows 8.1 Bluetooth method. But the keyboard still does not work fully. Here is what happens and how to fix it:
- After pairing, I noticed that the "Home" and forward and back Internet buttons worked when browsing the web, as did the volume buttons. Nothing else worked on the keyboard, it seemed. I noticed that if I press and hold any other key, after a couple of seconds it will register and appear on screen: so the keyboard worked at 0.5 strokes per second... Go to the Windows Ease of Access Center and turn off the "Filter Keys" option. This fixes the issue and the keyboard worked fine after that. So basically, both the pairing and typing issues are settings in Windows 8.1 that one needs to make sure are properly configured. Lenovo, however, should have taken care of this, not make me spend time researching the issue online...

You need to also go to the Bluetooth entry in the Device Manager and in the Properties, on the Power Management tab turn off the power saving option. That should fix the delay/disconnect problems

My unit also had problems charging - would say its plugged in and not charging, even though the battery was only half-full. Nothing worked to fix this. Lenovo tech support remotely troubleshoot my machine (quick response to my call to tech support, thank you) but could not fix the issue. They suggested I do a clean boot option, which brings the tablet to a fresh clean state. I did that, and the charging problem went away. After that, installed all "important" Windows updates (almost 1GB worth of them, 57 to be precise) and it still works fine.

So, after the above keyboard configuration and clean install "fixes" I now have a well-working tablet. Hurray!

The screen is very good (not spectacular) - great resolution, decent colors (fairly neutral), fairly uniformly lit (there is some light bleed from the edges, but netter than most laptop and tablet screens), fairly bright, decent gradation (ability to resolve fine shades of colors or greyscale). The screen is reflective, so you may see your reflection in it, but that's just how shiny screens like this are.

The camera sucks on mine - soft and not sharp. I think it is defective as it does not just look like a low resolution issue - it is just bad. Still, sufficient for video calls or a web photo, but worse than any other tablet or phone camera I have seen recently. If I had bought locally I'd have it exchanged for that, but since it is not terrible and I don't need that camera to be any better, I'll live with it. Colors are OK though.

The speakers are loud enough for quiet environments, but they are aimed sideways, so the high frequencies get lost and speech is not as crisp reaching your ears as it is going away from the tablet to the sides. Turn it sideways and it sounds decent, listen to it from the front - and the sound is somewhat dull/muffled. The headphone jack is a little underpowered for some low sensitivity headphones, but enough to still get loud enough to hear well (just can't crank it up to very loud/beyond safe levels with such headphones). With high sensitivity headphones it is more than adequate and the sound is clean and of very good quality over good headphones.

Battery life is great, better than what I see from most other tablets, even with screen brightness at more than half-way levels.

It is an Atom processor, so it will not be blazing fast. But it is great for movies, the Internet, office applications, and other such tasks. Very spiffy performance for such uses, no complaints.

The keyboard falls off too easy. Very weak magnets. OK for stationary use, but best to use carefully or off the tablet to avoid unexpected disconnects from the base and dropping it or the screen down.

The stand works very well.

WiFi is strong and reliable, no issues.

Pricey at full retail - I think there could be better options for that cost. For well under $400 though, I think it is still a good buy if you like that form factor. I like a large screen, but it is a bit heavy for holding when in bed - place on a pillow on your belly and prop with the stand rather than hold it as it gets tiring to hold for more than a few minutes.

title: The system was largely pretty good. It's a bit on the thick side
text:
The system was largely pretty good. It's a bit on the thick side, but not overly so. It's lighter than it looks too, which is a plus. The screen was really great. Bright and clear. The overall speed was excellent and battery life seemed decent. However, I had some serious build quality issues with mine. Firstly, the keyboard, which has good travel, feedback, and spacing, wasn't exactly well installed. It was solid on the left side, but the further to the right of the keyboard you got, things got loose and made a clattering sound like not everything was buttoned together all that well. The deal breaker and reason I sent mine back was the trackpad. I usually carry a wireless mouse with me, but I do have situations when I'm in a server room or otherwise don't have the room for mouse and need to be at least have the basic functionality of the touchpad. The pad installed runs on Elan drivers and they're seemingly unusable. The hardware seemed alright, because I could revert back to default Windows PS/2 drivers and it worked, albeit without anything other than absolutely basic functionality (no touch click, no gestures, no swipes). With the Elan drivers, every motion of the cursor was a new adventure. It was nearly impossible to reliably select text or hit a button on screen. After going over this issue with Gigabyte support, they offered me an RMA replacement, but I think that a new unit would have the exact same issue so I opted to return mine for a refund.
So, if you don't mind mediocre build quality in your keyboard and an almost useless touchpad, everything else on the machine is really great!

title: Scary install made me wet my pants
text:
These modules were stubborn during the install process. After I installed them the first time, I turned on my 13" Macbook Pro (Early 2011), and my computer started emitting a warning sound — three continuous beeps over and over again until I held down the power button and shut down the system.

I took apart my laptop, took out the RAM sticks and cleaned everything, removing any and all dust in and around the internal components of my computer. I reinstalled the RAM, put everything back together and turned on the system only to hear the beeping once again.

At this point, my anxiety has risen tremendously because I thought I may have fried something. I did some web searching and found my problem is quite common with these Corsair modules.

I decided to give it a third try. Only this time, when I reinstalled them, I very patiently seated the RAM with about three times the pressure as I had before, making sure I was applying equal pressure along the entire module. Once both were firmly in place, I gently pressed down on the memory banks and put the aluminum cover back on. I tightened the screws a little tighter while applying slight pressure on the aluminum cover (hoping all the little circuit contacts would be nice and snug.

That finally did the trick, but I definitely would not want to do it over again. In the forums I searched where others had the same issue, someone advised to go with either Crucial or Kingston sticks next time. Apparently those are the best modules for MacBooks.

As for the speed they're providing, the only thing I've noticed is that Mail loads faster. Perhaps when I play around with it a little more I'll notice some other speed improvements.

title: Keep on looking.
text:
These batteries have surprised me. I use quite a few batteries as just about everything I own requires them. For years I always stuck with the copper top brand and purchased them in either the hardware or drug store. Then over fifteen years ago I found Amazon and I haven’t purchased a battery anywhere else. I found the Duracell Pro brand here and they have become my battery choice. I’ve had no use for Triple AAA batteries until recently when I purchased a set of under counter lights. The main feature that sold me on the lights was the included remote control. I’m confined to a power wheelchair making it difficult for me to get close enough to reach the cabinets in my kitchen. The kitchen is lit by a couple of overhead lamps which are controlled by wall switch. The problem with this configuration is I’m completely in the dark once I turn those overhead lights off. The under counter lights would have been ideal as they could remain on to allow some light which while bright enough to see but dim enough not to bother you if left on. Well unfortunately the lighting kit didn’t work out for different reasons and are now sitting in a closet. The lighting group used AAA batteries and these being recommended by Amazon in the “ recently purchased together “ section of the description I took a chance. I should have stayed with my first choice, the Duracell Pro. We placed these Utopia Home brand batteries in the above mentioned lighting group. They worked great. That was the first three worked. We loaded up the rest of the lights, six in all, and out of the six only three worked. We decided to check the batteries to see if they were inserted properly and yet we still couldn’t get them to work. My aide checked to see if the batteries that were in the working lights would work in the lights not working. She took all three batteries out of the working lights and placed them in the lights not working and they lit up immediately. So now we proved it was batteries. But which one or ones? Over the next few days we checked the batteries by placing and rotating each one in the working lights. I’m afraid to say that out of the fifty batteries received thirty six worked. I thought it still wasn’t bad as the price wasn’t that bad. The real slap in the face was the batteries that did work didn’t hold up that well. The batteries were used in low powered LED lighting. The lights were set in the lowest setting and ran just about three hours per night. One light was dead on the second day and the others lasted from three days to longest being five. Not very good. I can’t understand. The reviews of the batteries were great. One of the reasons other than price were the reviews. Could it be I received a bad batch? Maybe, I don’t know. The lights had these batteries replaced with my Duracell Pro batteries and they have powered the lights now for over ten days without a problem. I’ll stick with the Duracell Pro batteries from now on. I guess you get what you pay for.

This review was written without any financial considerations. Not a free product nor a discount was received. Full Amazon retail was paid.
I enjoy writing reviews on the products I have purchased. If my reviews have helped you in your purchase decisions please let me know. I’m available to answer any questions about my reviews. Contact me here at Amazon.

Bob

text:
I've had these since September of '13 and I really love to mix on these when mixing at home.
I usually mix on a pair of JBL LSR6328Ps, but these are every bit as clear and non-coloring as
the JBL's. They don't have quite the same punch in the lower end.

I have them as my main monitoring path out of my Avid HD-OMNI box and also as the USB computer output
from my Mac. You have to turn off the USB driver otherwise there's a short (1/2 second) recognition that an analog
signal is coming in. Other than that, the cut over between audio sources is excellent.

The Vanatoo's have plenty of power for desktop mixing.

I have combined them with the isoACOUSTICs isolating speaker stand and the pair is excellent. While the Transparent One
does come with little adhesive rubber feet, they aren't isolating enough if you're on a smooth surface like a desktop. Sympathetic
vibrations and low-end resonance will result. But, with the isoAcoustics, that's solved.

The thing that I really like about the Transparent Ones is how true they are to the material and the accuracy of the stereo imaging.
Very nice.

The Transparent Ones are a lot like my Yamaha NS10's in that if you mix on them, the mixes translate very well to other
playback systems .. especially earbuds ..and portable devices.

If you're looking for a pair of excellent speakers when you have to mix at home, I would highly recommend these

Jeff Markham
AES, CAS

PS: Leave the bass and treble knobs in the back at center for true.

title: High resolution photos, Less than great videos.
text:
When this camera was new, I would have said, it's a pretty good, relatively inexpensive point and shoot camera, that records HD video. Now here in 2016, I would say there are better options available at this price point. That's not to say it's not still an OK camera, but it does have some issues you should know about.

Lets start with the good stuff. The picture quality in daytime photos is actually pretty impressive. It has several different settings to choose from to change the resolution of your photos. The highest resolution photos the camera takes look very crisp and clean, and very large. They need to be sized down typically for use on the computer. The close up/MACRO use of this camera is also quite impressive. I can get very sharp close up photos from several inches away. This is one of the reasons I still use this camera after 3 years. There are plenty of settings for picture taking, such as low light setting, color adjustments, filters, red eye..all the normal stuff you would expect. They all work OK, but practically, this camera is best suited for medium to bright light, and extreme close ups. Low light photos are grainy and unimpressive. Very bright light photos can get pretty washed out, and will likely need contrast editing on your PC. Not a huge deal, but one more step before your photos are ready to share.

Lets talk about the video recording features. So first off, all the fancy settings, filters, low light shooting, etc are not available for the video recording mode. So basically you get what you get. Night time videos are basically out of the question for this camera. They will be either pitch black, or very grainy, depending on how much light is available. Daytime videos actually look pretty good, although 720p is the highest shooting resolution, so keep that in mind. Another thing to think about is that this camera will not focus on a light source you choose. It will adjust the aperature based on the light that's coming directly at it. For example, if you are recording at sunset/sunrise, and the camera is facing the sun, and you are standing in between the camera and the sun, you will be completely blacked out, while the sun will be correctly exposed. To compensate, you have to move the camera, and the object being recorded so that the camera is inline with the light source, and between you and the light source (sun). Unlike modern cell phone cameras, where you can just touch the screen in different places to tell the camera what light source you want it to adjust to.

So comparing it to modern cell phone video shooting. I have recorded videos with iPhone 6s, Samsung Galaxy, newer HTC, and Google Nexus 5x. All of these video recording is better than this Canon Power shot. Plus they all shoot in 1080p now, so even better.

One more area to touch on - Sound Quality. The sound quality on this camera is definitely the worst part about it. For sound to come out "hear-able" in the video, you need to be about 1-3 feet from the camera. Anything further, will be so quiet, it's almost unusable. Anything closer will be very loud, and distorted, and low quality. Also, every bit of wind noise is picked up by the mic. Any sort of wind will completely wash out the audio you are trying to record. Any kind of hand movement close to the mic, will be dramatic in the final video. And the zoom feature of the lens is pretty loud in your video. So when recording its best to move the camera closer or farther away, rather than using the zoom. If not, the "Zoom noise" will be in your video.

So yeah, what it boils down to is, this camera is really only suited for medium light to bright light, still shooting, and close-ups. The other features it has are adequate if you dont care about quality.

title: A decent unit with still immature/buggy firmware
text:
This is a well-made unit that is certainly capable of doing what it is supposed to do. My previous experience with Garmin car navigators include Nuvi 3490 and NuviCam. DriveLuxe 50 is definitely heavier than 3490, but noticeably lighter and thinner than NuviCam. However, as of this writing, DriveLuxe 50 suffers from a number of significant firmware bugs, which are unfortunately so typical for Garmin devices. Here's a few things I think are worth mentioning after a few months of use:

Pros:
- Solidly built and not overweight for its size (NuviCam was definitely on the heavy side).
- Very good Bluetooth connectivity. Connects reliably, which is important for using it device as a hands-free device as well as for reliable communication with Garmin Smartphone Link app. (NuviCam is good at it as well, but 3490 fared much worse in that department).
- Screen image does not disappear even when looked at through polarized sunglasses, regardless of the angle.
- Garmin finally replaced their horrible ear-shattering incoming call ringtone with something that sounds a lot softer.
- Voice recognition works well. Pre-programmed commands are recognized reliably. Custom names (like business names) are recognized well too (multiple choice screen usually contains the right guess).

Cons:
- The screen is too low-res for this size. 800x480 is ridiculously low by modern standards. Sometimes the image looks like it is painted with a lipstick.
- The sound quality is adequate, but appears to be notably worse than in NuviCam. This is especially noticeable during hands-free conversations. Higher-frequency tones easily make the speaker to squeal and distort. In my experience, NuviCam has much better-sounding speaker with surprisingly low distortions.
- Voice command menu hasn't changed since 3490 era. It is still very deeply and annoyingly nested. Such simple tasks as redialing the last phone call require suffering through several levels of nested menus. Garmin redesigned their touch-based phone menu and made it much easier to use, but the voice-based menu is still stuck in its original state from many-years-ago.
- Partial street name search is unreliable. For some street names it works, for others it doesn't. For example, for some unexplainable reason searching for "El Camino" does not find addresses on "El Camino Real".
- A serious firmware bug: spurious voice prompts. When device is set up to use a non-synthesized voice, it often issues voice directions intended for the distant next turn as _current_ directions. For example, if you have 50 miles of straight highway driving ahead of you, followed by exit to the right, the device will suddenly say "Exit right" at a number of intermediate points along that straight route. This is startling and highly misleading. The graphical representation of the route remains correct, just voice prompt is misleading. The bug is 100% reproducible and always happens at the same points of the route. So, if you prefer to rely on voice prompts for navigation (as opposed to following the line on the screen), this device is not yet usable for that purpose.
- Another firmware bug: School Zone chime cannot be disabled. Garmin introduced a number of settings that lets user select which warnings should be accompanied with audible chime. The device settings GUI contains a number of checkboxes allowing user to on/off the chimes. The list includes the "School" chime as well. However, the "School" checkbox has no effect at all - the device simply ignores the user selection. Regardless of what the user selects, the School Zone chime is always audible. Apparently, Garmin had the right idea to make it possible to disable this chime and even included the option in the the GUI, but never bothered to actually implement it.
- (Fixed in fimware 4.10) Searching for businesses by name suffers from some strange bug. I have lots of Starbucks locations around me. However, if I perform a text search for "Starbucks", this device will only list some very distant locations in other cities (about 20 miles away). The same problem affects text search for "Subway" and many other names. Yet, search for "Nordstrom" works correctly. Meanwhile, if instead of text search I'd simply open "Restaurants : Coffee & Tea" category, all local Starbucks locations would be listed properly.
- Weather support is implemented crudely. When connected to Smartlink app the device supports Free Weather at Current Location feature, as well as paid subscription-based Live Weather Along The Route and Live Weather at Destination features. If a non-subscribed user hits the Weather icon while some route is active, the device apparently attempts to access the paid service and displays a cryptic error message ("invalid request" or something like that). This is ridiculous. If the user is not subscribed, then hitting Weather icon should still display Free Weather instead of splatting cryptic developer-level error prompts across the screen.
- Active Lane Guidance is a useful feature (where it works), but it quickly gets annoying on familiar routes. The user should be able disable it, if they so desire. At this time all we can do is manually close the guidance window every time it pops up.

The recent map updates also introduced a number of ludicrous map-related issues (my home address suddenly disappeared from the database), but such issues are not related to the device itself.

I am a very happy owner of this lens mounted on a d5100 camera body.

First off from 11mm - 12mm there is a difference.... But one that you will very rarely ever need, and in the event you do.. take a couple steps back.

F4 vs F 2.8 is one step.... One step isn't a killer in the world of digital. The noise created from one step can be fixed in 2 seconds in light room.... Shoot RAW.

On F4 the frames are SHARP, edge softness is not noticeable for any of the shooting I have ever done..

On the positive side 12mm is really wide.... You can capture alot in one frame for landscapes, but more importantly the depth perspective changes significantly over 18mm... You can get right up on something and really capture interesting frames.

Getting up to 28mm is fantastic. I leave this lens on my body about 80% of the time. My bag includes this lens, 35mm 1.8, 50mm 1.8, and an inexpensive Nikon 55-300mm. I have everything I need to capture stunning frames.

Notes...

Standard Hoya UV filter at 12 mm will be noticed in the far corners of the frame, find an ultra thin filter if you elect to use them. Circular polarizer causes some interesting effects in the sky. I avoid polarizers on this lens. I leave a normal UV filter on to avoid finger prints / ocean spray on the lens.

title: Great For The Surface Pro 3
text:
Looking for a way to connect the Mini DisplayPort from a Surface Pro 3 to an HDTV, this is the adapter for you. It delivers both the picture AND the sound (providing your device has speakers) from the Mini DisplayPort to the HDMI connected device (i.e TV, monitor). I used this with an "HDMI 2M (6 Feet) Super High Resolution Cable" from LB1 High Performance and a Samsung 32" 1080p TV.

How To:
Simply connect the male end this adapter to the Mini DisplayPort, then connect the female end to an HDMI cable, and connect that HDMI cable to an HMDI port on your TV or HD monitor. The Surface Pro 3 will probably mirror (duplicate) the two screens the first time you do this. If you are connecting to a HDTV HDMI port, this may reduce the resolution to 1920 x 1080 (or even 1366 x 768). Just right-click on your Surface Pro desktop and select "Screen Resolution". Set your HDTV or Monitor to be your second (extended - #2) screen, and you'll be able to return your Surface Pro table screen back it's recommended 2160 x 1440 size.

title: Not Quite Perfect But As Close As There Is For A Bluetooth Adapter
text:
While the Bose Bluetooth Audio Adapter is twice the price as many other bluetooth receivers, it works as a bluetooth receiver should while other, cheaper receivers I've owned just cause headaches, some quicker than others. As I learned in the end, sometimes you just have to fork over the extra money. Before purchasing the Bose, I had two Homespot bluetooth receivers, a Pioneer bluetooth adapter for my A/V receiver, and tried the Brightech Brightplay bluetooth receiver. The Brightech was returned pretty quickly. Although the Bose may not be perfect, it is as close as there is to perfect for a bluetooth audio adapter. After a few days use I purchased a second Bose adapter to replace the other Homespot. During the review I'll draw comparisons to my other bluetooth receivers.

Positives:
1. Very easy to pair. If nothing is connected to the receiver, you just go to the bluetooth settings on your tablet, phone, or computer to pair. Even if another device can be connected to it, you simply touch the button on receiver to start the pairing process. The Brightech is horrible. You have to unplug the audio cable and then reconnect the cable to start the pairing process. While the Homespot is easy to pair also no other device can be connected to the receiver if you want to pair a new one. With the Pioneer bluetooth adapter, I have to go into the receiver's menu to pair which isn't a user friendly process.
2. Three devices can be connected to the Bose at once. This is a feature which caused me to look to replace the two Homespot receivers I was using. Only one device can be connected to the Homespot. When my wife decided she wanted to start to streaming to the Homespot also this became a problem for us. One of us would try to connect but couldn't, so she or I would have to search for other's iPhone and iPad to see which was connected and then go to the bluetooth settings and turn the bluetooth off to disconnect that device. While the Brightech does allow two devices to connect, it doesn't always work. The Brightech also has a big problem of randomly auto connecting to devices. With that problem, it became a bigger nuisance than the Homespot. The Bose works perfectly! If multiple devices are connected, just pause audio on one device and click play on another. The Pioneer also doesn't allow multiple devices to be connected to it at the same time.
3. If you are connected to the Bose, then go out of range of the receiver and back into range within about a 10 minute period, the Bose will automatically reconnect you. This is very nice if you move around a lot in your apartment or house while streaming audio. If I walk out of range when using the Homespot or Pioneer, even for a few seconds, I have to reconnect to the bluetooth adapter to start streaming audio again. This is a nuisance. While the Brightech had auto reconnect, it was a needly little receiver and seemed to always want to be connected to something. It would randomly connect to one of our devices at home. Very frustrating.
4. The Bose, Brightech, and Homespot all feature auto connect when the receiver is powered on. This is great if you use the bluetooth adapter in a car or if it is powered by an amp. If the bluetooth adapter is plugged into a wall outlet it will stay powered all the time.
5. The Bose is powered by a USB cable and comes with a wall adapter. That means if you have an amp that has a powered USB port you can plug directly into it for power. The Brightech plugged directly into a wall outlet which I didn't like. The Homespot is powered by a USB cable also. However, when I plugged either of my Homespot receivers into the Orb Mini-T amp using either cable that came with them, I could hear noise and interference through the speakers. I thought it was the amp until I got a new mini amp, a Polk Omni A1, and experienced the same noise and interference through the speakers. I then became suspicious that it was the Homespot receivers that were causing this. When I got the Bose Bluetooth Audio Adapter and plugged into the Polk receiver, there was no noise or interference whatsoever.
6. When the Bose is connected it stays connected and when it is disconnected it stays disconnected. It may seem like such a small thing but neither the Homespot or Brightech could get that quite right. While streaming audio to the Homespot, well within bluetooth range, the receiver would occasionally disconnect itself while the Brightech as I mentioned earlier would randomly hijack the audio of my iPhone or iPad.
7. Audio quality from the Bose is excellent. If using the auxiliary out of the Bose, the audio quality is indistinguishable from the Brightech and nearly indistinguishable from plugging my phone directly into the amp with an auxiliary cable. Audio from the Bose and Brightech is noticeably louder than that from the Homespot but again the same volume as plugging directly into the amp.
8. The Bose Bluetooth Audio Adapter features apt-x codec for lossless streaming and digital optical out. iPhones and iPads are not compatible with apt-x so I'm not able to comment on that feature. If you have an open digital optical input on your amp or receiver, the Bose is without a doubt the bluetooth adapter to get. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the sound quality is even better using the digital optical out than it is using the auxiliary out. Using the optical out, music is more lively, punchier, and has better soundstage.

Negatives:
1. There is one disadvantage to the auto reconnect. On the Bose and Brightech if I'm connected to either receiver but listening on headphones and walk out of range of the receiver and then back into range within 10 minutes, the Bose and Brightech will reconnect to the device (that's great) but then the receiver will select itself as the primary audio output thereby stopping playback to the headphones (not so great).
2. All Bose Bluetooth Audio Adapters have the same bluetooth name in your computer, smartphone, or tablet. This can be a problem if you have more than one Bose adapter and are using an iPhone or iPad to connect to them. Unlike Android, Apple doesn't let you give a bluetooth device a nickname, although you can on a Mac. Therefore you can never be sure which Bose receiver you are connecting to. The Homespot is the only receiver I know that gives a number value, 00-99, to the name of their bluetooth device. That means if you have multiple Homespot receivers, as I did, you can easily distinguish one from the next. One of my receivers was GT BT-Receiver 35 and the other was GT BT-Receiver 67. This obviously isn't entirely Bose's fault but it isn't entirely Apple's either since competitors of both have found solutions to this problem.

Summary:
I understand the desire to try to get by inexpensively on a bluetooth receiver. There are several receivers in the $30 range and then the Bose at $60. You may think you're spending a lot for the Bose name and a $30 one will do the same for half the price. As I learned the hard way this isn't true. I got fed up with the Homespot and Brightech and Pioneer before finally forking the extra money over for the Bose. After using it for a few days, I ordered a second one. It works as a bluetooth adapter should work. If your amp has an free digital optical input that you are wanting a bluetooth receiver to plug into, the Bose is without a doubt the one to get. The sound quality from the Bose is superb, especially using the optical out. The Bose features auto reconnect and the ability to connect three devices to it at once. It's easy to pair to even if a device is already connected to it. It has the ability to be powered from an amp which has a powered USB port. Plus, it has bluetooth 4.0 along with apt-x for the best bluetooth streaming currently available.

*** End update ***

*** Original review ***

These fans are quirky. You need to know what you're getting into.

Firstly, they are reasonably good build quality. They don't feel cheap, the LEDs are consistent and the cable quality is OK.

However, I have some gripes about these:

1. The fan connection is proprietary and probably won't work without the controller. The astute among us would figure out the pinout and make a connector. But usually people want 'out of the box' compatibility.
2. The fan frame isn't super rigid, it's semi-flexible. The foam pads are cheaply glued on
3. The latch on the connection to the fan hub is a little wonky, it takes a little force to get it out
4. The fan hub seems to freeze up somehow. After changing many settings at once it seems to 'freeze up' and takes a while to become responsive again. A power cycle fixes it. I'm guessing it's a firmware issue.
5. The fan hub has 10 spaces on it. I wish they made it smaller so I could fit in my case better.
6. An extra few inches on the cable length for the fans would also be nice.
7. The IR LED component has a clear warning on it: It can short your other components. Be sure to place it somewhere well away from your motherboard and valuable graphics card!

There are also some good pros:

1. I confirmed this to work with Asus Aura Sync (I have an Asus Prime X470). Push the 'M/B' button.
2. The LEDs are bright and beautiful. They are dimmable and you can turn them off if you don't want them on.
3. You can control the fan speed with the hub! I thought this was a neat feature. It doesn't have any kind of software though, so if you lose the remote or break you're out of luck.
4. The fans, 24 hours in, are running quiet and moving a good amount of air
5. The LED color mostly matches my other RGB components
6. The fan hub doesn't need any memory-sucking software. It works by itself if you want it to.
7. These are extremely well priced. They are well worth the asking price considering you get three fans and get extra features on top of that.

Overall I'm pretty happy with these fans. They pair very nicely with a tempered glass case. They're pretty well built and all of the LEDs are on the fan cage so they avoid the cheapo illuminated fan blades look.

title: Best swim mp3 device I have ever used
text:
I bought this hoping to be able to use the bluetooth feature to listen to Pandora while swimming laps. That part is a mixed success. I have previously tried the waterproof ipods (they don't last), the finis bone-conduction devices (they get glitchy really quick and lose the ability to connect to computers), the Syryn, and several other cheaper waterproof mp3 players. None yet are perfect, but this one so far is as good as any.
The sound quality is excellent; better than the Syryn, comparable to the ipod. The earbuds fit well and it comes with several sizes included. A bit of vaseline and a swim cap keeps the water out and the sound good for over an hour.
The play from memory works well, although the volume changes rapidly when the up or down buttons are held; it gets louder or softer really fast causing occasional overshoots and the necessity of readjusting the other way. A single brief push of the same buttons skips a song ahead or back, but sometime this happens simultaneously, and unintentionally, with the sound adjustments.
As advertised, bluetooth does not work underwater. This is not a defect of the device, it's a property of the bluetooth RF wavelength; it doesn't penetrate water. Also, the distance bluetooth waves can travel is relatively short. I expected these limitations and found I was right:
Distance limitation: With the device strapped to the back of my goggle strap and my phone at one end of a 25 yard pool, the sound does momentary cut-outs as I approach the far end. With the phone to the side of the pool, the sound lasts the whole way back and forth.
Underwater limitation: The sound to disappears entirely during flip turns. If I don't glide too long before resurfacing, the sound resumes. Also, if I turn my head too far to breath such that the device on the back of my head dips under the surface the sound is briefly interrupted. These minor interruptions were expected and not a problem with the device.
However, a problem does arise if the device is disconnected from bluetooth for too long; either with a long glide after flip turn, or if I push pause, or press the bluetooth button to switch to memory play. In all of these cases the device does not automatically reconnect with the phone. I had to get out of the pool and manually reconnect the phone to the device. This happened numerous times as I experimented with the functions. Disconnection from the phone was caused by pushing pause while playing on bluetooth, pushing the button to switch to memory play and then back, and staying under water for more than about 1.5 seconds.
The instruction sheet says that once the device is paired it will automatically connect to the phone thereafter. This is not correct. Each time it's turned off and on, or paused, or switched to memory and back, or remains under water for more than 1-2 seconds it has to be manually reconnected to the phone. This is a nuisance, and involves getting out of the pool, pulling the phone out of the bag, unlocking it, getting to the bluetooth devices screen, and selecting the H2O device. It always reconnected after doing this, but it should be automatic as the instructions say.
Finally I gave up listening to Pandora while swimming laps and just finished my workout on memory play, then got out, reconnected the phone, and did 15 minutes of kicking so the thing would stay out of the water and connected while I listened to Pandora.
Bottom line: a good device with good sound quality, but for swimming laps it's pretty much limited to the memory play feature, unless you do open turns or don't mind getting out of the water after each good flip turn to reconnect to your phone. For anything else, including doing kicks with the device on your head out of the water, the bluetooth feature works (if it's on the side of the pool and you're in the end lane closest to the deck where your phone is), but if you want to switch back and forth between bluetooth and memory you'll have to manually reconnect to your phone each time, unless it likes your phone better than it does mine (iphone 6s).
I think it's still a good device just for the mp3 playback, which is what I'll be mostly using it for.

Addendum 4/19/2019. The device stopped being recognized by my computer. I got the battery low message. I took it home and plugged it into the computer. The charge light came on but the computer did not recognize the device was plugged in and did not read the mp3 files. When this has happened with other devices (ipod, Syryn) I have been able to restore connectivity by cleaning the port with rubbing alcohol. I tried that with the H2OAudio device and it became completely unresponsive; the charge light did not come on when plugged back in. Cleaning again did not help. The device is dead. Too bad, it was very nice while it worked.

Another Addendum 11/18/2019
My Syryn's power/pause button became increasingly glitchy so 2 months ago I bought another H2OAudio. Since my original one died the manufacturer has added a plastic tube device through which you plug the earbuds. It makes a quite tight seal that (probably) keeps out water. When I first opened the package and saw the new connector I was a bit doubtful that would be sufficient. I got out the earbuds that came with my first H2OAudio device (they are the same as the new one) which I had been using with the Syryn, and plugged those in. It made such a tight seal that when I tried pulling it out the insulation at the base of the earbud connector wire split. That warned me to be more careful with the new earbuds. It has been through 3 charge cycles now and no problems so far. Contrary to prior advice to disconnect the earbuds after each use so the connection can dry, the instructions now are to leave the earbuds connected to keep out water. I've done that except when it was time to charge, which is surprisingly long. I haven't counted the hours exactly but I swim usually 5 days per week for at least an hour a day and it lasts over two weeks.
The volume controls also work better than on the earlier version.
The sound quality remains very good. The earbuds are the best I've tried from any manufacturer. I now have a fairly large collection from my failed swimming mp3 players and the H2OAudio ones are the best fitting and best sounding, which is why I was using my old ones with the Syryn.
I like the feature of a voice telling you when the device turns off and on, rather than just a light, so you can tell when it's one or the other for sure while wearing it on the back of your head. The Syryn does not have that feature and several times I've run the battery down thinking I'd turned it off when I'd actually only paused it and hadn't noticed the light status. The same voice also tells you when you're in playback or bluetooth mode.
So I've again become happy with the device and use it exclusively for my workouts. I accordingly upgraded the rating to 5 stars. It's still fairly early days, however: if it fails again I'll post another update.

Update 8/17/2020 Except for about a 2 month break when the pool was shut down due to COVID I have continued to use the device for all my swims and have had zero problems. By far the best swim mp3 player I have ever used.

title: Best value in a lower-powered KT88 amp
text:
OK, so I wanted to live with my Gemtune Class-A KT88 amp for a while before I wrote a review.

First things first - There's some confusion in the reviews, and the questions asked/answered. *IF* this is a 13.3W/channel amplifier, then this means that this is running the KT88 in triode configuration. This is running the tubes at high voltage in their sweet spot, so you couldn't ask for much more. This is assuming that the specs are correct. One thing that leads me to believe that the specs are telling the truth is that my amp came, out of the box, biased to 70ma. Again, if you refer to the spec sheet, this verifies the configuration of the amp.

Another reviewer mentioned that the "VU" meters don't move. This is correct. This amp is known as a "Variable fixed bias amplifier". If you look behind the power tube on the right hand side, you'll see two little slotted knobs. Those are the bias adjusters for the left and right channels. The meters on the front of the amp are used to adjust the bias. As the amp settles in, and the tubes age a bit, the bias will drift, so you need to adjust the bias as time goes on. You can tell a tube has gone bad when the bias current is no longer stable. One of the stock KT88 PSvane tubes that came with the amp only lasted 3 months. Due to the configuration of this amp, I'd expect to get about a year out of a set of power tubes. You're pushing the grids a bit with this configuration, so the quality of tube construction is going to play a more serious role in how long they last.

OK, so now that we've covered some of the technicals, I guess it's time to talk about tube compatibility. I had to do some real homework to figure out a suitable replacement for that rectifier tube. 5Y3/5Z3 were the recommended rectifier replacement type, but if I'm reading the tube datasheet correctly, 5U4 tube types actually provide more current. I'm running a 5U4 type in my amp, and things are working fine. The preamp tubes are equivalent to a 6SN7 tube type, and of course, we know we've got the KT88's at the power position.

Ok, so my setup and impressions - I'm running a pair of Klipsch RB61's (original revision), and this amp is fantastic for my "home theater". I live in an apartment, and the amp is more than capable of filling my entire apartment with sound. I really really appreciate the natural compression that this amp has. It has taken the place of a NAD C375BEE amp, because the NAD just has too much power. If you're watching any modern TV or movie content, the dynamic range will rattle the windows, even with the sound at a reasonable volume. This amp solves that problem by simply not having 100W of headroom. That's not a dig either. This amp is extremely musical, and has a wonderful sound stage, even with the stock compliment of tubes. I will say, however, that the stock tubes had a very "scooped" sound, and were shouty at high volumes. This problem has been resolved with a set of Mullard KT88's. The Mullards are wonderfully flat. They have a more tame top-end that agrees very nicely with the brightness of the RB61's. I changed the rectifier tube at the same time that I installed the Mullards, and the bass is much tighter too. This is typically a function of better power delivery, so it's difficult to tell if it was the Mullards, or the new rectifier. The Mullard KT88 tubes seem to be running much cooler than the stock tubes too.

OK, so final thoughts -
Over all, this is probably the best value in a reasonably priced hi-fi tube amp you're going to find. KT88 tubes are a powerful, and dynamic power tube, and this amp really does show case the quality of whatever tubes you're using. You're probably going to want to run some fairly sensitive speakers to really appreciate this amplifier, but it does deliver on that delicious tube-amp goodness.

title: 10Gtek AGM734 clone transceivers work great with Netgear GS724Tv4
text:
Bought two 10Gtek AGM734-compatible transceivers for the SFP ports on my Netgear GS724Tv4 switches and they work great!

There's no official information about Netgear's own AGM734 being compatible with the GS724Tv4 (and a variety of other Netgear switches), except for a post on Netgear's forum (if that can be considered "official"), so I was a little hesitant buying an AGM734 clone. If it didn't work, then was it 10Gtek's fault for not being a flawed AGM734 clone or my fault for trusting that the AGM734 (clone or not) is compatible with the GS724Tv4. The price for a Netgear AGM734 is ridiculous for use, little alone just testing, but the price for a 10Gtek is worthwhile. I bought one and it worked! Bought a second one (as GS724Tv4's have two dedicated SFPs) and it also worked! 5 hours straight of full-duplex ~1 Gbps TCP traffic (2 Gbps total, according to GS724Tv4's SNMP reporting and the traffic generator) through both transceivers installed in a single GS724Tv4 and no problems.

After this experience I know: 1. AGM734 transceivers are compatible with GS724Tv4 and 2. 10Gtek transceivers are functional clones.

title: "Factory tuned," my shiny metal ass!
text:
This was the last commercial base station antenna that I'll buy. The assembly instructions are not great, but tolerable. My biggest problem, though is the claim that no tuning or adjustment is necessary. Bulls***! My antenna, fully assembled and tested at least 10 feet away from anything, including the ground, showed a 2:1 bandwidth from about 144.5 MHz to about 147.5 MHz. Not enough to cover even the FM portion of 2m. On 440, the situation is even worse. Resonance lands at about 435 MHz and the 2:1 mark is passed at about 438 MHz. In the transmit portion of the FM repeater section of the band, it's already over 3:1, so unusable on that band, and far from what is claimed.

Today, I built a "flower pot" vertical dual band antenna from about $10 worth of parts, and it outshines this piece of crap by a landslide in terms of both usable bandwidth and on-air performance. I'm going to give this Tram to my dad and let him see if he can get it to work or use it as a mono-band antenna. I'll be homebrewing my base station antennas from now on.

title: The best case! Held on by snaps and not magnets, but still the best case!
text:
Quick update 11-5-2016: After about 2 months of taking the case on and off, the snaps are noticeably weaker than when it was new. As the snaps on the case side look fine, I think the snaps on the tablet side are starting to wear. However, it still sticks well, only falling off if I hold it only by the case and shake it a little bit (when it was new this would not make it fall off). It still has no problem holding the tablet in stand mode.

Quick update: I'm changing my rating from 4 to 5 stars. I still believe my gripe about the snaps is warranted, but not enough to take off a star considering all this case gets right. The 3 angles of the built in stand are all extremely stable and useful, the case mostly gets out of the way when you're holding the device (I especially like how it magnetically closes around back so it doesn't flap around like most phone folio cases), and it just looks good. I can't count how many times I've looked at my tablet folded up into this case and just thought it looked extremely slick. If you own one of these great tablets, you're doing yourself a disservice by not getting one of these great cases.

Original Review:
Let me start off by saying that this case, as far as protection and functionality goes, couldn't be better. The three viewing angles are very nice and sturdy, the case looks and feels nice and is very slim. However, it doesn't seem like it was engineered to be removed.

Let me also mention that I really don't like cases. I don't like the weight and thickness they bring to our otherwise sleek devices. So when I bought the lightest (!!) 8 inch android tablet ever made, I intended to take advantage of that by using it bare. However, after I got a few light scratches on the screen even with careful use (I don't know how I manage it, but I scratch all kinds of gorilla glass), I thought I'd get a magnetic case that would be easy to put on and take off when needed. I unfortunately didn't do much research and then purchased this case because the first few top reviews mentioned it attached with magnets.

Spoiler alert: It does not attach with magnets, it just closes via the magnetic flap. I thought the case would attach to the tablet via magnets that went into the dimples on the back of the tablet, but instead it uses these plastic snaps. You apply the case by lining up the case and tablet and pressing very hard until they click. These snaps are much stronger than any magnets could be and the tablets safely will dangle from the case, unlike the iPad smart cover where if you shake the cover the iPad will fall off. However, removing the tablet becomes an ordeal. You have to pry at the right angle with a good amount of force.

Although this in itself isn't too much of a problem as it can still be removed within 10 seconds, I worry for the longevity of the snap mechanism if it is removed and attached several times a day as I plan to use it. Some youtube reviews report that after taking it on and off after a course of a month it was still good as new, but I'll watch it over the course of a year.

I will be sure to update this review and take off 1 star if the case snaps break within a year or 2 if it wears out the snaps on the tablet side. However, I'll give samsung the benefit of the doubt and assume it will last.

title: Finally, effective home networking!
text:
Setup was reasonably easy. There was a firmware update that I did not discover until after deploying the satellite to its location and updating the router before the satellite. Under such circumstances and in the case of difficulty updating the satellite, the documentation required temporarily relocating the satellite closer to the router, which we have located in the basement. Since performing this update subsequent updates appear to be happening automatically and without moving the satellite.
So far, after one week of operation, the Orbi system seems to have solved the problem we had with streaming cable programming to the upstairs bedrooms. There are still some jerks in programming but these are extremely rare and barely noticeable and certainly far less annoying than the previous, very frequent streaming stops and quits, especially with HBO programming. Can you say "ready for Game of Thrones"?
We have our living room flat screen, TiVo, and blu-ray player connected by Ethernet cabling directly to the satellite on the first floor. On the second floor, we have two more flat screens, a desktop computer, an Xbox, and another blu-ray player that connect wirelessly. In the basement, we have a desktop connected by Ethernet to the router. Across the room there is Securifi Almond wifi extender to which we have connected by Ethernet another TiVo and a Yamaha receiver. Through the latter, we airplay music out of our iTunes collection to booming basement speakers (something that I wish that I could also do with the Prime music catalog). I should point out that the Orbi system has made use of two other extenders unnecessary because they never worked that well on the upper floor levels. There are wireless-connected Fire TV sticks on the flat-screen in the basement and on the flat-screens of the first and second floors. There is another wireless connection of a blu-ray player in the basement. Finally, we have smart phones, a Kindle Voyage, a Kindle Fire tablet, a laptop, and an iPad. Everything seems to connect to the Internet without issue. I highly recommend the Orbi system.
We settled on the Orbi system because marketing diagrams showed its operation through floor levels and its effectiveness within 4000 to 5000 square feet. Videos showed an easy setup process and a browser interface for system administration. The technology appears to be proven with several competing home wireless network systems out there. Aside from Orbi, most of the other systems consist of routers and satellites dedicated to each floor level. Even Comcast is expected to deploy one soon for lease to its customers.

Number two, there is a definite scoop on the SE215 in what I would call the mid-mids (maybe leaking slightly into the mid-highs). In this range the SE215s loose some definition and feel a little thin. I noticed this before doing my comparison and it was proven out when I listened to the SE535s.

While these are noticeable traits and less than perfect, I don't think I'll ever feel bad about spending $100 for the SE215s. They have great isolation, great fit for me, and very enjoyable sound.

Honestly I didn't even use the wedges that come in this package, the foam isolate pads that came on with the headphone fit perfect for me. If you want more reviews of the headphones make sure to check their main page by searching for Shure SE215-CL.

title: Neewer DSLR Camera Backpack Review
text:
Today I'm going to talk about this DSLR camera backpack from Neewer.

So backpacks are one of those, “oh yeah” things. You need them, but you don’t really want them, and it’s important to make sure that they are good considering that they are holding all of your gear which is probably much more expensive and important. And on top of that, there are so many options out there, and I can tell you right now that this backpack is definitely worth you consideration. It is advertised as tear proof, and water proof, which really stood out to me. The bag I had before ripped within the first month that I had it. And this hasn’t ripped yet, and I am confident that it won’t rip in the future. As far as it being water proof, it comes with a flexible tarp that can be stretched around the bag to protect rain from entering the bag, which is handy if you need it. And this can be easily stored in a pouch when you aren’t using it. Now this bag is not meant to hold all of your gear (for those who own a lot of gear), and that is important to note. It is meant for the essentials that you need to have easily accessible to you while shooting on location. Taking a look around the bag, we can see so many compartments. There are two main ones which can house the largest gear like you camera, and a few lenses, as well as audio gear too. And then within those flaps are small places to store things like lens caps, and cables that you just want stashed away. And it also comes with little velcro pads that give you the ability to fully customize the interior of the bag to fit whatever gear you want. As far as carrying the bag goes, there is a top handle, and just one strap which definitely shows what this is meant for. This is for the photographer of filmmaker who is going out to snap a few pictures or clips. Definitely not for those who are going on massive shoots and need to bring a ton of gear. If you haven’t heard of Neewer, they are a company that specializes in creating professional filmmaking equipment with an affordable price tag. Definitely a reputable company.

title: Good, but not great scanner
text:
I purchased this hand held portable scanner to use while in my vehicle. This is a Radio Shack branded copy of the GRE PSR800/Whistler 1080.

1. It is not intuitive to program or use. The normal keypad is gone and has been replaced with a 4-way rocker switch controlled menu driven system. Don't get me wrong...initial set up is easy. Input your city/county/zip code and you're up & running. BUT...unless you dive in a little deeper you get EVERYTHING...including the trash collector. You can exclude labeled sub-systems like police or EMS or health department but it gets complicated. Search the internet for "Easier to Read Pro-668/PSR800 Digital Scanner" for much better documentation on programming the scanner.

2. BACK UP the included micro-SD card to your computer before you do anything.

3. Install the computer software that is located on the micro-SD card onto your computer. It is the best way to program the scanner for all of the custom functions you want. For instance, when my county fire dispatch channel makes a broadcast, I have the front panel LED light flash in red (or any other color you want!).

4. The provided rubber duckie antenna is absolute crap. First order of business is to replace it. In my vehicle, I attach a mobile antenna coax that goes to an outside antenna I have mounted on my truck bed toolbox.

5. Eats battery life quickly. Use the highest capacity NiMH AA batteries you can get your hands on (minimum 2700mAH) and when you install them, make sure you place the battery type switch in the correct position (NiMH). Takes FOREVER to fully charge the batteries, so I would suggest you keep two charging cords on hand - one in the house and one in your vehicle. It takes a standard USB cord, so you'll need one of those USB adapters that plugs into the cigarette lighter/auxiliary power port in your vehicle.

6. Front faceplate is plastic, which scratches VERY easily. Either leave the factory plastic film in place or purchase a universal kit for cellphones that you can cut to cover the main display at a minimum.

Overall, very pleased with the scanner. I would have provided 5-stars except for the poor antenna, battery life.

text:
The Cooler Master N400 is a great compact Mid Tower case.

Pros:
- Nice looking
- Compact yet will fit a full size PSU
- Full drive options; 2.5, 3.5, and 5.25
- Works with ATX, mATX up to 7-slot boards

Cons:
- The top lip makes it hard to screw in the top two/three motherboard screws.
- SOFT metal, be very careful when tightening screws!
- Paint chips off after inserting screws then unscrewing them

Warning, if using a full size ATX MoBo the motherboard sites recessed in a motherboard tray, it can make it difficult to plug in some side mounted SATA and side mounted USB 3.0 front case connector cables. I used an ASUS Z370-A and the USB 3.0 mounts off to the side on the motherboard, and the recessed motherboard mounting makes it so you have to bend the cables.

Over all:
With some challenges, it's a flexible and nice looking case, easy to build, and at a fair price for a mid size tower case.

I bought this sound bar upon moving to a new house where my much larger "separates" system would not fit in the great room. I own two full, high quality 5.1 systems in my home, so I am no stranger to what good systems sound like. I went to Best Buy with no price ceiling in mind, if the $1500 sound bar had the best sound I was going to buy it. I started with the Bose Cinemate ($1499), my buddy had recommended it highly, and ,while I do not love Bose historically, I was willing to give it a chance. It is hard to describe sound I always find, but the term that came to mind on the Bose was "tinny" it was really shrill sounding - the bass was weak and the sound just did not feel "full". I can honestly say I disliked it, I think there were probably $300 sound bars in the store that would have sounded better to my ear. The Sonos sound bar ($699, but no sub included - sub adds $699) sounded pretty darn good (particularly for music). It's music was clear, had the highs and lows and was pretty good. I did not get to tinker with their app, but it is supposed to be best in class. Then I arrived in the Magnolia section, one of the employees steered me toward the Def Tech W Studio, and played a demo. It was AMAZING, great sound (for a sound bar)! Truly a great piece of equipment, the sound is full and feels like you are at a concert (or a movie theater if you're watching Batman Dark Knight). It has been in my home for about a week, and absolutely have no regrets after dropping $1299 on it - great full sound, a high ceiling on volume - if you need to fill the house for a party, it will do it, huge impact for movies, and great sound for music. The engineers did a great job on this one. Oh, and it looks great too! I am shopping for a W9 as we speak to have a speaker for by the pool and around the rest of the house. Buy this sound bar, you'll thank me.

If you look at the CNET reviews, it gets 4 stars, but actually read the content and they highlight "This blows away our previous favorite, the Paradigm, for sound. I feel like they docked it a full star based on some early bugs in the app to control it. I wish the reviewers would give this thing some more credit so that Definitive Technology keeps making these magical sound machines for us! It is THE BEST sound bar in the market.

title: A cheaper Pioneer with few frills, but it nails the essentials.
text:
I've installed many Pioneer stereos in my cars over the years. (I'm a car nut and I have a whole fleet of vehicles.) I usually spend a bit more--around $80, give or take--and get a fancier model with a few more features. This time, the radio was destined for a car I only spent $350 to purchase, so I decided to go cheaper for its radio. At only $53, this Pioneer definitely fit the bill.

My top priority for any car stereo is a USB port--I rip all my CDs to mp3s, store them on a flash drive, and leave that plugged in 24/7 to play my music. I like Pioneer's file structure allowance; it recognizes 500 files and 15,000 files per storage device. This lets me carry 16gig of music, and I can easily search for any specific artist as I desire. Furthermore, the 13-character dot matrix text display always lets you know what's playing, and it is easy to read as it scrolls by (when necessary). In that regard, this stereo is every bit as good as the more expensive Pioneers I usually buy. This unit also uses the same equalizer and audio output configurations as the higher models, so the sound is also great. At the end of the day, this is what matters most--after all, it's why you buy a stereo in the first place.

A cheaper model has to be cheaper for a reason, and in this case it is easy to see where a few corners were cut: this unit lacks some of the fancy extras found on the premium models. For example, the small digital display above the left half of the line of text cannot be configured. On my higher models, I choose to have that area display the time, but that isn't an option here; instead, it will do its own thing and you better be okay with that. As another point, my higher models typically let me choose my own color scheme, but that option is missing as well. Quite frankly, these are minor issues... but since I'm used to them in my three other vehicles, I do tend to miss these features. If you put this stereo in your only car, I bet you'd get used to their absence quite quickly.

So this isn't the fanciest model out there. At this price point, you already knew that. But if you just want a quality stereo that has everything you need and an affordable price, you could do FAR worse than this unit. It's a solid value.

text:

Although I really like the device, I would not recommend it if you are planning on using it for a Linux based HTPC right now, Windows works great. I'm using one for HTPC chores and the other as an Ubuntu development machine.

The following issues are for Ubuntu only, but since the drivers are written by Intel for linux, I hold them responsible here. After putting on the latest Ubuntu 15.04, it still has the following issues. Screen tearing during video playback. After the OS upgrade, and bumping the ram reserved for video in the bios to 2GB, it's not as bad, but still present. This doesn't seem to be an issue in windows. Beyond this, when resuming from suspend, audio output is simply gone, and doesn't come back without a reboot, which only takes 10 seconds, but is still annoying. I'll be moving to Kodi on Windows soon.

Leaving at 4 stars, it is a great device, but I would only recommend it with Windows if you plan on using this as an HTPC device.

(Edited 2015-05-03)

----
2015-07-27 Update - About a month ago, I got an update that broke audio... after adjusting to use the dev/test repos for updates, the audio disconnect and recovery (audio would often die after recovering from sleep), seem to be gone. The tearing is also no longer as bad... Looking forward to seeing what 15.10, or other interim updates bring.

----
2015-10-23 - after upgrading to Ubuntu 15.10 and re-enabling most of the PPAs I was using, and re-installing Kodi, the video playback has no tearing, and doesn't seem to be locking up anymore. Bumping to 5 starts as a result.

----
2016-12-31 - Currently running Ubuntu 16.04, I had to enable a daily intel driver ppa that fixed the hdmi audio not working after suspend. Everything is working great, including 1080p HEVC (h.265) video, I have my other one hooked to a 4k screen running windows 10, and wouldn't recommend 4k at all with this box, it's too sluggish. Thinking of upgrading to whatever comes next at the high end and going to a 4K replacement to my big screen. This box has been a little champ. Seriously great all around since some of the 15.10 fixes.

My old MS BT mouse wouldn't work at all on our white table, but this one doesn't have an issue with the semi-gloss white surface. I don't really use the tilt functions on the mouse wheel or the Navigation button (the square button in the center), so can't give much feedback on those.

We tried pairing the new M535 to my wife's laptop and it wouldn't pair. Discovered in the process that she is still running Windows 8.1?! The older (just over 12 months old) M535 paired just fine with Windows 8.1, so something must have changed since these first came out. I had to try a couple times to get the new mouse to pair with my Windows 10 laptop, but once it is connected it doesn't lose connection. Connectivity issues are the only reason I can find to knock off any stars on this product.

Battery life seems decent. I might have changed the battery (it uses one AA) 3 times at most in the last year, but then, I do turn it off every time I am done using it.
