title: Fantastic Retro Style, but not always functional.
text:
Update: I've been using this half case for a while now and really love it. It really adds style and function (grip and protection) to the camera. The quality is top notch and feels like it will last a long time. Keep in mind the bushing is picky about the screw it will take. Make sure you are using a normal short mounting screw with a rounded top when using this case. Given the depth of the base, and I wouldn't want it thicker, I really don't think they could build a case to support larger mounting screws. Great buy!

I really like the half bottom. Also, I was pleased to find that it also came with a matching strap as well! I don't know if that was a mistake or if the product description is incomplete.

Pros:
Looks and feels great! The camera is a bit tough to grab and this allows me to grab it with a more comfortable grip. Also, the button down battery door brings me peace of mind and provides inceeased security and guards against the flimsy plastic door getting knocked off. That happened to my last Olympus micro 4/3 Camera, which had the door in the same location. I always had to put it back on the hinge whenever I changed the battery and memory card.

The half bottom also came with a matching leather strap with matching red stitching and accessory loops! Although I think the strap is a bit on the thin side for my taste, I like the loops and the way it mounts to the camera with a leather backing behind the attachment key ring. There are no instructions to help with attaching the strap, but I figured out that I had to remove the camera's triangle key rings and attach the strap with its own retro brass key ring. Picture included.

I will use the strap for a trial run, even though I purchased another wider cotton strap for this camera.

Cons:
So why only three stars? Well, the bushing on the bottom is very picky about what type of screw it will accept. It makes sense that it has to be shallow to make the case fit, but I am sure that there will be instances where this case may need to come off to accommodate some tripods, stabilizer, or monopod configurations.

For example: I have two quick adapters that have the similar size screws, but my MEFoto adapter's screw is a little shorter and more flat at the beginning of the threads and my Neewer screw begins with more of a tapper. At the bottom of the bushing, there is also a taper, so the Neewer one works but the shorter MEFoto hangs up and will not go in enough to secure the mount. There is more: the MEFoto screw not only gets stopped early, but it also gets stuck! The problem is that the beginning Flat edge of the screw easily jams itself into the tapered bottom of the bushing. To remove it, even after only lightly tightening it, I had to use plyers to hold the base of the bushing while I unscrewed and broke the screw free from where it had jammed. I guess since both quick adapters work with my tripods, I'll have to put the Neewer mount on this half bottom. Unfortunately, this is not ideal because this is my micro 4/3 canera that I purchased for its smaller size and the Neewer quick adapter is twice as large as the MEFoto adapter and so interfers more with the battery door. I cannot just switch screws either, because the Neewer screw has a d ring on the head that makes it too large for the MEFoto base.

To recap: the Neewer screw is a bit longer than the MEFoto, so the hang up has more to do with the taper than the size of the screw. Pictures included.

All in all, This is a good fit for me, but I'd only recommend it if you like the style and function of the half bottom enough to work around it's incompatible with some mounting screw and hardware.

title: Not for everyone
text:
I'm an audiophile. I researched for a months before I got my latest set of headphones. I'm the audio snob that devices like this are made for. I'm having a hard time seeing exactly who this is for, and I especially can't recommend it for most "gamers".

Pros:
-Hooks up quickly out of the box. Powers off a PC or PS4 USB port, and claims to run off a 5V "cell phone" type wall jack but I haven't tried that.
-Jacks include AUX (why are you getting this unit if you run AUX?), optical, and USB, all in/out.
-Nice big volume control knob on the front, with a lighted ring behind which dims or brightens to show volume level.
-Has a decent software suite, with plenty of options.
-Three programmable "profiles" that can be accessed with a button on the side of the unit. I could see this being very useful if you switch a lot of different types of audio, like games versus podcasts.

Cons:
-Requires a USB PC (or PS4) connection. I tried this unit hooked to my DVD player's USB slot, but got nothing. Maybe I could try the wall adapter solution, but that seems like a hassle so I'll leave it attached to my PC.
-No battery backup, so it's not portable.
-Expensive. List price at time of writing is $150USD, which requires some real justification.

So... who is this for? One use I can see is if you have (or want) a really good set of 5.1 or 7.1 Dolby Surround speakers, but you don't have a volume knob or 7.1-capable sound card on your computer. But almost any good motherboard for a modern gaming computer comes with an onboard sound card that is "good enough" for most anyone else. I run a set of Sennheiser HD 598 cans which "only" deliver standard left-right stereo, and although I'm eager for any improvement, I doubt I'm going to be able to tell a difference. My speaker setup is a puny set of Dolby 2.1 speakers, which is plenty for an apartment, but far too little to make full use of this unit. I just checked, and yes in fact my motherboard already does 7.1 audio onboard, I didn't even know since I haven't used it. The sound profiles and leveler will be nice, as I often listen to lower-quality audio off YouTube so it would be nice to have effects modes to eliminate the noise of podcast audio. But for a list price $150?

So maybe you have a gaming computer but you got a motherboard with stripped-down audio. Then this product should be right up your alley. But alternatives exist- even if you have to have 7.1 audio- starting at around $25 at time of writing, and for even cheaper if you just need 5.1 or standard left-right stereo. Even advanced features like the profiler can be easily replicated with a variety of free software options, although other- cheaper- competition have similar options.

This unit can also be hooked to a PS4, but honestly I'm not sure what you'd gain on a PS4. There's some really bad information out there due to Sony doing some heavy marketing of the "features" of PS4 audio. Suffice to say PS4's onboard audio can deliver some of the highest audio quality on the market, and any modern TV or monitor should all the onboard audio processing you really need. So you don't need this unit. Some users report success with Xbox One, but again, this isn't the right product for you.

Really, this unit is for PC users who are premium audiophiles. You probably built your own computer, and got one without any onboard audio because you don't trust a builtin unit. You're willing to pay top dollar, and you won't accept anything less than optical audio, because you want the most out of your Dolby Surround setup. You already know what "gain" is, and you can make serious use of hardware profile buttons to switch between vastly different types of audio. Anything short of this, and you're paying too much for hardware you don't need.

So this is a great amp. It functions as a DAC. It's a fully-featured 7.1-capable external sound card. But it's overkill for most "gamers", and really it's better in the hands of premium audiophiles who know how to extract the most from its features. I'll keep playing around with the BlasterX to see what I can extract from it, but honestly having gotten this unit as a review copy the part I'm most excited about right now is that I finally have a hardware volume knob that's visible in the dark, and headphone/mic jacks right alongside it. The amp will also be nice, for those times when audio (like YouTube) is excessively low. But in the era of good, low-impedance headphones, that's less of an issue than it used to be.

title: Junk; RAM slots failing within a month, total failure within two months
text:
I really wanted to like this board, I really did. The BIOS isn't bad and their tools for upgrading firmware are painless. However, my experiences with this board and MSI as a whole have been far less than ideal. I purchased this MB about two months ago, within the first month my PC started to freeze every so often for a few seconds without warning. At first, I thought it was an issue with my SSD so I purchased a new one and re-installed the OS on the brand new SSD. Needless to say, this did not resolve the issue and now my PC was only detecting half of my RAM I had installed. I tested both of my RAM modules and found them working without issue and the board was now failing to boot into the bios when both slots have RAM installed. It will, however, boot if only one slot has RAM installed. As of now, the freezing is happening more frequently than ever with one stick of RAM on the system.

This is the second time MSI has failed me and needless to say I will be avoiding them from now on; as an alternative, I would recommend going with a GIGABYTE brand who has never failed me in the past or an Asus board which is what I will be replacing this piece of junk with.

Still keeping my fingers crossed that factory warranty covers this so I can get a refund.

title: Beautiful image. Three practical issues.
text:
This is my 3rd Optoma projector in 10 years and my favorite so far. The image is super-bright and really crisp -- though I'm comparing it to a 720p projector, so I know I'm talking Clementines and Oranges here. Would I recommend it? Absolutely.

Three issues that cause problems for me - but are not problems with the projector itself.

First: The IR remote receiver lens is in the wrong place.
In my setup, I place the projector upside-down on a high shelf (with some spacers to level it). With my last Optomas, there were two receiver lenses: one on the top and one on the front. With those, even though the top lens was against the shelf, the front lens could capture the remote signal. With the HD142X, there is a "dummy" lens on the front (support told me they use the same case for a higher-end model) and the top lens is the only functional receiver lens. As a result, the remote won't work at all and I had to buy a short IR repeater to capture the signal from the front of the projector and relay it under the projector to the working receiver lens. Optoma advises using a ceiling mount, which would leave the lens unobstructed, but that's not my setup (or the setup of many others in forums complaining about the same thing).

Second: the minimum throw distance is too long for my screen.
After owning two different Optomas, I was lazy when ordering the HD142X. I didn't check the minimum throw distance! The problem here is not focus, but zoom. Yes, the projector can throw an image in focus at 10 feet, but the image is too big for my 106" screen. One would think the image would be too small, but in this case they overshot the zoom ratio and I have had to use the built-in digital zoom which means I'm not getting the maximum resolution and brightness for my setup (it's not a big difference, but it irks me to know that I made a mistake and that it's happening).

Third: the "signal power on" needs a strong signal to work
Because of the above remote issues, I enabled the "signal power on" to control powering the projector on and off while I waited for my IR repeater to arrive. The feature worked for a while but then stopped. I'm not sure why - but I think it has something to do with the fact that my HDMI cable is 30'. If I ever figure out the answer to this one, I'll update my post.

Conclusion: A bit quirky, but a solid performer at a competitive price. I'm looking forward to many nights of beautiful and immersive entertainment.

title: Great value and can be used for gaming with some effort
text: Bought this to replace my aging i7-860 cpu.  After reading several reviews and comparisons, I was a little hesitant to believe that this system being a new i-5 architecture would outrun my old i7, but it did.  I was able to install my gtx 760 into this system, but it fits very tight to the motherboard because the sata 3 cable connections on the motherboard  are in the way.  But with some effort, I barely got this card to fit.  The card is 10 inches long, and it also barely fit and had the narrowest margin of clearance to the hard drive enslosure., whew!  I also installed a 650 watt power supply which went in without a hitch.  There is a YouTube video of of someone putting an upgraded power supply in this exact system, so I knew it would be know problem.  I also added a ssd card that cloned easily and was no problem.  Having sata 3 and usb 3 is a awesome upgrade from older i7 860 system.  Remember if you decide to move all these dell components to your own full computer tower versus this mid tower, you still have the motherboard problem not designed for a long video card, but can be done with some effort.  Thats why for now, I am just going to use this mid tower, but I may later change it.  There is (4) sata 3 cables on the motherboard, I have one going to the dvd, one to the sata 3 drive and one to the sata3 ssd.  This info would of been of some help to me before buying and could not find it, so maybe this info helps you decide to try to use this system for gaming.

title: I love the fire tablets
text:
I love the fire tablets.
I preordered the Fire HD 8 -7th Generation tablet so I've had it since June 7th.

I had the Fire hd 8 - 6th generation tablet (black) and I loved it. I've attached photos comparing my new Fire hd 8 - 7th generation (yellow)

The first thing I noticed was the shape. The previous generation tablet had edges that were more rounded and the new 7th gen tablet definitely has a more pointed edges making it look more rectangular. I actually really like this feature.

The next thing I noticed was the weight. It weights slightly more but it's noticeable. I used my kitchen scale to compare their weight. The 6th gen tablet weighed in at 12.0oz exactly. The new 7th gen tablet weighed in at 12.9oz. A slight difference but you can definitely tell.

On the side of the new 7th gen tablet they added a microSD slot so you can expand your storage up to 256GB which is quite a bit of storage.

The new 7th gen tablet is actually slightly thinner, and the headphone jack and microphone hole were moved around a bit so sadly this tablet won't work in your previous 6th gen hd 8 case if you had one.

I noticed something about the display I don't think was mentioned in the description, the screen on the new 7th gen tablet is a bit different. It has more of a yellow tint than the previous 6th gen. I set the same screensaver on both tablets to show the comparison.

The camera on the new 7th gen tablet is a bit better than the old one. It looks better overall when taking pictures but it's not a huge improvement- the cameras have never been that great- unless you're in a very well lit area or outside in the sun.

Overall I love my new tablet and even though there are only a few new improvements. They're pretty great and I love the new expandable storage! So if you can do without these small new features then by all means- don't upgrade, but if you always find yourself running out of space, or you just want the next best thing.. then get the new Fire HD 8 - 7th generation tablet!

title: 600 Ohm. Horrible bass distortion even with quality amplifiers. Too much top end.
text:
I ordered the 600 ohm version, as I have several powerful headphone amplifiers, and wanted the sonic benefits of the higher impedance. However, either the headphones are simply distortion monsters, or defective, or none of my amps would drive them properly. I'm not convinced they are defective, because I think the odds of two bad drivers are slim, and the severe distortion was present in both channels.
I have a DarkVoice 336SE OTL tube amplifier, typically extremely well-suited for high-impedance cans, and it runs my Sennheiser HD650 300 Ohm headphones beautifully. But there was massive bass distortion at all but the lowest volume levels. I was listening to things like contemporary jazz and country ballads through a quality outboard DAC with no EQ. Every bass note sounded like blown woofers or massive amplifier clipping.
The Alex Cavalli CTH Tube Hybrid (Solid State and Tube gain stages) fared slightly better but was still bad. And, an XDuoo XD-05 fully solid-state amplifier couldn't do the trick, either.
Beyond the distortion, the upper treble was simply too prominent, like someone took the upper sliders on an EQ and cranked them up.
They get a second star for supreme comfort, looks, and apparent build quality.
Sending them back.

title: Read this first if interested in multiple speaker setup
text:
I continue to be very impressed with this speaker - so much so that I bought another one to pair with the first using the JBL Connect app.

The sound is great and I can attest to durability - one overnight rain storm and a drop from 5 feet later, the original speaker is still top notch.

My one caveat (and the reason for loss of one star) is that, while the setup and pairing for multiple speakers is straightforward, the operation in party/stereo mode is fairly clunky. Specifically, whenever you want adjust the volume in multi speaker mode, all but one speaker will go silent for 5-10 seconds. This is because In JBL'a pairing setup, on speaker serves as a "master" and the rest are "slaves" -- as a result, any change in volume results in a delay because the master unit has to recalibrate the signal it's sending to the slave units, and cuts volume until that recalibration is complete. I have verified this with JBL support.

Soooo.... if you're looking for sonos-like control over a multi speaker setup, look elsewhere. But if you're looking for an outdoor-friendly, multi-speaker setup and can abide the delay whenever you want to change the volume level, go for it. They are great BT speakers, esp. for the price.

title: Great Cameras for the Price - You Need To Work a Little for Best Results!
text:
This is the 4th one of these I have purchased and installed, and for general watchdog level security, I have found them to be excellent and reliable. There are a couple of things that I think you might need to know if you want to set up a "security system" based on these cameras from my experience.

1) Get a good 3rd party surveillance camera management software suite like "Blue Iris" to make this whole process much more painless. Blue Iris handles the recording and storage of video clips, sets schedules, motion alerts, and most of all, interfaces with their free app for mobile devices, which makes watching your house when you are away MUCH simpler. The Blue Iris software has a bit of a learning curve, but in my opinion, is priceless.

2) Make sure you use the browser interface built into the camera to set your video quality, frame rates, maximum exposure time, white balance, IR functions (use Smart IR) all properly. This camera requires a bit of tweaking of the settings to wring the best video quality out of the image. Be patient, and experiment until you get a combination that works for you. I know that you can make this camera work in almost any environment day or night, if you adjust the settings properly. I get best results using that interface in MS Internet Explorer.

3) Don't expect $1000 performance from a $150 camera. Yes, night vision is limited as with any "consumer grade" camera, but with "Smart IR" turned on and even a relatively dim (I use a 60W) incandescent bulb helping to light the area, night pictures are very clear even with motion for a considerable distance. Even without added light, I get a really reliable 35 feet or so.

4) If you opt for "Continuous Recording" rather than just motion triggered recording, set your software to store 2 or 3 frames per second at about 1/30 second max exposure, instead of trying to capture the standard "real" continuous video at 20 or 30 FPS. This way, you are actually storing a series of very closely spaced "still" pictures, which trap details like license plates and faces much better than a continuous stream, especially at night. You will use WAY less hard drive space, get much better and clearer results, and get way less ghosting at night. Experience shows me that 3 frames per second is plenty to capture motion. Believe me, you won't miss any action, and it will be much clearer to see. If, hopefully never, you have to give a recording to the police, they will get much more info from many fast paced "stills" than from a blurry continuous stream.

5) If you get the latest hardware edition TV-IP310PI camera, the reset button on the back is now soft rubber instead of hard plastic and requires a little pointed tool to push in instead of a fingertip, as it is now more flush with the back of the camera. BEWARE, if you push it even a little bit sideways, the button will stick IN because the edge of the rubber gets caught on the inside of the reset button hole AND KEEPS THE RESET FUNCTION ALWAYS "ON". Now your camera will still work, but lose its settings every time you reboot or lose power. It appears to be defective. All you have to do is get a tiny screwdriver and under a good light, "work" the button inside the hole straight again. Once it "pops" out again, everything will be back to normal. When you push it, keep it straight in and out, (which might be tough when you are balanced on a tall ladder!) and be sure you can hear the faint "click" of the internal reset button as you push the little rubber piece and let go again.

6) For the BEST results, run a dedicated PC as your DVR with the TrendNet 8 port PoE (like the TPE-TG80g ) switch with the huge power supply. It delivers gobs of available clean power that these cameras thrive on. Run individual Cat5e (minimum) cables from the switch to each camera. With 4 cameras recording a continuous stream of 2 or 3 FPS to an external 1Tb hard drive, I average about 20% CPU time on an Intel i7 processor PC with 16 Gb RAM, and Intel 4600 integrated graphics. So there is plenty of horsepower left over to view and edit clips, serve live video and alert clips out to my mobile devices on demand, and still allow for using the PC to download and install firmware updates, email tech support, and browse the web for other cool toys.

All-in-all I think these are excellent cameras for home security. With the right management software, some of the firmware limitations are inconsequential, and you can build a pretty good system.

text:
UPDATE: First the annoyance. The key cap for F10 keeps coming off. Often times when the cover is opened after the laptop has been in the Alienware sleeve and that is inside a double-padded Courier-style bag, the key will have popped up and need to be reset. I've taken Macro photos of both the key cap back and the keyboard switch where it seats and can see no damage or missing bits. But it is REALLY annoying and spoils the experience of having an otherwise excellent piece of luggable technology. After searching I see key caps on Alienware's products are a problem are a problem for others, but I imagine some of that is because it can be a great gaming machine. I don't know if buying a replacement key-cap will solve the issue. I actually comes loose while the cover is down, not just from pressing it. Indeed the keyboard gets little use as my setup is such that I use a separate Logitech USB keyboard and mouse. But I need to use F9 and F10 on the laptop keyboard to adjust brightness.

Original Review: Original rating still holds. I got this machine not for gaming but for remote on-location HD video production, editing, and rendering. Primary requirements were GPU and CPU performance and software compatibility. So far this machine has performed very well. I was concerned about and on the lookout for any issues with the display, critical in my work, that appeared in at least one review. I haven't yet seen any dead pixels. I needed a machine with an IPS display so that the screen could be viewed by more than one person, thus from oblique angles, with minimal darkening or color shift of the image. The display in the machine I received is excellent for my needs.

There was a mention in one of the reviews about unsatisfactory color on the display. After considerable testing that is most certainly NOT THE CASE with the display in my machine. The display is excellent and color accurate. Read on. . . Consistency and accuracy of color, brightness, tonality, and nuance are critical in my professional work. I use a professional colorimeter-based display calibration system (DataColor's SPYDER product [ASIN:B00UBSL3L6 Datacolor Spyder5ELITE - Designed for Professional Photographers (S5EL100)] to calibrate all my displays on all my systems to the same viewing standard regardless of the hardware. This is a hardware and software solution to calibrate monitors on different systems to a fixed setting (determined by user requirements) so that the images displayed are as identical as possible. The precision colorimeter sensor measures the color output and brightness of the display across the full spectrum of displayable colors. The display in my Alienware laptop matches the displays on my large workstation monitors in a side-by-side comparison.

I have run FurMark benchmarks on the machine, watching the CPU/GPU temp rise and then hearing the fans kick in. For a portable production system on a budget I think this will do the job. I'll update the review again if there are issues or Alienware/Dell steps up to this problem.

title: Toy or Tool?
text:
This is either a great little toy, or a cheap tool. Maybe both. If I needed a research-grade lab 'scope, I'd want something with a bit more native resolution, but I don't. Rather than try to make sense of the "power" magnification ratings, try this: at the lowest possible magnification (given the mount supplied, as in the manufacturer's pics), a penny fills the screen. At the highest, with the clear shield touching the subject, you can clearly see the individual ink droplets on a postage stamp; the field of view is just over one millimeter. Now, with the camera that close, you have two possible magnifications, the lower one has a FOV just over five mm.
For philatelists or numismatists, I would recommend some sort of extension for the gooseneck, in order to get the camera farther away from the subject; I couldn't get a whole stamp or any larger coin in the FOV. This shouldn't be too hard, at least in the US, the threads appear to be standard 1/4-20 so your local hardware store should be able to come up with something--maybe a couple barrel nuts and a stud?
I seem to have misplaced the penny picture, but the first is a US flag postage stamp at full magnification (the white area is part of the "R" in "FOREVER"), the next two are of a stainless-steel ruler's mm scale taken with the shield touching, both possible magnifications, and the last two are a rather dirty 45 rpm vinyl record at full magnification and lowest possible with the reflection of the LED lights showing. Ah, here I found the penny--again, lowest magnification. The preview looks elongated here on my screen, it doesn't in the actual pics, the penny is indeed round.
All in all, it would be hard to beat this microscope for bang-for-the-buck. Over the years I've cobbled together several 'scopes with photo capabilities, and probably spent more money doing so, but none have given this clear a picture or this wide a range of useable magnification. Anyone with schoolkids should definitely consider it.

title: Cheap, highly functional gaming-laptop with poor build quality
text:
After working with this computer for a few days, I'm left with heavily mixed feelings on it.

Primarily, the computer is a very suitable, relatively light gaming computer that runs perfectly well and is a great buy for the price. I am overall happy with its performance, but HIGHLY disappointed by the build quality.

On the other, you get what you pay for. As many reviewers below have listed, the plastic of the case is a fingerprint magnet. If I didn't know better, I'd almost say this computer was designed specifically to perfectly preserve every key stroke. permanently on the keyboard. The components also feel cheap and not up to snuff with other ASUS products. The maintenance cover on the bottom feels like its clips will start breaking after removing it more than once or twice; the optical drive tray feels like it's going to break off - when the tray is closed - when open, its own very slight weight starts levering it downwards away from its original horizontal plane.

My case came with a slight gap in above the USB-C port on the left hand side. I wish I had taken a picture of this before applying some downward pressure with my thumb to pop the case back in place, closing the gap.

The track pad is an oddly sensitive, flimsy piece of hardware, competing closely with the aforementioned optical drive tray for cheapest-feeling component. The bottom right corner of the pad actually dives about 3/16" into the the case when you use the right click button press. Additionally, the whole pad rattles a bit and oddly feels like it floats within the case and is a separate, unrelated component. The tablet style two finger functions are inconsistent at best, maddening at worst. If you're even a few degrees off of perfectly horizontal a two finger scroll can be confused with a pinch-zoom (even if your fingers are touching, oddly). In addition, the amount of pressure required to click via the track pad is highly variable, seemingly randomly and is always the opposite of what you're hoping to do. Buy yourself a mouse.

I can't speak to the quality of the AC wifi card due to not having an AC network to test it on, but it seems to be pretty stable and efficient so far.

As far as software goes, this came loaded with Windows 10, which this is not a review of. Of note, Windows 10's auto update, ASUS's auto update, and NVIDIA GeForce Experience did spend the first few hours of boot time re-upgrading the driver over each other before finally allowing the newest NVIDIA driver to go in. It also comes loaded with some extra bloatware, which you can remove. The overall quantity of bloatware is not too atrocious.

NOTE: If you want to add an M.2 drive, neither this laptop, nor most aftermarket drives ship with the necessary screw to secure the drive to the case. You will need to do some howework and look one up via Google or call ASUS customer service to find and purchase the correct screw.

EDIT: Lowering to two stars. Still not a one star piece of hardware, because it still runs very well, with the exception of being loaded with the cumbersome trash that is modern Windows. I was indeed correct and even after *very* delicately removing the maintenance panel for the second time, one of the clips that holds the panel in place (there are about 10, in addition to the "only two screws" advertised) has broken off and fallen into the 2.5" HDD bay. Finally, on only their second removal, I can feel the plastic threadings in the case beginning to strip slightly.

Additionally, after one week of travel to work and back in a laptop bag, the case is starting to show minor scuffs from rubbing against its own power supply (which is not even in the same pocket of the bag).

Finally, some sort of white fibrous material is beginning to squeeze out around the screen and its bezel. I can only assume this is some sort of flashing from an adhesive used that is slowly coming free.

title: Perfect size, great for plaster and lath walls
text:
Perfect size. I previously ordered a similar product on Amazon that was very large, and also didn't include the in-wall plug connection. This one is a similar size to a typical switch/outlet box and was easy to install.

Also, a tip for people with an older house with plaster and lath walls: DO NOT use a sawzall/reciprocating saw or drywall jab saw. The vibrations from those tools are likely to damage the "keys" of plaster that hold your walls together. Instead, use a multitool with a thin cutting blade--the tool will not shake or vibrate the wall nearly as much, and you will also be able to make much cleaner and more precise cuts.

title: Awesome little music player!
text:
I've had this music player for a few weeks and I really like it a lot. Unlike an iPod this AGPTEK is very inexpensive and oozes value:

- Small form-factor, similar to an iPod nano.
- Very lightweight which is great for travel.
- Sound quality is fantastic. I can't tell the difference between the AGPTEK's playback quality and the iPod's.
- Outstanding battery life. Some of the specs on Amazon say 50-70 hours of battery life and I believe it based on some of my own testing.
- Has played every media file I've thrown at it so far.
- Has a side-loadable uSD card slot supporting cards up to 128GB. If you have more than 128GB of music (wow!) then you can swap out cards in a snap.
- Can mount (connect) to your computer through a standard micro USB cable and read from/write to the uSD card just like any other USB drive.
- Has an FM radio built in which is nice when traveling abroad and curious about whats on the airwaves.
- Can make small voice note recordings using the tiny built in mic.
- Turned on/off with a simple toggle switch at the base of the device. No wondering if its really off.
- LCD is the ideal size, not too big to add dimensions to to the device and not too small that its hard to read what is playing, etc.
- Wide range of colors available. The blue one I got has a "soft-touch" coating which adds a non-slip property to the device.

There are a few areas where the product could be improved however since I do not think any of these detract from the overall usability (for me) it would be unreasonable to subtract a star over them:

- LCD screen is quite low-resolution and low frame rate. I just play music and it displays titles and album art and its perfect for that. You supposedly can play movies on the device but you'd really have to hate yourself to watch them on this 1in screen!
- Menu navigation together with control wheel layout is a bit odd and takes some getting used to at first. After a bit of use you get the hang of it and can get anywhere you want pretty quickly.
- The edge around the front face of the device would have been a bit more aesthetically and tactilely pleasing if it was a bit more rounded.

Overall this music player is great for traveling and for keeping your music collection within reach. I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this to anyone but especially I recommend this for the travelers out there!

title: Just Decent
text:
UPDATE: Although you would think this stand would be almost indestructible because of its aluminum alloy frame, the knobs on each side are just plastic. One day in the summer while trying to adjust the stand the plastic at the top of the joint snapped, taking the entire leg with it on one side. This made this stand completely useless. Considering the high cost of this stand I was furious that it lasted less than a year! As the warranty is for one year, I didn't bother contacting Furinno, especially since I don't want another of these stands. I used this stand daily for hours at a time and under normal conditions, so the knob snapping is just ridiculous. I switched back to a Cooler Master and am having much better results (review will be posted).

Original Review:
I was looking for an all-in-one type of laptop stand and this stand is adequate. I wanted a stand I could occasionally use on my lap while reclining in my bed, use while sitting at my desk and use in the living room as its own table. This stand manages to do two of these three functions amazingly well. In fact, this is probably the only stand I have found which works great in the bed. The width of the stand means it will fit over wide hips (like mine) and larger bellies without any problems. In the bed and when sitting at a desk, the three adjustable legs ensures I can always get the perfect elevation and angle on my computer without putting strain on my neck.

However, this stand is just not tall enough to be used as its own table. Although I have tried it with several different chairs in my home and when visiting others, its height as a table is just too low. Using it is a table requires looking down at my computer and leaning over it. this just puts too much strain on the eyes and lower back. Plus, in this position on a bare floor it was just too slippery and was unsteady even when locked into position.

The other feature I wanted in my stand was compactness. This stand, however, is too long and or wide to fit in my current laptop or luggage bag (yes a larger bag would hold it). However, it is very lightweight so it can be carried, even though this can be cumbersome. Of course, carrying it has also meant I have dropped it a few times and banged it into things. Thankfully, however, this has proven to be pretty resilient and durable. There is not a scratch on this stand and the fans still work great, even though it has gotten a little wet when carrying it in the rain. Wiping it off and waiting until it dried out before turning the fans back on has worked pretty well. The fans are also pretty quiet but considering the size of this stand, they could be larger. My 17-inch laptop fits perfectly and the stand seems to easily manage its weight, but it does shake some as I type which is distracting.

The stand is quite attractive and has gotten a number of compliments. I have the purple color which is really beautiful in person. The little levers that keep the computer from sliding off can be used in two positions. You can simply let your laptop rest against them or you can open these little levers. Once opened the laptop is basically wedged into the lever and wont slide off or down. I recommend using this feature if you plan on using your laptop on the bed while your laptop is over your head, in this position adjusting your body and bumping the stand could cause the laptop to tilt forward and hit you in the face if these levers aren’t open. However, even with these levers open your laptop could still tilt forward if the angle of the stand is to elevated. The levers are adjustable so they will move to fit different size laptops. I have dropped these little levers lots of times when moving this stand, so it would be great if the ends were closed so the stands could move but not slide all the way off.

The locking mechanism is different from any other laptop stands I have used, but once you try it out a few times it’s very easy to understand and adjust. It would be great if there was a hook on the back of the stand to help with keeping cords a little better organized and out of the way.

Overall, the issues I have with this stand are minor and it is the best laptop stand I have ever owned. The price is high, but if it lasts for a few years it will be worth it.

title: Not Recommended for Gamers - Input Lag Test Results
text: I purchased the SEK-3500U for my 2014 75" Samsung UN75HU8550 TV.  While there are positive things about this upgrade kit my review is going to focus on input lag which should be of significance to anyone who is using their TV for gaming.  Input lag is the delay between the display receiving a signal and actually displaying it on screen.  When you have high input lag you will notice a delay between button presses on a gamepad and some sort of action (firing, jumping, etc.) on the screen.  My test setup consisted of two different computers (one a laptop and one a desktop with secondary external monitor).  I also have a friend who has the same TV as me and I performed the testing on his TV as well to ensure the results were consistent.  I initially tested WITHOUT the SEK-3500U hooked up.  I tested with default settings (game mode off) then enabled game mode and retested.  I then hooked up the SEK-3500U and repeated both tests.  The results were disappointing (see my attached image).  With the SEK-3500U attached to my TV input lag increased by ~85ms.  Even with game mode enabled on the SEK-3500U my input lag was noticeably higher than my TV before with game mode disabled!  What does this mean?  If your primary use of the TV is for gaming stay away.  The lag is too high and noticeable.  If you use the TV for occassional gaming and primarily movies / 4K content then you should enable game mode when gaming and disable when viewing other content (a hassle but doable).  If you don't play games at all then the lag should not affect you.  After spending several hours testing the SEK-3500U I ended up returning it.  Even if it were free I would be reluctant to use it due to the input lag.  It's possible Samsung could release newer firmware to address the issue in the future.  If that happens I will retest and update my review.  Otherwise, i'll wait for the 2016 evolution kit and try again.

title: Be sure you know what MURS means before buying this
text:
Before buying this, make sure you understand that it's a MURS radio. This is not a CB. Nor is it the Family Radio Service radio you get in most stores even though it looks exactly like one, or the more commercial GMRS radio, or a Marine or Aircraft radio, or indeed a Ham radio. And it won't interoperate with any of those, only with MURS radios. MURS radios have their own channels, separate from all of those other sorts of radios.

MURS is the correct service to choose for unlicensed use in a business. FRS is also usable in a business. MURS has higher power (2 watts) than FRS (1/2 Watt) but FRS has a higher frequency that may work better inside of a building.

Here are what you use the others for:

* CB: was once for talking with people in your neighborhood, now you are at least as likely to find a raving nutcase as someone you'd want to talk with.
* FRS: family or group communications, business use permitted with no license.
* GMRS: licensed business or personal communications, $85 license.
* Maritime Radio Service: Talking with boats, services on the shore, and the Coast Guard.
* Aviation Radio Service: Talking with the control tower and between aircraft. Big consequences for using this if you don't belong on it, don't try it.
* Ham: talking with folks in your city or around the world, requires some studying and a test, the test is harder if you want international range. No more Morse code test!

title: Fantastic gamepad, with one super tiny and conditional flaw.
text:
nice resting position (because the pictures all show it more upright, understand that it does lay almost flat, watch a video of someone using it). Keys are easy to set up through the Logitech Gaming Software (LGS), with many presets already figured out for you, and easy setup of alternate layouts (for example, starcraft 2, it will list the "find worker hotkey" as "Select Idle Worker" instead of "F1"), which is helpful for when you find an action that you didn't know had a hotkey. And can be completely customized with any key or key combination you like, with programmable timing sequences, text blocks, and more being able to be assigned.

One drawback:
If you do go one brand for your peripherals, Logitech is the way to go. The only downside is this, and most people won't even notice it. I game on my laptop, while my wife games on the desktop. I use my laptop for work and school, but I only game at home while plugged in. I also happen to have the Logitech g700s, which is a fantastic mouse. Before I set up my g13, I had used the mouse both on and off my Lenovo one link dock. There's the option to have a button cycle through profile presets, which is kind of nice. Once I had setup the g13, this button no longer worked, since the g13 has the option to select among your profiles right there on the device screen. It's a nice feature, but unplugging from my dock, and taking the laptop and mouse elsewhere, that option to cycle profiles didn't come back. Only annoying if I happened to leave the profile on one of my games, when I have copy/pasta or my password database hotkey programmed to my g-keys (Logitech's name for the programmable buttons).

It's a small inconvenience that will probably only affect very few, but it is there. Everything else links and stitches together wonderfully well.

title: Definitely not worth your time or money
text:
This product is garbage. Do NOT waste your money.

I bought TP-Link 7020 when my girlfriend and I moved to a gigabit cable connection. Because the cable drop is in a different room, I wanted to run an Ethernet connection to my gaming PC in the other room. This thing seemed perfect for what I wanted.

I had problems immediately. I had no network connection, despite getting a solid green light on the powerline light on the side. I was getting 700MB straight from the router, and I tested all four cat6 cables. The problem was with the powerline adapters.

I downloaded their piece of crap utility to check on the connection, and voila - despite the LEDs indicating that the devices were paired, they couldn't communicate. I tried adding manually via the "password" on the devices and consistently got recurring errors. Finally, the two paired (despite the errors saying they did not). I moved the adapter to the other room and plugged in my PC...

And got 15MB download speed.

For those of you doing the math out there, that's a 98% bandwidth loss. What?!?!?!

I thought maybe the problem was my PC (despite having a gigabit LAN, but whatever, check every variable). Girlfriend's Windows 10 computer gets the same speeds...and then poof. No internet at all.

The two receivers lost connection. I tried another seven or eight times to connect them using the utility, but found no success. And why would I even waste my time? Even when "working," these dismal excuses for technology gave me slower download speeds than my own wireless BY TWENTY TIMES.

So yeah. Worthless. Look, I really wanted to love it. My alternative is literally stapling a 150 foot Ethernet cable to the ceiling. I took a chance on you guys, and you let me down really hard.

title: Buggy, poor UI design, original apps are worst than third party.
text:
I read a lot of reviews when researching baby cam options. I decided I wanted to buy an IP camera so there was some utility after a baby cam was not needed, as well as be able to check in while away from home. Foscam seemed to be best during my research compared to others such as Nest cam.

However, our experience has been wildly different than the reviews I read:

- Common theme "Set up is easy"
Couldn't be more false. Plug and play to me literally means, plug and play. The CD that came with the box does not support mac. So I had to dig around Foscam's website for a mac specific program. Of which, is a naive, pretty pointless app. All it does is open a web link. Trying to change settings on it does not work. You have to do everything through the web-based program. Which leads me to the next topic.

-Web based UI is poor. Having to download, and re-download, and re-re-download buggy plugins so it can work on Safari, and Safari only was just the first. Secondly, it does not control the camera well. Delayed responses, delayed picture, delayed everything. I downloaded a free 3rd party app which controlled the camera 10x better which leads me to the next point.

- Native Foscam iOS app is pointless. Doesn't do anything but maybe pan/tilt once and a while. No talk back controls work on it. "Zoom" function does not work on it. I used Owlr, and it has full controls compared to both the ios and web-based app.

- Connection issues. One day after setting up camera we get constant connection issues. I tinkered with settings (FPS, video quality, assigned IP, etc.) and no concrete fixes have been found. The camera is 30-40ft from router upstairs from router, of which all other devices have full signal.

I was looking for an easy, plug and play type camera, to set up as a baby cam. Although I am not an IT specialist, I am pretty familiar with computers and networks. This has not been "easy" by any means. UI can use a major overhaul, a real desktop app would be nice. I will try technical support for any miracle fixes, but if not it will be going back.

Setup was easy enough for the wife. She installed a 4TB hard drive and plugged it in to our home network. After that I took over remotely from 3,000 miles away by first with a remote login to a networked PC at home and using IE browser to login to my home router to get the IP address of the NVR. Then I used the NVR IP to login with the default username/password. After I was connected to the NVR I added our 3-1080p wifi cameras (updated the login info because it defaulted the password that was set by the oem.
I also update the internal and external HTTP/S ports (I didn't like the default ports).
Setup port forwarding in my Modem and then my router.

One note: I had to change the Audio that my cameras provided. After that I was able to hear.
Don't forget to change the default user name and password for your cameras and NVR.
Also the Android app is nearly plug and play. Enter the Serial number in the app and it will connect via P2P. ( I'm not sure I like the P2P method)

title: These are "the ones".
text:
I am a professional radio DJ and programmer. I got a pair of these back in the 90s and loved them for having a similar sound profile to JBL 4412 studio monitors, and for the closed back design with allows me to run them loud without feeding back into the mic.
I've heard the Sony MDR 7506 which is allegedly the same headphone... but I don't believe it. To my ears the MDR V6 has a smoother, crisper, fuller sound, while the 7506s have a midrange hump that makes them sound a touch "honky".

title: the sound of something
text:
There's a lot of confusion about USB and Digital Coax Audio cables, so maybe this will help:

USB and Digital Audio Coax cables aren't "digital" cables. They are analog cables. At one end, 0's and 1's are coded into electronic pulses which are decoded back into 0's and 1's at the DAC end, and the DAC synthesizes the audio. The pulses are either correctly encoded and decoded or they aren't. The concept of jitter as something that will make a difference in the quality of sound is swamp gas.

I think a Toslink (optical) cable is a true "digital" cable because it transmits pulses of light which obviously isn't related to the analog domain at all.

The quality of the DAC chip is of greater interest as far as sound quality is concerned, but many audiophiles believe the supporting analog components are even more important than the DAC chip itself.

I own this cable and it appears to be of good quality, but it doesn't sound "better" than a well designed less expensive cable. And I can't say it will last any longer, either. I own USB cables more expensive than the AQ, and they don't sound "better."

Perceived value is subjective, and if you just like expensive cables, I suppose this cable could be considered a bargain.

title: Best headphones I've owned
text:
"Yet another pair of headphones," I sighed when I first saw these. "Well, I guess I'll use them someday."

"Someday" turns out to be "now." These have quickly become my favorite pair of headphones, for several reasons.

First: As a professional video producer, I need good headphones. The ones I'd been using are very good -- but they're too bulky, take up too much room in my case, and the long cord on them doesn't stay de-tangled very easily. These new AKG headphones are now my go-to pair for using with my pro video camera. (See my photo #1). They store easily and you don't have to turn them on to use with a wired connection -- so I never have to worry about running out of battery charge.

Second: They charge easily (see photo #2). And so far, that charge is lasting a very long time. ("Up to 33 hours," claims the manufacturer. Hmmm. We'll see.)

Third: The bluetooth functionality works perfectly. These really can be paired with two devices at once (see photo #3). Very cool that you can use these with (for example) an iPhone and an iPod simultaneously, or a phone and an external speaker. You can play a song on one device and listen to it on the AKG headphones, then start another song on another device and the headphones automatically switch to that device.

Fourth: They work great as a wireless headset on phone calls. In fact, I was listening to music with them and got a phone call in the middle of the song. The AKG headphones automatically switched over the phone call. I heard the caller perfectly, and he heard me perfectly too.

How's the sound? Very good. Not powerhouse loud, even at full volume (really, would you want that anyway?) but certainly loud enough. Bass, treble, etc. -- all fine.

Finally, they're quite comfortable. So comfortable, in fact, that when I accidentally put them on backwards I didn't even notice. Did I mention they look great, too?

Five+ stars for these.

title: Excellent Premium Tab at a Premium Price.
text:
The Microsoft Surface Pro 2017 reminds me why I make jokes about Apple-only users. First, don't misunderstand as I was given an iPad as a gift and I love it in comparison to my Android Tablet. The iPad almost gave me reason to switch to Apple as I'm one of those Android people the Apple users laugh at.

The Surface Pro is a premium device, and comes with a premium price. That, and the extraordinary battery life are what reminds me of that other OS. Then I wondered, do people pay the premium for a better device?

I've wanted a device like this because I'm a Windows user (with all of it's good and bad points) and love the idea of being able to use it as a Windows hybrid of Tablet and Laptop. By the way, this loses one star out of the gate because every photo I've seen of this Pro "Laptop" does not come with the pictured keyboard. I don't quite understand that, but I'm cool with an on-screen keyboard and a very thin cover. In fact, the keyboard doesn't mean as much to me as it may many others, because I wanted a very thin, powerful laptop-like device that syncs with my PC and offers all the benefits of a Tab/PC minus a DVD - but this is mighty thin. It is slightly heavy, so using the built in kickstand comes in handy, even without including the Pen accessory, which is a hefty benjamin, Not including the removable keyboard cover that you might expect as it's marketed as a laptop, not so cool, especially for the high added expense. Who sells a laptop without a keyboard? My touchscreen laptop has a keyboard, just more cumbersome and find myself using it less and less.

I won't get into the specs that are listed, just my experience with it.

Setting it up was a breeze. It quickly unlocks after learning your facial recognition. *Occasionally it does not recognize me and I just use the screen pin lock instead, but it might be user error as I am not properly holding my head.*

The screen is beautiful. It's powerful like a mid-range laptop in the form of the convenient Tablet. And it's a large 12.3" Tablet screen. It's quick, and my number one issue with every device is always battery drain. I know this is a new battery, but it has lasted at least twelve or more hours at last count

As with smartphones which eventually morphed into phablets, this is the sweet spot between a small laptop and the average sized tablet. I've found my old huge phones and can't believe I ever thought a 2 and a half inch screen was huge! 5.5 inch screens are a minimum now, and I prefer my 6" phone. Sorry to get off track.

The bottom line: If you want the functionality of a Tablet AND laptop, you will have to purchase that keyboard. If, like me, where it gets used as a Tablet, it's fantastic. With Christmas around the corner, I may be getting the keyboard, but before I turn that gift down, I need to see it in real-world use as I do not want to add any bulkiness to this streamlined device. It's heavy enough for the size and if I want more bulk, I might as well switch back to my old 14" laptop. The Pen on the other hand, is going on my wish list.

Now that I finally have the chance to experience a great Windows device in the Tablet form I prefer, I do recommend it. Again, I call this a Tablet, not a laptop. It's convertible into a laptop. For the price, I think the keyboard should be included.

Devices like the Surface Pro appear to be the future. I just never thought I really needed one between the number of laptops from 14 - 17", the iPads, Kindles, Android tabs we have - but this fills that gap of premium power really nicely.

title: but it could have been so much better.
text:
Overall this case takes care of my needs, but it could have been so much better.

Pros:
5.25 bay support. I know they are becoming less and less common but I still like having one and it was a key point in my search for a new case.

Dual chamber design. Cable management is awesome; my temperatures are almost 10 degrees cooler than in my old case with the same equipment.

240mm radiator support. I don’t have one yet but I am excited about the possibility of adding one the case.

Cons:
3.5” drive cage is not removable. The cage that holds the hard drives in is riveted in place. This completely negates the large CPU opening. If you want to upgrade your CPU cooler at a later date and you need to install a back plate you’re going to have to pull you motherboard,

No rubber cable pass thru grommets. On Antec’s website site it shows no grommets, which is fine; but early photos of the case released on the web had them. It would be a nice feature to have.

Feel. The case feels cheap. The power and reset buttons are very light weight and feel flimsily when pressing them. The case is made out of a light gage metal. The front cover of the case is plastic that you pull off with brute force.

Dimensions. On Antec’s website the case it listed as 12.3” high. That is the height of the case without the feet on the bottom. The height of the case with the feet is 14 1/8”. This is important to know if you are putting the case in a cabinet or on a shelf.

Overall the case is nice but it does not seem worth the 70 dollars that is being charged for it. The non removable 3.5” drive cage is a big deal for me. I feel this is Antec taking the cheap way out. If I want to add water cooling I’m going to have to pull all my cards and cables and remove the motherboard to put a back plate in place. All of this could have been saved with a few screws instead of rivets. Rubber grommets would have been a nice touch and brought the case value closer to its retail price point

Powered on and in use the screen is almost flawless, no dead pixels, minimal IPS glow, even color. Overclocked to 100hz no problem, detected by my NVIDIA GPU without issue. GSYNC is excellent, 100hz is excellent and the slight curve is at best more immersive and at worse totally ignorable.

My example does have 2 minor flaws. All the way on the lower left side I seem to have a tiny spec of dust behind the glass, it isn't a dead or stuck pixel. I have to look for it on a completely white background to spot it so I deemed it so minor as to not worry about it. The other flaw is when there is a lot (90% or more) of light pixels (i.e. white) on the screen there is coil whine that comes from the bottom slight-right of the monitor. I have to move my head down and tilt my head to hear it, but it's there. I use headphones exclusively with my computer so it is a non-issue to me.
I also did have a stuck pixel in the same region as the dust but I tapped it and it went away. I've been keeping an eye out for the last week and haven't spotted it return.

All in all this monitor is fantastic. Excellent color, excellent refresh rates, g-sync and subdued physical design. It is my perfect monitor as it has everything I want, nothing I don't want and I don't have to compromise with odd scaling things like I would had I gone with 4k. Yes it is expensive but there are no other alternatives. If you can afford it it's excellent, if you can't wait for it to cheapen and roll down like it always does. 100hz IPS ultrawide with g-sync is absolutely excellent and I have zero regrets.

I used the Winegard LNA-200 amplifier with all of the antennas I tried. This antenna worked slightly better than the Winegard FV-30BB ($30), but not as well as the Xtreme Signal HDB91X ($40).

Pros: If signal strength is not a big issue for you, it has the advantage that it can be pointed in two directions at once. It has a sturdy build

Cons: While it has a sturdy build, it really catches the wind. Also, the two, round signal combiners in the middle of either side are not weather-tight. If you're struggling to get a distant signal, the HDB91X wins hands down. If you're trying to get weak signals from more than one direction, you could probably do better combining two or more DBB91Xs at a fraction of the cost of this unit.

title: Great action camera with a mulitude of features
text:
Just as a way of background, I have owned a previous version of this action cam, the Sony HDR-AS100V, for about a year. I was also an early adopter of the Contour Roam 2, and my son owns the GoPro Hero 4 Silver.

It is amazing how much the technology has developed for these actions cameras over the past several years. To say that this latest Sony camera is impressive is an understatement. Note that this camera is a different shape than the previous models and therefore may not fit all previous accessories. For example, it will not work with the waterproof case that came with my HDR-AS100V. I have uploaded a couple of photos that show both cameras side-by-side.

In this review I will cover the camera itself and a few accessories: the external remote screen, the finger grip, and the shooting grip. Here are the key things that I have found thus far:

Before turning it on for the first time find out where your location is in relation to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). It asks you for this when first setting it up rather than asking for your actual time zone. For me (US Eastern Time), it was -5. After that it will ask you for your local time, date, etc. You can select the format you prefer for this to display in.

If you are going to be shooting video in 4K, get the fastest micro SD card you can afford. According to the specs, a micro SDXC/SDHC UHS-I U3 card or higher is required for 4K 100Mbps recording. I am using the 64GB Sony brand and so far it has worked well. You can find it here: [[ASIN:B00X140GW4 Sony 64GB High Speed Class 10 UHS-1 Micro SDXC up to 95MB/s Memory Card (SR64UXA/TQ)]]

One noteworthy feature of this camera is that now you have a choice of three angles of view, “wide”, “medium” and “narrow.” Be aware though, that medium and narrow are not available in 4K, time-lapse capture, or high speed recording.

Most importantly, the picture quality is amazing. I generally keep it on the 4K setting when recording. I have a large 75” 4K television, so I want to make the most of the picture quality this video camera offers.

The image stabilization (IS) works very well. It does a really good job of keeping the image steady when walking, or even when running or riding a bike, and is a feature yet to be offered by GoPro. It definitely gives the resulting footage a much more professional look. Unlike some of its predecessors, the IS also works when shooting in 4K.

The battery has lasted me around 40 minutes when set to 4K and around three times that long when shooting in MP4. The sound the camera captures is also very good for a camera this size, and it has a built-in microphone port if you want to connect an external mic.

The live view remote screen works amazingly well. It will go blank about 10 seconds into shooting to save the battery, a feature that can be turned off if you prefer. It must be put in a cradle to charge, it does not have a direct charging connection. One thing cool about the remote screen is that when you turn the screen on and off, it also turns the camera on and off. It pretty much provides full menu navigation, the same as navigating off of the camcorder itself.

The Sony VCTSTG1 Shooting Grip [[ASIN:B01BY54HSA Sony VCTSTG1 Shooting Grip Shooting Grip Tripod, Black]] comes with an adapter to hold the live view remote screen, but for the one that works with this camera, the RM-LVR3, the adapter is not necessary. You can simply snap it directly into the holder on the handle of the grip. This holder also snaps off, so you can also attach it to a selfie stick or any other apparatus if you so choose. (see photo)

The Sony AKA-FGP1 Finger Grip [[ASIN:B01HD7EIVY Sony AKA-FGP1 Finger Grip for Action Cam]] is by far my favorite accessory for making use of the live view remote while keeping things compact. It almost turns it into a tiny “regular” camcorder. You can tilt the screen up and down to your liking, and it makes it really easy to maneuver and use the camera. (see photo)

I have been beyond impressed with this camera so far, as well as the various accessories that are available for it. If things change as I continue to use it, I will update this review.

I hope my experience has helped, and feel free to ask any questions you may have and I will do my best to answer them. Thanks for reading!

title: Surprised they sound as good as they do – Great Value - Here’s some tips - Grill solutions
text:
I installed these speakers yesterday. Use the metal clip that comes with the speakers to get the grills off – lift one side half way out then lift the opposite side of the grill and they come off easy. REAL EASY. To put the grills on – carefully line it up with the installed speaker and one side should go in very easy –but only go half way in or so. Take a sheetrock knife and with the razor blade GENTLY ‘pry’ in the grille and press in gently as you go around the edge – go slow and steady - put the grill in half way or so - when you get it completely in – press up on two sides of the speaker and the grill will easily go in flush. It didn’t take hours. The grill comes off in 30 seconds and it took less than a minute to get the grill back on. Use your head. Don’t put the grill in fully on one side thinking that’s the way to do it by trying to jam the opposite side in. It isn’t – you will only bend the grill. One of the worst things in the world to be is a GRILL BENDER. You do NOT want to bend the grill or have your neighbors calling you “GB”– so take your time and like I wrote – GO GENTLY. Use a sheet rock knife and use some logic or things most likely will get frustrating and you will screw it all up. Last thing, adjust the tweeter with one finger AFTER the grill is on.

Sound wise – for $37 - I was really surprised they actually were alright sounding - and now I understand the massive mark-up on speakers. These puppies hold their own. You will not be disappointed. Sound just fine cranked up and at lower volumes. The highs could be a little cleaner and the bass lower – but come on – for $37 bucks. They sound like you paid 3x - 4x that amount. So don’t be afraid to dip you toes in the water with these speakers – GREAT VALUE. They are much more than fine for most applications. I put them in my kitchen ceiling to rock out when I’m cooking and when I have guests over. Very happy with the purchase.

title: If you are thinking of using this as the center for your multi-zone system...
text:
Edit - 4/19/2015:
I received it back from the repair shop about a week ago. It took about 2½ weeks to get it back. The fellow doing the repair tested the unit extensively, and said that he was not having any issues using multiple zones. I don't know what got jiggled loose, but he decided to replace the HDMI board in the unit despite not finding any problems. One way or another, this repair has fixed 90% of the grievances I had with this receiver. I can now play different video sources with the respective audio in zone 1 and 2 simultaneously or individually. Zone 3 still requires a toslink optical or analog source, but this occasional reconfiguration is much less of a frustration since I'm not spending 20 minutes each day troubleshooting zone 1 and 2 issues. I have upped my rating from 2 to 3 stars. I would give it 4 stars just based on its features, but can only give 3 because it took 6 months of phone calls to Denon support to get a representative who recognized that the unit was not working correctly. By that time, I had lost half of my hair. I should bill them for Rogaine.

Edit - 2/15/2015:
It turns out my receiver has been malfunctioning all along, but the Denon tech support reps I spoke with didn't understand its features well enough to recognize that. Every time I called, they would tell me that it was working as designed no matter how incredulous I was. If I weren't also discussing the receiver on avsforum I may never have found out. After 5 months of calling them about it on a regular basis, I finally got escalated to a tier 2 support rep who apparently thinks that it should handle different sources to zone 1 and 2 without conflicts. With that information in hand, I am supposed to contact a local Denon authorized repair facility to get it fixed. I haven't contact a facility yet. I'll update this review with further information as this continues.

Original Review:
I would advise that you think again.

I have owned this since September 2014 and it is clear that I was greatly misunderstanding its limitations both before, and well after I purchased it. My intention was to use all 3 of its zones for my parents' home audio/video system, with a projector and 5.1 speakers on zone 1, a smart tv and 2 speakers on zone 2, and another pair of speakers on zone 3. It seemed to be a perfect fit. I was dead wrong.

At its best, the Denon will indeed run video and audio to all the speakers and screens, but with some serious limitations! Plugging a screen into zone 2 is just about pointless which I will go into details on later. If you want to be able to play an audio source on any zone you wish, it must be an analog audio source, making the plethora of HDMI inputs a bit of a joke. The smart phone app is pretty much indispensable as a tool for multi-zone management, yet for the first 2 months it would regularly fail to connect to the receiver, requiring 5-15 minutes of troubleshooting to resolve each time. That has improved recently, but the app still fails to connect occasionally.

1. Zone 2's HDMI out is basically useless.
Evidently if you were planning on having speakers and a screen on zone 2, you will need another receiver to go between the X4100W and the screen (unless you were planning on using the speakers on your television for zone 2 - in which case why are you looking at a $1500 multi-zone receiver?). When you are running audio and video into zone 2, if you don't have zone 1 turned on and set to the same source, zone 2 switches to "HDMI Pass-Through" mode, meaning that it no longer attempts to handle the audio for zone 2. Evidently the expectation is that if you are using zone 2's HDMI output, you want to use the TV speakers instead of the big, expensive speakers you have plugged into your big, expensive A/V receiver. Never mind that the main purpose of having an a/v receiver in the first place is to deliver an outstanding showing of the audio portion of A/V.

2. ARC: Zone 1 only.
In case you were planning on hooking up a smart TV to zone 2, the only HDMI out that has ARC is on zone 1, so you won't be getting any audio back from the TV in zone 2. If you were planning to use any of those smart TV features, you'll need to run some more wires back from the TV to the receiver to hear them.

3. Zone 2 is mono or stereo 2.0. Zone 3 is mono or stereo 2.0. Don't expect anything else.
I originally thought I was going to hook my second subwoofer up to the second subwoofer port and put it in the zone 2 room. Perhaps that was stupid of me. Probably was. Either way, don't make the same mistake. You'll have to hook your sub up to the speaker wires if you want a sub in zone 2.

4. If you want to play audio in all 3 zones, you are pretty much limited to analog sources.
The system has specific limitation on each of its 3 zones. Zone 1 can handle anything. Zone 2 doesn't like toslink. Zone 3 doesn't like anything but toslink or analog. If you are trying to decide "hey, what audio out should I use from my computer?" The answer is analog... unless you want 3+ channels, in which case you want to use HDMI, unless you want to be able to play it on zone 3 in which case you want toslink, unless you want to be able to play it in zone 2 in which case you want analog, unless you want to use the receiver's DA converters in which case you want HDMI again ... and round and round. In other words you basically need 3 audio connections from your computer to the receiver just to be sure you can play your junk on all 3 zones. You need a freaking PhD in home theater setup just to figure out how to configure it, and configure it you will! Every time you switch rooms, you're in for a good 5 minutes of turning screens on, flipping through menus in the smart phone app, swapping audio outs on the computer, power cycling the receiver, and on and on.

I have been fighting this thing for months now. By now I am very familiar with its limitations and quirks, and I know what to do when something isn't working, but I actually built this system for my parents! I know what you are thinking - but they are not the typical kind of parents who struggle with technology or can't figure out how to use a smart phone. They both have nice smart phones, and nice brains, yet trying to explain how to get the receiver configured to watch a movie in the theater involves a convoluted list of what-ifs and how-to's that aren't as simple as swapping a few settings. Sometimes all the settings are correct, but it still won't work unless you power cycle zone 2, or zone 1, or the whole darn thing just to get it to work. The process of determining what is wrong is fairly difficult too, since the one symptom is pretty much always the same: no sound. No sound? Try A. If that wasn't it, check B, if that wasn't it, try C - Q until the sound comes on. This process occurs several times per day.

Sometimes I walk in to find Mom watching TV on her little 24" monitor on her computer with crappy sound coming from the tiny built-in speakers. Her computer screen is literally right next to the $1800 65" smart TV we have hooked up to the expensive Denon receiver and a far better computer, with far better speakers. Why? Because she doesn't feel like trying to figure out how to get the receiver to do what it's supposed to do.

I was very happy to find this receiver when I was looking for a way to handle the installation for my parents' new home which has a theater, a living room TV, and then some speakers in other areas. It seemed to be the perfect solution for a central device to power all the speakers with clean, powerful sound, and get the necessary video to the two screens. 5.1 on zone 1, stereo on zones 2 and 3. It seemed perfect. Sadly, it just can't handle the job. If someone is using the theater, the screen in the living room is stuck with no audio. If someone is watching something in the living room, the theater can watch along, but that's it. I'm stuck with using basic stereo analog out from the computer 95% of the time, which leaves the subwoofers in the system sitting pointlessly dormant. This last bit is probably another bug in a long list of bugs, but there is nothing I can do about it except cross my fingers that another firmware update will come along and fix it.

At the end of the day I've got a receiver that does about 80% of what I thought it would do based on my reading of all the promotional materials. The last 20% is some pretty important stuff, though. Don't think of this as a multi-zone receiver. It's a nice 7/9.2 Dolby Atmos receiver with some underdeveloped multi-zone gimmicks that just don't pan out.

title: Finally an affordable external monitor for a Macbook Pro Retina; requires "Mini DisplayPort to DisplayPort" cable
text:
I used to use my (non-retina) 27" iMac as a large monitor for my Macbook but stopped after getting a Macbook Pro with Retina. Text on non-retina monitors now look too jaggy to me.

I would love to upgrade my iMac to a 5K iMac, but 1) it's expensive AF, and 2) current models do NOT support Target Display mode, so it can't be used as an external monitor.

So, I was happy when this 4K Samsung monitor dropped below $500. It works well with my Late 2013 MBPR 15" and Yosemite 10.10.3 but note you'll need a "Mini DisplayPort to DisplayPort" cable like http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00C7RJQPY. HDMI does work, but it only goes to 30Hz, not 60Hz. Warning: this cable is surprisingly hard to find. Don't be fooled by the Apple Store "Mini DisplayPort to HDTV adapter" , it is just an expensive HDMI cable.

There are no speakers, and angle view is kinda washed out. I use it at 3008 x 1692, text is a bit small but it's a lot of screen space.

Tip: run this command in OSX Terminal to verify the resolution you're getting:
$ system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType | grep Resolution
Resolution: 2880 x 1800 Retina
Resolution: 3008 x 1692 @ 60 Hz

title: Works Even Better Than I Thought It Would!!!
text:
I was hours away from going into the crawl space of my house, built in 1938. I sat down to make a list of all the things I'd need to expand ethernet access throughout my home. Cat 5e cable, old construction boxes, face plates, punch down tools, cat 5 cable endings, etc. Luckily, I came across an article describing 3 methods of extending ethernet access: running wires to new access points, using wireless repeaters that pick up wireless signals and rebroadcast them to boost the strength to low signal areas, and finally plug in adapters that send a signal through the electrical system of your house - effectively turning the electrical system into ethernet cables.

I had some difficulty setting the Powerline system up initially, but it was ALL USER ERROR. Initially, plugged the unit that creates the Powerline signal into the WAN port on my modem, instead of a LAN port. The result was that the units that were downline mirrored my wireless router name and password, but they didn't have an internet signal. Swapping the ethernet cord to a LAN port solved the problem. Other than that, setup was simple.

I've got 50MB/50MB download/upload speeds through Verizon FIOS, and my home speeds via the FIOS gateway regularly exceed that threshold, generally returning mid fifties on both download and upload. I tested the two wireless access points after setup, one returned 52/55, the other returned 55/67. In short, they are providing the exact same internet speeds via my home's electrical system that I get directly from the FIOS modem/router. I must add an asterisk here though ***my home has both older wiring and newer wiring throughout. Half my plugs are 2-strand wire (no ground), and the other half are 3-strand (with a ground wire). All three of my Powerline Adapters are plugged into new wiring that has been run in the house.***

Pros
