2) Auto time and date feature - Frankly it was unimaginably good at what I said it would do. I live in Florida and the signals for Auto time and date are often week or worse (wrong). This clock set itself completely accurately before i could even look at the screen after plugging it in. Amazing . . 3) Charging - One of those features I didn't know I needed, but this helps eliminate an electronic device from my house by combining which is generally a good idea.
4) Night Light - cool feature, I doubt it will get much use, but I thought it was a good brightness

Cons

Did not test the radio or the aux in, I'm sure they are probably marginally better speakers in the clock than your phone speakers, but eh to me.

Anyway, I highly recommend this clock, I hope that its longevity is as long as its feature list.

title: Worth the wait!
text:
The sound from this is 5 star!

Only ticking off a star because I ran into some quality control issues.

The motor on the first RP6 that was shipped to me wasn't fully mounted and was hanging off the bottom with a 1/4" gap between the motor casing and the plinth. This probably could've been easily fixed by tightening up some screws but with a turntable at this price I decided that it was worth returning for a replacement. Longest two weeks of my life.

The replacement arrived and this time there was an issue with the wiring. I went to attach my cartridge and noticed that the tonearm leads/wires were extremely thin. Like the thickness of 3-4 strands of hair. So thin that I was afraid they would break when trying to mount my cartridge. I didn't remember the leads on the first RP6 being so thin so I looked at photos online and these were definitely not stock tonearm wires.

By this points I was getting extremely frustrated and almost said screw it and changing my purchase to a Clearaudio Concept turntable. The distributor put me directly in contact with Rega who seemed a bit embarrassed and assured me quality control issues are rare and twice in a row was unheard of. I sent them photos of the tonearm leads and it was agreed that it was not the correct wiring.

Another return and another waiting period for the 3rd replacement to arrive. My patience was wearing thin at this point. Thankfully 3rd and final replacement showed up in perfect condition and WOW. It sounded great.

When I purchased the RP6 I didn't have the budget for the RP6 / Exact 2 cartridge combo so I was using it with an Ortofon 2M Red. It sounded good to my ears at the time but after I finally upgraded to the Exact 2 cartridge I about lost it. It sounded like my entire stereo system got an upgrade. The RP6 / Exact 2 combo is a match made in heaven and I wouldn't waste time trying to find a better paired cartridge for the RP6. Rega really took the guesswork of pairing out of the equation with this combo.

In the end, was it worth the hassle? Yes. I can see myself having this turntable for the rest of my life so the month or so of waiting on a working replacement was worth it in my opinion. And the chances you will run into a situation like mine are slim to none. The whole experience was a testament to Rega's exceptional customer care.

Pairs perfectly with the MM phono stages inside Rega's amplifiers.

title: Amazing connectivity and as good as a direct connection
text:
**Original Review**
Below please find my thoughts on this product!

OVERALL IMPRESSION
Excellent product. I can game online, stream HD video, and browse the web without any lag and without an unsightly cord going from my downstairs router to my upstairs PC.

SETUP
Extremely easy. Just plug in one unit and connect the ethernet cable to the router. Hit the "pair" button. Then plug in the second unit and connect the ethernet wire to the PC (or whatever device). Hit the "pair" button and they are connected. You have 2 minutes to hit "pair" on both units.

OUTLETS
This DOES NOT block the second electrical outlet, and you can plug the unit in either facing downward or upward (as in the stock photo above).

DOWNLOAD AND UPLOAD SPEED
I ran lots of speedtests across multiple different electrical outlets.

I have a 60 mbps / 5 mbps internet connection.
Average speed: 50 mbps / 5 mbps
Lowest speed: 25 mbps / 5 mbps
Highest speed: 66 mbps / 6 mbps

Why the variability? I think EVERYTHING matters with these units. The electrical outlet you use, whether or not you use the other outlet, the ethernet cables you use, EVERYTHING! Even your network adapter settings can cause changes in your speed. So be very sure that you run multiple tests and check multiple outlets to find the best connection speed.

LATENCY
Just as good as a hardwired connection. My average latency is < 50 ms, and the lowest I have seen is around 13 ms (but again, it's the same as using a hard wired connection, which is pretty fantastic).

ONLINE GAMING
I play online games (StarCraft 2 mainly, yes I know it's an old game but I love it) and it has been incredible so far. NO lag, NO stutter, NO buffering. Just a flawless experience so far.

OVERALL INTERNET EXPERIENCE
Amazing. Web pages load instantly and videos do not buffer (at least on YouTube, I have not tried other video yet such as Netflix). I can click on a YouTube video and it starts playing instantly. I can then click anywhere in the timeline of that video, and it plays instantly. There are literally no delays.

FINAL THOUGHTS
Overall, I'm extremely pleased with these units. My internet is silky smooth: I can play games, I can watch HD videos, I can browse the web, and it all works flawlessly. Setup was a breeze and truly plug-n-play.

The only reason I am deducting 1 star (and I may change this later) is that the raw download speed is not quite as fast as a hard wired ethernet connection. On average, I receive about 50 mbps download speed, but with a hard wired connection I can max out at 70 mbps. Granted, the units went up to 66 mbps once, but I do feel that a 1000 mbps network adapter should be able to reach speeds of 70 mbps. I am not sure why I only get 50 mbps instead of 65-70 mbps on average. My hypothesis is that these units are subject to electrical interference because if I plug the powerline adapter into an outlet away from my PC (in an isolated outlet) the speeds go up a bit. That's when I saw the 66 mbps result. But as soon as I plugged my PC into a nearby outlet, I'm back to 50 mbps average speed.

But in the grand scheme of things, it does not matter. These units are plenty fast for me. I just *wish* I could snag my full speed because it's an obsession with me. I may update to better ethernet cables and see if that changes anything (more shielding may help). But for now, I am very impressed with these units.

If you have any questions or comments, please let them below!

**UPDATE 6/25/17**
I have figured out a way to gain about 16 mbps download speed (on average).

I have two power outlets near my PC. I just had the power strip (containing all my PC electrical connections) and the adapter switch places. That's the only change I made.

Download speed before switch: 50 mbps average
Download speed after switch: 66 mbps average
Direct connection: 71 mbps (max speed / average)

So now I am getting about 93% of the speeds of a direct connection.

I even found that I can get a bit more speed if the TP link adapter is facing downward versus upward (I have it plugged into the top socket but facing downward).

Funny thing is that my download speeds can be horrendous if I put the TP link adapter in the bottom socket versus the top socket. Like, 3-4 mbps average horrendous, but that's if the power strip is also plugged into the bottom socket in a nearby outlet.

Bottom line is this: These things work great but are EXTREMELY SENSITIVE. You have to be willing to tinker with your connections to get the best speeds. I recommend conducting numerous speed tests on several consistent servers to see what effect your changes have.

**UPDATE #2 - 6/25/17**
Well, my increase in speeds was short-lived. Turns out, when I was plugged into that particular electrical outlet, the speeds took a turn for the worst. I was suddenly at 3 mbps average.

On a whim, I decided to try plugging the TP Link adapter into a standalone outlet even further away from my computer. This outlet had nothing close to it on the left or right (1 outlet is vacant to each side of it). And low and behold, I started achieving perfect speeds of 71 mbps download and 6 mbps upload (which is my maximum speed when directly connected on my 60/5 internet connection).

I was very pleased, but skeptical. So I did repeated speedtests, and the speed has consistently been near 70 mbps every time over the course of the entire day. I kept doing lots of different tests and my connection is rock solid with top speeds now. So the stability has always been rock solid, but I am FINALLY getting the same speeds as a direct connection, CONSISTENTLY. Whew!

Turns out, in case anyone is interested, other outlets further away from my computer also gave me top speeds. I truly think the problem is electrical interference -- you have to find an unused outlet far away from any other electrical sources. Luckily, I have plenty of outlets in my computer room, and I had a spare 75' ethernet cable (Cat 6) that I just finished running along the wall.

This will be my last update, unless something changes. But for now I will stand by my 4-star review. This thing performs incredibly well, but the fact that it is so finicky and does not handle electrical interference very well is a clear deduction of 1 star. I bought this so that I could avoid running cables across the house, and it has prevented that from happening. But I still had to end up running a cable along a wall and around a door frame so that it would not be laying on the floor. It was an easy job, and the wife will be pleased that I did not have to run cables across the whole house, but it would have been nice to have simply plugged it into any electrical outlet and had it work perfectly.

title: Less Sensitive, Decent Sound, Good Quality, and a Steal!
text:
It's hard to review discontinuing items that are being offered at a heavily discounted price, but I try to be fair here. I was always curious about the driver design of KEF, so when I saw the new price of Q100 I jumped on it. I thought if I don't like them, I return them or give them away as a gift. My current main speakers are Paradigm Signature S1 with Beryllium tweeters working in a 2.2 setup with two Martin Logan Dynamo 700s subs. In my other room I have a 2.1 setup with Paradigm Millenia 1 and Seismic 110 subwoofer. Over the years I've audition numerous speakers ranging from $100 to $15,000, and here are my takes on KEF Q100 based on their half retail price:

First impression, I wasn’t impressed with the sound, and I thought it was thin and less bright than my Paradigms. I was doing A/B with Millenia 1 plus Seismic 110 sub, and the amp was Marantz CR-611 with cut-off frequency set to100Hz for Paradigm. Paradigm shined in almost all music that I tried including CDs and iTunes. The best way I can describe the KEFs is that their tweeters are laidback and not as clear as Paradigm. The KEFs' sound has very good mids and lows (for their size), but their highs are not as impressive. Even so, I thought they sounded better than a pair of Paradigm Monitor v7 I had a couple of years ago. Lastly, KEF Q100 seems to be less sensitive than Paradigm. It requires more wattage from the amp to produce the same volume.

Overall, I think these are decent speakers and for the current price, they are truly a “steal” as in nothing comes even close. I like the front facing ports and the versatile positioning that they offer. The cabinet finish is good, and the back connectors are of high quality. The only problem seems to be that a matching stand will cost me almost twice as the speakers themselves! I like KEF soundstage, but I probably go for LS50 if I am getting the expensive stands.

title: 5 stars based on occasional use over 4 years
text:
Amazingly quiet, and while I had to use a dolly to move the box, once unpacked I was able to lift it with one hand. The handle makes the difference. Waiting for my magnetic dipstick to arrive, and then I will run it for longer than 5 min. Started on the second pull.

Instructions have pages of safety stuff, but very little useful information. Examples: Tells you to remove the access panel, but not a clue what that is or how to remove it. I figured it was the side opposite the starter, and that the 3 Phillips screws would be enough. When the panel wouldn't come off, I started to reach for a wrench to remove the hex bolt at the bottom, but then gave the panel a yank, and it came off. Good thing I left that bolt in place! It would have been easy to say this in the instruction book.

(Having to remove that panel with a screwdriver to check the oil level is a design error.)

[Gas cap has a on/off switch for a vent, but no information about which position it should be in and when. Readers: If you know the answer to this, please comment.] see updates below

Anyway, these are one-time problems, and I got past them. Hence the 5 stars. After I actually use the thing, I may revise. But it sure looks and acts like a honey of a generator!

UPDATE: From a Honda generator instruction manual:

"The vent lever must be in the ON position for the engine to run.

"When the engine is not in use, leave the vent lever in the OFF position
to reduce the possibility of fuel leakage. Allow the engine to cool well
before turning the vent lever to the OFF position."

(ON/OFF are confusing labels. Better would be OPEN and CLOSED.)

2nd UPDATE: I did find information about the vacuum relief valve in the manual. Didn't see it the first time.

3rd UPDATE after 4 years of very occasional use: Wouldn't start after sitting for about a year. Instruction book suggested dumping old fuel and adding fresh. That worked! So I withdraw my negative comment about the Instructions. This is really a fine little generator.

4th UPDATE: Again it wouldn't start. Dumped the fuel and replaced by what was in the gas can when I posted the 3rd UPDATE. No joy. Put that gas in my truck, got fresh gas in the can, dumped the fuel in the generator, put in fresh gas... and it started. Lesson: The fuel has to be FRESH! Not sitting around for 6+ months in the gas can.

title: Great if it wasn't buggy and freezing up -- lost data is a no go
text:
I've tried basically ALL the smart/sport watches/devices. I liked this one best, but there are some fatal flaws that I'll quickly state.
1) Freezes up every now and then with a notification and vibrates continuously unless you reset it. If it's at night, it will vibrate ALL NIGHT and until the battery is dead. And this is with the latest firmware 3.10...
2) After resetting, I lost all data unique to the Fenix 3 (settings, VO2 Max from runs, waypoints)
3) Waypoints don't appear to be backing up on Basecamp like they should
4) Altitude and barometer on my Casio work better.
5) The storm alert goes off in broad daylight, clear skies and no drop in barometric pressure
6) VERY IMPORTANT: The Garmin Connect Server connection stopped working and I lost data. Without the server/app working you basically have a $600 dumb watch. This is an issue with Fenix 3 and other Garmin devices using their app.

I'd love to wait, because it is the best looking (albeit HUGE) smart/sport watch that supports iOS and Android, but at $600 it has to work. I don't have time or money to Beta test Garmins products. If they iron out the bugs, I'd consider this sport watch, but for now I'm returning mine to the store. This was the worst Garmin experience I've had. My old Forerunner 305 was flawless.

One of my favorite things was the LCD screen that allows the battery to last much longer than all but Pebble. Color even cooler, though under utilized and no real apps to use yet. The sport features made me think, "This will be THE ONE." So it's too bad it's riddled with bugs.

Good luck fixing this up Garmin. I need technology that works though.

title: G-Sync is awesome and I'm glad I shelled out the extra money ...
text:
G-Sync is awesome and I'm glad I shelled out the extra money for it. That being said, this monitor is stupidly expensive considering what's actually going on - they took their already expensive BenQ xl panel and stuck an additional nvidia chip inside of it, making one of the chips completely redundant, so we're stuck paying extra for features we will never use. There's no sanity to this, and nothing to gain from the "hybrid experience." If you want to switch between the two, you'll actually have to use a completely different cable, and the manual warns not to have both plugged in at the same time. I was worried this would lead to some annoying cable switching and that G-Sync would be buggy in certain contexts. But none of that ended up being the case - I just keep this permanently on the G-Sync setting and everything's been great so far, there's no need to use the BenQ classic mode.

Ultimately though, this the cheapest gsync monitor available and the only one in 24 inches, and luckily it's BenQ and not ASUS so it actually looks pretty good and doesn't give you headaches. My experience with this monitor after a few days is that games look amazingly smooth, and the blacks are nice and deep for a TN panel. I was blown away at how smooth and responsive Battlefield and FarCry run now, even compared to running it on the ASUS VG panel at 144 hz (which I bought first and returned). Obviously, not every game is going to take advantage of G-Sync and there may be some titles that have problems - but I ran quite a few steam games new and old and they all ran just fine. So - don't expect this to breathe new life into Civ 5 or anything, but also there's no worries about glitches either.

GSync is more than just smooth fps, it means you can safely run your graphics card at much lower framerates without worrying about screen tearing. So if you are used to running games at 120+hz because you hate vsync and screen tearing, you will now be able to get a much better experience even at 60hz, meaning you are free to pump up the quality/resolution of your games.

I should take off a star for the silly / pricey design as well as a minor annoyance - powering this monitor on or off is surprisingly unintuitive. I had to watch a youtube video on how to do it because I couldn't figure it out. (You have to cup the corner with your hand and leave it there a while). I actually thought it was broken at first.... but I'm going to stick with 5 stars anyway because of how freaking cool it is.

title: This is a high quality monitor for a good price, and I'm very happy with it
text:
No edge light bleed, no dead pixels. Of course, that's what you should absolutely expect when you drop this much on a monitor. This is a high quality monitor for a good price, and I'm very happy with it. Turned factory brightness down a bit and turned off deep sleep, that's the only adjustment it needed. Color temperature from the factory is cold, probably too cold for most people. Easy fix.

Performance: I paired this with a GTX1070, and most titles can run 2K on high quality settings at decent frame rates making the monitor refresh rate a solid investment. DOOM (100-120fps) GTA5 (80-140FPS) Overwatch (100-120fps). Battlefield 4 (100-144fps)

GSync: You won't know what you're missing until you actually see your games running with GSync enabled. It's a great technology and it really does make things buttery smooth. You can absolutely tell a difference between software vsync and NVidia GSync. If you're going to get a high refresh rate monitor, it's worth the extra ~100 bucks to get hardware sync.

Real estate: This is the compromise for people who want to go to full 4K. Most graphics cards can't push 4K in the latest games anyway, so all you are giving up going down to 4K is screen space when in desktop mode. And things are already getting pretty small for the old eyes at 2K. For me anyway, this was the way to go.

Panel tech: IPS vs TN. Basically, I think the guys saying they can tell the difference are the same people who can hear a difference listening to music over gold plated Monster cable. This monitor has a beautiful picture and great color. The viewing angle is fine. I'm coming from a high end monitor that's about 5 years old, and this new one blows it out of the water.

title: Enabled my Vizio Soundbar to work with my 4th gen Apple TV
text:
I've had a 4th gen Apple TV for a while, connected to my Sony 32" TV. I recently purchased a Vizio soundbar (SB2821-D6) which required me to use the TV's optical output to power the soundbar. I was experiencing a noticeable amount of audio lag (lip sync) issues and tried numerous settings on both the TV and the soundbar to eliminate the issue. Determined the optical output on the TV was causing the issue, and since the Apple TV has no optical port itself, I did some googling and found this Tendak adaptor.

I purchased this because other reviews mentioned that this Tendak adaptor DOES pass through the command from the Apple TV to turn on/off the Sony TV which enables me to use the Apple TV remote as my "universal" remote for my setup. Also, because the audio is no longer passing through the Sony TV, my soundbar is no longer lagging and everything is perfectly in sync.

Worth mentioning that in order for the Apple TV to show up as a live input on my Sony TV, I had to connect the 5v USB power cord. Luckily my soundbar has a 5v USB. Once this is connected, the red LED on the Tendak box glows a brighter red and the Apple TV is able to connect.

Very simple and inexpensive solution to my audio sync issue.

The Roku is connected to a HDMI ARC input on a Samsung 8000 series plasma TV and the optical output from the TV is driving the AVR-4800. Again no 5.1 just stereo. I then inserted a device that splits out the optical from the HDMI between the Roku and the TV, again no 5.1 just stereo.

I spent a couple of hours talking to Roku product support and they indicated my settings were correct and unable to get me working. I've purchased 3 of these Roku Ultras and am sending them all back as 5.1 is a big deal for me.

title: VR Compatible Upgrade - Well worth the price.
text:
I bought this card to prepare for my HTC Vive coming in April / May. I replaced an MSI GTX 970 and the swap over was seamless. I placed the latest drivers on the PC, shut it down and installed the new card. It requires two X eight pin power adapters from the PS. Turned the PC on, it was recognized and worked perfectly with no issues (Win7). As I said this card will run my Vive, but I also got it for future proofing. I suspect this will last me for a couple of years. Many are waiting for the Pascal cards. I chose not to. When VR hits, the prices on VR cards will go up from demand and the Pascals are sure to be pricy.

According to the Steam VR Test tool, this card on my system was rated as a Spinal Tap 11 and pegged the bar in the green. It outperformed a Titan X by 0.3 on the same Steam test, so quite happy. The lesson here is if you don't have a decent CPU, motherboard, RAM and SSD any benefits given from this monster will be nobbled. The Titan X had medium level quality CPU and mobo. The 980TI is a performance card for serious gaming and VR enthusiasts. The next higher card is an MSI Titan X for $1700 and I just couldn't justify that level of expense for the tiny amount of extra CUDA.

Temps, even when playing Elite: Dangerous, The Division, Far Cry, Long Dark, World of Warships, etc. at 1080 Ultra are 60C max. Fan noise is negligible and I'm running on default settings. With v-sync off, I'm getting 170-180 FPS in Elite: Dangerous on Ultra settings. Had the card installed for a month with zero issues so far. I game an average of two hours a night on multiple high end AAA games. I do not overclock, but you have the ability to do so with the MSI Afterburner program. Honestly, if you have to OC to get reasonable performance, buy a better card.

My Motherboards are ASUS, My video cards are MSI and I have never regretted buying either brand. I recommend this card if you have the cash to spare. The MSI GTX970 is good enough for 1080 gaming, but you'll need a 980 minimum for VR.

title: Works like a charm!  Highly recommended!
text:
I was pulling what remained of my hair out trying to figure our why my JL Audio Fathom F212 subwoofer's internal toroidal transformer was at times very quiet and at other times audibly humming very in a very distracting fashion. Installing dedicated 20 amp circuits, moving the sub to the other side of the breaker box brought not a lick of relief. After reading many articles I decided that D.C. offset on the A.C. line maybe be the culprit. The two options for experimenting were to obtain a toroidal isolation transformer or a device like the CMX-2. Not having much luck in the past with isolation transformers (they can hum as well!) I decided to give the CMX-2 a try.
After hooking it up I can tell you I've reached audio nirvana once again. The F212 is as quiet as a church mouse even with my ear right against the cabinet! It's the best money I've spent in a long, long time and if D.C. offset is your problem, I can recommend the CMX-2 unequivocally! As a matter of fact, I'm going to buy another one just to have on hand!

I did a lot of research to select this particular laptop, so I was not surprised to be very content with the product. I use it for work (heavy on excel), photo editing in Lightroom and a little bit of photoshop, sporadic video editing and lots of web surfing with a hint of skype.

It's really a trade-off between the glossy touch or a matte non-touch. This touchpad is somewhat finicky and I find myself making touch errors with my smaller hands. A wireless mouse is recommended for anything more than casual use.

The full-size HDMI and 3 3.0 quick charge USB ports are something that really sets this laptop apart from it's peers. You just don't find this kind of connectivity on many (if any) ultrabooks.

title: Useful device—read for FLIRC case install and Raspbian setup instructions.
text:
I bought this little RTC because I was looking for one that would fit inside my preferred Pi enclosure, the FLIRC Raspberry Pi case. The case is inexpensive and doesn't completely break the onboard WiFi and Bluetooth, while still providing excellent thermal mass for the SoC (System on a Chip, the integrated processor and graphics chip basically). This one has the fits over pins 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 and doesn't itself replicate any of those pins, which is fine for my application.

If you're here just for the RTC software installation, skip down till I shout at you.

My first concern though you can see in my first picture. Those little prongs poking out of the board. That yellow-edged pancake thing is a supercapacitor. It's like a regular capacitor except it can leap tall buildings, etc. (read: It can hold a charge like a battery to keep the chip powered.) The bits poking out of the side of the board look to be the leads that go to the + and - of the supercap, and if they are shorted, well, basically you're going to lose the time stored on your clock. :) Only a problem really because my FLIRC case is metal, in particular this little post for the case screw (pic #2). You can see (pic #3) that those little metal nubs stick out real close to where that screw post is located. Should only be a problem when installing or removing the case, but let's solve that problem: A tiny piece of electrical tape. You could put this over the post just as easily as over the RTC board, but I have fat fingers which is why I've been pointing with a spudger. :)

Apply the heat pad to the case (a little off-center like I've done here is best for the 3B+ in pic #4) and remember that the heat pad has sticker tape on the adhesive side and clear film on the other side (pic #5). Notice the cotton round I used with some 90% isopropyl alcohol—this FLIRC case is being reused with a fresh thermal pad (thinner for the 3B+, both thicknesses come with new FLIRC cases) and I needed to clean the old pad residue off the case. Insert the case HDMI-side first, line everything up as well as you can (pic #6) and put in the screws (#7). I started with the one diagonally opposite of the screw hole you see closest to the RTC/header, followed by that one, then the other two, just to make sure the thing was secure and pushing the board into the thermal pad a bit.

I'll assume you don't really need step-by-step instructions to get Raspbian installed. Either format a microSD card for FAT32 and download NOOBS from the Raspberry Pi website or get Raspbian from that website as a zipped .img file and grab a little program called Etcher. "Yes but I'm a Linux expert and don't need Etcher because I can dd the thing myself…" Good for you, Mr. expert, so can I, on Linux, Mac, BSD, or even on Windows, but I still use Etcher because at 3:30am when I'm writing Amazon reviews for clock chips that include full tutorials for setting them up, I'd rather not blow away the wrong 64GB disk image. Oh, Etcher will warn you that 64GB is awfully big for an SD card, lol.

If you're reading this in the US, you'll probably want to configure your keyboard so \ doesn't generate a #, set your timezone, etc. Do that in raspi-config. And change the password, you know how many botnets people have made out of Raspberry pi's because some idiot left the thing on the internet with user pi, password raspberry? That's especially important if you're gonna enable ssh (which I did). A few other system tweaks so my router knows what IP to give this thing consistently, upgrade packages, reboot, and now we're going to connect via ssh from a Mac with ridiculously large terminal fonts for easy screenshotting.

RTC SOFTWARE INSTALLATION

TL;DR for Mr. Linux expert: Enable i2c in raspi-config, add "dtoverlay=i2c-rtc,ds3231" to the bottom of /boot/config.txt, reboot, "sudo apt-get purge fake-hwclock", "sudo hwclock -w", and "sudo systemctl enable hwclock.sh". Then reboot and make sure it worked. There's more steps below if you wanna know how to know it's not working if it's not.

The first thing we need to do is enable I2C. Run raspi-config as root (sudo raspi-config, pic #8), arrow down to Interfacing Options (#9), and select I2C (#10) and turn it on (#11). If you've never exited out of this thing before, when you get back to the menu, press the right arrow and it'll move from the menu to <Select>. Press again for <Finish>. Press enter and you're back to your $ prompt. Now reboot (sudo reboot) and wait for it to come back up. I'm using Raspbian Lite on a 3B+, so that's really fast. The green LED tells will stop going nuts when it's rebooted.

I'm still using ssh, so I'll reconnect that way and run "sudo apt-get install i2c-tools". It'll want a couple of extra packages (#13), say yes and let it go till you get back to your shell prompt. That will let you run "sudo i2cdetect -y 1" as I did (pic #14) and see this weird matrix output thingy. See that 68? That's your RTC, all there and visible to the system. We could've skipped this step, but we didn't because if you don't see that 68 there, or maybe a UU if you've done the next step already, your RTC isn't working. Since it's there, let's make it work!

Next run "sudo nano /boot/config.txt" and add a line down at the bottom that says "dtoverlay=i2c-rtc,ds3231". I added a comment line above that explaining what this line is for so I don't forget the next time I'm doing something at this hour (pic #15, we'll pretend that's nano.) Hold down the ctrl key and press x, safe the file with the default name of /boot/config.txt, and sudo reboot again.

Remember that "sudo i2cdetect -y 1" command we ran? Pic #16 shows you what happens when we run it with the ds3231 module loaded. We're almost done! I stopped at this point to "sudo apt-get install apt-file" and "sudo apt-file update" so I could do an apt-file search for ntpdate because I can't remember if that's in its own package or part of ntp or what… We might need ntpdate later. (Pic #17, and I'm obviously an idiot, why are you listening to me at this hour for how to do this?)

We need three more commands: "sudo apt-get purge fake-hwclock", "sudo hwclock -w", and "sudo systemctl enable hwclock.sh". (Pic #18)

There are several websites with different instructions for how to enable the normal hwclock after you purge the fake one. Most involve editing /etc/rc.local or editing some file in /lib that'll get overwritten the next time you upgrade the package it's in. Debian systems on the desktop don't need any of that crap and they don't break on upgrades because Debian already has stuff for handling the RTC built into most systems. As soon as Linux knows you have one, you can undo the Raspbian customization (to disable it) and it will just work. I hope.

One way to find out… Reboot and check check the date! Pic #19 is … SUCCESS! We didn't need ntpdate, but I'll probably go use it now to make sure my Pi is synchronized rather than a second or two off of the rest of my computers, watches, dinguses, and other stuff. This process goes a lot faster than this if you've done it more than once before (I hadn't done this particular thing before) and aren't trying to document the process as you go.

If I have any problems with this thing keeping time due to supercap failure or whatever, I'll report back. Otherwise easily a 4 star product. Would've been 5 star if I didn't have to Google for how to set this thing up and then figure out how to actually do it RIGHT since nobody seems to have bothered to look at RPi-Distro/pi-gen to see how they disable the hardware clock script provided by Debian. I did, which is why my last step before the final reboot was to re-enable it rather than bumbling about editing random files.

title: Canon's best snapshot camera yet!
text:
I'm no pro, viewing this latest Canon as a more full featured point-n-shoot. Yes, you'll see some fringing when dark and light meet, but if you want pro quality get a pro camera and pay accordingly. This thing has been great on vacations, where I usually leave it hanging from a lanyard around my neck or even in a front shirt pocket so it's handy for taking spur of the moment shots. The super zoom is pretty amazing for getting close, detail shots, especially in this day and age when so many attractions are using fences to keep the unwashed masses away. The preview screen on the back is bright enough to use in full sun, and the controls are well laid out and mostly follow the same conventions of previous Canon cameras I've owned. Some of the features are buried in menus that are not at all intuitive, so I keep a copy of the owner's manual on the iPhone for reference.

The camera is more battery hungry than previous models, and charging seems to take longer as the battery is bigger. The good news is that it will charge off the Canon version of the USB cable, though it seems to want to be nearly fully discharged before it will trigger the charging mode. So now for the first time ever I'm keeping a spare battery and using the wall wart charger for topping up.

The other issue is the lanyard ring, which is so small and poorly positioned it is very difficult to get anything larger than the small thread like end of the supplied hand lanyard through. I finally managed to find a 4mm split ring to fit it, but it doesn't swivel freely. It works well enough, but it's not "right".

At the end of the day this is a great snapshot camera, providing detailed 20 Mb images aided by that wonderful 40x super zoom lens. In other words, just what I was looking for.

title: BATTERY LIFE IS SHORT - Be wary
text:
These radios were field-tested in the mountains over a period of two weeks. Sitting basically idle (no transmissions, very little receive) the batteries would become weak enough to cause the radio to automatically drop from Hi power to Low power after 4 - 6 hours of idle "on" time. When transmission was attempted the radio would turn itself off. We found ourselves carrying and changing batteries out in the field.

Week 1:
1) Battery - AC Delco alkaline
2) Replaced batteries at least once daily

Week 2:
1) Battery - Energizer alkaline
2) Replaced batteries at least once daily

Reviewing the supplied owners manual, we attempted to turn off all settings which could consume battery power to minimize battery consumption but the result was the same. Batteries were consumed, rapidly.

To validate the test, we carried 5 year old Motorola radios with 25 mile range (theoretical). The Midland GXT1050VP4 did NOT provide greater value over the Motorola other than the NOAA weather capability. We did notice more background noise (hiss) while receiving from other radio transmissions to the Midland GXT1050VP4 than to the older Motorola. The Motorola was much more clear. The Midland GXT1050VP4 radios consumed batteries at a rate of at least one change out per day (4 batteries each) while the Motorola consumed a set of batteries once per week at identical use level.

I cannot return these radios to Amazon so I will give them to the kids to play with (using the supplied rechargeable batteries) and will begin the search for a good radio that is not built by a manufacturer with apparent stock in the battery industry.

title: Very nice and practical piece of travel/adventure gear
text: I'm not a fan of carrying a tripod in general, but this little Sirui is worth the hassle.  I'm not sure who first said "the best camera is the one that's with you" but I believe the same principle applies to tripods and perfectly describes the beauty of this Sirui T-025X.  The T-025X will easily fit into a regular men's messenger style bag or a medium sized women's handbag without any fuss.  The Sirui T-025x is remarkably small, sturdy and well made, but especially for the price point.  You could easily drop 2, 3 or 4 times the money for a comparable fancy name brand carbon fiber travel tripod, but I've played with quite a few and none of them seem better than this Sirui.  The T-025X holds my Nikon D7200 securely, but I wouldn't plan on doing a long exposure with this tripod (or any other small travel tripod) fully extended on a windy day. A compact travel tripod like this T-025X is incredibly lightweight and convenient but it requires some modest trade-offs from a realistic user.  Nine times out of ten I can find a sturdy perch like a rock or picnic table that allow me to elevate the camera to my eye without fully extending the tripod legs or using the extension tube if I want to compose shots while standing completely straight. Frequently I like to compose shots low to the ground while sitting, so the Sirui is perfect for those times. As a photographer who likes to hike and travel the trade-offs are well worth it to me, but if you never venture more than a few steps from the trunk of your car or your studio then you may want to consider a taller, beefier tripod made from less expensive materials. The included ball head is very smooth and remarkably stable for its small size just like the tripod itself.  The hinges, joints, legs and the rest of this tripod appear to be manufactured to exceedingly precise tolerances.  If you want a high-quality, small, light-weight travel tripod look no further. I wish I would have purchased mine sooner.

title: Good camera in comparison to many others
text:
Since the YI Cameras are cheap and well reviewed, I bought the YI Dome 1080p & YI 1080p Home Camera test out. Overall, I am very impressed. My basis of comparison are my mix of cameras from Foscam, D-Link & Samsung.

SETUP:
I have nearly every type of Foscam made & I am tired of the spotty connections/disconnections when trying to view the cameras remotely. The Foscam setup is not difficult if you know how to setup port forwarding, etc... but it's just a hassle. The YI camera was extremely simple to setup. You just hold your phone in front of the camera. That's it, no port forwarding or anything.

IMAGE QUALITY:
Very good. Similar to my 1080p Samsung.

SOUND:
Far superior to Foscams. In situations where I can't understand the audio from my Foscam, I can hear the audio from YI without a problem. Yi also has a "Hand-free" setting where you can talk & listen at the same time.
- Also, Foscam Cloud doesn't record audio, but YI Cloud does.

ADD'L:
- I got the "YI 1080p Home" & not the "YI 1080p Home 2" because, the non-2 version's camera pops out and fits into the Nest/Dropcam cases I bought. (I needed a piece of tape to hold the YI in one of the cases.)
- The YI app & desktop application are very simple. I haven't seen any ability to view the camera via web browser.
- I haven't tried to connect the YI cameras to Blue Iris yet.
- I haven't seen an option to imprint the timestamp in the videos.
- I would like to see an outdoor YI & YI with optical zoom.
- D-links are just terrible cameras & all 4 of my D-links are offline more than online.
- I have 1 Samsung, which is a good all-around camera, but they are expensive & I don't yet see an important functional difference between the Samsung & YI cams.

I had to send the first one back because it continually had playback problems from the sd card. I tried multiple cards and multiple formats and it would not connect consistently and hardly at all. I just received a new replacement. I have the exact same problems. The unit syncs well and it's nice that it is splash proof but without reliable sd card reading system I would probably look for another product, especially if you are buying this for the sd card option. I will be returning this also, not sure if it will be for a third time is the charm replacement or refund and look for something else.

Final Review Sept 16th: Well life got busy and I never sent it back. The best I could get it to do was play one very low quality mp3 before it would throw me out into bluetooth sync mode. Honestly for the money it wasn't worth the time to go through the hassle of sending it back and hoping for one that worked correctly or the refund. title: Great Cable
text:
Okay, so my review will be as to the point as it can be and I hope it helps others out. First, before anything please make sure that you are buying it from an authorized dealer, because if not, Monster Cable will not help you nor will you be eligible for the upgrade program.
So, when I bought the cable I had many other HDMI cables to compare, from a cheap sony $10 one to a best buy rocketfish $30 one and the Monster HD1000 and HD850 and my Favorite and number one cable the Audioquest Chocolate HDMI $120. I am using a Sony 1080P LCD TV as well as a Samsung Plasma with a playstation 3, an Apple TV, a Pioneer Elite Blu-ray player and a DVDO Edge line doubler HDMI Switcher.
I have to say that I noticed a major difference right away when I compared this cable to all of the above, it blew the cheaper cables away hands down, in color, the presentation, darker blacks, no bleeding whites, it was amazing. I then compared it to the Audioquest and there was indeed a difference that was noticeable, I wouldn’t say as much as an all around better cable, but it was indeed better than the more expensive Audioquest. Where did the difference come to play? To me it has to be the speed difference of the Monster Cable, the audioquest as good as that cable is couldn’t keep up with fast moving scenes and really wasn’t a good match for the playstation 3.
The Monster Cable gave a much better picture that was warmer, not brighter but warmer, more of a Movie Theater Tone which some TV’s have in their settings.
I had to remember that this cable used to cost a lot more and that the $60 price tag is the sale price.
Now, with that said, I can see why this is on sale the way it is and why no other cable of its kind has been made. This cable has a constant signal running through it and it has to be connected directly and only directly to a TV in order to get the full benefits of using it. Meaning that I was unable to buy as many as I wanted because I wasn’t able to use it with the HDMI switcher, if you have your switcher set to auto, it will never switch channels for you. And the most annoying thing happens, the LED indicator light on the cable will blink until it receives the full signal of the TV, and as small as that cable is, that light is bright when blinking at night when you’re trying to sleep.
So I was only able to buy two of these cables for that reason.
No, another thing, when it comes to premium cables and spending the money on them, please make sure that you are buying from an authorized dealer, trust me when I say that you will not be able to tell that you just bought yourself a bootleg and had to spend extra money in order to find out.
Is this cable worth the buy, yes for sure and for this price you’re getting a major deal.. It’s worth it…
Thanks for reading

title: A Few Cons
text:
Just received this Kindle Papewhite Case a few minutes ago and already have found a couple of cons. First let me tell you what I like about it. The case is a pretty orange which I like. I wanted a bright color so it would be easier to find--my old black one was hard to find if it was in a dark area. I like the way my Paperwhite fits into the case--was easy to install but it feels as if it is pretty snug and won't fall out. The feel was light and easy to hold. The open and shut operation was easy and my Kindle turned on each time I opened the case. Can't tell about weather it shuts off or not since I can't see any light to let me know.

The cons:

1. First of all, I do a lot of reading at a table and with my old one I could easily prop my Kindle upright using the flip cover--it bent back and made a stand. This new one will not do that. The metal claps on the cover causes the flip cover to slide and makes the Kindle fall down--flat. I am going to have to figure out a way to prop it up whenever I read it.

2. The second problem for me is that it has no place to store your stylus--so that they are kept together at all times. Now I don't use my stylus to turn the pages but I do use it when ever I have to use the keyboard. The letters on the keyboard is too small for my large fingers and I usually accidentally touch the wrong letter. The stylus is just right to use for typing. The photo below will show you how I stored my stylus with my old case.

3. The last con is the price. I don't think it was worth the almost $40 I paid for it. I got a promotion discount and it was still expensive--about $35 with the promotion. If I had it all over to do again I would not have bought this case for the reasons I just mentioned and mainly because I feel that there has to be cases out there that is just as good as this one is but for less money. Don't get me wrong, it is a good case, it just does not have the benefits that I am use to having. If you don't need to keep a stylus with your case, and if you don't mind your Kindle not having the ability to stand up, and if money is not a problem for you, then this is a good case to get.

In my mind that means a boom mic. Siri integration would be a plus.

What I got:
The technology on the headset was great. It connected to my iPhone and my Surface Pro (with some help from tech support, which by the way was a person in the US who speaks English-a plus). After briefly reviewing the button functionality in the user manual, everything was working fine: good sound quality (I'm not an audiophile, but I was happy with it), good call quality, and ready access to Siri from my headset.

There was one problem: the headset is. not. comfortable. It is not "over the ear." Neither are the ear cups "on the ear". They are very uncomfortably in between. I'm trying to say that they enclose a part of your ear, and they rub uncomfortably on the part they don't enclose. I think most adults will find this to be the case. And the profile of the headband creates a pressure point which eventually started digging into my skull.

I REALLY, REALLY, REALLY wanted to like them. They have all of the tech functionality that I wanted. However, I kept adjusting them and trying different positions. And by 1:30pm on the first (and only) day I've used them, I gave up. I just couldn't find a position where they would be comfortable, and for $200 (after California state sales tax), I just couldn't make any more excuses.

There is a review from a gentleman that mentions adding Bose ear cups, and other padding to the head band. I would try that, but I'm afraid Amazon wouldn't take them back in a modified condition.

VXi has a great idea, and is so, so close. I can only guess they product tested these on a 12 year old (thus allowing them to be "over the ear" on a preteen's smaller size), and no one in their test group wore them for more that 1 hr stretch to feel the headband dig in. The most I was able to wear them without adjusting might have been 20-30 minutes.

When I called tech support to ask about the bluetooth connection to my Surface Pro, I told them the headset was uncomfortable. They told me it was a common complaint. Apparently they have been waiting a few months for new memory foam ear cups to arrive from their supplier. The person I talked to wasn't clear if they were larger or not. In addition to the head cups, they need to improve the headband. I was told to call back in a few weeks to see if the new head cups arrived.

I'll be returning these over the weekend. I can't decide if I want to try another product or see if VXi can improve this one in the next few months. This was seriously so close to what I wanted! But they were adding to my distractions instead of removing them.

title: Simply.  Amazing.  A compact powerhouse of a camera.
text:
Sony appears to have another home run with the A6500.

I'll admit it, I've become a Sony camera fanboy. It all started with the ground-breaking NEX-6. Each generation of these mirrorless cameras just keeps getting better. I skipped the A6300, as it didn't really seem like enough of an improvement from my trusty A6000, but this release has compelled me to pull the trigger. Here are my impressions:

Pro:

+ They've managed to stuff in-body 5-axis image stabilization into the a6x00 body without adding much more bulk. Awesome. Now any lens is stabilized, even those old Canon FD film lenses. Prior to this release, you had to spring for a full-frame Sony to get this benefit.

+ The grip is slightly larger, and feels better in the hand than the A6000. They've managed to make it feel substantial without adding excessive bulk.

+ Touchscreen. Finally. Being able to quickly set focus point via touch is a welcome improvement.

+ The level is back! It was puzzling that it was missing from the A6000.

+ Mode dial now two has presets.

+ Burst shooting on hi+ is outstanding. On the A6000, it would start to stutter and choke after 3-4 seconds of continuous shooting while it tried to write to the memory card. To make matters worse, you had to wait to shoot again while the buffer flushed. Now, they've added buffer memory and some hardware updates that allow what feels like endless high speed shooting with no lag or delays.

+ Autofocus is fast and accurate

+ The eyecup mount has been revised and is much more secure. After losing two on the A6000, this is a welcome improvement.

+ The lens mount has been reinforced and is now metal.

Con:

- One of the Intelligent auto modes on the dial is gone - Intelligent auto +. No big loss for me, as I never used them, and am not sure why they were present at all on a prosumer camera.

That's the only (minor) downside. Build quality is solid, and it has a nice matte case finish. Image quality is, as expected, outstanding though not notably better than the A6000 from what I've seen so far (noting that I can't yet open RAW files), but with all of the other improvements, it makes a worthy successor and a great buy.

title: Really disappointing. Buyer beware. UPDATED January 2023 Outstanding Performance
text:
After setting up and testing the system in my driveway multiple times I was very pleased with this purchase. With the first camping trip the satellite worked well for two days. On the third day it would not work at all... I kept getting an on screen message "cannot locate signal, check all connections and call Dish." After several calls to Dish and checking all connections, re-booting several times I finally gave up and waited until returning home. I made several attempts to get through to Winegard and once I finally got through the tech person said to check the voltage at both the receiver and dish ends of the coax. I was showing a range of 13 to 19 volts and the system would work about half the time. I strongly suspect a bad receiver. The Winegard tech said I was covered under the two year warranty but since the problem was intermittent if I were to return the unit to the factory they may or may not be able to fix the problem unless they could duplicate the same issue I was having at home. After replacing my new coax cable with another new coax cable when I test the system I get the "cannot locate signal" message immediately followed by the dish working correctly then flashing back to the "cannot locate" message and then back to programming. Quite frankly, having spent $300 for a system that works intermittently and cannot get decent customer service from either Dish or Winegard I would not recommend buying this product with the Wally receiver. If you do buy, make sure everything is working correctly BEFORE the 30 day Amazon return window closes.

UPDATE 6-10-2018
Upgraded to three stars since my problems seem to be resolved. I called Dish Customer Service and finally connected with a very capable young man who spent 2 1/2 hours on the phone with me and checked what seemed to be almost every test in the book. The software was seriously out of date and one glitch is the button labelled "Upgrade my Software" doesn't work and only tells you that whatever version you have is already current and up to date... Wrong!! As of 6-9-2018 the current software version is U438. There are 3 ways to update: 1.) if you are already a Dish customer take the receiver inside and hook it up to your home satellite wiring. The receiver will update at 1 AM or so automatically. 2.) Clear the memory by unplugging the receiver, disconnect the coax to the dish and plug the receiver back in to reboot through the whole process. Of course the dish won't find anything because the coax is disconnected but the memory will be cleared. Then connect the coax back to the dish and reboot. After the reboot, and assuming you are receiving something, use the remote to turn off power to the receiver which puts it into standby mode where you will watch the dancing "tips" square. After a couple of minutes the receiver will begin a software download and install. 3.) As in step #1, if you are not a home Dish customer, leave the system plugged in overnight for the automatic update and download. To see what version software you have now, and to confirm if anything has changed, push the Home button on the remote three times and look for the software version in the middle of the page. If you have U438 (now U802 as of July 8, 2019) you will be current.
Since I am by no means an expert about any of this I urge you to call Dish technical support and have them walk you through everything. Don't waste your time with Winegard. I upgraded to 3 stars because I am willing to give Dish technical support 5 stars but I am not 100% sure that the software is perfect and may still have future issues. Overall this process should be automatic but at least I have learned there are answers to our problems with the Wally. My confidence is restored.
UPDATE 9-4-2018
My system is slowly improving with time. The software has updated a little but still uses the U438 designation. The reboot takes about 10 minutes or less now however the guide doesn't always download and I have to repeat the process occasionally. In the diagnostics area the "Upgrade my Software" button now actually works where the system will reboot on its own and try to find anything current. I am still having problems getting the complete loss of signal screen for one second followed by programming for one second then the signal loss screen then programming which flashes back and forth like a neon sign. I found that if I quickly use the channel up button to change channels when the screen flashes to the program for one second the receiver will change to that channel. When I then use the channel down button everything seems to work OK after that. As Dish will tell you on their website if you do not use the Wally receiver for two weeks or so the receiver goes into sleep mode and you will not receive programming until the receiver is reauthorized. One great improvement is to download the MY DISH app to your phone because you can now 'wake up' the receiver without having to make a phone call or go online to the website. In the app scroll to the bottom to find the Dish Outdoors tab, find and click the reauthorize button... works like magic!
UPDATE 10-20-2018
Three more week long trips and finally this system is working reliably. Works well using my generator or solar powered inverter and on-board batteries. I am still getting the flashing 'no signal' message followed by a working program but I simply push the channel up button to change channel and then come back to my original channel and all is working well. Start-up takes about 8 minutes or so. My only wish at this point is that Dish would include a memory for the receiver so once power is disconnected the receiver and dish would remember the last setting if nothing has changed in the interim. Another useful option would be to offer this system in 12 volt only so the inverter would not be necessary.

UPDATE: July 8, 2019
After being in storage for six months I reactivated my Wally receiver on the Dish website and turned on the system. Once the boot had completed the first thing I did was go into the diagnostic/tools area and hit the button labeled "Upgrade my Software". It promptly told me my current version of U448 from last December was up-to-date and would not reboot and look for anything newer. To clear the memory I then unplugged the receiver, disconnected the coax and plugged the receiver back in. As expected the process only went as far as giving me a message to "check all connections". USING THE REMOTE I then turned off the Wally receiver, re-connected the coax to the dish and waited while watching the 'dancing tips' square... After about 5 minutes the receiver started a new download since the memory had been cleared. In all it took about 20 - 30 minutes and upgraded everything. Do NOT turn off the power or unplug while upgrading. When the screen returned back to the dancing 'tips' square I then turned the system back on and checked the software version number: it is now current at U802.
9/14/2019
Repeated the exact same procedure as listed above, current software version is U806. Dish works perfect.

UPDATE January 2023
Continues to work well with no issues. I have added a hard drive which enables the DVR function and a wireless adaptor to bring in Netflix & on-demand features.

title: Clean Design with Strong Performance in my use so far
text:
I've had this for a few weeks now and mainly use it for general work use. This is my first 3440x1440 ultrawide monitor, but also use a 43" Samsung 4K monitor so it's not my first large scree/resolution screen I've used for PC's. The 1500R curvature is a striking feature and I think it actually works very well in day to day use as it keeps you from needing to tilt your head or adjust your position to view the screen. Which is of course why curved PC screens make sense, we sit a foot or two away from them, and why curved TV screens make no sense as you sit much further away. Compared to the 4K screen (really more of Ultra HD but splitting hairs here) you do lose quite a bit of desktop space, especially vertically - but if you're used to using a 1080P screen or 1440P monitor this Samsung ultrawide is a nice jump up and is close to using 2 of those screens without the monitor border (but also without all of the built in window management capability).

Pros:
Curve very immersive, beneficial for day to day use
Good value compared to some competing options
Zero backlight bleed on my unit
Good contrast and colors out of the box are good for my use with what is labeled "Basic Color" mode.
Built in cable management on the better end of what I've seen on other monitors
Good built in stand stability

Cons:
Not G-sync capable
Proprietary VESA adapter (which is included) makes for a very ugly conversion if you want to use a desk or wall mount and the back or side is visible

Neutral:
I can't comment on the Freesync since I don't use AMD graphics cards and am not much of a PC gamer in general.
Not IPS - however colors and off viewing are both strong on this VA panel

title: Quite the surprise...
text:
I did a build with a 4790k during tax time in early 2015. Went with a hyper 212 evo cooler and AS5 because they were a good team on a prior build (except the prior was hyper 212+). I expected great cooling with the tried and true only to have OCCT stop itself because of 85C safety. I did a 2nd attempt thinking I may not have a good application with the same results. This led to some research and I seen this TIM rating high with a couple others. The temp differences in the reviews were within 10C in many cases but this was still lower. I made the jump but didn't take the time to use it until recently...

Application was nothing like expected. Reviewers on websites and several customer reviews make it sound thick and difficult to work with. The difference between this and AS5 is actually very miniscule in application. In fact, I'd go as far as to say it's not worth mention.

Temp drops were better than expected. I've pulled about 8C drop at idle but I question the true accuracy considering the adaptive frequency/power at idle. Of course load is different since it's full freq and power in which case I'm able to hover around 82C in a 20C room while running OCCT. Real world scenario, GTAV went from 66C during gaming to about 54C.

This is still a rather high temp so I'm not going to bother overclocking until I get a better cooler and case. Either way, you should expect better temps if you're running a better cooler/case.

10C isn't something to shake a stick at. It can be the difference between throttling or worse... If you spent the money on a decent CPU, don't try to save a few bucks on a cheaper paste.

title: DON'T BUY THIS BATTERY!  It overheated and damaged my computer.  Read the review.
text:
This battery overheated my computer and melted the thermal gel on the motherboard. Lucky for me there was a youtube video to show me how to fix it. Don't buy this battery.

Background:
I bought the battery and loved it. It was the cheapest one with the best reviews. Easy install. Looking back I did notice my computer was much hotter than usual but I don't use it for more than a few minutes at a time to google things so it didn't bother me.

After a few days, the computer shut off while I was using it. It would not come back on. I assumed the battery failed and ordered a new one that cost a few dollars more. Today I installed the new battery but it didn't fix the problem. I googled it and it turns out the problem is the thermal gel on the motherboard melted because the computer overheated. I made the repair with the help of youtube. I believe most people would have given up and bought a new computer so I decided to write this review.

The owner contacted me and ask that I delete my review. I would have done so but that is not an option; you can only amend your reviews here. I regret that this will impact his business but I can't in good conscience leave this battery a positive review.

title: One of the more frustrating electronic devices I've purchased.
text:
Bought this GPS for our travel in Mexico during the summer of 2017. I thought that it would be useful in areas where there is no cellular coverage and the dash cam looked like a useful addition in case of an accident. I also thought the warnings (drifting out of lane, traffic ahead, etc.) would be important.

Turns out to be a mixed bag. The pre-loaded map got us lost in the middle of the downtown Dallas freeway system. Also, the maps were not entirely accurate about accessing the Cuota near Monterrey. Most odd of all was that we received completely wrong "Time to Destination" and "Distance to Destination" readings while in Mexico. The Garmin would say we are two hours away, while Google maps would say 75 minutes, and we got there in 75 minutes.

I like the lane and traffic warnings - once the camera is aligned they work well.

I bought a 32 GB mini-SD card to give adequate recording time on the camera. But every time I turn on the unit it says the card has to be formatted, erasing everything that was recorded.

As other reviewers have noted, Garmin should provide a charging block - with such short battery life, having to have the unit plugged in and the motor running is a pain. And the "Type D" USB means you can't plug the GPS into the same charging block you use for an Android phone or most anything else that uses Mini-USB. I don't understand why manufacturers can't standardize (this goes for Apple, Fitbit, and Netgear Arlo as well). How many damn different cords do I need to haul around?

Overall, this is one of the more frustrating electronic devices I've purchased.

title: Perfect 4096x2160 @ 60 Hertz
text:
My high-level specs:
- Windows 10
- AMD Radeon R9 200 Series
- LG 31MU97 Monitor

I was very frustrated purchasing a very expensive monitor capable in displaying true 4K resolution at 60p when I can only configure it in UHD resolution in 30p due to the flickering issues the monitor was having in the higher resolution, higher frequency modes. Reading in many online forums, users were blaming AMD for the issues, primarily around having driver issues. Other users were blaming the displayport cables, stating that the gauge (AWG) were too small or the plating wasn't the right conductive material. After trying 4 different displayport cables, all bought from Amazon and Newegg, I was about to replace my video card for a Nvidia-based card when I decided to look into the displayport spec itself. Little did I realize that there is an actual alliance / working group dedicated to maintaining the standard of displayport technology and requires manufacturers to certify their cables to prove compliance to the spec. It ends up being that all of the cables I've purchased, including those that were really thick, braided, gold plated, and fancy looking, weren't Displayport / VESA certified. None of them in fact were capable of sending 5.4 Gbps / 21.6 Gbps total of bandwidth down the wire (this is the key issue). When I opened the Accell B143B-007J package open, I had doubts about the performance of this cable because it was noodle thin -- ok slightly exaggerated -- but it was definitely much thinner than any of my previous cables. But after replacing my existing cable with this one, and setting my display adapter resolution to true 4K @ 60p, and working with the monitor for several hours, I was pleasantly surprised with the results -- no flickering, smooth transitioning, excellent gaming, the works. This is a fantastic cable, hands down, cheaper and more effective than my other cables. I can already tell the difference in the increase in resolution and especially the display rate. It is almost as obvious as seeing a 1080P TV in 30/60Hz and upgrading it to 120 Hz, which if you know what I'm talking about, is a game changing experience when viewing HD, high FPS content. Highly recommended and you should try this cable first before replacing your monitor or your video card for that matter. My lesson learned from this: cables do matter.

title: Fantastic, must-own product for music lovers with iDevices
text:
AWESOME product! Love how this brings all of my music to life! And I've gotten several compliments on how well-put-together it look!

EDIT: 16Dec2015
I've been using the Oppo HA-2 every day since I purchased in around October 2015. It proves to be the most valuable piece of audio equipment I own at the moment. Its aesthetically pleasing construction is matched with the superb performance of the device. Music has a wider sound stage and I am able to hear better instrument separation. The vocals in "Sound & Color" by Alabama Shakes make the hairs on the back of my neck stand on-end, Tosin Abasi's guitar strings in "Do Not Go Gently" by Animals as Leaders are given much more guts and oomph.

I use these mainly with my V-MODA Crossfade M-100s and Audio Technica ATH-M50x's. I have a pair of Shure SE846s, but beware that with lower impedance IEMs, the volume pot goes up very quickly. I don't think I've gone above volume level 2 for any environment.

The bass boost function is almost a hindrance for most music genres. I use it when listening to Kendrick Lamar or dubstep, but for rock, metal, acoustic works, and most other genres it is not needed and makes the mids and bass bleed into each other.

Hope this will prove helpful to some. All in all, it is a fantastic device for iDevice owners looking to get the best out of their music collection without having to buy a separate mp3 player.

title: Great grey market buy, but read the fine print.
text:
Edit: Still functions perfectly Still my favorite walkabout lens, no regrets and certainly put the money I saved towards good use!!

This is a really great lens, end of lens review. Seriously, their are many great professionally done reviews about it and they are not exaggerating about it's quality, it will not fail to please.

I mainly wrote this review for few different reasons that may be helpful to some.

I purchased this grey market from CW US. The grey market part I was fully aware of, the "Made in China" stamp I was not and was going to return it just for that reason.
But after some research I found Tamron manufactures in China as well as Japan, they have two locations/facilities in China so it is not being sourced to Chinese manufacturers and that makes all the difference.
I was still a bit wary of "Made in China" of course for reasons we all are aware of. But I have tested the lens extensively and it functions flawlessly, I have compared to the Japanese version and is identical, so my advice is don't let the made in China aspect bother you too much if you get one from there it makes no difference it is a quality lens made to Tamrons high standards.
Bottom line, No it is definitely not some cheap knock off.

Warranties = waste of money in all but a very small percentage of cases.

The extended warranties you see offered do not cover grey market items period and are a total waste of money.
The fact is companies that offer them do not go out of the way to make it known they do not cover international versions that have no USA manufacturers warranty, I bought a SquareTrade but after some research canceled it got my money back after they confirmed they do not cover grey market so read closely or call and ask for your self the other companies that offer them..
Technically they are doing nothing wrong since it is all in the fine print but truthfully they are dishonest cheats that bank of the fact most people that buy the warranties will never use them.
In many cases they would not honor many of them as well when then did not fall into a narrow set of guide lines and even those reasons are at there discretion.

Also on side note if you buy the drops and spills that will not be covered unless it is specifically offered at the time of sale for the item you are purchasing and it must be purchased at the time of sale as well, seriously that is right in the fine print.
So if you are expecting them to verify your item will be covered, you are quite mistaken.
Extended warranty providers are some shady characters so beware.

Tamron the company just to make things worse and something you must know before buying a Tamron lens is Tamron the company will not even look at these grey market lenses, Period. Seriously they will not fix them for cash. If you don't believe duckduckgo it.
So if it is in need of service you will need to find an outfit that can and has access to parts from Tamron if needed, as of now I have no idea of who would.
Basically if you break it that's that.

In my experience their is very little that can go wrong with these lenses, if it is okay when you get it probably will stay that way if you take care of it, they are very reliable under normal use. If you use it in extreme conditions and expect you may need maintenance or possible repairs you may want to spend the extra and go with an official import.

Tamron is the exception with repair issues, other manufacturers like Sigma are happy to fix any of their lenses regardless, Canon as well.
One must question Tamrons malfunction in this area of policy

text: The unit may be fine, but the nature of its very compact original packaging caused the cord (as it exits the unit) to be severely kinked (despite the cord protector that is in place where the cord enters the unit).  As a result, it actually intermittently shorted out (the wire in the cord must have been broken because of how hard it was bent to fit in the original package).  As such, I can't recommend the unit because it is a manufacturing issue that will likely potentially replicate itself with every unit produced (i.e., it will either arrive with this likely short, or the kinked cord will weaken the copper inside such that it will reduce the overall life of the unit).  It's a shame, because otherwise the unit seems well built and sturdy.

title: Satisifed customer
text:
The laptop delivers in every way. The only issue that others have reported as well is a little bit of light bleed on the bottom of the LCD. Honestly, that's not a problem for me and not what was important to me, so it's not a problem, but I thought I'd mention it because some people find that important.

The other thing I should mention is make sure to learn to use the Dragon Gaming Center software that comes with it if you are gaming. The default setting does not have the video card set up at maximum(more power consumption, more heat). Changing it to Sport mode significantly improves gaming performance. I use this in conjunction with the manual fan feature(button on the keyboard) when I play more taxing games on the system. Heat is never a problem with the fans on.

Other things:
-The audio seems pretty good. I've been happy with it.
-The network performance seems good(I've heard bad things about Killer Wifi). No complaints. It has two settings, one for max thoroughput and one for best ping. Seems to toggle between 5ghz and 2.5ghz modes.
-The screen is crisp and bright and the colors are good. There are 5 preprogrammed color modes as well for easy switching.
-The laptop is effectively silent when browsing the internet, watching video, and doing other productivity tasks.
-The keyboard is pretty solid and the backlighting is a nice premium touch.
-The touchpad is pretty good. As good as Dell. Way better than Samsung.
-Tons of USB connections. I like it.

Overall, I'm very happy with the purchase.

I bought the tablet like many parents specifically so my kids could do things off line, while traveling in the car, cryign about when are we going to get there I have to potty I'm hungry and so on. The only content available offline is purchased Amazon stuff. The 8GB of movies I loaded onto a microSD? Useless. There is no way to allow a child to watch them in FreeTime. I've seen a few hacks, I tried them. Since a recent update they no longer work. So. I either forget the kid profile with its parent controls and let the kid use the adult profile, I root the thing to make it exactly what I want it, or I return it. I don't love any of those options. The adult profile is also a huge pain in the neck. Android usually has swipeable screens on the home screen, you can put what you want on each screen. Not so with Amazon Fire. One screen and they've taken the liberty of filling it with junk for you that you can't remove. :insertangryface: So a little kid isn't going to navigate it well (much like a little kid isn't going to navigate the oodles of FreeTime apps well until a parent takes out precious time to wheedle them down.) Rooting it takes time and runs the risk of bricking it. Returning it is a pain in the neck AND I have to go find another tablet to buy. It sucks all around. title: w10 vs w20 vs w30
text:
I have owned the w10s, w20s, w30s and w40s all at some point. I currently keep the w30s but have been able to listen to the 10s 20s and 30s in the past month so I have a good impression

Here is what all of the westone w series earphones will get you:
-the most comfortable/ergononmic earphone avaliable. Super light and feels as if nothing is there
-Great sound, the w20 or w30 is the sweetapot
-Removable cables which allows these to last until you lose them. Removable cables provide an ability to listen wired as well as wireless.

The w10s are a good pair of earphones. They have the same perfectly ergonomic fit (besides being smaller than the w30) and all accessories as the higher end models. The design of the W series earphones are solely based on logic and the physical shape of the ear and makes it feel as if it's not even there so I love the comfort. The sound quality is pretty good but lacks the detail and impact of the higher end models, but I can still recommend these if you find them at a discounted price.

The w20s are one of the better earphones I've listened to. These are just as small as the w10s which are extremely small (although the plates are not interchangeable between w10 and w20). What the w20 brings over the w10 is much more sonic detail and texture to sounds with a very clear and concise sound. Bass may be a little lacking for some people, but it does very accurately represent the sound.

The w30s are what I would consider the best choice in the W series line for the majority of people that can really appreciate an amazing sound. The housing is a bit bigger than the w20s (same as the w40) but still extremely comfortable. These are surely a step up from the w20s in how full the sound feels and the bass is great. The w30's are the earphone a ton of people want but have no idea that they would want and appreciate. Wheres that marketing at Westone??
