title: Similar to LG for one third of the price.  Good Deal.
text:
I had the LG 730 ($55) and it lasted about 2 years before it broke (left ear no sound). Before that, I had the previous LG version, nearly identical headset. It also lasted about 2 years before it broke (again, left ear no sound, and it cost 10 bucks more at 65).

This time, I spent 20 bucks for the no-name brand, SoundPeats Q900.

The good
• About a third of the price of the comparable LG headset
• You get an extra 6 months warranty if you sign up at their web site
• The sound is about the same as the LG. Good, not great.
• Better reviews than the LG
• Initial pairing – super easy and fast.

The bad
• No fast-forward or reverse, which the LG had
• These are NOT audiophile headphones. They sound decent, but not wow
• The ear piece is a tiny bit less comfortable than the LGs

What else
• The buttons are in opposite places than the LG, so you have to memorize new placement. For example, the answer phone button is on the right, not the left. Not a big deal, just have to get used to it if you are switching from LG
• The “power on/battery medium/paired” lady voice has a British accent. Who doesn’t like that?

Overall
If this were a $60 headset I would give it 4 stars. As a $20 headset, it gets 5 stars.

If it lasts 2 years (or more) it’s a bargain. We’ll see.

title: Great Kid's Camera. Waterproofing Not Confirmed.
text:
Pretty solid construction, good for rambunctious kids. Certainly not indestructible, but it won't fall right apart, either.

NOTE:
Requires 2 AAA batteries (Not included). And this seems like it goes through the batteries very quickly.
Cannot be used at all without a micro SD card (Not included).

Photo quality:
I'd say this is certainly decent enough for a toy camera. Pretty clear with the right light. Things deteriorate pretty quickly if not, or if zoomed in on the subject. Reminds me of earlier (pre-smartphone) camera phones as far as the quality you can expect: possible to get something that looks pretty good, but just as easy to get a blurry, or overexposed shot. But again, it's a camera for little kids, not Ansel Adams.

NOTE: The pictures all have a timestamp, and if you can remove it for display, I have yet to find the feature.

My 4 year old uses this. It is extremely easy for her to take pictures right away. Just one button to turn on, and the one right next to it to snap a shot. If she keeps this a while, she will be able to access the more advanced menu features that are over her head right now.

There are actually a lot more features and configurations possible from within the menu. Enough that a kid could really learn almost all of the basics of digital photography on their own. Mine is still too young, but provided this lasts, she'll have a good time making adjustments to exposure, white balance, saturation, etc. As is, she has been taking it with her on all outings, and also using it to document her artwork!

Features of note:
Toggle between photo/video/gallery modes
Take photo bursts
In-camera effects modes
Preset picture modes like night, portrait, etc. via the menu
Zoom
Flash: on/off/auto (I don't recommend auto. I saw a couple of shots where the flash just washed the entire photo out)
Timer: cycle through timer duration by pressing the timer button. Click the shutter, and the countdown begins.
Slideshow feature from within the View mode can be set to display each pic for 3,5, or 10 seconds
You can also rotate, crop, and delete photos using the menu on the camera

NOTE: I have not tried to take a photo underwater. I am not at all confident in the water-proofing here. I do suspect it is water-RESISTANT, but not water-PROOF. So a photo in the rain? No problem. a photo in a fishbowl? Not about to try it.

Upload: Connecting to a computer was super easy, with nothing to install, both via (Included) USB cable and (Not included, but required for use) Micro-SD card.

Overall, this is a sturdy, feature packed camera that little kids will love. It is not professional, but does mimic certain professional features, which is great for the kids to learn and grow with.

title: Simply incredible - you won't believe your ears.
text:
These are, without a doubt, the best headphones I've ever listened to and, quite possibly, the best headphones in the world. I've spent a very good deal of time listening to these on Schiit Audio's Ragnarok amp and Yggdrasil DAC, and the experience is nothing short of awe-inspiring. Let me go through each aspect of it so that you can get an idea of how incredible these headphones are.

Design:

You will either love or hate the look of these headphones. There is no getting away from the fact that they are massive. They will take up the majority of the side of your head. The metal bar on the top does look a little funky when you're wearing them. Beyond this, they are expertly crafted and are of extremely solid design. They have a good heft to them without being heavy. The headband on the top is easily adjusted via the divoted slider on the sides. If you couldn't tell by the grill on the sides of the drivers, this is an *extremely* open-ear design. Anyone within earshot will be able to hear what you're listening to, and if you put them on without any music, it blocks out almost no ambient noise. The nanometer scale diaphragm is as transparent as it gets, but this is what delivers the incredible sounding audio.

Comfort:

These are extremely comfortable. The ear cups are supple and soft, the headphones have just the right amount of weight to make them stable without being fatigue-inducing, and the headband is easily adjusted to fit your need. It's superbly comfortable, even for long listening sessions (the longest I've listened to these is three hours at a time). The drivers are so large that I would challenge anyone to say that the cups don't fit over their ears.

Sound:

Overview: Otherworldly. I have listened to some of the best headphones in the world (markedly the Sennheiser HD800's), and nothing has delivered like these. Granted, they are on one of the best headphone amp/DAC setups there is, but I have yet to hear anything that delivers the kind of clarity, sound staging, bass response, effortless treble delivery, and openness outside of a $20,000 speaker setup.
-Treble: It's the most accurate I've heard out of any headphone ever. It will go far beyond your hearing range, and the accuracy and tonality of the treble is outstanding.
-Mid: Supple, warm, and delightful. Honestly, the best word I can think of for the mids is delicious. There's no roll-off, and it has great heft to it. Absolutely sublime.
-Bass: Bass heads need not apply; these do not have the bass of something like "Beats", and thank God for that. The bass is ample, punchy, accurate, and quick. In a word, perfect.
-Sound staging: This is the best part of the headphones. They have the best sound stage of any headphone I've ever heard. You can pinpoint where instruments and vocalists are; it sounds like you're listening to a huge stage of sound in front of you.
-Tonality: It's a planar magnetic driver, so it's going to sound a little less warm than, say, a pair of Bowers and Wilkins, but that isn't a bad thing. These aren't as neutral as the HD800's, but I prefer the sound of these. They're treble-focused, but not overly so.
-Clarity: These are the second clearest headphones I've ever heard next to the HD800's. The Sennheisers take the cake for most clarity, but this makes them the most discerning as well. I prefer a headphone with great clarity but that doesn't force me to listen to SACDs to enjoy them.

Value: Honestly, when you get to this level of audio, the value is always poor. Are there headphones that cost less than half that give you 90% of the listening experience? Yes, there is. The HD800s deliver 97% of the listening experience for about half the price. However, if you're a true audiophile and you have the money, there really isn't anything better at any price that I've experienced thus far. If you have to have _the best headphones_ out there, these are it. Just know you're paying an exorbitant amount to have them.

Overall: If you have the cash and you want the best there is, get them. They're worth it and you won't be disappointed. Please be prepared to spend another $3000+ on gear to make them work. The Schiit Audio stack that I listened to them on was $4100. You pay to play with these bad boys, so get ready for that.

title: Here are your many reasons to choose this lens.
text:
I spent several hours researching which fisheye lens was best for my needs at an affordable cost. I kept digging for a valuable review that gave me confidence in my decision to choose a cheaper lens, but never really found one with substance. I somewhat took a gamble on this lens and I am completely satisfied, so I wanted to write a thorough review that eliminated this problem for others. Stop your search here and please believe me when I suggest this lens for a recreational fisheye user. I am not typically one to write a review for a product, however, this product really deserves the positive feedback. I am somewhat a photography novice. I took a couple of classes about 7 years ago, but recently got back into it again, so my "skill" level is by no means advanced. I have never owned a fisheye lens before so I was afraid to purchase an expensive one. This Opteka Fisheye Lens is perfect for a first time fisheye user. It is an inexpensive way to get your fisheye fix. I took it with me on a trip to Niagara Falls recently and the pictures turned out beautiful. I used this lens for landscape shooting and was able to get the shots I was looking for with ease.

The lens is completely manual, so you should set your camera to full manual mode for the best results. If you don't have any experience shooting with a completely manual lens, I would still recommend getting it. Don't let "fully manual" scare you off of this lens. Just pay around with it and read a few 'How to' forums online. It is fairly simple to learn.

The lens is very well made. It does not have a 'plasticy feel' to it. It was considerably heavy compared to my Canon Digital SLR, so if you're going to use a tripod with the lens, I recommend a sturdy one. It has the white and red marks on the lens to allow you to mount it on your camera easily. It fit secure to my Canon Rebel SL1 and easily rotated from one aperture setting to another. The focus was also very precise and easy to maneuver. It comes with a nice thick bag with a drawstring to store the lens in too.

Overall this lens is amazing for the price. If I had to be picky, the only downside to this lens is quality of the detachable hood and lens cover. Given the ornate shape of the lens, the lens cover snaps on kind of loosely and can be wobbled around slightly, which is totally minor. I didn't shoot much with the hood attached to the lens because if it was turned out of position slightly it left a blurry black ring around the photograph. I haven't been able to play around with it more to try to resolve that yet though. The detachable hood is also kind of difficult to get off. I almost felt like I was going to break it trying to get the hood off. It doesn't just pull off, you kind of have to twist it and push in to release it. Maybe it was just me though, I was shooting in extremely cold weather so that may have had something to do with it. Honestly that is the ONLY negative thing I would say about this lens, which is very minor.

I shot these photos with a Canon EOS Rebel SL1 Digital SLR camera in full manual mode with this Opteka Fisheye lens. It was a very foggy day and was raining slightly, plus the mist from the falls made it extra moist and gloomy out. These photos are not the greatest example of this lens' potential given the s***ty weather conditions, but even with all of the moisture in the air this lens still captured great photographs.

title: Great, simple unit with LOTS of features
text:
Love this unit!! Recently installed one inside a dwelling for a client and most recently (today) two more, one under a covered porch and the other on the outside of a house. These are Power over Ethernet cameras that plug into a switch or router and are completely independent and do not require a dedicated recorder necessarily. You get 4 hours of free recording in the amcrest cloud and then it loops over. You also have the option to get emails, push alerts through the amcrest view pro app for motion detection and video tampering, downloading to a NAS or through an FTP drive, built in night vision up to 100 feet as well plus many other options.

Basically the camera is physically mounted by unscrewing the top white ring above the word "Amcrest" in the product photo there you have four screw holes to use provided phillips screws and drywall anchors if needed. Then feed your cable through hole in side of the structure or into a junction box if you're mounting it on a electrical junction box (a 2"X2" Junction box works well for this.) One side note here, if you are putting the cable through a structure or junction box for a clean, flush install you will need a 3/4 inch paddle bit. The Ethernet end of the pigtail connector is significantly thick. a 3/4 inch hole fits the connector perfectly.

If you do not wire through a wall/ structure/ junction box, the 8" pigtail connector can be routed out from under that four screw base which has four slots to slip cable under. After you have mounted the four screw baseplate and have decided where you're routing the cable, the cameras has the middle section that you can see below the product image's word, Amcrest. The camera sits in this and this is what is screwed in with ring that has "Amcrest" printed on it. The camera can be tilted only manually, NO motorized Pan Tilt Zoom or one/ two way audio.

This camera can be powered via two methods: a 12 volt power supply right at the camera IF you're fortunate enough for a convenient outlet near by. However most the time when in an attic or conduit, etc. this is not the case. Most often people will use PoE or power over Ethernet. PoE will input the correct voltage for the camera over the Ethernet line you are running for the data/ router connection. This is extremely easy and just takes plugging your Ethernet cable from camera into a "PoE Injector" or Poe Switch, both of which can be found here on amazon and then from that particular device to the router then you're set!!

Overall this is a great camera and you get a lot of functionality from the webpage (GUI) after finding the IP address through the provided software or your router webpage. These cameras are IP66 water and dust ingress protected and with the cast aluminum body these are not cheap feeling in the least. I love this model and brand of cameras and would definitely recommend them.

title: Great Value, even better if you replace the Pre-Amp
text: Let me start by saying I'm not a turntable expert by any means.  I am however a music lover and collect 70-80s records as a hobby.  I have owned cassette tape, CD and MP3 versions of several songs and have found the Vinyl copies to sound the best to me.  As with many others, Vinyl's warm sound is what draws me to it.  Vinyl does have its short comings however.  The most obvious being pre-stamping RIAA equalization.  Back in the 1950s the Recording industry got together and agreed upon a standard way of recording music to records.  This involves removing the low end (bass) and some of the high end (treble).  This is why, in my opinion, a raw Vinyl recording will never sound as good as a raw digital copy.  To compensate for this, good Pre-Amps restore the bass and treble with what I describe as a "Reverse RIAA equalization".  For those confused by the term pre-amp, a record player has three main parts.  1.) The table itself that spins the record.  2.) The stylus (needle) that picks up the sound.  3.) The pre-amp that amplifies the micro-volt output of the stylus to around 1 volt for line output.  Most also reverse RIAA equalization.  Old school record players did not include a pre-amp.  Either a separate pre-amp had to be purchased, or a receiver would include one behind its phono input.  For those who are just planning to connect their LP-60 to the line-in inputs on a receiver or speaker system, you'll need to either use the AT-LP60's built-in pre-amp or a separate, external one.  The pre-amp is where the AT-LP60BK falls flat on its face.  Although the built-in pre-amp in this turntable claims to be RIAA approved, it is far from it.  The sound coming from this turntable using the built-in pre-amp still suffers from a lack of bass and high end treble.  Some describe this as "missing hat", a reference to the fact that high frequency sounds like cymbals and high hat are missing from the sound.  It also has a lot of noticeable noise in the form of humming and extra pops.  Luckily, Audio Technica realized that the cheap pre-amp installed in the AT-LP60 may not suite everyone's needs and included a switch on the back to turn it off and pass the un-amplified phono signal to your own pre-amp.  You really can't blame Audio Technica for using a low end pre-amp in a unit priced around $100.  You can spend way more for higher end tables that include better pre-amps.  So what's the solution?  Buy a better pre-amp and use the phono output on the AT-LP60, or connect to a receiver with a nice built-in pre-amp using its phono input.  The sound on my Sony receiver using the phono input instead of the line-in input is drastically better.  However, I like recording lossless FLAC copies of my records to listen to in the car and on the train.  So I did what another reviewer suggested and purchased a better pre-amp to put in between my AT-LP60 and my computer. After doing some research, I went with the ART Pro Audio DJPRE II pre-amp for $34 on Amazon.  The recordings from before and after are night and day.  The DJPRE II does an excellent job of restoring the music to pre-RIAA equalization. I barely have to touch the recordings now in Audacity.  I usually just normalize the recording and sometimes add a little more treble.  The humming noise and extra pops are also gone.  On its own, this is a well built turntable and will meet the vast majority of people's needs.  However, if you are like me and feel like the sound coming out of the unit is a little flat, I'd strongly encourage replacing the pre-amp.  Also, I saw a lot of buzz in other reviews about the quality of the stylus.  I can say that with a better pre-amp, there is a negligible difference in sound quality between this unit and record players three times its price.  No, you cannot replace the cartridge / stylus with a better one.  Yes, you can replace the stylus with the same proprietary one if it does break.  However, I suspect the replacement will cost you almost as much as the entire unit.  Only buy the USB version if you are planning to digitize music and somehow don't have a sound card on your computer with a line-in.  The USB version has a similar pre-amp and will suffer from the same quality issues.  You'd be better off buying an external pre-amp with the $30.  A final note: As with many things in life, there seems to be a rapidly diminishing return on investment when it comes to record players.  Most people can distinguish a marked increase in sound quality when upgrading from a $100 unit to a $300 unit.  However, the minor differences between a $300 unit and a $1,000 unit is only worth it for Audiophiles with money to burn.

title: Not what I thought I was getting...
text:
As others has said, this cassette deck is not really what one would expect from a respected name like Marantz. Sure, it does play cassette tapes and can record to new cassettes (if you have any of those lying around). But the main reason I purchased this unit was to be able to play music from my ancient cassettes that have irreplaceable material from the past. (Yes, stuff recorded before most readers were born, back in the 70s and 80s). I realize that some of it is hardly "audiophile" quality, but it should still be listenable, right?

The problem with the PMD-300CP is that it severely limits you in terms of both noise reduction and playback bias. For example, you cannot select Dolby B or C noise reduction settings for cassettes originally recorded using these older technologies. I also was unable to specifically select the newer Dolby HX (although I don't have much material encoded this way). Similarly, in terms of playback bias, this machine does allow you to switch between "Normal" and "CrO2", but I found neither sounded particularly clear or faithful to the originals. The unit also seems to be poorly constructed; one doesn't get the impression it will last very long because it is lightweight and has a cheap, "plastic-y" feel.

In fairness to Marantz, it has been a while since I listened to some of the cassette tapes I tried in the PMD-300CP and my ears might now be firmly accustomed to listening to fairly antiseptic "digital" sound. The system I now use to listen to music is significantly more accurate and powerful than the setup I proudly owned in my first apartment, and thus reveals more in terms of detail as well as flaws. But I have to share with any perspective buyer that if like me, you are purchasing the PMD-300CP to play your old cassette tapes, you are likely to be disappointed. You will probably not consider what you get out of this unit anything like what you remember hearing from your old hi-fi system. (That is in some cases, perhaps a good thing... :-) I'll probably end up putting this unit in a bedroom or office for "casual" listening, and keep looking for a better unit...

title: Hey Jorge - how Does 80MB/s read-only sounds?
text:
<<< This review is (mostly) for Jorge [low read-only 20mb/s] ??? >>>

I drive my bicycle with a speed of 25mph (oh, forgot to mention this is happening mostly down the hill!)

It is not always a rule that what you measure it is 100% valid for everyone else! And measuring speeds for micro/SD cards is one of those "grey" areas. I’m pretty sure it matters a lot HOW you measure?
This is my second Silicon Power product; I have an S55 SSD for about 2 years that runs like a champ!
Here’s how I measure claimed speed for this Silicon Power microSD card:

Hardware: DELL Computer with i7-4790, motherboard Intel with Q87 chipset, 16GB RAM, Windows 7 (64 bits). There are 4 native USB 3.0 ports (blue ones :-D) and here’s where I connect a Unitek 4 Port USB 3.0 Hub (from amazon) via an AmazonBasics USB 3.0 extension cable. I did not use provided adapter, I insert the card directly into a Transcend USB 3.0 Card reader (from amazon).
The card was recognized right away, it was pre-formatted FAT32 and empty it shows about 14.4GB. I did not re-format the card.

First I ran ATTO Disk Benchmark 2.47 and write speed was about 13MB/sec while read speed was around 76MB/s!

Then I fired CrystalDiskMark 5.1.2 (64 bits) and I tested for 100 MiB (x5) and here are the results:
Sequential Read (Q= 32,T= 1) : 79.214 MB/s
Sequential Write (Q= 32,T= 1) : 14.647 MB/s
Random Read 4KiB (Q= 32,T= 1) : 6.095 MB/s [ 1488.0 IOPS]
Random Write 4KiB (Q= 32,T= 1) : 0.826 MB/s [ 201.7 IOPS]
Sequential Read (T= 1) : 75.080 MB/s
Sequential Write (T= 1) : 13.213 MB/s
Random Read 4KiB (Q= 1,T= 1) : 4.968 MB/s [ 1212.9 IOPS]
Random Write 4KiB (Q= 1,T= 1) : 0.819 MB/s [ 200.0 IOPS]

I also started AS SSD Benchmark (1.7.4739) and after seeing Sequential Read = 79.77MB/s and Write=13.32MB/s I stopped because it was obvious I will get similar results.

Now, does the card live to the promise of “up to 85MB/s”? Answer: NO, not in my case, but I’m pretty sure that in “ideal” or better conditions than mine, maybe using Windows 10 instead of 7 or a different machine we may get results closer or even a bit over 85MB/s. Is the promised claim speed on the spot? Answer: CLOSE enough, but today it is common to advertise a bit over the limit or the “ideal” value you will get. Not many will advertise for less than you will get! If I put this card in my tablet and check for speed will I get 80MB/s? Don’t think so. Am I mad about this? Nope, since I already know that the card delivers very close to promised performance.
If you want to complain about something you may complain about the slow writing speeds, yes, I think this is on the lower side; I would have been very happy with a 20MB/s write speed!
I intend to use this card in a tablet to store picture, music and books. Is this card ok for this purpose? Oh, I think it is!
Will the card last? It is too early to say, I just got it today, but if it fails, then I will come here and complain because it is a custom to complain when something does not work at perfection than when it does :-D.

Unfortunately, it only worked until the warranty expired, and then 12 days later it stopped recognizing the main internal hard drive. The solid state drive still worked, but not the main 2TB hard drive. Dell said tough luck. Dell recommended that I replace the hard drive which I did - no luck. A computer this expensive should not fail so completely during its early operating life. Maybe other purchasers will have better luck - but if you are considering buying this computer, I would definitely get the extended warranty.

title: Its more of a laplet!
text:
Laptop\Tablet
The packaging of this product was superior and it came without a scratch which was a relief. Right out of the box, it had significant heft to it. Considering it is all metallic, this is to be expected I guess. It looks sleek and I love the charcoal color. I didn’t weigh it per say but I think it might tip the scale at about 6lbs – meaning it is HEAVY. I’d not lug it around everywhere I go just because it is sleek and beautiful unfortunately. It is great to use it in an office space though. The setup was seamless. The tablet to laptop transition was satisfactory - the lid can traverse 360 degrees and the transition from the laptop to a tablet happens automatically then. It is a plus that you can place it on a table folded like a tent (an upside down V) and use it as a tablet this way too (at about 320 degrees) You can also use this angle to view whatever video you are watching. I wouldn’t recommend holding it as a tablet in your hand as it may be too heavy for that. I tried that and in about 15 min I was tired and my arm was feeling it the next day. So I would recommend you use it as a laplet (a tablet placed on your lap or a table). The power button and volume control are on the side of the laptop which is a new. Since there is not much thickness, the power button is really tiny. In a slightly dark room, it might take a few seconds to locate it. Talking about a dark room scenario, the keypad back light DOES NOT light up  I was super bumped about it because this feature would’ve made it so useful to work in bed at night. It lights up when you turn the laptop on but turns off after about 20 seconds or so. I’ve tried every setting and they don’t turn back on permanently.
The processor is i7. The display screen is 15.6” which makes it big enough to see things from a distance, 0. 8 GB RAM, 1 TB hard drive(so great storage space!!) and Windows 10 operating system(Meh! Not a big fan of windows 10) . No DVD drive is included but there are 4 USB ports along with one HDMI port so you could connect a DVD player to it if you wanted to.
No heavy duty computing or gaming here. Just your basic browsing, working and predominantly watching Amazon Prime videos and Netflix on our bed with this if you have other backups.
Watching movies on this is awesome especially because the display is great and there is no lag.
Wifi dropped a couple of times but I have a dual band router and I connected both bands to it. Now the drop in wifi is less frequent but I use the laplet(tablet on the lap) for a couple of hours once in 3-4 days. So maybe I’m just lucky that there is no wifi glitch during the time I’m using this product.
Overall, Good product. I’d give it 4 stars as it has served its purpose for me. Dock one star due to the expensive price tag.

title: Simply phenomenal
text:
This 49" LG LF5500 is an phenomenal TV! At this price point, this full 1080p beauty is a steal. My relatively new 42" Samsung LCD TV decided it was done with this world, and after three years of moderate use, it went out with a faint pop. It simply would not turn back on. I have several other appliances by LG, and typically, tend to be loyal to one brand. I have slowly replaced most of my Samsung devices with LG. My decision to go with this model was also influenced by the fact that my parents bought a very similar, higher end smart TV by LG and I really liked it. When my kids started complaining that the smaller 32" I had moved from my bedroom was really not adequate for our den, I had no choice but to upgrade. I did some quick research, noticed a lot of positive reviews about this particular model, and decided to give it a try. I had a $90 certificate to a national electronics retail chain, which brought the price of this TV below $400 after taxes.

Now, to somewhat technical side of this review...

Unpacking this TV was not difficult; the box it comes in is relatively thin and can be easily handled by one person. We have built-in entertainment center in the den and this LG is not wall-mounted in my case. Attaching the stands was easy, although to be fair, I had someone help me hold the TV to minimize the risk of accidentally damaging the screen.

I really appreciate the fact how thin this LG LF5500 is. It is not deep or bulky at all. The bezel is about 1/2" thick throughout and makes the viewing experience a pleasure. As far as the picture goes, the colors are accurate and are easy to adjust to your liking in the TV the settings menu. When you first turn it on on, the set will guide you through a quick setup process. You will have two options to choose from: store/display mode and home use. The first is only recommended for store display purposes and is too bright / saturated for home use. Choosing it will most likely shorten the life span of your TV. The picture quality is super easy to adjust; it gives you several preset options such as game, movie, vivid, standard, as well as custom settings for color warmth, brightness, contrast, etc. The menus are user-friendly and easy to navigate.

As for the sound, I'm extremely pleased with what this LF5500 has to offer. I'm actually amazed how LG engineers managed to achieve such deep lows and perfect highs in this very thin physical form. To be fair, right out of the box, you will be wondering what I was talking about. Not to worry, you simply need to adjust the sound settings. As in the case with the picture quality, there are several sound modes as well: standard, voice, game, movies, music, game, etc. Each option brings up either high, medium, or low tones depending on your listening preferences. In addition to that, you can manually adjust both base and treble, which truly makes this TV sound awesome. You really do not need a sound bar, unless you are a sound junkie and prefer to watch your games or movies with a hi-fi 8 channel sound system.

As far as comparing this LG LF5500 to smart TVs goes, I didn't need this feature and it was not a decision factor for me. These days people tend to rely on external devices such as Apple TV, Roku, and Amazon Fire TV which offer a lot more more channels and even games than any TV manufacturer could cram into a smart TV.

Overall, I'm very pleased with my purchase and highly recommend this LG LF5500 to anyone who appreciates high quality at a very reasonable price.

title: So far so good, a great router upgrade at a decent price.
text:
This refurbished unit does not come with a manual, but a link to a pdf file. No problem, I don't need a manual. Pretty straightforward, plug internet network cable in, plug power cable in, use the ssid/password sticker on the router to connect, done!
Reading other reviews about Netgear firmware issues, I immediately installed DD-WRT firmware, which was like doing a normal firmware update. According to DD-WRT, it should be easy to revert back to original firmware by using same method. I will be missing some features Netgear offers such as their Genie App, and a lot of other things. One thing I will miss is the Netgear web GUI. The trade-off was VPN client option in DD-WRT.
My main concern was having a router that could handle torrent downloading without freezing and needing a reboot (asus rt-n56 locked up many times for me). Also I wanted one that could maximize my Internet connection. I have a 50/5mb cable connection. Using the 5ghz wireless connection, I am able to achieve max connection speed tested with speedtest.net and speedof.me. With the 2.4ghz wireless connection (set at b/g ONLY), I am get around 25-30mbps connection speed. I have set it up like this so I get max connection speeds on 5ghz wifi, while the rest of my household gets 2.4ghz wifi. I'm sure this router can prioritize all the bandwidth traffic for everyone, but the only one that needs to download is me.
It has been a few days of using it, so this is an early review. So far no freezing or rebooting needed! I think the fast CPU and extra memory will solve any bandwidth/connection problems I had with my previous router. Will definitely update if anything changes

UPDATE 1-21-15:
DD-WRT VPN pptp client option was too confusing for me to setup so I decided to revert back to Netgear firmware. Downloaded/unzipped latest firmware from Netgear's website, and flashed it with no problems. The Netgear Genie app could be designed better and allow more advanced features. The bandwidth history chart is nowhere close to being as good as the DD-WRT history graph. That's probably the one thing I will really miss about the custom firmware. I was able to see bandwidth usage (Mbps) in real-time. On top of that it divides Wireless devices and wired connection bandwidth monitoring. Torrent downloading works great on Netgear firmware. I did run into one issue that almost made me go back to the custom firmware, I had tinkered with some QoS settings for 5ghz wifi that caused my laptop connection to be limited to 54Mbps 5ghz wifi connection. I re-enabled the 5Ghz wifi QoS setting and my connection went back up 100+Mbps speeds. I will probably stay on the Stock firmware until it gives me issues. So far it looks promising.

title: I know power management in OS X is good as well so your experience might come close to ...
text:
1 YEAR LATER - UPDATE:
-------------------------------------

This turned to be a good battery replacement for an old Macbook given its price/performance. I've been using it for exactly 1 year and the battery is at 86% of its designed capacity delivering 2+ hours of juice. On light load it might even give you 3+ hours. (See screenshots).

I will definitely recommend it. Hard to find a better one for this model/price range.

INITIAL REVIEW ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hi all, this battery went into an old MacBook 2007 Intel Core 2 Duo CPU 2.10GHz, Intel 965GM Graphics, 4GB RAM and a Samsung SSD drive. Nothing special about the machine as you can read, but it could give you an idea of its configuration to complement your own judgment. For example, as you know the SSD drive uses less power than a conventional 2.5 hard drive, which is what's originally shipped with this computer. This machine runs Ubuntu Linux 14.04 LTS and not OS X. I know power management in OS X is good as well so your experience might come close to mine. During my tests (and I've owned this battery for just a week) I can get 2 hours and 10 min (average) of continuous YouTube video playing before the machine hibernates because battery has drained to critical levels. Doing regular browsing, office work, playing music, you have it, the battery gives me up to 3 hours (maximum in average).

I have better control of power settings under Ubuntu 14.04 than that I had in OS X when I first purchased the machine years ago. What I want to share to give you a good idea is not to expect more than 2 hours our of any battery that goes in this price range for the OLD MacBook models.

Another thing is the battery capacity; it should hold 50.2 Wh (designed capacity). After few cycles (about 10), the battery is reporting 49.7 Wh. That is in itself 'ok'. To me, the designed capacity is a cosmetic estimate from the manufacturer (maximum designed capacity under perfect conditions) and it might or might not be reachable after real time usage since batteries go through the stress that comes with charges and discharges hence they wear out and that's not even considering the software algorithm used to measure them that can't be 100% accurate.

Case in point, I can't claim anything about this battery's life expectancy. If for whatever reason it keeps loosing capacity at this rate I'm ending up with a dead battery pretty soon. If it doesn't turn out to be a boner and it is capable of holding a good percentage of it designed capacity over time, it should keep it powered for about 2 hours per charge cycle.

With all and all, considering its price to be brought to my door and the fact that it is actually usable, I will purchase it again if I have to. Your experience may vary so good luck finding a better battery for an old MacBook in the 20ish price range.

title: Excellent Comfort & Fit for Sleep and Workout
text:
All of these headset types appear to be designed for exercise and work well for that purpose, however, I ordered these specifically for sleeping. Reviews on other Bluetooth headsets designed for such a purpose were convincingly lukewarm. I have used headsets similar to this model previously for sleep so I chose these based on my previous experiences. I prefer over-ear headsets which are difficult to find, and these are quite comfortable.

HEAD BAND

This model fits very securely and the thin spring-like band connecting the two over-ear ear pieces provides some significant advantages over the hard bands on other models.

The spring-like nature allows the band to expand or contract to fit any size head and neck. When expanding, the coil near the ear stretches and the ear pieces rotate while staying securely in place over the ear. The band always stays snug to the back of the head without gaps. Aside from general comfort, this is one of the features that makes sleeping with them possible as pressure on a loose, hard band does not dislodge the headphones from their position.

The thinness of the cable is small enough to rest over the ear without causing uncomfortable pinching during sleep. I am not an active sleeper, but I do change sides several times during the night. The band, while noticeable, is still comfortable enough to sleep when sandwiched between my head and ear against a pillow.

EAR PADS

The ear pads are a padded thin vinyl, presumably to resist sweat. I find the light padding very comfortable for sleeping and not so padded that the headphones are not secure in position.

CONTROLS

The majority of the controls are on the outside face of the right ear piece. There are subtle raised symbols but it is difficult to distinguish them by feel. Regular use of these headphones provides familiarity for the 4 main buttons. The buttons are very low profile and require enough effort to press that when sleeping, it is unlikely the buttons will ever be pressed unintentionally as I change position or rest with buttons into the pillow.

In distinction from other designs, the volume controls are actually on the outside rim of the right ear piece. This is ideal for sleeping as it is not possible to unintentionally depress these. The are also slightly raised and intuitively placed so that it is easy to locate them for use when resting or exercising.

SOUND

This is the area for which I deducted a star. The sound quality is not as good as similar, over-the-ear, Bluetooth models. The sound is a bit tinny and lacks bass (which is desirable for exercise mode). The sound also has a muffled quality, perhaps due to the padded ear cover. That said, the purpose of these for sleep and exercise to some extent demands comfort and secureness of fit over sound quality. The sound is loud enough to psyche up for some treadmill time or walking up steep hills and the quality is adequate at both loud and soft levels. Since listening to music critically for quality appreciation was not the primary reason for this headset choice, I can't penalize the product by more than 1/2 a star, although if you're looking for something to enjoy classical music on a 10 hour plane flight, this might not be the set for you.

LIGHTS

This is another 1/2 star deduct. These do have exceptionally bright blue/red LEDs which are quite bright during pairing and charge. There is also a continual blue flashing light during use. As the wearer, it is not possible to see the flashing light, but I imagine this could annoy others using adjacent gym equipment or other passengers on a plane. I will likely put an adhesive sticker over the LED to tone this down a bit.

title: Worked great with a Samsung 950 PRO -Series 512GB PCIe NVMe
text:
This worked great with a Samsung 950 PRO -Series 512GB PCIe NVMe. I'm actually getting the advertised 2500 MB/sec read and 1500 MB/sec speed from the Samsung 950 PRO. Seeing those numbers blew my mind. There are a couple of things to keep in mind if you are going to use a NVMe SSD with this adapter.

1. Make sure you put this in a PCIe 3.0 x4 or higher slot on your motherboard and remember that the number of available lanes in your PCIe 3.0 slots will depend on what is in use in the other PCIe 3.0 slots. If you have a MB that was built to run 3 video cards but are only running 1 or 2, then you should be good to go. Check your motherboard manual to be sure.

2. Windows 10 has NVMe drivers out of the box, but I don't know about older versions of Windows. Do yourself a favor and upgrade to Windows 10 first.

3. If your motherboard isn't seeing the new drive make sure that your PCIe slots are enabled for UEFI. I did this install on a ASUS Z87-Pro and the drive wasn't detected until I switched PCIe Storage from "Legacy" to "UEFI". I'm doing this from memory so the wording may not be exact as to the exact motherboard setting, but it was something like that.

4. Make sure your motherboard is using the latest "non-beta" bios before you install the adapter and SSD.

Tips:

2. On a Sony Bravia TV, ARC shuts off when you switch to the HDMI/ARC input, so just make sure to not be on it when you want to Chromecast or use other TV apps (if you want to turn ARC back on, you have to switch to another input on the Enclave and then switch back to Aux/ARC). If you have a smart TV and use the apps, use the ARC input for controlling the Enclave only (as recommended in the quick-start guide they provide) and plug everything else into your TV's inputs

title: Outdated
text:
On one level, this device is great. It's exactly what I was looking for: a simple AC bridge to connect wired devices to my AC wifi network. But the wireless radios used in this device are outdated. title: My Sonic Promised land
text:
As anyone who ventures into the the (expensive) and often frustrating journey of high fidelity gear knows, it often feels as a never-ending and self-defeating venture. Hours upon hours reading reviews, perusing forums, seeking recommendations. Hundreds (perhaps thousands?) spent on different entry level gear and yet never quite getting what you're after. Sure, incremental improvements happen as you start honing in on what type of sign signature you love. However, there's always that gnawing feeling that there's better things out there. Fast forward to a month ago or so when I had come across some unexpected money which I could responsibly spend on audiophile gear. At the time there were couple of nice drops going on in Massdrop for headphones in this price range. In discussing with fellow audiophiles these pair (AQ NightOwl) came up. After a lot of research and deliberation, I decided to take a chance. I can only describe my experience thus far as "life-changing good". My ears tell me "this is it, mate, look no further." There's something very visceral and soulful about these cans. With the right DAC and AMP, it's a sonic heaven -- or at least it is for me.

To start let's talk about comfort and ergonomics: the headphones are fairly light -- lighter than Senn HD 650s similar to AT-M50. Head pressure is only enough to create a decent seal and yet leave enough room to breath. Heat is very well controlled (incredibly so for a closed back, actually). The headband is the most comfortable I've ever worn, by far. The elastic capabilities are a stroke of genius quite frankly. Definitely designed for the extended listener in mind.

Sound:

Sub-bass and Bass: excellent detail, punch and sooooooo incredibly smooth and full of life. Nothing muddled, nothing clipped, nothing trumped up.

Mids: this is what makes or breaks a can, IMO. And this case, not only it "makes" the NightOwl, it makes it special. Much like bass and sub-bass the whole mid FR there's a lot of detail retrieval, very smooth and musical. Voices are just face-melting good. Guitars sound as if they were hooked straight to the cans, like the musician wanted to sound. Drums have punch to boot will leave having your favorite songs in repeat.

Highs: kept tight and well under control but not subdued or cramped. Smooth, punchy and yet not fatiguing. If you're treble-sensitive these cans will be paradise.

Conclusion: In the two decades as an amazon shopper I've reviewed few products where I've felt a product deserves not 5 but 10 stars. This is one of those very rare exceptions. If you're an audiophile or a hi-fi enthusiast you owe it to yourself to own one of these cans. I've trying to pick nits and find something to complain about, but the NightOwl have not given me any reason to. A truly impressive feat of design and engineering. The greatest injustice of all of this is that AudioQuest discontinued production of their headphone line. If you're on the fence about this pair or something else in the price range, just stop and get these. You will not regret it.

title: Fast booting, odd keyboard, touchscreen less useful, clean install of Windows 10!
text:
12/5/2016 Update: After a few more weeks of use, I have updated my comments on the usefulness of the touch screen. I still like the laptop. Also corrected the RAM that my model has.

PERFORMANCE: This is a surprisingly fast booting laptop. It boots to Windows 10 in about five seconds. It has a fingerprint reader so you can instantly log in at be using the computer in less time than my old Windows laptop could even get to the "loading" screen. 16GB of RAM and the 256GB SSD drive make it quite speedy for casual use. I am not a gamer, so I did not test anything that would try out the graphics.

APPEARANCE: The plastic case is about what you'd expect from a typical Windows laptop. I've seen much uglier laptops, and certainly much prettier ones (like pretty much anything made by Apple). But, if you were looking for something "pretty" you'd be looking in to much higher end Windows laptops anyway (or a Mac).

CONNECTIVITY: It has the basic ports you'd expect on a modern laptop (USB, video, SD memory card reader, etc.). It has no legacy ports (no floppy drive, no RS232, no VGA). You can get USB adapters for older hardware, and use a cable to go from the HDMI port to legacy monitors. It has modern Bluetooth 4.0, WiFi, and even an ethernet port. The ethernet port is interesting. The case is slim, so the port has to be opened a bit to let a the cable click in. One of the USB ports is "always on" so you can keep things plugged up to it that need power even if the laptop is suspended. That's a nice touch, since you would normally have to keep a laptop awake (sucking more power) just to charge via it's USB ports.

SOFTWARE: The Windows 10 home edition that comes with it appears to be a clean install, other than some drivers and Lenovo utilities. Maybe it's hidden somewhere else in Windows 10, but I didn't see any trial ware or junk ware cluttering up the desktop. There is no install media, but you can make a USB Recovery Drive to use in an emergency. You can also boot in to a recovery mode (hidden hard drive partition) and reinstalls WIndows. (Update: I've already had to do this once. It went well - took a few hours to reinstall and download updates.)

The keyboard is a bit compact. To the right where the SHIFT *should* be is the UP arrow. The UP/LEFT-DOWN-RIGHT arrow combination is moved there, so you may find yourself hitting UP instead of SHIFT until you get used to it. After several weeks, I am STILL not used to it since every other keyboard I use is NOT like this.

The unique feature of the Flex is the touch screen and how you can rotate the keyboard all the way around to make it like a big, clunky and heavy tablet. In this mode, the keyboard is behind you, so it would be sitting face-down on the table. You have to be aware of the cleanliness of the surface you set it on, or you might find gunk on the keyboard ;-) (Lesson learned: If using the laptop at a breakfast cafe, watch out for syrup on the table.) I do not like this design, but I understand it would cost much more to have the keyboard swivel around.

When you flip the keyboard back (to use as a stand, or all the way back as a tablet), Windows 10 can prompt you to switch to Tablet Mode. This was my first experience with Windows 10 Tablet Mode, and I have decided it's just not much use for me. None of the programs I am using support Tablet mode, so while you can touch the screen instead of clicking, it's just quicker and easier to use the trackpad (to me). Also, the smudges I get all over the screen end up driving me nuts. Also, the Windows 10 on screen keyboard is awful. It's so unlike Android or iOS that I can't type on it. I just spend so much time on Android/iOS that it will be difficult to learn the "Windows Way(tm)" to screen type.

Update: Since I wrote that last paragraph, I have actually found a use for Tablet Mode that works for me. I do online surveys and such for money, and usually do this on my iPad. Lately, I have been also doing them on this laptop. I can flip the screen around (like the thumbnail photo for the Amazon page shows) and sit it on a table next to me and tap away during commercial breaks. It's quite convenient. If there was much typing to do, though, I'd still prefer to use a Bluetooth keyboard with my iPad (even over the keyboard on this laptop, due to the odd placement of some keys). It's really nice for casual web surfing.

Update: Sounds is decent, but at full volume, it's not even as loud as my iPad! While it's convenient to set up (in tablet mode) to use as a portable "TV" for watching streaming video, I ended up plugging up cheap external speakers to make it louder.

WiFi works well. I have not tested bluetooth.

The screen looks nice, and performance is quite good for the apps I am running. I think it's the speed of the SSD that really helps things out. This is the fastest personal Windows laptop I have ever owned (not because of the CPU speed, but because of the SSD). I no longer do any serious data crunching on Windows, so it might not be a screamer when it comes to video encoding, but for the speciality software I use (mostly DMX light/show control software and development tools) it is fine. I am sure someone else has done performance benchmarks.

Unless you plan to only use it for internet stuff, be sure to get one of the larger models (like this one) with more RAM and a larger SSD. I do not think I would be happy at all with the entry level versions.

My favorite thing: The battery life is really good and the battery charges FAST. I do not think I have ever had a laptop (PC or Mac) that charged this fast.

MY ADVICE: If you are interested in the touch screen and "tablet mode," find someone who has a laptop like this and try their's. I thought it would be an amazing feature, but it is more of a novelty to me. The laptop is just too bulky and clunky to be carried like a tablet, but I do like using the flip back screen as a stand for watching videos (then it makes great sense, since you can do most features without using the keyboard).

I really should give this four stars since I know there are other laptops in this price range that are better, but, I do not know if there are other laptops with a touchscreen/fingerprint reader/etc. in this price range that compare.

Nit picks aside (keyboard, mostly), it is my favorite Windows laptop I have owned, though I may not have thought that when I was using Windows 100% of the time. I spend more of my time on a Windows desktop (at work), two Macs, and an iPad.

title: Great Floating GoPro Mount!
text:
First impressions, this is a sturdy little mount with a pretty good seal at the bottom for storing small items. The grip feels good in your hand and the small wrist strap is also very nice. I have a GoPro Hero 3+, and I tested this prior to taking on vacation. I did a quick test using a 5 gallon bucket to see how it would float and if it could still float with my extended battery pack (GoPro Bacpac). Needless to say, this thing floats pretty darn good, even with the extended battery pack attached. While submerged, the camera hangs down at the lowest point and the bottom of the mount sticks straight up out of the water about an inch an a half. This is a good thing since it keeps the screw cap up and out of the water, preventing water intrusion into the small compartment. The yellow body improves visibility while in the water, so that's a plus. The screw cap itself has 2 o-rings, which is a neat feature.

Overall, great mount that does exactly what it advertises. Would recommend to anyone.

title: ION Tape2PC works great but check your recording settings
text:
The ION Tape2PC is a good tool for converting old audio cassettes to modern digital formats. I have used it to convert over 700 cassettes of varying ages ( some going back over 40 years), brands and types (Ferrous, Chrome, Metal) and sources (home recordings, pre-recorded albums, LP to tape as well as radio and special mixes). Works great for these - I still have about another thousand tapes to convert so doing at least one tape per day I’ve got a few more years of transfers ahead :)

A Note on Sound Quality : The ION device itself has been compared by other sites to have audio quality at equivalent to CD level, however I have also noted some persons making the complaint about less than Hi-Fi results. There are some real limitations with any digitization process starting with the quality constraints on the audio cassette in the first place - whatever you have recorded is as good as it will ever be given a few adjustments for EQ and levels.
Next the ADC (Analog to Digital Converter) in the ION that takes the tape analog audio to the digital stream coming over the USB cable. This seems to be at a very good level that exceeds or matches the limitations of most audio cassettes.

Critically the audio recording input process on the user’s PC is the next big challenge. I would suggest that before making any tape conversions that the user ensures that the recording input settings from the ION device is set to max - i.e. DVD quality.
On a Windows PC, check the Sound Settings > Recording Tab then look at the Device Properties in the Advanced Tab. The highest level there is 2 channels, 16 bit, 48000Hz (full stereo with DVD quality). You will not get the best from the ION at any lower setting.

I had the unfortunate experience of recording well over 100 tapes, that on later listening review, had slightly muddy sound for quite a few and poor stereo separation. I discovered that my recording input was set at 1 channel, 16bit, 22050Hz (mono with AM radio quality). After fixing that little issue I recopied my tapes at the DVD recording level with the vastly improved results that came alive with clear sound and good stereo separation.

Finally, after making sure you’re getting the best from the source material, the choice of recording software and the encoding format - loss-less or lossy - gives the final touch. A tough choice here between the large file sizes from loss-less vs. the space saving but lower quality lossy formats. It comes down to personal choice and storage space realities. You have to try some test recordings and listen to the results for several formats and quality levels. As a general rule try a level or two up from what you find as a good recording - disk space is getting cheaper, your tapes are getting older and you don't have the time to do it over if you find that it could have been better recorded.

I settled on 2 channel mp3 at 320Kbit - this was better than the quality of the source audio cassette and provided a good quality reference to replace my aging cassettes. The originals can go back to storage while the digital files allow them to live on again for hours of listening.

title: Great Product! A Little Short Though
text:
Note: I have been given this product to write an unbiased review on it.

I have purchased previous Anker cables for other devices before (Micro-USB), and they have all been of very high quality. This product is no different. The box it comes in is nice and compact, although I would . Inside the box, you will find the cable, and a little "booklet" (its just one sheet of paper folded), that tells you what to do if you were satisfied/dissatisfied with the product.

The cable comes with a velcro tie that is very handy in my opinion, and looks much better than standard twist ties.
This product is very short though, although you would probably know by the description of the product. In my opinion this cable is only useful as a backup when you go out, or for charging stations, Also, you probably don't want to leave your phone or worse, your iPad dangling like the icicles on the edge of a roof (like I did for the photo I included), so if you have a plug that is not near a desk and is too high up, I suggest you either invest in a small desk, make a "table" out of things like books/binders, or just buy a longer cable.
The cable certainly does feel a lot sturdier than the standard Apple Cable. It is a little stiffer than the standard cable as well, and will not bend as far. The Anker cable is also thicker, but not by too much.

The transfer speeds/charging speeds are about the same as standard Apple Cables, and I have not received any "Charging May Not Be Supported With This Accessory Errors", which I have received before on the cables that came with my device.
Previously, I had bought cables that have both been MFi certified and non MFi certified, but many of them have felt very cheap, or the plugs would not seem to plug all the way into my iPhone/iPad, and I was starting to believe that only the Apple Official Cables were any good, until I received this product.

Overall, I like the cable a lot! It feels like it is going to last a long time, and if you told me that this cable costed $15-20, I would not be too surprised.

title: Review!
text:
Hi!

I was using the IP Camera Baby Monitor for some days and I found a lot of good things, and other things that could be better. Then, I am going to talk about this product from my personal experience and my professional opinion as an electronic engineer.

Good things:

- The information about specifications is clear and enough.

Things to improve:

- I have a Huawei P8 LTE and I don't know if is because of my phone or what, but when I activate the defense system (movement sensor), I receive the alarm only with the app running, not even with the app running in the background.

- Move the camera position in the movil APP is a little bit difficult. If it works in the same way that the PC app it would be better.

Conclusion:
If you are looking for a baby monitor or security cam that provides a good video quality, alarm system, recording function and night vision for a good price, you are looking for FREDI.

text:
I certainly am confused by all the positive reviews on this unit as I just gave it a nearly 11K mile test drive (USA Four Corners tour) and it is quite literally the boy who cried wolf (or the radar detector who cried radar, as it were).

My motorcycle was equipped with this unit while my buddy was carrying an Escort Max 360 connected to an iPhone running the nifty Escort Live software. I looked forward to checking the Adaptiv units sensitivity versus the Max 360. Unfortunately, the adaptiv unit has no discrimination whatsoever therefore it picks up EVERYTHING (and I mean everything) transmitting near K and Ka bands. After about the 30th time of calling him on our intercom and asking “where is that coming from?” (he has the directional arrows on the 360) to which he responded “nothing here”, I gave up.

On any busy corridor, even with it selected to a mode with no X and no K, it is almost squawking constantly. As it was mixed with my Sat radio via an Sena SM10 it was nearly impossible to get through an entire song without pointless interruption unless we were cruising in remote areas with no other traffic.

Pros:

Neat design, buttons easy to manipulate with gloves (and you will be pushing one in particular ALOT to suppress all the bogus warnings).

Remote LED nice touch.

All inclusive package, aside from the add on handlebar mount (which was fine except the mounting screws are junk instantly rusting once we hit any humidity).

Trick clip on mount and cable setup – easy to remove at the end of the day.

Has the ability to turn off X AND K warnings in areas where one is mostly certain the LEO’s are only carrying Ka (or Laser) – BUT – this is only cool because the spurious K alerts are almost non stop.

This thing IS as waterproof as I would need. Florida repeatedly tried to drown us and it kept clicking along with no damage.

Cons:

While it DOES detect radar (some Ka anyway and one verified Minnesota boy in blue with K) it also detects everything else. One can assume all the fancy new proximity sensors on the newer vehicles are setting it off (though not the Max 360) as well as the frequency oscillators on other dirty radar detectors. Because of this it is all but useless in any environment where there are ANY other cars, buildings, sun spots, snow owls with tracking collars, etc. I got so I only really paid attention to steady building Ka warnings. The other 16,723 alerts were nothing and therefore ignored. A couple of times it failed to detect K band speed signs (that my buddies 360 did) which are normally quite strong. I would see my speed flashing on the sign but the Adaptiv would be silent (yes, K band mode was on) – I would call back to my friend and say “that sign throwing anything?” to which the answer was always “oh yeah” usually followed by the exact frequency courtesy of the Live app (very cool). And NO, the “City” modes only performed marginally better.

It did throw a few false laser alerts (which get your attention for sure) but so did the 360 (once they were in sync but we didn’t see the source, if there was one). I have not had a laser detector yet that didn’t throw a few false laser alerts so no biggie here. As they say, if you get a real laser alert, it will be shortly followed by flashing lights (if you were speeding).

Long story short, maybe I got a bad unit but I give this thing 2 stars, because it is slightly better than nothing. Works okay in VERY remote areas. Neat design but too many false alarms to make it usable to avoid any speeding entanglements. Might be worth $100 – if that. You are probably better off adapting an automotive unit to the bike, hack as it may be. The 360 is a nice unit and while it occasionally detected non LEO K band warnings (and a few false lasers) it is a pretty darn nice product.

title: Great amp but...
text:
Had my 3 channel version for 2 weeks and I just wanted to share my impressions with it so far. Sorry, can't compare it to any other versions or amps for that matter because this is the first I'm incorporating an external amp to my home theater setup. For those wanting to know, my theater consists of an 11.2.4 Dolby atmos setup using a Marantz sr7009 as a pre amp for the LCR's with the Marantz powering everything else. My speakers are the Bic Accoustec PL 980 towers, PL 28ii center and the PL 66 for SR's and SRB's, 2 PL 200 handling sub duties and lastly 4 JBL Control One outdoor speakers for the overhead sounds. Didn't feel the need at the time to go for expensive speakers just for overhead sounds but may consider changing this in the future.

Now on to my impressions. After rerunning Auydssey, the sound quality in both movie and music listening has changed dramatically. With the Emotiva now doing the heavy lifting up front, so much more detail and nuances can be heard. Not only up front, but with all my other speakers as well because the Marantz is now more capable of driving the surrounds and overheads. One of the biggest difference is the bass extension. Although my speakers are very efficient I can now see or hear for that matter how more power was needed to put out the bass that I always felt was lacking from my system and thought it was a limitation of my speakers until I got the XPA Gen3. Especially in 2 channel listening. With such a boost to my listening experience I will definitely be adding more channels to my amp in the future.

Now to the bad. I know that I am probably one of the very rare cases but none the less it was very unsettling to me, especially as a first time customer of Emotiva. I had the amp for 2 weeks then all of a sudden when I fired it up 2 days ago the amp was stuck in protect mode. I tried everything from disconnecting everything and connecting one item at a time to troubleshoot to connecting it all back up on a different breaker to see if maybe I was getting a DC leak into my AC line but still no luck so I called tech support. After a brief diagnosis, the tech agreed that I have a faulty unit and emailed me a return shipping label and put in an order for a new 3 channel amp for me that I should have in about 10 days. Although I'm still in my 30 day home trial window I feel that they still would've given me that first class support and take care of me had I been outside the window. Best part is once I receive the new amp I will still have 2 weeks left to audition it should I feel dissatisfied and want to send it back for a full refund however from what I heard so far I don't think I'll be sending it back. I will be adding more channels and will be hopefully enjoying the amp and maybe a second one once all 7 channels are filled up on the first one, for years to come.

text: Be careful when buying this product. Do some research before you buy the product, not after like I did. After talking to the Samsung tech support about an issue I had with a new Install, I found out that not all cables are created equal.  I purchased a 100-foot cable to reach the furthest corner of my home. The camera connected to this cable wasn't as clear as all the other cameras. I switched the camera with another one and still the same problem. What I found out is that some cables are built with 3 wires and some with 4 wires. The 3 wire cables share one of the wires for power and signal wich can cause an issue called ghosting or double vision. This is the issue that I had. The 4 wire cable has the extra wire to separate power and signal for no interference. At first, you can tell no difference but after closer inspection, the cable was slightly smaller than the originals. I replaced this cable with another 4 wire cable and the results are a crisp clear 1080p picture. ​

title: Sounds very good in a 7.1 system
text:
My Onkyo HT-RC260 AV receiver is highly adjustable. I can instantly switch from stereo with only the ELAC floorstanding to all 7.1 speakers. With the stereo playing only the ELAC speakers,the sound was good but not great. Adding the extra speakers made a huge difference delivering a sense of space and veracity handling human voice very well. For awhile I was a bit disappointed hearing large orchestras because the sound was muddy until I realized the crossovers were set wrong and the auxiliary speakers needed to have the crossovers set high. After a lot of fiddling with the Onkyo I am getting a nice convincing sound for large orchestra classical. However the reproduction of piano is imprecise and not quite right - cannot get the feeling that a real piano is in the room when I close my eyes. But jazz plays beautifully giving a strong feeling of being in the room with the group. Similarly blues. And modern pop comes through very well.

One caveat to this review. Maybe the ELAC speakers would have sounded much better with a better amplifier. My Onkyo is decidedly mid-grade and not high end. I bought these speakers to replace Sony SS-F6000 Floorstanding 4-Way Speakers that cost a great deal less... $150 7 years ago, in hopes of substantially improving the sound. The upgrade has not made a strongly noticeable difference. Maybe I'd be saying different if I was playing at high volume. Or if I had a better amplifier.

title: Small, thin, striking design, but pay attention to advertised clearances to avoid headache.
text:
(+) Plenty of room for larger GPUs - up to 330mm in length. Bracket is solid and comes with supports if you decide to cram a full size card into the case.

(+) ATX Power Supply compatible.

(+) Thick enough to mount a solid cooler on your CPU. Many users find watercooling possible... I am not so much of a masochist to try.

(+) Design stands out, though the LED bar is a tad bright at full force.

(-) Efficient air / temperature management is a must. My system is configured with the GPU portion on the bottom, bringing in cold air from the intakes by the GPU itself, with hot air being exhausted by the force of the CPU cooler on top, set to push air out rather than pull in. This has worked so far, but might prove harder when using a card more punishing than a RX 570.

(-) While ATX PSU support is a selling feature of this case, take care when choosing your PSU. SilverStone recommends no longer than 140mm for better clearance, anything 150mm will be possible but very difficult. Do note that you can simply use an SFX PSU bracket and use a smaller PSU - I went this route since this was cheaper for already owning a capable SFX PSU.

(-) Choose your CPU cooler carefully. The cooler's heatsink will need to fit within the confines of the board itself, as anything that would extend over the edge of the board will not work based on how the case is constructed. A be quiet! Shadow Rock LP was sufficient in this regard, but required some clever cabling.

Overall: very solid little case. Departs from traditional HTPC cubes and approaches a more lithe form by offloading the GPU to its own area. Make sure to pay attention to posted clearance allowances before buying; no matter your cable management skills, space WILL be limited. Would recommend for more experienced builders, but maybe not the best beginner case, especially for one's first foray into ITX territory.

title: Not without flaws.
text:
If you're looking at this model, you are probably looking for a bridge camera and considered various models from the "old" SX60, the Nikon P900, the Sony 400V and the FZ300. I didn't get the P900 because I wanted to have RAW and the Nikon was also very big compared to this..plus it's around 150$ more expensive. The Canon is too old and missing features..I don't even remember why I didn't want the Sony. I ended up trying to decide between the FZ300 and the FZ80. If you don't want to read further, I'll sum that today I would probably get the FZ300 for 70$ more. I chose the FZ80 because of the extra reach..1200mm vs 600mm. I thought it would be a deal breaker but now I'm not so sure. The 20mm is really nice though. So..I'll just write pros and cons.

Pros:
-Amazing reach at 1200mm.
-20mm is very useful.
-Auto HDR is a great feature.
-4K (video and burst).
-Camera can charge the battery so if you travel you can just carry the USB cable. Even charge from power bank.
-4K support.
-In camera editing.
-Custom button.
-Touch screen works well.
-Video is great.
-Small size.
-Tons of features.
-Wifi works great and very easy to transfer photos to my phone.

Cons:
-Cheap plastic feel.
-Images are kinda soft. Especially in the tele end.
-OIS not that effective in tell end.
-barely usable in low light.
-Very noisy sensor. Even at ISO 80.
-Dial is really bad. Hard to scroll without pressing on it.
-Prints on buttons deleted after 2 weeks of use.
-Bad D pad design.
-Fixed screen.
-Kinda small EVF and it doesn't​ switch automatically. (Missing sensor).
-cant zoom in panorama mode. Can't take vertical shots for panorama.
- Audiable noise from camera in videos.

I know.. it's a low end model. Maybe 18MP is too much from a 1/2.3" sensor?
I do like the zoom but I feel that having the Leica with the fixed 2.8 and the bigger pixels would yield much better performance.
So, not a bad camera but could be better.

The camera box was not factory sealed (from Ritz) but it was new and untouched. No fingerprints on the camera. I'm pleased with Ritz. The bundle was great and the price was right. The UHS1 card works with 4K BTW although the manual states that 3 is required.

title: A Tale of Two Routers
text:
This review is my experience with both the 8 port version and 4 port AC3100...
I read some pretty poor reviews regarding the 8 port version so I purchased the 4 port version from my local big box store. My home is wired for internet with a central location so there are a lot of hardwired cat 5e cables that need to be plugged in. I got a cheap network switch and connected it to this router and I was done. Signing in to the router was a piece of cake and I had everything up and running out of the box in 10 mins by just following the directions. I am not a networking expert, but have plenty of battle scars from pc problems over the years so I would describe my level of expertise as "I can search on google and follow instructions."

I was so impressed at the ease of setup that I thought--gee, why am I being so paranoid about the 8 port version. The people who wrote the reviews must not know how to use google or be computer illiterate. Ha! It was so perfect--if I got the 8 port version I could get rid of my switch and just have 1 device. It is the same just with more ports, right? So I ordered this and made the changeover. The end result was 2 hours wasted. What was the problem? Everything... First, the wireless antennas did not transmit. This took several reboots and a firmware upgrade to correct. Then, I couldn't connect to the router with any device. I tried changing security protocols, using a psk key, not using a psk key, going to no security with an open setting. The router scolded me but still nothing would connect. Fed up, I finally went back to the 4 port version of THIS SAME ROUTER and like magic everything just worked again. From everything I have read on the internet, there is no apparent difference between the 2 products except for the number of LAN ports. Did I just get a dud? I don't know but the experience left me scarred. The 4 port version was a trouble free nirvana that just worked. The 8 port version was a hellish, endless journey into a dark forest of networking hell. In fact, I am so irritated I am wondering whether I should even keep the 4 port version of this router. My opinion of this company, however, has definitely been affected negatively and it will influence future purchasing decisions.

title: Definitely good and improve over the original B652's, but not quite perfect.
text:
For the past few months I have been looking for the ultimate audiophile budget bookshelf speaker system. So far I have tested the Fluance SX6'S, Micca MB42X's, Dayton Audio B652's and these B652-AIR's. Here are my thoughts on the AIR's and overall conclusion from my comparisons.

The Dayton Audio B652-AIR's are an excellent speaker for just under $70. They are definitely an improvement over the original B652's-which were renowned for their amazing value. I'm always on the hunt for audiophile sound on a budget and the AIR's ALMOST fit the bill and here's why.

Although they do sound amazing for the price, they are not perfect. I found them to be a lacking a bit in the mids. The 6 1/2" woofer produces some amazing lows for a non-ported speaker and the Air Motion Tweeter (AMT) produces wonderfully crisp highs. Where they fall short is in the midrange. Mids are there, but just fall flat. Perhaps a better way of saying it is that they are overpowered by the highs and lows. If I used an EQ to pull the high end out I could definitely hear the mids better, but this produced a much flatter that was overall unpleasing.

For my system I am using a Macbook Pro running iTunes 11:4. That is connected to the Behringer UCA202 DAC via USB. The DAC is connected to an older, but still good, Aiwa AV receiver that is rated at 120WPC but only produces about 30. The EQ and DSP was turned off on my receiver and I used iTunes to adjust the sound for optimal sound reproduction.

The B652-AIR's are one of, if not the, best speakers I've heard for around $65. The main reason I can't give them five stars is that for just a little more there are far superior options out there. At only around $15 more I would definitely choose the MIcca MB42X's. They have better mids and produce a better soundstage. My ultimate choice for budget audiophile bookshelf speakers would be the Fluance SX6's, at $100 refurbished they are an amazing speaker!
