title: Poor product support for failed Wi-Fi connection
text:
[[ASIN:B01CW4BG4K YI Dome Camera Pan/Tilt/Zoom Wireless IP Security Surveillance System 720p HD Night Vision (US Edition)]]The camera appeared to work fine as it cycled through its start up and reset process. I got clear and easy to follow audio prompts on the camera speaker, and easy to follow step-by-step guidance with the Yi app for my iPhone 7 plus. Unfortunately, the camera would not pair with my household Wi-Fi network. Support from Yi was marginal. There were voids in the online support, for example a contact page on the website with email information that said "email removed" for the email link. Yi did contact me several times via email that the company initiated as part of a customer satisfaction survey loop. There is no real time tech support available. In my email reply to Yi I detailed the steps I had followed, my equipment configuration, and the failure to connect. Their email replies came in the form of boilerplate phrases along with 3rd party YouTube video links that would supposedly solve my problems.

During my problem solving attempts, I reset the camera multiple times, bought a $10 micro SD card (luckily I already had a reader) to manually update the camera firmware, and logged into my Netgear gigabit router and reconfigured my basic and security settings. I'm not an IT professional, but I can do some things on my own. Again, no success. I passed the baton to an IT professional acquaintance who worked on the problem for hours, along with tech support from my internet provider, on gateway and router settings, camera firmware, and system resets. Still, the camera would not pair with the Wi-Fi network. The camera may be good, but I wouldn’t know, as I never got past the basic set up.

This camera, at least in my experience, is anything but plug and play or user friendly. Tech support is almost non-existent. I returned the camera to Amazon for a refund. I will buy a Nest Wi-Fi security camera instead.

title: He loved that 1400watt rating
text:
I bought this off a friend who bought it here on Amazon last year. He loved that 1400watt rating. I have to teach him about RMS lol. Anyway, its a little too weak for his pair of 15" sub's, but its fine for my single Audiobahn DVC 10" sub. I ran it mono then parallel to each voice coil because it implies its 2 ohm stable. It pounded my 10. I have never seen that much excursion on it before o.O It was loud! I ran it for about 30 minutes and checked the amp. It was running fine but EXTREMELY HOT! Protection was still off (green normal). Scary hot though. Read up on the amp online and realized that 2 ohm stable is only in stereo mode. Bridged mode only allows for 4-8 ohm loads. Went back out and ran each voice coil to each channel of the amp. It hit a little less hard. Turned the bass boost from 6db to the 18db setting and it sounded pretty good. Runs cooler now. Still hot, but it shouldn't set my trunk on fire now. My sub is rated at 400wats RMS and I'm only giving it about 160watts RMS. I might upgrade, but overall I'm satisfied.

At around $50-60, this is good bang for your buck. I wouldn't use it on any competition level subs. In fact I think its best for a single 10" or 12". Something around 100-200watts RMS. The complainers in these reviews are probably expecting the "1400 watts" lol. Or they just hooked it up wrong lol. You can't be mad at a $50 amp unless you thought you were getting a $200-$400 amp. And if you think that, your are just dumb.

title: Good Enough for an Audiophile!!!
text:
if you really care about sound, you will love the NAD D3020.

I am an audiophile. I sold all my equipments because I had to move between countries but I used to have a stereo system that was around 20K. I have had solid state amplifiers, solid state ones, DHT, triodes, etc. I have had horn speakers, open baffle speakers, etc. I know my audio.

Nowadays, I had a 120watt solid state asian amplifier Qinpu that I bought new for 1.2K but it died a week ago. So, I needed a new amplifier for my living room. I did not wanted to spend much money because I do not have the space for a real audiophile stereo system but I needed good sound. My speakers are NHT bookshelves, 6 ohms, 86 db sensitivity, so it was not easy to find a proper amplifier for them in the 300-400$ range.

First, I tried the Onkyo TX-8220 2 Channel Stereo, the sound was not bad but it was a tiny sound, like the sound you would expect from a bad car stereo (in audiophile terms, the soundstage was really small). Also, the instruments did not have any clear separation. The tone of the instruments, which I am very sensitive to, was wrong, it did not sound real.

The next amplifier was the Yamaha R-N303BL Stereo Receiver. The Yamaha produced much better sound, a fuller sound. Also, the soundstage was not small. The problem tough was it sounded really muddy, I noticed this mostly with voices. Somehow, the sound seemed to have a veiled. I tried to fix this with the bass and treble controls but it did not work. So, I returned it.

Both the Onkyo and the Yamaha are around 50-70 watts per channel in 6 ohms. The problem is that while the THD (total harmonic distortion) in 8 ohms is pretty low for these two amplifiers, in 6 ohm (for my speakers) it gets really high, like 8 or 10 times higher.

I knew I needed at least a 40 wattt amplifier to properly drive my speakers. I saw this NAD (the V2 version because I want to add a turntable) and decided to try it. The V2 is the same as the normal version with the difference that the V2 has phono input and the V1 not. In any case, this is a 30 Watt amplifier that keeps the same power, and most importantly, the same THD (very low) from 4 ohm to 8 ohm.

I tried it and I was really impressed!!! The soundstage is big enough, the instrument separation is very good, and it has a full sound. There is no way to compare this amp with the Onkyo or the Yamaha in terms of sound quality, the NAD is simply in a different league. More importantly, the 30 watts were more than enough to drive my 86db speakers to loud levels. This is solid evidence of what a well built power supply does for sound, small amp with good power supply will outperform an amplifier with more watts power but a bad or cheap power supply. Bluetooth works like a charm. As for heat, it gets warm but not hot.

This is a small amplifier with a lot of power and a great sound, even for a real audiophile!! So, if you need good sound for a small living room stereo, this NAD D 3020 (normal or V2) is a real good option!!!

title: Nightmare to set up and impossible to decipher instruction manual
text:
No stars. Returned it. Massive PIA to try to decipher the tech argot of the directions and it didn't work anyway. I bought it to extend the range of my router's wifi signal for an outdoor camera. Even after all the irritation involved with getting it paired to the house wifi and then plugging the extender into an outlet closer to the camera, it had zero impact on the camera's signal. The location receives a strong 4-bar signal from the router, too. There's no phone number to call for help with the setup unless you register the product first. The website you have to go to for the setup process doesn't even bother to tell you up front, where it might be helpful, that you won't ever see the setup assistant until you access Netgear's web pages through the extender's wifi, not your home router's wifi. The website has links for setting up with a PC or Mac, but the one for Macs doesn't work--the page never loads. Well, not until you've accidentally come across that information, on a completely different page that you found while looking for set-up help, that you have to access NetGear's pages through the extender's wifi signal, not the wifi from your own router.

If you finally get to the setup assistant you will be asked questions you have no clue how to answer because they're all in tech-speak. Why is it necessary to call a password a "network key"? Why don't you just say "password"? "Make sure your computer is set up to use DHCP". Really. I'll get right on that. I've been using personal computers for 30 years and have never seen the term "DHCP" and have no idea how to check that my computer is set up to use it, but since you bring it up, why don't you tell me how to "make sure" of that? Worthless. The whole instruction guide is like that and the setup assistant is worse by far. And hey, did you know that "WPS does not support WEP network security"? Who cares, if you don't know what either of those things are and if they don't tell you how to determine which your wifi has? The manual will tell you things like, "Click the Next button and the status screen displays". Wrong. Like a lot of the other steps. You know what happens when you click Next? The setup assistant completely vanishes and you end up back on NetGear's main web page. You are not offered something logical for the next step in the process, like a log-in setup option, or a flashing neon sign that says "setup complete" or any information on the status of the device you think you maybe might have possibly just set up. Nothing. Here's our web page. Enjoy this total lack of feedback about what you were just trying to accomplish and whether it worked or not.

No idea whether their phone tech support is any good or not because I put the device back in the box and printed a return label, but phone support is good for only 90 days anyway. Besides, you have to register the product first--so they can have your personal information and probably put you on 20,000 mailing lists for spam--before they'll give you access to the super-duper-secret-classified help line number. Never trust a company that won't give you free phone setup help in its instruction manual.

title: Love it!
text:
I upgraded from a GoPro 4 Black. Not much difference in video quality that i could notice. Bit rate seems to be slightly higher with the 5 than my 4 Black, it it's recording more details in 1080p. I don't really have a use for 4K as the max frame rate is only 30fps. I need at least 60fps and 1080p is more than enough for what I use the GoPro for.

The main selling feature for me is the image stabilization and GPS for telemetry overlay in the video. I did a quick test in my car and the overlay feature is nice as it will show my speed, G force, and all the other good stuff. I plan to use this for my motorcycle rides through the canyon. I can see the electronic image stabilization working on the video play back. Seems like I'm using a 3 axis gimbal which is cool. I think it actually electronically stabilizes all 3 axis (pitch, roll, and pan). It seems to work pretty good on my car test shot, but not sure how well the image stabilization works when holding the GoPro hand held or using it on a motorcycle which has more vibrations.

The cons about the newer GoPro 5 Black:
1. The built in mic sucks. Audio sounds really muffled and not clear like my GoPro 4 black. Probably due to the water proof design. It sounds very similar to using a GoPro in a full waterproof case.
2. You can no longer plug in an external mic directly and need to use an expensive adaptor. This sucks as you can only use the adaptor that GoPro sells and this is not cheap and adds more stuff just to use an external mic.
3. The screen is required to access the main settings. You can still change the camera settings without the screen, but not able to change the other settings such as WiFi, GPS, and other things like the previous GoPro models. I have to remove my motorcycle gloves to use the touch screen. Also I heard the touch screen doesnt' work under which I haven't tested yet.
4. The GoPro 5 Black is advertised as waterproof, but I'm not going to take that chance without using a real waterproof case. Ive read some reports from other people that their camera lens fogged up when using the GoPro in water or water got inside and fired their GoPro. GoPro doesn't cover water damages. Too much money to test out so purchasing the insurance may be a good option if you going to use the GoPro around water.

Overal I give this GoPro a 5 Star rating because it does exactly what I expected. There are other sellers selling refurbished ones for cheaper but I choose to buy new as I wanted to have the best and not a second hand unit. Also can't bet Amazon's same day shipping for dirt cheap and saved me the time of having to go to the retail store out of my busy schedule to buy one.

title: Bought to use in my dedicated Plex media server and it works great!  Best bang for your buck hard drive out there!
text:
I have a veritable rainbow of WD drives (red, green, blue) between my PC, Drobo and newly built NAS and they are all real workhorses. I have yet to have any of them fail or misbehave even after 8 years. I know certain colors are best suited for certain applications, but I find the blue drives to be the best bang for the buck and most versatile. I bought this most recent 4TB blue to install in an old PC that I turned into a Plex media server/home made NAS. I've been wanting to have a dedicated media server for some time and finally had the chance to do it but needed more storage space. The PC I had has a 1TB hard drive that I wanted to remain dedicated to running software and store all of my movies, tv shows, documentaries, and kiddie crap (haha) on its own drive. I installed this the other day and loaded all my visual media on it (I keep pictures and music on yet another drive) and I still have room to spare. I immediately connected the new server to Plex through my Roku 4 and watched a movie (1080p) on the TV while streaming another to my phone and had no trouble whatsoever! I know a lot of the buffering problems stem from inadequate CPU and mine is good, but just in case you're wondering, these blue drives have no trouble streaming content from when you've got adequate transcoding power in your machine. A lot of people would tell you you need red drives but old blue does just fine in my experience and is so much cheaper!

For those of you who are new to installing new hard drives, it's a piece of cake but just be aware that this drive does not come with any cables or mounting hardware, so you'll need to be sure you have your own SATA cable and an available power source cable as well as screws or whatever you need to mount it in your case. Also for the newbies, you can't just plug and use, you'll need to go in to your drive manager and name/format it before you can use it. This is also very very easy to do and only takes a few minutes and then you're ready to go!

I don't use these WD drives to boot and run software anymore (it's all about SSD's for that now - buy one, it will change your life) but I use these drives to hold and back up all of my data for me and I love them! You really can't get more storage and a more reliable drive for a better price than this. And don't be freaked out because the picture shows the inside of the hard disk, this is a fully enclosed drive (see pics). Hope this helps! Happy computing! I did NOT receive this for free or at a discount.

title: Great HD FM tuner for the audiophile
text:
Pros greatly outweigh the cons. The FM tuner is very sensitive, and picked out stations I didn't know were in my reception area. Connecting this unit is plug-and-play. I connected the FM antenna to my rooftop antenna, optical TOSLINK to my A/V receiver and started tuning around the FM dial. All FM stations in my listening area have at least one HD channel most 3. Audio quality for HD stations is definitely clearer than standard FM. Not all HD stations audio quality is 100% great. However, I think this is more an issue with the compression/bitrate than this tuner. A few stations have definite digital artifacts; tinny sounding highs with poor bass., while other HD channels from the same station sound is excellent. Having analog output and optical/RCA digital covers all bases for connecting this unit to your A/V receiver.

The cons. Biggest issue is the poor performance for the remote control. The viewing angle for reliable remote control operation is very narrow. I've tried fresh batteries (a couple of times, just in case the "new batteries" were tired), no better. I've programmed a few buttons from the Sangean remote into my learning universal remote, no better. The issue is with the IR sensor on the radio has a very narrow viewing angle. If you are not pointing the remote pretty much straight at the IR sensor, the radio does not respond to the remote at all. Second minor issue: even brief power outages causes the radio to loose the clock time setting. Fortunately the programmed stations are retained in memory. Third issue: 10 buttons for preset FM stations is not enough for a large metropolitan FM listening area. Last issue: AM performance is not very good. However, I'm surrounded by power lines, and AM reception is pretty difficult in my area without at least a ferrite rod AM antenna. The supplied AM wire loop antenna does a poor job of nulling noise sources.

Overall: Good HD FM receiver for the audiophile. Once stations are preset, operation is extremely simple, and audio quality is outstanding for HD radio stations.

title: Don't buy: it doesn't wake up from sleep/hibernation and ASUS Tech Support is clueless!
text:
Do NOT buy this computer unless you want to spend hours on the phone with tech support and be the beta testers for ASUS because it won't wake up from hibernation and randomly turns off. I read the Amazon reviews prior to purchase so I was aware of the possibility that there could be a power/screen issue, but there were plenty other reviews that were silent on the issue and/or customers were able to quickly resolve the issue w/ driver updates or settings so I bought this for my daughter. After I received this laptop I followed the Windows instructions for set up and updates, and immediately had problems w/ the laptop: when ever the lid was closed the computer would go in to some type of sleep or hibernation mode that I couldn't wake it up from. There were power light indicators on that showed the computer was on, but the only way I could get it out of this mode was to do a hard restart (hold the power button for 10 seconds or longer) and that prompted the computer to turn off and on again. The problems kept on coming: whenever the computer went into sleep mode from lack of usage/typing, the same black screen and unresponsiveness returned.

ASUS customer service is horrendous! The first call I made to tech support resulted in me spending 20 minutes on hold (not including the initial 10 minutes to get a live tech to speak to) when the tech advised me he would investigate the problem and get right back to me. But, he never did return to my call; instead, I was sent to a customer service survey prompt asking me how my service was that day. I gave my opinion! I then called back, and spent 50 minutes on the phone (about 25 minutes on hold) w/ a tech who initially spent 20 minutes trying to instruct me on where to find the "hibernation" setting in Windows10, and eventually advising me I could resolve the problem by setting the computer to never go into sleep or hibernation mode after being turned on. Since such a setting would use a lot of power, and potentially harm the screen, battery, processor, etc I said that was not an option. The tech then investigated the problem and instructed me to do a "clean install" of the computer. To do so I first removed the two upper screws on the crossmember. I then pushed the table down as far as it would go and through the screw holes marked on the tubes where the screw holes were. I then removed the top and the two tubes that now have screw whole mark. Then I simply cut just above those marks and reassembled everything. Works like a charm

title: Good CPU, Not Best Performance/Price
text:
Low power consumption, works fine for normal light use and NAS applications. Support for DDR4 ram, new connection standards, etc. It also comes with a stock cooler. iGPU is Intel HD 510.

One thing to take into consideration when buying this processor is that unlike the G3258 20th Anniversary edition, the multipler is locked. This means that you can't overclock it. Without overclocking, they perform roughly the same, but if you overclock the G3258, it would smoke this processor.

However, by buying this processor you get a much better platform in regards to future-proofing. Skyline brings native support for NVME drives which have blistering fast speeds, USB 3.1, DDR4, Skylake upgrade path, etc.

TL:DR
Future proof platform & slightly better iGPU= G4400
Pure Performance/Price=G3258

3/2016 Update- Intel has released a newer microcode which blocks BCLK Overclocking, however I would recommend this processor over the G3258 due to falling DDR4 prices and future-proofability.

I have a set of cheaper "Bluedio" phones that I hoped would offer the same quality sound but they did not.
These are worth the price!

title: sturdy, and easy to carry while in use
text:
We order a lot of Lenovo laptops on the Edge E series (14" and 15"). The model we chose came with 16GB RAM and a 500GB SSD.

Overall
For a 14" laptop featuring Skylake, this laptop comes at a convincing price point. You get lots of hardware packed into a sleek, small package. I walked around our facility for a week with this laptop in hand while I provided support for our infrastructure and end-users and found it to be lightweight, sturdy, and easy to carry while in use. The fingerprint scanner is particularly useful if you're frequently logging into a locked system.

Performance
The i5-6200U is a dual core, hyper-threaded CPU with modern features. I'm a system admin, and power user, and have a desktop workstation for my complex workloads, so I find this laptop to be perfect for every-day tasks such as Office, web, network and infrastructure management, and photo and audio manipulation, and more. Unless you're a gamer or heavy power-user, this laptop has plenty of performance for almost all needs. Having 16GB of RAM and a 500G B SSD also helps the system remain snappy, responsive, and usable. We've had a few laptops come in with Samsung 850 Evo SSDs, but our last model came with a Sandisk X300 SSD.

Screen
The screen is bland, boring, and nothing to write home about. Viewing angles are poor, and the 720p resolution is extremely dated when 1080p, 2.5k, and 4k screens are becoming the new thing. I'm really disappointed to see 1366x768 on a 2016 mid-grade laptop. Lenovo needs to step up the game and make a 900p or 1080p screen the minimum. Docking a star for the low-res LCD.

Usability
The trackpad is abysmal, and the function key is where the Ctrl key is supposed to go. The trackpad tries to mimick some of the big-names like Apple by removing buttons from the trackpad. Clicking and dragging doesn't work well, left clicking when you meant to right click, clicking not working, etc. After over a week of using the trackpad, I hate it more than I did when I opened it and realized it had no buttons. Good luck getting used to it! The function key is also located where the Ctrl key normally is, causing you to hit Fn instead of Ctrl. Since 95% of every other keyboard in the world is different from this one, it doesn't make any sense to try to just get used to it. There is a setting in the BIOS that allows you to swap the keys, but then you have a button that is labelled differently from what it actually does. Why Lenovo does this, I've never understood. Docking another star for these as they are pretty big issues.

Battery
The battery lasts me 4-8 hours, depending on how heavily I use it. It charges quickly, giving me 50% in about 35 minutes. For the form-factor and the amount of hardware inside, I can't complain at all.

Took a while to figure it out. I've posted a photo to help explain things. A few things to remember:
1. Insert the reference coin as shown in the photo (this is what the manual refers to as a "yellow plastic token")
2. The most helpful guide is on the sticker on the device itself (see photo)
3. It is powered by 12V
4. The coin signal output (white wire) can be set to NO (normally open) or NC (normally closed) by a switch just above the wires.
5. Yes, it works with Arduino, RPi etc. Make sure the coin acceptor and microcontroller share the same GND. Best to set the NO/NC switch for the coin signal output to NO. Have a pull-up resistor on the coin signal line (in Arduino you can just use INPUT_PULLUP). When a coin passes through the acceptor the coin signal output will be pulled to ground.

So i know a different review touched on this aspect so I think I should as well, just to show some continuity on the matter.  So the company says these are over the ear headphones, that's a bit of a technicality.  They technically are over the ear, but the area that's supposed to go around the ear isn't very big so unless you have small ears part of the cushion will be resting on your ears.  If you have big ears, sort of like myself, there is a way to, as you put them on, to fold your ears into the hole without it being uncomfortable.  Another negative is the headphone cord, now it's not necessarily the cord, the jack that's on the earcup isn't the best design so you can easily not plug it in all the way.  Though you will know when you don't because, while the sound comes in on both speakers, it sounds like you've hit the "concert hall" theme on the equalizer so it's very echoey.  Once you plug it in correctly it's hard to tell the difference in sound between the headphone jack and the bluetooth.  The last negative is the "multi-function" button on the earcup, it's got more functionality than most headphones, though half of those functions will only work with their proprietary music player.  Only the general functions will work across devices.The proprietary player is really nice looking i just wish it would be able to interact with other source audios.  As an example itunes or google music, i already pay a subscription fee for music I'm not going to cancel one that works very well for a different one that only works really well with one set of headphones.

The internal pockets are relatively deep and about 3.5' wide, I can fit the MAC charger and cable in one pocket, keep a highlighter and spare pen in pen holder and the other pocket holds a portable Hard Drive and its USB cable. There is another major compartment that can hold lots of stuff, I keep my other USB cables in a satchel in there. Loose papers, needing a temporary home are placed in the rear zippered compartment to provide protection to the laptop from that side of the bag as there is no pad on the side for some reason. There also appears to be no padding on the bottom of the laptop compartment, but seems to have sufficient material to protect it during normal use. title: D4s Review
text: The D4s is a great step up for me. I shoot travel and studio photos and the dual-axis ergonomics really was an unexpected plus. The FX sensor produces flawless images with fine granularity and color balance. I like the format flexibility because I usually know pretty much in advance if the resulting images are headed for smaller head sheets, the web or large color prints. That lets me adjust the capture size and quality to maximize storage and not waste a lot of time in Lightroom or Photoshop dealing with 30 MB images. The pro metal body has already paid off in being able to be banged around and keep on ticking. Be aware that this is not a lightweight camera and that when mated with lenses like the Nikon 70-200mm or the 16-35mm, you are holding significant weight. It's not a D40. I upgraded from my trusty D300s, which is no lightweight either, so the weight was not a big shock for me.  If you are considering the D4s and you have one of today's lightweight cameras, make sure you hold the D4s with a representative lense before you plunk down the money. That said, it is not too heavy or cumbersome and it has a very nice feel in your hand. All the controls are where they should be and it all feels natural to me. The large number of features necessarily leads to a layered menu system that can be intimidating to those unfamiliar with the Nikon system. But then again, this is not a camera for a first time buyer or casual user. If that's you, you would be best served with other choices. In the end, great photos are not made with pro cameras, they are made with great glass like the 70-200mm or 16-35mm f/4 and an artist's eye. Don't waste your time or money if you don't understand that simple fact. If you have a limited budget, and who doesn't, invest in the glass and the training/books that will make your a great photographer. The D4s is just the paintbrush. It can't make you a great painter.

title: LG 65UB9200 experience - Also comparison to 60UB8500 (2015 model)
text:
Update (6/3/15)
I found that this TV works seemlessly with my LG Bluray. I can control TV, Bluray with just one remote.
There is also nice feature when if HDMI signal present, it'll turn on the TV.
I have this TV attached to Yamaha receiver, and I had 4 HDMI cable connecting 4 different sources on to the receiver. For example I had Bluray on HDMI1 and PS4 going to HDMI2.
TV is connected via only one HDMI cable, buth when both Bluray and PS4 were up, it let me select Bluray or PS4... Not via Yamaha interface....
You can also down load Android LG remote and you can even capture screen on your phone!

I recently purchased LG 60UB8500 (new 2015 model) because I've been wanting to have 3D tv and it was on sale for $1299 from local giant computer store. This TV has WebOS 2.0, which my 65UB9200 is missing. It also has fancy LG Magic remote, which I really like.

Despite all the nice feature and ultra thin 60UB8500, I still like the big screen of 65 inch (didn't realized 60 vs 65 has big difference in size) of 65UB9200.
I tested 4K video because many people noted on HEVEC codec incompatibility of 65UB9200. They play the SAME 4K videos and both would not play some 4K video (as many people point out how 65UB9200 cannot play HEVEC encoded videos). Except for one of the LG demo 4K video, which 60UB8500 played much more smoothly. I think it's just too early to tell how 4K works on this TV or any other LG TVs. Both of TV has ability to update their software (both of them updated the software automatically when I connected to the internet.) The problem is that only LG knows if they will keep supporting 65UB9200 os and upgrades... WebOS seems to be their flagship OS, so I'm not sure if LG will spend resources other thei their WebOS....

I've noticed that 65UB9200 keeps network connection more secure than 60UB8500 which if I idle, it'll loose connection to the cloud hard drive and I have to go back to the beginning of selecting cloud HD.

Not sure it's just me, but 65UB9200 seems to have better looking screen that 60UB8500.
When compared 4K videos, they both look amazing and fantastic, but then I played over the air HD or 1080p Video, 60UB8500 show softer iamge with higer darker tone- I switched picture mode on both the same "cinema" 65UB9200 showed much more crip image.

So here is my recommendation. If you don't care about 3D, air-mouse like remote (which you can buy separately for 65UB9200), and just watch downloaded content from HD (leagally, of course) or stream move over internet tv service, I think this may be a good choice considering the screen size. If you are worry about HEVEC codec and future enhancements, you may want to look for something else.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I had LG TV when I was a little boy and back then they were dependable and more high tech then Samsung, who just came out as a new brand. I never had an issue with LG product, so I didn't hesitate when this TV was on sale at local computer store (Ever since Amazon start charging tax, thanks to Mr. Jerry Brown, I tend to shop around elsewhere).

I paid about $600 less then current listed price.

TV is very thin (about 1/3 of the thickness of my old Panasonic 55 inch flat screen and wider screen size), and I was able to lift it all by myself.

The leg assembly was very easy (need to screw 4 screws on each leg) and is very sturdy despite its look.

It says it'll cost $17 year to run the TV on the Yellow energy sticker. This TV would be much cheaper to run then my Panasonic plasma TV which had 4 fans on top constantly working.

It has all the connections you need; 1 composite, 1 component, 3 HDMI, and 3 USB 3.0. I have AV receiver which can upscale to 4K resolution, so I probably need only 1 HDMI and 1 USB, but nice to have all options....

I have not configured built in wifi (per LG Website) yet, but connected via LAN cable.

I read many review about 4K content not playing on this TV, and Smart app does not work. Not sure why LG would sell 4K TV if it does not support 4K resolution. For me 4K worked and the Smart app worked absolutely flawlessly out of the box. It also did auto Smart App update when I tried to download free app.

I was not able to verify YOUTUBE channel 4K videos playing 4K or 1080p, for I could not figure out how to get what resolution it's playing on the TV. However, I found a website where I was able to download 4K resolution videos.

I know it's not fair to compare image quality on my previous 720p TV to this, but one word.. OMG. The image is so clear, I could even see a person's nostril hairs. No latency playing the video either....

Smart app also worked fine. It played all of my movie on USB hard drive, played movie over LAN on my network Hard drive.

One thing I was annoyed was the remote control that came with the TV. Smart app icon is right above up arrow button. So for example, you try to create a LG account to download free app, while you are typing new user ID/password, you trying to hit the arrow key to select a letter form onscreen keyboard, but you hit Smart app button. You are thrown back to the main screen and all your typed info are gone.... I think I repeated about 4 times before I made it. I think I'll look into Smart Remote option.

Overall this TV add style to your room and give you perfect picture.

It doesn't have wireless, it's not particularly attractive and it's probably not a good fit for 99% of the Apple Fanboys who don't care about the terrible quality of the audio files they're streaming. In fact, the vast majority of the digital audience will likely not understand this device.

But it's strangely beautiful, listening to such a crisp, clear, deep noise emanating in a way that makes you realize you've been asleep and forgotten what music should sound like. The fact that the whole thing comes in a wooden box is absurdly prosaic when it should be packaged in some plastic clam-shell that will never biodegrade. title: Very bad.... Port 2 does not work - also no VPN pass-thru support, intermittent ping issues, not really supported.
text:
As of 3/31/2014

Update: 4/7/2015
After hours of diagnosis, and a replacement unit, I have determined the core problem is that Ethernet port 2 is unstable on this device. It is unable to keep a connection with my Dell or Lenovo, producing intermittent 4000+ms pings. Support claims this is related to the power management on port 2. Port 1 seems to be OK.

1) The unit only supports VPN pass-through with a hotfix. The hotfix doesn't quite work. The VPN will not be stable and will require frequent restarts. So this is basically useless if you need to VPN into your companies network
2) This unit periodically 'stalls' with producing 1000ms+ pings even for machines *not* on VPN. Possibly related to 1) above. Basically renders you connection useless for voice, realtime video, and games
3) Support - is of course comical. Hours of wait time, dropped call, passing the buck. The usual.

5/25/2015 update
Still no firmware update for port 2 problem. Looking at the Netgear KB, it looks like there is no user-update capability. So this may never be fixed. Many of the other features don't work either (parental controls). I should have stayed with my 2003 RCA modem. It worked better.

title: Android app lets it down
text:
GoPro really needs to pay attention to usability to stay in the market. Pairing this device with my Android is a very hit and miss affair and transferring files to my PC with a USB cable is also very error prone. The Android app doesn't seem to communicate with the camera correctly.

For example, right now the app says the camera has 40% battery but the camera says the battery is empty. Which is correct? I have no way to know. The camera seems to act as a wi-fi router that my Android has to connect to. I don't understand why they don't use bluetooth - it would be simpler. Every time I want to pair I have to re-acquire the camera's wi-fi which rarely works. It's a complete mess.

When I first tried to download files to my PC the file explorer could see the video but every time I tried to copy it I got an error saying the SD card was empty. I had to disconnect the cable and reattach it (same cable - not a cable problem). The file explorer could then download the video. Very flaky.

My last complaint is that the packaging is deliberately not reusable. You have to destroy it to get the camera out. That means I have to find somewhere to store the camera and the stuff it came with. Perhaps GoPro is forcing us to buy one of those camera cases. I don't appreciate that.

The camera itself is pretty good and has a nice high-contrast display that I can actually read without a magnifying glass. The two button control is difficult to use though - doubly annoying as the app is such a let down.

When I turn the camera off there's a blue light that still flashes every five seconds which probably explains why the battery was empty after leaving it overnight. I have it charging now but the app simply says it's charging - I want to know how full it is while I'm charging it. Another fail from GoPro.

title: Great Pocket Camera for Travel
text:
[Update 9/25/2017] After using the ZS60 for a few thousand shots, I have some additional comments. I like the long zoom, the RAW format, the viewfinder and the fact that I can put it in my pocket. But it just has too much noise under lower light conditions. In bright sunlight it's great but as soon as you get in a lower light situation, the picture comes out speckled, especially if you crop it at all. And by lower light, I mean something like inside a church with light coming in through the windows. I'll go looking for another camera that meets my needs for long zoom, RAW, viewfinder and pocket size and with better low light performance. Maybe it doesn't exist
[Later update] I think what's happening is that the imager is small so not a lot of light falls on it. Then, when you zoom a bit, the f-stop gets fairly high which reduces the amount of light coming through the lens. To compensate, the camera has to increase the ISO which leads to a grainy image. I have the Panasonic FZ300, which has the same size imager, but the lens is f2.8 for the full zoom range. With that f-stop, enough light gets to the imager and they don't have to increase the ISO so much - so the images are not so grainy. I bought the ZS100, which has a one inch imager so I'll see if that does better. The ZS100 has a viewfinder, RAW and it fits in my pocket but it only has a 250mm lens equivalent. I think I can do everything I want with that much zoom. [end of update]

I bought this Panasonic ZS60 because I wanted a pocket camera with a viewfinder. I had been using a Canon PowerShot SX720HS which produced good pictures but lacked the viewfinder and a panoramic function. So far, I'm pleased with the Panasonic ZS60. I also have the Panasonic FZ300 and the ZS60 has almost the same menu options so it was easy to pick up the ZS60 and feel comfortable with it.

I use the pictures in a travel blog so the quality is fine for my use. I really wanted a camera that I could put in my pocket - the FZ300 is just too big for travel use. I have to have it around my neck and it's too easy to have it hit something and damage it.

I looked at the ZS70 before purchasing the ZS60. The extra features in the ZS70 - mainly the ability to swing the LCD upward for a selfie - weren't of any value to me and the ZS60 was quite a bit less expensive.

I wanted a long zoom for travel and the ZS60's zoom is adequate for my needs. The Canon SX720 has a longer zoom but beyond a certain range you just can't hand hold a good picture.

All-in-all, the Panasonic ZS60 meets my needs for a decent price.

title: Do not buy this for use in the Dell Venue Pro 11 (7140) Core M model!
text:
Do not buy this for using in the newest Dell Venue Pro 11 (7140) Core M model. It will fit, but there are big issues.

You have to disable Intel RST "Link Power Management" feature for this to work, or else it'll lock up and reset the tablet, with the ssd not being acessible until you turn the system off and on again. Meanwhile, it'll will cook your tablet displaying a "boot device not found" boot screen, while getting things REALLY hot.

With the Link Power Management turned off, the battery life becomes very poor (the 7140 gets about 10 - 12 hours normally, and with this, you will lose about 50% of battery life. The increased power usage is ridiculous! From 2-3 watts in idle to 6-7 watts! That's unnaceptable.

Things I've tried to fix the problem:

*Updated Intel RST to the latest version.
*Enabled HIPM / DIPM in Windows 8.
*Using the Microsoft driver with HIPM / DIPM. It is more stable than using Intel's driver with LPM. The system does not Wake up from suspend, but it does not lock up and heat a lot.

I tried to contact Transcend about a future firmware update (or anything else), to fix this issue, but had no response after waiting for almost a week.

It's really frustrating that this ssd is one of the only that fits the Dell tablet and yet all these people have issues with it.

title: text entry a constant headache
text:
I don't understand the logic behind the T9 text entry algorithm on modern flip phones. If I enter the beginning of a word, and then hit "next" until the characters I want to see are displayed, then if I type another character my selection is forgotten. So if I type 4376 it gives "hero", I hit NEXT (0) until "herm" shows up. Then I type 37 to try to spell "hermes" but it comes out "heroes". I.e. the "m" changes back to an "o". Why would I have hit NEXT at "hero" if I wanted to stick with the original suggestion of "hero"? No one has been able to explain this to me. On the first phone I bought over a decade ago, which used Motorola's "iTap" algorithm, I swear this wasn't a problem. With modern flip phones, you have to constantly switch from T9 to Multi-tap whenever you enter a word that's not in the dictionary. Before, I never had to use Multi-tap to enter words. I would just delete the last character and hit NEXT until the correct prefix was visible, and then continue entering characters. Keep in mind that just about every other text message has a new word in it, either someone's name or some other proper noun or just an uncommon word. Multi-tap sucks because there is a preset delay for entering two consecutive letters on the same key. I hate to use it, it punishes you for typing fast. (why doesn't multi-tap adjust the delay to match the speed of your typing? good question!)

If I enter some text and hit the "right" direction button, the text is saved, but it isn't used for predicting what comes after it. Example: 946 gives "who" but if I put 9 NEXT (to get W) -> (to save the W) 46, it results in "win". That's because even though "who" is more common than "win", after I hit the right arrow it ignores the "w", and "in" is more common than "ho". My older phones did not do this. I type 9463837 and it shows "whoever". On a Samsung I type 9 NEXT -> (to save the "w") 463837 and I get "winfuer". Not a word!

Finally the treatment of new dictionary words is truly bizarre. For example at some point I must have entered "6am". Now whenever I type "man", which is the same keys, "6am" appears as the first selection, and I have to hit NEXT until "man" appears. Even though I'm sure I've entered "man" more recently and many more times than "6am".... The worst is "Ok." which is very common. It for some reason completes as "O5?". I don't remember ever entering "O5?" but it's possible that I did. Now, no matter how many times I change it back to "Ok." and continue typing, the next time I hit 651 up comes "O5?". The street number of my house also happens to share keys with a common word. I must have entered it twice, versus 50 times for this word, but nevertheless the street number always comes up as the first selection. This is a peculiar flaw in the Samsung Gusto 3, and it makes me want to vomit.

If I type 2 NEXT NEXT NEXT NEXT, the phone starts cycling through all the NEW words it ever encountered starting with A, B, or C. Why would I want to enter text this way? Keep in mind it's only cycling through words that were uncommon enough to not have been found in the built-in dictionary. Most of them I only used once. Why would I want an easy way to enter words I only used once? All they have in common is being super random.

I wish I could change the software on this phone, but I wish even more that Samsung, Nokia, et al would produce a flip phone with decent software. Why spend $100 on hardware that was programmed by a retard with a drunken product manager? Answer: because you have no choice. Because Motorola stopped making dumb phones!

title: Extremely happy with the sound and functionality
text:
This thing has great sound, great design and great functionality, making it unique among the such devices.

The tweeter is great for better voice understanding, the woofer in all that wood is absolutely strong enough for most locations where you would use a speaker like that (kitchen, table, nightstand). You can control treble and bass so you can tweak the sound to your situation too. The design is better than other internet radios too, no plastic on the front and the side, simple, logical controls, presets that get you to your favorite internet radio station with only one touch (beat that, smartphone:), even a very nice remote control is there. No silver colored plastics and no light colored unwashable clothes, how cool is that:) Multiroom functionality is there, Spotify Connect is there, aptx and nfc are there, a 5V USB port near the audio input for Chromecast and similar is there, USB input is there, a nice control app is there. And then the portability and the water resistant wood. Two timers too. You can't complain about the price when there is no real competition...

But, well, I do have a wish list... Not saying others are doing better, but then again, in today times, there are many thing that, theoretically, could be done better. Here is my list:

You have to be very careful not to tilt the speaker by pressing the buttons. I tend to hold the speaker with my other hand when pressing the buttons. It could be that the problem is only present on the vertical Amico and not on the horizontal Solo, Duetto etc, but still. The click mechanism could be a little lighter.

Dedicated treble and bass control would be nice and also a reminiscence to classic radio designs.

A real EQ instead of the simple treble-bass control would help in some situations.

Volume control is OK for most usage, but imprecise in the low level setting. Especially for a nightstand radio it should be much finer.

Different internet radios can have very different basic volume. Bluetooth tends to be very low volume. An input volume control, or some kind of global normalization would be helpful.

The rubber extensions for the buttons work well and look great matching the preset buttons in color. But why not add a spare one or two to the package, just for the peace of mind, if my children start to play with that thing?

My oldest smartphone has better WiFi!? No big problem for me, but why?

The processor power is just OK, but for 10$ more it should be possible to buy at least 5 times faster processor. Just go and ask how much that processor costs. Same goes for the display. The display is also not perfectly centered (which I don't care about:)

When I switch on an internet station and the WiFi is not stable, it is not possible to switch over to an another input for minutes, because the radio autistically thinks it should first search for that WiFi for ages and is not obeying to any other commands during that effort:)

Podcasts can be put on the preset buttons, but not the folders of the podcasts. I rarely want to hear the same podcast again and again. But accessing a specific folder of podcasts would improve the functionality greatly. I could access a podcast that I want to hear in a couple of clicks.

Why not add the audiobook functionality, with bookmarks and saving the last position? "Audible" functionality would be even better. Especially on a portable speaker.

Spotify is cool, but what about Chromecast built in, Tidal etc? I would also be much happier to be able to select my Spotify playlists on the radio itself. A radio that is able to function as a standalone device should be able to do that.

If showing the name of the song is the only real functionality of the display, I would prefer a monochrome high resolution display.

When do we will get lyrics on the display of an internet radio? The name of the song is there, the internet is full of lyrics, the radio is connected with the internet, when will somebody from a company that wants to sell internet radios invest a couple of weeks of programming into that?

I find it is a pity that almost no company seems to be really interested in developing the experience of modern audio media consumption on a standalone device. Maybe only Grace Digital seriously is trying to develop the idea of a modern standalone audio player further. The ubiquitous alternative, streaming speakers with smartphone control will always be dependable on, well, a second device:), which has to be there, be charged, be connected, be used with clean fingers and not be used for something else in that moment. I really hope I will not be forced to control my bathtub and WC with my smartphone app in the future:) All the things I would like to see are achievable with a small display like the one on the Amico. Maybe something like Echo Show is the future of an audio device. Because some visual information about the music is really helpful and is also needed for choosing stations, podcasts, playlists. Touchscreen can also help with control of some complicated functions, although I would like to retain a set of dedicated buttons, which make control of some simpler functions faster and more intuitive. On the other side, Alexa & Siri are still far away from understanding every word fast and reliable and I don't understand how could they help me choose from a long list faster than a touchscreen or a click wheel.

So, that thing has great sound and great functionality, even if there are a couple of things regarding standalone device abilities like streaming services, podcasts and audiobooks which could be done a little better. However, the alternatives are almost not existent, especially not with that sound quality. On the other side, regarding multiroom functionality, there are some better (bigger) options on the market. But, as a combination, I haven't seen a better device.

title: A technical marvel and at fantastic price!? Yes, it is, but not suited to color-critical uses.
text:
Well, there's plenty to love about this monitor and some and a few, more important things, to hate. Let's start with the love...

The wider range of colors and accuracy in the steps of the colors, they bring picture/video to a whole new level. Streaming has never looked better. That's probably because the monitors large color range, AdobeRGB is closer to the NTSC television standard than the typical sRGB standard monitors use. For videos, this monitor puts my plasma TV to shame.

Now, the not so lovely.. out of the box the color settings were awful. Glaringly bright, colors way too strong and unusable. With family photos, skin tones were like demon clowns. I searched the internet only to find that this model has some very unusual characteristics that made calibrating it a hard job, and some professional online reviewer said a waste of time for critical work with photography. You see, this monitor is set from the factory to display the AdobeRGB (despite the included fake sRGB option) and Windows and most video cards don't use AdobeRGB. What you're left with are oversaturate, falsely high, colors. On top of the oversaturated colors, magentas pushed to red, muted blues, and gamma setting options being off made for a heck of a long calibrating session over a couple of days. I had to resort to modifying my video card's output significantly to get the monitor usable for photo editing.
In the monitor's OSD: brightness 20, contrast 50, gamma 2.0 and Smartimage: Standard
Video Card Red: Brightness and contrast: set down to +20 (or down 30 from mid-range of 50 on a 100 point scale) and red gamma 1.2
Video Card Blue: Brightness +60 (or up 10 from a mid 50/100) and Blue gamma 1.1
Overall vibrance set to 40 (down 10 from a mid 50/100)
NOTE: Though take these with a grain of salt as I had to recalibrate almost times over a couple of days.

I hope to fine tune this setup more and I'll update this review. Bottom line is, this is technically advanced monitor and if you're' ready to put the effort into it and have the know-how to tame it.

UPDATE: I've recalibrated this motor almost ten times, each time and way I get different results. I've noticed that when it come out of power save mode/powers up the panel, the display starts our red tinted and that diminishes over a few minutes to different degrees each time. Another thing is the bleed from the red cells to surrounding cells in various places on the screen and this is particularly noticeable with high contrast such as text. For dependability, regards color accuracy, this model doesn't even match the monitor I'd hoped to upgrade/replace... an old Acer TN monitor.

UPDATE #2: I sent the monitor back. It's just not reliable for color. The last straw was when it had come out of powersave with blue think that faded over a few minutes, and then started tinted to red. Also, I'd started noticing cells bleeding in a couple areas (bad for office apps) and uneven lighting on the screen (bad for photo/video) too.

Despite the promise of the technology and marketing this I can't use this monitor for critical photo or video processing, it's color calibration just doesn't make the mark. It's a solid desktop monitor, and really great for video streaming once you get the color settings right.

text:

Also, the programming manual comes with the unit, and it is complete. I got a 6160RF keypad, and also a 6162RF. I mistakenly thought I wouldn't be able to easily program the system with the 6162, but that's not correct. The 6162 keypad is very nice looking. (Both are totally functional, however.) Now we can make any changes or repairs needed ourselves, at reasonable prices, and we can choose our own monitoring company, at good savings. There were no frustrations at all programming and hooking up this system.

Others have mentioned: connect the resistor to Zone 1 before you power it up, or you'll get a fire alarm, very noisy! Also, if you are replacing an existing panel, it would be helpful to label the wires as you pull them off, so you know what's connected to where.

title: Excellent as a doorbell, marginal for surveillance, and capturing video will cost you
text:
I installed a Ring doorbell as part of adding SmartHome devices to my house. Let me say right off that the only Amazon Echo device the Ring works with is the Echo Show (e.g., "Alexa, show the Front Door"), and that's pretty cool. Ring includes a nice installation package with the doorbell, including screwdriver, level, mounting screws, screw anchors, and even a masonry drill bit for brick or stucco siding. My old doorbell was installed when the house was built in 1973. I have wood siding at the front door and my doorbell uses a 20V (AC) transformer, so my installation went exactly like the Ring instruction video. Apparently most doorbells use low voltage AC produced by a simple transformer wired into a house circuit. For a wired installation Ring requires the transformer produce between 8VAC and 24VAC. My transformer is located in the attic so it was easy to check its VAC rating, but if you have a volt meter you can simply use its VAC setting to check the wires at the push button connection. Newer doorbells may be digital, so Ring supplies a diode to wire across the contacts to handle that scenario. If the Ring is installed as a battery powered device, you have to have your smart phone on hand to notify you when someone is at the door.

Setup can only be done with the Ring removed from its bracket and running off of its internal battery. It also requires you to be online using Ring's smart phone app. The setup is easy and you can quickly verify functionality. Once installed on the bracket, press the Ring's button and your inside chime sounds plus the Ring makes a chime sound itself. After that you will probably do what I did and figure out what else it can do, which is where things get a bit annoying since the documentation for the app is a bit buried on Ring's rather annoying website. The doorbell actually runs off of its internal battery, which can be charged via USB, and which for a wired connection recharges (slowly) from the VAC source. Heavy usage will draw the battery down faster than it will recharge, requiring you to remove the Ring from its bracket to recharge the battery externally (the software will warn you when the battery is too low).

From my perspective, sound quality is marginal and video is good, although the camera is easily fooled by lighting contrasts. As a doorbell device performance is excellent, for surveillance, less so. With the fish-eye lens you get great coverage, but with the distortion might have trouble making identification after the fact. The motion detection uses IR and is a bit slow on the uptake, where recording may not start until someone approaching the house has been in range a few seconds (possibly missing them entirely). As delivered, my Ring would only activate by the doorbell or motion sensing, but once I updated the firmware, live view worked, enabling the app to view the camera on demand. It took some hunting around to find out how to get the firmware updated, which turns out to be simple (in the Ring app, in the live view settings you just activate, then deactivate live view, which triggers an update check).

I might have given this a 5 star rating if there was some way to capture video other than relying on Ring's rather expensive cloud service ($30 per year, a lot considering that they only hold your video for 60 days). At least the company seems to be responsive to its customers, as evidenced by continuing to provide firmware upgrades for nice to have features like live view and Echo Show.

Update: I've had my unit installed for over a month and it's doing fine. As for the Echo Show, you can only access live view, not answer the doorbell, something Ring acknowledges on their web site. That's is a major mis-hit on Ring's part, or perhaps it is a case of the Show's software being too beta to be able to adequately deal with a device like the Ring at this time. I decided to pony up for Ring's cloud service to be able to check the doorbell when away from home. That generally works, but I've found the motion detection is often too slow to react to a delivery person in a hurry (either failing to record anything, or recording their receding backside). Also, on some occasions the camera image is simply black (in broad daylight conditions), which may be a function of my Comcast internet service dropping out at random times during the day. All in all I remain positive about the product and see no reason to change my rating.

Update 2: I've now had my ring doorbell for over a year and it continues to work well. Performance has actually improved since I put in a Google mesh system to distribute wi-fi throughout my house, ditching a hodge-podge of range extenders that went South with every power interruption. The Ring was particularly useful when we had to vacate the house for 4 months this Spring due to hurricane related repairs (fortunately the power could remain on). With the ring outside and a couple of cameras inside I was able to effectively monitor the house and work progress. The Ring activated whenever crews came to the door, and enabled me to run off a guy nosing around who was not a subcontractor. That alone justified the price of the Ring. Live view also enabled me to determine things like rain and wind conditions. Most cars don't trigger mine, but large trucks usually do (it's about 70' to the street) . The only real complaint I have is that detected motion does not activate the device soon enough, plus the delay of getting through the cell network is likely to preclude effectively answering the door bell.

title: Build the perfect point of sale system
text:
I've installed dozens of these square POS systems. They work fine on their own, just be sure to get the proper size/version to match your ipad, the connectors differ. To expand the system you pair it with a printer, cash drawer, scanner, and chip reader.

If you plan to get a printer with your system, then stick with lower cost serial (not usb) based cash drawer and tie it into the printer instead, which also frees up one of the precious and limited usb ports on a square stand. This is important when you need a chip/nfc reader, printer, drawer, and scanner.
To put together the perfect square stand system, at minimal cost, this is what you need:
Square Stand of your choosing
APG Cash Drawer VB320-BL1616 note: this is NOT usb, it uses an RJ11 connection to piggyback off the printer
Start TSP143IIU Printer
APG CD-101A Cable to link the drawer to the printer
Motorola LS2208 Scanner OR a Socket 7CI bluetooth scanner
Square chip reader OR the Muria model (don't be misled by the paypal branding, it still works here after the firmware automatically updates).

title: Good but install problems.
text:
Ok, first, ordered this little card on the Oct 4 for prime delivery on Oct 6. It made it as far as Lake Charles then it got notice of delay. Not prime's fault, but lame excuse (mechanical difficulties) by UPS. Item arrived on Oct 9th.

Pros: Very small card. The Noctura heatsink dwarfs it! Looked for this form factor for future build even though it is in a Riotoro CR1080 case on a full ATX board. This will eventually go and downsize to mini-itx. Since it uses PCIE power, another point for future build. Ran some benchmarks and it performs as expected. I can run the limited gaming fine at full resolution and framerates.

Con: Install is not good at all! The unit it replaces was a GeForce 650TI(1Gig), so should have been as easy install, but NOOOOOOO. Black screen after the BIOS. Hmmm. The limited instruction pamphlet (one little paper stating to go to geforce to download the drivers..:p) is pretty useless when you run into problems. So, replace it with the 650ti and computer booted again. Hmmm. Removed all the current drivers, put the 1050ti back in and black screen. Long story short, eventually got it to work and instructions are below for others to follow if you run into problems. zuse at your own risk..It may work for you, it may not. Fans are small and a little high wine is expected, so not a con. System still pretty quiet.

Instructions for my system:
1. With old card still in, and if you have on-board graphics, go into bios and set to use the on board graphics.
2. Shut down, remove the old card and hook up video to on-board.
3. Put in the 1050ti, but do not hook the video up to it.
4. Boot the computer go to geforce.com and download the drivers. I could not get the latest drivers to work, so used the 385.69.
5. Run the program and let it find the card and install the drivers.
6, Shut down and hook video to 1050ti and hope it works. If not, well, you are on your own.

My system: I7-3770 (nonK.. fast enough), Gigabyte Z77 Ds3h, 16G Ram, Samsung 850 EVO 128G(Win10), MSata 120(Linux Mint), 500G WD Black 7200, Riotoro CR1080 case with 650W PSU(way overkill now). Two 120 front case fans and one 80mm rear, Noctura NH-C14S with 120mm fan with idle temp at 32C.

Would have gave it 5 stars, but when you run into install problems, it will set most off. I have quite a bit of experience in building systems and I try all things to get something to work before I send it back. Overall, not a bad card and maybe it would have work better on newer motherboard. I can't try it on my other system due to case not having any vid card slots(mini-itx with small In-Win case.

title: (+)Far better than my previous T5i
text:
The first few paragraphs outline my journey, reasoning, and learning curve for the T6i purchase.

(+)Far better than my previous T5i. I resold my Amazoned T5i purchase in 2016, and shopped for months for the next move upward. I had heard that many were ditching Canon and Nikon for Sony, and looked at the rx100ii and the a6000-6500, but kept coming back to Canon for great optics at affordable rates. Canon has such a huge lineup of lenses that have been around for years, it didn't make sense to dump my 24mm, 40mm, 18-55mm, and the 55-250mm, that I kept while selling my T5i on Amazon. I took some wonderful pictures with my T5i too.

(-+)I like shooting animals, birds, flora, and landscapes. I use my cameras primarily with center point auto focus on M. I'm a hunter! I have tried taking auto-focus pictures with the T6i and the T5i at parties, and I guess I'm just too picky to like the outcomes. I want flash and auto working great, but I never see great results. Faces are very often a little soft(with built-in flash). Now, my friend at these affairs has a Sony RX100ii which is the ultimate party camera IMHO. Multi-face detection and more AF points make that camera a no-brain winner for candid pics or poses at parties, with a powerful pocket camera and Zeiss lens. On the other hand, shooting hummingbirds, the T6i is awesome, the RX100ii, forget it(stay with parties and vacations). If I wanted to work harder, like a wedding, in manual mode with a better flash, the T6i would then be the clear party winner. Low light without flash, the Sony RX100ii is amazing. I tested it against a Canon 6d at Yosemite and beat the 6d for those dark scenes(like inside Ahwahnee Hotel). Enough about the RX100ii. The T6i has a video snapshot feature that stitches several seconds of video together into a single movie, which is a much better party option for this camera, and super for trips. In a few minutes people can watch a video of your entire trip to somewhere without boring them to tears with hours of video.

I had used the T5i for about 2 years, and rented the Canon 6d and 80d in the last year while running tests for the next camera purchase. I really wanted the 80d or 6d, but ended up spending money on furniture that was earmarked for camera gear, and had to set my sights on affordability/quality. I rented the 80d for a trip to Eagle Lake in Lassen County, and paired it with a 400mm to shoot eagles/birds and other far off objects. I really don't know why, but that combo did not produce good photos. With my EF-S lenses, I had better luck, and from much closer, like dogs and people in the campground. Again, I'm picky. I'm a bit of a pixel snob. I was very disappointed, but remember, I rented these and do not know how they have been handled previously. 80d is over a $1000 new, and under that used. As for the Canon 6d and its full frame sensor, WOW! Now that is a $1500 camera worthy of its entry fee. Photos were the best I've ever taken. I took that on my new favorite two day trip circuit, Yosemite and then Fresno Zoo. Don't laugh people, the Fresno Zoo is up and coming with world class amenities!! Amazing animal/bird photos and landscapes in Yosemite. I was also using the Canon 70-200mm f2.8L for a super combo. OK, I couldn't afford that $3000 combo option after my furniture spending. So I came back to earth, with awesome photos in hand, and set my wallet towards something more practical but hi-tech.

(+)So the year long journey ended at the Canon T6i. I had the four lenses already, so that made this purchase even easier. By the way, remember what I said about party photos, I purchased the camera from someone that had shot several weddings, and I can see why he sold it. There are other far superior wedding cameras, like a 6d for sure. I rated this camera 5 stars, because it combines great features, photos, and a great price. I can definitely see better photos with the same lenses listed above. The Digic 6 processor with 24mp is producing far nicer pictures than the T5i. When I bought the T5i, many people did not move to that camera from T4-3-2, because they just didn't see the better features. I think this is the first huge jump from one iteration to the next. My pictures of birds are far better than T5i. There aren't flowers out yet, so nothing to report there. I have only used this with STM lenses and the primes of 24mm/40mm. I can't wait to connect a Canon 70-200mm f2.8L lens on this T6i, and hopefully see a big jump up from my 55-250mm.

(+)My first big outing with T6i was to the Sacramento Wildlife Refuge. Millions of birds, no really, millions! I took the best hawk photos I've gotten to date, best birds in flight, and video of thousands in flight. I paid $550 for the T6i, and that is the best camera at that price point. Refuge had deer, eagles, ducks, geese, hawks, and tons of varieties of each. The video on the T6i is really good HD at 30 frames per second. The other more expensive cameras give you 60 frames per second or 4k video. The 80d had time lapse video with 60fps which sounded really fun, but never got a chance to try it. I don't own a 4k TV yet, and didn't need 4k video. The T6i kills the competition(and higher end Canon cameras too) with one big, tilt out swivel feature, and flippable LCD screen. 2nd huge one that beats most other cameras(again other $$$ Canons too), is the touch screen, and is completely awesome. A movable touch screen moves this camera to the head of the line for most Canon cameras and the competition. Most pros, always say they thought it was a gimmicky feature, until they started using one. Try shooting a shot overhead or down at your shoes in water or mud, forget it!! You will move on or take a dumb pic. None of Canons cameras above this(OK, T6s) have a tilt out and touch screen LCD screens. I still cannot verify, from my use, that the 80d was a better camera which has tilt-touch. Video is touted as better, but I did not use it.

(-+)I was liking the fact that the T6i had NFC and wireless capability, compared to my old T5i which did not. I loaded the Canon software on my android phone and controlled the cameras basic functions from the phone for remote shooting. Fun feature, but usually for full auto applications that I don't usually utilize. NFC, I set that up and tried it out, but i usually shoot in RAW mode, and phones don't display RAW, I'm guessing, and my android is 4 years old now. So again, a nice add-on, but connecting a USB to the computer or pulling the SD card is more functional for picture or video transfer. Reviewing your photos on the camera, is again, way better than other cameras NOT offering touch screen. You can zoom in instantly to see how good that photo really is, instead of jockeying buttons or dials!! BIG PLUS!! Of all the Canon cameras I have used in the last two years, the T6i, has the worst battery life. Now I say worst, and that sounds bad, but you can get a full day of several hundred pics on a battery. The T5i and T6i are rated the same as 440 pictures on a battery(what is that the lowest jpeg quality with 440 shots in a row and then shutting down??) I have never seen 440 shots from either one of these cameras, which at single shooting mode, could take a couple days for many people. I purchased the camera with three batteries and do burn through at least one battery in half a day of a couple hundred single shots, with camera being on a lot. The Canon 6d and 80d, have ridiculously good battery life, which is hard to burn through in a day of casual shooting. I still think the T5i has better battery life, which is a subjective analysis. I had three of those batteries, and rarely got to the second one or spares. All batteries charge fairly fast. Get a USB charger or an AC/DC cigarette lighter adapter for the ultimate in recharging on the go. AC charges devices much faster and they are cheap to buy.

There are a lot of great cameras out there now, and they are exponentially getting better. Like the giant steps from T5i to the T6i, the advancements are bigger. Canon has two other cameras above this, not counting the T6s, 80d and the 6d, and the 6d is the clear winner beyond the T6 lineup, but again at another $1000!! I still have hopes for a 6d, and a 70-200mm f2.8L(with IS or not). I got so-so results from my 80d usage. That 6d+f2.8L combination for picture taking is all you need to approach professional photography at $3000+ new. My recommendation for new buyers on a budget, get this or the T6s body only, and spend a couple more dollars on great lenses. I find I use a 40mm and 55-250mm STMs, with the 24mm and 18-55mm STMs getting less use. A couple of better lenses than these will yield even sharper graphics. Many times the 18-55mm kit lens is FREE with the purchase, nice bonus. Read the manual, or get David Busch's T6i/T6s manual on Kindle or print(Kindle is better). His version actually teaches many camera basics along with the T6 usage/features, smart guy. I'm still learning every time I pick up the camera. Read these things with camera next to you, and pick it up and try everything.

For dedicated music listening, I would probably look at something else. Listening to music on my laptop, I just couldn't hit that 'sweet spot' with the EQ. I could get close, but just... not... there. For my listening preference I had to dial the mid bass and treble back to about half of my normal settings. Once I did this, the sound cleaned up nicely. They seem to be pretty sensitive above 12kHz and if I boosted these bands to my usual preset, the sound was harsh and distorted. I could set the 70Hz band to my usual level but the low mids had to be dialed back similar to the high end. Of course this is all subjective so your experience may be different. My reference music was several tracks from Acoustic Alchemy and included both live and studio recordings.

Comfort 5/5
Value 5/5
Construction 5/5
Sound Isolation 3/5
Sound Quality 3/5

One note: I had one of the ear pads come off of the phone and stick in my ear. I reinstalled it and it hasn't happened since so it probably just wasn't completely on the first time.
