title: Great light for a great price!!
text:
I did my due diligence when looking for a light for my 8 gallon aquarium (18"x9"x11"). Other lights considered were NanoBox Reef and Ecotech Radion series. This light won it for me due to cost, control-ability and overall fit for my size tank. I am already eyeing an upgrade in the future to a 36" aquarium and two of these Primes linked together (through WiFi) will be perfect.

The spread on this light is just enough for the length of my tank. It is listed as enough for coverage of an 18"x18" square and that would definitely be the coverage limit for this light. If you are keeping moderate light demanding coral I would shoot for 14"x14" for perfect coverage. I have a few SPS corals in the aquarium and positioned them more towards the center (they are doing great and coloring up more than with my Current Orbit LED) with soft corals towards the outside. I am running the blues, UV, and violet just over 65% right now, with white around 30% and red and green below that. I am noticing more fluorescence in my corals and everything is growing well. I am noticing a bit a hair algae growing, whereas I had none with my Current LED maxed out at 100%, so I can tell this light is definitely more powerful.

Pros:
1. WiFi!!!!
2. Each color is controllable for the perfect spectrum that you want
3. Size - This thing is tiny for the amount of output!
4. Customer service - The original mounts the were shipping with these lights were defective and caused the lights to droop. I contacted support and received a whole new hanging kit (not just the defective piece) for free. Great customer service.
5. Link-ability - For my future upgrades I will be able to link more of these lights together and control them all at once!
6. Smart fan - Depending on the temperature the fixture is operating at, the fan turns on and off accordingly, great feature!
7. Lunar phase - The LEDs can follow the phases of the moon (new moon = no moonlight, full moon = moonlight at what you set it, other phases vary in between in intensity)

Cons:
1. Dimmer buzz - Although not noticeable from more than a couple feet away, the LED dimmers buzz slightly when the intensity is higher (like mid-day sun intensity). Reading online from some LED gurus, this may be due to using slightly cheaper quality dimmers. As long as the dimmers have good longevity, I am okay with the slight buzz when I am standing next to the tank (my Vortech MP-10 makes more noise).

Overall great light for a great price and hard to beat!!! You can find them used on some on-line forums for even cheaper (~$150).

title: Don't Buy If You Want to Charge a Canon OEM Battery
text:
As MANY OTHER reviewers have pointed out, this unit WILL NOT CHARGE a Canon OEM battery; the charger works great on the off-brand batteries. Even if the unit worked, it seems a little pricey at almost $80. Some reviewers said that they used a screwdriver to adjust the contacts in order to charge a Canon OEM battery. Straight out of the box, the charger worked great for the non-Canon batteries, but was DOA when it came to the Canon OEM batteries. So, being very mechanical, I too tried the "screwdriver trick." It seemed to work at first, but then I noticed that the battery would disconnect from the charger. No matter how much I tried, I could not get a stable connection. So, I looked at the battery terminals and the charger's connection pins; I also tried to see if I could discern a difference between the OEM and generic battery.

I am convinced that trying to adjust the charger terminals with a screwdriver ISN'T THE ANSWER. It appears to me that the issue is the height of the charger's connectors. BUT, at $80 why are would you try to make chicken salad out of chicken sh*%! Watson's engineers need to fix the problem and stop selling a defective product OR, in the alternative, sell it as a charger that ONLY WORKS WITH NON-CANON batteries.

PROS: Pretty good build; has a readout on the front advising you of the charging status; heavy duty electrical cord with good length; heavy duty car charging cord; seems to do a good job charging NON-CANON batteries.

CONS: No instruction book; has a test button -- what does it test; the price -- way too high; WILL NOT CHARGE CANON OEM BATTERIES (isn't that what you bought it for?)

Too bad -- I've been hunting for a decent Canon dual charger.

title: Great surge protector.
text:
Works great. Nice spacing to use multiple bricks for external drive enclosures and what not. USB is a nice option if my charger goes missing and someone else is using it.

This device has already saved me once. I had a leg massager that I use on a dialy basis because I have restless leg syndrome and that helps. The other night I was using it and in a big flash I heard a pop and everything on the surge protector went out, including my newly built desktop and 42inch TV. The cable on the massager had become loose and I didn't notice it. It twisted and broke, and the positive and negative collided in a loud pop and sparks. I was extremely worried that my new desktop and TV were done. To my surprise, the surge protector just tripped itself and turned itself off. I switched it back on (after pulling out the massager of course) and everything is fine. The Messager is done for which I could care less about, but all the other electronics survived. I didnt know it would protect a surge on any of the outlets on itself, so that was nice to know. Because of that, I highly recommend this product.

title: A very capable and silent switch
text:
This switch is perfect if you want something that just works, where you don’t have to tweak QOS/Routing/VLans/Link Aggregation/SNMP/Port Mirroring etc. It requires no setup. Just plug in your cables and you are ready to go!

Since this is a fanless design, it is also very, very silent. Another advantage of not having a fan is that it is less likely to suffer from dust build up that can lead to overheating. Though not mentioned on the box or product description, this has an internal power supply (no cable bricks or large wall plugs).

This can easily be used for a 24x7 setup, and can be completely neglected in a closet/desktop/rack mounting. I can't say yet how well it will hold up over the long term, but I'm not too worried since it comes with a lifetime warranty too. So far I have had zero issues with downtime, speeds, latency, heat, etc. This switched replaced multiple smaller switches, and every device that was working on the original switches, immediately came up at 1Gb on the new switch.

As an added bonus, this switch came with an excellent pair of rack ears for rack-mounting, and also some rubber feet stickers in case you decide to use this on a desktop. This is great forward thinking from TP-Link as in my experience all desktop placed switches scratch and ruin the tabletops.

title: Price, Power, Quality, look no further!
text: So for starters I bought two of these surge protectors to use for my media room. They are both loaded down to the USB ports and have yet to encounter any flickering of lights or maybe a situation where lights and electronics run at a dimmed power level. This baby can handle 4000 joules I believe which is more watts than the average person will be demanding from it on a daily basis. I run a few Xbox's, a PlayStation, 3 tv's, surround sound system, all kinds of accessories and to top it off a custom built PC running a 1000 watt power supply. All in all it clean looking, provides safe power to your electronics and has a 6 foot power cord! Also the smart USB chargers crank out some power at 3.1a when your little iPhone charging block does either 1a or 2.1a at most. So if you have smartphones and tablets alike rest assured they'll be charged in no time! As far as the bad review from another customer, people need to understand whenever you mass produce anything it won't always be 100% so if you run into some bad luck don't sweat it that's why Amazon's return process is there and it's simple. Thank you for another great product from Amazon.

title: A Better Choice Than the Onkyo CS-265
text:
I bought this to be a bedroom system for listening to MP3s via flash drive, FM radio and as the aux sound output for my bedroom TV set. It has been just great so far. I had bought an Onkyo CS-265 for my daughter as a present and had been impressed with the sound of that unit and how seamlessly the Bluetooth works. But I did not like the glossy plastic finish of he Onkyo (a real dust and fingerprint magnet) and it does not have a line-level output for a subwoofer. After researching other units, I settled on the Sharp XLF-102B. I really like the metal case on the main unit and the metal grills on the speakers, which are also made out of MDF instead of plastic. They sound better than the Onkyo speakers to me and the stiffer cabinets don't resonate at higher volumes. Plus the Sharp has 5 watts more per channel than the Onkyo. When I added a small 100-watt powered sub to the system, it really came alive. Freed of trying to drive bass notes, the Sharp now plays louder and clearer.

I have bought both the Onkyo and Sharp units, set each up and listened a lot to both.This unit is better made than the Onkyo with metal and MDF surfaces instead of plastic, has more power, and a subwoofer output, plus it's $75 cheaper. The Onkyo is sleeker-looking and has more name appeal, but that's it.The Sharp plays reasonably loud, sounds at least as good, has more features and is better-built. Don't criticize this unit as some have for not playing at 110 decibels. It isn't built to do that. If you want the kind of power that delivers ear-splitting volume, you are in the wrong price range here.

title: No Gimmicks, Just Great Cooling With Low Noise
text:
Excellent cooler and great value.

With four fans included you get a great push-pull effect, although obviously that makes the total depth of the ensemble quite large. You'll need to check your case to see the best way to fit this in.
On the packaging and on reviews that I've seen the LGA 1366 platform is not mentioned as being supported. This cooler does indeed work just fine with an LGA 1366 motherboard (in my specific case i7-920 CPU, Asus x58 motherboard). Just use the standoffs for the 115X and you'll be good.
With careful positioning of the fans and routing the fan cables you can get a nice daisy chain effect that helps reduce cable clutter in the case and this also ensures that all fans are equally controlled from one source.
At full speed the fans can be noisy but typical speeds are quiet. The pump itself is very quiet with no noise at all.

Update 3/24/2016 after allowing Thermal Paste to cure and then applying overclocking and stress testing.

I could not get my CPU temperatures above 50 degrees C, which is about 20 degrees better than with my previous (Arctic) air cooler.
Once the stress test was over the temperatures reduced to 33 degrees in about 3 seconds.
Awesome heat removal capabilities and the fans remained quiet during the entire test.

title: A very average notebook that is almost unserviceable
text:
I have considered purchasing this notebook for an older ailing Lenovo that has been very reliable for the last six years. I have read a lot of positive reviews and I have done a lot of research on this particular model. I have taken the time to go out to retail stores and physically look at this machine as well. If I purchased it, I would only buy it from Amazon.com as their customer service is incredible.

Here is my counter take to all the positive reviews: (I think people should know some of the negatives as well before buying this product)

Positives:
A lot of bang for the buck - new Broadwell Intel i5 processor, 8GB of RAM, USB3 ports, HDMI output, etc., DVD writer and for a reasonable price. It's also a nice looking laptop and I like how they have textured the plastic to keep finger prints down. It's also nice that you get a 1 year accidental breakage warranty for free. More on the warranty later.

#1: It has a 500GB 5400 Hard Drive. This is a crippling component for such an otherwise fast notebook. ASUS could have at least put in a 7200rpm drive for a few bucks more or even a hybrid SSD/HDD drive for just a little more. Many people don't realize it but you are typcially waiting on your hard drive to retrieve data most of the time. It doesn't matter how fast your processor is if it has to wait on a pokey hard drive all the time. The net is you end up with a poor performing laptop due to this one component.

So you say, "no problem" just go out and buy a Solid State drive and replace it. Not so fast! First you can't get access to the hard drive without tearing the entire machine apart. What does it take to do this? First you need to remove all the screws from the bottom of the case. You then need to carefully pry open the plastic tabs around the case, (which is not for the faint of heart) Once that is done, you need to remove multiple ribbon cables from the keyboard. You then take out 4 screws and change out the hard drive. This might not be that difficult for a PC technician, but the average individual would never want to attempt this. So - in summary: By ASUS putting in a 5400rpm Hard Drive in this notebook is like putting wooden square wheels on a Ferrari.

#2. The battery is not user reaplaceable either. Same proceedure as #1 above. We all know that laptop batteries only last so many discharge/charge cycles and they usually need to be replaced after a couple of years. Be ready to spend some big bucks to have the machine sent in or pay your local technician to change out the battery when it dies. This laptop also only uses a 2 cell battery (3700whr) which, I highly doubt, will give anywhere near 5 hours of useage that ASUS claims. They could have easily put in a larger battery if they wanted. They could have also made it user replaceable, like companies have been doing for the last decade.

Oh, and did I mention that if you do go in and try to replace either of these components, ASUS says you void your warranty. (I verified this with ASUS directly) So - if you want to make the machine faster, you take the warranty on yourself.

#3. Only 1 memory slot. Not a huge deal, as 8GB's is typically all anyone will need, but the machine is not utilizing dual memory channel mode which will have a small effect on performance. Also - forget about ever upgrading the memory beyond 8GB's with only one memory slot. You may not need more memory now, but as software keeps getting more bloated, you might in the future.

#4. 1366x768 diplay panel. Not exactlly high resolution when other manufacturers are touting 1080P for almost the same price with much smaller screens. This is not just Asus, but all the manufacturers who are still making cheap low HD laptop displays when for a few bucks more they could be giving us a much better panel.

#5. Keyboard has a lot of flex in it and users of previous models have complained that they keyboard quickly wears out. Only time will tell on this and your mileage will probably vary depending on what you have used in the past.

#6. Trackpad is not very responsive and the left/right mouse buttons are on the same plane as the rest of the mouse pad. This makes the buttons difficult to press and use. Who decided that the old raised mouse buttons were bad on a trackpad? Once again, I'm sure this was cheaper to make.

Unfortunately ASUS is not the only manufacturer who are doing these things on low to moderately priced notebooks.. They all are. Why are they doing this? To be more price competitive and make more profit. You can't blame them for this, but in the end, it's the consumer who is going to suffer.

Is this a terrible notebook? No. I'm even thinking about keeping it, but I can upgrade the slow hard drive to an SSD and I can also replace the battery when it dies as I have been a professional PC technician in the past. I'm not happy about the display resolution or the trackpad, but at this price point, almost everything is a compromise. My only other choice is to pay more than $1000 to get a machine that is user serviceable and has a higher resolution display along with better keyboard and trackpad.

This is my dilemma. Let me know your thoughts.

Unfortunately, in my opinion laptop manufacturers are not making better laptops for the money. They are making disposable products in hopes that consumers will just throw them out and buy new ones. I think this is a very bad trend for the consumer.

Update: July 26th 2015

I decided not to keep this laptop and instead, purchased the ASUS TP500LA which was also a mixed bag.

First, when I received the laptop, there were was stuff loose inside of the machine. I took the bottom panel off and found two screws and a couple pieces of plastic loose inside the machine. It's a good thing they didn't short out anythingn on the motherboard.

I'll post a review of that laptop later, but I'd give it the same rating as this computer. The trackpad is terrible on it and the high resolution screen is poor. It's sad how laptop manufacturers are no longer building quallity products these days.

text:
I bought this as an inexpensive camera to take on an upcoming diving trip. I have not had a chance to test it underwater and will update my review after my trip. (BTW I bought the VVHOOY underwater camera case for it because it include a red filters that I do not have for my other cameras. The camera fits nicely in the case, I probably won't know if it is waterproof until it is too late. )

I read the complaints about the manual and yes the print is small and I had to use a magnifying glass to read it. But I could read it and the instructions were clear. The part that was a little unclear is how to connect to an iPhone using iSmart DV or as other have recommended PNJ iCam.

I thought both applications would not connect to the camera via wireless, then I went back and read the manual. The steps are:
* Turn on wireless on the Akaso EK7000
* For an iPhone or iPad, go into Settings ... W-Fi and look for a network called "iCam AKASO"
* Select that network then enter the password 1234567890
* It will connect with a warning that there is no Internet access

Now go back to iSmart DV or PNJ iCam and click on the icon to "Add a camera". After that both apps worked. Also, I tried to download PNC iCam onto my iPad first and it was not available in the App Store. But I checked on my iPhone 7 and it was so I downloaded it. After it was on my iPhone it also showed up on my iPad. I was able view, download and delete photos and videos from both apps.

So far, I like the camera for the videos and photos it takes and the ability to navigate the menus. It seems similar to GoPros I have used before but for a lot less money. I will update my review after my trip. Also, I would like to confirm it did take my 64 GB memory card even though the manual states the maximum is 32 GB.

title: A Very Handy Antenna Balancer/Splitter/Combiner
text:
This is a great piece of antenna tuning gear. Not only will it combine a UHF antenna with a VHF antenna, if you have a strong UHF or VHF band signal you can use this to attenuate just the band that's too strong.
In my case, the UHF signal was so strong it would blank out my distribution amplifier. My VHF signals were barely strong enough for good reception. An attenuator had to be installed on the antenna feed on the nights my wife would watch PBS. With this device installed and a small attenuator on the UHF leg, the signals are nicely balanced. The main antenna feed goes to the 'Combined' port on this unit. Add the attenuators that are needed to the UHF or VHF ports on this unit. Use coax from the UHF/VHF to a 2-way splitter/combiner to mix the signals together again, and connect to your distribution amp. No more 'fiddling' to get the UHF in!
Thee metal combiner/splitter comes in a plastic box made to be installed on an antenna mast. By artfully prying around the sides, the metal unit will come out of the plastic box. Much smaller and neater for an indoor install.

title: Quick to install, easy to adjust, very sturdy

Very easy to install and it moves side to side very easy. You do have to loosen the screws the adjust the height. For my use however, I just needs some side movement which it does well. It also rotates clockwise and counter-clockwise quite easily, which I'm not using, but seems very fluid.

Mounting took a few minutes, there's no template, but I was able to mark the holes by holding the unit up as it's pretty light. Given the ease of adjustment of the arm, it was easy to put the monitor onto the mount, especially with the notched top screw holes for the monitor screws. title: Fantastic sound quality comes with included balanced headphones or any headphone
text:
I got this yesterday & there is a learning curve, so I will save you a lot of time & frustration. Your micro SD card must be formatted to the old FAT32 which the device will do for you. They have a firmware update which you download then put it on the micro SD card & boot up the device. It then seems to see it & upgrade (I think...). I formatted a new 64 gig card then put it in my iMac & clicked & dragged about a zillion Album folders from the iTunes Music folder. Formatting the card creates a folder called MUSIC: this is where you click & drag the music folders or individual songs.
All of my music is Apple Lossless ripped using iTunes.
When you install your micro SD card the device says "No music found" so I went into the settings a selected "update database" then the songs were available.
I must tell you that you need to go to HiFiMan.com to see the PDF user manual which gives you only the basics. The device does not come with a manual.
The device does come with in ear monitors which use the "balanced output" & the sound is outstanding. I am also using the super excellent Cardas A8 in ear monitors in the regular phone jack & the sound is EXTREMELY good. With this combination it is hard to stop listening. I also use the HiFiMan 400s headphones with great sound.
Once in a while the device locks up the use of track selection & volume control for about 2 minutes but the music keeps playing from song to song.
Here is the conclusion & the BOTTOM LINE: Considering that this has the sound equaling Astell & Kern for a $1000 less I am very happy. Dr Fang Bian is a brilliant designer & a really nice person that I am able to visit with at the HiFi shows for several years. It just keeps getting better for us budget music lovers. Buy this & find out how great it sounds!! Keep a micro fiber cloth handy to keep the screen fingerprint free.
*** Update After listening for another day I like the SuperMini better than my Chord Mojo which costs $699. The Super Mini seems to have a bigger soundstage & more detail. The mojo is larger size & requires a smart phone, tablet or computer. I am now really happy with the SuperMini & the Mojo will get sold but it was great for 6 months. The battery life on the SuperMini has been great unlike the Mojo.

I didn’t have the WDR and DNR features on my old system either, and I have to say the difference is huge. I tried different lights on and off and tested it during different times of the day, but the system adjusts to show faces and other important stuff clearly in pretty much all lighting situations. I am pretty confident that I would be able to provide footage with identifiable traits to police if the situation of a break-in ever came up.

Cons:
None really so far. I would say that if you aren’t good with tech stuff, the manual seems to be on the basic side. However there are videos on youtube which are really clear about how to set everything up. One other thing to note is that Chrome is NOT compatible as a browser with this system. You can log in (as I tried at first) but won’t be able to get live view or playback to work or control any settings. According to my research, this compatibility issue seems to be true for other security brands as well so it’s not really a con.

text:
Edit: 02/14/2016. The problems below still persist after the recent iOS Nest app update. It has been months since I bought them in November 2016 and they still have not resolved this basic issue. I very much regret buying four of these expensive cameras. 

Edit: 04/02/2017. Chatted with Nest support about my snapshot history for the last three hours being totally blank (I don’t have a NestAware subscription and am limited to these snapshots). This has happened quite often since getting these cameras. I know there should be activity there. They tried some things like remotely resetting my camera which didn’t make much difference. During the chat with them, my history will suddenly be viewable on the iPhone. Then a few minutes later, it will be totally blank. This is true for multiple cameras. This gives me zero confidence that I’ll be able to view my history in a timely fashion in the event of an emergency. Also doesn't encourage me to give them any money for NestAware when I'm so often disappointed with how things work as it is.

Edit: 04/14/2017. Tried getting notifications working again as I periodically do since my original bad support experience in late 2016. The menus have changed slightly in the iPhone app and on the website which makes me think they attempted to improve notifications. Long story short...they still don't work. After walking around in front of the camera on and off for a half hour (alerts set to "only when away" and I currently have it set to Away), I finally got one single email to come in SEVEN MINUTES AFTER THE MOTION ACTIVITY EVENT. This is with me on wifi and monitoring my (push) email, so the problem definitely is with Nest and not my email. Ugh. Sigh sigh sigh. Please see my original review below for even more reasons not to invest in Nest. Will attempt to get notifications working again in a couple months. Not at all reliable now.

Original Review: 2+ weeks of dealing with Nest senior level support has left me beyond frustrated. 

I'm getting notifications for activity when I'm home despite "only when no one's home" being enabled in settings. 

After jumping through a ton of troubleshooting hoops and ultimately creating an entire new Nest account, the problem persists. 

Got a final phone call today after the "engineers reviewed my case" and senior support passed along the word from up top that the engineers say I need to have location services on for my issue to be resolved (which does not have anything to do with my problem as I've described it countless times). 

After explaining (for the 10th time) that I have the problem with location services both on and off, he proceeded to tell me that "it's a known issue and they're working on it."

I bought FOUR of these expensive cameras for several reason but notification support was a huge one, and now I've been asked to "keep an eye on updates" for an indeterminate time to see if it is fixed. (Also found out after buying them that notifications only show up ONCE every 30-minute interval for each camera, which is totally unacceptable.)

Except for this frustrating experience, the iOS and web apps are pretty good. But that does not ameliorate all of the other issues here and I refuse to rate the app more than one star until this is fixed. Will update this review if something changes.

PS: What you're viewing "live" on your cameras is sometimes 5-10 seconds delayed. I have fast internet with excellent wifi. This is ridiculous. Does not make me want to pay the monthly subscription for Nest Aware when they can't even get free functionality performing well.

PPS: My cameras go "offline" sporadically quite often. There's nothing else I can do to optimize their location or wifi settings. All cameras are within 10-15 feet of an 802.11ac wifi router. The one that goes offline most is actually about 5 feet from the router. I wish I had the option to plug in a cat6 ethernet cable, but it's wifi only. I'm at a loss with this product.

title: Abysmal - already sent it back.
text:
Like reviewer Axion below, I was looking to upgrade to this from the Edge 510 I've been using for a couple of years (and an Edge 500 before that). I echo most of his sentiments, though unlike him I actually LIKED the 510. I admit it was buggy, but that's been true of every Garmin Edge product I've ever seen, mostly because Garmin is simply a disaster in terms of their firmware/software. The only significant bugs I've experienced with the 510 are 1) Fussiness with uploading rides; sometimes it auto-uploads rides immediately upon completion, sometimes it doesn't. When it doesn't I have to fiddle around trying to do it through my iPhone, which involves closing and reopening the iPhone Connect app until it syncs with the device, or plugging/unplugging/plugging the device into my Mac until it shows up as an external disk, at which point Garmin Express will open and sync. Unfortunately, there's no way to force a sync with the iPhone Garmin Connect app - you've got to close/start/close/restart the app until you get a sync (why neither the Garmin Connect iPhone or Garmin Express Mac apps allow a forced manual sync is beyond me, but - hey - this is Garmin we're talking about). But I've had a lot less difficulty with this after the last firmware upgrade; 2) when you install a new firmware upgrade it will often reset a bunch of stuff on the 510. For example it might switch your current activity profile to a different one, and you might even have to reenter some settings. But other than those two glitches I've found the 510 to be very reliable and accurate. Also, unlike some, I like the touchscreen as it makes doing things on the fly a cinch.

In terms of riding experience, I ride 2,000 - 3,000 miles a year (will actually break 3,000 for this year in the next week), mostly on a Felt Z5.

Now, on to the 520.

The first thing I noted is the absolutely exasperating nature of the interface. The complexity and illogic are simply mind-boggling. As reviewer Axion noted, nothing is where you expect it, and some of the most essential stuff is absolutely buried. In addition the use of buttons over a touch screen exacerbates the problem by an order of magnitude. Instead of two buttons and a touch screen (I'm ignoring the power on/off button), you've now got six buttons. Worse, they're hard-press, chiclet-style buttons that require some force to press, so there will be times where you'll think you pressed the button but the press didn't register, and others when you'll press harder to ensure it registers only to find the button double activated (advancing a screen more than you wanted to, or scrolling up or down farther than a single item). Additionally, the start/stop button is now located on the bottom EDGE of the unit, rather than the bottom FACE, which means when you have the 520 attached to your bike using the "out-front" mount you'll find it a tight squeeze between the button and your handlebar.

I'll give an example of a common action. Let's say you want to set up a new profile. On the 510, you swipe upward on the screen, then press the tool icon get to the selection screen, then press "activity profiles" to select that feature, then press "page 1" to get to the first page for the profile you're establishing (all on the screen itself). At that point you'll see the screen layout with five fields (the default) and an overlay indicating "5" with arrows below and above that allow you to decrease/increase the number of fields you want to displayed, and then a checkmark you press to confirm. Once that's done you can press any of the displayed fields, and a list of options for that field will display: press up or down arrows on the screen to get to the one you want, press it, and now that parameter displays in the selected field. Repeat for the other fields and in a minute or two you've got the exact layout you want, and changing it on the fly is a piece of cake.

Now, try it on the 520, but before you do print out the manual because you're going to need it. A lot. Put it in your wedge pack or jersey pocket so you have it with you. And even when you do, you'll still get stuck since a) the material isn't arranged logically, and b) it assumes certain things are obvious that actually aren't (for example, it might show that the way to get to something is via Menu\Activity Profiles\Settings when it doesn't explain how to get to Menu in the first place). Anyway, to set up an activity profile, you hit a the topmost button on the right side of the device, which takes you to a list. You then use the two buttons on the left side to scroll up or down until you get to what you're looking for, in this case Activity Profiles. Now you use the top right button to advance to select this and go to the screen list that allows you to pick an existing profile or establish a new one by using the left-side buttons to scroll up/down. When you're on the one you want, it's back to the top right-side button to select it and advance to the next screen, in this case the pages screen. Scroll to the page you want using the left-side scroll buttons (though a lot of times you'll just want the top "page 1" screen, so you won't actually have to scroll), then hit the right-side top button to advance to the screen where you select the number of fields you want to display. Scroll up/down to get to the number and confirm it with a button. Now, you need to set up each field by selecting it - using the right-side top button - and then scrolling through a list of options; once you get to the parameter you want (and pray you haven't accidentally missed it by not hitting the button hard enough to get to it or hitting it so hard that you skipped past it, in either of which case when you use the top right-side to select it you'll find you've got the wrong parameter in the displayed field and you have to start over), hit the right-side top button and hit the back button to get to the preview screen so you can move to the next field. Repeat for all fields you want displayed, then scroll in the list to select the checkmark option and lock the screen page for that profile. Accidentally hit the bottom right-side button and you'll end up somewhere you hadn't planned and will be trying to figure out what to do next. By the time you get everything done, you'll probably be spitting teeth. I can't imagine trying to use the buttons on the fly. Using the out-front mount like I do, it's a tight fit to get to the bottom buttons, and awkward to fiddle with the side buttons. You really want to be cradling the unit in your hand to use the buttons precisely. If Garmin was dead set on using buttons instead of a touch screen, then they should have used soft-press rocker buttons on either side which would make things at least a little easier.

Okay, enough about the user interface. Suffice to say it makes the original Windows 8 Metro tiled interface look super-intuitive.

Another issue I encountered is that the unit grossly undercounts total ascent. It was so far off on my first ride that even though I already knew I was going to return it in disgust, I decided to do a second ride as a test. I have a close-to-home short course of 20 miles that I do when I want to be able to interrupt the ride and get back quickly if I need to. It's a 20-mile course where I'm never more than 5 miles from home. The total ascent for the course is just over 1,000 feet as consistently measured by my 510 over two years, my 500 for a couple years before that, the calculated Strava ride, and numerous other riders I know who use other Garmin devices, or devices from other manufacturers. There might be a max of 5% variation among those various sources, and some of that is likely due simply due to the fact that barometric altimeters found in Garmin Edge and other devices may report different results based on overall weather conditions affecting atmospheric measurements. The 520 reported 744 feet - about a 25% variation - on this course. I did a Google search and quickly found this is essentially a known and widely-discussed issue; there are many comments about it on the Garmin forums (and the 1000 appears to have the same issue). It's been speculated - and my ride seems to confirm it - that the reason is Garmin chose to use a new "smoothing" elevation algorithm that essentially ignores gentle climbs of less than a certain duration (if you ride a mile, it will report the proper ascent regardless of how gentle the slope is, but if it's a short segment, it ignores it). I could observe this phenomena as I was riding. There are parts of the course that have short, mild elevations - think of these sections as undulating - and the 520 simply ignores them whereas the 510 would recognize 5 - 15 feet of elevation gain. Thus, I wasn't surprised when the 520 reported 744 of total gain on a course that has actually has more than 1,000 feet. A few commenters in the Garmin forum have expressed a preference for this on the premise that's it's "more realistic", whatever that means. To me, accurate means counting all gains. If you're a trail rider or MTB guy who wants to know total ascent, you should definitely walk, not run, from this device. I was ready to send it back at this point but decided to test it on a longer ride with more pronounced hills, so I did one more ride over a 33-mile course. Again, my 510, Strava calculated course, and other riders consistently report this course at roughly 2,000 feet of total ascent; the 520 recorded only 1,676. BTW, you can observe the algorithm differences in action; on the 510 you'll see the elevation gain updating almost immediately on short modest inclines, whereas on the 520 it can be 5 -10 seconds after you've reached the peak of the incline before you seen any change in your total elevation gain, if it records any at all.

UPDATE ON THE ASCENT: Today I borrowed my buddy's 520 (since I'd already returned mine) and mounted it alongside my 510, then went for a ride. My specific target was a 2-mile segment with a total KNOWN ascent of approximately 210 feet (as determined based on elevation data from various map sources as well as numerous rider experiences using a variety of devices). The 2-mile stretch begins with some gentle ascent segments interspersed with some very short flats (100 feet max. each); about 1/3 of the way up the ascent becomes continuous with varying degrees of steepness, while in the last 2/10ths of a mile there's another short flat. The 510 recorded 208 feet, the 520 recorded 156 feet. This is what riders around here universally regard as a 2-mile hill, yet the 520 doesn't treat it that way.

Some may argue that total ascent doesn't really matter; one should only care about RELATIVE total ascent from one course/ride to another for the individual. But when you've been tracking the parameter for over 10 years, and when you regularly track it against others you ride with, it doesn't make much sense to suddenly find yourself with a device that registers such a difference.

Next up: display of average speed. My Edge 510 displays average MOVING speed (which is the speed I'm interested in) when I select the display parameter "average speed". The 520 appeared to display average speed as in total distance/total elapsed time (including auto-paused time); in both instances when I got home and uploaded my rides my "average moving speed" time was slightly higher than the final average speed time displayed on the 520 when I ended my ride.

So far the main advertised advantage to this unit seems to be the Strava segments, but I've heard those are coming to other Edge devices eventually via firmware updates, so while those are all that important to me, I'd rather just stick with my 510 and wait.

The only advantage - and it's a very slight one - I found for the 520 over the 510 is the display. It's noticeably sharper, but under normal rider conditions only marginally more readable because the screen's contrast is just slightly better than that of the 510.

YMMV, but I found this unit to be a major disappointment.

title: Outstanding Quality, But Heavy Build and Poor Sound Cancelling
text:
Note: I bought these headphones during the Razer 50% off CES Appreciation Sale

I really wanted to love these headphones, I really did. I owned a pair of hammerheads for a while, and absolutely adored them. As a drummer, the Razer Hammerheads had decent quality, amazing quality, and a button for media control. They were perfect until they broke. I decided not to replace them because my warranty had almost run out, so I got these Razer Adaro in ears.

At first, I thought that the loss of a media control button would be ok. I could deal with it. Besides, if I got a Razer Nabu, that would fix everything. I was expecting the same fantastic sound-cancelling and audio quality. I knew they were big, but I thought "Hey, the Hammerheads were big, but not so bad".

I got them in the mail and wow, was I surprised. They were much bigger than I expected. People tell you they are big and heavy, and they are not lying. They stick out of your ears a good bit, and are heavy enough that its impossible to do any physical activity with them on, unless you use a beanie to keep them in. The smaller ring on the back is about the entire size of the hammerheads, and about 2x as heavy. This was a serious downside for me.

Then came the audio quality. I thought I knew what music was but when I first switched them on, the heavenly chorus of perfectly tuned treble notes and the superb coordination and sheer power of the bass made me almost cry tears of joy. These are the best pair of headphones/earphones/speakers I own today, as far as quality. Comparing them to the remaining ear in my hammerheads (left was out, right still worked) I knew I couldn't buy another pair of Hammerheads again.

And then, the sound cancelling. I was excited for this. I needed it so my ear drums don't explode while I'm performing or practicing. It was a serious downer when I found they were little better than almost any standard earphones with replaceable tips. My ears are small so I had the the smallest ones in. They might work a bit better with the bi-flanges on, but this was a disappointment. I could now only use these for sitting down and playing a game or studying.

So overall, these are headphones with amazing quality, but low grade sound-cancelling and sturdy yet heavy construction. I would recommend them if you only need them for playing games, but not if you need them for biking, running, drumming, or any other physical activity. My current set-up are these for gaming, and Apple Earbuds for nearly everything else. My brothers Sony DJ's work for some half-decent sound cancelling. My plan is to buy some decent Seinhiesers or Razer Krakkens, and possibly another set of Hammerheads if a new version with slightly better quality comes out.

title: *** BUYER BEWARE *** - Maximum possible resolution is 1920 x 1080 (1080p)
text: Buyer Beware - I ordered 3 of these cables based on the product description stating they support up to 4K resolution. I have two monitors that are 2560x1080 native resolution that I wanted to use for them. However, I was unable to get any resolution higher than 1920x1080. After much research, I learned that it's not possible for HDMI to convert to Dual-Link DVI at full 2560x1440 (1440p) resolution with a passive adapter because HDMI doesn't have enough pins. It requires an active adapter and I'm unable to find any manufacturer that makes an HDMI to Dual-Link DVI active adapter that supports resolutions above 1920x1080. The HDMI page on Wikipedia states that, although HDMI is electrical compatibility with DVI, it is practically limited to single-link DVI rates. If you're looking for 1920x1080 or lower resolution, these are great cables. Higher than that, they will not work.

title: Perfect as part of a wired setup for letting one's spouse/partner watch TV in bed while the other lays in blissful silence.
text:
If my girlfriend and I go to bed early enough to make me happy then she almost always wants to watch a show which prevented me from falling asleep because I just can't tune it out. For this particular application I chose to go with a wired setup because the biggest advantage of wireless (mobility) was irrelevant since it's not like she was going to be wearing these around the house; she was going to be using them night-after-night in the same location. Therefore the disadvantages of a wireless setup (extra weight of the electronics package and batteries, poor sound quality, poor and/or intermittent reception) weren't worth it. I needed to get the audio signal from the RCA line-out "line out" jacks on the cable box to her ears 20 or so feet away so (in addition to these headphones) I got the following:
1) a Male RCA to Female 3.5mm adapter http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B000I23TTE/ref=od_aui_detailpages00?ie=UTF8&psc=1
2) a 50' "headphone" (3.5mm) extension cable http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00I0XPCE8/ref=od_aui_detailpages00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 and
3) a tiny headphone amp that would take the "line out" signal and boost it to headphone level. http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B002T6NZMS/ref=od_aui_detailpages00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

The Adapter plugs into the cable box on the dresser and feeds the extension cable which is long enough to run along the baseboard and up behind her nightstand to then hit the headphone amp on her nightstand. The amp on her nightstand is nice because it gives her volume control, mute, and has an on/off switch since it's an active (powered) unit (this particular model uses a battery but others are available that use a powered wall adapter or USB power, etc.)

At the time of my purchase these headphones and all the goodies listed above were 87 bucks and I'm so happy I could do a little dance. She put them on and watched a video and I couldn't hear ANYTHING.

title: Very Good Sony Earbuds
text:
Very good in-ears.

Pros
+Cord: Very different to what I'm used to - it's wrapped in a rubber-like material which doesn't tangle easily! If you've ever worked on screen doors, the material is similar to spline. It's also long enough for me to easily have my phone in my pocket and not have it tugging or unplugging.
+Sound: (subjective) The audio is good across the board. Clear, and somewhat crisp. The bass, though marketed as "Extra", honestly isn't something I'd say should be considered extra. It's definitely there, but won't satisfy most bassheads. I listen to a wide range of music genres, EDM being one of them, and some of my favorite bass heavy songs can't compare to more open headphones and speakers. Good thing about these earbuds is the bass doesn't drown out the mids and highs, so it's nice to have bass with details.
+Fit and Construction: These are very lightweight, making them easy to wear for long periods of time. The hybrid silicon/rubber eartips are also comfy. With 4 sizes, it'll be hard not to find the size for you. And if you still cant find the right fit, try Comply foam eartips. With Comply, you can squeeze them to fit, and they expand when you place them in making them fit for your ear (their website can be used to find the correct size for the MDRXB50AP).
+3.5mm Right Angle Plug: One design feature some people either ignore or is underappreciated. The plug is also slim, making it easy to plug into phones with large cases. I like the right angle plug because I do sometimes place my phone in my shirt or jacket pocket, and I'd rather not have a cord jutting out so much with the risk of the cord getting pinched and damaged. Normally right angle plugs are built tougher, and this one is no different.

Cons
-"Extra Bass": was honestly expecting a bit more. The response frequency is very low (4 Hz), just it's not bassy enough. BUT. I am using these with the LG V20, so it's most likely the sound signature from the DAC.

Overall, a very good set of earbuds. Multi-function button works fine with the V20. Play/Pause/Answer, 2x to skip track. Haven't tested in iOS.

title: Works really well if you experiment with different antennas
text:
I just completely rewrote this. So I'm now giving it full five stars but with a caveat - GET A BETTER ANTENNA!! I dug around in the junkbox and found a six foot heavy telescoping antenna with PL-259 termination - sweet! So I built up a plate to attach to a standard camera tripod to elevate it a few feet. I made up an RG-58 coax soldered to an SO-239, the other end BNC to hit the AA7C. Lastly I added four 1/4 wave radials for 20-meters (my only band of interest with this) - and just doing that, 20m CW and SSB signals jumped through the roof in signal strength.

I've got this paired with a Ramsey 20m 2-chip $44 receiver that I rehoused with an added 10-turn main tuning pot, 2k bandspread and an active audio filter for CW. With the addition of the much improved antenna, I hear TONS of signals without having to crank the AA7C into overdrive which the very simple 20-meter receiver chokes on if I do. I can see why Ramsey can't "be all things to all users" - the whip they provide may well do a great job on scanner frequencies but it's all but useless on HF - so just so's you know that, and have a way to up the antenna a bit you'll do fine. For me, I'm building all this up so I can take a 20m CW/SSB SWL-only rig on a cruise next week - just for the heck of it, so I can log CW and SSB along with the GPS coordinates of where I heard them and send an SWL email QSL to all the stations I copy - just seems like a fun way to sit on our Owner's Suite balcony while the wife is playing Bingo :-)

All in all, it's now working really well!! I'll try to remember to add a photo of the setup

title: Functional, but mediocre poor-performing antenna
text:
I've had experiences with this 2.5" stubby antenna similar to what others have reported.

It works, and its sufficient for use around the facility where I work, mainly hitting local repeaters and a simplex channel dedicated to a pair of adjacent buildings. On the upside, it's very short and extremely flexible, and it's super handy for not getting in the way and keeping the whole radio very compact and easy to wear and work with.

On the other hand, it's really just not a very good antenna. As much as folks complain about the stock Baofeng antenna, this one is clearly less efficient and sharply reduces the range of the radio. If I want to use the radio for simplex communication outside my small workplace environment, I need to switch to the stock one or my longer whip antenna. This, I suppose is not totally unsurprising for its size, but it's a little disappointing.

Most of my disappointment is about build quality. It's certainly a very flexible antenna, but they achieved that by making the antenna out of ... well, it's not really even a "spring", it's just a soft coil of wire, that they've covered with a sort of silicone sock. And they attached that silicone to the base of the antenna by about the worst way possible -- they *glued* it. This is an obviously terrible idea, to anyone who has ever handled anything made out of silicone. One of its most important material characteristics is that almost nothing adheres to it. Predictably neither does their adhesive, and so one can expect the cover to come loose from the base in very little time. title: A Budget Priced Monitor With An LED Backlight!
text:
Yes, it has the newfangled LED backlights at this low price! Lower than some other non LED monitors of the same screen size. Why is it a big deal? Because most flat screen monitors use florescent bulbs which burn out after a few years of almost constant use. Once they begin to age, florescent bulbs start to flicker too, just like the ones in the ceiling of so many buildings. This flicker will really get to you if you spend a lot of time in front of a monitor. Besides, some studies show that florescent light is not good for our eyes and can contribute to increased irritability. Then, there's the eco factor. LEDs use a lot less electricity to be just as bright or brighter than florescent bulbs. They are also made with less toxic and lower toxicity materials. Florescent bulbs even contain gasses that are harmful if the bulb is broken.

I'd give this full stars if the stand was the same height as my other Acer monitor. I bought this one thinking I'd use it for a second monitor on my desktop PC setup. It is close to the same model, but not exactly the same as my other one. It has the same screen dimensions, but for some reason, the good folks at Acer decided to make the pedestal for the base two inches taller. The base itself is round rather than oval and is an inch narrower in diameter too. This may make it use a little less desk space, but it also makes it slightly more wobbly on my computer cart's monitor shelf. Both monitors fit side by side on the shelf nicely though the 'two eyes' appearance of having dual monitors is slightly cockeyed due to the difference in height. Update: I thought I could get used to it, but I must have just a little case of OCD, because it was distracting the heck out of me in a few hours. I put a inch and a half thick book under the old monitor so that the screens are now the same height.

My old one doesn't tilt at all, but I don't mind because straight up and down is how I need it for where it is sitting at almost eye level. The new one tilts a little bit, but the tilting is quite stiff. Trying to adjust it makes you feel that you may break something before you see how far it tilts. I'm keeping it at straight up and down.

I've noticed that the new one has a different design to it too. It's not glaringly different, but enough that it's noticeable when you look at them side by side. The corners of the new monitor are more squared, the frame around the screen is a little thinner, the base is round and has ridges on the front half rather than being smooth, the back has more vents (a great thing actually!) and is more squared, and the ports are on the bottom of the housing instead of on the back. This last one would probably be a big deal if I was thinking of hanging it on a wall. Not sure I could even hang the old one on a wall without messing up the cables since the ports stick straight out the back.

Since the new one is taller, I'll have a little more room under the new screen for the inevitable collection of knickknacks that find their way onto a computer desk over time. :) With the old Acer monitor, I'm more limited in how tall these knickknacks can be.

The brightness, color settings, etc are almost identical to the other model. If I put them on the same settings, they are virtually indistinguishable when showing the same wallpaper. But, the settings buttons are in a new more obvious place. On the old model, they were on the bottom of the screen frame and almost invisible unless you tilt your head to see under the monitor a bit. On the new one, they are on the front of the screen frame where they can be seen in the right light. They may as well be on the bottom however, since they aren't labeled. You still have to tap buttons and try to line them up with the graphics that appear on the screen above them to figure out what they do. I find on both that the best bet is to put them on 'movie' mode for my usually semi-dark office. Funny to see them on the front in this day and age of designers trying to make everything look sleek.

It has a DVI input like my old one does (a main reason why I bought it, that and the LED backlight replacing the fluorescent lights that all LED flat screen monitors used to have.), though it didn't come with a DVI cable. They aren't hard to get though, so I'll go get another one. The difference between VGA (the usually blue plug that comes with every monitor) and DVI isn't too noticeable in text websites and 'productivity' software, but I'll be quite apparent when I try playing 3D rendered video games on this new monitor with a VGA cable if I don't get a new cable. Monitors that come with a DVI cable often cost a lot more than what it'll cost me to go and get a DVI cable myself, so its okay.

It's a good quality monitor that does all it should for its price point. It's not a cutting edge thin frame monitor that costs more than my computer did to build a few years ago, but it will get the job done for me. Just getting LED backlight at this price is a 'wow' factor for me.

title: Setting The Record Straight "Faulty Capacitor Issue..."
text:
I figured I’d write this review to set a few things straight… “I” too hit the “Dreaded Capacitor Issue,” or what others refer to as a blank screen/blinking red LED. Why am I still giving this TV a 5 Star rating? Upon reading all the negative reviews online & on Amazon regarding this particular defect stating; "no replacement parts,” “brick,” or just being absolutely infuriated in general, I opted to pull my TV off the wall & rather than repairing (assuming that a repair would just delay the inevitable), I’d just go to the “Dark Side,” with a Sony XBR65X930D 65-Inch 4K HDR Ultra HD TV. The funny thing was, the Magnolia rep (non-commission based) @ Best Buy asked me while I was shopping, “Soooo, what kind of TV are you replacing?” When I said, “A Samsung PN64F8500,” he said, “Whoah, you’ll have to go OLED to get a comparable picture.” We’re talking about a 2013 Model TV that STILL outperforms the best of the best LED’s in the current market! I didn’t just take his word for it, Google “PN64F8500 vs OLED.” You’ll see that up until the 2016 HDR model, this Samsung outperformed even the best of LG's top-of-the-line OLED's....

Onto the story… I didn’t just take the reps word for it because I for damn sure didn’t feel like shelling out $7k for an LG OLED, so I gave the XBR65X930D a try (great reviews). I paid the same company who installed my home theater to swap the TV while I was at work (being too lazy to mount/level myself) & my Wife texted almost immediately afterwards stating, “The Plasma was better….” Sure enough, by the time I got home, she was absolutely right… Where picture quality was the most noticeable was in standard modes via Comcast HD content. Though HD content streamed via Netflix or via Blu-ray were nice, something “wasn’t quite right…” I was trying so very hard to make myself love it, but I kept comparing the video quality, the motion resolution, the black levels (so black, I was afraid my TV died during a scene of complete darkness,” etc… For the next week or so, I watched HDR content on Netflix (upgrading to the HDR, 4-Screen plan), binge watching the entire Marco Polo Series in HDR. I must admit..., HDR is GREAT. I’ve never seen Blue’s & Green’s in those shades, so my eyes were immediately drawn to these colors which popped, visually. Despite the colors (& 4K), the picture quality STILL didn’t live up to my expectations/comparison w/ the Plasma. Days had passed & I had pretty much written off the Samsung, submitting to a less superior TV (due to my fascination w/ HDR). That was until I was invited to my buddies house who has the Panasonic equivalent…. He’s an audio & videophile who spent a ton on his home theater, yet opted to keep his Panasonic. When I told him what I had & what I replaced it with, he said “FIX IT & RETURN THE SONY!” He then cycled through a series of content on his Plasma explaining the superiority Plasma STILL has to this day, with the only worthy challenger being a much more expensive LG OLED…

So I went home…, looked at my Plasma (looking as beautiful as ever, though non-functional) & opened a case (despite my warranty expiration) w/ Samsung support. After a series of absurd back & forth case updates (“YES, this happens regardless of Input,” or “The screen ITSELF doesn’t not turn on,”), even explaining the behavior or recording/uploading a video of the blank screen & blinking LED or providing an online thread pointing to the exact issue, I FINALLY got a # to call. No, it was no longer covered, but they did refer me to a local authorized repair facility that made house-calls. I suppose I could've just done the legwork myself, but I was hoping Samsung would own-up to this mfg defect (I was mistaken). Where I wasn’t mistaken though was that the repair centers are already keen to this issue & have UPGRADED CAPACITORS to replace the insufficient, defected (bulging & leaking) old ones. The technician was in/out of the house in about 30 minutes stating “w/ these new capacitors, you shouldn’t see this issue again.” He also stated, *sic “Your plasma is badass & one of the best TV’s around.” How much was the repair you ask? $250… I tore my Sony off the wall after a 2 week test drive (THANK YOU Best Buy Elite Plus) & mounted/leveled this one myself (just in time for Game 7 of the NBA Finals…) Just in time to see my Warriors end what should’ve been a historic season… (though ended up being historic for the Cavs)…, though I digress…

Bottom line, don’t believe the negative hype online. Board parts are no longer available (this is true), but the capacitors are still in stock, have since been upgraded & brought the BEST TV I’ve ever owned back to life, hung back atop my Fireplace mantle… You’ve got nothing to lose to quote a repair & unless you go OLED, you’ll be watching what you know in your heart is a far less superior set (I felt so disgusted with myself). Had every channel on Comcast or every video on Netflix been HDR, I’d have strongly reconsidered, but the content is minimal & life is too short to settle on crappy video… I work all day & the little time I have in front of the set needs to project the best picture possible… Shame on you Samsung for shaving a few $ w/ these crap capacitors, but THANK YOU Samsung for providing such a perfect & legendary set…

I like this case a lot. It fits my 2017 iPad perfectly. The holes are very slightly skewed, but not so much that they prevent anything from functioning. My camera still works fine, the charge port and speakers are clear, etc. I really like the sleep wake feature because I have autism, so I use my iPad for a lot of vital things (speaking when needed, emergency info, sensory calming apps, etc.) which means I need my iPad to be on me and switched on at all times. This case is very slim and lightweight, which I also appreciate, as I didn’t want to add any extra weight, given that I carry the iPad everywhere. The only minor complaint I have is that the power button is rather difficult to access through the case, and it takes a bit of pressure for it to register. Overall I’m extremely pleased with this case, and would recommend it to those soloing for something slim and functional.

title: They DO sync together!
text:
[[VIDEOID:fcdc50c8ccce61faf45203289a400739]] So far, so good. We just got these a couple days ago, and while I was concerned based on the reviews, they synced together very easily. They sound great, but I wasn't sure about the volume. So we took them outside and spaced them out where we'll be using them. Without even adjusting the volume within the phone, they seem like, at the highest volume setting, they will be the perfect volume for party ambience... not so loud they'll overpower conversation and not so soft that you can't hear them. The true test will be at a party we're hosting this weekend. I'll try to update the review if my opinion changes. They also match well with a bunch of flickering solar torch lights we'd also bought on Amazon and put around our pool.

As for the syncing, ignore the comments & reviews that say they don't sync. They DO. Here's what we did:
1) Turn on one of the speakers and pair it with your phone or other device
2) Turn off the speaker
3) Turn both speakers on and hold down the bluetooth pairing button until the white light ring on each of them blinks
4) When the white light ring on both devices turns solid, they are connected to one another and will automatically link to the phone or other device that you previously paired.

Enjoy!

text:
This is an INCREDIBLE center channel speaker for the money. I purchased this Pioneer SP-C22 based solely on the size of the speaker. The reviews helped make the decision easier as well. I built a custom entertainment center for our house, and when the final design was taking shape, it was determined that I would need a smaller (footprint) center channel speaker to fit the housing that I made for it. Our existing JBL Arena Series center channel was simply too big to fit in the entertainment center. That being said, this little center channel speaker, COMPLETELY transformed our movie watching experience and was worth twice what I paid for it. title: Don't waste your money
text:
UPDATE: Square Trade finally agreed to reimburse me the cost of the television, and they paid me the full original purchase price. I appreciate this and upgraded my review to 2 stars, but because of the hassle I don't think I'll be purchasing any future replacement plans from them.

My TV started to act up about 2 years after we purchased it. Good thing we bought the extended warranty, right?

When I first called in a claim, Squaretrade assigned a repair but left it up to me to schedule. That's okay, not great, except the repair company would not answer my calls. After several frustrating calls to Squaretrade, they figure out that repair company doesn't service my area. Finally they find someone, two weeks later, to come fix my TV. He does, it works, I was inconvenienced but not put out that much.

Two months later the TV has the exact same issue. I file a claim at Squaretrade and they schedule the exact same repair as before. I tried to ask them why they would do this if it only temporarily worked last time and all they said is "It's company protocol." Repairman comes again, remembers me, tells me he has no choice but to do the repairs they requested. He does so, even though he knows it won't fix the TV, and luckily for me the TV replicates the issue immediately after he does the repair. So he tells Squaretrade the TV is unfixable and they finally agree to replace the faulty unit.

After a full week I get information on my repair. They're willing to send me a new or refurbished TV with a value between $300 and $400. This is very much less than the $500 to $600 listed right in the total of the plan I purchased from Amazon. I don't fight this, though, because I just want a working TV. I select a lesser TV and they ship it to me. It arrives and one of the four mounting screws on the back is broken. I can't use this TV; a few days later Squaretrade agrees and sends me a return label. I send the TV back. A few days after that they tell me another one is on the way.

The second replacement TV arrives and I notice immediately a big gouge on the box. The TV has been dropped or hit with a forklift or something, and it has penetrated all the way to the screen, cracking it and making the TV 100% unusable. I have to send it back. Squaretrade agrees to expedite this service, but it's been 4 days and I still haven't gotten a return label for the TV yet. I'll update this when it's resolved, but at this point I regret getting a warranty. I'd rather spend a few hundred bucks and get a new better TV.

title: This Bag is Amazing!! Great for the Beginners and the Experts! I am in Love with this bag!
text:
I got my camera bag loaded up with all my stuff and I still have so much room! I'm so glad I went with this bag. The first one I looked at was smaller and cost more. I ended up only paying $35 for this bag and it was worth every penny. The dividers are removable and the whole inside of the body of the bag is the soft side of Velcro so you can arrange the compartments the way you want. And the net pocket on the inside of the lid zips up. I just love that it zips up! A lot of bags I looked at had a net pocket on the lid but they didn't zip. They just had a piece of tight elastic.
I am absolutely in love with this bag! I rearranged the dividers as soon as I got the bag out of the box. In this bag I currently have my Canon T5 camera body, a 18-55mm lends, my T5 battery charger, two T5 batteries, my Canon A2300 PowerShot Point-and-Shoot camera in a case, the PowerShot's battery charger, and one PowerShot battery in the body and in the top net pocket I have my 12 slot SD card holder, the T5 manual, and two lens cloths. I still haven't put anything in the side or front pockets. And I still have one compartment left in the body of the bag. If I put the PowerShot, all three batteries, and the two chargers in the side and front pockets I can fit 3 more lens, or 2 lens more and a flash, in the body of the bag. The side pockets are bigger than I thought. They could fit a battery charger and a battery or two easily. This bag is bigger than I thought it was going to be and I love it!
It is really well made too. All the grey parts are that water resistant fabric, the Velcro is super strong, and the outside is made with the fabric most electronic bags are made from. The shoulder strap on the bag (which I forgot to get a photo of) is really nice. The shoulder pad is a little stiff at first but if you bend it around for a few minutes it loosens up. I love this bag. This bag fits so much stuff! And it's only $35! There are also straps on the bottom front of the bag for small tripods.
I just love how much this bag can hold! In the body of the bag you can fit one camera body and four lens, or two camera bodies and two lens, or a body, or one camera body, 3 lens and a flash. I'm sure you could play around with the dividers and get all different types of combos. The side, front, and lid pockets are big enough to fit all of your batteries, chargers, SD cards, and other little things. This bag is amazing!
I included a lot of photos of the bag. For anyone wondering what the white thing is on the body of my camera, it's the slip the camera came it when you take it out of the box. I put my camera in it when it's in the camera bag or when it's just sitting on my desk to protect my screen. And the DS case has my point-and-shoot camera in it, a Canon A2300 PowerShot. It fit really well in my old DS case so I figured I'd use it instead of buying a new case. I keep my PowerShot in the case while it's in the bag for a snugger fit and for an extra layer of protection.
The bag was bigger than I expected so I included a photo with a water bottle next to the bag to show how big it is. I was very happy when I learned it was bigger. I absolutely love it. The price for this bag is amazing! Most bags from Canon are crazy expensive. There was a bag at Wal-mart that was in between 1/3 and 1/2 the size of this bag and they wanted $50. Sometimes you really just cant beat amazon's prices.
I would recommend this bag to anyone with a camera that is more than a point-and-shoot. I am in love with this bag! It is great for anyone, whether you are just starting out or you have a ton of equipment. This bag is huge and spacious. It is big but you can rearrange the dividers to fit your needs and change them as you collection grows. I love this bag all the more for that reason. You can use it if you have just started and once you build up your equipment you won't need to buy another bag. If you are considering this bag I say get it. It is totally worth the price and if you don't like it you can always return it. This bag is seriously amazing!!

title: Why Spend More Than You Have To?
text:
I wanted to get a camera carrying vest to use with my cameras. I have a Nikon D750 and a Nikon D810. I use a Manfrotto RC4 tripod mount with these cameras. I like the RC4 - it's solid and easy to use. I looked at vest from Cotton Carrier (635RTL-S), Opteka (MCH-25) and Movo (MB1000). They all looked the same, but the difference in cost was significant. The Cotton Carrier came with a Universal Adapter Plate, but I would still need to buy a Manfrotto RC4 camera plate to use with it ($149 & $18.29). The Cotton Carrier was set up for one camera. Both the Opteka and Movo came with an extra holster for a second camera. They did not come with a tripod adapter. The Opteka cost $5 more than the Movo - other than that I could not see a difference. You could also get upgraded metal mounts to use with the Opteka and Movo ($14.95).
I opted for the Movo with the upgraded mounts and a Manfrotto 394 RC4 adapter that included the plate for both the camera and a tripod. My order total was $92.97 delivered to my home. This saved me $74.32 over the Cotton Carrier and $5 over the Opteka with the same accessories, but I also got a belt holster to use with a second camera. An extra belt holster from Cotton Carrier would have cost me an extra $40.
Before I ordered anything I tried talking to support staff from each company. I could not find a phone number for Opteka anywhere. I found a phone number for Movo and they answered their phone and were very helpful. They even suggested that I not get the upgraded mounts until I first tried the ones that came with the MB1000 - they didn't think I would need them. It took numerous calls to speak with someone at Cotton Carrier. The message on their machine was not accurate. When I did speak to people they gave me conflicting information and one rep even contradicted himself in his emails to me. There's more to it, but I don't need to elaborate further.
So, I bought the least expensive rig with the most available and most helpful support staff. I have no regrets. My setup is solid. It works like a charm. My RC4 tripod plate stays on the vest. I have not had to change a single thing on my camera - it has the RC4 camera plate I've always had on it. I can go from vest to tripod without a problem and the camera is centered over the tripod because the Movo does not offset the mounting plate from the camera base like the Cotton Carrier's Universal Adapter Plate does.
This was a no-brainer for me. I've attached some photos so you can see what I'm talking about. If I were using a different tripod mount other than the RC4, I would buy that to use with the MB1000.
Most of the reviews for the Opteka and Movo listed the lack of a tripod adapter as a negative. Just buy a tripod adapter - save the bucks - go out for a 4 star meal with the money you save.

text: As a student, I like to listen to music when I do homework, and my old speaker recently broke. This cube is totally worth it. Because it is generally near me, I, unlike a plethora of other reviewers, listen at low levels of music. The speaker does pretty well, as it is controlled by your device volume. This works /fairly/ well (iPhone doesn't get as quiet as I wish it did). At the lowest iPhone volume, the speaker is relatively clear with little fuzz, but classical music can sometimes have a little more due to independent musical volume range within the piece. Another awesome feature is the aux in cord which allows me to listen to my antiquated iPod nano with no Bluetooth. My family actually liked it enough we bought a second one for the kitchen, where it is played at higher volume levels with retained sound quality. Another reviewer states that this cube is roughly the size of a stack of sticky notes (3" X 3"), and they are absolutely correct. Very nice and compact, which is useful for transportation. On transportation: the Bluetooth is wonderful at retaining a connection. I have repeatedly moved my phone closer, further away, gamed on it, etc. with no issues, and also repeatedly moved the speaker too. Seemingly hardy outer shell too, but it has a sort of pleasing, somewhat squishy texture. It's difficult to describe. (OCD customers: it can get a little fingerprinty) Also have had no issues with battery life, the red blinker is a nice, subtle reminder and it charges after the initial time very quickly.  If you are looking for a well-priced Bluetooth speaker that also has non-Bluetooth options to play at lower volume levels, in my experience, this is a great choice overall. Currently loving mine and expect to for a long while.

title: Something You Should Know
text:
I don't usually rate a product on the basis of it's delivery to me. However, in this case, I think it applies. I received the wrong battery. I was supposed to get a pair of new batteries but, instead, I got just one, in a cellophane wrapper with the correct label but the incorrect product. There was no commercial packaging, even though the batteries were described as new. Instead, the cellophane wrapper was open and the wrong battery slipped inside. It seemed pretty obvious that this was a returned item, sloppily handled and re-shelved.

Now... there are some things that I NEVER want to buy as a returned item. Batteries are high on that list. A well-used (or used-up) battery looks the same as a fresh one. The only way a person can know that he's receiving a fresh product , as promised, is if it is delivered in original, sealed packaging.

If you want to trust a system that actually encourages bad or used-up products... fine. But, I just though it was necessary to warn you.

title: Great option for a family that likes to travel
text:
Our family travels a good bit, especially in the summer, and the Canary provides us with a simple cost effective way to monitor the house when we are not there. We have had it now for about three weeks. Here is the rundown:

PROS:
- Quick/easy set up. It appears that all of the early issues that I read about on the installation side have all been worked out. Just plug it in, follow the instructions in the app to connect to your phone and you are up and running in minutes.
- The wide angle on the camera allows us to easily cover all three entrances to the main floor of our house from one position.
- Very high quality video
- Intuitive user interface makes it easy for the whole family to use
- Auto arm/disarm when you leave or enter the house is a nice feature

CONS:
- The unit tends to jump in and out of night vision mode periodically (especially at night or around dusk), which currently triggers a notification.
- Canary is extremely sensitive and will send notifications for any motion including small movements of light, shadows, and reflections on the wall from windows and doors. You have the ability to tag these notifications to train for future monitoring, but it can result in a lot of notifications early on especially in a house or apartment with a lot of windows or glass doors.

All in all, we have been very happy with the Canary and I am planning to pick up one more for the house and another for my office. This is a great product and I recommend it without hesitation.

title: EDITED several days later Edited again
text:
Installed on a macPro 3.1, OS El Capitan. The USB3.0 pcie card works with all USB drives directly connected to the card. Put this thing in, with power, and it does not work. DOA. Drives do not appear. Not for a spinning HDD nor for a flash drive. Yes, I did turn on the port so it shines blue LED.

So I pulled cable from the hub and put it in directly to the card, BAM...the drive pops up.

HUB IS POS. Edit: <B>Hub is OK. I was wrong</B>

The drive that could not be seen was a format OSX 11 didn't want to see....NTFS. I have a utility on my other macs that allows NTFS format to be seen by OSX and I thought i had it on this box as well.. It took crawling under the desk and switching cables to Win 7 box (worked OK) and then to W10 box (ditto) to show the canary feathers on my lips.

Appologies!!

The issue was not disc format but a really antique pci-e spec in which the USB3.0 card had to be plugged into in this 10 year old mac.
