We had a brief, two-year relationship before I realized it was just not the same as my original, which I re-charged and returned to. After seeing it pop out of that confounded plastic shell again, I decided to try one more time.

This time, miraculously, I found a case that was made for that five-year-old Kindly. I got it yesterday and it fit perfectly. And I can use my Kindle right-side-up. The charging port is easily accessible, and the Kindle looks brand new.

So, after five years, I found this case and am loving it. My Kindle is still good-to-go, and I've put the "newbie" in a bin in case I ever need it again. My 2012 fire and I are good to go for at least another five years.

So glad I found this case! It's perfect.

title: I love this Chromebook
text:
I love this Chromebook. It's not bulky nor is it very heavy. I was looking for a laptop that was simple for doing online work and writing. Google docs is great to work with and it allows you to save your documents offline. I researched what laptop to get for about a month before finally settling on this. I'm very happy I went with a Chromebook, as I wanted to get away from windows but a MAC was out of the question. This Chromebook was very affordable and gave me the ease of access I needed. Since it runs on Google and most everything is done online, you don't have to worry about it constantly running loudly. This thing is more quiet. You wouldn't even be able to tell it was on if you were sitting next to me. The speakers are nice for listening and my favorite feature is the backlit keyboard. I do a lot of writing so that was a plus. The ONLY drawback is I still find the keyboard to be a bit small. If it was up to me I would have the keyboard take the place of the speakers. Other than that, the screen is a good size and changing the brightness and volume is simple.

There are drawbacks to writing on a Chromebook if that's what you do, such as if you'd rather write on word or openoffice/libreoffice. However, I still would recommend this for any writer out there that doesn't mind using google docs. It is very easy to access docs from my desktop and download the files into libreoffice after I've written them on my Chromebook. The only thing I have found to be frustrating is when you want to share something by downloading it to your computer, only to remember that it is to be done through Google Drive. You can, for example, convert a Google document into a PDF or ODT or wordx file, and download it to your drive to share with others, it just has to be downloaded to your drive rather than a hard drive. That sort of stuff takes some getting used to for new users, but I'd take this over dealing with windows any day.

It isn't loud, there's no overheating, and the boot up is quick. I hardly ever shut it down, as I use it daily, but when I do and turn it on, everything is up and running in less than ten seconds. There are no loading screens and you don't have to constantly be hassled with updates. Battery is average. If I listen to music in the background through youtube it will drain it quicker, but if I just browse the web or write on docs it'll last a few days without having to be charged. Hands down, a great Chromebook. Lightweight, affordable, simple and all around perfect for getting simple things I need done. If you're a writer or student, I highly recommend it. Transitioning over to a Chromebook can be a bit frustrating at first, but eventually you'll ease into it and you'll probably not want to go to anything else after.

title: Works with unRAID
text:
NOTE: Picture on the box I received was of an LSI Logic SAS 9207-8e (note the "e" at the end, instead of an "i"), even though the sticker on the box said 8i. This worried me until I opened the box and found that it is the correct card (internal SAS ports vs external). My guess is the manufacturer just doesn't bother having separate boxes printed for every variation of their cards and uses the stickers to differentiate the actual models.

I bought one of these for my unRAID server (running version 6.1.8) to hook up more hard drives as my motherboard only has 6 SATA ports. I shoved it in an x16 slot, which it feels a little weird doing with an x8 card but seems secure enough with just the backplate screw. Works fine with no configuration needed and, in fact, there really doesn't appear to be anything you really *can* configure in the card's BIOS. I guess that makes sense for just using it as a SAS/SATA (non-RAID) card.

One of the SAS breakout ports doesn't lock the cable in and the cable came loose after installation, preventing half my drives from showing up on the first boot. I'd just spent a great deal of effort routing data and power for 12 total SATA devices though so I wasn't about to pull the card and cable out to determine which was at fault, hence not docking a star as it could be a problem with the third-party cables I bought. It works fine with the cable plugged into the port, it just doesn't lock in place like it's supposed to. title: the default ASUSWRT features are really easy to set up but the advanced DDWRT features are ...
text:
was looking for a router that had either DDWRT or TomatoUSB support for better security and QoS which is the key optimizing your bandwidth, happened to hear about these ASUS series of routers which openly endorse DDWRT on their site and since my network is entirely LAN based it came down to either the 52u or 56u and the 30$ difference for twice the cpu and ram was the final decision maker to go with this. the default ASUSWRT features are really easy to set up but the advanced DDWRT features are what i really wanted. super easy to install, just download the firmware file from DDWRT's site and simply load it. you'll immediately notice not only a faster UI (it could take close to a minute for certain changes in the ASUS firmware) but a bevy of features that will suit your every need, being that this router's hardware is more than sufficient to support the FULL version of DDWRT (something to think about when purchasing lower end models because DDWRT does have lesser versions as well) that being said if you arent using a high end internet service you COULD opt for the cheaper 52u which will still have more than enough overhead to support the DDWRT install, however it does come with almost a 50% slower cpu, again this is not taking the WIFI technology into effect which is the only differences above the 56u which has the same cpu and ram as the higher end versions as well as all the other additional features.

another key feature that i love about ASUS compared to even the "top names" in the routing world is the fact they openly state their hardware specs, not just the WIFI signals, things like CPU and RAM are essential to networking, that's what specifically handles the traffic and makes sure all your devices traffic can be processed easily, being an actual computer company you can see how they value that type of open and upfront info to the customers over the other "router only" companies who just use vague buzzwords and the PDF manuals or "technical specifications" wouldnt specify either.

another cool feature is the so called inability to "brick" the router with any changes or firmware updates because it will simply fallback to a recovery page to reload a firmware of your choice again (check their comparison chart on ASUS DDWRT page for this feature in lower end models)

it is also fully supported by TomatoUSB which is just as highly regarded as DDWRT and both have a bunch of guides and forums to help you learn all the features.

if you are a Verizon Fios user you can simply disable the DHCP in the Actiontec and attach it via a LAN port and use the other 3 ports and the WIFI if you choose as an extension from the ASUS which will also handle any traffic to your set top boxes or VMS units for Quantum users that get transferred via the COAX connection from the Actiontec. and if you're wondering, the DDWRT firmware blows way the Actiontec features but also does it with actual terminology your can understand (just try setting up QoS to see my point)

id also recommend getting some Cat6 (thats Six not Five) cables if you're running LAN, they're extremely cheap now, CableMatters via Amazon have great size options an colors

title: Limitations to recording on USB stick
text: While the ability to rip music from a CD to a USB stick is a compelling feature, you should be aware that it doesn't pull any of the associated meta data - like the name of the artist, album, or song title.  The MP3 file that is loaded to the USB stick has a name like "Track 001".  And all of the files go into the same folder on the USB stick, so if you rip several CDs at a time, there won't be any way to tell which songs came from where.

title: Great camera, lens, EVF, and flash
text:
This is a beautifully designed, solidly build camera. I purchased both the 25mm prime and 12-40mm Pro zoom. My intention was to use the Pen F mainly with the 25mm lens, but the Pro zoom is a superb lens and the one I preferred. Despite the zoom's size, I used the camera almost exclusively with the zoom. For me, the zoom flexibility outweighed the significant advantages of the 25mm prime's size/weight and portability. It's a personal decision, but I regret thinking I could look past the obvious constraint of fixed focal length to achieve portability. Don't be swayed by what others choose - decide what you need and what you prefer before going with the diminutive but very good 25mm. The zoom is a capable, beautifully constructed lens.

The auto focus is fast and so far as I could tell, accurate. Exposure was perfect. The auto focus mechanism made enough sound as to be distracting to me, though.

The included flash was versatile and powerful. It's a great tool to have in your bag for the times you need to augment available light. Its tiny size and tilt-head capability adds to its usefulness. It is a wonderful accessory to the camera.

The quality of the EVF and LCD was superb. I have no complaints except, for me, flipping the LCD panel out was a fussy operation. The info on the panel was dense in the full-content choice of display options.

I did not find the menu system quick and easy to use. To me, a menu should start with the most-used functions and work down a hierarchical tree to the least-changed options. I didn't find the menu system intuitive in this goal of a top-down structure. It's one of two characteristics of the camera that was a deal-killer. I recognize a menu system is highly subjective, and you may not be bothered at all, but I found it distracting and frustrating.

The image quality was excellent, but not better than that of my Sony RX10. I purchased the camera both for its appealing design and portability, but also was seeking improvement in IQ over the RX10's 1-inch 20MP sensor. Shooting the same scene with both camera sequentially, I could not detect any difference in IQ. This surprised me, because a MFT sensor is substantially larger, and the price of the Olympus 12-40 Pro zoom approached the cost of the complete RX10 camera - which features a 24-200mm (35mm equiv.) F2.8 lens.

Battery life was excellent, equally as good as my RX10. Handling was better with the Olympus, but both cameras have a control disk that's too-easily moved by my thumb joint. For all the great ergonomics of the Pen F, that control disk and menu system detract from it's intelligent design. The disc is too-easily depressed.

A fully discharged battery takes about three hours to fully recharge, about the same as my RX10.

I was disappointed to find that wi-fi connectivity did not include connectivity to my network, only to my iPhone. So, downloading images to my PC required a direct connection. Download time was adequate, but not outstanding, at a rate of about 7 MB/sec sustained. The included software for image management was good, about the same in features and usability as Sony's mediocre PlayMemories app.

If I did not already own the RX10 I would have kept the camera, but given that the menu system was a disappointment and IQ didn't beat the RX10, I decided to return it and wait until I can afford a full-frame camera. I don't want to go to a system with larger, heavier lenses, but it probably will take a full-frame sensor to achieve a noticeable improvement in IQ.

Please include the Pen F in your consideration of a high-quality mirrorless camera. Its design and build quality are very impressive (subjective) and the lens system is superb. Camera and zoom lens together are expensive, though.

title: Hewlett-Packard HP EliteBook 8740w Upgrade of HDD Boot Drive to this SSD Boot Drive Can Work. Here's How.
text:
My mission: upgrade the original 300 GB HDD hard drive that came with my HP EliteBook 8740w laptop to this Samsung 850 EVO 500GB SSD to use the SSD as the primary drive / boot device.
The included Samsung Data Migration Software CD will not work for this purpose because “OEM recovery partitions generated at the factory by computer manufacturers cannot be replicated.”
HP OEM software has multiple partitions that include a Recovery partition and a Tools partition. It’s my understanding, creating a clone boot drive using ordinary software (including Windows 7 system image backup) will not work to properly copy these partitions. [I’m sticking with Windows 7 Pro (and am not being forced into Windows 10 thanks to Never10) as I lost an entire week of my life trying to recover from a Windows 10 malfunction that stopped search functions.]
Acronis True Image 2016 [[ASIN:B013LIFUNO Acronis True Image 2016 (1 Computer)]] worked great to accomplish the multiple partition boot drive cloning task. The CD I bought from Amazon in June 2016 is out of date and refers you to the Acronis website to download the current version. The 71 characters for the serial number you must enter appear on the paper included in the box. (You’d think we were launching a nuke.)
I attached the StarTech SSD/HDD - Hard Drive Adapter Cable [[ASIN:B00XLAZODE StarTech.com USB 3.1 (10Gbps) Adapter Cable for 2.5" SATA SSD/HDD Drives - Supports SATA III (6 Gbps) - USB Powered]] to the SSD and plugged it into the USB port. Then I rebooted to the Acronis media which started right up. The Tools and Utilities tab on the Home page offers “Clone Mode” and “Automatic” which accomplished the migration perfectly.
Next, turn off the laptop, (remove the battery), remove the HDD from the chassis, separate the HDD from its holding “cage” by unscrewing the two screws on each side, and slide the SSD into the cage. (The two screws nearest the connection don’t seat deep enough on this SSD and make the cage too wide, so don’t use them; just use the remaining two.) Slide the cage into the chassis, and replace the chassis cover. (Replace the battery.)
It booted right up for me. At this point, the included Samsung CD can be installed to use the Magician software which enables RAPID Mode for up to 2x faster performance by utilizing unused PC memory (DRAM) as a high-speed cache. The newest version of Samsung Magician supports up to a 4 GB cache on a system with 16 GB of DRAM.
I am storing the HDD for any emergency rather than using it for backups should the SSD fail. I hope this review saves you all the hours I invested to learn how simple this can actually be.
P.S. If you upgrade your memory, you’ll have to remove the keyboard on this laptop, but I was able to fold it back and make the installation without disconnecting all the cables.

so far my experience with the Arlo system has been positive. i'm coming from 2 logitech circle gen 1 cameras and was a looking for more coverage. logitech just updated their system to be more modular and flexible leaning towards Arlo's strengths. but their cloud storage is only 24 hours on the free tier with a pricier per camera package paid option.

the accessories ecosystem for the arlo is well rounded offering plenty of mount options, sleeves to make the cameras more discrete, and power solution to make sure the cameras are alway running. the basestation also makes it possible to install the cameras quite a bit further away than i was able to install my old logitech circle cams, i think they used poor wifi chips in their camera because the range was abysmal.

the biggest downside to this system is the image quality. that is not something to be ignored. at 720p there is not much resolution to discern much detail. it's dynamic range is poor and doesn't handle contrasty scenes very well often leading to blown out images in the sun or very muddy looking footage in the evening .

overall its a bit of a mixed bag. for me, the flexibility the system offers in mounting, placement, and power along with the 7 day free cloud tier outweighs the mediocre image quality. we'll see if their Arlo Pro 2 fixes the image quality issues.

title: Worked great right out of the box!
text:
Unpacked, attached this to my 2 year old Vizio TV and had it working in less than 3 minutes. Projecting from a recent Windows 10 Home laptop which is Miracast capable.

1- Plugged the unit into an HDMI port, & it's USB plug into a USB port on the TV
2- Switched TV on, then selected TV input to the HDMI port - TV should show a Microsoft logo and an ID for the Display Adapter. If you don't see this make sure you have switched the TV to the correct HDMI port, and that the device and it's USB connector are firmly plugged in.
3- On the PC - went into the Win 10 panel (slide left from the right side of the screen)
-> clicked project
-> selected a mode (e.g. duplicate screen)
-> clicked connect
4- The panel on the PC should then list the Display Adapters Id -> click it. The PC should say connecting.... and finally connect

That's it.

Smooth rendition of picture and sound with imperceptible delay. I played back a full screen YouTube music video to test it.

Have not yet tried to project from Android and iPhone - will come back and post once I do.

Was a initially put off by some of the negative reviews almost didn't buy it. I had also tried one of the 'generic' devices that claim to do Miracast and airplay; that was awful and I had to return. Glad I didn't give up and finally bought this.

If you have a PC, check the specs on the manufacturer's website to see if it is Miracast capable and will project.

title: Affordable, quality bedside and reading light

I've been through multiple "regular" booklights, all of which have burnt out and fallen apart in short order, as well as a dimmable, clamping desk lamp that cost $30 and broke apart after a couple of months of regular use. So, my requirements for a new light were:

1) rechargeable. With multiple kids who tend to leave the light on after falling asleep, I can't be buying batteries x 3 or 4 on the regular;
2) dimmable. Brighter for reading, dimmer for ambient light;
3) sturdy and can stand up on its own (and, ideally, have a clamp option); and

I'm so glad I found this light! The first thing I said when I pulled it out of the box was, "Wow, this is really nice!" It feels like it's a quality product. The design is sleek and simple, too. And it comes with a USB cable -- added value.

The dimming button is a bit sensitive, but the 3 lighting strengths are perfect. Then, the ultimate test: Does it *really* work with a USB cable *with* the brick that plugs into the wall? And yay, it worked!

I definitely recommend this light!

title: Cheap, easy to set up and use and it sounds pretty good but needs an On/Off button.
text:
It's what it is...a method of playing the music from my iPhone and Kindle Fire tablet through the home system. It's simple to set up and it works. The sound is not as good as playing CDs and the volume is slightly reduced but it's better than the sound you get through normal bluetooth speakers.

Once unpacked, I read the instructions--really pretty basic. The booklet referred to plugging the device into speakers but that's not possible with a standard home system. I plugged it into the Aux inputs of my amp (red RCA plug in red input, black RCA plug in white input). I then plugged the power cord into the power outlet of the amp and it powered up immediately and the blue pairing light started blinking. I turned on bluetooth in my iPhone and it paired and connected. To test, I played a little of the Martha Argerich/Nelson Friere "Saltzburg" recital recording, a little of Jimmy Buffett's "A1A" and a little of Charlie Haden's "Quartet West". There is definitely a reduction in output volume but this varies with program material. There is also a small reduction in the quality of the sound compared to playing a CD of the same recordings. It's not so bad to be a deal breaker for my purposes but it's something others might want to consider. Older recordings suffer the most in sound quality (as should be expected) but more recent downloaded recordings and home-brewed MP3s from newer CDs and SACDs sound very good to my ears.

There is one fly in the ointment that I've discovered--automatic reconnection with no On/Off switch on the device. The only way I can keep this device from automatically reconnecting with my iPhone, tablet, etc., is to manually press the pairing button to take it out of the automatic pairing mode and then connect to the other device. You have to do this every time you want to use another bluetooth device because the receiver jumps back to pairing mode after a short time and there's no way to prevent this other than unplugging it. A simple On/Off switch would make life a lot simpler for those of us who own and use multiple bluetooth devices around the house. That drops a 5-star device to a 4-star item in my opinion.

I'm pretty pleased with this device. It's my first foray into playing music from my phone, tablet and computer through the home system. Heretofore, I've relied on wired earphones and small portable bluetooth speakers. It's nice to have the home option. I believe I can install a simple inline On/Off power switch that will take care of the one negative aspect of this receiver.

title: My favorite lens in my bag
text:
This lens is quickly becoming my first pick out of my camera bag. It is such a versatile lens for so many different scenarios. As a walk around in suburban/urban environments this lens rocks. It has a very low profile, sans lens hood, and is fairly light. I use it with my Rebel T3. On a crop sensor, this lens is a go-to, but it won't be a full time replacement for indoor shooting. I do still keep my 18-55mm kit lens with me.

The one major callout that I'm going to give is towards the argument that I kept running into as a beginning amateur photographer: Do you need to buy a prime lens or is the 18-55mm kit lens all you truly need for basic photography? The answer that I have come to is: it depends on how you like to work. I can set my 18-55mm to 50mm and I can tweak a lot of settings on my T3 to get a similar image from this prime lens. However, I tend to rely more on flash, due to the aperture, and I have to do a lot of post processing to clean up the image. With my prime, I do less work. I also have more moments where I may only need to process the image with one go. I also have moments were I look at the picture I captured and deem it to be of good enough quality to let it be without anything more than an onboard jpeg edit.

The TL;DR of this story: Its up to you if you want to buy a prime or stick it out with a kit lens. Just know that in my experience, I tend to really work the kit lens and process the image, whereas I can shoot and worry less with my 50mm.

The one thing that I would say that you might want to be aware of is the focus. My in depth study of this 50mm and its older brother is that AF is finicky. I have noticed it and overlooked it until I went out on a cold night. Ambient temps were right around 40 degrees and it seemed that this lens body was much colder in a shorter time versus something like my kit. This, I believe, threw the AF off even more. It's not enough to knock a star off, but it make the expected behavior of the AF to exaggerate itself compared to similar subjects with warmer temps.

***TWO YEAR UPDATE***

This lens is still awesome. I recently upgraded my camera (Rebel T6) and I have found that this lens is getting better and better. Using a 50mm on a crop sensor presents interesting challenges and rewards. In some cases, the DOF creates some unique bokeh. At other times, the sharpness from this lens surprises me. Each time I push this lens it shows me that it can do more. The one fault that I can say about the lens (not worth knocking a star off because the price point doesn't allow it) is that it is difficult to work with in astrophotography. The two main issues are: 1) this lens lacks a physical indicator of focus, i.e. hard to find infinity, and 2) The focal length + crop sensor combo doesn't allow for long exposures before star trails happen. Stopped to f/4, you'd get about a 5 second exposure before trailing is evident. Its enough to capture a fair amount of stars, but not enough to get something like the Milky Way without having a specialized mount that corrects for trailing.

title: If you have a Pro or Pro2 this is a MUST BUY!!
text:
If you own a Surface Pro or Pro2 you know about poor battery life and if your like me where your primary devices for work and other is a Surface Pro then you will have to live next to an outlet (or some sort of external supply). When I would go on work trips half way through my plane ride my Surface Pro would be stone dead or pretty close to it. I will still need another 20 mins to finish a movie and at least another 2 hours to finish what ever program or document I was working on at the same time.

After my last trip I said enough is enough, I could not justify the Pro3 price tag when I purchased a Pro 1.5 years ago brand new. I searched for external battery packs and I could not find anything, getting rather frustrated I went to best buy and there was the POWER COVER! I already had the touch cover (which came with my device) and the Type cover 2 which I purchased last year to make it easier to work as the touch cover is great for some light use not good for every day use. I did not want to spend another 200 +Tax on added features for my Surface Pro at some point it gets cheaper to buy a new i7 model. I went home and checked Amazon as the product had been out for a while I was hoping to get a used one for cheap, to my surprise Amazon Prime had the Power Covers for 90. free two day shipping. I have had this cover now for about a month and the battery life on my Pro running Windows 10 (tech preview) last for about 12 hours with light usage and 11 hours with movie watching and other applications at the same time. I could not have been more thrilled to figure out that it all charges on the same power cord I have and does not add that much more time to the charging (40 mins or so).

As for the keys on the keyboard, they are as smoother if not better then my Type Cover 2, however they have NO Back-light, which on a plane makes a lot of difference to me. The case is made out of the same felt material that the other covers are made out of, and the keys are hard plastic. You may have to rest your device to get this cover to work as I did, the process is simple and took less then 20 mins. All in all it help me reach the real potential of this little Surface Pro which at the same time saving me money in the long term.

title: Definitely worth buying, easily compatible with portable chargers
text:
Not much to say about a backpack. Comfortable and fits well, and the straps are adjustable. The metal zippers are a nice touch, and make the backpack feel premium. Lots of pockets to store things, as well as some secret pockets (two of them, one where you rest your back and one near the Matein label under the front-most pocket, it can't be seen in the pictures of the product ). The extra strap on the top makes the backpack easy to carry with one hand if you don't want to wear it on your back, and the area where you're meant to store your laptop is compatible with small locks to keep in place. I also like the buckle that attaches to the inside front pocket which allows you to store your keys (unfortunately I lost mine, oh well).

Another great feature is the charger, as the backpack supports portable charging. Keep in mind that you, of course, will need your own portable charger, but it's a great addition. You can store your charger in a mesh pocket inside the lockable section where you can also put your laptop. The backpack comes with a wire one the inside (that unfortunately isn't detachable) that is long enough to reach anywhere in the pocket and can connect to your portable charger. Then you can subsequently put your own charging cable in the USB on the outside, such as a Micro USB charger, a USB Type C charger, or an Apple Lightning charger if your portable charger supports it. You can then put your phone in your hand and charge and use it simultaneously, or you can put it in the mesh pockets on the side to keep it idle. Just know that you might get your phone stolen in doing this, so I just recommend putting your phone in the second mesh pocket on the inside (there are two) without using the backpack's USB if you don't want to use it while charging.

I only have one problem with the backpack, which is the adjustable straps. The straps often adjust by themselves accidentally when moved around or when pulled on a little, which can get annoying. This, though, isn't enough to deduct a star, but just know that you will have to deal with this problem once you get it, even though you get used to it pretty quickly.

Conclusion: Well made with nice features and hidden pockets, works with locks to keep your stuff safe and an easy-to-use portable charger compatible method of charging your phone on the go.

TL;DR: Get it if you don't want to spend money on a name brand backpack, works well with portable chargers and feels high-quality.

Edit: Unfortunately, in about May of this year, the backpack zipper on the pocket closest to the straps unfortunately broke (after over a year of daily usage, aside from summer break). However, I liked this so much that I picked it up again, and needless to say I love it even more! They made BIG changes from when I got this March of 2018. They changed the color to make it closer to black (which I really like) and they made it so every large pocket is able to be used with a lock. Used the upgraded version for the last two months of my school year and loved it. Still an excellent backpack over a year later.

title: I do audio engineering. This clips, pops, and distorts regardless of input level
text:
I know what you're thinking: 1) I must be overdriving it, and/or the distortion is already there in the source.

Neither is true. Multiple known and proven sources that sound fine on other similar speakers (and headphones) sound fine.

It also happens to perfectly good, high-bitrate MP3 files played on MicroSD card, that sound great played on other devices, and playing at low volumes on the DOSS. (Which alone categorically rules out source signal problems such as existing distortion or overdriven input.)

It's not bad enough to return, and it's not constant. And I can't figure out why it WOULDN'T be dependent in input level, that's a real head-scratcher, because the characteristics are exactly that of overdriven input, especially with cheap AD and/or DA converters.

That said, for the price I'm not surprised. Actually I'm a tiny bit impressed for the price, clipping and distorting aside.

So I'm not going to one-star it. It deserves a tiny bit of respect. And I do still use it, clipping and all.

The battery doesn't last as long as some other (slightly more expensive) similar devices. Also the bass is much thinner than others. (Though many others have cartoonishly boomy, muddy, over-loud bass. Maybe lack of bass is better than over-compensated bass.)

title: but this has such amazing sound quality and versatility for what I consider to ...
text:
I rarely leave reviews, but being the tech savvy woman I am, I needed to let everyone know about this product.
First off, I am not being paid to review this Bluetooth Stereo and this is my honest opinion. I own a Bose System, Sony Wireless Bluetooth speaker, Alexa, I could go on, but this has such amazing sound quality and versatility for what I consider to be a great value.

We bought this to replace an antiquated boom box that my husband refused to part with at our automotive repair shop. It was only because the old radio finally broke that he gave in and replaced the old boom box with new technology! When I hooked it up and my husband heard the sound quality and his favorite band Metallica,coming through the speakers he was floored and said, "Wow I should have listened to you awhile ago, this system kicks a$$!"
This was cake to set up, it took me literally 4 minutes, and one of those was to install the batteries in the remote, which, by the way, is a nice bonus to have. It is a cinch to stream music directly from our smartphones, or via a SD card or Flash drive if you store music that way. With this system, we stream Pandora and XM radio, mixed with our local FM rock station at the shop, in the bays, and office and the sound quality is amazing. The bass rivals most high end systems. While Bose is the gold standard, for the money this is a great sound system. It can be used in conjunction with your television as a surround sound system if you so choose, or for gaming, which I think would be awesome. We are extremely pleased with our purchase and will be purchasing another.
The only con is, which was not an issue for us as we intend to keep this stationary, but if you are looking for a system to cart around with you for the park or a the beach,this is rather bulky, and you would have to be sure to charge the battery, to be able to use it as a portable unit, so this would not be the best system if you are looking for portability. However, for a party or by the backyard pool, this would be a great system. We are actually ordering another one for our cabin in Upstate NY, as the price point and sound quality are a "sound fit" for us!

title: 3x Cable Speed Increase in Apartment ... No Neighbor Interference ... Works on Mac & iOS
text:
Achieved a 3x upgrade to my wireless speed (22Mbps -> 65Mbps) over previous WRT54G in the same room, and 20x in the back room (~3Mbps -> 65Mbps) with the change to 802.11N vs. G.

Having the 5GHz band means no more interference from neighbors around my crowded apartment setting, but even the 2.4GHz band is clean and fast (about 40Mbps in the back room) due to better technology, N-spec., and admittedly better placement on my part.

Kept the old WRT54G by the TV/Entertainment cabinet and wired it back via CAT-5 to LAN the PS2, PS3 and TV, effectively giving me 6 ports in the living room. Also supports a Guest network.

Note that I'm using Macs and iOS devices, and the Cisco set-up software does not support Mavericks well, so I had to IP into the set-up, but that worked fine (IIRC Safari was a problem but Firefox did the trick).

Considering the price of $35 for a refurb., this deal cannot be beat.

title: This stereo is a great head unit for a very reasonable price
text:
This stereo is a great head unit for a very reasonable price. I installed it in my truck with one of the dash adapter kits and a wiring harness adapter kit. Very easy to do and the unit sounds great. Do yourself a favor. They provide you with like ten feet or so of wiring to wire the mic any where you want. I saw YouTube videos where people wired in behind the dash and up the A-pillar, across the front of the headliner between it and the front windshield and then used the double sided tape to stick it to the top of the rear view mirror. This is kind of tacky looking so I just drilled a small hole that was the exact diameter of the mic through a spot on my dash bezel( part that covers your instrument cluster and maybe other stuff like vents) and had it poke out through the hole about a half an inch. On my dash I had a blank spot that would have had some buttons for a more highly optioned truck (probably for rear wipers or maybe fog lights or even a cargo light or something) so it was sort of a blank area. I used the two sided tape provided and the gimble mount provided and basically installed it on the inside of this area of the dash cover/bezel and had it just poke out of the hole I drilled. It actually looks very professional and almost stock.
Pros: I like the blue lighting instead of red which many units are. The blue tooth capabilities were easy to set up with my phone. If I don't want to deal with Bluetooth I can always just plug in to the auxiliary jack for music. It is Pandora compatible which honestly I thought I wouldn't use but now that I paid for the Pandora app and don't get commercials its like having satellite radio on the cheap. It charges your phone through the USB port. Accessing my phone while it is in my pocket for making or receiving calls is great.
Cons: My biggest pet peeve with the unit is that there are so many things to learn to do and button combinations you have to push to access certain settings and info. It's kind of overwhelming and I don't want to pull out the manual and read page after page of directions while I'm driving down the road. The main dial does most of the work but I am still trying to figure out how to use all the features and set it up the way I want. Many of you very tech savvy people out there will undoubtedly not have any issues with that.
Overall it is a great stereo for a great price that is pretty feature rich. I'd recommend it.

title: Faux Leather Genuine Fail by OPPO.
text:
The sound and build of the Oppo PM-3 make the price almost worth it.

My reservation has to do it the poor quality padding. Unlike premium models, the pm-3 used faux leather on the ear and head cushion. This faux finish began to peel away a month or two after my warranty expired. While it’s true OPPO has a plan to replace them for under $100, instead of sending a customer the replacement parts that customer has to ship the headset to OPPO for repairs. So, not only does one lose OPPO’s headset for a week or so, OPPO is replacing the rotted items with the same poor quality materials. I had asked if they would allow me to pay for an upgrade to leather, but it was not possible.

So, I have just endured years of black vinyl bits sticking to my face every time I listen to my headphones. Sometimes I’ve missed a patch and people thereafter would find it on me and think I was suffering from some kind of skin disease. Ha!

I think OPPO should offer a chance for customers to upgrade to a better quality material. Why would I pay the fee to replace poor quality materials that have deteriorated in a year with same again? It would be a vicious and costly cycle just to have to replace them all over every year. In the end, purchasing an OPPO PM-3 headset would require ownership with long term hidden repeating costs that frankly make these great sounding headsets really not worth it.

title: Generally Working with MC-11 and A6300
text:
Using this 85 with the MC-11 on my A6300. I am still learning to use the combination of this lens, my camera, and the MC-11 but just wanted to say that it works with some caveats and it is capable of producing some very nice and sharp images in my experience with it so far.

The lens is made up primarily of plastic but it feels well built and sturdy enough to get banged around in a camera bag. The focus ring isn't great but it works. It is a little stiff and grimy but with some use you get used to it. I don't want to go over the image quality too much as I'm still learning to use it with the mount converter and the A6300, both of which it was never supported to work with. From my experience so far, the chromatic aberration can be pretty bad at the wide apertures although with some work in lightroom this is easily fixed. Stopping down does improve this but it does seem to be a common and constant problem with this lens. The contrast and colors so far have been decent to good but I'm not sure if that is only the lens or the compatibility issues with the MC-11 and my camera. Other than that the images are pretty absurdly sharp in the center and in the corners even wide open.

I don't want to comment too much on the additional stuff that came with the lens from this seller because they're just ok at best and I never would have got any of it unless it was free. For the most part all of this stuff is functional although the case provided is too small for this lens and the hood screws into the inner threading of the lens where the filters attach. It was shipped fast and well packaged on a positive note.

I can't recommend this lens for the MC-11 and the A6300 despite all of its good qualities. I know this is a great lens for the system it was designed for and for that and what I have seen I can easily give this 5 stars, however I recommend that if you're planning to use this with the MC-11 and a Sony E-Mount, you find a way to try this combination before you buy it. I like it and I'm going to keep it but I recommend really exploring your options and your budget before jumping into the MC-11 or any lens adapter and this lens.

I'll update this review as I have more time and experience with this lens with the MC-11 and the A6300 and I will answer any questions I am able to.

title: 0 Star - Don't make my mistake! Expensive, useless brick and I'm out $300. Thank you NetGear!
text:
I purchased this router from Amazon in Feb 2015 for $285 because it was one of the first AC routers to have TWO USB 3.0 ports (this was one of my requirements). At first, no real issues but I wasn't floored by its speeds either. I had other, more urgent things to deal with (death in the family, etc) but eventually, I spent some time analyzing speeds I was getting using it, with Speedtest.net and comparing my hard-wired PC performance and my WiFi devices (iPhone 6, iPad Air 2) and realizing I was not even getting 30Mbs throughput on any of my devices even though my TWC service was rated at 300Mbs!! - And yet I could achieve these speeds if I connected directly to my TWC modem. I contacted NetGear and they diagnosed my unit as a defective one. I was sent a new, replacement unit fairly promptly, I shipped my old unit back to them. This was in June 2015. And yes, I immediately saw a HUGE jump in connection speeds, with the replacement unit, I started achieving the Internet bandwidth which I had been paying for.

We jump now to Feb 2016.. Now I should say that in general, I have felt that something was wonky w/ my Internet setup.. Speeds varied greatly, Internet would drop in and out at various times, etc.. Also, quite often, either the 2.4 or the 5G SSIDs off the router would not be available (but a router reboot would fix the issue). But since the iPhones/iPads are quite stupid devices that don't have the sophistication to switch automatically to a different WiFi network if the network they're on loses connectivity (or the speed is degraded, etc), I had to constantly switch WiFi networks via the good old manual process (test, troubleshoot, switch)..

A week ago (Mon Feb 22 2016), after losing my Internet connection in the middle of an important work day, I did the usual troubleshooting with TWC and they determined their modem was bad. I went right away to their local store and they gave me a new modem. I plugged it in, tested it, all seemed good. But later that day, I lost the Internet again.. WTF? The rest of the week was like that.. In and Out Internet, up, down, up, down. All the while, I'm cursing TWC..

Today, (Mon Feb 29 2016), I was having Internet connection issues again and I finally reached my wits end. So I started dissecting my Internet set-up. I first connected hard-wired straight to my TWC Modem (a Ubee, btw).. Great speeds.. I switched back (hard-wired) to my Nighthawk X4 router. No Internet. Huh?. I checked my TWC connection via WIFI on my iPhone, it's up and fast.. OK so it's something in between. I replaced the Ethernet cable (I had ordered a pack of 5-star-rated CAT6 Ethernet patch cables over the weekend) between my hard-wired Dell PC and the Router. No Internet. I switched the port that I'm plugged in to, on the router. No Internet. I fired up the NetGear NetGenie app. It showed the Internet as being down. (But it was not, I was still monitoring the TWC modem and its speeds from my iPhone).. And btw, the Ethernet cable between the Router and the Modem was also tested. It was fine. I should mention that I RESET (ie unplugged Modem and Router and even restarted my PC over and over again. Several times (Power on the Modem. Wait 5 full minutes. Power on the Router. Wait 5 full minutes. Start my PC. Check. Same problem. OK it was time to call NetGear Tech Support.

I got a very nice, very polite lady (Case # 26541046) at NetGear and I explained to her all of the above. It was a 40 minute call when all was said and done but even though I proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that the NetGear router was clearly the issue, she explained to me that my 90 day support window has expired and that in order for her to support me, I would need to pay anywhere from $50 (for one incident support) to $229 (for 24 months of support). Yes, because I should spend even MORE money for NetGear to help me troubleshoot my obviously defective unit!!

I explained to the lady that I also have the option of going straight into my TWC Modem (which has WiFi) for a total cost of $0. Okay so it's not an "AC" router and it doesn't have the fancy USB3.0 port or all the other cool technologies.. Dear NetGear: Your advanced technologies are USELESS if the Router doesn't work.

So I have now switched to my TWC Modem for now. I don't know that NetGear is any worse that any of the other Router manufacturers (as far as the quality of their products or their generosity when it comes to support) but they have let me down.

Also, considering that I am able to "see" (via WiFi connection) in the very rear of my house a $20 Router (a TP-LINK TL-WR841) my next door neighbor (I share a duplex, ie a house with two apartments, one on each side) has installed in the front of their house, 100-120 feet away - whereas I have NEVER been able to see my own Nighthawk in my own place when I'm at that same (shorter, actually) distance away is deeply disturbing to me and tells me that I will never blow this kind of money again on a "bleeding"-edge router.

My point is if I had invested $20 like my neighbor and the thing don't work, big deal. Spend another $20, $30, etc.. I have to earn my money and I thought I was investing $300 for a super-duper router which will last me at least 2-3 years. My replacement router is about 7 months old (Since I got in June 2015) and there you go. Not very cool.

Lessons learned. Looks like I now have a $300 brick that I cannot even resell for $10, ethically. And I will never buy another NetGear product thanks to their lovely support policy. Please build "Quality" products and THEN, enforce a 90-day "free" support policy. I didn't get a quality product and you have made me lose a lot of time needlessly. Hmm, class-action?

title: UPDATE 03/16/15: Disappointing Motion Detection
text:
UPDATE: After several emails and then a phone call from a Level 2 Tech I feel the motion detection sensitivity problem is solved. One of the first email suggestions to me was to set the motion detection sensitivity to 100%, I thought I had done this step prior to the email so I complained to Netgear Tech Support again. More suggestion came but all of them had been done by me previously. After I received an email from the Level 2 Tech (Christine) I re-checked by settings and found the sensitivity was NOT set to 100%.

So with egg on my face I called Christine and explained that I must not have saved the sensitivity setting and would need some time to let the system run with the new sensitivity setting.

After a week at 100% sensitivity the Arlo and the Foscam were both at similar detection rates. I did a some false positives with the Arlo but I am happy at this time.

I think the Netgear support is great with excellent follow-up. When I came hear today to enter this update I was amazed at the Netgear replies to Arlo owners comments. I am very impressed with the support. Great Job Netgear Tech Support!!!

I have changed my rating from one start to five stars.

I bought this system because it was battery powered.

The system is easy to setup in random locations because they don't need to be plugged in. The image quality is great, the online image storage system is easy to access although I would prefer to have local video storage. The IR lighting is very good for the Arlo. There isn't much that I can complain about except the motion detection which in my setup I would rate as poor, this characteristics forces me to rate the whole system as poor.

I thought the Arlo system was missing activity but had no may to measure if I was or wasn't. I placed a Foscam FI9831P next to one of the Arlo cameras. I scheduled both of them with the same schedules. Over a month I found that the Arlo only caught about 10% of the activity that the Foscam caught. To put it to numbers the Arlo might have 5 motion detection and the Foscam would have 50 to 60 motion detections. Reviewing the video clips I found the Foscam detections were real.

I am very disappointed with the Arlo because of the poor motion detection in my application of detecting the activity of house cats.

I first bought [[ASIN:B017WTANCG iPad Pro Keyboard Case, New Trent Airbender SmartPro with Detachable Wireless Bluetooth Smart Keyboard for the Apple iPad Pro 9.7"; Not for iPad Air, iPad Pro 12.9, iPad Mini]], which had more ratings/higher ratings. The Trent is bigger and heavier, the support bar is hard to pull out, you can't use it in portrait mode, and when I detach the case from the keyboard it has large awkward hooks on the ends. And the rubber 'latch' does little to hold the case closed during transport. But I do like that it has a full 6 row keyboard in proper layout, albeit with slightly smaller keys. But back to the Spigen... I've had a Spigen case on my iPhone for years and have a strong respect for their products, which is why I took the leap to buy this without a ton of reviews. I am so glad I did.

Pros:
– Slim and lightweight, almost as small as the iPad Pro
– Super easy to swivel from landscape to portrait orientation
– When detached from keyboard the case is almost unnoticed, as if you don't even have a case on it, but you do
– Includes a stylus which stores right inside the case

Cons:
– On one hand it has full size keys, which many will like. But, they altered the keyboard a bit to accomplish that. The ;/: button and the ?// button are to the right of the space bar instead of a copy of the Command and Option buttons. The space bar is shortened, and my right thumb that I use to hit the space bar just barely hits the right side of the space bar. Personally, I'd rather have smaller keys and have all the keys where they are on all my other keyboards, and the space bar should extend all the way beneath the J as well. Also, the 6th row function keys are now on the 5th row by using the Fn button. These are definitely on my Con list, but overall this is still a preferable unit to me.
– Perhaps a small issue, but you have to get used to how you hold it, the tablet and keyboard at once, because of the design. Otherwise it could flop about a bit.

Overall I am very happy with this product. at least a 4.6. With the key layout improved I could easily give it a 4.9 or 5.0. :-)

title: Guide on how to program these and test them.  Couldn't find anything online and wasted days because this is ESP-01s and not ESP-
text:
I will increase star by one because seller is really trying to do the best. English is about broke and is really trying to help solve the problem even after I was refunded but I will not change my original post because I did get the ESP-01s and not ESP-01. He keeps insisting I use a 10k resistance when it isn't need. You probably just heard that from someone. Did you test it? I tested these and know what I have. So please be happy I am helping you get a 4/5. Here is my unbiased and truthful observations. Please stop emailing me about this item because posted below are details on how to program these for people who don't know.
---------------------------------------------------
First I did not receive the Esp-01, but the Esp-01s. So you may have too. I finally figured out how to program it and because a lot of people having problems I will post how I did it. I will attach image with how to connect it in programming mode and list instructions step by step.

Programming Mode: FTDI - USB
Guide to Programming:
Buy an FTDI chip. (search "FTDI USB to Serial") I don't like to advertise items or URL but people asked, so I use the one from HiLetGo FT232RL which has the 5v and 3.3v Jumper for easy voltage switching it is perfect for what I am doing because it was only 5$.

Step 1. Connect ONLY the ground, RX, and TX to the ESP-01s (Only connect the VCC if you are using same FTDI as me and have tested the voltage to 3.3v with jumper in correct position.)
Step 2. Use External power supply instead to VCC from the FTDI if you are unsure. Some fit on breadboard that do 5v and 3.3v or if you have the same FTDI I am using you can skip Step 2 and just use the correct 3.3v power supply jumper.
Step 3. Connect GPIO0 to Ground. (This tells chip that you are going to be entering programming mode)
Step 4. Connect GND to Ground.
Step 5. Connect CH_PD and VCC to the 3.3v (Double check your voltage or you will burn chip up by applying 5v)
Step 6. Plug In Everything. FTDI, USB, Power.
Step 7. Briefly touch the RST (Reset) pin to the GND (Ground) and it will now boot into firmware flashing mode.
Step 8. Go to the Arduino and get the ESP8266 Board Collection. If it doesn't show up in newest version 1.8.3 then, use older 1.6.5 and add the URL under preferences is what I had to do. (Google it)
Step 9. Open Arduino IDE and go to Menu Tools> Board> Select the "Generic ESP8266 Module".
Step 10. Make sure baud rate is correct, same as setup under your Serial in Device Manager. Should be 115200 and set flash speed to 80MHz.
Step 11. From Arduino IDE choose menu. File>Examples>ESP8266>Blink (not same as normal "blink").
Step 12. Upload/Flash the code to your ESP8266 and I hope this can help other people who are having problems.
Step 13. Un-Ground the GPIO0 and Reset.
Step 14. You are now booted in 'Normal' mode and your program you uploaded should be running.

Enjoy! Let me know if you found it helpful.

title: Some Initial Issues...Then Nothing But Fun!
text:
I'm a first time, rookie drone owner/flier. I was skeptical about spending so much money and on which drone to spend it. I decided to go with the Karma because it seemed to represent the best value by far when all the extras you get are considered.

So far, I love the drone. This particular buying experience with Amazon was a monumental PITA, though.

Anyway...back to the Karma. I chose the Karma Hero6 bundle that comes with an extra battery and the usual items...very nice backpack-style carry case, the Karma Grip (haven't had a chance to use that yet), Hero6 camera, 2 extra propellers, misc GoPro mounting hardware, etc. It was well packed and protected inside the boxes (double boxed).

The Karma is much heavier and larger than I expected. The construction, materials and fit & finish of the various components all seemed to be extremely good. This thing feels solid as do all the parts and accessories. It took a few hours to get everything charged up and ready to go. Once the charging was done I tried to do the software updates and that's where things took a bit of a turn. I downloaded the GoPro app to my Android phone. Now, I'll admit, I don't use a lot of phone apps. The GoPro app seemed to be exceptionally useless to me and I couldn't get it to work downloading the various updates. So I downloaded Quik for my PC. That was just as bad. Not a big fan of it, either. I'd heard that all you have to do for the updates is turn the controller on and follow the prompts. Well, I couldn't get that to work. Nothing was working for downloading the updates. After about an hour of trying to get everything to update I gave up in frustration, shut everything off and went to bed.

The following morning I decided to tackle the updates again. I opened the controller and powered it on. Miraculously there was an update icon on the home screen. I tapped it and an update screen opened and I was able to download all the updates just like everyone said. I have no idea why it didn't do that when I initially tried. But, whatever. They were all successful, batteries on all the components were charged and I was ready for my first ever drone flight.

Just in case, I practiced a little on the flight simulator. It's actually pretty helpful...not so much for the flying but for control familiarization. After a bit on the sim I took the Karma for a spin. It didn't like the first location I chose to fly and would not complete the initial compass calibration. I moved to a different location and it worked first try.

Once the calibration was good I was all set to fly. Taking off is easy since all you have to do is tap the screen and press a button. I followed the on-screen prompts and instantly my Karma was in the air hovering steadily at about 6'. I flew it around the backyard keeping it below 50 feet. I flew it around, hovered, brought it back to land a few times and basically just got familiar with the controls. It's actually quite easy to fly and it's extremely responsive to the controls. Mine is rock solid when you release the joysticks. It doesn't wander around at all (to be fair, there was absolutely no wind for my first flight). Each time I ordered Karma to return and land from the launch location it returned to the precise spot it took off from. One thing to be mindful of (and I almost learned the hard way)...Karma returns to the launch point in a straight line...not on the path it took to get to wherever it is when told to return. So make certain there aren't any obstacles (like trees) in the way. Landings were quite soft and dead-on accurate. I was actually surprised by how much downdraft this little drone makes. It's quite powerful. I flew around for about 18 mins and never got a low battery signal on the controller so I'm guessing flight times will be pretty close to 20 mins or so.

I don't have experience with other drones to compare to Karma. Having said that, I'm glad I chose to go with the GoPro instead of one of the other popular choices. I think I'll use some of the extras like the Karma Grip more than I'll use the drone. I'm also glad I got the extra battery. The update issues were a challenge but that's all behind me now and once I got to fly it around they didn't seem all that important.

So, so far, so good with my Karma. I can't wait to get a few more flights and videos under my belt.

***UPDATE 12/9/2017***: I've had my Karma for a week now and have several flights of various duration under my belt. Of course, a few flights certainly doesn't make me an expert but this is what I've found:

I live in a fairly narrow river valley. I can't get a certain satellite emergency service for vehicles at my home. I was worried Karma would have difficulty with GPS disconnections or other issues. Fortunately, that isn't the case. I have yet to have a "Lost GPS" or "Lost Connection with Controller" message come up that so many others have complained about. Function has been perfect.

If you're new to drones like I am, don't worry. Karma is REALLY easy to fly. Once I got past the initial worries of having a $1k toy (I'm no pro so this amazing pro-quality tool is just a "toy" to me) a hundred feet in the air above me I've really started to like this thing. It is a blast! I'm very happy I bought this particular setup.

The hardest part for me is controlling the camera and knowing what settings to use for the particular conditions of the day. Having said that, the Hero6 takes fantastic video, even from a rookie like me that doesn't know how to use it. It is just rock-solid and steady when mounted on the Karma.

The first time I flew it with a fairly good breeze going on the motors were constantly adjusting to keep it steady. When that happens they make a lot of noises that can be very disturbing for a beginner. It's just Karma adjusting to the wind. I didn't want to take my eyes off of it so that made it difficult to follow on the controller. So, controlling the GoPro was a NoGo until I got used to that. I haven't used any of the built-in camera modes (like "reveal" or "follow me") yet, either.

title: Great Backpack, don't hesitate!
text:
After looking at tons of backpacks in stores and online, I settled on this one. After half a year, I am still in love with this thing (didn't realize I could get so attached to a backpack, but I am).

Pros: As a motorcycle rider and a college student, I really love this thing.
- Sturdy. The material feels strong, I'm never nervous about rips on the pack, handles, etc.
- Spacious (but see Cons). Always held everything I needed (laptop, books, and clothes). Laptop pocket is great and nothing has been damaged.
- Waterproof. Even on a motorcycle in the rain, I would always come home with dry items.
- Straps: The chest strap really makes a difference. Buy some carabiner clips for the front straps and you can attach anything to this pack.
- Cupholders. Minor detail, but they are tight and deep so I never worry about my stuff falling out. 2 sizes as well.

Cons: The pack is really tall, but not super long (outwards from your back). It has always held everything I needed including a laptop, books, and clothes and the design stops things from moving around, but if you carry multiple textbooks and a laptop at once, this might not be long enough.

Would definitely buy this again for a friend or family member. Great pack for daily use, especially for students and people on a motorcycle.

title: lots of crisp accurate sound for the money
text:
I replace my front ceiling mounted Yamaha entry level surround speakers with thees Polk S10s and made a tremendous improvement to the sound of my system.
.
The S10's seem to produce sharp sound output at every audio frequency from lows to high. I got the smallest signature series Polks so i could replace ceiling mounted speakers in the front with them.
.
My system that I added these Polks to: I have a pair of rebuilt Cizek stereo speakers with Pioneer mobile 8" woofers and Visonik dome tweeters that at least match the original Peerless tweeters in sound and high end output. My bass is well taken care of with a home-made Kicker 10" X2 sub box on a 150W X 2 Onkyo stereo amp. But then I had barely adequate sound from six more speakers including 4 entry level Yamaha NS SP1800 surround speakers and 2 Advent shelf speakers with 8" drivers I bought years ago for $100 on sale at Crutchfield, new. For the money the Advents reproduce mid bass well but there never has been any crispness to them and the Yamaha surround speakers sound just like them. Consequently, my system sounds brilliant to mediocre depending on where you stand in the room, I noticed after months of fine tuning the sound in each speaker to my liking. But the treble is at max on everything and only the Cizeks in the rear (on the front channels because they are 4 ohm impedance and only my front channels support 4 ohm speakers, plus the Cizeks are not shielded) perform brilliantly at the top end.
.
I am very happy with my investment in these S10s. I think they should have better mounting options on the back, such as a pair of 1/4" threads in the raised sound reflector on the back instead of the middle of the back below the reflector.

title: Great Picture and Value for the money!
text:
Several of our friends have upgraded to large around 65" TVs and we were very impressed at the quality of the picture. Our current TV was a 40" Samsung which is over 8 yrs old. I have always found Samsung quality and customer service to be top notch, so I saw no reason to jump ship.
We settled on the 65KS8500 Curved 65 Inch which we bought through the Video & Audio Center on Amazon.

We did have a few problems with the delivery, The 1st was that I was given a tracking number for UPS. The number did not look anything like a UPS number, believe me I have seen a lot of them! And when I tried it on the UPS site it told me it could not be found. I sent an email to the shipper and got an immediate response telling me that it was not shipped via UPS, instead the used another 3rd party shipper since because of its size it would have to be hand trucked in from the road. Once that was taken care of we waited for it's arrival. The truck driver was great, he told me that I would probably not want to accept delivery... he was right, on corner of the box was crushed. Looked like it was dropped. I did not accept delivery. The driver gave me a receipt and the phone number of the shipper, Video & Audio Center. I called and talked with a wonderful CS Rep who offered to credit my card with the sale or ship a replacement. I saw no reason not to have another set shipped and she set it up on an expedited schedule. The same driver delivered the replacement and moved it into the living room where he helped unpack it so that I could inspect it. It appeared perfect so I excepted the shipment and I am so glad I did!

The picture on 1080P is outstanding, and on 4K it is simply beautiful. This is also a smart TV with built in WIFI which was easy to setup. I wasnt totally sure that I would need or much less like having a Smart TV, but since I have Amazon Prime I thought we might get some use out of it... and we have. We live in a ponderosa pine forest in the mountains of AZ. We had a pretty decent snow over New Years which took out our DirectTV dish. We switched over to Amazon Prime and watched several episodes of Grand Touring in 4K and then the movie Sully also in 4K. When the movie was over the storm had blown away and the dish was clear so we watched football on DirectTV.

Another not so small problem was that my 20 year old Denon surround sound receiver amp was not compatible with the HDMI inputs that the Samsung wanted. After a bit of research I bought a Denon AVR-S510BT for $279. It is so much better than my old Denon that I had paid over $2000 for back in the day. It was an added expense but well worthwhile to end up with a very flexible home entertainment that should be future proof for many years to come!

I have to give Video & Audio Center a lot of credit for their excellent customer service. Things do sometimes get damaged in shipment, it is nice to see that some companies put the customer 1st and help to get the product replaced as quickly as possible.

The Samsung UN65KS8500 is a real bargain offering a great deal of value and a reasonable price.

Would definitely recommend it to my friends...

title: Great for kids but have odd technical issues.
text:
First, let me give a little info about our living situation. We live in a semi-rural area with no access to cable internet. We currently have our home internet through Verizon. Why is this important? Because these tablets seem to need a constant connection. We knew the tablets needed a connection, obviously, to download apps and to stream movies. But, as you can see in the attached photo, sometimes the downloaded apps icons go blank. The only remedy is to connect to the internet. This is fine, even for us at home, but when we leave the house for the day, blank icons can be an issue.

The second issue I have is the app menu. Unless I am doing something wrong, you only see a portion of the app title (even at smallest font). You literally have no idea if the app is a game or book unless you actually download it. There is actually a "books" section to download books but some of the apps in the "apps" section are also books. Plus, there is no description for the apps of what they do (i.e. if its a game, what kind of game). You won't know until you fire it up and start playing.

If there is fix to the issues above that I don't know about, please disregard. But this brings me to the next issue. There are no instructions on how to use the tablet. Granted its a tablet and fairly simple to figure out, some sort of instruction guide or a more advanced wizard would be nice.

The positives are the tablets seem to be fairly durable with the foam padding and the battery life is good. Aside from the complaints above, there are a ton of apps to choose from. I added 32 gig SD cards to both of our tablets and loaded them with games. Once the games start, they are fairly easy for the kids to understand (mine are two and five).

From what I found out by comparing kid tablets, I still think theses offer more bang for the buck, because as my kids grow, we can alter these tablets to grow with them.

title: Fine starting kit, but could improve teaching
text:
For each of the 12 circuits it shows how to create, the booklet provides:
* A formal circuit diagram
* List of parts used
* 3D and 2D diagrams, showing the finished breadboard / Arduino
* Table of component used (e.g., a 330 ohm resistor), and which breadboard positions to use.
* Short discussion of C code used in the IDE
* Expected results
* Short troubleshooting section
* Very brief example of a real-world application

In the booklet, what we don't see much of:
* Thorough teaching of electronics, troubleshooting, etc.
* Instruction on the meaning of the circuit diagram.
* Instruction in WHY those components are used. Why is a resistor needed? Why is it a 10K ohm, and not a 330 ohm? When do you need a transistor or capacitor (the kit includes no capacitors). Note: there is some discussion of pull-up resistors.
* A diagram showing how the current flows through the breadboard (be sure to read the section "How's it all connected" on the page titled Breadboard -- and WHY aren't there any page numbers???)

The result is that if you make a mistake in a circuit, you may have difficulty correcting it. If you want to create a new circuit of your own, you probably won't have the knowledge to do that.

To be fair, there is some teaching in the *.ino code provided for each circuit. It's not all in the booklet. So, you definitely want to read the C code and comments. There are no quizzes, nor code to complete, or anything like that. It's all basically done for you. There could be far better explanation of what resistors, transistors, capacitors, diodes, etc. do. If you somehow learn to create your own circuits, it's going to be on you, or YouTube, or somewhere else.

It includes a Made in USA, Arduino (genuine, not clone, derivative or, I think, counterfeit), which helps support the Arduino community.

It does include a parts list of the entire kit, near the start of the booklet, so ignore the reviewer who said there isn't.

Some sensors that would have been cool to include, but weren't:
* Motion
* Humidity
* Air quality
You can, of course, purchase these cheaply elsewhere, and use with this kit.

The English is good throughout.

The 12 circuits are:
1. Blinking an LED, similar to Blinky.
2. Potentiometer (using a dial to vary LED brightness)
3. RGB LED
4. Multiple LEDs
5. Push buttons
6. Photo resistor (like to control a night light that gets brighter when it gets dark)
7. Temperature sensor (it's not a very accurate sensor)
8. Single Servo (that you would use to grasp things in robot hands, for example)
9. Buzzer
10. Spinning a Motor ** Note: I got a bad motor, apparently. My circuit perfectly matches the book. I tried other parts (diode, 330 ohm resistor, transistor, even wires). The code uploads. I entered various motor speeds in the Serial Monitor, which the booklet never mentions is needed. All the motor does is a high-pitched hum. **
11. Relays (to turn things off and on)
12. Shift register

title: BEST CAMERA FOR THE $$$!!!!
text:
Best camera on the market for the money, period!!!!

READ ENTIRE REVIEW

First impression: When I pulled the camera out of the box I wasn't very impressed, the instructions was lacking especially if you are a first time installer (not going to take away a star for instructions, your taking the project on, do a little research on basic camera installation beforehand) and the camera itself was smaller than I imagined by the picture which made me wonder how the quality of the image was going to be.

Installation: Very simple installation, has a power wire close to the camera and a power wire with the RCA cable (radio side). This gives an option to power it from the reverse wire or from the accessory power wire at the radio (only need to connect one of the two power wires). For most installations, including mine, you can simply ground it to the same bolt that is going through the bracket. Depending on your vehicle you may want to work your way from the camera to the front of the vehicle being as the RCA is smaller than the adapter end that plugs into the camera (some vehicles it won't matter, just plan before you install) It's setup to mount to a tag, but in my scenario I just had to drill new holes to mount it because I wasn't mounting close to my tag so I can't comment on using it with a tag. Once it was mounted, it was angled slightly downward (this is where I thought I would have an issue), the camera was made onto a small metal bar that was actually super stiff (this is what I thought was going to be flimsy), I slightly bent the bar upwards and BAM! PERFECT! I drove my van around on some rough roads and the camera never moved!

Night Viewing: I previously had a $100 camera installed that took on water inside the camera,that's why I purchased this one. My old camera had "night vision" with 3 LED lights on each side, this camera puts that one to shame for night viewing even without the LED's. this is one of the best cameras I've personally seen for night time.

Added bonus: you can turn off the guide lines simply by flipping a switch at the camera side of the connection. This doesn't take effect until the camera is powered off and back on, I personally like the guide lines but if you don't, easy to take them away.

Overall: VERY impressed with the camera, it has a 1 yeah warranty and if it died on day 366, I would buy another one the next day, no questions asked. I wouldn't even try to search for a better camera.

title: Best touchscreen for Raspberry PI
text: Great device! Absolutely love it. The thing I love about it is that there are no dangling wires or extra little PCB boards to maneuver out of the way. The PI fits perfectly on the display board via the GPIO header pins and the case fits it well with a little extra room to spare in case you do want to add extra PCBs. Couple this with an external battery like an Allpower AP-12000, http://amzn.com/B00EF1PIA2, and you've got a great little standalone computer. I am using this device for serial data logging when I am out in the field. The case is slanted in such a way to help it stand up-right, and its fairly sturdy in that regard. Of course, glue the external battery to the bottom of the case and its even more sturdy. My only concern so far is the little plastic screws that hold the backing to the case. It doesn't seem to secure the PI in place very well, but it does hold. A little hot glue helps there. As for external connections to GPIO pins, the device uses the first 26 pins (for power and mouse/touchscreen), so you have the last 14 pins left to use (assuming you are using RaspberryPI model A+, B+ or B2). The backing to the case has a slit to allow external wires to come through. At some point I want to try to use this as a small oscilloscope, so I intend to use the last remaining 14 pins and modify the case to have test lead hookup wire ports. I imagine it should work well. Given the quality of the display and the touchscreen capability, and this little device could be used for just about anything. I highly recommend it to anyone. Also, remember, this device does NOT work out-of-the-box. You have to modify your configuration to support HDMI hotplug and define the proper resolution (or you can use their Raspbian image included in the download link in the product's description).

The desiccant packets are sealed and must be opened before inserting them with the phone into the larger pack. Yes, that seems obvious, but for some reason I didn't think I should open them up.

title: If you are an Amazon Echo home, this is a great investment for hands-free calling.
text:
I have Echos in the bedroom and in the kitchen - and it always seems to be those two rooms when I don't have my phone handy. So for 35 bucks, I thought this was worth a shot.

Not a bad call.

Setup was a snap. You DO need to have a smartphone with the Alexa app installed. Obviously, you need to have at least one Echo device.

Ten minutes after unboxing it and following some simple prompts from the app and it was working with Ooma and my landline phone (I use my old phones with the ooma VOIP system). My contacts on my phone synched with the Alexa app and all is well. I called out to my phone and it worked. I called my home number from the cell and it worked.

My wife called her sister and had a nice chat. The only issue was her sister reported that we sounded 'distant' - I guess the microphones aren't as powerful as the speakers because she was pretty loud.

A few more commands but they are simple ones. This is another example of why I am betting that Amazon is going to win the smart home contest. This product works fine - and I have played around with it enough to know it's pretty reliable. Amazon will continue to tweak the connect and make it better. And let's face it - I have a google mini and I like the Assistant just fine, but the Echo system came out of the gate first and they have a commanding lead.

Devices like this make it clear that they are not planning on losing it anytime soon.

So, easy to setup, commands are intuitive, the Alexa contact list syncs with my phone when I make changes, and it's reasonably priced. It works with my existing hardware, so it enhances my investment. And the only strike seems to be a minor one - and most phones don't sound that great on speaker either.
