title: BUYER BEWARE! This is a SCAM! Took device to Microsoft store and they said hardware does not work
text:
DO NOT BUY ANY PRODUCTS FROM DAVE PARKERS.

The product comes as a "Certified Refurbished" or so Dave will have you think. Within minutes of receiving the product, I upgraded it to Windows 10 (as it is clearly the better processing system). The device failed to work properly after the upgrade. I took the device to the Microsoft Store and the technicians (equivalent to "Apple Geniuses") did a workup on the hardware inside and told me that this device does not have properly functioning hardware.... Wow... Certified Refurbished right? They told me that whomever sold this to me as a functional Microsoft Surface Pro clearly was misleading me.

Now I know what you're thinking. "But Derek, when you got the device, it was working... You upgraded it to Windows 10 and then it stopped working. Why are you blaming Dave Parkers for this?"

Well, I'll tell you why. This device should not fail to work because of a software upgrade... a ROUTINE software upgrade. I did not try to download a random application. I was upgrading the device to the next processing system and it failed. The Microsoft Store technicians told me that it must have been on its last leg if all it took was a simple software upgrade to make this device fail.

What gets me the angriest is this device might not have failed until after the 30 days return policy that Amazon offers. What would I do then? Nothing. It's almost as if the device was made to work for a limited time period and then fail. I would have been far less angry had the device failed to begin with.

Do what you want but I would personally not recommend Dave Parkers and his Surface Pros to anyone.

title: Top-notch sound quality and comfort.
text:
In this review I won't be going through technical charts or DB graphs showing how much the signal is attenuated at different frequencies. I won't use pompous adjectives to define the sound characteristics either. This will be a straight-to-the-point review based on how the headphones feel and perform when playing different music genres.

## Hardware Quality
**Rating: 10/10**

You don't see this level of quality in headphones often, not even in high-end offerings, category which is definitely occupied by the Momentum headphones. The metallic head band is wrapped in yellow-stitched leather. Although the ear cups are made of plastic, it's high quality and feels very solid. The matte finish helps repelling those nasty fingerprints we've come to hate.

The parts of the cups touching your ears are made of a very soft and pleasant leather. The included cables (yes, there are cables, more on that later) are not extremely thick (i.e. not like the ones you would find on Shure earbuds), but that's not a bad thing. The case is made out of leather, very soft to the touch but sturdy at the same time.

If I had to criticize something about the quality, it would be related to the play/volume/skip button. It has a plastic feel that somehow seems out of place in headphones like these.

## Hardware Design
**Rating 10/10**

The design of the Momentum headphones exudes minimalism, thoughtfulness and good taste. It's really hard to pull that off without being austere or overly simplistic.

Buttons are almost hidden in the right can. However, they are very easy to reach out to thanks to the raised dots and ridges in the cup. The included cable doesn't have the fancy stereo connector the original Momentum headphones had. However, it makes sense to do away with it for a headphone that is meant to be used primarily on wireless mode. One thing to note is that you have to properly align the stereo plug before inserting it in the right cup hole, then twist it so that it stays in place. I guess Sennheiser went for this design to prevent the cable from being accidentally pulled when in wired mode. A decision I must say, I'm not a fan of.

The new Momentum Headphones can be folded before being stored in the included case, which is great for travelers. Talking about the case, it perfectly complements the looks and feel of the headphones.

You can't talk about design without talking about comfort. On that department the Momentum headphones also excel. The headband provides just the right amount of pressure in your ears, and the leather lined cup cushions effectively go over the ear without leaving areas uncovered, not even while using eyeglasses. These are also much lighter than similar offerings from competitors, which is a huge advantage when using them for long periods of time.

## General Performance
**Rating: 10/10**

Let's get to the really important part: sound performance. The Momentum headphones can be used in two independent modes: **wired** and **wireless** (i.e. Bluetooth 4.0). In each mode, Sennheiser's proprietary noise reduction technology *NoiseGard* is used. You can also use the headphones turned off in wired mode for passive noise isolation.

If I had to describe it with one word, it would be **balanced**. I couldn't sense a particular range being prominent. Lows are bold and well defined, mids and highs are crisp and clear. Daft Punk's One More Time is great for testing the bass performance at the beginning of the song and high frequency response towards the end. The guitar and vocals in Creedence's Fortunate Son and Travelin' Band are nice and detailed. Diana Krall's voice in Glad Rag Doll sounds crisp and clear (all these songs were played in their lossless format)

### Noise reduction

As mentioned above, Sennheiser uses their proprietary technology - *NoiseGard* - for noise reduction. I have never been a fan of active noise cancellation as it seems to drown music when the *canceling* signal is introduced, especially low frequencies. I have noticed it with several pairs of Bose headphones and it's not pleasant at all. I'm happy to say that I didn't get the same feeling with the Momentum wireless.

I also performed some tests using the headphones in wired mode and turning *NoiseGard* on and off (by turning on and off the headphones as a whole), and although there was an noticeable difference in performance, I wouldn't say it was considerably detrimental.

## Ease of Use
**Rating: 10/10**

Using the Momentum wireless headphones is pretty straight forward, for the most part. Operations associated to the Bluetooth connection like pairing, pausing music, skipping tracks, making calls and adjusting volume, are made by clicking/sliding one of the only two buttons in the headset. This is pretty standard for wireless headphones and Sennheiser has included graphical instructions on how to perform these tasks.

## Other Pros
**Rating: 10/10**

This section is intended to account for features not usually found in similar products. In the case of the Sennheiser Wireless Momentum headphones, *NoiseGard* is definitely one of those features. As explained above, it's basically active noise cancelation that really works.

## Battery Life
**Rating: 8/10**

Sennheiser included a 600mAh Lithium-ion polymer battery inside the headphones. They claim it lasts 22hrs, but I could only get 18 hrs out of them. Although it's a good amount of time, I'm disappointed I couldn't get the rated duration. Also, it takes approximately 3 hrs to charge them, which it's just too much for such small battery.

## Price
**Rating: 7/10**

These headphones retail for about $500, which is a pretty high price. You can find similar offerings from other manufacturers for much less than that, but you would obviously lose on quality and most likely features.

title: and this case is beautiful. I got my new mobo
text: I WISH I COULD GIVE THIS 5 STARS.  But I can't.  Why they decided not to make the main chamber just another 1 1/2 - 2 cm wider, I'll never know.  Huge design flaw in my opinion.  I read review after review trying to see if one of my GPUs would fit.  I'm trying to go to a smaller form factor pc, and this case is beautiful.  I got my new mobo, my ddr4, my skylake cpu and a water cooler, my psu, and was all set and ready to build.  I put the mobo, cpu, and ram in first with no issues whatsoever.  Then came the h80i water cooler.  This is where the first hiccup begins.  You have to really get creative to fit even the smallest of water-cooling systems in this case.  I removed the front fan, and had to place it there, and even then it just didn't look right.  But it worked with a little elbow grease.  Went to bed that evening, and woke up the next morning.  I'm not sure if I had a nightmare that night or why I woke up thinking about it, but I woke up so worried that my gpu wasn't going to fit.  So before work, I was taking measurements and it was soooooo close.  I thought that maybe it might be snug, and the psu wires would be touching the glass, but that would be okay.  Went to work, came back home, and the build commenced.  For about 5 minutes until my hopes and dreams were broken.  First I tried my MSI 980, and it was so close.  I got it to fit inside, but the heatpipe stuck out too far to close the side, and once you attach the psu wires, it would be even worse.  Next up, EVGA Classified 980 Ti.  Oh hell no.  Not even close.  This thing couldn't even fit inside the case.  You know what did fit?  My PNY (spelled PUNY) gtx 650.  The oldest gpu I had for the newest computer I'm building.  Like I said before, I read so many reviews saying that their cards fit, and many of them were 900 series cards.  In 2015, if you are making a computer case like this, and you don't factor in the sizes of high-end gpus, that is a huge oversight.  Well, I love the case, and I'm just building a new computer for my wife using some spare parts and the 650 with this case.  I'll be searching for another, slightly larger case for my apparently gigantic gpus.

title: I... I've never felt this way about a monitor before...
text:
This 24" monitor has become my favorite thing about my office. I plug this into my 13" retina macbook pro for work. Then whenever I work remotely on the rMBP, I just want to go back to the office so I can work on this big beautiful monitor instead!

I can't say enough about this thing. It's big, it's got very high contrast, retina-level density. My office needs involve research and communication, and this monitor is a joy to read and write on.

The construction is also superb; It has the most extendable stand on the market (for the first time I don't need a pile of books to set it on), and it swings smoothly off with the push of a button if you want to mount the screen elsewhere.
Best of all, it has PHYSICAL, VISIBLE BUTTONS ON THE FRONT OF THE SCREEN so you don't have to grope blindly around the back of the !@#$ monitor every time you want to change the input! The buttons are all robust and click solidly, the chassis is solid; it's got all the classiness of a german luxury car. Also, it has a bunch of usb outlets which saves me all the messiness of plugging peripherals into my laptop.

I've researched the competition, and as far as I'm concerned, this is the ONLY monitor worth buying, period. Don't get the 27" version. This one is WAY cheaper with just as many pixels. If you need more space, get two of these.

Save your comparison-shopping time and just buy it.

title: An interesting bit of technology
text:
ODB-II ports are found on almost all US production cars after 2004 and import cars after 2007. This evolution of the ODB standard provides a candidate list of vehicle parameters to monitor, along with how to encode the data for each. In short, this is the type of information that your car polls to provide dashboard information and your mechanic uses to help diagnose or maintain your vehicle. Of course, this port is user accessible, so you have access to that same type of data.

The Techstick 5.5 inch E300 HUD Multi-color Screen Car Heads Up Display provides an interesting way to access some of that data, and that's, as the name suggest, as a heads-up display reflected onto your front windshield. It provides a laundry list of data display, including vehicle speed, engine speed (RPM), water temperature, battery voltage, fuel consumption, local time, single driving time, mileage measurement, shift reminder, fatigued driver reminder, low voltage alarm, high temerpature alarm, speed alarm, engine fault alarm, and fault code elimination. Naturally, you can also change between units of measurement.

In the box you get the main unit with 5.5" screen, ODB-II cable (which also works in EUOBD-capable vehicles), dashboard mat (to keep the main unit in place), wipes, windshield reflectors (allowing you to see the multi-color heads-up display on your windshield if it's dual layer construction, otherwise, it's not necessarily needed), and a comprehensive user manual. The device automatically powers on and off with your vehicle, as well as automatically adjusts brightness for a variety of lighting conditions (this can still be adjusted manually if desired).

On my 2014 Toyota Prius, I installed this without issue. Since my front windshield is dual layer construction, I probably needed the reflector, but the slight double image didn't bother me (and the photos, for obvious reasons, don't do the display justice), so I didn't stick one on. In any case, the colorful heads-up display worked great. Needless to say, it all feels kind of futuristic and is a nice way to display data that your dashboard may not otherwise provide, or even as a complement with an adjustable line-of-sight.

Thanks to Techstick for the discounted review unit.

title: Way too many issues make it a frustrating experience
text:
It's a sleek looking keyboard with a reasonably responsive touchpad and the good things end there.

First of all it has a very poor signal for a media keyboard. If the receiver dongle is plugged into a USB slot in the back of the computer, the signal doesn't penetrate to it consistently. As a result it loses key clicks and trackpad swipes. So you need a usb cable to move it to the front of the computer or to plug it into one of the front facing USB ports on the media computer.
Then if I am relaxing on the couch with my feet up and the keyboard on my lap, my feet end up blocking the signal somehow - even without shoes on. So the lost key clicks and touchpad swipes are again an issue.

Then the issues with the trackpad: the right click press is more like the very rightmost corner press. Anything else and it counts it as a left click. Sometimes even a rightmost corner press still gets counted as a left click. This is the single most annoying thing about the trackpad. Two finger scrolling works sometimes. Othertimes it doesn't work and I need to use the page keys or the scroll bar - but it's still not nearly as annoying as the unpredictability of the right click.

Overall I regret buying this keyboard and also regret not sending it back.

title: Random Volume Drops
text:
The UE Boom is great when it works. A product defect was reported several years ago where the volume would drop by 20 to 30% each time the playlist transitions from one track to the next. The only way to fix the problem is to physically go to the speaker, and manually increase and then decrease the physical hardware volume button to reset the speaker back to its original state. After I purchased the UE Boom I found several Logitech forum posts saying the problem had been fixed and all that was needed was a simple firmware update. Unfortunately after applying the latest firmware patch, the problem still pops up every three songs or so. This is true on a Windows 7 Dell laptop, Windows 10 Surface 3, and a Windows 8 Surface 2, all which strongly suggests that the problem is not the audio software or the device the UE Boom pairs with but rather with the speaker itself. I have attempted to reach out to Logitech's customer support for additional assistance after trying to fix the problem for over a week, but after waiting over two weeks now I have yet to receive a response -- just long enough for the speaker to no longer be under Amazon's warranty. Not only is the device unusable like this, but it also appeared to be physically scuffed even though it supposedly was shipped brand new. All round a very frustrating experience and a sketchy product.

5/17/2016 Update: I received two automated emails last week, one on May 11th and the other on May 13th, from Logitech reading, "You’ve recently been in contact with Logitech. We’d like to follow up and ask if your request was fully addressed. If it wasn’t, please feel free to respond to this email or visit our online Support Community." I replied to both emails explaining I never heard from anyone at Logitech. Unsurprisingly, having waited another week now, I have yet to get a human response. The device in functioning state would have received a 4/5 (higher frequencies don't carry as well), with its various warts a 2/5, and with nonexistent customer support a 1/5.

I also have a picture of this monitor next to my existing IPS monitor which uses an LG IPS panel. While both monitors do have IPS glow, which is expected from IPS-type monitors, the Acer has more of it. Also the glow on the LG panel is more silver-colored and fairly easy to ignore once you're used to it. title: AMBIVALENT CUSTOMER
text:
8/31/2017 . . . I had to reset this HP to to factory settings today. Since this laptop was delivered July 19, 2017, I have encountered more and more slow responses, freezes, and blue screens of death. For Windows 10, it's a much lighter shade of blue than it used to be. Very frustrating. Wasted lots of time dealing with what the HP analysis tools reported as Windows 10 failures and problems with the partitions it created. Equipment checked out according to the HP analysis program, but it has been behaving suspiciously like the hard drive failure on the Dell this one replaced, I' beginning to discover there are no reliable hard drives or virtual drives. They WILL fail. HP seems to have problems accommodating Windows 10, as do ALL anti-virus programs. Nothing good for my computers on which I installed Windows 10.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
My observations after 3 days:
RUNS COOL! No overheating problems so far.
Nice screen resolution with responsive touch screen.
Camera seemed grainy, could have been lighting.
Keyboard is OK (After all, it is a laptop)
Touch pad is weird. Will require retraining your finger/thumb muscles. Although it does have left click and right click buttons, they are UNDERNEATH the touch pad, so at first, you'll occasionally click on the wrong thing. The cursor will move if you don't hit the buttons dead on. Not that bad, just different. I got used to it fairly quickly.
Updates didn't take long . . . maybe an hour or two.

6 GB RAM is adequate, but seemed odd to me. Why not build evenly? Max 16GB. Holds 2 X 8 GB memory sticks.
DDR4 Memory. Description lists DDR4, but additional Information shows DDR3. It really is DDR4..
The 2.4 GHz CPU speed is good, especially for a computer under $500.00; it is NOT slow.
Haven't put much stress on the processor yet, so can't tell how it will perform in the long run.
Used laptop without the charger for about 6 hours (mostly online w/ minimal disk use) before warning appeared that only 20% battery life remained.
It runs Windows 10, and to create a recovery drive you must use a USB flash drive. It took up 8.6 GB on a 32 GB USB 2.0 drive. Probably need at least 16 GB drive to be safe. I used USB 2.0 rather than 3.0. It was cheap and took minutes, not hours. (May encounter errors first few attempts, but keep trying. Third time was a charm for me.) I still miss Windows 7 and computers that came with manuals & system CDs.
The hard drive storage capacity of 1 TB is probably more than you can use before it eventually fails. The life of a USB drive is not that predictable either, but if only used for the recovery drive and written to only occasionally, it should outlast the hard drive by years.
If computer develops problems, I'll revise this review.
So far, I have been pleased with this purchase.

title: Fast, and easy to use!
text: [[VIDEOID:f0994b8031d7b9ffbc3b31c2449481c1]] I’ve been wanting to upgrade my home network to 10G speeds, so I bought the solo for my network adapter for my Alienware 17 R5 laptop. This device does achieve the rated 10G speeds. I have this wired to a 10G UniFi switch via cat6, the switch is also connected to my server with a 10G nic that has a m.2 SSD drive. And in the attached video you can see that a 15 gigabyte file transferred across my network in 15 seconds!!! Don’t forget that your speeds will only be as fast as other bottlenecks in your system as most mechanical hard drives top out at 150 MB/sec and even standard SSD top out at 500 MB/sec. (non-raid). m.2 SSD drives are really fast and will allow reads and writes at or above the 1Gb/sec transfer rate. Most of the time this device runs slightly warm, however during long durations of high speed transfers it does get hot. But I have had no issues after 2 weeks of usage. I’m very happy with the product and highly recommend for laptop uses, as a standard 10G nic is more cost effective for a desktop application.

And, I don't really expect the battery power to be exactly as advertised, but it would be nice to be able to make apples-to-apples comparisons, so here are the actual numbers I get with the new battery:

Original battery is marked 5600maH, 62.1 watts; powercfg -energy reported capacity as 62160 mw, so that's right on the report's numbers.
This battery is marked 5200maH, but powercfg -energy reports 48840 mw capacity, that's (48840/11.1) = 4400 maH.
The last full charge appears to be 47097 mw, that's (47097/11.1) = 4243 maH

Arrived about 40% charged. I let it discharge and calibrate to get above numbers. The discharge time from 40% to shutdown at 5% was very good (about 2hrs., idle). Overall, probably equal to anything in this price range, and it clearly works fine, but I'd prefer correct numbers!

title: It's my first 2" eyepiece and I'm very pleased.
text: I recently added a 2" Dielectric star diagonal to my C8, after seeing a gorgeous view through a neighbor's scope. When I looked in his 2" eyepiece, it was like looking through a spaceship window instead of the pinhole view I was used to with my 1.25" EP. Your eyes will thank you for it. I chose the Celestron line of 2" eyepieces due to their affordability, good reviews, and my overall comfort with the brand as a novice astronomer. I couldn't be happier. The 23mm EP, in conjunction with the new diagonal, provided a wonderful view the Orion Nebula on my first viewing. Although Jupiter was bright and sharp, as well, I found that my Celestron 8-24mm 1.25" EP offered a similarly good image. The retractable eyepiece is a nice touch, although I find it harder to get a full view with it fully raise. In most dark environments, I probably will not use it. The build quality of the eyepiece is impressive. It's stunning to look at in person. What surprised me most was its size and weight, Sure, the specs listed the weight before purchase, but I didn't realize what it would feel or look like in my hand. Overall, I feel like I made a great choice for my first 2" eyepiece, and I have already begun adding more.

title: Does as claims when used properly
text:
Reading through other reviews it seems to be a mixed bag. Some obviously don't know how to set it up and others don't seem to know how to use it at all. I think the issue here is expectations. It is 1080p but it's not 20Mp. For what it is it does a great job. I've not had any of the issues some have reported such as failure to record or cutting off randomly. In my experience it takes a good quality video and works reliably. One thing I do rather dislike is the SD card slot. It's quite recessed and removing the card can be a bit persnickety. It also should be noted that inserting the SD card at an off angle won't end well so be mindful as you do it to keep it straight in all axis.
Tips; Make sure you have it powered reliably. Cigarette lighter type ports are not reliable as they depend on friction for their connection. The battery is very small so if you lose power for long enough it will power down in a few minutes. Make sure you have the exposure settings set according to lighting conditions. You will have to change this according to time of day and weather etc. There is not a 1 for all setting that will give you good results in all circumstances. Like most digital cameras the audio is not intended to be studio quality. The microphone element is tiny as it has to be but the audio is usable in most cases. If you want a high quality audio record of conversations in your, for instance with police then buy a digital audio recorder. They are very affordable and do a great job. Most modern cars have a fairly heavy UV/Anti-glare coating across the top part of the windshield so mount the camera as high up as possible to reduce flares and washout. Mounting it too low will also divert a lot of reflected light from the hood into the sensor which will lessen video quality. Try to angle the camera in such a way that puts the front end of the car out of frame or barely in frame. The battery usually lasts long enough to do a quick walk around to document collision damage or to move the camera from one vehicle to another without interruption, maybe 5 to 10 minutes max. There are a lot of settings options so read through the manual and get to know your camera.
Conclusion; This is not anywhere near a DSLR camera and it isn't designed to be. I bought mine from a national big box retailer before it came available on Amazon and paid twice as much and to be honest it is still worth it. I've even turned it around to make a few vlog episodes and both audio and video were quite good once I post processed them in audio and video editing softwares. I've used Uniden communications products for decades with no disappointments and this product is no exception. I'm not being compensated for this review and it faithfully and truthfully represents my honest opinion. Hope this helps.

title: Functions much better than expected. No voltage backfeeding on host port.
text:
Functions much better than expected. All the devices (2.0 and 3.0) I threw at it performed at the same throughput they do when using direct connections. The hub switches to external power when a USB 2 micro-B cable is plugged into the appropriate port and switches back to host power when unplugged. I did this repeatedly in rapid succession with no disconnects of either the hub or any attached devices (two HDD's and two USB sticks). Impressive. The current on the host port zeroes out while external power is connected and devices do remain powered through external power whether or not there is a host connection (i.e. whether or not the computer/host is powered on). It would be nice if there was some mechanism that would disconnect external power when the host goes down, but I'm not sure that feature even exists on any hub.

I also tested the host port for voltage "backfeed" using a [[ASIN:B00J3JSEG6 DROK USB 2.0 Digital Multimeter]] connected by gender-changer + adapter from [[ASIN:B073PWP5FW 4 Kinds of USB 3.0 Adapters]] to the hub's host port while an external power source was simultaneously connected. All devices on the hub powered up and no voltage was seen (multimeter/tester did not power on).

One little niggle that I'd be remiss not to mention: the USB cable that comes with this hub is ridiculously short; about 12 inches, sans-connecters. It also comes with an instruction leaflet and a "satisfaction card" (support information) in an easy-to-open cardboard box, so no blister pack with which to cut yourself.

title: It works, but the Amazon specific UI is poor compared to other devices.
text:
My views on this are mixed. I got it to replace a failing Roku stick. The Roku was annoying me as it kept losing the remote and requiring hard resets and re-entering account info for every service I use. The Amazon Stick I had hoped would be a fast experience with better features.

My opinion on it is mixed. It has a nice startup. Setup is not as annoying as the Roku, but still annoying. The speed and performance of the device is exactly the same as the Roku, so much so that I suspect they use the exact same hardware. But not a bad thing, except that the Amazon costs $10 more...

My biggest issue with the Amazon Fire stick is the Amazon App and Menu system. I am an Amazon Prime member, I also have quite an extensive Amazon Library of movies and television that I have bought. I frequently like to view from this library, first and foremost. Amazon however seems determined to make getting to my purchased library as difficult as possible. Instead force feeding me new shows that I might wish to purchase or watch on Amazon Prime instead. After 10 minutes of digging with each login I can finally reach the single narrow strip that contains my purchased content. I now have to punch the left right buttons several hundred times to scroll through it all to find what I wish. All while Amazon tries to entice me to buy other stuff over the remaining 90% of the Television screen. Manipulating your purchased video content using the Kindle Fire Stick is just awful. Hats off to Roku, they do it 1000x better, for Amazon. The Netflix app on the Fire Stick is similarly much m uch better presentation and UI than Amazon's own. As is the Hulu and the Funimation, and Crunchyroll (seeing a pattern?)

My second negative comes from a more unique situation to myself and my household. The Voice Navigation. My voice was medically compromised via a surgical error many years ago. I can speak well enough for humans, but the truth is only one vocal cord functions. So voice recognition machines cannot handle me. They are nothing but frustration in every way possible.

The Fire TV Stick With "Alexa" is an ok experience. So far it has not had the number of repeated problems I had with the Roku stick. But this is countered by the Fire Stick having its own negatives including performance, a horrible and slow Amazon interface, the idiotic Alexa Voice Services that are useless for many people. It does have a nice responsive remote. Gotta give them that.

If you like shouting into your remote trying to explain that you want to watch Star Wars, and not something far far worse, over and over, like a bad comedy routine, this might be for you. If you have that perfectly pitched announcers voice, with every crisp cadence exactly where it should be, you might actually find what you are looking for. Everybody else seeming gets a random selection from the "worst of the Saturday Afternnoon SyFy channel movie playlist. You know what movies I'm talking about. You really do.

text: Best Garmin watch yet.  Previously had the 920xt which I loved, was actually hard for me to switch, but after using the 935 for a few months now, I love it, mostly.  It's a great looking watch!  My only issue is there is a lot of data screens you need to go through to get to what you want; not really a big deal.  BUT (big problem for me), I have found that in the 25 yard indoor pool at the local YMCA my 935 does NOT track all of my laps properly.  Every workout, it miscalculates at some point.  For example on Saturday (3,700y total swim) during my 4x200 pull set, it counted my first 200y as 50, the next set as 175, the next set 200 and my final set 150.  Later on in my workout it calculated a 100y interval as 150 and another at 25.  It's not consistently off on every set but I can trust that every single time I get in the pool it will be off during some part of my training swim.  To make note, I am using it in non-gps mode for my indoor pool swims.  My 920xt started doing this after 3-years of everyday use, which is one of the reasons why I upgraded to the newer 935.  This is a HUGE disappointment, especially at the $500 price point.  Because of this I would be very hesitant to purchase this watch again, I would most likely look for the 920xt at half the price and buy that one again.

title: Love this amp!
text:
I was really surprised by this amplifier. I had read in many places that Chinese stuff is junk and that you have to pay thousands of dollars to get a decent class A amplifier. Well, that's not true. This amplifier is wonderful! It looks great. It sounds great. The build quality is great. I'm just amazed that I got this for the price I did here on Amazon. The shipping was incredibly fast too which was a surprise. When I ordered this I was afraid that 6.8 watts per channel was just not going to be enough. Well, it powers my bookshelf speakers very well. In fact, I never even turn the volume up more than a quarter way. It turns out that this is way more than enough power for me.

This amp is compact. I have enough room for a few of these so I might get another one.

I was going to upgrade the tubes but decided not to because it already sounds great. To upgrade all the tubes would cost me three to four hundred dollars. I did lots of research to find out how much and where to get all the replacement tubes. It would have to be a combination of Mullard, RCA, and Winged C tubes. It's just not worth it in my opinion. Maybe someday if these tubes ever burn out.

Anyway, I love this amp and would recommend it to everybody.

This amp inspired me so much that I'm going to try to build one soon.

Update 12/10/18: I'm still using this amp for about 12 hours everyday and it hasn't given me any problems at all. It sounds great.

I ordered all new tubes which cost way more than this amplifier itself. So far I have replaced all the 6J1 tubes with Russian Winged C tubes. I don't notice much difference if any at all. This tells me that the tubes that come with this amplifier are good to begin with.
I'm still waiting for three more tubes that are hard to find and get. Wow, they were expensive. Hopefully they will make this amplifier sound even better. However, as it is I'm totally happy with this amp. It's great. I love it!

update: 1/12/19
I have upgraded all the tubes and been listening to it like this for more than a month. I didn't think the sound could get any better but it did. Now this amplifier sounds even more incredible. Now I know that vintage tubes can really make a difference. Here's the tubes I installed:

(4) WINGED "C" (SED) 6P1P-EB (these are Russian tubes, not vintage but they were the only upgrades I was able to find
(2) RCA 6SN7GT / GTB Black Plate (I was able to get these used off ebay for about $50; they're made in the 50's or 60's
(1) Mullard 5V4G (I was able to get this tube on ebay for around $120; it's the rectifier tube I believe and definitely the most expensive)

So something with this combination of tubes really works excellent for me. I couldn't be happier.

I still have had no problems with this amp and I use it at least 12 hours per day. It always gets very hot but I guess this is just normal for tube amplifiers. Sometimes I turn it off for 30 minutes or an hour to give it a break.

It's also probably worth mentioning that I bought another tube amplifier that costed 6 times the price of this and it doesn't sound as good as this small amp. The only thing I can figure is that this Nobsound 6P1 amp is just designed and built really well and maybe adding the vintage tubes makes it even better. Unfortunately, I've seen some other reviews on here about this amp having problems or failing. I guess you kind of have to take your chances on getting a good one. I feel lucky to have received a good one.

One other thing that somebody else had also mentioned is the blue power led light on the front of this amp. It really is bright. That's why I eventually put a piece of tape over it. Now it doesn't bother me at all.

For the ceiling mounts I cut half inch plywood circles using the mount templates and mounted the wood between ceiling joists with insulation behind. Each speaker comes with a paper template which worked perfectly. The sound for all of them is very impressive- clear highs and surprising bass although my system also uses a 12 inch sub. title: **35" Monitor review** It would be hard to go back after going so wide ...( cheesy, but deal with it XD )
text:
[[VIDEOID:7c1cf5056d0dad6d8a4d51ade444d9da]] I have waited a while now before writing this review. I wanted plenty of usage time before explaining my experience with this monitor. I am sure many people looking to buy a 35" ultra wide monitor have probably never used one before as I hadn't in my case as well. Obviously though, the experience is subjective in the end. As with my case, I have loved having such a large monitor. Being immersed in what I am doing is quite a good experience. I can have 5-6 different things open at once and I can see all of them in their full glory (depending on what I have opened lol, Steam, discord, friends list, cam, and others). My perspective is going to be based on general web browsing and gaming. Mostly gaming though. I dabbled a little into watching youtube/netflix and what not, and the experience was great. I had to sit back a little farther than usual though. Being in my usual spot just seemed way too close for a 35" display of what I was watching. Technically a good thing in my opinion though. As for gaming I really only play 2 games. I purchased this monitor for PUBG play. I also play CSGO, but mainly PUBG nowadays. The PUBG experience is amazing! ... This alone made the monitor worth it. You really get immersed into the game play so much more. The wide screen res also helps with being able to watch multiple corners at one time since you can see more to the sides. I also pick out many opponents much faster than people on my squad since I can see more to the sides than them. It does give you quite the advantage. As far as csgo. It was a MEH,.... kinda experience. I actually play it at native 1440p res for this game ( where the sides are cut and they are just black at the edges ). I tired the widescreen thing for a bit and I just couldn't get used to it. Again this is subjective, but CSGO just isnt a good game for widescreen imho. Depending on the type of games you plan to play, widescreen is amazing. Especially for open world type things. I tried GTAV for a little bit and I also really liked it for this as well. I am sure you can think of the great implications that a wide monitor can have for certain types of games.

The bad - Really this is the only reason I am giving this monitor a 4 instead of 5 stars. I absolutely love this monitor, but it does have a HUGE flaw that is hard to overlook. IT GHOSTS TERRIBLY! ... I contemplated sending it back for a replacement, but it seems many people have experienced the same issue. Although, mine seems pretty bad and I have often wondered if it is worse than others. If most of these monitors suffer from this, then I would recommend spending a little bit more and going with the acer or asus widescreen. Its mostly noticeable with dark colors, but it still does it with most all of them. In game it is not as noticeable unless there is a very dark object (typically black). So because of this I decided to just deal with it since during gaming and watching videos, I don't really notice it. But, if you are moving a tab on the desktop, it is verrrry noticeable. Everything looks like the nyan cats rainbow trail. ... Quite annoying lol.

In the end, I do recommend this monitor. I could write so much more about this gem, but this is already a pretty long review lol. Maybe mine is worse than others when it comes to ghosting, but I am not sure since I have not seen another one in use. I know the monitor has a 3 year warranty, but I dont want to NOT game with this thing for 2 weeks to a month lol. If the problem somehow gets worse though, then I will definitely suck it up and send it in.

P.s. Yes I tried every setting to help minimize the ghosting. I also looked up the best settings to set the monitor to, and in the end, it still ghosts. :/

I may upload a video of the ghosting if enough people show interest in seeing it----

title: First impressions
text:
This is my second smartwatch. The first watch I ever purchased was a Samsung Gear Neo so I'll compare theSony to my Samsung Neo. The Neo has a Tizen operating system so there are many limitations whereas the Sony Smartwatch 3 has an Android operating system. The Sony has a built in GPS and you can use OK, Google because it's an Android; BUT, unlike the Neo it doesn't have a speaker. I can receive calls from my Neo and keep my phone in my pocket.

The Sony is way easier to pair with Bluetooth (I had to 'reset' my sons phone just to get his Neo to pair with his Samsung S5). Battery life is on par with the Neo (two days of operation without the need to recharge). Because it's a Sony and has Android it will take me some time to work through all the features and settings. The watch thickness is not bulky and the face makes it more traditionally dimensional as an everyday wear (I hate bulky watches), so it's about the same as the Neo's. The Neo needs and comes with a charging dock, which means it can be lost because it's small - I believe a replacement dock costs about $30. The Sony doesn't require a dock, just a mini-USB cable that comes with the watch.

Here are my initial assessments:

Size, resolution, price, and charge length: All even.
Operating system: Sony due to Android operating system.
Weight and face dimensions: Even.
GPS: Sony (none on Neo).
Speaker: Neo, but limited to Bluetooth range (none on Sony).
Charging: Sony (no charging dock required).
Camera: Even, none on either watch.
Functionality: at this point I would say advantage Neo, but I'm sure Android has an "app for that" and I'm still getting used to refer Sony's functions.

Overall: At this point I would probably lean towards the Sony because I can speak commands into the phone, like sending a text, email, or start my car without having to take out my phone (although I think my phone's security needs to be off).

title: Before you install this “art” on the wall...
text:
Honestly, this was a disappointing purchase, especially for the massive cost.

The art mode was a major factor in our decision, but it’s more of a screensaver or digital picture frame. If you were wanting a nice piece of art on the wall that doubles as a TV, this isn’t it. It’s a TV with a screensaver.

On top of that, the color temperature and brightness of the art would fluctuate, from really dim and orange, to overly bright and too blue, making it worthless to try to adjust the brightness and color level.

And if you still buy it and aren’t sure if you’ll like the art mode, set the TV up on its stand first and see if you like it. Don’t do what I did and spend a ton of time installing it on the wall, only to turn it on for the first time and find out it looks pretty fake. And realize that you now have to take it all back down and try to pack it back up.

If you’re 20+ feet away, then maybe, sometimes, it might look like art. But that illusion fades quickly. You can use your photos for art mode, but the colors are washed out. No one is going to be fooled — guests will think it’s a digital picture frame or a TV. Even kids ask about “the light up screen.”

IMO you’re better off with a better TV for half the price, and an Apple TV with a screensaver.

title: No Buyer's Regrets--I'm very satisified
text:
I am so pleased with my new Sangean RCR-20 clock radio, I wondered what others were unhappy about. The biggest complaints were poor AM reception, and low Bluetooth playback. I compared the RCR-20 with two AM radios and found it generally comparable. Radio-Locator.com lists six AM stations I should receive in my zip code, and the RCR-20 picked up five; the sixth came in when I rotated the radio for the best reception. However, only four were noise free enough for regular use. For AM, you'd want to listen to a strong local station.
The low Bluetooth complaint is justified. I needed to set the RCR-20 and my Galaxy smartphone near maximum volume, but then got clean, room-filling sound.
Another complaint was difficult programming. I am very sensitive to that and returned another model because it was too confusing. The RCR-20 is digital, and therefore more complex than older radios. You need to hold some buttons down, and that is not intuitive, but I learned the pattern quickly.
Some complaints are personal opinions about appearance and sound quality. I find the radio good looking for any room, and the sound exceptionally clear for a small radio, even at maximum volume.
The RCR-20 does not have an atomic clock--it does not receive the government time signals from Fort Collins or Hawaii. Instead, it receives less reliable time and text signals from some local FM stations. If you tune the RCR-20 to one of these FM stations, you will see text under the time on the display and the clock and calendar will be set. The setting is retained if you then tune to AM or to an FM station that does not transmit these signals. The time will be wrong if you tune to a station in another time zone or to a station that does not transmit time signals when Daylight Saving Time changes. For more information, read the Wikipedia article on Radio Data System. An advantage of the RCR-20 is that it displays RDS so you can read the station name, programming type like Rock Music, and the title of the song.
To explore complaints about backup I did some experoments and came away very pleased. The RCR-20 wakes you up on time even if the power is off and has been off for hours. If you set it to wake up to radio,and the power goes off, it buzzes instead (beeps really). One quirk: It the radio is playing when the power goes off, it won't turn on until you press the On/Off button.
Finally, some users complained that they could not locate the buttons by feel. Three suggestions: use the remote control buttons, don't touch any buttons and the radio will go off in an hour, or fasten a small shirt button on top of the RCR-20 button (but don't let any glue get inside).
In conclusion, no buyer's regrets--I'm very satisified with the RCR-20.

title: Good audio performance for both music streaming and TV at a modest price.
text:
I purchased this model based on decent reviews for both TV and Bluetooth audio quality, as I use it connected to an Echo Dot. While I make no windy claims to being a "golden ear" audiophile, I've dabbled in decent quality audio equipment since before CDs. This is not a life-changing piece of gear by any means, but for this price it's unfair to expect that, and it performs both tasks quite admirably.

Modern TV speakers almost by definition are very poor, with insufficient space to move enough air and awkward directional placement. Stringing a 5.1 system across your living room is not an aesthetic choice I'm happy with, and not even all that useful unless you principally use your TV as a display for Blu-Ray or DVD content. Hence soundbars/soundbases. Since I prefer to look directly at a screen at home rather than look up at a wall-mounted TV, the latter made more sense with my setup.

Sonos' new base then? Good reputation, fancy innards, but a persistent refusal to use Bluetooth even by offering an auxiliary port for a receiver killed them from consideration. I'm often streaming local content not just Spotify et al. ZVox in various sizes? Like the volume-leveling and dialog features but music playback quality is far from the greatest and reputation is...variable. This then competed for my business with the usual variety of Yamaha, Sony, Bose equivalents. It was the music playback reviews and relatively modest price that swung the deal.

Everyone wants to justify their choice retroactively but I am trying to be objective. This I feel is a very good match for my needs. The audio quality is just fine in the upper consumer range with nice tonal separation, a fairly good soundstage for a combo unit, and more than ample power for anyone not trying to rattle their neighbors' windows. In the current bass-obsessed zeitgeist I should mention that it has a solid even hefty low end given the lack of dedicated subwoofer, especially with bass boost selected, although I personally prefer the cleaner and less needlessly boomy standard EQ setting. Again likely not enough for the folks who like to shake their black Escalades to bits with garbage-can sized subwoofers, but more than enough for anyone who actually likes music, even in percussion-heavy genres. On the TV side of things it provides a huge improvement to the TV speakers. Admittedly this is not difficult, and soundbases or bars at half the price can make the same claim, but the discount versions are often either muddy or weak or both. No such problems here as we get good response and clarity across the frequency range, with much more distinct volume in the all-important spoken registers all too often lost in the mushy middle with TV audio.

Physical setup is childishly simple as is operation of the unit itself. You may need to fiddle with your TV's settings however, especially to get the audio from external HDMI connected devices like DVD or Blu-Ray passed through the optical connections here. Be sure to check the dimensions of your TV base or feet of course, as this is likely too tall to sit between the wide-set TV feet of most models. Luckily mine can be moved from the edges to only a couple of feet apart.

It's not perfect, admittedly. The lack of feedback from control settings is a bit of a niggle. What volume level am I on? (It will likely need to be higher for Bluetooth than TV by the way, as the former was initially barely audible even with the Dot turned up to 10 until I pressed the Fluance's volume up button a whole but unguessable bunch of times, but luckily switching from Bluetooth to optical inputs remembers the relevant audio settings and my feared deafening on return to TV listening never happened). There is no indication either on the screen, on the unit or on the remote. Same for 3D or Bass Boost settings. The latter is immediately apparent most of the time but the former seems to vary in how much difference it achieves so often hard to know current setting. The switching from various Bluetooth sources is a bit fiddly, and I'd prefer an option to eliminate the initially slightly distracting LED source indicator light altogether or at least make it turn off a few seconds after any change.. I'm pretty sure I can tell which input the sound is coming from without Fluance's help.

All in all though a good choice if you want to combine very respectable Bluetooth music streaming audio quality with a solid mid-level TV audio upgrade in one easy cost-effective package which is handsome and well constructed.

title: Durable and good performance - trustworthy drives - recommended.
text: I'm in the enterprise storage industry, so I've seen many different drive types come and go.  WD is in the enterprise space with the HGST acquisition, but these drives are from the legacy WD side.  Even though I'm in the industry, my home lab suffered from frequent failures of consumer-grade drives.  White not devastating at home, it was inconvenient and expensive - short warranties and the need to correct issues when I could have been doing other things.  I decided to invest in these - WD's entry-level enterprise-grade drives - and I've been extremely pleased with them.  They perform as you would expect for a 7.2K drive, operate at reasonable temperatures, and in the years that I have had them I have yet to have a drive failure.  If you have appropriate expectations for performance (understanding that these are not 10K or 15K drives and rather high density) and availability (they are SATA, so single connection vs dual SAS), these are excellent drives for smaller arrays.  Highly recommended for the appropriate use case.

title: Got the Chinese-voice-prompt version, would't connect
text:
I was excited to get this camera because of mostly positive customer reviews. Then, when I plugged in the power cable for the camera, the excitement immediately turned into disappointment and frustration.

First of all, the voice prompts were in Chinese and I didn't understand them. I was hoping that they were the default voice prompts and I was using my phone to Google-live-translate them. However, this was difficult to do as I also needed my phone to set up the camera. I had the QR code, in which the phone app puts the W-Fi credentials read by the camera. I didn't understand if the next Chinese prompt was Wi-Fi connected or not connected, but the setup failed every time no matter what I tried. I tried turning off the 5 GHz in my router completely and that didn't help either. I also checked that my Wi-Fi SSID was not hidden. I tried setting the region to China in the phone app -- as it warned that the app only works for the same region the camera is intended for -- but that didn't help.

I read on the Internet that if the camera firmware is for a different region, the camera won't connect. I looked for the firmware on the YI website, but the download link was unavailable -- very poorly designed website!

With so many things going wrong from the get-go, I decided that it's not worth calling the customer service for this poorly designed and built camera with poor Web support. Just the fact that there are a multitude of firmware versions and the app works for only specific regions is a sign that this camera is poorly built. I just returned it.

As additional notes, the physical design of the camera is not great -- it's somewhat large -- and it doesn't come with good mounting hardware that most other cameras come with -- comes with only a flat mounting plate.

I strongly recommend avoiding this camera. There are better products.

title: Nice compact unit - well made with plenty of features
text:
I bought this to replace an older MP3 player, and I've been very pleased with it. While it's UI (user interface) isn't perfect, the overall product is very good.

The quality of construction and fit and finish are excellent. Particularly welcome is that it came with several screen protectors, including one that is pre-installed. Nice touch!

It also comes with a small plastic tray that protects the back without adding any noticeable weight or bulk. This is a small unit. It easily fits into my a shirt pocket. While I didn't buy this for its compact size, it is something to note.

I've had no problem adding many songs. It's a slow process even with USB, and it's because you are adding gigabytes of data.

The display is quite nice, and there are several color schemes. I'd like to see some larger fonts. I'd also like to see a better way to enclose the Mini-SD memory card. Perhaps a small door that flips upward. And the Mini-SD card would slot into place rather than the pressure spring that is widely used.

I'm very pleased with the audio quality of the files. You should keep in mind that your speakers or headphones play a major role in how these files sound. I just bought some Sennheiser CX-400 II earbuds, and the X1 has no problem driving them loudly. With several headphones, there wasn't enough volume, and the X1 probably could benefit from pairing it with a headphone amp.

After you add music to the Micro-SD memory card of your choice, be sure to rescan the folders, unless you've set that option to "Automatic." Depending on how many files are on your card, this could take a couple of minutes to scan and index.

I like that it has the option for gapless playback, which really makes the listening experience for a number of albums in which one song leads directly into the other.

The rotating rubber ring doesn't depress. It merely allows you to navigate your songs. I'd like to see the Creative Zen approach of allowing you to flip through your albums by major letter A, B, C, D, etc. That would make navigating a large number of albums a quicker process. The rubber is soft to the touch with soft detents (clicks). It also allows you to quickly lower or raise the volume.

Overall, I have no major complaints - just a couple of suggestions here and there.

I really like this unit and can see me using it for years to come. I already have begun re-ripping all of my CDs.

title: Fast easy voice activated set up.
text:
I’m not a gamer or hobby level computer engineer. This won’t be that kind of review.
I am a tactile person. I appreciate how things look and feel. I enjoy the feel of quality design, and construction.
First let me say I enjoy the aesthetic of this computer. The brushed metal with a matt black, and red accents is both interesting and exciting. This will be the primary computer for my 11 year old. He loves gaming, and graphic design. He is currently working on a comic book, and I know he will make great use of this computer for his creations.
I absolutely loved the setup. This is a windows machine. I have not set up a windows machine in years. We have mostly used iPads and iPhones for most of the last decade. I’ve purchased and set up many of those. They are simple for sure, but this windows machine made setup interesting. Now maybe that says more about windows than Acer, but it’s included. I enjoyed it. So it’s in the review.
Why was the setup so interesting? Cortanna. The whole set up was voice controlled. She spoke, I answered, and she did the setup. I felt like I was at a pro desk, having a knowledgeable customer service rep set it up for me.
The screen has a matte finish, and feels a little plasticy. This may be a side effect from coming from iPads, which have glass screens. But I think I do prefer the look of glass. I do think the matte finish helps reduce glare. So this computer would likely, literally shine, out doors. It’s a bit big, in my view, to be easily portable. But I’m sure kids and teens lug these around. I prefer the iPhone 7 Plus for portability. Anything bigger than an iPad mini is staying at home.
The machine attaches to WiFi quickly and easily, and with stability. Thanks to google, most of my settings were there after setup and google log in.
The back lit keyboard is a neat feature. The keyboard it’s self provides a nice tactile experience. Key strokes feel fluid, and smooth. The keys feel more rubber or silicone, than plastic. Their motion seems to have been intentionally engineered for a positive user experience.
The hardware inside is sufficient for any computer tasks I threw at it. I had numerous windows open at once, everything from shopping, to video streaming, to audio streaming. No hiccups, or glitches.

title: Really fast router
text:
I cannot understand the many bad reviews regarding this router.
I upgraded my wireless n netgear router with this one iin early December.
The first thing I did was to upgrade my internet subscription from 50mbs to 100 Mbps since I found that the internet speed was was maxing out on my wireless devices. With the netgear router, the max wireless internet speed was in the 30 Mbps range, now with the upgrade I get 100 to 120 Mbps on my iPad and other devices that have AC. I am sure that with this router, I could use faster internet and have it delivered to my devices but getting a higher tier would not justify the costs for me. It might help that I have the router connected to the modem in my living room in the center of my house.
I bought two routers and use one as a bridge in my office, to replace the power line adapter that only got me about 15 Mbps. Before deciding to use the bridge, I was contemplating to use a wired Ethernet connection, but it would be difficult to run the wires invisible since I have mostly tiles. With the bridge in the office, computers there can now use the full internet speed and I can finally use my Synology NAS to stream movies to the living room. As an experiment, I used the NAS to check the download speed between the router and the bridge and found that the transfer speed was between 300 and 700 Mbps averaging over 500 Mbps. (Connecting the computer directly to the NAS gives me nearly gigabit speed; so considering the distance the result I am getting are close enough.)
The office bridge is about 30 feet away with one wall in between. The link speed is mostly at 1300 Mbps. With this router there is no need for wired gigabit Ethernet anymore!

I did had initially problems that the router was losing the 5 ghz connection once per week. I found that the router was not updating to the latest firmware automatically. I checked the installed firmware version on the asus web site and found a note that the version installed requires a hard reset in order to install a new 5 ghz driver. I performed the hard reset by holding down the reset switch for more than 5 seconds (and lost all settings in the process; that's why I gave only 4 stars). After that, the router recognized the latest firmware automatically and installed it. Since then, I installed one more update, which was automatically detected. I did not experience any problems since then.

I use parental control for time and content and have my son complaining sometimes that he either cannot download (when I blocked file transfer), or that the Internet is down (when I blocked it for the night). Therefore I know that the restrictions work. The anti virus software in the router informs me by email of blocked sites in real time. It also keeps logs of visited sites and statistics of device and app usage.
I have about 20 devices connected (wide range: TiVo, tivo stream, vonage, fire tv, AV-receiver, blu Ray player, phones, tablets, printer, laptops, desktops, ip cameras, NAS, TV, Wii, access point, kindle,...) no problem with any of them.
Overall it is an awesome product for my needs.

The only downside I've found after months of use is that the raised bezel annoys me greatly when I'm writing with the Surface pen and have the unit flat. I'm not sure if this is partially just the way I tend to write, but it digs into the edge of my hand when I'm writing and is painful at times - especially if I'm trying to take quick notes. title: A Great Kit and Building Base for a Lot More Than Weather Data!
text:
I really like this kit! At first, I was a little put off at the cost. But after researching the parts, I realized that if obtained domestically in the US, they add up to just under the cost of this kit. And that is without the Wemos interface board. Sure, you could get the parts from overseas and pay a bit less and get them in 30 days or more, but I wanted to play with this tech now and Amazon Prime got it to me within a couple of days.
The kit also includes some hardware that gives you mounting options. After “dry” assembling a few configurations, I decided that I wanted to keep the SD card mount which also allowed me to use the female socket headers to insert the display into. Being a guy that likes to prototype, I wanted the clean option of removing the display easily to use with beefier hardware with more I/O. The ESP32 perhaps. Hmm. There are two spacers and 4 screws included for this option. I would have preferred four spacers and 8 screws so I could solidly mount the interface board with the display. I had more on my bench so no worries. Also included is a nice set of headers to accommodate other options. I was impressed!
The interface board is solid and took to soldering well. The mounting holes were a perfect fit to the display and that was an awesome plus! My only complaint would be that there should be some additional printing on the board indicating what the first display pin would be. Not all the pin descriptions, just the first pin. This way, the end-user knows that the board is oriented correctly and not flipped upside down. I had to do a bit of research to determine my dry-run layout was correct. And the seller was awesome in quickly addressing a question of mine by linking a site showing the connections. Two thumbs up!!
The Wemos is a fully functional D1 Mini Pro and has 16mb! That gives you tons of creative room for enhancements! I planned to rewrite everything to meet the needs of my project, that needed a touch screen and to be wifi connected so I was pleased with the processing power. If I had a complaint, it would be that the only pins left after interfacing with the TFT, is the serial pins, an analog pin (A0), and a digital pin (D0). That does not leave much room for expansion to sensors, etc. Not a design flaw though, just a limitation and workable. So long as I can attach an interrupt to D0 status change, I’m good. I have not tested that yet.
The software setup was almost in-sync with the online instructions at github and other places. Maybe I missed a step with the instructions and ended up using an older version of the Arduino package, but it did not work as expected out of the box. I had to make a couple of modifications to the main ino code. There was an undeclared function that needed to be prototyped, and I had to add a wifi.disconnect to the wifi_connect function. Why? Because after uploading an updated sketch, the weather application would not connect to my wireless network unless I cycled the power. With the disconnect addition though, it worked like a charm!
Additionally, with the sketch, the settings.h file was very convenient! The whole project is pretty well written. With MY version (remember that it might not be the latest and a mistake in versioning on my part), the time settings were all setup for Zurich. I had to adjust them for the US and although I do not fully understand the parameter meanings with the DST library, in the end I found that changing the GMT adjustment was what finally allowed the time to be displayed on my device as it is on my computer. And right down to the second too. NICE!! It is also important to note, and the settings.h file recommends this in the comments... TEST YOUR WUNDERGROUND API KEY on a browser, to see what the JSON has to offer. This is critical and proved to be a major stumbling block for me as I omitted that step. It turned out that the city I was setting in the variable did not have “_” (no quotes) for spaces between words, as in “SAN_TAN_VALLEY” for “San Tan Valley”. And finally, change the country code to the STATE abbreviation. I had to change what I set “US” to “AZ”, the state in the US where I live. After I did this and updated, the display lit up with all my weather data as expected. If you do not have these set correctly, you will get question marks in your weather data. Maybe I will write a validation function that fixes that.
The settings.h file also has constants for your wireless network login information.
I cannot speak for the seller, but I do not believe this kit was meant to be a 100% out of the box working project for weather. Rather, it is a fully functional Wemos ESP8266 controlled touch TFT display. And for that, it does it very well, with smart components selected! And at a very reasonable price! I am very impressed and happy with this purchase!! I just scratched the surface on what is possible with this gear through my sketches or modifications and it is a great building base for that geek that envisions touch control panels and wireless connectivity for all their embedded projects. INVENT! ENJOY!

now... on to this unit.

pros.

Cons.
1. ever since D-link updated the Firmware on this camera, it has been useless. I even used older firmware for a long time to try and fix some of the issues. the camera will stay connected for a while, and then just drop off.
2. D-links customer care is useless. I've contacted them several times with no response.
3. even though this camera records at 720 P, the picture quality seams wors them my 3 non-HD cameras. the day time mode is ok, however night time mode is super grainy, witch defeats the whole purpose of having an "HD" camera.

the bottom line?
I know in most cases a newer model is better, however in this case, stick to D-links older cameras, they have better picture quality and are more reliable then the newer ones.

title: Invaluable and a MUST HAVE for Cinematographers... PERIOD
text:
If you are not using a color checker for referencing then you are doing it wrong.

I am not talking about using it as a color picker even though that does come in handy when matching cameras. I am talking about when you are color correcting before your grade.

We all know unless you spend a fortune on the right monitor and calibrate it -- nothing is going to be better than your scopes. Using this to reference accompanied by scopes and other tools we have at our disposal, I do not see how anyone serious about nailing imagery can go on without something like this.

There are too many YouTube tutorials that teach the wrong thing and it is frustrating to see this being done. This is why I like the X-Rite. Let me elaborate.

People teach the wrong way to white balance and correctly white balancing is ABSOLUTELY CRUCIAL for getting all the color information that was there when you were recording. Especially if you record RAW or ProRes. You want all the dynamic range in not just your highlights and shadows but you want it to show in your colors. Without properly white balancing first; this is not possible. The X-Rite has THE BEST white balance reference on the rear end that I have used and I have used so called 'certified' white balance cards. Simply crop your clip with the white board, set your vector-scope to 2x and boost your RGB levels (NOT SATURATION). Then bring your kelvin (if shooting RAW) or warmth/cool and tint to a point where the cropped white balance card shows as a dot right in the center of your vector-scope. DONE.. NAILED every damn time. White balance in post perfectly every time in less than 30 seconds.

The next thing I like to do is use the clip of the front of the X-Rite to make sure my exposure is perfect a la scopes. Make sure the front of the board is in the light of your scene and adjust your highlights to ensure the white (highlights) are showing as 95 IRE in your waveform, adjust your gamma so the mid-tones (second to last grey swatch) are roughly in the center and adjust your shadows so your blacks (shadows) are right around 0 IRE in your waveform. This way, when you look at the scene with your talent and the highlights are not hitting 95 IRE, you know you are where you should be and don't boost your highlights too much. Then, adjust mid-tones for taste and start your grade. (I don't like crushing my blacks so I will clip them in my grade, not my color correction). I don't usually adjust exposure in the RAW file and will almost always use my levels for exposure. However, if I over exposed a lot in a scene (which I often do when shooting RAW) and highlights aren't clipped (otherwise the footage is scrapped), I may dial down the ISO (RAW adjustment only) so I have a better starting point (general crushed wave is in the center of the waveform scope).

Sorry to turn this into a tutorial but I just feel this is an invaluable tool and worth every penny because of how fast it can help you get a scene color corrected and on to the fun stuff.

Feel free to comment below for any questions.

title: A beautiful monitor plagued by major backlight bleed issues
text:
I want to like this monitor, but for $620 (at the time of writing this), what I got was unacceptable.

First, regarding the build quality: I have no complaints. The stand on which the monitor rests is nearly all metal, and keeps the monitor very sturdy on my desk. I witnessed no wobbling in the day I spent using it.

Second, regarding the features: I mainly bought the monitor because I plan on upgrading my graphics card in the near future (from GTX 980 to GTX 1080 TI), but since I haven't yet made the upgrade, I tested out the monitor with a few games on my current GPU. On R6 Siege and Battlefield 1, my fps had a very wide range, dipping into the 40s in both games and maxing out around the 110's at max settings. This is where I noticed a slight difference using G-Sync for the first time. As many people say, G-Sync did in fact make the games feel smoother at the lower fps range and I appreciated that. Also, the fact that you can overclock this monitor to 165hz just like its direct competitors (the Asus PG279Q and Acer XB271HU) is a nice addition for anyone who has the equipment to achieve framerates that high. Also, this is the first IPS monitor I have ever used, and I must say that on colorful scenes, the colors did look a bit more vibrant/lifelike (after calibration) than on the TN panel I currently own, the Asus VG248QE, and the viewing angles are also noticeably better. The higher resolution of this monitor also made everything look more crisp and clear than what I am used to at 1080p. I did not realize how insane the difference was between 1080p and 1440p until I used this monitor. For the features this monitor has, it is an absolute steal at it's current price at the time of writing this review ($620), considering the Asus and Acer equivalents are both $800, nearly an entire $200 more than this monitor.

Unfortunately, that price is probably a result of the amazingly bad quality control this monitor has. At the time of writing this review, I have just returned this monitor a second time for a third and last chance of getting a panel that does not have horrendous backlight bleed. You can see what I'm talking about in my pictures below. Before I continue, note that the camera makes the backlight bleed more pronounced and worse that it actually is, but despite that, it was still quite noticeable and distracting (for me, at least) on both monitors in dark scenes. The first monitor I received at a large amount of bleed in the bottom right corner, and small and medium splotches of yellowish bleed in the the other 3 corners and along the top. The second monitor I received wasn't quite as bad, as it had a more equal distribution of bleed in all 4 corners. And before anyone asks, yes I did in fact check both monitors from several angles to confirm that this was not just the standard IPS glow that most IPS monitors have. However, you'll notice in the one picture I have with a lit background that the bleed is hardly noticeable. This would be just fine for me and I wouldn't have returned this monitor, if the only time I ever had to use it was during the day. That isn't the case, though, and usually the only time I have to use this monitor is during the evenings after work and on the weekends. Either way, I strongly prefer to play with lights off at any time of day, and the quantity of bleed that is visible in that scenario makes it unpleasant. Also, you can see a comparison of this monitor against my VG248QE in another one of the pictures I took. The only reason why the left side of the right monitor is significantly brighter is because it's a TN and I took the picture from an off-center angle; otherwise, the black color is uniform across the monitor and there are no distracting discolorations, unlike the AG271QG that I compared it against.

Other thoughts: I found the OSD kind of uncomfortable to use, but considering how rarely I would use it, I wouldn't take a star off for it.

So here I am, having returned this monitor twice now and currently waiting on the third one, hoping the third time's the charm. If the third monitor still has an unacceptable amount of backlight bleed, I will be returning it for a refund and trying one of the other more reputable brands that people seem to have better luck with, as well as updating this review. One last thing; I must say that I am amazed that neither of the two monitors I received came with dead pixels. But I think I'd almost rather have a few dead pixels than all this bleed.

I am giving this monitor 3 stars because although the build quality is generally good and the monitor has all the features the average gamer would want for the current price, I'm not sure if it's worth returning multiple times in hopes of getting a good one. Also, any daytime users might not be so bothered by the bleed issues as a nighttime user like me, so I think a daytime user would have a greater tolerance for the bleed and thus be less likely to return the monitor.

If you are willing to keep making returns on this monitor as I am, I would say you might as well give it a try while it's still under $700. If you get lucky, you will have saved a LOT of money. If not, you can always get your money back and go for a different monitor. Once this monitor goes back up to its supposedly regular price of $750, though, it will no longer be worth getting or even trying for a good panel, imo.

title: $30 GGMM Nightingale - AMAZING!
text:
This was my first GGMM product. Didn't really feel like I took a leap of faith purchasing it given the high feedback score on Amazon coupled with the low price. Upon arrival I was impressed with packaging. You can tell GGMM spent some time thinking through the design to showcase the product. It was an easy to open package and the cables/earphones were nestled in the case snug. Many other reviewers have noted the cable size and weight. This is the absolute first thing I noticed about the earphones as well. The cable material doesn't seem to tangle as easily as many earphones out there. Also the connection is super small and I had no problem inserting into my iPhone 6 plus even with a case....Can't say this for all of the earphones I've purchased in the past. The speakers are well built and although I was expecting them to be heavy since they are all metal....they weren't! The rubber end pieces fit snug in my ear and even during my morning run they didn't come out. Honestly, I have some other earphones that work better for runners but these still worked well today and I can see myself using them again for most exercises.

Alright enough about the aesthetics, let's talk about the sound quality. I mean c'mon that's why we buy earphones right? I've had everything from $6 Panasonics to $300 Bose/Beats, etc... and all I can say is WOW. You can tell that GGMM spent some time developing these. They have nice tight bass (not ear shattering) and very clear mids/highs. If you select the correct rubber earpiece for your ear size they will seal tightly and you'll get great noise cancellation. This plays into the impressive sound quality IMO. For $29.99 you'd be hard pressed to find a better set of earphones. You could always spend more...that's easy right? However, to find a nice product for a very fair price is tough these days. From a scale of 1 to 10, including all price ranges and brands I'd give these earphones and easy 8. For earphones under $50, they are an absolute 10.

Some of the other goodies you get with this product is a microphone with one button for answering and ending calls. GGMM included a metal "sleeve" on the cable that allows you to slide it up/down the two upper wires to make it tighter or loosen them. In addition, GGMM included a leather carrying case that is very unique. It was actually pretty darn smart along with being so simple and very functional. Would I buy the earphones because of this case? No. Would I buy the case by itself? No. I do think it's a great addition to the earphones though and very nice touch.

So, what's the consensus on this pair of $30 earphones with a lifetime warranty? Simple. Buy them. Period. Enough said. They are priced fairly. They have amazing sound and the build quality is close to what you'd get in most $200 pair of earphones.
