What's even worse is the RMA process. First, they try to hide their advanced RMA offering, insisting that you send in the defective one first, which in the case of a mostly functional unit is unacceptable. After insisting that they send you one first, they'll give you the extensions of three people in the company that can handle that. If you thought it couldn't get worse... they take your credit card info, which is standard for an advanced RMA, but they charge it and say they'll refund it once they get the unit back. Well, it's been just under 60 days since they charged my card, and it has been at least 45 since they received the unit back, and I still have no refund. I'm going to have to contact my credit card company to have them charge it back since EnGenius isn't replying to my emails on the matter.

Bottom line, we expect reliability, consistency, and good customer service when there's a problem. EnGenius provides none of this.

title: ABSOLUTE JUNK!!!
text:
Nothing about Roku is impressive. I have purchased 4 of these (2 Roku 1's, a Roku Stick and a Roku 3) and only have one left on my account. The only reason that I have one left is because I can't sell it.

Roku is absolute junk. The interface is unimpressive. It the modern age of smart tv's, Roku doesn't match up.

Then you have the remote. The remote likes to work when it wants to. For every 4-5 times you push the cursor, you will be lucky if the controller actually moves.

Next is the sound ... I have tried to hook up 4 different units to my Onkyo receiver and none of them worked no matter how I set up the audio options. The only time I can get audio is if I turn off the stereo feature to place it directly through my television.

Then the software is terrible. Only the Roku Stick and Roku 3 have updated applications. So if you want to have multiple profiles on Netflix, you will not get them on the Roku 1 or Roku 2. Instead you only have access to the main profile on the account which limits which person can watch Netflix on a particular television.

However, my biggest complaint is the motion judder. 3 out of the 4 units that I have purchased have motion judder. Right out of the box, they seemed to work fine but right around the month and a half mark, shows on Netflix or Prime would like to skip every 7-10 seconds to the point where shows are almost completely unwatchable. Which leads me to me next issue.

Roku's customer service is TERRIBLE!!! I have dealt with a lot of customer service issues in the past and Roku's might have easily topped the list. I owned my Roku 3 for a little over a month before the motion judder got so bad that you couldn't even watch it. Since I paid $100 for the unit, I wanted it fixed but it was beyond the 30 day Amazon return period. I reached out to Roku's customer service department and two hours on the phone with them. They kept having my unplug it and change out HDMI cables. I am fairly competent with electronics and explained that I had tried everything over and over again. However, they refused to let me return the unit for repairs. Finally after 2 hours of arguing, they agreed to fix it but wanted me to pay $10 to ship the unit back to them. I had owned this $100 defective device for 33 days and now I was expected to pay $10 for them to fix it. Absolutely not. title: Nice case for the new Paperwhite. Material feels different vs the last gen - will it be as durable?
text:
After years of eschewing e-readers, then gradually using mobile versions, I bought a Paperwhite about a year and a half ago, during a sale. I was going back and forth between the Paperwhite and the Oasis, as I was an Audible user, and also like to read in the bath.

I bought a denim/dark blue Finitie folio case for my chosen Paperwhite, and was really pleased with it.

Now, I’ve upgraded to the new Paperwhite for its Audible and waterproof functionality. I was pleased enough with my last Fintie case (still looks brand new!), that I ordered the same for the new Paperwhite model, albeit in a different color (Denim Gray).

My first observation right out of the packaging was that the fabric material is softer. I don’t mean more pliable, although the cover does not seem as thick/sturdy, but the fabric itself is a brushed texture, like flannel, whereas my older case’s fabric is definitely more like a hard wearing denim or stiff canvas (Denim Indigo folio).

It’s actually a pleasant tactile change, however, I’m concerned whether or not it will wear as well as my old case has, although I’ve only has that one about a year and half.

I’m pretty careful with my electronics if they’re near water - so I’m not sure how well this case would hold up to an accidental dunking (say, in the bath) - I wouldn’t expect it to be anything more than water resistant. With the non-fleecy, tight weave of the old case, any accidental drops just bead and spill off, though I certainly wouldn’t try to subject it to more on purpose.

As careful as I say I am, with my older Paperwhite and Fintie case, I’ve definitely had it fall off the bed, chair, get accidentally dropped, stuffed in bags and luggage, etc, and the Finitie came out of everything just fine, and again, is still brand new looking. I am hoping this new case follows suit!

Another detail, in the definite positive, for me, is that the branding on the lower corner of the outside edge of the front cover is now a small logo, rather than a logo and “Fintie.” It’s much more subtle than on the last gen folio (and possibly other Fintie styles), and complements the case well. There is a “full,” logo on the left inside edge of the front cover.

All told, this Fintie folio case is a nice, snug fit, with a good feel while reading. It adds a little bit of bulk without being too much, which I greatly prefer to snap on “low/slim profile,” cases - I don’t want my e-reader to feel like my phone!

title: Unbelievable Sound and Value
text:
I've been buying several of the highly rated Chi-Fi budget in ear headphones from KZ, Auglamore, and others just to see what you can get for under $50. I also have the 1More Double and Triple drivers and a few other higher end in ear headphones. I love to compare and see how much quality a little money can buy. I read the reviews on the S2000 and decided to give them a try. I mean, for $25 why not.

So I just recently got these and plugged them in to my iFi Nano iDSD Black DAC/Amp to see what Advanced Sound was serving up. I started out with a few Enya tracks because I like to see what kind of presence and sound stage they have. Wow! These in ears are fairly small and really comfortable, but they sound like something far more substantial. The bass and sub-bass is rich and powerful, but not overpowering. The overall clarity and detail from bass to treble is crazy good. Two small observations are that male vocals are a bit reduced compared to the low end and high end and every once in a while at high volumes certain highs can be very bright. But that's being being pretty picky as the overall listening experience is really amazing.

I also tried several classical, rock, and jazz hi-res tracks from Tidal and Spotify and got consistent results. Instruments have a very live sound. Listening to a jazz trio I could hear the noise from the bow on the bass strings and the excellent sound stage gave the sense of being there. This is my second Advanced Sound product and I am super happy with both. The S2000 out-performs all my budget in ears and sounds nearly as good or better than anything I have purchase in the $100 to $200 range. I really am enjoying these. Thanks to Advanced Sound for knocking the quality and value out of the park.

title: If the Garmin engineers only knew how to design displays......
text:
This is my 4th GPS running watch and if it were not for the display, I would have given it 5 stars. It seems that Garmin engineers just don't seem to get it when it comes to readability of their sports devices. I have two Garmin cycling computers, one is color and when I race with it, I have to leave the light in the constant on mode in order to be able to reliably read it. Unfortunately, the light on this watch is quite dim and not changeable as are the lights on their cycling computers. Don't be misled by the graphics always shown on the faces of their devices in their ads and manuals - if they looked like that in reality, I would be ecstatic!

Apart from that, I love it. It has every feature that I would want to have. It is accurate and comfortable. I love the fact that it tracks running dynamics, estimates VO2max, suggests an adequate recovery time based on the intensity of your workout, guides interval workouts, and even predicts your race times for 5K, 10K, half marathon and marathon races assuming you have done adequate training to negotiate those races. I also love the fact that it connects to the Garmin software through your WIFI or can be connected to a Bluetooth device.

From what I can gather, it is the best running watch out there at the moment - that's why I purchased it. As an aside, I owned one of the older Forerunner watches, and currently own the Nike sports watch and the Fitbit Surge - both of which I dislike.

title: For the price, a good mount that will require a little bit of thought to install.
text:
I'm using this on an Optoma HD141x. As noted by some reviewers, it takes a little thought to use this. Two of the shorter arms will work on the OEM mounting locations, but you will need a third short arm to utilize the third mounting hole (which it doesn't come with.) You will need M4*3 (10mm) screws from your local hardware store to attach the arms to the OEM mounting holes.

For the third arm, I mounted it on the tilt adjustment feet, utilizing the same adjustment screw from that feet.

There's a lot of adjustment available on this thing, and i thought it would be difficult to adjust with so many screws to tighten. But, it wasn't as bad as initially feared. Still took a bit of effort, but it can be done. The system also has a built-in "hook" of sorts so that even if the lower half (not counting the rod) loses its screws for any reason, the projector will stay hung (albeit obviously off-kilter at that point.) Good insurance, i guess.

My only point of improvement would be to widen the plate that attaches to the ceiling. With such a narrow strip, even bolted to a stud, there's a little bit of side-to-side play. This is likely due to soft drywall. To combat this, i used the extra arms as a point of leverage, as you'll see in the photo that i included in this review.

Please note that this is still while i was still in the process of adjusting, so don't mind the mess. :)

title: Can't be disappointed with the quality and the price!
text:
OK so I'm actually typing this review on this exact Qisan mechanical keyboard right now :)

I purchased this exact model with black switches just week or so ago - the quality and the price were so good that I ordered the blue switch version which arrived yesterday. I have to say, this is just as nice as the black switch version and the blue switches are definitely "clicky". I would say they are clickier than a NORMAL Cherry MX Blue also because the keycaps themselves are quite cheap - not doubleshot PBT or anything nice like that. Therefore, the tactile click is that much louder on this model. Let's keep in mind - this is a VERY loud keyboard and will probably not be usable in the office setting or even home setting, unless you have it in a room / office hidden away from everyone's ears.

I put some run of the mill keycaps I had laying around on this thing, and I have to say, just in general, price considered, this is a great mechanical keyboard for the money. The switches are responsive, solid and tactile - absolutely on par with MX Blues. I would say the tactile response is even a bit more noticeable. If you like the satisfaction of the blue switch - this keyboard will certainly scratch that itch. And for under 40 dollars, you can afford to beat it up a little bit.

Note: My right shift key does not "click" like the rest of the keys, but that seems to be the only key that is slightly subpar - I will not dock a star for this, not at this price point. Again, this is not a Pok3r or nice import - please don't expect that. Connoisseurs that are expecting top shelf? Keep moving along. Otherwise, expectations tempered, this is a great Mech for entry level and vets alike.

title: Amazing Value for Budget Gaming - Adtl Update on MSI Afterburn
text:
Excellent Bang for your buck, Play's Crysis 3 with G3258 flawlessly at 720P 60fps on Plasma TV with Vsych engaged for me. The fan is large / low noise and the components look absolutely solid and well made all around. Attention to detail is great and each video connector has a protective insert. I also would like to say it may be worth going with a 2GB card at this point if you plan to play the most advanced games that use a lot more textures. Certainly if you play at higher resolutions as well. Crysis 3 is a couple years old and would have required expensive hardware at the time it came out, looks beautiful much better then Xbox 360 and for sub 100$ card that is quite impressive. For an all around budget performer this card performs beautifully. This model is stock with solid state capacitors large fan and is overclocked to the tune of about 4% boost over a non overclocked R7 260. In my case this card is perfect, if you want a little more horse power to play at better resolutions such as 1080P you would benefit from a 260X, for those wanting an all around budget performer this model is great. Solid card and is one of the best cost to performance cards you can get. Enjoy!

Update: I am now using MSI Afterburn at 1150MHz GPU core giving me about a 12% boost over stock and closer to the R7 260X performance. I found a lot of users of the R7 260X reporting black screens periodically and did some research and tests of my own. This card uses the same memory and GPU with some of the stream processors disabled for the non X version. I figured due to this it should be able to achieve at minimal stock 260X frequencies. What I found was after bringing the memory clock up to 1600MHz; that while the card passes benchmarks & game tests when it idles down to desktop mode the screen can go black as other reviewers posted. This is why some 260X users report dropping the memory clock back to 1500MHz resolves their issues. Also the 260 R7 Cards have a higher memory clock then the other cards in the lineup. It appears when the card cycles down to 300MHz from 1600MHz memory clock their is some instability. Keep in mind running full power for games etc. works fine. As a result I left my memory clock at 1500MHz and GPU at 1150MHz for a nice performance boost. MSI is overclocked by default to 50MHz and the OC 260X is 1150, MSI leaves that at the max OC without taking off the limiters which is also a sign that this is relatively safe OC for this CPU with the extra cooling capabilities and controls on this card.

Other 260X users have reported hacking their card GPU BIOS and changing the low end frequencies can correct the problem, in any case it appears the R7 line up does have problems with the low power throttling logic resulting in stability issues. The good news is their are several band aid work around's on the internet until this issue is patched with an updated driver. I am running current Omega drivers and as long as I'm at 1500MHz memory clock all is well. That is my suggestion to anyone having the issue, down clock 260X's memory to 1500 and you should regain stability of your card. If you still have problems you may go lower. Its unfortunate that this is the case. It may also be an argument to stay away from the higher clocked cards. I have an R7 240 and R7 260 and these both do not present the black screen lockup issue that the 260X users are reporting, although there can be some variance in component quality. MSI did a great job with the build quality and temps are perfectly fine at 1150, completely stable even playing RYSE which is very demanding. Keep in mind with 1GB ram you are limited to low detail for this game / RYSE is a current AAA title meant to run on quad cores with a medium to high end card. The fact that it plays great at 50-60fps consistently at 720P was a great surprise on my dual core G3258 at 4.4GHz per core.

I don't fault MSI for the current driver issues with these cards since all the manufactures putting them out appear to be having these issues. The good news is the 260 version is great for budget gaming and is less susceptible to the memory clock issue as it runs a tad slower then the 260X variant. The reality is a simple adjustment in the throttling of the cars would likely fix this for all users. Hopefully AMD will correct this soon, I have also contacted them to seek resolution. This card is still an excellent value especially if you get the rebate and free games, my recommendation is test it in your configuration before cutting out the UPC, the odds are if you go with the either the 260 or 260X and set memory to 1500MHz you will be stable and running until a driver patch corrects the issue.

title: Serious system is a big step-up from IP cameras...Passable mobile app...
text:
SUMMARY: 4 stars - Good with opportunities for improvement. Solid, quality system with intuitive interface and good overall usability. Video quality is not HD, but impressively sharp and more than adequate for my purposes (home security) Mobile app functionality limited to live view, though more stable than two competing wireless IP cameras. Wired installation takes time and requires a monitor for setup (VGA or HDMI input, not included). Audio requires additional hardware. Note: free item (960H 4-camera system with 500 GB DVR) was provided for evaluation.

BACKGROUND: I've had an IP cam ([[ASIN:B0096YORV4 Lorex LNC104 LIVE Ping Wireless Monitoring Camera]]) for about 3 years, and added a second one ([[ASIN:B00FLQM768 Lorex LNC216 Wireless HD Dual Lens Network Camera with Real-Time HD Resolution (Black)]]) last year during our kitchen remodel (we had tons of contractors coming & going for 4 months). In my experience, WiFi based IP cameras are super easy and fast to install, but are not that robust/reliable. In addition to router and reception issues, the app/computer based interfaces are typically less ideal with worse image quality (focus, lighting, graininess, frame rate, lag) compared to a direct video feed.

GENERAL IMPRESSIONS: Good build quality overall. Base unit is compact. Device boots quickly and menus were intuitive so I didn't have to refer to the manual too much during setup. While the manual seemed a bit sparse so far It's answered all my questions, so no complaints there. There's the occasional typo in the instructions, onscreen menus and mobile app, which give a less polished impression than the hardware. This unit is branded Amcrest, which is apparently part of Foscam. That linkage gives me a little more confidence over no-name security camera systems, particularly considering installation time and costs.

RESOLUTION/SENSITIVITY: This system is 960H (960x480) putting it between the D1 (704x480) and 720 (1280x720) formats. Note that full HD is 1900x1080. Like digital cameras, however, the pixel count is only part of the image quality. The optics and sensor size affect how good your low light sensitivity is. The Lorex 216 IP camera is a good example - it records in HD but the optics are minimal and it reverts to "Night Mode" way too soon. Also note that there is a tradeoff with higher res systems - you need more storage space. One way you can offset this is by changing the frame rate. This system allows you to change the frame rate at each camera - good if you figure that outside a building you may want a higher frame rate to capture license plates as cars drive by, but inside people can only move so fast, so lower frame rates might be acceptable.

SETUP: Easy and intuitive. I set it up in my office first to make sure everything was working. YOU WILL NEED A MONITOR TO ACCOMPLISH SETUP. Change your password as soon as you start it up. I configured the system to record at 15 FPS instead of 30. I also opted for motion sensitive recording to better utilize the storage. An uninterruptible power supply is recommended, but I did test how long it takes to reboot if power is interrupted. Less than 30 seconds. That's impressive. This system does not have WiFi built in, however I am using a [[ASIN:B00D5G00XI Belkin Universal Wi-fi , Dual Band, Av Adapter]] so I didn't have to string CAT5 out to the garage. Works like a charm.

INSTALLATION: This is a serious 4-camera security system which requires hard-wired installation of the cameras and the base unit. Even if you plan to use only the mobile app, you still need a monitor to set-up. An HDMI cable is supplied but the base unit also has VGA out - handy since I used an older 17" LCD monitor. Each camera comes with ~65' of wire (although the documentation says 60'). The wire is ~ 1/8" diameter, so concealing it isn't an issue, however the BNC plug requires a 5/8" drill to get through various walls, etc. 1/2" will NOT work. Base unit uses two 12V wall warts for power. Installation took about 2 hours (Driveway, front door, garage, rear of house)

MOBILE APP: Google Play has about a half dozen Amcrest apps - look for "Amcrest", not "Amcrest Link" listed in the instructions. It installed fine (Galaxy S5 on Sprint) and was easy to connect to the system. Mobile playback was pretty easy once I figured out what icons to click (It's the one in the upper left corner that looks like 2 video cameras stacked on top of each other) You can also switch between "Fluent" and "Sharp" video modes to improve clarity. Manual says "Main Stream" vs "Sub Stream" for this, which isn't explained. The app does have some issues besides lack of documentation and being less intuitive, however: 1) No zoom feature - there is a PTZ menu for cameras that Pan/Tilt/Zoom, but this wasn't noted anywhere in the documentation, so it took me some time to figure out. 2) Aspect ratio is OK when you look in portrait mode, but flip your phone to the side (as you would so you can see all 4 screens tiled) and it stretches the images to fill the screen. 3) Video playback freezes after a few seconds - perhaps 2 seconds when on a mobile network, 10 seconds when on WiFi. Very annoying. If you want to see what happened, you have to go to the base station 4) No fast forward in the playback mode - particularly an issue since the playback freezes after 4-5 seconds.

NITS TO PICK.
1) The cameras are supposed to be weatherproof, but the connectors are just typical BNC and power connectors. I've used dielectric grease and will plasti-dip to waterproof the connectors that are exposed to the elements.
2) 12V power adapters had 2 different current ratings, but I couldn't find anything that told me which goes to the cameras or base unit. After reading the box carefully, I did some math and figured out that THE LOWER CURRENT ADAPTER GOES TO THE CAMERAS. A larger power adapter which fed both the cameras and the base unit would have made more sense.
3) Conflict in documentation - camera specs say up to 983 feet cable run is possible, however documentation says 300 feet max.
4) System can record audio but as equipped you will have to run a separate microphone for each camera. If they are all looking at the same space (Inside of store or home) then a single mic would work - as it is, I'd need at least 3 with the associated wiring.

title: A Ridiculously Great Value Tech Upgrade for Older Cars
text:
When used in a 2003 Dodge Durango with the stock radio/CD player and with an I-phone 5SE, the performance is beyond any reasonable expectation. I read the short directions and had it set up and paired with my I-phone in ten minutes. I was hoping for a decent sound by using my phone with a bluetooth (wireless) connection and a static-free signal to my FM radio. I got more than that. The phone connection is adequate - not fantastic - adequate and usable. If you are the kind of person who wants to yak on the phone a lot while driving, then you'll probably want to keep your ear blue tooth device - but if all you need is to be able to adequately communicate, it works fine. When using Mapquest on my I-phone, verbal directions interrupt the music for a few seconds just as hoped. When I start the car when first getting in - it pairs to my phone within just a few seconds. The magnetic mount that gently and firmly clips to my air vent fins works exceptionally well. After attaching the thin metal plate provided to the back of my I-phone 5SE, the mount works flawlessly. As an unexpected bonus, the unit charges my phone from its USB port faster than the lighter socket charger that I had been using.
I have a CD in the stereo and a matching Album stored on my I-phone. I played the CD version of Diana Krall's "California Dreaming" cover and then directly compared it to the MP3 version playing through the unit from my phone. I was very impressed. No static, excellent volume range, no engine or ignition whine. The only difference in sound is the difference between a true CD track versus an MP3 file. I stand duly impressed it is as good as it has turned out to be.
I had been planning to buy an aftermarket stereo head unit that had bluetooth and a video screen for Mapquest or Google directions, but no more. I actually prefer the smaller screen of my familiar phone. I plan on buying two more to "upgrade" all of my cars, one of which is a bone stock 1996 Nissan 240SX SE that I didn't want to alter in any way.
I purchased this with Amazon Prime. It was delivered early ( the next day after placing the order).
Knowing what I know now after hearing the fidelity of the sound and how efficiently it functions - I would have gladly paid twice the $16.99. It is a ridiculously good value. If I have problems with it's durability - I'll be back to edit this review.

title: Ignore the positive reviews...this monitor has a major design flaw. Trust me...you will regret buying it.
text:
I did not understand what other negative reviewers meant when they said that it had "image retention problems" so I ignored it. What this term means is that whenever there is an image on the screen for more than a 2 or 3 of minutes the monitor leaves a ghosted image behind after you move the window.

So imagine trying to work in Photoshop...or even a web browser...and every time you move a window or load a new web page you see a ghosted image from the previous page. This burned in image stays behind even after powering the monitor completely off and back on.

Dell was good about sending us a quick replacement. They acted as if they never heard about the image burn in problem and said that we must have received a defective one. When the second unit arrived we were quite shocked to see that it had the exact same problem.

They insisted on sending us a third monitor but we were very skeptical that it would solve the problem. The third monitor arrived and "strike three", it had the exact same problem. We sent the Dell tech the link to the reviews on this page and he finally told us that it was a known issue. I for the life of me understand why they would waste anyone's time sending out replacements knowing that it is not going to fix the problem.

We paid $979 for this monitor and it took Amazon more than 3 weeks to refund our purchase after shipping it back. (not cool Amazon).

As of the writing of my review the price has dropped to $879 and I would expect it to go even lower.

We ended up buying this LG monitor for $698 which has turned out to be much better and less expensive: [[ASIN:B071WMP77C LG 43UD79-B 43" 4K Ultra HD IPS LED Monitor w/ Accessories Bundle Includes, SurgePro 6-Outlet Surge Adapter w/ Night Light, 2x 6ft High Speed HDMI Cable & Universal Screen Cleaner for LED TVs]]

title: Among the best of the dash cams I've tested.  Great functionality, easy to operate - even while driving!
text:
First, please note that in the photos I’m posting, none of the blurriness at the side of the photos appears on the videos in any videos I’ve shot. In the videos the entire image is very clear, no blurriness anywhere. I would post a video, but so far as I’ve been able to determine the Amazon system degrades hi-res video, and uploading video that I’ve res’d down seems counterproductive when I’m trying to convey the quality of an HD camera.

I’ve reviewed several of these dash cams at this point, and I now know fairly well what attributes I want them to have. Different people will have different requirements as to the features they’re looking for, e.g., video cycling, locking files, battery back-up (in case of a crash), etc. However, while I recommend looking at and considering those things, keep in mind that if the cam isn’t easy to operate while you’re driving those features might as well not even exist. This cam has only four large buttons and is very easy to operate.

I’ll try to put somewhat random thoughts in an order that makes sense:

Attachment to the windshield is easy, and the suction mechanism provides among the best hold I’ve encountered while still being easy to remove. This is important in the event of a crash, but also because there can be the extra weight of the power cord pulling on the cam. The cam swivels in all directions, X, Y, and Z axis.

The power cord and the (required) micro SD card are installed on the right side of the cam. There is also a “Reset” button on that side. It hasn’t happed for me yet with this cam, but an easy reset is great if the camera ever freezes. (That’s happened to me with a cam I have used but did not review – long story - and it was a big problem.)

The four control buttons are along the bottom, facing toward you as you drive. They’re limited to “back,” “up,” “down,” and “OK,” but the functionality of those four buttons is expanded by the symbols/icons that appear on the screen just above each button. That is, the icons and menu choices on the screen change based on your input, but the basic function of the four buttons remains essentially the same. I’m not sure what I just wrote will make sense, but I think it will when you use the cam. Regardless, AUSDOM has got a system that provides full control and settings within a framework that’s very easy to follow. You won’t get lost in the menu items and you won’t have a hard time finding the settings you need.

I was able to simply plug-and-play right out of the box. Power it up and it starts recording, although of course you can change that, and the red dot on the screen makes recording very clear. I like very much that you can power the cam not only through the cigarette lighter, but also by USB cable, including USB cable to a battery pack, the type used for charging cell phones, etc. That means you’ve also got full video function away from the car.

With some cams the controls have been complicated enough, especially while driving, that I’ve controlled the recording on/off by plugging in or unplugging the cigarette lighter. With this cam that function is so easy it’s actually easier to use the single touch of the “OK” button to start or stop recording.

This cam can also take still photos with a single touch of a button; you’ll even hear the artificial shutter sound. However, unless I haven’t found the way yet, I don’t think you can take snapshots while recording video. It is of course, easy to capture still images during playback on your laptop or whatever you use.

This cam has so many features I could right five times this amount, but I’m already over 650 words so I should stop. The only potentially negative thing I can even come up with to mention is that this cam does not have GPS. However, while I found that to be initially interesting in one cam I used, it did not really prove to be very useful, and in the cam I used but did not review the GPS didn’t work properly.

I received this dash cam at a discount in exchange for testing and writing this review, but as I wrote, at this point I know what to look for in one of these, and this cam has just about every feature I’ve come across. It does not have the rear-view camera, i.e, you can swivel the cam to a rear view but it does not record front and back simultaneously. While I initially thought that was a great idea, in practice the way to record front and back in a way that’s actually useful is to mount a second cam in the back window and run it off of a battery pack. Shooting backward from the front windshield gives you a very small rear view in video. That seems to be because these cams shoot at a very wide angle, and the portion of that wide angle that’s represented by the rear window is tiny sliver of the entire view being recorded. (I hope that makes sense. Just know that you don’t get a good rear view when shot from the front windshield.)

Anyhow, I can easily give this camera my highest rating. That’s based on its features, the quality of the video (and audio), ease of use, the ability to shoot still photos, and whatever else I’m forgetting. Easiest five stars I’ve awarded in a while!

title: There is no reason to spend more than $10 for an HDMI cable
text:
This cable is a rip off. There is no reason to pay more than $10 for an HDMI cable. None. Do a web search for "4k hdmi cables are nonsense" and read why.

There are four kinds of HDMI cables:

High-speed with Ethernet
High-speed without Ethernet
Standard-speed with Ethernet
Standard-speed without Ethernet

Nearly all cables that are sold these days are High-speed with Ethernet. Per the HDMI spec, *any* High Speed HDMI cable will work just fine with a 4K HDTV.

HDMI cables carry a digital signal. There is no such thing as signal degradation in a digital cable. Either the signal goes through, or it doesn't. There is no quality issue. The cheapest High Speed HDMI cable is just as capable as an overpriced cable at carrying a digital signal.

Don't waste your money on overpriced HDMI cables.

title: Fantastic, future-proof TV for a solid price!
text:
First things first. This TV is dang good at what it does. You'll have a difficult time finding something of this caliber at this price (currently, the 50" can be had for $900). While this is technically an LCD TV, it has several enhancements (brought to you by the SUHD series) that make it very good at displaying vibrant colors and deep blacks (sure, not as deep as OLED, but you're not going to get OLED 4K at this price for at least four or five years, and there's NO guarantee that OLED will move downmarket).

If you're interested in pure blacks and outstanding contrast, AND have the $$$ to spare, than by all means get a 4K OLED (it won't be from Samsung, as they've decided to put their $ in SUHD enhancement). But if you're interested in fantastic and vivid color, then this is the TV for you. Although (and please see my sample photos), the blacks in this TV get *pretty* close to what you get from OLED. Further, thanks to the Quantum Dot display, colors really do pop. Not to mention the possibility for future HDR content -- the way the TV technology sphere is moving right now, you really want to buy a display that will be somewhat "future-proof." Enter the QD display (i.e. Nanocrystal Color), full array backlighting and contrast enhancer -- these all help to really move the TV to a premium level, without the premium price (which really helps when you want to ball on a budget). Bonus points if you have other Samsung products -- they all work SEAMLESSLY together (i.e. my Samsung Galaxy S6 Edge +).

It's important to remember (and this goes with any TV), that you have to spend time tweaking the color when you purchase the TV -- otherwise it'll look terrible (just like any 4K HDTV will). This TV is pretty solid at "Movie" mode (if a little muted) and I usually have it in "Natural" mode -- never put it at "Vivid," as this just introduces lots of noise. It took all of 10 minutes to set-up, and the Smart TV interface is pretty solid. One thing it does not have, which affects only some programs (and even then, most people won't notice it) is a *native* 120Hz refresh rate. But, again... minor quibble. However (and this may matter since we don't really have THAT much content), this TV is amazing at upscaling 1080p content, especially on a Blu-Ray player w/ HDMI 2.0 cable (rather than the typical 1.4 cable). Even the morning news looks better -- it's not 4K quite yet, but it is a step up.

I cross-shopped this with the regular UHD curved TVs from Samsung and I feel like the price was more than reasonable for the level of quality (at least from what I have seen) you're getting -- every Samsung SUHD TV has the same basic features, even this one (its "entry" model, so to speak). Is this TV the absolute best TV? No. And, at $900, you're not going to get one. BUT, this TV is one hard-working machine. Honestly, I got tired of reading so many negative reviews, because from what I've seen so far, this TV doesn't warrant them.

Check out my pictures below for reference. I believe all of these images were taken while the TV was in "natural" mode, and none have enhancement from my phone. I was watching "Jessica Jones" on Netflix, a show on Amazon, and some YouTube 4K demos.

title: Bad camera, bad software, bad customer service
text:
[Edit: Since I posted this, Foscam commented in an attempt to show how much they care about their customers. They asked me to get in touch with them, which is funny because I totally mention in this very review that I already tried this and they shafted me. Wait...they wouldn't just be mass-commenting on every negative review to make it look like they actually care, could they? Gasp! Never! They also linked me to a page that supposedly would help me with my issue. A PAGE THAT WAS BROKEN. See the comments below for details and proof.]

This product is easily one of the worst things I've ever spent money on. To make a long story short, it gave me problems straight out of the box (set up would not have been possible if I did not work in IT), half-worked for 4 months, and then gave out completely. It now only works if I reset the camera every few hours, which, besides being unnecessary, I can't do since I use it as a video monitor for my 7-month-old and I much prefer it when she's not screaming because daddy just woke her up so that he could keep his eye on her. Tried contacting their customer service to make use of the warranty they have with the product. Turns out they do not give out refunds for their poor-quality work, but they'd be more than happy to send me a replacement unit that will have the same issues (at least half the issue is with the really buggy software that you have to use with the camera that won't get fixed with a camera replacement).

The long of it:

Pulled it out of the box the day it showed up, glad that we'd be able to make sure our daughter wasn't going crazy at night whenever she started crying. Found a CD in there, along with some instructions on how to set your camera up "easily." They describe this camera as "Plug & Play". They *should* describe this camera as "Plug & Die Horrifically From The Stress Of Dealing With This Awful Camera". (Unless, of course, they have a very different definition of the word "Play" than I do. If that's the case, then I apologize.) The software that was supposed to automatically detect my camera didn't work, so I had no clue what the IP address for the camera was (which is step 1 in setting it up). Okay. That's annoying. Thankfully, I work in IT and I knew to pull up the DHCP server page on my router and just started plugging in the addresses that were actively in use until one worked. If this last sentence means nothing to you, good luck setting this thing up.

After fighting through the incredibly poor UI in their setup software for an hour (an HOUR - I really do need to discuss the definition of "plug & play" with Foscam, apparently), I finally got it up and running. When I pulled it up to test it, the time on the screen was completely wrong. It wasn't a set amount of time off, either. Over the next several weeks, it turned out that it would just (seemingly) choose a random time to display and then do that. ("3:38 AM, I think", it would say to itself and then giggle as it displayed that time knowing full well that the sun was out.) I once looked at it and saw it displaying 12:10 AM as the time (again, wasn't even close; it was like 3:00 PM). When I looked again, it was saying it was 12:08 AM. Wut. I watched it for a bit as it counted up for a few minutes before hopping back to 12:08 AM and starting over. It apparently just gets stuck in a time loop now and again. Good luck using the "nifty" feature that allows you to tell your camera to start recording at a certain time. If it makes it to that time at all instead of just hopping back to 12:08 AM every few minutes, it'll most certainly be nowhere near the time you actually told it to start recording.

At this point, I knew that I had made a terrible mistake. However, I had spent the money and so I sucked it up and decided I had to deal with it (also, I was out of forget-me-nows). Over the following 4 months, my wife and I put up with UIs that would frustrate Satan, a video feed that would randomly lock up without reason, and enough connection issues to make Time Warner Cable jealous (seriously, though, sometimes it just wouldn't connect and we'd be video-feed-less). Finally, last week, it died almost completely. I now have to reset the camera every single night by unplugging it and plugging it back in to get a connection to it at all. And the connection we finally do get dies during the night and leaves us looking at a frozen screen.

I contacted Foscam today to get a refund on a clearly worthless product and they said I'd have to go through Amazon if I want a refund, which I'm pretty certain is not possible after 4 months of owning something [Edit: The return window ends within a month, something I'm sure Foscam is aware of.]. They would, however, be very happy to send me a replacement devil camera that will likely have all the same hardware issues and will definitely have all the same software issues, since you can't really replace software. I will never again purchase another Foscam product. I strongly urge you to not even buy this one. So, basically, what I'm saying is:

Foscam. Not even once.

title: Great photos, battery door opens when exposed to vehicle vibrations or small shocks.
text:
Well I'm going to start with 3 stars.. Why 3... well on the first use of the camera the battery compartment opened (yes I did check it was closed multiple times) and the battery fell out into the water - sploosh. Oh great. What I figured out was that the vibration had worked the latches open over a period of about 1/2hr. The camera was never submerged (thankfully), so no damage to it there. But now I'm down a perfectly good battery.

The photos were wonderful. Great quality excellent focus, I was really starting to get the hang of it.

I think if I rig up some sort of wedge that prevents those latches from opening, the camera will work just fine. I'll also try not to expose the camera to too much vibration. I'm pretty sure if nikon did a few tests of low impact shock (minimal) bumping, that over time the battery compartment would come undone all by itself. I will update review if I figure out something worth sharing.

So, waterproof, yes. Shockproof, not really. While the camera may survive a shock, the compartments wont stay shut. I've got an old sanyo waterproof camera that has a battery door compartment that is bulletproof compared to this one.

Update: Upgrading to 4 stars. Well, I did a pretty low tech solution that works wonders. I made some small plastic wedges that fit into the small depressions that appear when locked. I think use electricians tape to hold it in place. Now it's impossible for the compartments to work their way open. The replacement battery pack I got is also working well. I've now got the waterproof lens and I got the silicone protection sleeve. I'm also putting a screen protector on the back. I plan to ensure this guy lasts a long time!

title: Excellent Hardshell Bumper Screen Protecting Case with Customization!
text:
I recently purchased the Trentium 6L iPhone 6 Plus Case (NT636CR-L) by New Trent. This case is for my iPhone 6 Plus, and is a nice product that does its job well, with a snug fit, and is clearly a durable solution for protecting my phone.

The initial impression with the Trentium Case is that it is comfortable to hold, thoroughly protective of the device, while not compromising the snappy response of the touch screen and other buttons on the body of the phone. I like the added screen protection beyond the normal bumper/hard shell case. Built in screen protection is a nice addition to the "classic" styled case.

The one feature that New Trent is obviously featuring is the exchangeable color covers (Black, Gold, and Silver). They are attractive options (with black being the least conspicuous as a separate piece from the case itself). I like the idea of customization so that I can keep mine and my wife's phone clearly distinguished. Also, I own the version of this case for the iPhone 5, and New Trent has greatly re-tooled the switchable covers, with great success. The older (iPhone 5) version's switchable covers much more readily dislodged from the case. This version (for the iPhone 6 Plus) clings to the case wonderfully, making this customization feature a great asset, and in no way a liability, as it was for the iPhone 5 case.

One feature that does require some "breaking in" is the small flap that covers the various ports. It is obvious that this case will protect from debris and even provide minimal water resistance (from splashes), but straight out of the box, the flaps are a bit challenging to use. They loosen up with use though.

This case leaves very little to be desired by way of a customizable, durable, protective case. New Trent has another winner on its hands!

text:
I feel somewhat unqualified to review this item because I don't understand why a CD player should be so heavy or expensive. But I can tell you about my naive experience using this one for the last few weeks.

First, if you put a CD in it, then it will play the CD. This sounds like a trivial observation, but I have owned several mini-systems that refuse to play CDs some of the time. This one's not picky. It accepts your CD and turns it into sound.

It plays scratched CDs that skip heavily in my car. It passed over one heavily scratched part of a track, and then I rewound it and played fine. Pretty impressive.

I plugged two different flash drives into the USB port. It couldn't read one of them, but found all the songs on the other one just fine. I tried reformatting the flash drive that it wouldn't read. It didn't help. My guess is that it isn't compatible with some flash drives.

It also only plays mp3 and WMA files. FLAC seems like a notable omission. You'd figure they could fit a FLAC codec somewhere in the 12 pounds and third of a cubic foot that this unit occupies.

I don't dock it any points for having some USB and file shortcomings. All that stuff is a bonus for me. I bought this thing to play CDs, which it does perfectly.

title: Rendered Virtually Useless Due to WiFi Issues!!!!
text:
This product is amazing, in theory.

Fresh out of the box it could not connect to any wifi networks. After hours of googling and troubleshooting I eventually was able to get my chromebook to connect to my Office WiFi. It is still painfully slow compared to the internet connection my laptop, phone, and desktop can pull.

Now my chromebook will work in my office but it will not connect to any other network. I have tried two separate home networks and a public networks but the chromebook can't connect to any of them. Well, it will connect for a second but immediately drop the connection. All three of the other networks are working fine and have no connectivity issues with any other devices.

I have tried every tip on the web in order to solve this problem but nothing worked. I even tried installing Ubuntu and trying to connect to the internet with a clean OS I knew worked flawlessly. It seems to me that this is a hardware issue and it is a pretty well-known issue! The fact that Dell would continue to sell this product with full knowledge that their device is defective is troubling.

The only way I can use this product is if I use an ethernet to USB converter or if I use a USB WiFi receiver and run Ubuntu, which completely defeats the purpose. Considering this device was built to be used in the cloud, it is ridiculous that it's main flaw is internet connectivity. Without internet this device is useless (Chrome OS won't play videos or let you install/transfer certain files via bluetooth or USB).

Since it was only $200 I guess it isn't that big of a deal. After installing ubuntu I now have a laptop without a wifi receiver that weighs 2 pounds so i guess that is ok.

On the bright side, when I am in my office on the one WiFi network that works with this chromebook it is a great experience. Battery life is incredible, screen is very good for the price, keyboard is comfortable, it looks better than the picture, and the device doesn't feel cheap at all.

If this device actually worked it would be 5 stars for sure.

title: Skeptical?  So *was* I
text:
As an individual in my mid forties, I have distant recollections of rabbit ear antennas and the constant struggle to pull in a clear picture without having to balance on my head in the corner of the living room while holding a coat hanger in one hand and the tip of one antenna in the other. I had never really considered going back to an antenna until recently, when I realized just how much money I was dumping into a cable television subscription which I rarely even watched. This window antenna was my (fairly skeptical) first dip of the toe into the cable-cutting pool. After the initial setup, however, I was completely blown away by just what I'd been missing!

About the product itself: it's not exactly subtle or ascetically pleasing. You're going to be looking at something which wouldn't appear out of place in an Aliens movie and which is about the size of a piece of loose-leaf paper hanging on your window. I also have to echo a complaint which other people have had--the suction cups used to attach it to your window suck...or, don't suck. Whatever, they do have a tendency to fall off from time to time, which wreaks havoc with reception. On the bright side, one has stubbornly clung in place for the two weeks it's been hanging on the glass, while the other is currently extending its record-setting hang of 26 hours (and counting).

That being said, the positives well outweigh the negatives. The price point is extraordinarily fair, the picture quality is outstanding (truly high definition), and the attached coaxial cable should be more than lengthy enough for any hook up. I'm pulling in more than 60 (!) channels without any further amplification equipment, although I'm fortunate enough to live just outside of two major metropolitan centers in the DC-Baltimore suburbs; your mileage will vary. For a fraction of the cost of a single month's cable fees, I've got more television than I could ever want...I just wish I'd taken this plunge sooner!

While I haven't used any other HD antennas for comparison, I can heartily recommend this one.

title: Comfortable, effective. Makes working from home much easier.
text:
I ordered these headphones strictly for the active noise-cancelling because I work from a rowdy home. While I work, I don't even need to turn on the active noise cancelling in order for the headphones to block most of the outside noise. In fact, the active noise cancelling can be distracting itself (it is a soft static noise) when worn in an environment that isn't "too loud."

I work in a room alone with the door closed, but (without headphones) much of the noise in the rest of the house is still very loud and prevalent in my office. However, these headphones have made quite the difference. Some noises are still audible, but muffled enough to not cause distraction (and I am a very easily distracted person who hates noise).

In addition, I recently wore these headphones on a cross-country flight. The active noise canceling basically blocked the roaring "airplane noise" completely, although it made voices of the people sitting directly next to me more audible, assumingly because the airplane noise was eliminated. However, all other distant voices were blocked.

I have a considerably small head, but the headphones don't slip around. They fit nicely when adjusted for size and feel very comfortable-- almost a leather cushion-- over the ears.

I have owned these headphones for over a month now, and they remain one of my favorite "work" purchases. They are definitely effective in improving my concentration and work environment. Would definitely recommend.

title: A Good Monitor at a Fair Price
text:
I purchased this monitor factory refurbished from Amazon's Woot.com to save a few dollars, and have been very happy with the monitor so far after about a week of work. The design is sleek looking and the screen has a very thin profile. The monitor comes bundled with a Displayport cable and an HDMI cable. The display is so bright out of the box that I have since reduced the brightness within the monitor settings. Settings are accessed via a single joystick on the back bottom right hand corner. Contrary to some other reviews, I actually think the joystick interface is easy to use and the menus are easy to navigate. You are able to adjust the monitor tilt within a limited range for viewing angle. Full 4k resolution is really a thing of beauty and, for the money, this is a great monitor for everyday use if you have the hardware to drive it.

Now for a couple of negatives. I agree with other reviewers that the stand is rather flimsy and could be approved upon. The monitor will shake if it or the desk is bumped, however, you should be fine if you have a stable work surface. In my case, it seems like the monitor's resting position is slightly crooked, leaning a little to the left. This bothers me more than it should. Be advised that there are only 3 input options; HDMI and Displayport 1.1/1.2. I also would like to see some form of height adjustment for the screen. I am over 6' tall, so my higher viewpoint causes the color to suffer slightly due to my viewing angle. And yes, as others have said, colors can suffer due to extreme viewing angles. You may want to think twice if you plan to use this monitor for tasks where color is important e.g. photo or video editing.

The remaining information below pertains to my setup. If you're an Apple user, you might find this helpful. I am using this monitor with a brand new 13" MacBook Pro Retina Late 2014 using a Mini Displayport to Displayport cable. The best advice I can give is to be sure that your hardware can drive a 4K monitor. I had ordered my new laptop and this monitor at the same time and thought I had done my research. Before the monitor and laptop arrived, however, I discovered that the Intel Iris graphics card in the 13" model only supports 30Hz at full 3840 x 2160 via HDMI, and I believe this is true using Displayport as well. The 15" rMBP however is able to drive this monitor at 60Hz at full resolution using Displayport. This is no fault of the monitor, only my own stupidity, so this has not negatively affected my review. Take a look here for Apple 4K info: http://support.apple.com/en-us/HT202856. This monitor is also not listed as supported by Apple

If you are a 13" rMBP user and are going to order this monitor, here is some advice: Download SwtichResX to create custom resolutions. The full version costs $15 and it's worth its weight in gold. You can unlock many resolution options not offered by your Mac. Using this program, I was able to create a custom resolution and achieve 3840 x 2160 at a 52Hz refresh rate. It's not perfect and some lag is noticeable, but it's darn close and turned this into a great experience. I also use SwitchResX to go between various resolutions depending on the task at hand.

We have also tried this monitor with a MacBook Pro 13" mid or late 2011 model. I was unable to get any sort of picture on the monitor after trying both a Mini Displayport to Displayport cable, and a Mini Displayport to female Displayport adaptor connected to the Displayport cable that comes with the monitor. I thought Displayport 1.2 compatibility may have been an issue, so I changed the input to 1.1 within the monitor settings. This did not work either. We were only able to get the monitor working on this MacBook by using a Mini Displayport to HDMI cable at 1080p and this looks good.

title: Solid product BUT one spec is way off.
text:
The product is well built (for the price) and had no issue getting a good solid mount to my desk and once all tweaked, it is a sturdy setup, the monitors don't rotate or move on their own even when the desk wiggles a little etc.

The main issue I have is that the specs clearly state that the VESA heads can be adjusted by 1" for leveling your monitors (I had pre-measured the difference in the holes in my monitors and needed 7/8" of adjustment). Where they get 1" I have no idea, the adjusting screws have exactly 3/8" of threads on them. That means it can be adjusted slightly less than 3/8". So about 1/3 of what the description states. I guess this may not seem like a huge deal but since it was my primary reason for buying this one over the other brands, it was aggravating. I ended up fashioning up my own adjustment bolt (cut the head off a long bolt of the same thread size, and used a couple washers and several nuts to create the resting point for the bracket) which now gives about 1.5" of height adjustment. Another benefit of this setup with extra washers and nuts, it is a lot sturdier with less flex/play than the included bolt.

As mentioned in some other reviews, when you use the height adjustment (even the stock 3/8" one) that monitor will have some "rotational play" in it, but this is easily fixed by adding a few layers of electrical tape (or whatever tape you prefer, but the rubbery texture of electrical seems to be ideal) to both sides of the bracket, before sliding it into the mount. Hard to describe but you'll see what I mean, the vesa mount slides into slots in the mounting arm and the tape makes it a much tighter fit and eliminates the play.

Attached picture has the custom height adjustment/mounting bolt I made circled in green, and the electrical tape circled in red. Note you're only seeing the tape on one side of the vesa head, the other side has the same thing (you can barely see it at the bottom right of the green circle). I believe I used 3 layers, but folded over so it is on both sides of the metal, so in reality 6 layers per side.

I've also noticed the difference in height of the 2 arms side to side, around 1/4" in my case. If you have identical monitors, the 3/8" of height adjustment should be enough to resolve this.

The included mounting screws are OK but the plastic heads were a concern, so I used all-metal ones I already had. One of my monitors had lousy threads, filled with powdercoating it seems, so even with my sturdy all-metal screws the heads stripped out some, so the plastic ones would have been useless in that case. Not the mount's fault (blame Lenovo for this one) but just bear in mind that the included mounting screws can't be tightened very hard due to plastic heads which will strip out very easily. With most monitors this won't be an issue, my 2nd Lenovo monitor (newer version) was very easy to thread in and the plastic ones would have been fine (other than being a bit worried about long term strength).

All in all, it is working great, just wish I didn't have to make a trip to home depot and cut/fashion my own mounting setup. Basically if you want your monitors to be level with each other, you'll need identical monitors, as the 3/8" of adjustment is just enough to compensate for the side-to-side difference in this mount, leaving no room for monitor differences, unless you want to fashion your own adjustment like I did.

title: A geek's new best friend
text:
So this thing is seriously the best computer I have ever owned. I've owned a couple old XP Desktops, a windows 7 Toshiba laptop and a Windows 8 Convertible laptop and none of them can top this Chromebook.
The build:
- The texture on the exterior casing is really really nice, it keeps it from feeling like it's going to slip out of your hand, and makes the plastic more tolerable.
-The keyboard doesn't have a whole lot of travel, but it is comparable to a lot of MacBook Air keyboards I've fiddled with. It's not quite there, but it's definitely not bad at all.
- The trackpad is fantastic! It never misses a two or three finger click, it is equally easy to push down no matter where you press.
- The hinge is really steady and hardly wobbles at all, which is definitely a good thing.
- The display... Oh my word, this display is gorgeous. It doesn't beat out the retina MacBooks, but it is as good as any 1080 panel I've seen. The viewing angles are great, it has deep blacks and vibrant colors, A+
- Speakers: The speakers are amazingly loud for such a compact machine, and for the price they offer very good quality, only distorting at very high volume. They could afford to have a little more bass, but generally A+
The Software:
Chrome OS is fantastic. It is my favorite operating environment. Mac, Windows, and even Linux OSes don't come close to the pure simplicity that is Chrome OS. The dock is great, clean effective, out of the way. The application menu does just that, applications, no attempts at unnecessary eye candy or access to spots within other apps. The menus are very easy to navigate, the settings area on the dock is well designed and intuitive. It doesn't have anything extra and that translates to everything just working. I never have to think, "Man I hope my document saved" or "Dang it did I get a virus." Google has taken out all things that aren't necessary, and it is awesome. The fact that this is so lightweight also translates to amazing battery life. At half brightness with music playing I can get a solid 9 hours, and if I don't have audio and I turn the brightness all the way down I'm able to get nearly 13 hours of continuous use. A few great features of chrome OS are the two finger horizontal swipe to go forward and backwards in a tabs history, the 3 finger swipe down for the "expose" feature, and the various hotkey combinations.
All in all, this is my favorite device I have ever owned, 10/10 would recommend.

title: Dysfunction enhanced by Dell Tech Support incompetence and apathy
text:
My ownership of the D3100 UltraHD Universal dock is a story of dysfunction enhanced by Dell Tech Support incompetence and apathy. The dock failed to work properly when connected to my system. The source of my problems was originally not clear, although ultimately identified as the dock & Dell tech support. Here's the long version of my problem. I purchased the Dock along with a Dell XPS 15 laptop and Dell U2713HM monitor, all purchased new at the same time. Both the computer ($2000) and the monitor ($500) are made for ultra-high-resolution display (maximum 3200x1800 and 2560x1440 respectively). They do not match resolution, despite the assurances I got on this point from Dell before purchasing the equipment. Prior to purchase I was told by two separate Dell answer-line people that these three products (laptop, monitor, Dock) were designed to work together. It is obvious they were not.

Initially the monitor did not work (black screen) when connected through the dock, or directly to the laptop. Two different Dell tech support technicians spent a cumulative 5 hours (with me a hostage assistant) working remotely on my system, resetting and re-installing every possible driver and setting and cable configuration, plus having me purchase additional cables. Unfathomably, the DVI and VGA cables supplied with the UltraHD monitor do not support its full resolution; you must purchase additional cables for it to reach its full, advertised resolution.

With no help from Dell tech support I accidently discovered that the computer-monitor connection (either with or without dock) will not function if the Screen Resolution setting is "Duplicate these Displays". Any other setting works. After solving that "problem" my monitor works fine when connected directly to the laptop. Connections through the D3100 Dock work only intermittently. This includes both monitor display and keyboard communications.

After Dell Tech Support recommended purchasing additional cables, which also did not solve the problems, my case was elevated to Dell's "HD resolution specialist" who confessed having never worked with a D3100 dock before, so wasn't sure what to expect of it. After having me perform more tests and having me install more drivers, communicating only by email, she eventually concluded that either the dock is faulty or maybe I need to re-install the computer OS. It took 2 weeks' of occasional email to reach this indecisive conclusion.

It has taken one month to get to this point, the source of the problem and its resolution are still not known decisively, and Amazon is out of stock on the D3100 dock until end of February. I asked the Dell Tech Support specialist if they could handle the Dock replacement in order to expedite finding a solution to my problems and she promised to let me know. That was 5 days ago; still no response. If the replacement Dock doesn't work I'm faced with an OS re-install that also may or may not work. This is not Dell's cheapest equipment by a long shot. I expected a lot more of both their equipment and especially of their tech support. It will be a long time before I think of purchasing Dell equipment again. I can only wonder: how would Apple have handled such problems if it was their equipment?

Update 1/18/15: I exchanged my D3100 for the same product two weeks ago and the new dock has worked well during this time. Apparently my problems stemmed from a hardware failure in my original dock. I would give the new D3100 a 5-star rating if not for the fact Dell tech support was both helpless and apathetic about assisting me to diagnose what was the cause of my connectivity problems (I was on my own to figure out if it was caused by my new computer, new monitor, or new dock). I'm raising my rating to a 3-star because the hardware is good if it is functioning, but lack of product tech support and misinformation from Dell denies it a higher ranking.

Then you have to tap on the screen to invoke it again. So much easier to just unlock my phone and say stuff. Even on a run.

title: Great machine, but needs better Chrome OS office compatible software
text:
You get a lot of machine for your money, especially if you buy it refurbished from the Acer factory store. The machine looks a lot more expensive than it is. The Ram and hard storage are more generous than a lot of other chromebooks. Don't forget to apply for the extra 100 GB on Google Drive that came with my machine. The near instant startup is a great feature. Battery life on the Acer 14 is good, but not nearly the 11 hours advertised.
Beautiful large screen and sharp picture - great for movies and videos. Sound quality is OK, but the volume is not loud enough in a noisy environment or to fill a room.

My main problem is not with the machine itself but rather the limitations of the Chrome OS. It does not have a decent word processor of its own.
Chrome compatible versions of Google Docs and Word Online are not capable of working with the MS Word tracking features, which makes it impossible to use the Chromebook to work properly with Word files which have tracked edits. This is a big problem for someone who wants to use a Chromebook as a more affordable replacement for a full fledged business laptop.

There are a few other things this machine could use. The lack of a slot for a micro SD card is a nuisance. You can use a flash drive instead, but why waste a scarce USB port? It would also be nice if this Chromebook could recognize a plug and play external DVD drive. Also, the procedures for working on documents with this machine offline are absurdly complex and confusing. All of your files have a tendency to wind up getting dumped in the Chromebook's download directory. The system needs a more flexible and easier to use file manager.

The Acer 14 Chromebook is slated by Google for an official software upgrade to make it compatible with Android apps via the Google Play store. That should make this machine much more versatile. But that still will not solve the problem of the lack of a fully functional Chromebook app to substitute for the MS Office suite.

By the way, if anyone from Google or Microsoft is reading this, please give the Chrome OS the respect it deserves and stop choking it with crippled apps. I would be willing to pay a reasonable amount, say $25-$50, for such a full featured Chromebook Office suite, and I bet a lot of other people with machines as capable as the Acer 14 would do so as well.

The Acer 14 Chromebook gives us a peak at just how useful these Chrome OS devices could be if the OS and the apps can catch up to the capabilities of the hardware.

title: Very nice sounding speaker if you have the room and cash, but does not approach high-end speakers
text:
We decided to go full Nelson with Sonos and own play:5, play:1, the soundbar and sub in various rooms in the house. These have replaced a number of conventional speakers and subs. The sound quality of the play:5 is much better than the play:1 in maximum volume, frequency range (high and low), and overall clarity. I'd highly recommend getting a pair because of the better stereo separation. The play:5 will not distort much at high volumes for most music, except bass heavy hip hop. There is some painful distortion in the upper mid-range / lower high range which creeps in near maximum volume.

The play:5 matches the quality of conventional speakers in the $600-$800/pair range. When you consider that the amplifiers are included and the extreme convenience of the streaming software it is a pretty good value. If you are an audiophile, you are better off getting the Sonos connect:amp and adding a sub.

One great convenience of the Sonos system is that you can add units over time and still get full functionality because of the long production runs of each unit. We've added speakers over a few years, singly or in pairs to avoid large cash outlays and as we reconfigure rooms.

Pros:
Excellent sound and convenience
3.5mm mini-plug audio input (for bluetooth adapter, PC input, etc.)
Plays fairly loud without distortion
Good bass for regular music listening.
Wireless (2.4 Ghz) or wired Ethernet input
Vertical or Horizontal Orientation
Add units over time. Even a single play:5 is very functional. A pair is a lot better.
Any input can play on any speaker, or group of speakers.

Cons:
Won't play loud enough for a DJ-style party
Bookshelf speaker sized, 14 lbs.
Requires AC, somewhat limiting placement.
Optional Sub does not rock the house
Distortion creeps in at high volumes

IMO the sub is unnecessary for music. The play:1 is good for smaller rooms or if you don't play music very loudly.

title: Excellent USB hub. Power cord sold separately, though.
text:
Works perfectly with my Surface 3. Using this hub, I've attached an external 1TB hard drive, mechanical keyboard, and optical mouse, basically converting my Surface 3 from a tablet/laptop to a 'desktop'. So far, the hub has been working seamlessly, to the point where I basically plugged it in and forgot about it. I haven't had a single problem. For convenience, I did put some velcro on the bottom to anchor it in place on the side of my desk... The USB cord is thick and the hub is super light, so it has a habit of wandering around whenever the cord's bumped. Also of note, the cord is about 3' long, which makes it very convenient to put 'where I want it' instead of 'right next to the port' like a lot of other similar hubs expect you to do.

Really, I'm not sure what else to say. It's nice to purchase a product that just simply works. My only complaint is that the AC power cord for this hub has to be purchased separately. But at the same time, you really only need the power cord if you're planning on charging smaller devices or using devices that require more power than your device's USB port can provide in the first place. If you don't purchase the extra AC cord, the device is entirely powered by your USB port, which is typically sufficient to run all but the particularly power-hungry USB devices. With the AC cord plugged in, I can use this hub to charge my bluetooth headphones and my USB battery backup... But it doesn't put out enough amperage (2+ amps) to charge my Surface 3. If it could do that, it would be better than perfect.

title: Setup a little difficult, but pretty good otherwise!
text:
We've been in need of a new replacement speaker for our main living room. We've had a small bluetooth Panasonic that we often ran into issues with it not remembering pairing properly. It also didn't sound too great

Then came along the Heos. I was surprised to read about how small it was, and yet how great it sounded. Decided to give it a try. Since it was wireless, I expected we'd be able to get around the bluetooth issues we've had with the other Panasonic speaker we had. Boy was I right! This things sounds amazing, even with the volume cranked all the way up. It doesn't break up, and really brings all types of music alive. We've tried classical, new age, pop, rock, and more. I couldn't be more happy with how the speaker performs once it's setup.

Setup, however, was a pain. You're supposed to hookup your iOS device (iPhone 6 in my case) via the headphone jack to the speaker. Then you run through the setup, and it's supposed to pull the wireless info into the speaker. I couldn't get mine to work no matter how many times I tried. We have an Apple Airport Time Capsule, and it refused to connect. I pressed the reset button, read the manual troubleshooting tips, and couldn't get it to work at all. I finally resorted to hooking it up via ethernet to my router, and then manually changing it to be wireless (as suggested by the manual). That worked after one try, but I would've rather just wish the speaker could've seen my wireless through the regular setup. Hopefully your results will be better, but this was hands down the worst part of the product use for me.

The iOS app isn't bad, but it did quit a lot on me. This may be due to me using the iOS 9 public beta, however, versus the app itself. Once you're in, it allows you to use many music services (i.e Spotify) or use the library on your phone. I tried it with both music on my phone as well as Spotify. Both worked and sounded great. The app could be a little more user friendly, but overall, it's not bad. I did run into a few issues trying to play Apple Music songs, but ran into some DRM issues. Perhaps this will be fixed in the future, since Apple Music was just recently released. Adding my wife's iPhone 5s was simple too. Just downloaded the app, it instantly recognized the speaker, and she was able to play songs just as easily.

We're happy with this, and thrilled to have a nice speaker for our listening needs. Other than the setup, as described, we're just fine with our Heos 1.

title: Needs 462 Gigabytes more to get that last Terabyte
text:
I do not typically buy entire external drives with enclosures; when I do I usually pull the bare drive out. So far, I just finished unpacking the drive and hooking it up to start transferring files; pretty straightforward process for anyone who has used an external drive before.

The housing for the drive is all plastic and, without taking apart the enclosure, there appears to be minimal metal framing to hold the drive and circuit board. The rubber feet raise the drive up quite a bit and there are plenty of louver type slots for airflow. Still, I greatly prefer all metal housings for heat dissipation but if you aren't constantly using the drive, plastic is probably fine.

I am not sure why companies label their drives in terabyte increments since they never quite get the full terabyte. For anyone interested this drive has 5,000,946,249,728 bytes. Divide that by 1024 four times to work through kilo-, mega-, giga-, and tera-bytes and you get 4.54TB. That's about half a trillion missing bytes.

I do not have any kind of benchmarking software but doing a file transfer of 1.61TB from an internal drive to this external, it started at 90MB/s and tapered off to about 65MB/s and could take 7 and a half hours to complete.

Until a company makes real terabyte increments I probably will never give a full 5 star review on a drive of this size.

title: Every subsequent insertion has gone in easily. Shortly after that I noticed that the earphone ...
text:
I bought this to use to fall to sleep with music without disturbing my ultra-light sleeping wife. I use it with a single earphone that combines both channels into one so I can have one ear against the pillow and the earphone in the other and still get both channels. With this extension cord, I don't have to worry about turning over in my sleep and pulling the phone off the bedstand to possibly be damaged in the fall.

The first time I inserted the extension cord in my fairly new Galaxy S7, it was hard to insert all the way, and the phone immediately started doing some crazy stuff that I had to restart to phone to stop. Every subsequent insertion has gone in easily. Shortly after that I noticed that the earphone outlet on the phone was only outputting the left channel. I've set the phone earphone outlet to output in mono, so I'm still getting my full music at night, but I can't enjoy in stereo at other times when I switch the phone back to stereo and use stereo earphones inserted directly into the jack. This isn't a devastating problem with the phone as there is always the mono output option, but it IS disappointing in a fairly new expensive phone.

I don't know if the physical resistance when inserting the cable was due to the plug breaking something in the jack, but I'm suspicious, hence the 3 star rating instead of five.

[Edit: I've subsequently found that getting the right channel contact in the phone jack bent back to where it doesn't make contact is a known problem with the Galaxy S7, so I don't think this was the fault of this extension cord. I'm restoring my rating to 5 stars.]

I've had no similar problem with either cord when inserted into the earphone jack on my tablet as a test and have no problem listening in stereo there, except I seldom use my tablet for this purpose.
