title: Excellent Monitor For Photo Editing & Gaming!
text:
I chose the backlit LED BenQ GW2470H for professional photo editing and some gaming with the rest of the family (Plants Vs. Zombies Garden Warfare, Sim City, Civilization IV & V and various zoo and theme park tycoon games). I chose the 24" screen because at 1920x1080, it uses a .274 pixel pitch size compared to the a 27" using the same resolution, which would use a .31 instead. The smaller pixel pitch equals sharper detail for photos and for closer viewing.

After reading ENDLESS amounts of monitor specs and lots of reviews and forum posts, I finally determined the right type of monitor for me was the AMVA + (SNB) panel, for reasons listed below. Many of these online sources will direct anyone seeking a photo editing monitor toward one with an IPS panel. The truth is that IPS panels produce no better color response than a VA panel does. VA panels also have two very important advantages over IPS and one lesser one. First, VA panels are capable of producing much better native contrast ratios than IPS (those dynamic contrast ratios mean absolutely nothing, especially when it comes to photo editing/accurate image display). Secondly, VA panels produce better blacks than IPS, which is also an important factor in accurate image display. The lesser advantage is the lack of light bleed in the corners, which is a shortcoming of IPS panels. The advancements of the AMVA + (SNB) design also improves refresh rates a bit for gaming.

The BenQ GW2470H has an AMVA + (SNB) panel, which produces a 3000 to 1 native contrast ratio, compared to 1000 to 1 from an IPS panel monitor. It also has a 4ms refresh rate, making it slightly better for gaming than the 5ms rates of any IPS panel I've found. I also bought a Datacolor S5P100 Spyder5PRO to calibrate the color and contrast response, which (after calibration) lists this monitor as actually producing 74% of the color spectrum (slightly higher than the standard 72% of NTSC color, also known as 100% of the sRGB color spectrum, or 8 bit color). This is the standard color gamut to look for when buying anything short of a wide gamut monitor. Wide gamut monitors are only effective when the entire signal chain from software to printer are handling the image at 10bit color processing and are usually quite expensive themselves. They also produce mixed results when trying to simulate 100% sRGB color, which defeats the purpose for my needs.

Using a professional hardware color / contrast calibrator is absolutely essential for making your monitor produce the best results. Having three times the native contrast ratio (the difference between brightest and darkest levels the screen can produce and how smooth those transitions are) is a huge plus. Regardless of what a manufacturer says about their monitor being "pre-calibrated" or color accurate right out of the box.... it's a load of you know what. It's not possible for any manufacturer to calibrate a monitor to be "accurate" without it being connected to your video card, using the cables you've chosen, and knowing the specific ambient light levels/color levels of your viewing area. All those variables affect the monitor output and a hardware calibrator like the Spyder5 Pro allows you to properly calibrate your monitor, including all those variables. You can also re-calibrate it anytime you like, to maintain image quality and know what you are actually outputting as a photographer. Ignore anyone saying a monitor's color looked bad out of the box. Of course it doesn't look as good as it could, regardless of brand or price.... if it hasn't been calibrated as mentioned above.

The BenQGW2470H comes with two HDMI ports, one HDMI cable and a VGA port, with cable. It has a 178 degree viewing angle and looks really good at far off center angles, both sideways and from above. This means more people can enjoy what you are seeing (the way you're seeing it) without crowding together in that sweet spot. That's not the most important feature for me, but it is much nicer than the 170 degree monitor I had before.

Is this monitor everything I hoped it would be? Yes! After much research, I'm happy to say that this is a great monitor for all my needs and at a great price! Performance for both offline and online gaming have also been great, without any smearing or ghosting. I wish it had the height adjustable stand of some of their gaming specific models, but that wasn't a deal breaker for me. It also includes flicker free technology, which is a nice touch.

The BenQ manufacturer product page includes more information than the Amazon product page, so some people may find this link useful:

http://orwww2.benq.com/product/monitor/gw2470h/specifications/

I posted all this information in the hopes that it might be useful for someone with similar monitor needs as myself. With all the misinformation out there and the fact that this particular model seems to be pretty new, it might be easy to miss this really great performer.

title: Format it and it's good to go! *see update*
text:
Updated to 4-stars from 2 [3/26/17]

So after a few emails with WD Support instead of just sending this back to Amazon, I took it upon myself to do a long format on this SSD. Long format in that I unchecked the "Quick Format" box..
I popped in my Kingston HyperX 120gb, reinstalled Windows for like the 3rd time that week, and did a format of this WD Blue. When everything was done, I opened up the WD Dashboard, and bam! Everything is good! Status says drive is good and the firmware updated. Speed is up to where it should be - passing my Kingston in 4 of 6 categories.

SO just watch out, that you might have to format it right out of the box! Left off 1 star because of that fact..
- - - - - - -
I bought this to replace the 2 SSD's I had been running - one with OS and other with Adobe Suite and a few select games [Skyrim, which is slow loading on HDD]. The idea of having just one SSD and one less drive overall was great - coupled with the great reputation of WD Blue, how could you go wrong?!

Well, installing it and plopping Windows 7 on it is where things went wrong. The first attempt at installing Win7 went ok for a week or two. Then suddenly the whole system came unglued... . It dropped to a slow performance and a literal 4 minute boot time. Not having any of that, I did a fresh wipe and tried it again. This time it boots at normal speed, as I've since isolated the problem driver, but this drive still preforms pretty slow.

Looking up some benchmark/performance testing software, I ended up with a good ol' fashion UserBenchmark, and even that confirmed my system was about half the beast it was pre-WD Blue. I attached a screen shot of a drive-specific test for you to see how abysmal it really was! Barely better than my aging Toshiba 2TB HDD!

The 2nd Windows7 install on this Blue drive gave the proper 20-30 second boot time, but then quickly started having lags in window response times, desktop response times, and overall Explorer.exe responsiveness. Really?!

Doing some more searching on SSD-optimizing software, I found that WD actually released a Dashboard for their new SSD line. That would've been nice to know right off the bat...
So I installed it and immediately it tells me the drive is bad. Great...
There was also a Firmware update. ...Great, one more piece of equipment that needs to be kept up-to-date.
Then it tells me it's not compatible with my system.
What??
It's not a driver incompatibility, it's the drive. Since when is a hard drive not compatible with a computer system?!?! WHATT?!

WesternDigital, I expected so much better from you! Looks like i'm returning it and putting back my HyperX 120gb.

Only reason I give this WD Blue 2 stars is on the chance that I just happened to get a lemon. Otherwise it's been a 0-1 star experience.

title: Almost Perfect
text:
I have tried ear buds, in-ear monitors, even custom-molded quad-driver monitors and none have been able to withstand the tortuous use to which I submit them. The biggest complaint I have about any headphone of any type is that the cables fail, usually where the right and left leads separate to the speakers. After throwing away 3 pairs of Etymotic ER4 ear buds at $300 each because the cables failed and the the cables could not be replaced, I stopped buying Etymotic ear buds in this price range. When I saw that the ER3XR has replaceable cables, I figured I would take another chance on the higher end Etymotic ear buds.

First, my list of likes:
- These ear buds produce even better audio fidelity than the ER4P ear buds. That's quite an accomplishment. I prefer to hear the high notes, and most ear bud manufacturers tend to emphasize the mid-range with abundant bass. These ear buds open up the high end with a nice balance of mid-range and bass. If you want head-thumping bass, the ER3XR might be a little disappointing, but I find the bass response ample enough.
- Cable construction feels more rugged than I remember for the ER4 series. Time will tell how often I have to replace the cables, though.
- The triple flange tips that I like, and were left over from the ER4 and other Etymotic ear buds work with the ER3XR. That has saved me a little expense since I could use them without having to buy more right away.
- The connection between the driver and the cable is static. There is less chance that the contacts on the driver will wear out over time like I experienced with another brand.

Now for the only dislike I have for now:
- I buy ear buds because I use them while riding motorcycles. The ER3XR driver assemblies are larger than the previous Etymotic ear buds I have tried. It is going to be difficult getting my helmet over them, and this might also cause a problem with comfort.

title: Nice battery power camera, but with only low resolution images
text:
VueZone cameras does not require AC power and thus it is easier to install. However, the image resolution is lower.

I have tried more than 5 different kinds of DIY home surveillance cameras, including Dropcam, Homeboy, P2PCam, and VueZone (above are available in the US market) and GoSafe, Skywatch, and Unieye (these are not available in the US market).

There are a few general problems that I ran into
(1) Many cameras need AC power or USB power. It creates trouble on where a DIY user can set up the cameras. Homeboy and VueZone are those cameras that can operate on battery. VueZone has extremely good battery life (at least 6 months in my experiment). Homeboy has a rechargeable battery. However, it lasts two about two weeks (probably because it needs to emit infrared lights during the dark).
(2) Many cameras stream every image to the cloud. Besides privacy concerns, it eats away my upload bandwidth. When I have more than 10 cameras in the house, it becomes a big problem. VueZone on the other hand will not capture (and transmit) any images when there is no human motion in the scene.
(3) Many cameras that stream the images to the cloud like to charge monthly service fees. It is a little bit annoying that we have to pay extra fees after the initial equipment cost. Homeboy, GoSafe, Skywatch, and Unieye does not charge any extra.
(4) There are two kinds of motion detection. One uses image processing to detect motion. One uses a second sensor, e.g., PIR sensor to detect motion. Using image process are often inaccurate. In particular, some of them tried to do it on the camera, which has limited computational power.
(5) The majority of the cameras have a slow response to stream the video the smartphone. Dropcam is one of the best. It takes about 2-3 seconds before I can see the live video stream. Some others may takes tens of seconds. Homeboy is the worst. I cannot view any life stream. In order to adjust the camera angles, I have to record a small segment of the video and wait for the whole segment to be uploaded into their cloud before I can see the images. The process often takes minutes.
(6) Most of the camera cannot work well during the dark. Some of them that have AC power have built-in night vision lights. VueZone requires a separate IR light source.

In general, I am not extremely happy with any cameras at this point. I would recommend Dropcam if you don't care about the monthly fee, the need of AC power, and the upload bandwidth consumption. I would recommend VueZone if you don't care about its low-resolution images.

title: Junk! -- AVOID as if Ebola --
text:
I should have searched the Internet for repair information concerning Polk products. It's amazing how many of their subwoofers fail just after the warranty expires. And that caused by a known manufacturer defect.

Then, when one wants repair information about the unit, such as schematics, it is refused because "intellectual property". Of course it's "intellectual property" -- as is every book published and on the market; it's an irrelevant excuse by means of which to withhold information, else the customer might be able to save repair costs by fixing the unit himself.

What it comes down to is returning it to Polk -- shipping both ways on the customer -- for repairs which cost the same, if not more, than the price of the product new. (In one instance Polk wanted $100 to repair one of its subwoofers -- $1.00 more than the cost of it new; the problem turned out to be a burned resister costing .49 cents.)

Customer "Support"? I was told to remove the rear electronics panel. I removed all the screws holding that in -- and the panel wouldn't come out. I was told to remove the "metal grill" -- the model doesn't have a "metal grill" -- and "push the woofer in" so the panel could be pushed out from the inside -- which can't be done because the woofer is attached to the _outside_ of the cabinet. That being unhelpful, one continues to be limited to the options of either paying through the nose a second time, or trashing the item.

And when one notes those facts to the "Support" person, one is subjected to crude insults.

The long and short of it is that Polk is in the repair business: it sells products designed to fail just after the warranty expires. Then it charges at least as much to repair it as the cost of the item when new. The denial of information based upon the irrelevant claim that it's "intellectual property" is how they limit the customer's options to either paying through the nose a second time, or tossing that which is overrated junk.

This fan in particular is not quite as solid feeling as a resin-compound Fractal Design stock 140 fan, but the look and performance is what I'm after.

So, why just 4 stars? Good question. This would've been a 5-star review were it not for the very weird PWM Sharing thing they do with this line. Okay, I get it. Save us a bit more dough by not making us buy a PWM splitter to daisychain fans together. But leaving a thin (what is that, 28 gauge?), unsleeved wire dangling from the fan is a recipe for disaster. It's so fragile that I worried about how I was going to manage the cables. My fix was to remove the piece intended for daisychaining and then sleeve the lone, fragile wire used for the PWM control to this fan. I have the tools and materials to do this. Others may not. What do they do?

title: Great sound at all volumes and with a variety of music!
text:
I know there are several other reviews stating how great this thing sounds, and many such reviews talk about how "loud" it can go and the "bass". The reviews are true and accurate, it really does crank and is very clear when loud. I wanted to also address how it sounds with typical music and play. It absolutely excels at any sort of music I throw at it, and at lower levels also sounds great. We tend to listen to older classic rock, some newer music, some alternative, classical, jazz, whatever the mood calls for. This Aiwa excels at all music and is very well rounded at all volume levels.
What amazed me is the battery life. At the claimed wattage, I did not think the battery could last more than a few minutes to be honest, but even when listening at very loud levels it goes for many hours as claimed. After 5 hrs or so at a moderate level, the battery is still at about half, which I find amazing.
It has a nice equalizer, which I have almost flat for my taste, but it is nice to be able to adjust 5 bands, (low bass to higher treble-not just the standard treble and bass adjustments). It will remember your last adjustment, or you can select from 4 presets, or turn it off (flat).
I have heard various expensive Bose units and other nice units over the years, and this Aiwa at under $300 in my view absolutely blows away anything in this price range, especially being a portable unit! That is what got me to consider it, it is big, but you can easily pick it up and move it outside or anywhere, and it sounds fantastic. Many other units with this sort of good sound are not portable like this one is.
I also considered a Fluance Fi50, but found no comparisons to this unit, but this unit being truly portable with battery option, and with the rave reviews sold me on trying it. I have not heard the Fluance unit or a lot of others really recently, but I can very confidently tell you if you get this Aiwa, you will probably love it. Just for the audiofreaks, I turned it up to about 75% and with my SP meter measured it at around 95 decibels, and it was still clear and running on the battery. It can play loud enough to satisfy most people and yes, the bass/low end is very nice indeed. For me the most important thing is good overall sound, which this has plenty of, and clear music at decent volume, which this has in spades! To totally sweeten the deal, the battery life is very good in view of having basically a portable stereo with you that you can tote around. Amazing product!
Another great feature: It actually has a Rotary Volume Control-you never see that anymore and I miss that in modern day equipment. It is very nice to just reach up and turn a knob for fine adjustment.
OK-overall I really love this player-it just sounds great. I also love that it also has a 3.5 AUX IN Jack to play anything else without Bluetooth you might want to play through it. (Hint-you can also buy a really cheap blue-tooth adapter for non-Bluetooth items to avoid "the wire" if you wish).
PROS: Fantastic Sound, Good battery life, Rotary Volume Control, big but still very portable, Aux-In Jack for older equipment.
CONS: No Remote, (but can operate functions from I-pod or other device)
Touchpad on unit sometimes not real sensitive so might require a few taps for the function to work (But ultimately always works)
Note: Some may find non-detachable speakers a "con", but that would in some ways probably make it less portable and perhaps be subject to rattle and other issues. I like the solid structure of the unit. I did see in only one review that someone thought the unit had a "rattle", and I actually thought that at first with this unit, only to discover it was the surface I had it on as this unit puts out so much lower end. Since I realized that, I have not had any other rattles or unpleasant vibrations from the unit, just be aware of position if playing it loud.
The "Cons" are really almost not worth mentioning as this unit sounds fantastic and is such a great value. I really enjoy it. Happy listening.

title: Great specs for the price in the current market
text:
If you know what you are looking for in a PC and know how components perform, this one does as you would expect. I bought this to use as a media PC for my bedroom connected to my TV. I don't do anything particularly demanding, although I wanted something relatively powerful for a couple of reasons. I like to stream 1080p content at 2x speeds (sometimes higher), and eventually 4k - I can't do this with a Roku set. Nor can I do some light gaming with a Roku, and instances where I can't run a game well enough, I intend to use Steam in-home streaming. (I do have a Steam Link, but that's an entirely unreliable product.)

I haven't used this computer a ton, and it's probably more than I need - but I like to be in full control and have flexibility, especially later on down the line if I re purpose this. I knew exactly what I was getting, and it cost me less than it would have to build, and without the hassle - in the form factor I was looking for. I can even use this as a secondary work computer later on down the line - especially once I set up a NAS and I don't have to worry about file storage. It won't be the fastest, but it'll get the job done for light Graphic Design work.

There have been some minor issues that drop it a star:

1. When I took the PC out of its packing, I gave it a little shake and heard a loose rattling - a screw was floating around somewhere - inside of the power supply in fact. Thankfully after several minutes of shaking I was able to get it loose. Not a huge deal.

2. When put to sleep, the front LEDs blink bright blue which is kind of an issue as a matter of principle. I shut it down at the end of the day anyways, so it's not brightly flashing, but I think that it's a bit absurd. I'm sure there's some workarounds, like blackout tape, or disconnecting the LED's, but to have to do that is a bit ridiculous.

3. The display won't wake up when I wake the PC from sleep. I think this is something I can find a fix for, and it may be my display which is currently an older samsung TV connected via HDMI.

4. Not really an issue for me, but the lack of space for additional hard-drives is something to take into consideration. At the current time of writing, though, I forgot if there's an available M.2 slot... I should know that... However I'm referring 2.5" drive space for a traditional hard drive for file storage. I don't need more than the 128Gb since I really only care that my major apps and OS are on the SSD, but it'd be nice to have more room. I'm sure it can be done though with some modding or jerry rigging.

Bottom line, if you like the specs you see and the price, it works as intended, at least in my case. I'm happy with my purchase.

title: Slightly improved, yet vastly the same.
text:
BACKSTORY:
I purchased two of the original Canon 6D bodies in 2014 to use as a backup to my two Canon 5D Mark III bodies. It was a "just-in-case" purchase that I could use if my primary camera failed while covering a wedding. Eventually they started to accompany me on hikes, trips, and other daily life routines. Using the less expensive camera for unpaid moments in life just made more sense. Why risk having an accident with my 5D Mark III when I could bring the less expensive Canon 6D, right?

It didn't take much time for me to realize that the image quality was superb, dynamic range was acceptable, and ISO performance was not that much different than the 5D Mark III. So I made a cost-savings analysis, ended up selling my 5D Mark III bodies, and purchased 2 Canon 6D bodies with money left to spare. Yes, I have 4 Canon 6D bodies. And yes, I use them to photograph weddings. You can read more about this decision in the "final words" section, but for now let's get to the cream and butter.
----------

REVIEW:
**********
WEIGHT and ERGONOMICS:
6D: Approximately 1.6 pounds including battery and SD card.
6D Mark II: Approximately 1.8 pounds including battery and SD card.
Difference: Negligible

Note: They both weigh virtually the same amount of weight, and both feel virtually the same with one exception. That exception is the rear thumb placement. I personally think the Mark II has a slightly more comfortable rear thumb placement than the 6D does. This solely has to do with the thumb ridge extending onto the SD card slot door. This point is more subjective than objective, but two photographer friends have agreed -- so take that for what it's worth.
----------

VIEWFINDER COVERAGE:
6D: 97% coverage
6D Mark II: 98% coverage
Difference: 1%

Note: A 1% increase in coverage is VERY hard to notice. If I didn't know the 6D Mark II had 98% coverage I would have assumed it had the same as the original 6D because I see absolutely no difference.
----------

VIEWFINDER INTELLIGENCE
I don't use it very often, but once-in-a-while I will deploy the 6D's electronic level for either landscape or real estate photographs and sometimes the grid for still life photos. The pain with using them was the need to switch between two separate LCD live view modes. I would have to use the electronic level, go back to compose my shot, and then check the electronic level again to make sure it was still in alignment. And although the grid was able to be superimposed over images in live view, I still disliked using the LCD screen because it felt unnatural to me.

The 6D Mark II has made electronic leveling and grid display available through its "intelligent viewfinder" which is a really neat feature. This means you can now look through the viewfinder and superimpose an electronic level OR grid display onto the screen. Gone are the days of having to use the live view function on the LCD screen to see these features.
----------

LCD SCREEN
6D: 1,040,000 dots, non-articulating & no touch screen features
6D Mark II: 1,040,000 dots, fully-articulating touch-screen

I love unique vantage points and try to utilize them as often as I can, especially for getting-ready and dance photos. I routinely hover over the shoulder of hair and makeup artists to get POV photos, and when the dance floor is crammed I put my camera overhead and point it downwards to get a wide-angle, top-down view of people. Both of these caused me to either A: literally be on my tippy-toes while looking through the viewfinder with my chest against the hair and makeup artist, or B: raise my hand in the air on a dance floor and hope for the best -- because I literally could not see what I was shooting. If I had a dollar for every missed focus dance-floor shot I got while doing this I would be a very rich man.

The articulating screen on the 6D Mark II eliminates these problems for me. I no longer have to say, "I'm going to be right behind you and over your shoulder for a few shots, so don't backup..." Instead I can hold the camera out at arms length and articulate the screen for an easy-to-see live view. And it has eliminated missed focus shots on the dance floor now that I can accurate aim at subjects and no longer have to throw hail-Marys while hoping for the best.

I use a Glidecam for real-estate videos and the articulating screen has proven to be a huge convenience for that as well. Just like the dance floor scenario, I used to flip my Glidecam upside down for sweeping ground shots and also to glide closely over furniture and would have to hope for the best because I was unable to see what I was filming. Now I can articulate the screen to face upwards and see exactly what what is being recorded while the camera is down by the floor and I'm standing upright.
----------

VIDEO
I hate it when my wife says we're having pizza for dinner, and when I get home from work I see a hot mess of cheese that originated from the freezer at Walmart. Imagine the disappointment I feel every time that happens and you will understand how underwhelming and disappointing the 6D Mark II video capabilities are.

I like shooting at 60fps because it allows me to slow the footage down 50% in post and get silky-smooth slow motion. With the 6D I was forced to choose 1280x720 in order to shoot at 60fps because 1920x1080 had a maximum frame rate of only 30fps. Now with the 6D Mark II I can shoot in 1920x1080 at 60fps, which is a slight improvement.

One thing I absolutely could not stand about the 6D was the fact that I needed to manually focus while recording video. I'm not good at it, and practice has not made me any better. Anything under f/8 with a moving subject would result in footage where 50% is kinda-sorta in focus, and the other 50% is me trying to get the subject in focus. In other words, it was like looking through the eyes of a heavily intoxicated individual. Some people are very talented and can shoot at f/2 while keeping their subject within the depth of field -- always making manual micro-adjustments to the focus ring as they move. I'm certainly not one of those people.

Therefore the new dual-pixel continuous AF is a very welcomed feature. I shot video of my 5 year old son riding his bike today at f/1.4 with a Sigma 35mm f/1.4 Art lens, and it was glorious! The 45 cross-type AF points kept him in focus the entire time. It didn't matter if he was riding at a moderate taking-it-easy kind of speed or pedaling as fast as he could, there was absolutely no indication of focusing lag. It was if the continuous drive system was proactive rather than reactive, successfully anticipating where he was going to go next. I was very impressed!

Other than those two points, the color rendition for all profiles is still the same, and ISO performance is regretfully not much improved.
----------

MORE ON AUTO-FOCUS
6D: 11 AF points, cross-type limited to center point only.
6D Mark II: 45 points, all cross type.
Difference: HUGE!

If you're like me and rely on auto-focus for 99.99% of all pictures you take, you may have cursed Canon's 6D quite a few times when peripheral AF points failed to lock while the center AF point locked on just about everything -- even under the dim light of a full moon on a cloudy night. If there is one thing I consistently cursed about, it was the need to always lock focus with the trusted center and then recompose for the rule of thirds. This was especially hard during weddings when people were constantly moving during getting-ready photos. I would be a rich man if I had a dollar for every time I locked focus and recomposed only to have my subject move out of focus while shooting between f/1.2 and f/2.8.

Take the 6D's over-competent center AF point and multiply it by 45. That's what the 6D Mark II is essentially equipped with. I can lock onto a dim star at night with any one of the 45 focus points. Dimly lit churches and dark dance floors are now a walk in the park. After so many years of locking focus and recomposing, it's actually quite hard to break that habit when you have an auto-focus system that is abundantly capable with more than just the center point.

One thing that baffles, though, me is Canon's decision to place all 45 AF points within the same area that the 6D's 11 AF points are located. While the overall auto-focus ability has been put on steroids, there is unfortunately no increase in AF coverage across the frame.
----------

IMAGE QUALITY
As you can see from my sample images, the image quality of the 6D Mark II is astounding. I can't say that the increase in megapixels from 20.2 to 26.2 is a difference between night and day, because it's not. Overall it equates to a slightly noticeable increase in detail when an image is cropped, but that's about it.
----------

FINAL WORD
You will inevitably come across a plethora of professional photographers who claim that the 6D and 6D Mark II are not worthy of being considered professional grade cameras, and therefore should never be used for a wedding or paid work. But I have to disagree. Having shot with the 5D Mark III for quite some time, I sold them and opted for 6D bodies because the image quality was essentially identical, ISO performance was essentially identical, and the 6D did a better job at focusing in low light conditions. Do not let anyone tell you that the 6D or 6D Mark II are not worthy, because they are! I fully plan on replacing all of my 6D bodies with 6D Mark II bodies.
----------

Note:
The 6D Mark II camera, just like its predecessor, is only compatible with Canon EF lenses and Sigma DG lenses. It is not compatible with Canon EF-S or Sigma DC lenses. If this is your first full frame camera and you have only EF-S lenses, you will need to make an additional purchase of new lenses.

Addition****

DYNAMIC RANGE:
When I originally posted this review, it was brought to my attention that I had forgotten about Dynamic Range. Which is fitting when taking into consideration that Canon forgot about it too.

White and black clipping is still a problem when it comes to images that have a lot of inherent contrast. The 6D Mark II spec sheet touts it as having a greater pixel size and pitch than the 6D, which should more than just theoretically translate to an increase in dynamic range. But unfortunately -- in this case -- a hypothetical increase is all that we get because it just doesn't exist. Anything beyond an EV +2 push and you'll have an unusable image, regardless of how much you play with the tone sliders.

title: Great travel cam for the price!
text:
Like others, I upgraded from this from the SX260HS. I live on a sailboat and upgraded for the 40x optical zoom. I am very amateur and just snap pics that are later shrunk to 400 Kb and posted on a blog, so the fact that this camera doesn't shoot massive RAW files didn't bother me. I love how it can go from wide-angle to ultra-zoom -- perfect for travel! I find I tend to shoot a lot in LIVE mode, with two clicks up on 'vivid' for my outdoor landscape shots, as it produces a more subtle look right out of the camera than just upping the saturation in Photoshop afterwards. This camera is also better in low-light than my old camera, although it doesn't come close to a DSLR with its massive lens, which is expected. But if you are walking around a dark cave or cathedral without a tripod, setting it on 2-second self timer to reduce shaking when you press the button and leaning your hand against a rock while it fires a pic without flash results in much better shots than with the old version.
I have only two complaints. The first is the flash. My old 260SX was annoying as well in the fact that the flash came up right under your finger while you held the camera. This camera has the same location problem, which I can deal with, but my flash stopped smoothly popping up after just two weeks of use. Now I literally have to pry it up. It's possible I got some dirt or something in the mechanism, but I can't find anything. This flash seems more complex and breakable. I don't use flash much, so this is not a deal breaker. The other problem is the autofocus. It is quite touchy without a tripod. Even without zooming out a lot one has to hold the camera quite still to get the focus to slowly come to a decision, regardless of "image stabilization". I find I have to take two or three shots to guarantee I have a focused one. I also often have trouble getting it to focus on what I want -- if a rope close to me is in the foreground of a pic of a boat far away, it prefers to focus on the tiny rope in the corner of the giant autofocus area, instead of the big boat, despite my attempts to lock the focus on something else. This may be my inexperience or just what happens with a pocket cam versus a DSLR that's five times the price. Regardless, I still make this my go-to travel cam as it has to be the best compact cam for travel given its amazing 40x optical zoom (I even use it as post-hoc binoculars to see the names of boats from far away!) and I am very pleased with my purchase.

title: I will never buy another computer brand besides Origin again. Love this PC.
text:
So our desktop died less than a year after we bought it and I wanted a decent PC but one I could upgrade with better hardware instead of just tossing dead pc's every year because I always buy super cheap ones and they spend most of their life with the sides off.
I've heard good things about ORIGIN PC Corporation but did not want to pay for a custom built rig. I found this inexpensive pre-built and got it with with the intention of upgrading as needed. I don't think I will need to upgrade for a while.

This is the most professional packaging, dust cover, a solid shipping set up, absolutely no bloatware, I was plugged in and online in about a minute, everything is updated, it's ridiculously fast because of the SSD hard drive, I got a free t-shirt in the box, USB back up dongle with a snapshot of my system when it was shipped, it has everything I need, they sent extra mounting screws for if you want to add anything to it, and it's a beast- took two of us to carry it, the part of the computer I usually use as a "handle" was clearly marked that it was NOT a lifting point.

Obviously the thing could die in a month, but I doubt it. There was an inspection sheet with it where they marked off what they tested and it was signed by three different people with real signatures, the CD's for recovery for Win 10, the dedicated graphics card, motherboard etc and I could go on and on, but seriously, look at them for your next PC. It reminds me of the first PC I ever bought which was also the most solidly constructed computer I ever bought and was built by a little computer shop near my home in the late 80s.

It's also the first computer I've had that can actually keep up with my fiber internet, it hits the wall on both uploads and downloads. It plays games (Overwatch and World Of Warcraft: Legion) great. It has 2 HDMI ports- one of the dedicated graphics card, an ethernet port and plenty of USB ports.
The side is not screwed on, but connected with a magnet system that works well for easy cleaning and upgrading.
I am happier with this computer than any other I've bought in decades. Completely sold on the brand and happy to tell anyone else about them.

title: Shame on Garmin for this poor but expensive GPS
text:
Simply put, this GPS unit has provided me inaccurate guidance. Note, I'm a large motorhome and inputed that into its settings, and as such really need an accurate GPS. But after using it in over 4 USA states and over 2000 miles, I have not confidence in it. I returned it, Amazon has a great 30 day return policy. During my experience I also compared it to several other programs and apps. The free apps and there are many, are no worse in route guidance. Note, I updated the unit and checked for updates during use.

Even the speed limit indicated on this unit was wrong much of the time, i.e. I drove along I-75 in Michigan, and approximately 90% of the time it gave me the wrong speed limit. The other 10% was by luck (I think). And I'm not talking about recent construction changes to limit speed along the route. Why would I even want to look (again) at the speed limit on this Garmin model if I can't get accuracy for something this simple.

It would take me down longer routes instead of the more direct. Such as a I-295 connector from I-95 North connecting up with I-95 South. I don't understand such ridiculous mapping. I ignored it and stayed on I-95 directly and there was no problem. Note the unit is set for the fastest route. Also, twice it took me down dirt roads, instead of the paved roads accessible in a shorter run.

What am I paying for if not for confidence in accuracy? Not once did it display low clearance avoidances in any area on screen. This makes me wonder if it has such vital information or complete data? Very important. And, I've read comments that it is quick to calculate, well, I was not impressed. Its not even better than Google maps.

Even the interface is strange. When you want to see upcoming fuel or restaurants etc., it will only provide you with a limited number of advance opportunities, say for 45-60 miles. I don't know how accurate they are, but I may want to get fuel or eat at the same stop say 60-90 miles ahead. That is not available as its limited to only so much in advance, and it should show what is along the route, like other apps.

And I guess Garmin only wants to show you logos on the map that pay them. I only saw Krystal or a Steak N Shake logo here and there, and all other times just a ridiculous symbol of Garmin that you can't disseminate from a campground, service facility or restaurant during GPS. You will have to tap on each similar looking symbol to understand it. Not convenient, nor efficient and safe while driving.

Here's something else that really bugged me. There is no display of the time. How difficult can it be to display time?! You can if, you don't want to know other information, i.e. remaining miles or arrival time. But I want to see as much details on my GPS screen, and conveniently displayed. Not to have to constantly tap through the screen and take my hand off the wheel until I find what I want. Especially when the map display is so blank, it has plenty of area to display pertinent information. One other comment, it would be great to have steep grade percentages in advance. Many times it did not display such.

Because I only can see the main road I am on. Again the canvas is mostly blank with only the road I'm traveling on, whether its zoomed in or out. Sometimes cross roads show, and there is no indication if its interchanges. I'd like to know, say you want to stop. Not to mention there is no indication for rest areas. And, forget seeing the town name you traveling in. That's not displayed either. But the unit has room for including all.

Oh, and when I am going to take the upcoming exit, say I-65, it would not indicate east or west exits. That's simple enough I would think for a $400 unit? Consider this, driving 60-70 MPH in a 40,000 # motorhome I would like to know in advance to take the east or west I-65 exit and prepare or even double check the indication. Especially, when Garmin does not provide a compass or the direction you are traveling in on the display. Sure you can get it get a direction, but then you loose the other information you need. They only have one little box to choose what you want display.

There were times when it showed an arrow to go left, but I had to go to the last right lane out of 5 or 6 lanes to pay the toll. If you didn't take care, you would stay left, be in the electronic paid lane, and perhaps get a ticket or fine for not paying. And it did not tell you in advance of a toll booth.

So, when you link it to their app on your phone, its counterintuitive. It will not remember to connect each time. So, say for "live" traffic reports, get connected or refresh the Garmin unit each time, the app gives you a list of reports. But, its impossible to determine which are on your route. I would have to study the list, or see a map on my iPhone with many reports to zoom into. But, why not only display those delays or detours that are on my route? That is the logical? Sometimes, if you are lucky, it will, but only show up as a different color line on your display and its hard to see it. There were many many times it was not showing the congestion or detours I encountered on my route, that it took me on. And.... I couldn't disconnect or tell the Garmin unit not to display alerts, texts or phone calls from my iPhone. What an annoyance each time on the Garmin unit when I got a call, reminder or text!

I think someone was half asleep at Garmin that approved this unit. Nor are they field testing it enough to make sure the mapping information they buy is good enough. My gut feeling is that Garmin is all about show bells and whistles, corporate profit or marketing an all in one unit. Instead it lacks on providing the best GPS directions, alternate traffic guidance for detours and delays, and low clearance information for a RV or motorhome it purported the unit is for.

And every time you start up, unplug the unit when not in use, or reconnect you get the warning message to agree to all terms. If you don't agree, you don't get to use what you bought. Sorry, but I paid for the unit and that should entitle me to not have to agree to your conditions every time I turn it on. And, the battery life is horrible. You have to keep it connected to the cigarette lighter or forget it.

Too much wrong. Shame on Garmin. You can try it. But this is my experience and opinion of a high mileage traveler.

title: Stand-buy.....or not.
text:
Bought for Vizio S5451w-C2. After reading reviews of the various stands available, some of which were less expensive and rated higher, I chose these for two reasons. Simply put, I liked the Euro styling and preferred a stand with feet for carpeting. These also appear to be the stands that Vizio feature on the side panel of the box.

A Phillips #1 screwdriver is the only tool needed to assemble. Of note, even when a screw is tightened it's still possible to move the speaker and/or bracket. They simply don't lock down tight enough.

To repeat what others have said, they work with some Vizio speakers, though you have to use the Vizio screws to attach them to the bracket. The height adjuster knob is plastic, will probably eventually fail, and gives the stand a certain cheap feeling.

The center columns are narrow and will not accommodate Vizio (or any other speaker wire) with RCA plugs attached to them. You could cut/ splice/solder/tape if you really needed to feed the wire up the middle. I chose to simply wrap the wire around the pole.

They support the speakers well, look fashionable and, more importantly, are extremely stable. The bases are nicely weighted and two running cats barely make them wobble.

However.....USE CAUTION when unpacking. I'm not sure if every shipment arrives like mine but I discovered two items of concern.

One: There were very small spiral metal shavings, probably from when the base screw holes were machined, that were loose and wedged between the top and bottom portions of the bases. These were extremely sharp! If stepped on or hit with a finger, they'd probably draw blood. I'd hate to think what would happen if a cat saw this tiny, curly, silver thing on the floor and decided to eat it.

Two: Of equal concern is that the bases (both of them) had residual oil on them from the machining process. One, in particular, to the point of dripping.

I read a lot of reviews and found no mention of these issues. Perhaps mine were just a fluke. $50 stands (made in the U.S.A.) shouldn't have these issues. Still, overall, I'm pleased with the stands and decided to keep them.

That said, had I known about the shavings and oil issues ahead of time, I probably would not have bought them. Give them a thicker pole, metal height lock down knob, get rid of the shavings and oil and you'd have a new five star, top rated #1 seller on Amazon worth every bit of $50.

title: Small, light, and works great
text:
The drive dock is very small, smaller than a 6x9 envelope. The power button on the back is a simple push/click type that is easy to reach and takes very little pressure to turn on or off. Both 3.5" and 2.5" SATA drives fit in the bays.

Offline cloning is simple. Place the source drive (drive intended to be copied) into the rear slot, place the destination drive into the front slot. Plug the Inateck unit into the wall with the supplied power adapter, press the power button to turn on the cloner. Wait a few moments for the drives to be detected (orange lights beside the drives will light up when they are detected). Then press and hold the clone button until the blue LED beside where it says 100% blinks. Let go of the clone button and press it once more releasing it quickly. The Inateck unit will start transferring the data from the old drive to the new one. Then its just a matter of waiting until the 100% led lights up solid to let you know its completed.

title: Great quality and durability
text:
I love Belkin products and am seriously impressed with this cord.

The exterior is a flexible nylon material - reminiscent of shoe strings for boots- and it protects well without getting snagged (by cat claws). Unlike other cables with a braided protective layer, this one has movement and flexibility. Others are extremely rigid and difficult to maneuver into difficult spaces.

Let's talk about the protection for the lightening and USB ends. Usually, my cords bust right at the connection with the USB or the lightening side. The protective coating cracks and exposes the wiring, making them no longer safe to use. (Try it and your iPhone will not recognize it. Apple is too smart for my wallet.)

Both ends have an aluminum shield, then a much longer rubber cover that eventually molds down into the nylon cord. (See photo) This helps protect the cord from breaking at the connectors - which always happens after continued use. Add to that the flexibility of the nylon cord and you have a cord that won't break easily.

No issues connecting, or with having the iPhone recognize this cord.

I took photos to compare this to the StarTech cord I recently received from Amazon Vine. While I think StarTech is a good medium-quality brand, I would pay the money for this Belkin cord for the extra quality and durability. The StarTech just looks cheap next to this one.

title: Solid
text: I bought this product after a lot of researching and reading up on reviews, and also with a lot of uncertainty as to if it would fit my needs. This one did fit my expectations perfectly. It's not the best or top of the line router in the market but a very good one for me. I live in a one story house with lots of walls, and my old netgear modem/router was just not doing so well. I decided to help the performance of my poor old modem/router with a good router, and this was the perfect fit. It looks like a spaceship and is kind of bulky, but it does its job well. My range increased and used to get 1/3 of a signal from my room, but now get almost full bars. This router is great in managing how many devices are connected. To give you an idea there are about 10 devices connected, including gaming stations that use up lots of wifi. We've got two smart TVs that needs lots of WiFi for streaming Netflix and amazon prime videos, then we got cellphones and tablets and laptops watching YouTube videos and surfing the web. Surprisingly my WiFi doesn't need to buffer when streaming with all that going on anymore. I also play games online on my Xbox, unlike before I never get disconnected from live, but not anymore. Cons would include the size for me and how bulky it is, but that might not matter for you. The signal is decent; I have it setup on a shelf in the middle of the house and I can get some connection outside my house. Pros include how it manages your WiFi, it's really good because streaming things before was bad because I always had to wait for things to load in a good quality, but this fixed that issue. It was also easy to set up and so far haven't had any issues, unlike my last setup id always have to reset that thing and do a power cycle and wait 5 mins ect, but I have never had a problem in the several months I have had it. This router is a huge upgrade . I am with Comcast and get 12 ping 23.33 down 12 up, not the fastest WiFi in the world but works well for me. Overall, Netgear did very well in making a solid product here that gets the most out of your WiFi.

title: Love The Keyboard (Had Some Initial Quality Issues That I Was Able To Fix)
text:
*Update 8/30/2016: This works great with everything I've tried it with: Desktop PC (Windows 8/8.1 and Windows 10), Laptop (Windows 8). Mac Mini (OS X Yosemite 10.10.5), and with the Raspberry Pi 2, 3, and Zero running KODI, RetroPie, and Raspbian OS. Plug it in and it just works. Edited to give 5 stars instead as the pros outweigh any damage in shipping (as it could be exchanged for a new one). Had it for 9 months now and it's one of the favorite things I use and the battery life is exceptional.*

This is a pretty nice product and feels pretty good in the hands and has a decent amount of buttons in the places for easy access for common functions/procedures. The media buttons work great and "out of the box" with VLC. I've used it on different laptops and desktops and it works just as it should like a true keyboard (and love that it is so small but still easy to use versus a larger keyboard that would sit on your lap). The only reason I am giving it 4 stars however is because when I got mine it did not work right away and there was a sound coming from it like something was loose. It worked when plugged in, but would not charge - I figured it was the battery and that it had lost a connection so I was going to return it as I wasn't sure what was inside and then I wondered about overall quality, etc.

I ended up cracking it open however unscrewing the four screws on the back (star bit screwdriver) and found that the battery was not stuck properly onto the back as I had thought which caused the noise and one of the wires was then disconnected from the battery to the board so it would not charge. I stuck the battery to the board in the square lines and the adhesive on the back of the battery stuck like it should (it must not have been placed correctly) and then re-soldered out the red/positive wire and everything has been working/charging as should. My guess is that something did not get pressed correctly in assembly but still didn't make any noise right away so it was shipped in the condition it was (otherwise it looked and worked new as I thought it should have). I could have returned it easily but also wanted to check it out myself to see if I could fix it easy.

Now that it's working - love it and definitely recommend it.

title: Excellent Gaming Monitor with great Contrast
text:
I was hesitant to buy this monitor at first because I couldn't find any reviews for this model. However, this monitor turned out to be very good. My main requirements were to get a gaming monitor with low input lag and good color reproduction for under $200. At first I was thinking of getting a high 144hz monitor but I realised the quality of TN panels was horrible. I thought about an IPS monitor since it gives a wide color gamut but the contrast ratio and black levels were bad. I finally settled on buying a VA monitor which has a 76% gamut compared to the 82+ for IPS panels. The main advantage was the immediately noticeable high contrast and deep black levels. The VA drawbacks of high input lag and ghosting have been overcome by the new generation of BenQ panels. I read on some Korean website (http://playwares.com/dpreview/47604706#) that it had slightly less than 10ms input lag which is good enough for anyone. The color reproduction is a little off though. More towards the cooler side. However you can fix it with some tuning.

Pros: low input lag, 2 HDMI ports, blue light filter( very useful), excellent black levels and contrast

Cons: color calibration will need to be done, not as good color reproduction as IPS panels

Update: I have found a dead pixel right in the middle of the screen after 3 months. BenQ policy states that they won't replace it unless it has 3 dead pixels. So I've downgraded the review.

text: I bought the Nuvi to replace my Magellan Maestro which Garmin stopped supporting several years ago. Quite frankly I picked this model largely due to its modest cost. The Nuvi is very similar to the Magellan and so far, except for the up to date maps, points of interests and larger display, is not noticeably superior. I have not had a chance to give it much of a workout yet so the jury is out. The program which updates and registers the Nuvi was easy to use. I immediately got updated maps, points of interests, and software from the Garmin web site without a hitch. The Nuvi works very much like my Magellan and I didn't need the users manual to program in my favorite regular destinations. I don't rely on my sense of direction and almost always use GPS to go anywhere outside of my immediate locale. I like the crutch it gives me and the possibility to easily go around traffic tie ups via the GPS 's ability to quickly recalculate the route to  bypass around an accident. For instance, if I95 is backed up, I can exit it and take a detour with relative ease. The window mount that comes in the package is much smaller than the one supporting my smaller, lighter Magellan. I don't expect it to stay attached to the window for long and have therefore ordered a larger one from Amazon. I will update my review after I take it out for a workout. UPDATE: I have now had several weeks use of the Nuvi and it has worked flawlessly. I love being able to locate commercial enterprises with the the POI. As I expected, the window mount that came with the Nuvi was insufficient. It regularly fell off of the window daily.I don't know why Garmin scrimped on the mount. Surely a slightly larger one would not have cut into profits much. I purchased an aftermarket window mount From Amazon for about $12.00, which works wonderfully.  I now wish I had gotten 57LMT, for the advantage of having traffic information. The extra cost is not a factor when amortized over the years of service I expect to see with the Nuvi. title: Great for quick & easy bird identification, even in your yard..
text:
A beautiful book using detailed paintings of birds along with arrows to highlight details for identification between similar species, drawings & small paintings of tail shapes & feet details, and sometimes of how the bird looks in flight from below. I often find bird ID books using drawings and paintings not helpful enough, but this book is different, very useful for recognizing birds, even for a beginner. This is the one I went to to verify that the bird I'd seen swooping across my front yard was, in fact, a red-headed woodpecker and not something else.

Not overwhelming in the amount of information it provides, but enough to be useful. The intro chapter gives general information on how to look at birds to identify them, bird habitats, etc., and ranges and commonness or rarity. This is followed by listings of birds by grouping, with intro, then by subgrouping, with details of the birds, comparing them side by side, with paintings of male and female of each and juvenile or breeding plumage sometimes, close-ups of bills for comparison, sometimes with paintings of underside and topside. The listings for each are brief, giving just enough info to identify, including seasonal range maps and vocalizations. The back contains more detailed range lists with how common or unusual the bird is within parts mof the range, along with a species "Life List" checklist for users to keep track of what they have seen. The index is by both scientific/Latin names and common names. The back of the book contains a few pages of silhouettes of the most common birds in their respective habitats - shore, flight and roadside. This is especially helpful because it shows relative sizes, and differences in flight shapes you'd see from the ground.

Thick, but not too big to carry along. Cover is coated for protection while still remaining reasonably flexible. Glad I bought it.

title: Launched 6 months too early....
text:
I want to love Canary. It's a cool concept, the ID is great, and the interface is relatively easy to use. For me it boils down to this just being a product that was probably launched 6 months before it should have been. The only way this works is if the alerts are useful. Here's the alerts I consistently got over the last weekend when I was out of town. Times are approximate.

4am - activity detected - lights came on in house
5am - activity detected - canary shifted from night vision to day vision
8am - activity detected - lights turned off
3pm - activity detected - roomba vacuuming
4pm - activity detected - roomba vacuuming
8pm - activity detected - lights came on in house
10pm - activity detected - lights turned off
12am - activity detected - bug in front of camera
1am - activity detected - bug in front of camera
2am - activity detected - bug in front of camera
3am - activity detected - bug in front of camera

Obviously I'm not going to let these wake me up at night, which sort of removes the usefulness of a security system.

Canary's response: "Over the coming months our system will be analyzing data from thousands of Canary devices. This aggregate data is going to be used to set baselines for motion detection, safe temperature and air quality ranges, normal indoor humidity, sound levels etc...Canary will learn to recognize and categorize activity and trends specific to your home based on the feedback you provide within the app...Canary will combine this supervised learning with machine learning and computer vision to build a home profile that will identify patterns, recognize alarming activity, and filter out unwanted notifications over time. Unfortunately, it takes a little while for all this to come together and provide you with more intelligent notifications, but we're working on making it faster."

Lots of wills, not many does. It takes faith to believe they'll get it right.

I read this as I just paid $250 to be in their Alpha data collection program.

I want this device to work - kudos to the team for getting it this far. Just buyer beware that the gap between marketed functionality and actual behavior is quite wide currently.

text: This is a eulogy for my ASUS PRO C432AQ monitor, manufactured Jun 2015, left this world in a horrible accident Jun 28, 2018. I wanted to leave a review for people considering ASUS Pro monitors. I felt like I was taking a risk buying it because there just weren't many reviews nearly three years ago when I got it and there still aren't a lot. I'm glad I took the chance as the C23AQ proved to be an excellent monitor at a good price back then and an even better price now, considering it has an IPS screen. While it may not be the best technology for intense gamers, it is an excellent monitor for the basic consumer or office professional who wants a solid monitor that has excellent color. Good for business applications, media consumption, and light gaming. It has basic DVI and D-sub video connections,  Audio in, Earphone jack plus USB 2.0 ports added flexibility (though I never set these up so can't report on but expect they would have been useful). In daylight when the motion detection is tripped it takes a second for the camera to come online. Then once online there is a bright light as if someone shined a flashlight into the lens. This is the camera adjusting to the lighting conditions. By the time the camera gets around to capturing the video the subject that triggered the motion is nearly out of frame. I was hoping that the camera would capture vehicles coming down the alley in case of a later event in the neighborhood in which the vehicle was involved. By the time the vehicle triggered the motion and the camera started capturing the vehicle the vehicle had already passed. I had the settings set for max range on motion detection and had on the zones selected. At night the camera is even worse. The IR images are horrible. There is still a time lapse between motion being detected and the camera capturing the event. Detail at night from the camera is poor. I would not recommend this camera for surveillance. On the good side, the solar panel works great at keeping the camera battery charged. I also own the Ring Floodlight Cam and it is tons better both at day and night then the stickup cam. Considering the total cost of the stickup cam plus solar panel is about the same as the Floodlight Cam, the stickup cam is just not worth the price.

title: Great little keyboard for my Surface RT
text:
Hands down the best keyboard ever! I bought my Surface RT (don't laugh) over a year ago as a replacement for an old work computer that was blue-screening me every other day. I was told I needed more RAM or something which would require a lengthy trip to the computer hospital and I have a hectic schedule, just no time for that. Anyhow, I bought the Surface RT and it didn't come with a keyboard. Someone I knew had an extra so I had been using that one. I should have just splurged and spent the $35 to get this Type Cover 2. This thing is brilliant!

The keys are sharp and easy to feel as you're pressing them. Whatever model keyboard I had before for my Surface had keys that didn't quite go down as far as these. This feels really amazing on my fingers. Keys are super responsive and I definitely like the sensation that I'm using springy new keys. Hand me down keyboards are the worst. Actually after that hand me down keyboard died, I "borrowed" a keyboard off a Surface Pro at my office and was using that. It was too big for my RT but fit fine as a sub until this new keyboard arrived. Keys on the Surface Pro keyboard are not as nice feeling as the Type Cover 2 in my humble opinion.

Another great thing about this one is the backlighting. My other keyboard also had backlighting so this is not new to me but I'm literally in the dark right now sitting by a fireplace writing this review and it's great to be able to see all the keys. Once I stop to think about what I'm going to type next, it fades to dark for a second but as soon as I start moving my fingers it lights up. Great energy saving feature!

All in all, super happy with this keyboard. And I should write a separate review for my Surface RT which is also turning out to be the best computer I've ever had. Great for work and super portable! A+'s all around. Thank you, Microsoft!

text:

After that I upgraded my OS from Windows 8 to 10 on a new drive and ran two different SSD benchmarks. Read was good (above 500 MB/s) but write was about 240. Googled it - it is a common problem even with the latest firmware. My Plextor drive has both read/write close to 500 even when configured as a second drive in a SATA caddy. I hope that Intel will do something to fix the issue. If it does will bump it up to 5 stars. Now only 3 stars - half of the advertised write speed only!
Upon further research I found out that this drive uses a Sandforce controller that has a slow write on uncompressed data. Compressed works as advertised (checked with the benchmark) but not all data can be compressed in a real usage scenario.

title: Chromebook R11: a great little laptop and so so tablet and tent
text:
I bought the 4gb version on eBay as a refurbished unit. It only cost around $200 and had a single issue which made me learn even a bit more about how Chrome does stuff. It was stuck on an OS revision three versions old so auto update would not. I had to restore it from my other Chromebook, an Acer Chromebook 14. Once having done that, all my apps and even my smart lock using my Nexus 6p was restored although the smart lock thing took one additional step of disabling and then enabling to make it work. Here are some findings of the 4gb model.

The size and form factor is perfect for use while binging on beer or Netflix. It sits very comfortably and seems to be just the right size for this type of use. Since its a chromebook and many come in at the 11 to 13 inch screen size, its something to accept as a normal size.

Speed and use to me is quite good. It operates with a number of tabs and a few apps open and does the normal stuff like play Play Music, Youtube, etc without stuttering or anything. It seems snappy when opening up new tabs or windows. Feedly works quite nicely on it.

Tablet and tent use could be better hence the 4 stars. Chrome just does not seem suited for tablet use yet. Perhaps when new laptops come out which support the Play Store, we will see enhancements to Chrome browser functionality when that happens. The main reason I got this was that the Acer Chromebook 14 is big! Big and beautiful but meant for a table at Starbucks. This convertible is better when I'm moving around. Folding it around is a mixed bag and I cannot really recommend the tablet form factor yet. It can be used and you may get some use out of it but I don't think the R11 can be used that way. I find the Surface Pro 3 to be just as frustrating in tablet mode though. I have one of those which used rarely.

We'll see when Google rolls out the Play Store integration in June what happens here with the R11. It seems difficult fo find the 4gb model except at Costco. Amazon only has the 2gb model. I don't think I would go there on a chromebook.

title: Great laptop for the price, some variations from listing though...
text:
Overall this is a great laptop, and great value for the price. “Refurbished” is important to keep in mind here as you may notice (as I have) that there are some minute & spiderweb-type scratches on the side and on top of the laptop housing. This of course does not affect performance, which is why we have the “refurbished” classification.

The speed is fantastic for what I do. Word processing, email, facebook, interwebbing, etc. Streaming Netflix is fast and flawless with great picture quality. There are some important notes however. Great speed aside, I did not exactly receive what was advertised.

1) The headline for this item states the processor is a 3520M 2.9GHz chip. From the Start menu, click on the gear-like “Settings” icon > click on “System” > click on “About” ...there I saw that the processor was stated as a 3720QM 2.6GHz chip. Like I said, the speed is great for me but your requirements may be different.

2) The RAM is stated as 8GB of DDR3, but this must be “built-in” ram. The “About” tab did in fact verify that that I have 8GB of ram, but as you can see from the photo I have posted that there is NO ram chip(s) in the memory slots. Interesting, to say the least.

3) Another spec that was promised but not delivered was 128GB SSD. When I checked the status of the harddrive on my EliteBook, I discovered 238GB of storage! That's right, I came out ahead in this department. So I'll take that every day of the week and twice on Sunday, of course.

As for the rest of the laptop, there are some minor issues that I had to rectify. The touchpad setup has some redundancies. From the listing photos you can see that there are 3 buttons along the top and bottom of the touch pad for a total of 6 buttons. I think the majority of us are used to only having two buttons – left and right click. The top and bottom buttons are mirrors of each other – both left top and bottom buttons are your main selection tools, both right top and bottom buttons bring up click options, and the center buttons are a variation on if you were to have a clickable wheel feature on a peripheral mouse. It seems the top and bottom are only set up for user preference to click in front or behind the touch pad; it would have been nice if one could assign a different function/shortcut to the unused buttons. The touch pad itself requires some getting used to. I feel as though sometimes I have been needing to click twice on an object, compared to only clicking once on my previous laptop. Clicking into a new/different window for Explorer takes some getting use to. There are some touchpad sensitivity settings that you can fiddle with, and so, your mileage may vary.

And lastly, audio is not great out of the box. I am not an audiophile and do not require my laptop to deliver performance in that category. But even to my amateur ears, I notice something was off. Netflix and songs did not sound as crisp as they did on my previous laptop. Go to the “Controls SRS Audio Settings” icon in bottom right and mess with the settings for a needed improvement.

Overall, I'm keeping this laptop. I'm happy with this laptop. And for the processing power, the price is right. I do not have any buyers remorse.

title: Good sound, poor interface.
text:
Picked this up after I reading a few reviews. I decided to give it a go over another television manufacturer's soundbar/subwoofer combo. After researching the Vizio, I decided to take a gamble.
I'm glad I did.
I experienced the other soundbar in person after I got this. And, while the other was okay, the satellite speakers/subwoofer just blew it out of the water.
The vizio gives great surround and multiple input options. I've had it a few days and I've been running it through the paces. So far, it has exceeded my expectations.
I've run it through optical cables, bluetooth pairing, HDMI ARC, 3.5 to RCA, and 3.5 direct.
I would avoid 3.5 direct and just leave the included 3.5 to RCA plugged in in case you ever want to utilize that method. I have the 3.5 to RCA plugged in and ready for friends that want to play music through their phones.
I noticed a very slight optical delay, but the HDMI ARC is basically flawless on my Samsung TV.
Bluetooth can fade in and out a bit, especially initially, but I was walking around while streaming from my phone.
MP3 using USB does not work at all, but this is already specified in the literature. Doesn't hurt to try, though.

The bad:
If this had an LCD display, this would have been a 5 star review. As it is, there is an odd series of LED "dots" that give the readout. By this, I mean: "Two bottom dots, then two unlit dots, then two lit dots above the unlit indicate that you are in XYZ mode." Sound confusing? It is. I have no idea what I'm doing or what mode I'm in half the time. A simple LCD that says: BT/ AUX1/HDMI/BASS/VOL etc would have made this considerably more user friendly. Sure, if you look at the no-backlight remote in good lighting, you can see what mode you are in. But if you're watching a movie with the lights down or using a third party universal remote? Forget it. And chances are: if you're using DVD/Blu-Ray/TV/cable/DVI/Sound System/Game consoles all at once... you're probably using a universal.

End thoughts:
It's a good system at a fair price. (EDIT: I PICKED THIS UP FOR ~200. THE PRICE WAS ~$230 RETAIL AT THE TIME. I WOULD NOT PAY MORE THAN $250 FOR THIS PRODUCT) The inputs give good versatility, but utilizing the device can be difficult without the manual close at hand at all times.

title: I was pleased with these
text:
I bought two of these for ~$240.

Initially, I was pleased with these, but I became progressively more dissatisfied with them that I was compelled to return them - and I am grateful that Amazon facilitated free return shipping.

Sound quality is okay - if you're looking for bass, look elsewhere. These speakers do not feature passive bass radiators (something that is necessary to get deeper bass). If you like this size of speaker, I'd recommend the JBL Flip series.

Battery life - this is what really upset me the most. Logitech rates these speakers at "up to 15 hours *depending on volume and content". Okay, fine, I figured at half volume this would be achievable. However, I played these speakers in unison at ~75% volume and to my dismay, the first speaker powered off due to low battery in less than 4 hours!!! That's not even a third of what they advertise!!! I spoke with Logitech support via phone and they wanted me to perform a factory reset, which I declined to perform because I'm pretty technically savvy and I knew that this was no software problem. The second battery read at a level of about 40%, which extrapolation forecasts it would last 6 hours, still under half of the advertised battery life...

The only reason I'm giving this two stars is because of the 'surround sound' aspect of these speakers, however, it is not "360 degree sound" as advertised - it's really only 180 degrees.

Update:
I was originally going to give this speaker 2 stars, but there are just much better options out there for the money.

I upgraded to the JBL Xtreme, which I was fortunate to have gotten under $240 on sale here on the great Amazon. Worlds better in sound quality and battery life. I've gotten numerous compliments on the sound quality, and this thing gets many times louder than the two UE Booms combined. I played the JBL Xtreme at about half volume during an afternoon (4 hours) of disc golf and the battery life indicator did not lose one light (there are five).

All in all, take it from someone who tried to like these buy buying two, but was consequently let down in the end. Spend your hard earned money elsewhere.

The only reason why I knocked off a star is that as others have said the groove that holds the ipad upright is so shallow that I end up using the top row of the keyboard to do so instead. If I were to make a suggestion on how to better this awesome product I would highly suggest making the ipad holder magnetic and thus detachable as well, because when I'm not doing homework I like to Pinterest and holding the whole case for that purpose, even without the keyboard, is a bit cumbersome and I usually end up pulling the ipad out of the holder.
