title: Exceptionally Crisp and Detailed 4K Images and Excellent Color. Super Fast 1 Millisecond Response Time for Gaming.
text:
This is my first BenQ monitor. I’ve been tempted to purchase one for many years, but I just wasn’t familiar enough with this brand to make a major purchase. Now I can see it is probably the best 4K monitor I have, except for being the smallest one I own. The diagonal panel dimension is 27.9 inches and the resolution is 3840 X 2160 with a 16:9 ratio. That puts a lot of detail in a relatively small area. The text is exceptionally crisp and easy to read even if the font looks quite small at 4K resolution. I have three other 4K monitors: Dell UltraSharp 34 inch, Asus 32 inch and a Philips 40 inch monitor. I learned that the 40-inch monitor was too big and bright and gave me bad headaches, virtually blinding. I am trying to sell it now even though it works perfectly. So I decided 32 to 34-inch monitors were optimum for desktop monitors. But the more I use this BenQ 28 inch monitor, the more I realize it is also a very good size. I can bring it closer to me and it offsets the font size being so small. So on a shallow desk, it is an ideal size. Everything has exceptionally crisp detail at the 4K resolution which equals 4 times the resolution of an HD monitor or television.

This is also my first TN panel type. I did not know anything about it until now. The main upside is the ultrafast 1 msec response time which is ideal for gaming. I am not a gamer, even though it is very tempting with today’s fast overclocked computers and super fast monitors like this BenQ monitor. I am approaching 74 years old and I don’t want to be wasting what little time I have remaining on earth playing games. My wife is much younger, so maybe she will waste some of her time gaming.

Compared to an IPS panel, a TN panel doesn’t have such a great viewing angle. However, if you are the only person using it at a time, this doesn’t matter. You will be looking at it dead center where it looks perfect. I’ve noticed that if I walk toward my desk from the side, the monitor face is obviously at an extreme angle as I approach it and the white background has a noticeable yellow color. Even if you are not thinking about it, you will notice it. It is not what you are expecting. But when I sit down directly in front of the TN monitor, it is bright white and colors are excellent just like an IPS display panel. Other colors on the monitor also change shades and appear a little faded at extreme angle viewing. I am the only person who uses the monitor, so all this extreme angle viewing is of no consequence. If two people are seated next to each other in front of the monitor, they will be able to see the background white color start to appear as a faint yellow color, but not a lot until you get to a much wider viewing angle. However, the response time is so much better than any IPS panel if you are really into some fast action gaming.

This display has a highly desirable feature called High Dynamic Range (HDR), but it is emulated and not hardware based. The point of HDR is to have deep blacks and bright whites if they are present in the source video without it being washing out or blended together. However, you cannot create something out of nothing. If the source video is not HDR, then the dark shades of blacks will probably blend together and the near bright whites will do the same. However, if there is some differentiation still apparent in the dark black and bright white scenes, the HDR function will help pull them out of the background so you can differentiate the hidden person or scene in the dark background. There are currently five versions of HDR on the market or in development. You have probably experienced this when taking a photo or video of a person in front of a bright window. Their face will appear quite dark because the bright window fools the camera sensor into believing it needs to close the aperture. When you do this, you may be able to see the blinds over the window, but the person’s face will be so dark you can’t recognize them. Our brain knows how to ignore the bright light while taking the photo, but not afterward. Some highly advanced cameras will take upwards to 10 different exposures and then blend the images to bring out the person’s face and tone down the light from the window – similar to what our brain manages to do through experience.

The main versions are HDR10, HDR10+ and a proprietary Dolby Vision. BenQ has another feature called Brightness Intelligence Plus Technology, which they abbreviate as QI. You can cycle through four combinations of HDR and QI by sequentially pressing a front panel button on the lower right-hand side. These four modes balance the maximum contrast and what they call vibrancy to optimize HDR performance. It automatically adjusts the brightness in abrupt steps as a function of the amount of ambient lighting. I saw it change brightness automatically after sunrise today.

There are one white power button and 5 other buttons underneath the right side to set up the monitor including HDR and BI. Some of the buttons will override the front panel button for HDR and QI. It is not all intuitive in my opinion, but no monitor I’ve ever used has been intuitive. I downloaded the manual, but I have yet to get any motivation to read about all the control buttons underneath the front panel. I wish they would put some abbreviations on the lower bezel to designate where the buttons are and what they do. On the other side are two HDMI inputs and one Display Port input. I am using the Display Port input with a cable to my desktop computer. I am using the video output from my Intel i7 4790K Computer Processor. It is so good, I do not need a separate video card.

Then there is the blue light technology, which I personally dislike on all monitors. However, at least BenQ gives you several choices of blue light reduction. All the other monitors are just on and off. The other brands just look horrible with blue light reduction. A better description is Very Low Contrast and Extremely Faded Image. Maybe there is a lot less blue light, but it is so difficult to read, you will turn off the monitor resulting in no light at all. In comparison, BenQ has reasonable steps of blue light reduction, especially the reading mode. It will probably prevent some headaches if you plan to be reading a lot of text at one time. However, it’s not convenient to fumble through a menu just to get the monitor back to the way you normally use it. I don’t think I will ever use blue light reduction for that very reason. But the front panel button for HDR is mostly the way I want it. The maximum number of times you need to press the button to get the HDR and BI combination the way you prefer it is four times and then stop pressing the button.

The image quality of this BenQ monitor is absolutely superb. It is a very good size for a small depth desk area. I’ve been viewing it for hours and no headache. I frequently get headaches with the other monitors. My 40-inch 4K monitor is so large, it emits a blinding amount of light. This 28-inch screen size is smaller and doesn’t generate a blinding amount of light. Until I purchased the 40-inch monitor, it never occurred to me how much bright light it would emit. It was expensive, so I tortured myself for almost a year before I gave up and bought a 32-inch monitor. What a difference it made in headache reduction. And going from 32 to 28 inches, I expect it will reduce my eye strain and headaches even further. Bigger is not always better.

title: Awful Vizio customer service
text:
I purchased this unit two weeks ago. After my experience with Vizio customer service it is going back and I'm purchasing a different 4k tv. My previous TV was a Samsung Plasma 60' which developed vertical lines after 18 months. Given how Samsung took a "too bad for you" stance for repairing the plasma - I decided to replace it with the Vizio m65 based on the reviews here. After setting up the unit and watching a few shows...a glaze or haze would show on the screen - not there all the time but enough to make me wonder if there was an issue. I opened a ticket with Vizio and they asked for pictures (see attached). The pictures of the Star Wars dvd were deemed a possible problem so more pics were requested. The other two pics were from my directv input. The problem I had is parts of the pictures look ok, but the background haze/lack of detail was upsetting and not what I was used to with plasma.

When I reached out to Vizio after the second set of pictures I submitted - I got a different person. He looked over the pictures and thought everything looked great and didn't know what my problem was. I told them my problem is the picture on my new $1500 tv is worse than my broken plasma tv. Is there anything that can be done via settings or perhaps a new unit to take care of the background fog. Again, the answer was that the pictures looked great to him and he didn't see a problem. He then had the nerve to ask me if there was anything else he could do for me.

Vizio made it clear to me that 1) They make an inconsistent product with some truly awful pictures which apparently is what they expect and 2) Their support will say whatever they have to in order to get you off the phone and close your case.

Maybe you will be lucky and get one of the units that work - i only got insulted and told I had to accept what I had.

title: Great performance for the price.
text:
Great performance for the price, a nice upgrade over the previous Evo Select, and a huge upgrade over last year's Evo +.

The U3 64 GB card is rated at up to 100 MB/s read, 60 MB/s write. I benchmarked it at 92 read, 70 write, and observed sustained 65 MB/s write speed in use, which is fantastic as the read speed is already fast enough and it's the write speed that's important. There are certainly faster cards out there, but they're also twice the price.

This is a marked improvement in write speed over the previous U1 Evo Select (26-56 MB/s write, large sample variance), and a huge write speed upgrade over last year's Evo + (80 MB/s read, 18 MB/s write).

The only negative I see to the U3 Evo Select is that the random read performance is down to ~5 MB/s from ~8 MB/s of the previous U1 Evo Select, which decreases the card's read IOPS - relevant if used for the OS in a Raspberry Pi.

As always, buy direct from Amazon and/or test the card to make sure it's legit. You may need to re-format the card after doing the test.

If you are using this card for a Nintendo 3DS, you will need to re-format it to Fat32.

For the utilities I used to test and format, please see the comments.

title: Easy Installation, Fast Speeds
text:
So I moved into an old house with really thick walls, and of course my PC is on the opposite end from the modem/router downstairs. As such, my WiFi connection left a lot to be desired. I looked for different solutions, ran across this and figured it was worth a try. Boy was it. Installation could not possibly be any easier. Ethernet cable from the downstairs modem to one device, plug that device into a wall outlet. Go upstairs, plug the other unit into the nearest wall outlet, then an ethernet cable from it to another router I had, hit the pair button on both devices: we're a go!

The speed is amazing and now I have a fresh WiFi source upstairs, as well as the ability to hardwire devices to the router up here. I'd definitely suggest this over a WiFi extender in almost every case, since there are always tricky spots in the air, but your home has electrical cables everywhere.

title: Works well with digital landline
text:
This is a product category that doesn't get a lot of attention anymore. There are new call blocker products being offered, but very few simple caller ID boxes. Not too surprising, given that most phones have integrated LCD displays these days. If someone could convince Panasonic that they should put an LED into their base units that would flash for missed calls and digital landline voice mails (stored by the phone company) I wouldn't need a separate caller ID box anymore.

There is a lot to like about this little box. It doesn't require batteries. You don't have to set a clock on it. It displays both the number and the name. The LED flashes green when there is a missed call, and red when there is voice mail waiting. (I really, really, like that feature.) It's very reasonably priced. title: Have my Doubts
text:
I figured I would try this since I needed a low profile antenna. First off this is very pricey. The Wilson magnetic mount with vertical antenna is 40% cheaper and this is just a simple plastic housing.
Upon install I accidentally broke it. My fault trying to put it in with a mallet lightly. Not the manufactures fault. But upon braking it I decided to look inside and low and behold a simple wire. No wire would loading like on normal antennas. So having a background in antennas somewhat I know the correct antenna for the duty. The higher the wavelength the shorter the antenna. So it’s a formula (Hz, wavelength and speed of light) to determine the antenna size. So for example a half wave antenna for a specific frequency may be 18” tall if the wave is 3ft tall. A quarter wave will be smaller and require more of the grounding plane to be effective.
So hanging a wire off the device can cause more issues than good. So judging by the tiny wire sticking out I cannot possible see how this can even be effective one bit. I would expect some sort of pc board antenna like what’s built into the phones and devices.

My conclusion aside from being overpriced is that this cannot possibly offer any performance benefits. I could be proven wrong but looking at the design it leads me to think not.

title: Fantastic value for this CPU and a great upgrade to run Windows 7!
text:
If you have an older computer and want to run Windows 7 like I did, then this CPU is for you. Windows 7 (and other new OS like Windows 10) will require quite a bit more of CPU horsepower. I have a Vostro 200 that will run Windows 7 just fine if you do a few upgrades like CPU, RAM, and a cheap SSD. I upgraded my Vostro from E4500 (2.2GHz 2M cache) to this E8500 which is 3.16Ghz 6M cache and the performance was night and day with Windows 7. Windows 7 used to stall for a few seconds especially with FireFox that is a CPU hog. If there are any Flash elements in webpages then the stalling pauses would be even worse. Not to get too technical, but running CPUs and memory close to 100% has a dramatic performance drop off towards the last 20%. This is because things starts domino effect as the CPU waits for the L1 cache or the RAM and then the RAM starts waiting for the CPU etc and you get into a situation where a computer's performance drops off exponentially towards the end.

This CPU is a 3.16GHz Dual Core CPU with 6M cache. The reason I didn't go to the E8600 for 3.33GHz is because of price. It was not worth paying the extra $$$ for 0.17GHz more with the same amount of L1 cache. Also, because I have an older motherboard, it will only take up to the E8600 and so I could not go to the Q6xxx series quad core CPUs. This is a LGA775 socket processor and supports 64-bit OS.

I upgraded the CPU after Windows 7 was already installed and Windows had no problem recognizing the CPU. It will ask to be rebooted several times as it updates the OS drivers.

Overall I am very satisfied with this CPU and this upgrade. For the record, I upgraded the CPU to E8500 ($16.75), the RAM to 5GB ($30), and a new SanDisk 120GB SSD ($42) for a total of ~$89. Beats paying for a new PC and honestly, Windows 7 runs just fine for almost all use cases and I prefer Windows 7 over any of the later operating systems. Of course this isn't a config for gaming PCs but for web surfing, movie streaming and checking email, these specs are just fine.

Gets very cold. If you size the packs to drinks well you can actually get the drinks frosty without any additional ice.
Fits well in my RTIC 65 cooler, and Pelican 65.
Usually mix in ice with it to make the ice last longer.
Been able to make an entire 6 day camping trip without having to get additional ice.
If you use only the freezer packs, then food can stay dry.

CONs:
Assembly required. (but helps keep cost down)
Due to the foil type material, have a few concerns with the durability.
Also due to the material, it is a bit clunky. Meaning, seems that the edges and the heat seal lip are always needing to bend. Have poked myself with them several time unintentionally and it's a nuisance. Seems to me after enough bends it may puncture. B/c of the foil type material it takes damage. Must be careful. Can't be rough with it like your old hard blue freezer packs.
I wish they could put them in different packaging for the gel. Not sure why the foil is necessary. Maybe due to the better cold transfer, who knows.
I would not recommend them for softpack coolers like the YETI hopper or the RTIC softpak coolers, but would recommend them for high end coolers especially with ice.

Great product, but could use a little improvement.

title: Still a nice graphics tablet in 2016
text:
I know this isn't a perfect, new product, but I've had it for 1 day and I'm satisfied with it. It might be a little better than I was expecting. It's pretty big. I like the big drawing surface but I wouldn't mind getting rid of all the extra, blank space around the edges. That would cut about 3-4 inches off the size.

PROS:
* Customizable buttons: Some of them are out of date or applications I'd never use, like MSN or Excel, but you can change their paths which is nice. I changed them and then put a little piece of tape over them--the pen WILL write through tape and paper--with a new label. I included a picture of what I did.

* Feel: It really does feel like writing on a piece of paper. You have to press a little harder than I thought to create thick lines, but I've made sure pressing hard won't damage the surface and I'll get used to it.

* Pen: It's a sturdy pen and when held the right way, the buttons on it are extremely helpful for scrolling. I've found that it can really replace the mouse as long as you practice using it and adjust the screen size.

* Drawing: The reason we're all here! I don't think I could be happier with the actual performance of this tablet. For reference, I'm a digital artist who regularly draws detailed images. I use Photoshop, Illustrator, Sketchbook, and a few other programs. Until I bought this I was doing most of my digital art on my Samsung tablet with an S-Pen, which if you've used one, you know is very precise and high quality. This pen is much thicker which isn't a draw back, simply something I need to adjust to. I find this just as accurate as drawing on my Tab!

CONS:

* Pen: I like the pen itself, but putting the battery in was a hassle and I thought I was going to break the whole thing. It's set up very oddly, and might give me trouble in the future.

* Button delay: It isn't every time I push one of the left-hand buttons, and it isn't that long of a delay, but it's still there. Not a big deal, but something to be aware of.

There are no other cons. I'm pleased with this product and would recommend it to someone looking for an affordable graphics tablet.

title: There's a reason why both sizes are typically ordered together...
text:
Without a definitive guide to selecting the correct size the FIRST time, you're likely going to have to take the Goldilocks approach to discovering which device fits best - unless you know you have small or very large hands.
I made the mistake of allowing one reviewer's opinion guide me to the wrong size: "...unless you have gorilla-sized hands, you should choose the small model."
Learn from my mistake...
The width across my fingers, where I grip the joystick, is around 3.75" - which happens to be 1/4 finger-width too large for the small model, and about 1/4 finger-width to small for the large model. In other words, 3.75 is about a tween size for these two models.
At 3.75" - I'm much better off with the large model:
I stack my pinkie, ring and index fingers on the base - allow a slight bit of space between my index and fore fingers - and support my thumb on the top of the joystick stem.

My search of the internet reveals that at least for the time being both XDA developers and Kinggo have given up on this model. There is no indication that Samsung will offer Marshmallow or higher for this device..

Because bootloader is locked the Samsung bloatware cannot be removed or moved to SD card leaving just 4GB usable memory. Most application cannot be moved to SD card.

Why would you want to upgrade to Marshmallow? Because with MM the SD card memory becomes seamless with the on board memory. Add 64GB sd card and you have a device with 72GB memory.

With the SM-T280 you will have a device which has 4GB usable memory. Data storage can be on SD card but most useful apps will not load from SD card and many apps will not offer to save their data on SD card. This leaves me with a device pretty much the same (a little faster) as my 2012 1st Gen Google Nexus 7 which this was to replace.

It is my fault that I did not research this issue more thoroughly. I had assumed that an unlocked device would be rootable even if Samsung did not offer an android OS upgrade. Hope this review is a warning to others. I don't think I can return it since I have opened it and it is not DOA. Perhaps I can donate it to some non profit that can use a device with so little memory.

Update: 10/13/2016
Apparently android OS 6 (marshmallow) has been released for this device but adoptable memory is disabled. So my review stands as originally posted. A one star review. Lots of bloatware + disabled adoptable memory + locked bootloader make this a tablet I cannot recommend.

title: Good compact usb powered travel charger for the NP-FZ100 battery.
text:
This seems to be a decent option for a compact USB powered travel charger. I found the charger less aggressive than the Sony A7RIII in camera charging except for a slightly higher charge rate between ~80 and ~90% battery capacity. This charger appears to be a safe inexpensive option for charging OEM batteries.

Below are the results from ad hoc tests of different chargers.

Testing method:
USB power provided by 5v 2.4a capable Anker USB charger(s).
Power draw monitored by a YZXstudio ZY1276 in line USB power meter.
Tests run multiple times with two new OEM Sony NP-FZ100 batteries. (Each battery had around 3 full charge cycles at the start of these tests.)

Kastar LCD Slim USB Charger (Item being reviewed.)

Total charge time for a fully exhausted battery until charge cycle complete: ~4.25 - 4.75 hours. (In camera battery meter showed 100% around 4:15 but continued charging the battery itself at a very low current.)
5.1v ~1000ma USB power draw between 0% and ~90 - 95% charge. (~4hrs)
5.1v ~0 to 400ma constantly varying current from ~90 - 95% until ~99.5 - 100%. (~+15 mins)
5.1v ~0 to 130ma constantly varying current for the last .5% charge or so. (+15 to 30 mins)

Notes:

Between ~90% charge (as reported by camera) and the end of the Kastar charge cycle, the current being drawn by the charger was constantly varying but progressively lower as the battery neared full charge.

4200+ma of current @ ~5.1v passed into the Kastar charger during a full charge cycle. (Keep in mind that only a portion of this 4200ma made it to the battery as usable power due to inefficiencies of the charger & charge process.)

Well after the Kastar charge cycle completed (via monitoring the usb power draw), the in-camera meter showed 100% charge but consumed an additional (nominal) ~40ma before the in-camera charger considered the battery fully charged. This is a strong indicator that this generic charger is not likely to over-charge OEM batteries.

Vivitar dual port USB charger: (Included in a bundle with my camera purchase. Looks identical to the DSTE DUB167 dual charger.)

Total charge time for fully exhausted battery until charge cycle complete: ~4.0 - 4.5 hours.
5.25v ~1300ma USB power draw up to ~80% charge.
5.25v ~1200ma from ~80% until ~90% charge.
5.25v ~700ma from ~90% until ~95% charge.
5.25v ~700ma down to ~32ma between ~95% and 100% charge. (Constant but progressively lower current draw until the end of charge cycle.)

Similar to the Kastar charger, once the Vivitar charge cycle was complete I moved the battery to the in-camera charger which drew another ~32ma or so before ending the in-camera charge cycle.

A7RIII f/w v2.0 in camera charging via the micro-USB port:

Total charge time for fully exhausted battery: ~3.5 - 4 hours.
5.1v ~1500ma USB power draw between 0% and ~75-80% charge.
5.1v ~600ma from ~75-80% until high ~9x%
5.1v ~290ma down to ~40ma for the last 1 - 2% or so of the charge cycle. (Constant but progressively lower current draw until the end of charge cycle.)

title: Its ok, usable and functional
text:
This is a nice compact camera. I am very impressed with the quality of the video it records. But there are some negative moments as well.
Pros:
- compact size
- has a metal frame, not plastic
- stable during high and low temperatures. Just have not tried it during our hottest summer month.
- it records nice quality videos during day time.
- pictures are usable too
- great function to save currently recorded video without been in accident yourself. This one is useful, when accident happened without your involvement. Those kind of videos are helpful when you were a witness and are willing to help someone else.
- cord is very long and more than enough to go around the dash board to hide it.
- cigarette lighter plug will stay in no matter what. Well made.
- cigarette lighter plug has additional USB input, which is a nice feature, so you can use it for cell phone charger
- great idea about connecting the mount to the power instead of camera itself. With this one you basically mount your camera and don't have to deal with the cord itself, it's already plugged in to the mount.
- box, that came with this camera is professionally made and looks like a high quality product.
- customer services is relatively responsive if you have any questions.

Cons:
- A lock on the mount, which also serves as power cord connector, fell apart at first use. It is easy to put it back together, but should of been made better for the price
- Suction cup is not holding well, I had to purchase suction cup buddy to make it work. That's additional $3-6.
- Video looks like you are watching through the fish eye. Kind of weird feeling.
- >>>>> !!! GPS function requires additional attachment purchased separately. This is a huge disqualifying minus!!! <<<<<
- Green lights are blue on the video. Most white lights are blue as well.
- No memory cards included.
- Camera comes with installed system which is not upgraded to the latest available. After reading many feedbacks about camera failing as the result of updates, I decided not to play with it at all. Will rather use it as is as it is usable.
- Night video recording is not so good. You can see some cars, some objects, but car numbers, colors and most other details are not visible in most cases. In case of the accident this video will help only to see who is at fault. And if it's not you, I doubt that insurance or police will be able to find the other one involved, if they diapered from the place, especially if you are going to use it during night time to record movements around your car.
- This camera is ok for $80-120, but not for $199.

As the result: for the front I decided to use an other dash camera because this one has a lower quality of the night time video than it's competitor. But this one will be used as the camera facing the back of my car, to record all the cars behind my vehicle. It is great for that!

Took about an hour to get used to the DXT mouse. At first it felt different, and I was skeptical. But after an hour I just about forgot I was using a mouse! It was that comfortable. I've been using it for two months now, and don't plan on looking back. Battery life lasts about a month for me with lots of use, and a light will let you know when it gets low to recharge it. Takes 2 hours for a full charge and you can use it while charging it with the cable. Originally I wished it had replaceable batteries, but now I don't mind.

Prior to using this mouse, I had been using the Logitech M705 for many years (my favorite 'standard mouse'). After repeatedly suffering from carpel tunnel, I started looking for something better. I tried several other ergonomic mice including the Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Mouse, and the Anker Vertical Mouse. But both were worse than the Logitech M705. A good mouse should keep your thumb and index finger close together, and be small enough to let your fingers do precise movements without entirely relying on arm movements. The Microsoft and Anker mice failed on these 2 important points, even for my larger than average male hands. The Anker also had stiff buttons, which is not good for carpel tunnel.

title: Woah.
text:
[[VIDEOID:be3368cc94fdc195ff4d351255887db9]] [[VIDEOID:8136c34fbfd509cd4298d71195a78c68]] This review is for the [[ASIN:B01IDJ5U40 Jelly Comb Mechanical "Gaming" TKL Keyboard - Blue switch]]. NOTE: It does not have an official name, and they have two TKL mechanical keyboards. This is for the one with "gaming" on its name, currently

TL;DR │ At it's current price, you cannot go wrong at all. Better materials than leading $100+ keyboards. I will review this at its current price, at approximately equal to $32. I am still stoked by how much of a bargain this is. So much good stuff in here that makes me think negatively of mainstream brand names.

CONTENTS: Intro │ What I Like │ What I Don't Like │ Package │ Notes │ Verdict

- - - - -

Ah yes, another keyboard. The list of mechanical keyboards I have tried is as follows: Roccat Ryos MK Pro - Cherry MX Brown ($170), Corsair K95 - Cherry MX Brown ($190), CM Storm QuickFire TK - Cherry MX Blue ($80), Redragon K555 - Outemu Blue ($90), Redragon K551 - Outemu "Purple" ($100). That is the list in order of when I bought them. I started with brand names, with Cherry MX switches, and gradually changed to "cheaper" keyboards, then-unknown brands, and non Cherry MX switches. And now this.... $32 with a a switch I haven't heard before (Long Hua Blue⁽ⁿ⁰⁾).

So what do I think about it? It is now my primary office keyboard. My Roccat and CM? In storage. Corsair? Sent it back to them. I now use at home the K555 while the K551, I only use to salvage keycaps (The Redragons, as well as this keyboard uses superior keycaps than those expensive name brand keyboards).

WHAT I LIKE │ + │
+ Nylon braided cable. Yes, this is important to me.
+ Included and storable on-board keycap puller.⁽ⁿ¹⁾
+ Usable keyboard cover!!!⁽ⁿ²⁾
+ Cable routing channels.⁽ⁿ³⁾
+ Disable keyboard Button! (Fn key)⁽ⁿ⁴⁾
+ LED On/Off Button! (Fn key)⁽ⁿ⁴⁾
+ Little details, like the USB plug and USB cover
+ OMFG $32 ???!
+ I love that they did not use yellow LED. I hate yellow.
+ What looks like doubleshot injection keycaps. Nooice!⁽ⁿ⁵⁾

WHAT I DON'T LIKE│ × │
× Non-removable cable⁽ⁿ⁶⁾
× Non-RGB lighting⁽ⁿ⁷⁾
× Yellow keycap puller, which is irreplaceable.⁽ⁿ¹⁾
× This particular silver paint and branding. Makes it look cheap.

PACKAGE │ ✓ │
✓ Plain brown box without branding⁽ⁿ⁸⁾
✓ Foam package wrap
✓ Keyboard cover
✓ Keyboard
✓ Keycap puller
✓ Printed materials

- - - - -

NOTES

⁽ⁿ⁰⁾LONG HUA Blue???
▶ After having used Cherry MX Blue, and Outemu Blue, I feel like these Long Hua Blue is closer to Cherry MX Green (75-80 grams). I haven't done an official nickel test yet (maybe in a review update), but these switches are heavier than the Outemu Blue (60-70 grams), which are a tiny bit heavier than the Cherry MX Blue (55-60 grams).

Do note that the weight of Outemu Blue varies. My Redragon is heavy, kind of like this keyboard. However, my [[ASIN:B01E8U8HKW Jelly Comb mechanical numpad (which by the way is also an unbelievable steal at $16)]] is lighter.

I did find info on the internet that says it is 50 to 70 grams. I am leaning towards the heaviest 70g for this particular keyboard. It could also just be that it actuates light, but bottoms out heavier. It sure does feel heavy, and I like it. One more thing I like about the switches in this keyboard is that they are clear, which helps spread the light around.
···

⁽ⁿ¹⁾Key cap puller is installable at the back or the keyboard for storage. Note that it uses a "proprietary" clip to connect to the keyboard.
⁽ⁿ²⁾There's a plastic keyboard cover. Call it what you like but I use it as dust cover. The only other keyboard I had that came with it was my Roccat.
⁽ⁿ³⁾You can route the cable exit at the left, center or right. Only other keyboard I had that has this function is my Cooler Master.
⁽ⁿ⁴⁾There are function keys for LED off and keyboard disable. I cannot stress how much this is important to me.
⁽ⁿ⁵⁾This is the reason why I like these "cheap" keyboards. For some baffling reason, expensive brand name keyboards only use inferior keycaps. It boggles the mind!
⁽ⁿ⁶⁾This is a feature that I like. However, since this already have superior cable, I do not see myself replacing it.
⁽ⁿ⁷⁾The lighting is as per line. From top to bottom: White, Red, Orange, Green, Blue, Purple. I love that at least it uses orange and real purple lights, unlike my Redragron RGB keyboards that produce pinkish and yellow lights only (by mixing colors). Also, the white is like "real" white, not RGB white.
⁽ⁿ⁸⁾The keyboard came in an unbranded yellow brown box. I guess that helps keep the price down.

- - - - -

VERDICT: I highly recommend this product.
★★★★★ | 5 stars out of 5. Usually, I give 4 for a great product with the 5th star reserved for cool surprises. Well, the inclusion of the keyboard dust cover, the little details, and the very useful Fn key functions make it more that deserving of that 5th star. Kudos!

Questions? Hit the comments!

This review is for the [[ASIN:B01IDJ5U40 Jelly Comb Mechanical "Gaming" TKL Keyboard - Blue switch]].

title: WH14NS40, so far so good
text:
Just got this installed minutes ago. Easy as usual, detach the sata and power cable from behind, unhook the latch that's built into my case that holds optical drives in place, slide old drive out, slide new drive in, reattach power and sata cable, secure locking latch. My previous model, WH16NS40 lasted me about four years, so I can't complain about it much. I used it to rip countless DVDs, but I only watched about a dozen blu-ray movies with it, which is what actually failed. It would still see and play DVDs, but it stopped recognizing blu-ray discs all together, and that was my main purpose for buying it, to watch blu-rays while sitting at my pc.

As others have stated, you will need to buy or purchase additional software capable of playing blu-ray movies. Others have stated where to get it. I chose to buy PowerDVD 14, years ago. a word of caution. If you choose to buy it also (the newest version is PowerDVD 17 as of this writing) make sure you save a copy of the install and the registration key. They will only keep the download link on their website for a limited amount of time and you will not be able to download it again, even with proof of purchase and they will not reply to email. Luckily, I saved the install and registration key on an external drive, but enough about that.

I have owned countless DVD burners, as I suspect most people have. These things are not designed to last. I would say, with the exception of the last one, that I have had to buy about one a year, for the last, eh i don't know, 20 years? If you factor in the amount we have bought at work, (I work in IT) internal and external, it's been in the hundreds. Seeing as the return window is small on this, I plan to put this through it's paces and play one blu-ray a day for 30 days straight to see if it fails. If it does, I will update my review to reflect that. I should also note that the drive that is shown here on Amazon for is different than the one I received. I like the look of it better, but some may not. I'm including a picture of what it actually looks like, taken directly from the LG website.

title: The reviews are right -- this is a top notch residential wifi router
text:
I bought this (plus an Arris cable modem) to replace the integrated modem+wifi device for which Comcast was charging me $10 a month. I've installed maybe 15 wifi routers over the years. Almost all of them have been Linksys until now, but after having had good experience with TP-Link PowerLine adapters, I went for this because of the high ratings in the reviews. In addition to the cost, wifi from the Comcast wasn't reaching into our kitchen which is around a corner in a 2500 square foot condo laid out along a long hallway.

The Archer C5 installed very quickly. It comes with two preset SSIDs, one for 2.4 GHz and one for 4.8 GHz. Each SSID has a default password, an 8-digit code stamped on the bottom of the unit. So it's very easy to install it, set up mobile device with the default SSID. You just walk to any dead spots in your home to determine whether the Archer C5 provides better coverage than the router you're using. In my case, it definitely did. My iPad can connect and download at a reasonable speed from anywhere including the kitchen - a significant improvement over the wifi signal provided by the Comcast device. (You can change the SSID and the passcode easily using a web utility rather than having to type the DNS address -- a number like 192.168.1.1.)

title: Great ESP32 board with screen standoff
text:
Unlike some of the other ESP32 boards with screens attached flush to the printed circuit board, this board has the screen mounted on a translucent standoff which is proud of the board by 0.2". This is very nice for packaging into a bigger project - the board can be mounted inside of a project case with the screen mounted flush to the outside of the case The boards with the screen mounted flush on the board have about the same height as the ESP32 package itself and are not as suitable to building into a case for a polished final product.

Note that you will need to solder the header pins on yourself. In my opinion this is not a bad thing as it allows you to mount them backwards or use a 90 degree header pin depending on your needs.

The example code on the board will scan for open wifi access points. It found mine and my neighbors with good signal strength. Additionally, there is a power connector on the back of the board. The connector type is Micro JST, and it's commonly used with small RC airplanes and helicopters. A quick Amazon search will give you a number of battery options. Given how flush the connector is to the board, you will likely need a pigtail to make the connection.

title: Beautiful and functional, but weak on several fronts
text:
This is a fantastic camera on many levels and really excellent overall. But I deducted stars for several reasons and ultimately am returning it. I am not a "Nikon guy" but I do currently use a D750 which is really a phenomenal camera. Unfortunately, it is also heavy. With a 24-70 lens attached, it is quite a whopper to sling around your shoulder. The whole point of getting the Sony A7II was to get the photo quality of the Nikon in a nice small and light package. I also have a Sony a99 with Zeiss 24-70 and I am absolutely in love with it. But, it too is a giant unwieldy beast. So I figured the A7II would be the best of all worlds.....wrong:

What I love about the A7II
I could rehash all the details and statistics about this camera which can be found online, but I think these reviews are more useful when you put it into perspective of a real person. So to put it in perspective, I take a lot of indoor shots and lots of pictures of fast-moving kids and pets. I am VERY picky about good focus, fast camera operation and ease of use. So here is what the A7II did right for me:
+ Beautiful - I think it is a gorgeous camera, and with a 55mm f1.8, it could be in a museum of modern art.
+ Phenomenal focus accuracy - as with all mirrorless cameras that focus primarily with contrast-detection, *WHEN* the Sony gets focus, it get's it dead-on, tack sharp and perfect.
+ Nice video - Unlike DSRs that focus during video by clanking in and out trying to keep focus, the Sony works just like a camcorder: smooth and quiet.
+ Nice electronic viewfinder. Some love EVFs, some hate them. I love them. The picture is bright and it shows you a lot of information you could not see in a DSLR viewfinder like a real-time histogram, the actual white balance the camera is about to capture and an immediate review of the picture you just took right in the viewfinder. Many times, you can see things in the EVF you could not see in an optical viewfinder, especially when the room is dark.
+ The camera and lens is lighter and more compact than any DSLR that I am aware of (in this category of cameras).
+ Built in steady shot is nice

What I didn't like:
- It is still heavy!! It is not exactly a pocket camera, and when you put a 24-70mm lens on it, this things is not exactly lightweight either. With the latter lens, it is about 2 lb 5oz while my D750 with 24-70mm lens is 3lb 15oz. Big difference, yes. But the Sony is far from being a feather around your neck.
- The auto-focus system is accurate when it actually focuses. But it is primarily contrast detection (CD) in bright light (with some phase detection) and totally CD after about f8 and in low light. So, like all CD focusing methods, it is slower than phase detection. This is maddening when you are trying to capture spontaneous moments or fast moving action. In low light, you might as well be taking pictures of statues in a museum, because if your subject moves at all, you will either get soft focus or be out of focus completely. This is 90% of the reason I gave up on the A7II. Sony also has an "Eye AF" which will focus on a subjects eye. Again, when it finds the spot to focus on and does it, the results are perfect. But if your subject is moving or it's a bit darker, forget about it. You will miss half your shots and start yelling at the camera (at least that's what I did).
- The battery life is horrendous. This has been griped about extensively online, but it's true. It makes me feel insecure taking it on any meaningful trips without several extra batteries. No big deal right? But there's the weight again! You just added more weight to this seemingly lightweight package.
- You cannot get a native zoom lens from Sony faster than f4 for this camera. Yes, you can mount a giant lens on there from Nikon with an adapter, but there's the weight again! Why would I buy this camera that is supposed to be light and easy to carry and then strap on this giant contraption to make it do what I want? Forget it. And sorry, but f4 is not fast enough for indoor shots of people with ISO less than 6400. You also lose out on some bokeh there as well. This was the other major reason I decided to forget about this camera.
- Low light performance leaves much to be desired. I am comparing to a D750 which uses the same sensor and the D750 blows the Sony away. Look at the dpreview site and compare them. Once you get to ISO6400, the Nikon puts the A7II to shame. Also, Sony RAW files are compressed to 11-bit while the Nikon is lossless14-bit. So even if the low light performance on both was identical, you can pull a lot more information out of the Nikon for noise reduction and other improvements in post processing.

In summary: I bought this camera because I wanted a light and compact full frame sensor camera. What I got was a slow focusing, battery devouring and sluggish device which doesn't live up to it's potential...and with crippled RAW output and noisy low-light performance (compared to a comparable sensor in the D750) to boot! And all this doesn't come cheap! It is a beautiful camera though, and it's certainly smaller and lighter than the D750 or any Canon, for that matter. But for my purposes, taking higher ISO images indoors and of fast moving objects, the Sony just could not keep up and it doesn't hold a candle to the D750. I am sure mirrorless cameras are the future. There is little doubt about it in my mind, but that time is not here yet. At least not for me.

title: Draw size
text:
So, first thing's first.

I'm a beginner artist. I am mostly going towards 3D modeling specializing in character sculpting.
However, taking note from an artist I respect and admire, drawing is essential. So I thought, well might as well learn digital drawing as I'll need a tablet for sculpting.

So here I was, thinking what the best option would be.
Everywhere you go, the vast majority will recommend a Wacom for 'beginners'. I was going to go that route, but I saw that they were 70 - 90 Dollars ( at the time of writing this). That was a bit expensive, so one thing I took to account was the drawing space.

Wacom may be famous for their work in tablets, and huion might be the second choice for most. I for one, have fallen in love with the XP-PEN Deco 03 (who knows what happened to 02).

The draw space is huge. Especially compared the lesser expensive, yet famous, a tablet from Wacom ranging around 80 dollars.

The wheel?
I was skeptical at first...then after spending a whole day with it, I thought to myself, hell why isn't this implemented in most nonscreen tablets?

The buttons?
You can customize them to your liking.

The pressure?
Superb. 8 f*** thousand pressure sensitivity.

The pen?
it's wireless, fancy and comes with an intuitive pen holster that also sports replacement nibs.

The wireless?
It may be me, it may be the interference, it may be the tablet that I got....but it lacks in range.
I can get up to at least 3 ft without losing much response. However, there are times that the response in general just stops.

The wired (USB Type-C)?
It helps, it's long enough to be comfortable to hold the tablet like a sketchbook.

The weight?
Weighs a little less than a sketchbook.

The verdict?
If they can fix the wireless connection, this is by far worth the extra 20-30 dollars over an 'entry-level-beginner-tablet' that Wacom Offers and/or Huion.

I dare say that Wacom should be worried about this rising king.

title: Great device for traveling
text:
This little product is a gem for travelers who need a lot of connectivity options for different devices. If you spend a lot of time in hotels you'll know that not all hotel WiFi are equal. Some hotels will not allow you to use a ChromeCast or AppleTV on their WiFi because it needs to go thru a sign-in page. Some hotels also limit the amount of devices you can connect per account/rooms. You just need to connect your computer via wireless or Ethernet cable to the router and then connect the router to the hotel's WiFi or Ethernet (if available in your room) and then go to the sign-in page to log-in.

If you are going to use the hotel WiFi, you need to connect to the router first, then set it as a repeater and select the WiFi name you want to connect to. Once that's done, maybe your browser will trigger the hotel's log-in page, maybe it won't. No worries if it does not, you can manually trigger it yourself by going to this URL: www.msftconnecttest.com/redirect (save that in your favorites, it will always be useful as you can use it anytime you connect to a WiFi and the log-in webpage doesn't trigger).

It's really that easy. Also, once you've connected to the internet for the first time with the router, go to the Upgrade section and upgrade the device's firmware as to avoid version 3.003 because it had a bug with auto-reconnect to WiFi if it disconnects for some reason.

You don't need advanced knowledge of IT or networking to work the device as it is fairly simple.

I'm enjoying it thoroughly and I'm sure you will too.

title: Fantastically easy to use fitness tracker keeps me more active at the office.
text:
I work at a desk and purchased one of these to help me stay a little more active during my day. I had been considering the original VivoFit; although I wanted the VivoFit 2 it was a little out of my price range. I saw these refurbished models at a lower price and purchased one. The unit I received is an official Garmin-refurbished unit, and came with everything a new unit does. I don't know what on my unit needed refurbishment; it looked brand new. No wear or damage.

Setting it up was easy. I already had Garmin Connect on my laptop (because of a GPS), and just followed the instructions to add the VivoFit 2. I synchronize using the Ant+ dongle; I haven't tried bluetooth.

I went with the VivoFit 2 for the following reasons:

* I needed a simple unit that would monitor my activity, help me set goals, and encourage me to be active at regular periods during the day.

* I wanted something with replaceable batteries. I like to use something as long as possible, and am not comfortable with disposing of a device because, say, the lithium-ion batteries soldered into it have worn out.

* I wanted something with backlighting and something more than a visual reminder/prompter. The original VivoFit had neither.

Using the unit is easy. In the morning after getting up I synchronize it with my laptop and then go about my day. I'll either have the unit display the total number of steps I've taken, or the number of steps remaining until I reach my step goal for the day. After I've been inactive for a little while the VivoFit beeps quietly, reminding me to move about. When this happens I usually go for a quick stroll in my office building. When I reach my goal for the day, it beeps to let me know I've done so. In the evening I put it into sleep mode (hold the button until "Sleep" appears) and snooze.

The biggest benefit I've gained from the VivoFit 2 is it helps keep me aware of my need to be a little more active and fit. Because I wear it on my wrist, each time I see it I'm reminded to do things that are more beneficial to my health. When I'm at my office and need to do something (get some water or visit the rest room, for instance), I take the longer route--few extra steps means a little more exercise. The regular reminders to be active work: when the VivoFit beeps I get out for a few minutes.

I synchronize once a day. It's easy: I sit at my laptop, and with the Garmin Connect application running I press and hold the VivoFit's button until "Sync" appears. Release the button, and it communicates with the laptop. A few seconds and you're done. After synchronizing you can go to Garmin's web site and see your fitness statistics. I usually manually sync (meaning I have to push the button to start synchronization) but once the VivoFit surprised me with an automatic synchronization. I don't know what caused that.

There are a few annoyances with the VivoFit 2. Because this is intended to be worn on the wrist, it can pick up some arm movements as steps, artificially inflating the step count. It doesn't seem to be affected by things like working with my computer or other office tasks, but brushing my teeth really fools it and my step count increases significantly. I've placed the VivoFit it in my pocket before, and it seems to still work, so I guess that's one option. The band is very comfortable to wear (I wear it a little loose), but it's extremely annoying to remove. Every time I try to remove the band from my wrist I expect to hear a snapping sound and see broken pieces of band or the closure. I suppose the band's closure design is good for those people who are very active and never want to take the VivoFit off, but for someone like me who doesn't like to wear watches etc. in the shower, it's frustrating. I may go with an aftermarket band if I can find a nice one.

title: Great Solution for Reasonable Situations
text:
From the outset, I have to admit I have a predisposition for this manufacturer. I own several of their other products, most notably cases for a few of my point-and-shoot Canon cameras.

Like those other products, this case is a smart purchase if you have a clear sense of how it and the device it contains will be used. What I mean by that is you should be aware of the nature of your device and the context in which it's going to be transported.

What this case is NOT is a military-grade storage solution; don't expect to take a standard laptop out into the wilderness or to some gritty warehouse via a Vespa during a downpour and expect everything to be OK. Likewise, if you're inclined to fling your case around like so much excess lumber, this probably isn't the case for you if you want your expensive laptop to remain intact.

However, if you're taking your laptop to a coffeehouse or library via any means of transportation that doesn't involve exposure to the elements, this will work well. It will securely hold your laptop, using padded sides and a retention strap and will also hold a few accessories, pens, etc.

Transport is easy via a padded, built-in handle and a wide, comfortable shoulder strap. Well worth the pittance they're charging.

For people who need to use electronics, but want a little less EMF/less Bluetooth, having a way to enjoy the functionality of portable iOS devices with some buffer distance, this adaptor plus a keyboard is really nice.

title: DO NOT BUY! Unreliable device. Drops internet signal several times a day, even though ISP signal is OK
text:
DO NOT BUY THIS PRODUCT!

I bought the AC1600 C6250 unit back in February 2017 and it worked fine until about 3-4 months ago when I started noticing intermittent loss of internet signal throughout the day. I rotate for work overseas so I missed the fact that this problem was rather frequent. every time I came home, I thought it was a problem with Xfinity and they would fix it. Eventually it became obvious that the problem was not going away but by then my warranty had expired! What a coincidence that this starts happening right around the time the warranty expires??!!

I finally called Xfinity and they were able to establish that the problem appeared to be with the router//modem I have installed and recommended I contact NetGear.

After reading a number of reviews here and calling NG customer support, it turns out, there are appears to be a glitch with the firmware and NetGear is aware of it. NG customer support told me that they are quite sure that they know why the Modem is behaving this way, which I found rather strange. Based on reviews and comments on NG community forum and reviews here on Amazon, I learned that others have had the same problem, and to fix it, the unit needs to be either reset remotely by NG or the firmware needs to be downgraded. But NG chose to profit from this known problem and I was asked to pay $90 so they would fix it for me!

This is ridiculous. Why should customers pay to fix a known problem with the device such as this?? Why doesn't NG simply release an update that either fixes what's wrong with the current firmware, or reverts it to one that actually works, instead of trying to make money out this situation?

I'd give the unit a 5-star rating but the frustration of not having reliable internet makes me wish I would give zero stars if I could!

I WILL NEVER BUY NETGEAR PRODUCTS AGAIN!

title: Overhyped and Overheated
text:
There's this amazing thing about commentary on the internet. Many times, there's a snowball effect, and what often happens is that when something is reviewed as being good, you'll see other reviews of it being good, and then more and more. However, as the old saying goes, you can't always believe everything you read.

If you read critical reviews, these may be among the best reviewed speakers of the past 18 months. Based on these reviews, I bought a pair, without hearing them, and then auditioned them at home (along with a pair of the UniFi towers [which actually were pretty good] and a center channel [which was better than the bookshelves, but not exemplary]). After listening to these bookshelf speakers a little while, I compared them to an old pair of Mission bookshelf speakers (made in England) which had cost me substantially less.

I was astonished to hear a difference that was literally night and day, but not in the Elac's favor. Whatever advantage that these speakers may have had in "clarity," and "soundstage," etc., they give up in bass (this is much less of an issue in the floorstanding UniFis). The bookshelf UniFi speakers do not give much at all the low end and can sound very flat. The high end, and the mids are okay, but without the contrast of the bass, you are hearing half the sound and it becomes very apparent when you compare them to other speakers which do have the capability to produce some bass. After noticing this, I went back to the reviews and wondered whether they were the same speakers. Researching further, I noticed that this particular quality of the UniFi bookshelves is explicitly stated in some reviews, and in others it is intimated. It is not insignificant that many of the Top 10 lists do not include the UniFi Series, but instead, include the Debut B6 Series bookshelf speakers (which I have not heard and cannot comment on them) as they may produce better bass. There are also comments about the UniFi bookshelves' lack of bass on some audio enthusiast board postings. Thus, these speakers may sound nice with a good subwoofer and a carefully selected cut off frequency, but beware before buying (so you can avoid the hassle of packing them up for a return) as to their limitations. I am not an audiophile, but I do have a decent ear, but most importantly, speaker preference is very subjective. These may be good speakers "for the price" (a phrase you'll see in most of the reviews), but it may be worth spending a little more to get better speakers overall. I would strongly recommend auditioning them and not buying them exclusively based on other people's reviews and opinions.

Another tale of caveat emptor for these speakers. They are extraordinarily power hungry, as they have a rare combination of low impedance (4 ohm, when 8 ohm is standard) and demanding sensitivity. In my set up, I was using a Rotel RSX 1550 (a very good 5.1 AVR) to power five ELAC UniFis (2 towers, 2 bookshelfs and their massive center channel). After auditioning the speakers on two channels, over a few weeks, including these bookshelves, I decided to test out all of the Elac speakers on a 5.1 set up. After playing for about 8 minutes, the Rotel amplifier apparently went into something called protection mode. Not understanding what happened, I went and pressed the power button again and heard a sound and then saw smoke come out of the top of the Rotel. After this happened, I had the chance to speak to a retailer (as I am in the market for a new receiver) and he advised that many people have complained about these speakers causing their receivers to clip due to power demands. Needless to say, I boxed up all of the Elacs and returned them. After what happened, I really could not get them out of the house fast enough.

As with everything, you need to make your own decision about whether the sound quality of this speaker appeals to you and overshadows other potential issues or concerns. If someone runs into the same circumstance that I did, I do hope this post helps that person realize what is happening with their receiver and saves them the trouble that I am now going through. If you do decide to go ahead with these Elac speakers and are buying a new receiver along with them, make sure that the new receiver is "4 ohm stable." It is hard to find this information on websites, but a call to the retailer should help.

Best of luck with your shopping decision.

title: Mixed Feelings about the R-4B)
text:
I want to love this sound bar but wish I'd spent another hundred or so to get better functionality. Ya it's my fault that I cheaped out since this is only a temporary measure (I broke my leg and can't go to other areas of my house where my real sound systems are set up. I do believe u get what u pay for and I do understand this is the least expensive, entry-level model that Klipsch makes. I do know a little about sound systems my other two being a Yamaha 7.2 receiver, and an Onkyo 5.1 using a combination of floor standing and bookshelf Bose, Harmon Kardon, Onkyo, and Atlantic Technology speakers and subs.

What is really lacking on the R-4B is the ability to tailor the sound to the room and adjust it to find the sweet spot. There are no equalizers or adjustments other than volume +/- and Sub +/-. Mode buttons include virtual surround, voice enhance, and sleep (does nothing more than turn off the sub). Virtual surround makes it sound muffled so voice is the only mode button that makes a difference by itself. Turning on voice and surround at the same time is about the best solution. Only music videos and Bluetooth offer enough depth to really make the R-4B show off a little, but just a little. Unless u watch a lot of music videos, want to stream to the sound bar via Bluetooth, or listen at higher volumes, you should probably pass on this one.

title: Great speaker for normal use around water!  Great sound, too!
text:
First, the disclaimers...I'm a veteran, and as such, have an average 35% hearing loss. With that said, i loved the quality of the sound from this speaker! I take my waterproof bluetooth speakers kayak-surfing in 4'-6' seas in downwind conditions where I'm constantly flipping the boat. Having a 6' saltwater wave crash down on top of a waterproof bluetooth speaker is the ultimate above-and-beyond test of endurance.

Even with the issues, I gave this speaker 5-Stars, simply because few people will ever put this speaker through the rigors I did in such a hostile saltwater envirionment!

PLUSES: I loved the sound coming out of this speaker. I also loved the fool-proof physical case-design, making it easy to secure it to my Surfski Kayak. I surf downwind in anything from 3'-6' cross-off and cross-on wave conditions. The minimum time on the water is two-hours and will go up to and above six-hours. These runs are always in rough saltwater in a surfski, which is a narrow (20'x19") racing style kayak. Not once did the speaker come loose or shift because of its unique shape. The sound was phenomenal for a bluetooth speaker!

CONS:
I've had five "waterproof" bluetooth speakers with one going out in 3-days. The best speaker, prior to the Lansing iMW575, went out in 45-days. The Altec Lansing iMW575 lasted 173-days, which included 45-days of downwind and surfing conditions, 6-races, 41-days of training, and only 4-days of freshwater use. The speaker was rinsed after each use in saltwater, but as you all know, saltwater creeps into places freshwater can't because of the salt-crystals that result. Saltwater is also a natural electrolyte, adding to the issue of using electronics around saltwater. The only other complaint I had was the length of time the battery went dead. Understand, the battery actually lasted longer than the manufacturer said it would. I would like a bit longer battery life for those endurance days lasting >6hrs.

FINAL WORD: This speaker should last the "normal" person a long time! Even though it was covered under warranty, I didn't have the heart to claim it under warranty and simply bought another speaker. If I can have great music without reducing my already limited hearing with earbuds, for the cost of two of these speakers, it's a cheap fix in the end. That's how much I like these speakers. I truly believe nobody will ever come out with a saltwater-proof speaker for a price we are willing to pay, as the sea is the most hostile electronics environment on the planet!

title: High Quality, Easy To Set Up
text: I am writing this review to dispel the notion that this system is too complex to set up.  I actually purchased this back in March and I just got around to setting it up yesterday.  I simply pulled everything out of the box, connected the power supply to the DVR and to the cameras, connected the cameras to the DVR, connected the DVR to my router (Internet) with cat5 cable,  and I connected the DVR to a computer monitor.  The first thing I noticed was a helpful start up 'wizard' that automatically appeared on the monitor.  That process took about 5 minutes to complete.  Then I noticed that the cameras were all showing on the monitor.  (I did this in my living room.)  Then I downloaded the Amcrest View Pro apps on my smart phone and iPad.  I clicked on "add a device", and then 'P2P'.  It asked for my Amcrest password (that I set up on the wizard), and then it asked me to scan (using the app) the QR code that is on a sticker on top of the DVR.  All of a sudden I could see what the cameras were looking at on my devices (phone and iPad).  It was that easy.  The whole thing took 15 minutes.  My initial impression is that this is a quality system with a lot of complex capabilities.  Now that I have everything working I'm going to look at the manual (which I downloaded on my iPad because the little manual that came with the system was difficult to read) and learn all of the complexities.  Of course I also have to hang the cameras in their permanent location.  The cooling fan in the DVR is a little loud (and I did purchase the recommended replacement fan), but I'm going to install this system in an upstairs closet so I don't think it will matter.  I'll connect the system to the Internet using a WiFi 'bridge' or 'extender'.  I'll update this review once I've installed the cameras in their permanent locations (I'll use my phone or iPad to 'sight' them in), but I'm thinking that this is going to be an awesome surveillance system,  and I'm excited to permanently install it.  Now I wish I hadn't procrastinated so long.  I guess I had been intimidated by all of the reviews that to me implied that you had to be a computer engineer to get the thing up and running.  Trust me,  if I can do it, you can too.

title: Happiness = Speedy New Boot Drive
text:
I bought the 250 GB version of this drive to upgrade my existing system's boot drive. The original drive was 1 TB however it was very loud (it's a server-grade drive).

The drive came with the normal warranty paperwork, installation CD for Samsung Magician and Data Migration as well as a pictograph guide for setting up the drive in both desktops and laptops. Unless you have mounting screws on hand, you will need to purchase some as none were included. This is the same as the SATA and power cables (if you're using a modular power supply); you will need to either use what you have or purchase more.The installation guide is extremely simple and does not cover troubleshooting so beware! I did a fair bit of research to make sure that I had everything I needed. I happened to have mounting screws and extra cables so I was good there.

Another thing to keep in mind is the fact that this is a 2.5 inch drive; unless you have a mounting bracket to fit this form factor into a 3.5 inch bay, you will need to purchase one. If you're using this in laptop, be sure to read your paperwork to see if this drive is best for you and get any/all hardware you may need. If you're not planning on using it as an internal drive, then this is not a problem.

After installation, I booted up and configured the drive as a new volume and installed both Magician and Data Migration. To be fair, I was leery of using the stock migration software as I've read that a fair portion of people using it to transfer their OS were having trouble. I used MiniTool Partition Wizard's OS Migration Wizard (available at www.cnet.com) which was seamless. Keep in mind that this is my two cents; your mileage may vary.

Word of caution: Back up everything. I backed up my system on an external hard drive and copied all important data (pictures, documents, music, etc) again onto a flash drive. I could be paranoid however better safe than sorry.

After rebooting, I started Magician and enabled RAPID mode. Another reboot and presto! While my boot up time isn't all that improved, the entire system is much more responsive and snappy. Programs open quickly and painlessly. When moving through pictures I no longer have to wait for them to load. Opening Adobe Lightroom used to take up to a minute and now only takes about 4 seconds. Likewise opening my iTunes sometimes took almost a minute now opens and is ready in less than a second. My read and write speeds are both near the advertised maximums.

All-in-all, I've very happy with my new drive. Installation was easy and straightforward. I would purchase one of these again in a heartbeat. Below I put two links for a mounting bracket and screws. Remember: YMMV.

title: Size matters.
text:
I thought mice were pretty much interchangeable. I'd had many computers at work, all with corded mice, and never had an issue. The corded mouse on my home computer was failing, so I thought it would be better to replace it with a wireless mouse. I carefully compared sizes, selecting one close to the size of what I had.

This mouse works well, and I don't have any complaints about function. I like the off switch so I can save battery life. What I don't like is that the wheel takes twice the effort to roll, which can cause fatigue if you scroll a lot. I don't like the textured surface. The smooth surface of my old mouse felt better to my hand. I also don't like the size. It's only slightly smaller and not quite as "tall" as the mouse I had, so it fills only about half my palm. My hands are very small, so I thought a slightly smaller mouse would be OK. After 5 minutes of use, my wrist and little finger were aching. I know I can get used to it, and i will, but I liked my old corded mouse, that came with my Dell computer, much better. If I could have found an identical one, I would have bought it, but mouse design is constantly evolving.

Potential Issues...

There is any audio out port on the front of the dock, but not the back - great for headphones, but not wired speakers. No matter to me since the Surface 3 has built in speakers.

I have a USB cable coming out of the station to power the tablet. Sometimes it charges, sometimes it doesn't. I've tried the back USB 2.0 and front USB 3.0 jacks. I'd imagine this has something to do with how much power the dock can actually produce at a time, or it might be something screwy with the tablet's charging circuitry (it recognizes that it is plugged in, it just doesn't actually charge all the time). However, when the tablet is asleep or powered down, it definitely charges, so the setup is still effective.

title: Pretty good.
text:
I was researching different photo LED light boxes looking for a sturdy assembly, strong tent fabric, roomy, bright, with multiple openings for different shooting angles. This product fit all of my requirements. Assembly instructions fit on one sheet and the whole apparatus was pretty easy to put together. It was much larger than I anticipated. Since I'm not very tall, I can crawl in and install the backdrop. Overall assessment: nicely designed, good quality, and easy (but not quick) to setup. Here's a quick list of my findings:

Attributes:
Compact carrying case
Bright LED lights that attach via magnetic strips already in the tent top (which means they are movable and can be adjusted a little)
Strong tent material
Inside tent material is foil
Multiple velcro bits to keep the tent opening flaps in place
Three tent openings (one on top - just remember to remove the diffuser if you have it up, technically two openings in the front, the entire tent front can open or a smaller section can open and be held up with a velcro bit at the top of the tent)
Sturdy zippers
Metal frame rods
Hooks to hold the corners of the light diffuser

Cons:
- It will take some time to assemble and disassemble if you plan on taking it apart and carrying it around. You'll have to swap convenience for quality in this case. The rods are sturdy and will keep the form of the tent.
- Make sure the rods are very secure in the joints because the tent covering is a tight fit. It takes a little jiggling to fit it over the frame.
- There is a problem with the backdrop staying up. There are extra slots sewn into the tent fabric to keep the backdrop in place. Unfortunately, gravity is stronger and I have found the backdrop slipping in the back like peeling paint. I have had to use tape to keep the backdrop in place.

Since I have a small room I do wish it was smaller, but the next size smaller in other products is 24" and that is too small. I also wish it was very quick and easy to disassemble and reassemble, but like I said, quality over convenience. There's now a huge black cube in the middle of my room.

title: Excellent replacement for Bluetooth
text:
This is more of an anti-bluetooth post but I think that part of the reason people text so much is that cell phone calls are so low quality. Some of the companies are addressing this with HD calling, but in general, the call quality is terrible. That brings me to Bluetooth. We love the convenience of wireless, but at every point you add a step to the cell call process, you lose quality and you get a delay. So when you add it all up, poor call quality to start with, signals bouncing off cell towers, bluetooth delay/degradation and even wi-fi delay, and you have a mess. It is just hard to communicate much of the time with these miraculous devices we all carry.

That leads me to this headset. Wired eliminates an additional wireless delay. The sound quality is excellent and it is very comfortable. If you call the same person from the same place using bluetooth and this, this will win hands down, and the person on the other end will want you to call with this headset every time. I know this seems like a step backwards, but if we all used these, we would text less and communicate a whole lot better.

title: If you loved inserting Tab A into Slot A as a kid, you'll love this tool
text:
I wish I'd read the reviews before purchasing. Had I, then I would not have expected a precision calibration tool made of - oh, I don't know - precise hard plastic. Imagine my sheer confusion and dismay when I opened the Amazon box to find the "pyramid," yet it was flat. And made out of bend-and-fold-tab cardstock. You know, the photographer cousin to Steak-n-Shake's kids' menu (fold tab A into slot 1, bend until B folds into C, and now you have a nifty car!).

So okay, moving on from the cardstock material and the absurd price of $25 (they even printed on the bottom to recycle it instead of throwing it away. For $25, I'm going to hold on to it until it's yellowed and brittle and must be kept in a nitrogen sealed environment to slow decay), as other reviewers pointed out, due to the material and tab insertion and whatnot, it doesn't exactly sit flat. Or level. Or consistent. If a precision calibration tool is not precise, what good is it?

If it were made of hard plastic, I think it would be a winner and I - along with several reviewers - wouldn't feel gipped. As it stands, $25 for an inprecise cardstock bend-and-fold pyramid leaves a bad taste in my mouth - and question over whether my lenses are actually calibrated correctly.

title: Super Speed Card -  connect this directly to a USB 3.0 port
text: Bought this card recently, initially disappointing as I was only getting approximately 40 MB/s read and write speeds. Tried a number of things to troubleshoot: Bought another USB 3.0 card reader, updated motherboard BIOS, looked for USB 3.0 drivers, opened up the computer to check that the USB ports were connected to USB 3.0 "headers" on the motherboard. Nothing improved the read write speeds. In the end I found the answer: my card reader was actually connected to an USB extension cable. The moment I removed the USB port extension cable, ran the speed tests, immediately got the 85-90 MB/s read AND write speeds I was looking for. SO lesson learnt for the benefit of all readers here: 1) If you want a fast card, this is it. It is faster than most cards in the market. 2) Make sure you have a similarly fast Micro SD card reader. The cheap ones at the discount store is going to slow down the read/write speeds. 3) Avoid USB extension cables if you want to realise the true speed potential of the card. I hope this helps.

title: Loses Functionality a Few Months After Purchase - Bait and Switch
text: I was given this product as a gift. It worked beautifully, and as advertised - at first. After a few months of use, you lose the ability to watch live from your camera or record any events and watch them later, unless you are willing to pay for the cloud subscription service. Canary changed how the products works starting in October of 2017, but new buyers get a working product for a few months, and then they too will lose the functionality of their product unless they pay extra. I noticed that in one of the photos for this product right here on Amazon it says in black and white that the product is free to use without a monthly subscription. That is deceptive advertising. It works beautifully at first, but only until you can no longer take it back to the store for a full refund. Imagine if this business tactic was used in the car industry. You would buy your car and it would drive beautifully for a few months, but then, after you could not longer take it back to the dealership for a refund, it would suddenly become deliberately disabled by the manufacturer and the terms of your purchase contract would say you can not sell your car to another owner. Imagine if your expensive car would not work again unless you paid the manufacturer extra money, in the form of subscription service, to make it start working again. So. Not. Cool. Buyer beware!! Canary could be a great product, but extremely shady corporate business practices make this product a hard pass for me. There are better systems out there that do not rely on cloud storage.
