title: Good product for the price
text:
UPDATE (3/20/2018): my star rating and original review stays the same (see below). Here are some few updates/add-ons for my original review. I live in MN so this winter has been quite brutal. We had a week or two with below zero temperatures. What I have noticed (in my unit at least) is that in freezing and below zero temperatures the back/forward button on my steering wheel doesn't work until 8 - 14 mins into my commute, but the touch screen works perfectly fine. I don't know what causes this but in warmer temps it works just fine. There was an incident where music wasn't coming through any CD/Bluetooth/radio sources. I had to reset for it to work again, but seems fine now. This happened once only and the reset seems to have sort it out. I tried connecting my wife's iPod via Bluetooth but the Hizpo unit doesn't connect or recognize the iPod so I guess the Hizpo unit only connects to Android devices(?). Other than these little hiccups everything else still holds to my original review. I will try my best to continue to update my review as time goes on.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
I've been using this product for about two weeks now. So far I feel that it is a good product for the price. Used the product in our 2007 Toyota Camry.

Things I like: this product is that it's an easy installation. It's a plug n play. No need to hunt around for the correct wires. Everything plugs in with the included harness and gives the dash a much more dated look than the original radio/CD player. The build seems solid. Fits well in the original location and looks factory. It retains the controls from the steering wheel (see dislikes for more details about this), but you have make it learn the buttons in the settings menu. The backup mode works well, but I didn't use the camera that came with this product, I used another camera I had around. This product is simple to use and if you know your way around a smartphone then there will be no problem using this.

Things I disliked: one thing I noticed right away right after installation is that the software is buggy. There were multiple times that apps would just disappear every time that I try to switch them around, so be warned. The only way to bring these apps back is by resetting the unit, which I had to do multiple times when I was trying to setup my main lower apps. The screen is very touch sensitive. Many times I have accidentally selected something else when I was just simply trying to scroll down the screen. There is no way to turn off the radio and it defaults to the radio every time you eject the CD so if you had the volume higher at the time listening to CD and you happen to eject the CD, prepare for a blast of volume from the radio. Even though you retain the controls from the steering wheel, the "mode" button cannot be mapped to two tasks. For example, the "mode" button switches modes from radio to CD (or vice-versa) on the original radio and can be powered off by holding the "mode" button, but on this product the "mode" can only be programmed to power off or to change modes, not both like the original, even though you can map the "mode" in the settings for both so choose either the "mode" powers off or changes modes. This product also eliminates the automatic volume adjustment, where the factory player adjusts the volume depending on the road/cabin noise. The GPS animation is quite laggy and slow. There are random moments where the GPS voice blasts up to the max volume for a fraction of a second, giving everyone in the car a sudden scare. Sometimes the GPS voice volume is very low or does not even come on when instructing.

All in all this product is a good product for what the price is. The build quality is good but don't expect the software quality to be as good as the more expensive similar products.

title: these are very good looking headphones
text:
Okay let's get this out of the way, these headphones are gorgeous and just a beauty to look at. I would have to look very hard to find anyone that would disagree with me regarding the look of these cans. I will break this review into 4 parts: aesthetic, build quality, comfort, and sound.

Aesthetic: as mentioned before, these are very good looking headphones. Just from the look alone, ones can tell that Master & Dynamic has put much thought into designing the MH40, making sure that the design translates to the user. Aside from being a tool to listen to music, I think these are also a fashion statement for many people who like to stand out from the crowd (especially the tan/silver color scheme). These are probably the best looking headphones at any price point. Note that they offer these in many colors and should appeal to many individuals.

Build quality: unfortunately, I have to take one star off of the review due to the build quality. Let me be transparent and upfront, the build quality is solid overall, but suffers from a few issues. The first pair I received had a loose adjustment hinge that keeps slipping around; this affects the fit of the headphones. The second pair was much better but not sure how well they will hold up over time. If you are individuals who constantly adjust their headphone band, it might wear out over time. The sliding metal rod is simply held together by a rubber gasket. Another problem I experienced with the 2nd pair is the fact that the magnetic ear pads keep sliding around and are not tightly attached to the metal housing. I am sure it won't fall off, but an annoyance regardless. I believe this is because the three alignment rods holding the leather pads are a bit short and cause the pads to have a little play. I'll have to see how well these parts will hold up through time.

Comfort: given how heavy these headphones are, they are actually very comfortable over longer listening sessions. This is thanks to the super soft lamb skin ear pads. Also, the clamping force of these headphones are not too tight and won't slip around while on your head. I wear glasses and still find it comfortable enough to listen to about 2 hours at a time. I cannot say the same about other over-ear headphones such as the Beats Studio 2 Wireless. They are almost as comfortable as the Sennheiser Momentum M2 over-ear, which are the most comfortable I've used to date. You might have to play with the positioning while they are on your head to get the best comfort and sound.

Sound: Okay, the sound quality of these headphones is what REALLY got me. I didn't expect a fashion oriented headphone company would make such great sounding headphones. These are the most balance sounding headphones I've had, as compared to the Beats Studio 2 Wireless, B&W P5, and the Sennheiser Momentum M2. The lows are very well defined and never mask any other frequency range. The bass make its present but never overwhelming. The midrange is not overly exaggerated like the Sennheiser Momentum and not as bright also. Treble is where these shines for me. They are airy sounding and not piercing at all. Overall, the sound signature of these headphones lean towards the darker side and sound very intimate. Furthermore, they are good for extended listening since they are not fatiguing. They sound similar to the B&W P7, but a bit darker. One thing they can improve on is the soundstage presentation. While the soundstage is realistic and convincing, it is not as wide as the Sennheiser or the B&W P7. But at the end of the day, I think the M&D MH40 is well suited for many music genre and will give listeners a well balanced listening experience. If you ever listen to Sonus Faber speakers, these headphones sound exactly like them.

Conclusion: these headphones are surely geared towards higher end fashion oriented individuals who also appreciate great sound. From an audiophile point of view, these headphones are a great tool to a great musical experience without sacrificing aesthetic.

***Note: I used my MacBook Pro Retina, iPhone 7 plus, and Fiio K1 to power these headphones.

title: Took a week to get the 5Ghz wifi to work.
text:
Now that it is working i have no problems, but it was an unpleasant process getting there. I tried every driver i could get my hands on, but it would either not see the 5Ghz wifi, or see it but not be able to connect. This device uses a common chipset, so you can drive yourselft crazy looking for drivers because there are a million of them out there. So here's how i Fixed it:
1. Uninstall the Asus/whatever WiFi driver if you have already installed any, power down the system and remove the card
1. on a Gigabyte MB, go into the BIOS
2. Go to "Miscellaneous Settings"
3. Change "Max Link Speed" from "Auto" to "Gen 3". Note: this option could be called something like "PCI speed" or something like that.
4. Save changes, power down, and install card.
5. Both the default Windows 10 driver and the driver from Asus should work now. Don't install the Asus network utitlity, just the driver. It was really buggy for me and doesn't really give you any additional features that make it worth it.
So, changing the BIOS PCI setting was mentioned by another reviewer, but they said it had to do with them having two graphics cards. I only have one GPU, and my PCI settings were called something else so it was hard to nail this one down. I kinda feel bad for deducting 2 stars for this, but if you google "PCE-56 5Ghz", you'll see a million posts from people having this exact problem, and Asus doesn't give any information on their website regarding how to solve it. It's clearly a common issue with a pretty simple fix, so it seems childish to not put it in a FAQ.

Also, if you are looking at this card, be aware that it is several years old and there are newer options for the same price that also come with built in Bluetooth. In hindsight, i wish i had known that.

title: Easily controls both the TV and the Apple TV - can set it up so you can control both without switching between modes!
text:
This remote was just delivered and I had it set up in about 10 minutes!

I wanted to use it to control the TV and Apple TV in my living room. Previously, we had two separate remotes - the TV remote was needed to control the volume, and the Apple TV remote was needed to control the Apple TV. My kids were constantly losing the tiny Apple TV remote in the sofa cushions or behind / under the sofa, and we'd have to search for it just about every time we wanted to watch TV. So I used velcro dots to attach the Apple TV remote onto the back of the larger TV remote. That worked for a while, but eventually my daughter decided that it annoyed her having the remotes back-to-back and so she would always un-velcro the Apple TV remote and we were back to losing it in the sofa cushions again.

The final straw came when the battery compartment cover on the TV remote broke. We needed a new remote and I thought we might as well get one that would work with both devices! This remote does exactly that.

It is supposed to work with the Apple TV on the A mode straight out of the box, but ours didn't. After some trial and error, I discovered that you have to unpair the Apple TV remote that came with the Apple TV (just go to Settings - General - Remotes - Unpair Remote). Once the original remote was unpaired, this remote worked immediately. Therefore, it appears that you cannot use both this remote and the original Apple TV remote at the same time - it's either one or the other.

I set up our TV on the D mode using the codes that I found at the Inteset website - took about 4 tries until I found the correct code.

Once I had both devices working, I took the advice of another reviewer, and I combined the functions into one mode, so I don't have to be constantly switching back and forth between A (Apple TV) and D (TV) modes. Following the instructions that came with the remote, I copied the volume and channel functions from the D mode (TV) and copied them to the Volume Up/Down and Channel Up/Down buttons in the A mode (Apple TV). Now, in the A mode I can control the Apple TV using the menu, round and arrow buttons at the top of the remote, and I can control the volume or switch to another input on the TV using the Volume Up/Down and Channel Up/Down buttons that are lower down on the remote. Easy peasy!

The remote feels well made and I think it should hold up well to use.

It frequently overwrites the timestamps for the GPX tracks, Moveslink (their syncing app) crashes after each use, and the Movescount website goes down for maintenance more often than its up, meaning you can't actually view your run until they turn their servers back on. The only way to access your data is through their closed social network, which leaves you S.O.L. in these instances. When it finally does get posted, you have to go through additional steps to sync it with your preferred tracking service (Strava, Mapmyrun, etc), which you undoubtedly have because Movescount is so terrible.

title: Cheap motor for a cheap telescope.
text:
The Meade 616000 motor drive turns the right ascension (RA) fine control for you to compensate for the rotation of the earth. If you've polar aligned your telescope mount well, this will keep objects from drifting out of your eyepiece.

Unfortunately, the whole Polaris system is an exercise in cost minimization, so the way you attach this drive to your mount is to replace your RA knob. There is no way to do manual fine motion control in the RA axis once you've attached this motor to your mount. Good luck zeroing in on anything with just coarse adjustment.

If you have a Meade Polaris telescope system, skip the motor, turn the knobs for yourself, and save up for a better mount.

title: Impressive Performance!!  Light Speed!!  Quality by a known manufacture!  Complete Solution!
text:
First things first - I had the opportunity to beta test this for the past two months. I am not biased for nor against Netgear.

My history - I am a virtual systems administrator for a major fleet truck manufacture. I am A+ (CE), Network+ (CE), Security+ (CE) and a Microsoft Certified Professional (MCP). I have over 15 year’s experience working with Microsoft Windows Operating Systems and associated networking.

Netgear R8500 – This is a first class device meant for speed and just about anything you want to do with it. The initial impressions is that it is defiantly larger than any other router I have ever owned. The unique shape prevents stacking things on top of it and becoming a harbor for heat sensitive devices allowing for a good natural air flow. The lay out allows for the device to be on top of a desk or behind the entertainment center. I personally like the blue tipped antenna allowing me to glance at it to ensure it is operating. The blue LED lights do not flash and are the color of an “aircraft taxi light blue”. The activity lights are on top of the device not pulling your concentration away from the performance.

The R8500 is designed for both low and high performance devices separating the two intelligently by separating the bands they use. The R8500 has both a USB 2.0 and 3.0 port. Netgear supplies a backup application called ReadyVault for all devices on your local network to back up to the attached USB devices. I personally have a Seagate Backup Plus 5TB drive attached to this for file sharing with friends and family while also performing backups of the family computers and mobile devices. Its use is through the Netgear Readycloud application that now shares a folder vs. the single file it once used to. This makes it easier to share a folder of pictures with a single link and can also be restricted by amounts of times accessed. Each time it emails you allowing you to know from where (IP Address) and when. The Nighthawk x8 has an android application that creates a VPN for mobile devices while away from the house for a theoretical network drive ability and continuous backups of for example pictures being constantly sync’d. While internal to the network I have been able to move 4GB ISO files at a speed of 40MB per second to the USB 3.0. with an Intel 7260. While connecting at 867 MB, a slower speed than the available speed of the router, I was impressed. The router also supports a aggregated dual 1 GB Ethernet connection (2GB link or redundancy) to a NAS if configured so speeds could be even better. I was not able to test this.
The R8500 supports a DDNS (Dynamic DNS) which allows you to connect via a name like a URL while at the same time supporting home users that are on DHCP and the IP address can change. This makes it helpful for persistent connections.

The nighthawk X8 also supports the ability to configure as a gateway vs attaching just as a router if performed with another Netgear device (in my experience). For example I have a gateway modem that gets excellent speeds that has wireless on it but not the wireless performance the Nighthawk X8 has. It recognizes that this feature is available and offers to shut it off in order for the R8500 to be the wireless router gaining the performance of both devices. I personally use it in this configuration because I have two modems/gateways that have a different amount of bonded channels increasing my ISP speeds available to the home network. Although both modems are DOCSIS 3 one has 4 channels and the other has 8.

For those who want or need the feature this router DOES support VLANS to isolate network traffic thus increasing the performance even more and offering even more benefits to the end user.

The R8500 Nighthawk X8 employs “Smart Connect” (One Wireless Network Name (SSID) for both 5GHz radios) which helps load balance the connected 5Ghz devices.
At this point I see no cons by adding this router to your environment to compliment another or simply to replace the one you had before that had so many features, until now.

Overall – I am very happy that I was considered to be a beta tester for this unit and had the opportunity to suggest different features, enjoy the individuals I worked and collaborated with to bring this product to a retail and to again work with the engineers with Netgear.

Other features I noticed in the GUI but did not utilize:
IPTV
VLANS
Ethernet Port Aggregation
VPN Service
ReadySHARE Printer
Dynamic QoS

-Snarf2948

title: I would buy more anytime.. Wait, I WILL buy more
text:
These fans are simply amazing. They are not as silent as other fans like the P12, but its expected as these can run faster. However, when you put them side by side at the same RPM, the noise is about the same, but the performance of the new NF-A12 is just better.

I have a very demanding rig, with a Silverstone Raven RVZ01 mini itx case with a 8086K @4.7 ghz, cooled by a Cryorig C1, and have been using a NF-F12 PWM for almost a year now (never used the fan that came with the Cryorig), and another two NF-P12 PWM for the 1080 graphics card on the other side of the case.

The 8086K proved to be quite difficult to maintain cool while gaming, and it usually reached about 78-80°C when using the NF-F12 controlled with PWM by the Asus Z370-i strix itx MB. Now, with the same PWM setting (turbo mode), the cpu barely reaches 72° C while gaming. Thats about 6-8°C drop!!!

Now, I have to say even if the PWM setting of the fan controller is called turbo, the PC can barely be heard, and the WD Blue 1TB is louder than all the 6 fans COMBINED (1x NF-A12, 2xNF-P12, 2x EVGA FTW 1080 fans, 1x Silverstone SX700LPT fan).

When I put all 3 Noctua third party fans (I mean, not touching any setting from the included fans of the VGA or PSU, which are not even running because all the good work Noctua fans are doing) at the 100% setting, you can here the noise, but the CPU runs not hotter than... wait for it... 65°C !!! Thats about 15°C drop! And let me remind you, this is a Mini ITX build with a really really cramped case!

I love Noctua. I would buy more of these NF-A12 to put them everywhere. Wait, I WILL buy more, I need more of these.

PC Specs:

Case: Silverstone RVZ01
PSU: Silverstone SX700 LPT, 700w SFX-L power supply.
VGA: EVGA FTW 1080
CPU: Intel i7 8086K
MB: Asus Z370-i strix itx
Storage: Samsung 970 pro 1TB, Samsung 860 evo 250 gb, WD Blue HDD 1 TB
Cooler: Cryorig C1, ALL NOCTUA FANS
Monitor: Dell S2716dg 144 Hz gsync 1440p (the reason everything runs so hot while gaming)

title: Held well to my CD slot, but the cradle couldn't hold an iPhone 6S long enough to leave the driveway.
text:
My old Koomus CD-slot phone holder failed (the thin plastic surrounding the ball-joint cracked from sun and heat. Otherwise, it had worked very well for a bit over a year. I tried this one, since it's supposed to be the most sturdy offered by Koomus. Okay... this one is functionally almost identical to the old one, significant differences being it has metal shafts on the gripping cradle, where the other had square plastic shafts (the parts that slide side to side when a phone is inserted or removed from the spring-loaded grip.

The other difference is what's killed it for me, and why I sent it back to Amazon.

The little "arms" that extend out and actually hold the phone, DON'T HOLD THE PHONE. The grip has less grip, somehow. There's less pressure squeezing in on the sides of the phone, and this is an iPhone 6S, not even a 6S Plus... it simply couldn't hold my phone long enough to get out of the driveway. Complete fail, made worse by the less-grippy rubber or plastic covering on the arms. The old Koomus had a softer, grippier textured rubber. This mount has deeper grips to hold thicker cases, but the combination of weaker springs and relatively slippery arms rendered it completely useless in this instance.

title: Terrible reliability, horrible Harmon Kardon Customer Service... great sound though
text:
I've had two pairs of these now: an originally purchased pair that started falling apart after 6 months and the warranty covered replacement pair that have started falling apart after 3 months. Both pairs traveled a total of 2 feet every day, back and forth between my desk surface and my ears. They received virtually no wear and tear, since I only use them at work. I can't, in good faith, recommend that anyone spend any amount of money on these headphones based on my experience:

- After the first 3 months of using the original pair at my desk, the black plastic pieces on the back of both earphones had fallen off due to the cheap glue Harman used, which exposed the wiring and rendered them useless for anything more active than sitting in a chair.
- After 5-6 months of use, they developed the nasty and unpredictable habit of producing tiny shocks every once and a while that would be strong enough to travel down my ear canal and tingle my tongue.
- After 8 months, one of the shocks was strong enough to elicit a loud and involuntary swear from me in an otherwise quite office setting, and so I set out to file for a warranty replacement with the company.
- Harman Kardon makes it incredibly difficult to file warranty replacements. The website won't allow you to submit a request without a serial number, which these don't have, and contact information otherwise is difficult to find. Once I found contact info for one of the technical departments, I wrote to them directly and somebody quickly contacted me back in scripted English with explicit instructions on where/how to return the defective pair. He said that once he received the defective pair with the RMA number he had provided, he would contact me and it would be a 2-4 day turn around. I quickly sent the defective pair to their repair depot and then waited 3 weeks, hoping with each passing day that I would be surprised with a shiny new pair of operational headphones despite receiving no communications from the company. I finally broke down and contacted the company again, and received a response, again in broken English, reassuring me that they had received my package and that it was mere moments away from shipping out. I gave them another 3 weeks before contacting them again and demanding a shipment number. They did not respond for several days, then finally wrote back that the shipment was on it's way and would be there in a week. Again, I waited 2 weeks to no avail before contacting them and asking for proof of shipping with tracking information. They said that the package had arrived a week prior, and sent tracking records that showed they had shipped the replacement from a location in India to a warehouse in California (I live in Virginia). At that point, I angrily, yet patiently demanded that they rush deliver another replacement to the address I had previously provided. Thankfully, they complied and I received my replacement headphones after 2 and a half aggravating months.
- I've had the replacement headphones for 3 months now. They are gold tinted for some reason instead of the silver that they are manufactured in, but otherwise they sound the same. The black plastic pieces on the back of both earphones are starting to fall off again. Additionally, the foam earbud tips are deteriorating, which is a shame since none of the included rubber tips will keep the earbuds in your ears.

As for performance and design:
-Sound quality is top notch. This is the only good thing I can say about these earbuds.
-On both pairs I've had, the left earbud has been clearer and slightly louder. I assume this has something to do with the wiring of the volume controls on the wire for the right earbud.
-These come with 4 earbud tips: 1 small pair, 1 medium pair, and 1 large pair of thin rubber tips; and 1 pair of conforming foam tips. The only pair that reliably stays in ear are the foam tips, which have mostly fallen apart on the replacement pair after 3 months. The rubber pairs do not seal in sound as well either, even though the medium fits perfectly.
-The earbud design is back-heavy, which means they slide out over time unless they are pushed in and "locked" against the bottom inside curvature of your ear. Since the earbuds also have sharp edges on their backside, they become uncomfortable over time if you move your head around a lot.

Bottom line is that these earbuds sound great, but that is the only reason I gave them more than one star. It's a shame that Harman put out such an expensive, yet poorly designed product that could be fixed with such minor tweaks, and spends so little effort on the quality of their Customer Support.

title: A good product with one very annoying quirk. If you...
text:
Let me begin by saying that I am an Anker fanboy, I've owned a bunch of their chargers and cables (oh yeah...their flashlight too which is awesome), and Anker products and packaging rocks. This is the first Anker product I've had an issue with and boy, it's a humdinger!

I have two issues with this product. The first is that it has a major issue with unpausing your audio app. So imagine this scenario. You're driving along and there's an accident in front of you, cars are serving and slamming on brakes and you pause your podcast app to give driving your full undivided attention as any responsible driver does. Then the podcast app starts playing again! So you jab at it quickly in disbelief to turn the damn thing off. And it turns back on again! So you close the podcast app. Then it starts playing again! Sheesh!

Lol, it sounds incredible as I'm sitting here typing this but that is exactly what this device will do, it will re-open Pandora or whatever you listen to and start playing once you've paused or even closed the app. It's like the thing is possessed and on a mission to kill it's owner!

Because of that issue this product is definitely not ready for prime-time. It's in dire need of an update or recall that fixes this safety issue.

The second issue I've had with this device is the support, or lack thereof. I messaged them about a month ago to complain about this issue. They do respond but it takes them about a week. I get extremely busy for days at a time, when things finally slow down I message them back. So to be fair part of that delay was my fault, but if they got back to me quicker we could move the ball much farther along.

Here is where we currently are after about a month of messaging about this stupid thing:

"The problem I'm having with it, is it constantly unpauses my audio app whether it's Pandora or my podcast app. It's very dangerous because I will pause listening while driving so I can focus on the road when there's congestion or traffic and this thing will unpause whatever audio app I'm using and start playing it again which is a huge distraction and very dangerous!

Even if I go so far as to close the audio app it will re-open the audio app and start playing the audio app-it's hugely annoying! Yesterday I had to yank this thing out of the electrical port to turn it off to keep it from doing that because I was crossing a bridge with congested traffic--I mean I was at the point where I was considering rolling down the window and chucking the damn thing off the bridge!!!

Because this support for this product has taken so ridiculously long I am now copying and pasting this message into an Amazon review. You can choose to support it or not, you haven't supported it very well up until now.

The serial number is B315CB0008.

Reference Ticket#57726283 if contacting a CSR
Cathy
AnkerDirect Customer Support
"

So there you have it. I purchased this because the aux cable was producing an awful whine in my new vehicle. This does alleviate that problem. And audio whine will be an even lesser problem if you're dead because this Anker product distracted you causing you to drive off a cliff.

So there's that.

title: Keep 2 for dual view, hack the other two for 3D :)
text:
First, let me say this: Dual view is flipping AWESOME.

Second, this is a weird set, because, well...it's DUAL view, not quad view. Why would I ever need 2 sets of these? I wouldn't.

The good news, though, is that if you take the second set and swap the right lens of the "B" frames into the "A" frames and vice versa, you wind up with an extra set of 3D glasses, which genuinely is a useful thing to have.

It's really easy. I used the tip of a knife to simply pop the inner frame out of the right side lens on both the A and B frames, then swapped the lenses between them. Voila, 3D. Why does this work? Well, because Dual View relies on the same technology as 3D. With 3D glasses, the left and right lenses are each seeing a different image presented by the TV, creating the illusion of depth. With Dual View, both lenses in a set of glasses receive the same image, and by having one set of "A" glasses and one set of "B" glasses, blammo, two people can see totally different things on the same screen at the same time.

Dual view isn't perfect, of course: you'll get a bit less resolution, which might make some games look a bit worse, but given how great games look these days, it's a marginal reduction in quality and is more than counterbalanced by the fact that you're turning your single HDTV into two HDTV's.

For reference, I use these with an LG 55UB8500 55" 4K TV, and I'm so happy I can't stop giggling. It's awesome.

title: Great replacement for my Harmony 890
text:
My Harmony 890 remote finally started to have issues with the buttons not working. I needed a new remote that would allow control of my z-wave lighting and the equipment in my rack.

This new remote works better at this than the old one. The z-wave equipment can be located on buttons for easy access and my gear is all controlled by rf through the remote.

It is unfortunate that few devices are controlled over WiFi with this product. This requires using an IR blaster on the front of the rack instead of it all being hidden in the rack. My receiver has a remote port on the back which is hardwired to the hub. This requires a converter because the plug on devices is larger than that found on the hub. The hub only has 2 outputs which limits the flexibility of the hub. The Elite remote only supports a single hub unlike the 890 which supported multiple RF extenders. The lack of multiple hubs and WiFi support also required me to add an RF repeater to go to my projector from the hub IR output in the top of the unit.

This new system allows configuration through an iPhone app as well as a computer. I found it necessary to use both in my setup. Simpler setups could get by with the app only, but there is more flexibility in resetting the hub in the computer product.

Typical with complex Harmony setups I had to call support to fix some issues with my system. Oddly commands were missing on the Elite for one device that were in the 890. I tried copying them and learning them to no avail. Harmony support was able to do this over the phone.

I also had issues binding my z-wave devices with the optional extender. Harmony supports solution of reloading the hub through the computer did not work. I finally was able to bind my Leviton lighting with many attempts without their help. Even though they said they were not compatible. After that my z-wave devices wouldn’t always work. I fixed this with the balance network utility for z-wave.

After all of this I have a system that works reliably every time.

Savant or Control4 would be an alternative to this, but those products are typically going to cost many times more to professionally install. Even though the process of getting this product to work was difficult it was the cheapest option to do this without a lot of custom programming using some Linux based device.

title: As close to the ideal ball head for still photography as I have found.
text:
This is turning out to be as close to the ideal ball head for still photography as I have found so far. For me, the main problems that it solves are ease of use, packable weight, and reliability.

What I have found most annoying about most of the ball heads out there is that every time I get the head properly adjusted, tightening the locking mechanism causes the head to move. If they moved the same way every time, at least I could compensate for that, but that is not how it happens; the movement is always random and unpredictable.

With this head, when I release the lever, the head stays where I put it — provided the tension is enough to hold the weight of the camera and lens, of course.

The variable tension is a very important feature. It is something to play with and get familiar with before actually using the head to take pictures. I imagine it taking no more than a half hour or so of experimentation to get up to speed with that for still photography. I doubt very much this would be a viable option for video. Similarly, I don't see it as an optimal head for panoramas, although with a little practice, I can see it would be possible.

In the horizontal position, I have found this head to be remarkably stable, so much so that I have little desire to test how it performs in the vertical or "joystick" orientation. Someone else will have to answer any questions about that.

This head loses a star because, for my purposes, it has what so many other heads have, a bias towards downward angles, rather than upward. A simple work-around is to mount the camera such that the handle is aligned with the lens. The head can then be operated with the handle in front, rather than from behind or to the side. Again, this is quite viable for still photography, but probably not useful for video.

In regard to the mount, I find greater versatility and sanity in standardizing on the Arca-Swiss system, so I have added a light-weight Arca-Swiss compatible clamp atop the supplied Manfrotto plate. It works for me, and YMMV.

title: DVI-D adapter started shorting out after 3 months
text:
As a summary of my review, I would avoid this product as this disconnect issue seems to be pretty common if you look at the other reviews left by other purchasers. I suspect that corners were cut including using cheaper glues and an inefficient method of attaching the wires to the board.

The DVI-D to VGA adapter did its job for a little over 3 months. However, for the last couple weeks, my monitor kept randomly disconnecting and displaying a black screen. Fortunately, I was able to get the monitor to reconnect by wiggling the wire connected to the adapter.

I finally decided to take the case apart to determine what was wrong and to see if I could repair the problem. Unfortunately, the protective glue had come off the solder points on the PCB board. In addition, there were exposed wires extending past the portion attached to the PCB board. This caused the wires to touch each other after putting the case back on after taking it apart to check what was wrong. This then caused the adapter to short out when I tried plugging it back in.

If you look at the attached photos you will see that the wires have several exposed sections of copper wire, along with cheap glue used to cover the solder attachment points.

title: Gunk on the bristles
text:
I tried this brush as a low cost alternative to the Arctic Butterfly and had high hopes it would work. After all, they both perform the same function and work the same way, what could go wrong. See the before & after photos of my sensor as displayed using Lightroom's Visualize Spots feature.

As reported by many others in their reviews, it actually left the sensor dirtier. MUCH dirtier. It was so bad it almost looks as if the brush was spun while it was inside the camera, but that didn't happen. Although the gunk this brush left behind looks like dust spots, it wasn't dust. Wet cleaning was needed to get it off the sensor.

To get to the bottom of this, I performed a really simple test using a lens filter. Just Google "The Pixel Sweeper" and you'll find an article about finding, preparing, testing, and using brushes to clean the sensor on your digital SLR. The filter test method is described about half way down the page. The brush failed the test, my filter looked exactly like the gunk deposited on the filter in the article.

It turned out the problem with the Movo Photo MV-B100 is a really cheap brush head having bristles contaminated with a coating, most likely size residue as found on inexpensive artist brushes. The residue on the testing filter was apparent after just 30 brush strokes and looked like a white film. However, on the sensor which only received 2 strokes, it wasn't visible with the naked eye. That made me wonder if this product received so many positive reviews because folks just eyeballed their sensor, although I can't say if the gunk would be visible through a sensor loupe. But it's certainly more than obvious when taking a test photo and using software to view the results.

If you are thinking about buying this brush I strongly recommend performing the simple filter test BEFORE using it on your sensor.

title: I like it!  Some features could be improved but well worth the price.
text:
Had this unit for 2 weeks. So far, it is well worth the small price. There are a few things that could be improved upon.
PRO's: it has a very good tuner, able to identify and process 4 additional tv channels that my Samsung television missed. The setup was easy and intuitive. The recordings, both in HD and SD are very good when using an external WD passport hard drive or a 64Gb Kingston USB drive. I can set recordings in one of 3 ways...either instantly while watching a program, or choose a program from the EPG (electronic program guide), or manually set-up a future recording by inputting the channel, date, time, duration. Able to 'train' the remote to switch tv power, tv volume, etc.

CON's: The remote must absolutely be pointed at the unit to work. The EPG responds fairly quickly to program names and time, but slow to display the episode description. (This may be the fault of the transmitting station, though.) The unit will not remember the EPG when switching from one channel to the next. (Each time you tune to a different station, it re-learns the EPG for that station). The remote is not very intuitive when it comes to recording/playback functions. Starting a playback is a little delayed (2 or 3 seconds) but I believe much of the delay is waiting for my hard drive to spin-up. The USB stick is faster. It has 'time shift' mode feature (pause the TV to answer the phone), and works fairly well, but it does not have the ability to rewind to review that spectacular 3-point shot (unless you're recording or in timeshift).

All in all though, for the $35 delivered price, this is a great unit. Other than and external USB recording medium and maybe an HDMI cable, the money you spend for this is ALL that you will spend. No monthly DVR and cable bills or TIVO charges. It feels great to cut the cord!!

title: I spent hours trying different configurations on my home network and I was amazed at some of the havoc caused
text:
A newer version of this product, 3.0., can now be purchased for nearly the same price.

[[ASIN:B00TO8SX7G AGPtek LKV373 100M HDMI Extender over LAN Routers/Switchers Ethernet Network RJ45 CAT5 CAT6-Single Source from 1080P Full HD STB,DVD,PS3 - w/DLP,LCD,LED ,Supports TCP/IP by Ethernet, DC 5V/1A]]

The product on this page is version 2.0 and it doesn't sync as reliably as 3.0.

Neither of the products work very well if you put them on your network. I spent hours trying different configurations on my home network and I was amazed at some of the havoc caused. The most interesting thing was the specific ability to complete disable router wifi transmission. I was able to do this to my xfinity gateway, as well as two different netgear routers (X6 and X8). This happened with repeated experimentation and the wifi broadcasting returned when i removed the extender from the network.

Even though the device works, it fails for me because at times it renders my network useless.

It actually works just fine if you want to use CAT5e or 6 cable to connect the transmitter and receiver directly.

I also works pretty well if you connect it to an un-managed switch, rather than directly to a router. I don't know enough about networking to understand why this was case.

My goal was to connect to it a router (or even a switch connected to the router) on one end and a high quality multi-band wifi-extender on the other end set up as non-broadcasting wireless access point and placed in reasonably close proximity to the router. Doing this resulted in a signal that constantly went in and out (85% out, with 15% flashes of low quality picture) despite measuring INTERNET download speeds of > 100Mbps from the ethernet port of the access point. Clearly though, I didn't have enough bandwidth to receive the transmitted HDMI signal. In fact, using the product specifically found on this page gave no picture whatsoever. The version 3 linked above had the signal that went in and out, an improvement over no picture, but not up to an acceptable level.

title: Waiting for the next version, which will hopefully be better
text:
[SEE UPDATE BELOW] I did quite a lot of research and figured out that this isn't for me. Some of Sonos' advertising is quite deceptive, so you need to understand what you're missing if you "upgrade" to the Playbar. I'm glad I tried it out, because I almost dropped $3,000 kitting out my home with this system.

In theory, the Playbar is a godsend: hook it up to your TV via TOSLINK, hook all of your devices to your TV, and you're done. Even better if you already have a Sonos system for your music. Given that my TV sits above a fireplace and I hate running wires, this should have been ideal.

Unfortunately, the Playbar comes with a lot of caveats. I have a lot of devices: a PS3, two different Xbox, and the cable box, all run through a Denon receiver and controlled by a Harmony remote. The receiver is a necessary evil: with several HDMI devices, I don't want to run half a dozen wires to a TV above a fireplace. Trouble is, my Samsung TV--like almost every TV--downconverts any 5.1 audio from the TOSLINK to stereo. Sure, the Sonos then performs a make-believe 5.1 "simulation" on the resulting signal, but if I spend $700 for a playbar, $50 for a bridge, and $600 for two Play 3's for back-channels, I'd like real thing, thanks. (If you have any interest in sound, you'll immediately be able to tell when the system is getting real 5.1, and when it's faking it.)

Sure, you can buy an HDMI splitter, connect that to an AVR, and then run the splitter's optical output to the Playbar. Hope it works--but that rather defeats the whole "simplicity" point. And if you do adopt that solution, but have a Blueray player that gives a DTS signal.... you're out of luck, because Playbar doesn't do DTS.

I suspect that Sonos' next offering will include something other than a TOSLink connection, because for $700, this kind of "simplicity" is insane. Especially as Play-Fi options proliferate, Sonos will need better hardware and software to stay in the game.

[UPDATE 3/7/05]: I finally made the leap and purchased the Playbar, as I needed to upgrade my TV when the old one's capacitors blew out. This device is as awful as I suspected.

I have a new Sony XBR-55x850B, and I've spent two days trying to get the Playbar to operate. I can get sound when I play a show in Netflix, but none of the TV's system sounds (like the click you hear when switching options on the menu) will work. Nothing will come through HDMI.

I suppose that when it works, it's great, but if your TV/input device/SONOS systems don't get along, it's awful.

title: Peachtree exceeds expectations again with sound quality and build
text:
I am new to the powered speaker marker as generally I love to power them with my own amps. Being a big fan of Peachtree Audio owning two of their Integrated Amps, I figured these would be good, but wow. They blew me away.
I needed speakers for a small space so I could listen to a bit of music but mostly watch Netflix. I have a few different subs that I wanted to connect for depth. In order to stick on these, I tried several different combos:
-Edifier R1700BT: Great speakers and great value. Peachtree is better for music and movies. These are powered.
-SVS Prime Wireless. Big sound, but not as much detail and sound separation during loud scenes as I would like. These are powered.
-SVS Prime Satellite powered by a Sonos Connect Amp. Too small and not powerful enough. Even with a sub. These are passive.
-ELAC Debut 2.0 6.2 powered by Sonos Connect Amp. These provided perhaps better musical quality and a much bigger sound, but not being powered and being the size of regular bookshelves I decided to pass.

So after all of that, these Peachtree’s are the winner!
-Beautiful Finish
-Come with Rubber stands to angle them slightly up.
-Being self powered the integrated and crossovers done internally are beautiful.
-They image very, very well.
-Bass is solid, but when paired with a sub they are big loud and fantastic and could easily power a large room music and decent volume.
-Great connections do you could have multiple devices connected and not need an Amp, pre-amp or reciever.
-Excellent quality amplification that allows these to play at loud levels well.
-Pair very well with Sonos Connect passive system.
-Great remote.
SVS Prime Wireless has an app, but no remote.

A stellar value, these are high end with sound and finish.

title: Fantastic
text:
On the a6300, having used the Metabones and Commlite adapters, this thing is far, far better. While it only officially supports Sigma EF mount lenses, I have found that a number of Canon lenses work as well (however, you will only have AF-S and AF-C modes). For example, the Canon 50mm 1.4 USM, which doesn't work at all on the Metabones or Commlite, works on the MC-11 quite well. You can even get a degree of focus tracking by setting your shot priority to AF and choosing AF-C (Wide seems to work best). No, it's not what you'd get from a Sony native lens, but it's quite usable. My Canon 70-300mm IS USM takes comparable images, and performs almost as well in AF as the Sony G 70-300mm. Certainly there are reasons to buy the Sony, but for most, this would an effective bridge. On supported lenses like the Sigma 150-600mm Contemporary, I have to say it's almost like using a native lens. I say almost because under normal shooting conditions I wouldn't be able to tell the difference; some native lenses perform far worse, some better.

I have tested the adapter with these non-Sigma lenses (assuming AF-S or AF-C mode) -
Canon 24mm IS USM - Works
Canon 40mm STM - Works
Canon 50mm 1.4 USM - Works
Canon 18-135 IS USM - Does Not Work Properly
Canon 70-300mm IS USM - Works
Canon 75-300mm IS USM - Does Not Work Properly

Sigma 150-600mm Cont - Feels like a native lens.

Quick update - I shot a lot of pics at the Indy 500 this weekend using the a6300 and the Sigma 150-600mm Cont. The combination performed quite well, but you really have to know your AF modes to get the best performance.

The only negative I can think of is that it doesn't support EF-S lenses, which is a shame and the only reason I have to hang onto my Commlite adapter.

title: Good thing which comes with a few major problems
text:
I've bought it on BestBuy before it was available on Amazon, and gonna return this thing today. There are a few things I want you to know before you buy Karma Grip:

Good things first:
1. They fixed the motor noise with the update, so now you can't hear that noise that was initially ruining the footage audio. That's good.
2. Grip does a good job for stabilizing your video. You just have to be really careful when walking, but that's alright.
3. The battery life is pretty decent. I've heard a lot of bad reviews saying that this thing is charging for 10 hours, but working just for 2, but they are not true. You can charge it with your cellphone charger for something like 3-4 hours and it's gonna be working for something like 2-3, which is pretty decent, especially if you have a good powerbank available.

As for bads:
1. You can search Youtube for horizontal tilt issue. It looks to be a common issue, but GoPro can't find a solution yet. During the video the camera just can't stay horizontal (the angle could be like 45 degrees and you never know what was the trigger for that). A lot of my footage was wasted and that's the main reason why I am returning this thing.
2. Grip really lacks controls. You can get the OSMO which allow you to change the direction of your camera with simple joystick controls. Can't do it with Grip, which is really painful if you are trying to do some filmaking with it.
3. When the Grip is attached, you can use external microphone with Gopro. Mic on GoPro Black 5 is decent, but still, it's not of a pro-quality, so it is something you have to consider while purchasing that.

I really liked GoPro, but it looks like the company is having a lot of troubles at the moment. You can't use their software on Windows 10 (check the topic on their forum). lot's of hardware issues, karma drone recall and the worst thing - the company IS NOT responding to them. Really hope this thing will improve in future. For now, I'll have to change it for OSMO.

title: A 4-Speaker Comparison
text:
My need was for a small speaker that could be stand-alone by playing MP3s loaded onto a TF card. There were a number to choose from that had the same basic functions, and sound quality. But there were pros and cons to each of the 4 units I tried out. All of them connected via Bluetooth, had AUX input, charges via USB connector, had a little (though insignificant) FM radio ability (Silver unit had none), and had relatively good sound considering the small size of the units (don’t expect superior sound – they are small, inexpensive, portable units). However, they all had weaknesses regarding the use of the TF card (a Micro SD card). The TF card could not be inserted straight into the Purple and Silver units – they went in crooked and would not play. The Green unit accepted the TF card and was recognized (identified by a flashing light, but would not play). The Red unit played the files on the TF card, but I had to push it in very far, but couldn’t get it to eject later - - I had to use needle-nose tweezers to pull the card out. But since I could at least get it to play from the card, I ordered a second one - - this one worked and ejected – but once again, I had to push the card far in, using my fingernail to push it far enough. I went back to my 1st, identical unit (not having mailed it back yet), and sure enough, if I used my fingernail to push it in far enough, it would insert and eject.
Thus, I rejected: 1) the Purple, “ThinkBox” (2*); 2) the Silver, LotFancy “SuperBass” (3*); and 3) the Green, “Kcrtek” (4*).
The Red EasyAcc “Mini-Cannon” was the winner when it came to my needs, and I will keep both of them (one to serve as a backup) – it gets 5*. If you have no need for the TFcard MP3 player, then all could be in contention, but this unit would still be my preference.
More Pros and Cons provided with the individual units.

The Red EasyAcc “Mini-Cannon” – 5*:
I liked:
-- Had a quality feel to it - - largely due to the weight
-- Note indicating the desire to make the customer happy – contact them in the event of any problem.
-- Had the best volume control – slow enough to be able to achieve the desired level.
-- Is the only one of the 4 units that could play the contents of the TF card.
-- Modes were identified audibly with pleasing tones (no voice)
-- Was the most significant packaging of all the units – well protected for shipment.
-- Had the most complete manual.
I didn’t like:
-- Mode was more difficult to recognize without any English description – only tones
-- Difficult to insert and eject the TF card - - probably due to the thick aluminum exterior.
Worth noting:
-- The buttons seemed to be more substantial than on the other units.
-- No good way to tie off this speaker – 2 very minor grooves in an otherwise smooth body.
-- No obvious indicator if the unit is well charged, or is receiving a charge – work-around is to use a power bank with it’s lights as a charging indicator.

title: Awesome radio for AM\FM. Not so much for Shortwave.
text: I received the radio and I have to say that everything said about it is excellent and on point except shortwave performance. If shortwave radio is the reason for purchase, I suggest you look elsewhere. After reading online reviews and watching various internet videos, I have to agree that if you live near strong FM stations and\or have many noise sources near you such as appliances, phones, TV's, etc, you will be swamped with noise when attempting to pick up shortwave signals. It is definitely sensitive including picking up noise. Even if you don't have issues with that, the radio itself generates internal noise that is picked up and does not go away. I have years of experience with other shortwave radios and I have owned many from $20 up to $500 and I have made comparisons with my experiences. Having said that, the radio build quality and operation is excellent, sound is fantastic, and AM/FM performance is great. Nothing to complain about that part. For a $25 radio, this is a bargain even if shortwave is subpar. But if shortwave listening is your goal and wanting a cheap option, the Tecsun R9012, which I compared it with, is an amazing radio as well as other Tecsun and Degen radios in this range. When making the comparison, the Tecsun came in clear and easily found stations that the TivDio couldn't pick up through all the noise. Maybe if the user doesn't live close to a city or other noise sources, it may work better. So, other than shortwave, the radio is pretty cool.

title: Bluetooth Speaker Comparison -- 2017 Edition
text:
I was in need of a new portable speaker, and like many of you, I was a little overwhelmed after doing an Amazon search and finding literally tens of thousands of options to choose from. It's especially frustrating because probably the most important part of the product -- how good it sounds -- is not something you can really evaluate until after you physically have it. So I picked four speakers to compare: Cambridge Soundworks OontZ Angle 3 Plus, Anker SoundCore Sport XL, Geek Beats Jolt5, and the JBL Flip 4.

First, the [[ASIN:B01LZV6TYQ Cambridge SoundWorks OontZ Angle 3 PLUS Bluetooth Speaker with 30-Hour Playtime - Richer Bass Greater Sound Quality & 10W+ Loud Volume, Water Resistant Splashproof, Portable Wireless Speaker]], is a slightly larger version of the best-selling speaker on Amazon with over 17,000 reviews and a $30 price tag, and this only costs $5 more, so why not give it a shot? I chose [[ASIN:B01DZ56MX0 Anker SoundCore Sport XL Outdoor Portable Bluetooth Speaker - 16W Output and 2 Subwoofers, IP67 Waterproof & Dustproof, Shockproof, 66ft Bluetooth Range, 15H Playtime, Built-in Mic, USB Charging Port]], partially because I have other Anker products that I'm pretty happy with, but also because the 66-foot advertised range seemed like it could come in handy if I were working in the backyard with my phone in my pocket and the speaker sitting on the porch. I selected the [[ASIN:B01AO1QAA8 GEEK BEATS JOLT5 10W X-Bass Wireless Portable Bluetooth Speaker and USB Power Bank - Green. IP65 Water and Dust Resistant with 5200mAh Samsung Battery.]] because it's the same price as the Anker, it has an average of 4.9 stars (wow!), and it can be used as a battery to charge your phone. And finally, I chose the [[ASIN:B06X1GLH1C JBL Flip 4 Waterproof Portable Bluetooth Speaker (Black)]] because in my search, I kept seeing the JBL Flip 3 pop up in reviews for other speakers, and this is the newest (and supposedly slightly better) version of that speaker.

Sound Comparison: Sitting in my living room and swapping around between the four options, it's clear that the Flip 4 is the most, well, clear. Considering it's also the most expensive, I kinda expected that to be the result. Surprisingly, the OontZ was a solid second place with a bit more rumble in its bass compared to the Flip 4 but at the cost of less clarity. The Anker and Jolt5 were noticeably flatter in their sound, seeming to favor the lows instead of an overall range, and this caused some distortion at higher volumes. When I took the speakers outside, it's a slightly different story. With the speakers on the patio, I walked into the yard about 25 feet and compared the sound quality again, and again I'd put the Flip 4 in the top spot. This time, however, I'd actually say the Anker was a solid number 2. At this distance, the distortion from having the volume up the whole way was not very noticeable and didn't detract from the music I was playing, and the Anker is a bit louder than the OontZ. The Jolt5 is a distant last place being not only flat but also not as loud. It's comparable to listening to the radio on a boombox from the 90s.

Bluetooth Range: With the speakers inside, all four started cutting in and out around the same spot about 30 feet away. It's around a corner, so having a wall in the way seems to even the odds here. Having an open space outside didn't seem to make a difference to the Jolt5, though, as it still broke up around 30 feet. The product page on Amazon says 33 feet, so that's pretty accurate. The OontZ fared a bit better and almost made it to the back gate about 60 feet away. The Anker is pretty spot on with its advertised 66-foot range as it went a bit further than the OontZ, even onto the other side of the gate and almost into the road. The Flip 4 was still going strong when I got to the other side of the road and couldn't go any further in a straight line, maybe 75 feet.

Other Things: Depending on what exactly you plan on using your speaker for, and just for comparison's sake, there are some differences that may be worth note:

-- All four speakers come with a mini-USB to USB charging cable but not the plug. If you've charged a cell phone in the last 10 years or so, however, you should probably already have one.
-- The Jolt5 and OontZ come with a 3.5mm cable so you can plug your phone right into it instead of using bluetooth (though all four speakers have this option, just not the cable).
-- The Anker and Jolt5 have a USB port so they can be used as a portable battery to charge your phone.
-- The Anker, Flip 4, and Jolt5 have hand straps. The OontZ does not come with one nor have a place to attach one.
-- The Anker, Flip 4, and Jolt5 have audible cues when they power on or off. The OontZ is silent. All four speakers do, however, make a noise when you successfully pair a device through bluetooth.
-- All four speakers are splash resistant, but only the Anker and Flip 4 are likely to live if they fall into the water (submersible up to 30 minutes)
-- The Anker and Jolt5 are shock resistant, so they likely won't shatter if you drop them
-- The OontZ has the longest battery life (30 hours) and the Flip 4 has the shortest (12 hours)
-- The Flip 4 can be paired with other Flip 4's (through an app) to provide a wireless multi-speaker experience. There are Bluetooth adapters that would allow you to do this with the other speakers if you wanted, as well as physically connecting them with 3.5mm cables.
-- The Flip 4 comes in a variety of colors.
-- They are all roughly the same size, just differently shaped (see pics)

Conclusion: The best bang for your buck is the OontZ Angle 3 Plus. It's a measly $35 and sounds almost as good as the $100 Flip 4, especially inside. In addition to being inexpensive, you can literally keep it blaring music for an entire day. It's not quite as loud outside as the Anker or Flip 4, but it's also half the price. If you're willing to pay for premium sound, go with the Flip 4 or even the Flip 3 if you want to save 20 bucks. Supposedly the sound is comparable, just the Flip 4 has a longer playtime. It really is noticeably clearer compared to the other options, so if you were using it with a projector to watch a movie, for example, the rumbling and distortion aren't going to drown out the dialogue, and likewise vocals on a music track don't get lost in the rest of the noise. If you're planning on a bunch of outside activities, like mountain biking or camping, the ruggedness of the Anker and ability for it to charge your phone makes it your best bet. I didn't do a drop test with any of these, but the Anker feels like a rubberized brick and would probably survive a fall. Other than battery life, there's no reason to ever choose the Jolt5 over the Anker, especially considering they are the same price. The Jolt5 is just worse in every way, and I honestly don't understand its 4.9 rating.

The Jolt5 is going back. The Flip 4 is staying. I'm still debating between the Anker and OontZ and may keep them both since the cost combined is still less than a Flip 4.

EDIT: After further testing, the Anker is going back and I'm keeping the OontZ. When plugged in with a 3.5mm cable, the sound is dramatically better with way more bass and a louder volume. And it's still somehow the cheapest one.

TL;DR:
-- On a budget? Cambridge SoundWorks OontZ Angle 3 Plus
-- Best sound? JBL Flip 4 (though I do wish it had a bit more bass)
-- Most likely to survive the apocalypse? Anker SoundCore Sport XL

title: Sounds great in a smaller room.
text: This is a beautiful soundbase, it’s like “electronic art”. It has a jet black scratch resistant glass top and touch controls. There are a lot of features packed into this budget friendly speaker. WiFi, Bluetooth, usb, music subscriptions, it has it all. However, the sound is really only made for a small room, like 15x15 ft only. I originally bought this speaker for my large living room. It was grossly under powered. Maybe the surround speaker options would have helped, but it would have still been lacking. But once I moved the speaker into a smaller spare room, “WOW” the sound really fills the room. It’s almost like high definition sound. The clarity is great and the different sound options for other types of music or movies is great. This sound base is rated for TV’s up to 55 inches; this is true only if the tv and the soundbase were in a small room. I knocked off one star because this soundbase isn’t capable of powering a large tv in a large room, although the ads advertise it this way. But nevertheless sounds fantastic in a smaller room.

title: Best budget power supply I've used.
text:
First, I have to say that I've only been using this power supply for a week and will update my review if anything changes down the road. I was trying to build a relatively inexpensive PC around some components I acquired secondhand (specifically an LGA1156 i7 and MB for it). Here's what I ended up with in terms of hardware/power draw in addition to the aforementioned processor/motherboard combo:
1. 2x DVD-RW optical drives
2. Raptor 10k rpm hard drive
3. Seagate 500GB 7200 rpm hard drive
4. PNY GeForce 740 2GB video card
5. 6x case fans (not counting the PS and CPU fans) - I won't keep this in the system long term, but was trying to add a little more draw on the supply for testing

With the components listed above and having overclocked the CPU slightly with the biostar mb's overclock tool, I burned the system in with SiSoftware Sandra. The full system burn-in completed with no issues. I have also used the system to render some 3D models and run some high fps games (well, as high as the video card would allow).

All that said, the system has performed well and voltages have remained as expected. Assuming the PS doesn't fail early I can't see anything about it that I'm not happy with.

I strip off the plastic and see a black coating on the wire - no matter how much flux I use, these wires will not solder, and are a huge pain. A bit more quality in the wire would help. Not all the wires are like this, I've noticed it happens a lot on the white wires in my batch.

UPDATE: Elegoo contacted me and ended up replacing the wires. I haven't had time yet to check if these have the same issue trying to solder, but I did raise the rating one star, as Elegoo seems to really care about their customers. As soon as I get a chance to solder one of these (it has to be a place where I need one end with a connector and I'm soldering the other end), I'll update the review again. Anyway - great customer service - Thanks Elegoo!

title: Headroomy when Headless
text:
Agreeing with reviewer @Dan Teo, this NUC improves upon my [[ASIN:B00L2C3VAQ Gigabyte Brix GB-BXBT-2807 Ultra Compact Mini-PC Celeron (N2807) 2.17GHz Gigabit LAN (Intel HD Graphics)]] in almost every way (clock, cores, speed, BIOS, build). With the N2807, there was too little headroom to remain responsive. OTOH, the N3700 CPU is fast enough to handle remoting with around 50% headroom remaining, enough for typical headless home serving tasks.

+ Better BIOS (compared to Gigabit N2807)
+ Wake On Lan works

+ Full size HDMI connector

+ Excellent build quality

title: Simply the best monitor in its class on the market
text:
Simply the best monitor in its class on the market. This had low input lag, beautiful and accurate color reproduction, sharp text, and great thin bezel. If an IPS, 24inch, 2K monitor without costly g-sync is what you want this is THE one to buy. Its great for office use, artist use, and gaming. Good for gaming a long as you are content with 60hz. I am, and given I do digital art and game, this is fine compromise for me.

Its IPS so the viewing angles are amazing. There is absolutely zero color shift when viewing this monitor at any sane angle.

It has a best in class refresh rate and less than 10ms input lag meaning you will have decently responsive gaming. You might not win a CSGo tournament using one of these, but if your idea of fun is slapping on an action RPG or even playing an FPS in anything less than hardcore competition mode you will do fine. Again this monitor does compromise as its an all-around performer rather than a single-focused product. Still I game on this and I'm quite happy. I even play racing sims on this and I'm happy.

Its got DC violate controlled backlight LED's Thus 100% flicker free and NO headaches from s***ty PWM lighting. The backlight its not 100% uniform but from what I've seen scouring reviews nobody's is. These have found to have no more than a 5% variance in luminescence across the panel in the two I own. There is IPS glow, its inherant to the IPS technology. Until we get affordable AMOLED displays this is just the price of getting good color.

Its not a perfect monitor, but in terms of an all around great 2k display this one wins. This monitor also quite acceptably down-scales/interpolates to deliver a 1080p source. Their is only a minor blur effect, and most of the fuzziness is inherent to having a 1080p source on such a large display. So this will be able to drive Blue-ray or console content with a quite an acceptable experience.

I could go into great detail about this montor's color reproduction but its easier just to say I'm a digital artist with far better than average-joe's color sensitivity. Not only do I not have color blindness but I've carefully trained my perception to pick out very subtle changes in color. Trust me when I say this is an *accurate* colored monitor. Mind you accurate is less saturated than most people think. Most display (like your samgsung phone that every gushes over, are over-saturated. But these can easily be tuned with a colorimeter or spectrometer to produce print-accurate color. With these I can produce paintings and order a finished print that is exactly what I expected. I use a colormunki colorimeter and use displayCAL to tune my color profiles.

The slightly matte screen prevents glare and doesn't produce any graininess that I can see.

Display port in and out lets you daisy chain in case your graphics card (like mine) only has 1 DP and you want dual monitors. Its a modern monitor that only supports modern ports, which thank god. VGA needs to just die already. That being said it doesn't have VGA or DVI connectors so plan accordingly.

And hooray for VESA mounts. It uses 100mm mounts. I'm able to mound them monitor arms and free up desk space for more junk and clutter!

As a final thought. IMO, eventually the VESA standard Adaptive sync will end up winning the format war between AMD and NVidias absurdly priced, proprietary G-sync. But I think we are several product generations away from a GPU-montior synchronization technology becoming standard on all mid-range and up monitors. Thus its a safe choice to buy one these today if you cannot afford an Acer predator. For anybody who doesn't game at all, this is a no-brainer. This is the 2k monitor you have been looking for.

title: Great set of tubes!!
text:
Good extension tube set. It does the trick.

I'm new to macro and I had bought another set previous to the Movo, [[ASIN:B00PQ4WXKA FODSLR Red Metal Auto Focus Macro Extension Tube Set for Canon SLR Cameras CANON EF EF-S Lens]]. After spending a few hours with it, I noticed that the FODSLR could harm the equipment because the locking pin (the little pin that protrudes from the metal edge and is what prevents the lens from rotating) wasn't flush with the rim, and dented one of my lenses. However, this Movo has a much better design.

Pros:
1. Fairly solid construction. Yes, it's a plastic casing with metal (aluminum, I suppose) contacts with the body and lens. However, it holds the lens without bending or flexing (the max I've placed is Canon's 24-105mm F4).
2. Good design. As stated in the intro, the lens attaches and detaches from the tubes with ease. In my case, with the same ease as attaching and detaching a lens to the camera body. The release leaver is comfortable and easy to use. The contacts with the lens element and body elements (the pins that transmit information and allow for AF and metering) are either copper plated or gold plated (my money is on copper plated), which talk of longevity. Note, if you're new to macro (like I), the AF doesn't work well at this level of magnification, even if you spend hundreds on extension tubes.
3. Light weight and compact. These tubes will not be to hard to carry around.

Con:
The only slight downside with these tubes is that they rotate a bit. Once locked in place, they each can move a bit. Maybe a MM or something like that. However, this did not cause any issues when shooting, at least for me. It moved only when I "forced" it, not when I was focusing (think, zoom lens after it reached its max extension and you want it to extend a bit more type torque).

Happy shooting

title: Very clever design but sound isn't the best.
text:
Really clever design with the removable battery that can be used by itself to power/charge other devices through USB. It is stylish and well made with a lot of attention to detail. Although not waterproof it would probably stand up to some moisture. The DC charging and Aux. In ports have a rubber plug that seems to seal pretty well. The top buttons are also rubber and look to resist a light mist. The most vulnerable part is the USB ports on the removable battery. No protection there.

The 2600mAH removable battery can be charged with the included USB cable. A little short but it works. To charge the internal battery I had to plug in the included AC adapter. There are two rows of lights on top to tell you the battery levels of each separately. A thoughtful feature. The Bluetooth took more than a few tries to pair but that is probably more my phone than this speaker.

Now for the not-so-good. The sound is thin and lacks depth. I didn't expect much but I have other speakers of this power and size that sound a lot better on the bottom end. Using an equalizer helped a little but there just isn't much there. That's OK for convenience but my ears tired quickly of the lack of bass and somewhat edgy mid/highs.

I gave it 4 stars mostly because of the innovative, compact design, reasonably priced and build quality. I wouldn't go so far as to say the sound is bad, just that I have heard better from other portable speakers. But, if you want the other features and are not too picky about sound quality, this iHome may be for you.

text:
Update: Anker's customer service is aggressively helpful, meaning they will help you whether you want them to or not! I received an email a day or two after posting this review. The rep told me "Regarding the play time, please understand that the playtime varies according to volume level and audio content. But normally, the play time is around 6hrs at 60% volume." They advertise 8 hours of battery life at least 5 times in their listing but never once explain this caveat. They did insist on sending me a replacement pair to solve the crackling issue if I confirmed the serial number and my address. I was not interested in receiving another pair as I am not overly impressed with the quality. After three emails asking me for my info, I finally caved simply so they would stop emailing me. I received the replacement pair as promised. Sound quality and battery life are the same but I haven't yet noticed crackling. I have now received three MORE emails asking me to update my review. I had no idea a simple review of $30 headphones would become such a big part of my life. Now please stop emailing me!

Bought these as a replacement for my JayBird headphones which were starting to have battery life issues after a couple years of daily use. These definitely don't have the same caliber of sound quality and the battery does not last 8 hours. They seem to last about 6 hours at best. There is also some crackling issues with the sound from time to time, maybe once or twice a day. They are okay as a cheap alternative but I'll probably splurge on another pair of high quality earbuds soon.

The product itself is very portable, and very comfortable to hold despite its all metal casing. There's a nice weight to it, which makes it not feel cheap. The speaker has a tactile base which prevents shaking and stays in place well.

Bluetooth is easy to setup and syncs automatically. Like the audio-out feature just in case you're low on battery and still want to use the device.

Design is very cute with Hello Kitty on the side of the speaker and a bow on the grill

There are volume up/down, play/pause on the device just in case you don't want to unlock your phone/bluetooth enabled device to enable to those functions. I just wish there was a track selection (forward/back button) on the device

The speaker can get very loud, but there's a set volume limit so kids won't blast the music and ruin their ears. The volume controls on the device goes as loud as the set volume on the bluetooth enable device. For example, if you put the volume on your smart phone half way, that will be the max output the speaker will make on it's on board controls. .

Love the cute beep sound indicators it makes when reached high volume or when sync is complete

Sound quality is very good with no distortions at high volume. Very impressed with the feature set seeing how small the device is.

I'm very impressed on what this speaker can do.
