Then to proceed to shut my vehicle off and put in aux, then wait for radio to start up, then start my vehicle again, and then find that the radio would not play sound; only the bluetooth and aux port would play music. I diagnosed the radio function not playing music issue to the fact that the radio does not like the cold weather (works after it warms up). Also making an educated guess as to why the radio does not start up unless put into aux, I'd say the radio doesn't have a stellar (cheap resistor) resistor to protect it from power "surge" or "discharge" from the starter pulling all the amps away from the battery while cranking the engine. This makes the radio surge or start up protector (really just a electrical reader that "checks" for voltage using the ground connection, it also will supposedly save the radio if the ground wire suddenly breaks) think there is not enough volts/amperage to work the radio so it does not power up. It works, but you have to figure out how to baby it to make it work which I don't have time for. Also I feel like it won't last long if it already has functionality issues. Guess i'll just have to spend the extra $40 for a slightly better one!

title: and like other reviewers I was overall satisfied with the product
text:
I have waited a bit to write a review to make sure it works, and like other reviewers I was overall satisfied with the product. Yes, the buttons are small, but it is not hard to turn off the alarm since the two alarms are on the opposite sides of the clock. It was not hard to setup at all if you read the manual, and the total process took about ten minutes. It has a nice test feature, so you can adjust the max brightness of your alarm, as well as the radio function which I enjoy.
The only thing, which may be a concern for some, is that I'm a very heavy sleeper and the light alone does not wake me up. Now you might say 'but wait, isn't the whole point of this alarm clock to have a gradual light to wake you up gently so you feel refreshed and peaceful?!'. Yes. But for those of us who sleep like rocks, even a brightly lit room isn't enough. It has been about a week of waking up at 5am, and still only the radio feature makes me wake up, and not the lamp itself. I have it on max brightness, directly facing my bed, and still nothing.
I still find this alarm useful, because I find that I spring out of bed when the room is well lit, so it does make getting up easier when it is still dark out. I'm hoping that after a month or so usage of this light, I will become more sensitive to it so I will wake up as 'gradually' as others describe.

Conclusion: Is this a good product? Yes. Could I have done the same thing with a desk lamp and a timer and not spent 100$? Yes. For those of you who are REALLY heavy sleepers, you may want to test the light alarm method out first on a cheaper product before you go full sunrise imitation alarm clock.

title: Just wait for DOCSIS 3.1
text:
As stated below, someone showed screenshots showing that the DOCSIS security is disabled on these modems. That person that posted the photos made that thread on Nov. 1, after all the connectivity problems had supposedly been sorted out with Comcast. This suggests to me that all the bugs have not been ironed out yet, and that this puppy isn't ready for mass deployment just yet. It's always a good practice to give new things time to mature a bit. The problem with that is that with DOCSIS 3.1 just around the corner, by the time that comes I'd recommend to people looking to upgrade to just wait for that instead if they already have a solid solution in place already. So I don't see this model really being an informed decision.

If you need an immediate solution get the SB6183 instead. It's a great modem and has been time tested and proven by now. And quite honestly although the 6190 in theory should out-perform it, in actual real world testing I've seen very little difference between the two in benchmarking. You could run 10 different tests and have each win 5 times, with every result, again, being very minute in differential. There could be a variety of reasons for this. Aforementioned kinks yet to be worked out. Most areas not supporting 32 channels anyhow. The unfortunate degradation that comes with the territory of cable internet from house to house as you distance yourself from the source. Many or all of the above...

I don't give it a 1 because these are well made, quality modems. My favorite in fact, and a testament to the beauty of simplicity... just one RJ-45 jack in the back for an ethernet cord, the cable outlet, and slot for power cord. I don't like the all-in-1 solutions, I like to have an independent, dedicated router. I just don't see this particular model being a wise buy for reasons mentioned above. The day Arris Surfboard's line releases a DOCSIS 3.1 modem I'll be keeping a close eye on it. Again, I will first lurk in the bushes until I can confirm that it's all clear before tossing my hard earned money at it. This is always wise to do and it looks like many here have failed to do so.

title: It just works.
text:
I don't think I've ever experienced such a simple set-up process for a router since my first AirPort Extreme. I always assumed "the other" routers in general would never become as easy to set up and use. I held on to my 5 year old airport for as long as I could, but unfortunately the range wasn't reaching a new and critical part of our house. So I started doing tons and tons of research trying to find the best router replacement. I came across "mesh routers" and discovered how popular they are for people with coverage problems. I then did even more research trying to find the best mesh router that wasn't astronomically expensive. I initially ignored the Velop because of it's high price, but kept it in the back of my head because of the strong performance it offered in comparison to the majority of it's competitors. I started to become dead set on getting the Netgear Orbi, because of it's high performance and the fact that it was on sale during Black Friday. I kept hesitating though because I'm not a fan of Netgear products and became worried that the quality and experience of the product might not live up to my standards. Then I casually looked again at the Velop and was shocked to see the new sale price on Black Friday and immediately pulled the trigger.

Set up took no longer than 30 minutes. The companion app did it's job well and everything was up and running like nothing ever changed. (I kept the same wifi name and password as my old router and everything reconnected.) I immediately noticed the speed and range differences throughout the house. I'm now getting between 200-300 mbps throughout all of my house. Even in my backyard. I pay for 300mbps down 20mbps up.

I did have to restart the modem and routers once since I've had it because I was getting abnormally slow speeds, but I'm not sure if it was the router or my internet providers fault. We'll see with time how often this occurs. So far though, It's just a set it and forget product. Like how they all should be.

I'm a happy camper with better range and faster speeds. I'm definitely happy that I skipped the Orbi and went with the Velop.

title: Decent speakers on a low budget
text:
I've had these burned in for around 80-100 hours so far, and to me they're really just "ok' speakers. They're not bad, but they don't really seem to really excel at anything either. Maybe expectations were just too high because of the very high rating they received here.

The main thing they seem to have had going for them was the price, though it seems they went up to $120 now at the time I'm writing this review. The prices on speakers seem to fluctuate pretty heavily, and these are the cheapest 2.0 speakers I currently own. I wouldn't pay or recommend paying $120 for these, but they may be a decent choice at like $80. TBH I haven't tested many speakers at that price range.

At first listen, It seems like Micca aimed for a more monitor type sound with these, as opposed to the the more normal bookshelf speakers. However, the clarity really falls short for monitors. They simply don't sound very clean compared to the other monitors I have (M-Audio BX5a and Yamaha HS5m), and the separation is lacking from a monitor standpoint as well. They do however have a clean sound and overall better separation compared to regular 2.0 desktop speakers I have/had (Simple Audio Listen and AudioEngine A2). They may very well be comparable to lower end monitors, though I don't own any to compare with.

As bookshelf speakers PB42X are severely lacking in bass. I don't mind the lack of low bass and sub bass since I always connect my 2.0 speakers to a sub anyways. However mid bass is severely lacking, and almost feels hollow especially for 4" drivers. Before going to watch Furious 7, I re-watched the other 6 Fast and Furious movies while switching though different speakers and headphones, and couldn't help but notice that these were absolutely terrible for any sort of action scenes because there's just no impact. The other smaller 3" driver speakers I have/had did significantly better at both mid bass and lower bass.

As a final note, The PB42X isn't especially compact either, but I did like the simple clean looks and magnetic grilles. It's just hard to recommend these when the Monoprice clone of the M-Audio BX5 was recently on sale for $100, and those speakers are much better sounding.

title: Actual Factory Refurbished Router in Fantastic Condition!
text:
I researched high and low for the right router. I decided the Linksys EA7300 met all my needs with solid reviews. Face it, all reviews for every router has some people saying that it didn't work, drops connections, has poor support etc etc. I have a lot of experience with these things and am quite comfortable setting them up.

This router came in a sealed box with seals that said "factory refurbished" etc. Now here's the thing about "refurbished"; if they're just "seller refurbished" it probably means that the item was examined for obvious visual damage and then plugged in to see if it appears to be working. In other words, they just check to see if works or not. A genuine "factory refurb" goes back to the factory and actually receives 2 quality control checks in its lifetime. If it's given a thumbs up by them, there's a good chance it will work perfectly for years.

When you receive this router, do a hard factory reset by holding in the reset button on the back for at least 10 seconds or until the Linksys light starts to blink. You may need to do a few of these to get into the factory setup page on your web browser at IP 192.168.1.1. Linksys software is pretty good at automatically setting up your router to get it up and running. I had some difficulty because I'm running it behind my Uverse modem/router. After a few resets, I had to go into my Uverse router and look up the IP it was assigning to the new Linksys router to get into its setup. Once there, I was able get things configured just the way I like.

One word of advise... You need to be fairly competent in setting up networking equipment to get them up and running properly, especially if you have a variety of devices connecting to it. I'm convinced that most negative reviews on routers (of all brands) are user error or due to improper configuration. Everything in your network has to be on the same page and talking the same language in order for everything to work properly. Once you have a sold setup, everything should work properly, especially if you keep the router in a cool location where it can easily broadcast its signal.

title: Great motherboard. Meh manual.
text:
Motherboard is beautiful with plenty of overclocking options.
The manual that comes with it, however, is rather terrible as it doesn't give you information you should really know like:

The extra 4pin power connector by the CPU and the extra 6pin connector by the PCIe slots are optional and only there for use in extreme builds with lots of extra needed voltage. The 4pin for extra juice to the CPU and the 6pin for extra power to the PCIe slots in case you're using 3-4 of overclocked GPUs.

EDIT: It took me a while to get it, but I can now confirm that installing anything in the M.2 slots won't impact your PCIe lanes but will instead just take over the lanes the SATAe ports would be using. This means you can install your beefy GPUs and M.2 drives without worry. Just check the manual for what SATA ports you'll still have available for other drives.

The BIOS is great and easy to navigate. You can set up fan curves easily though there aren't any pre-made profiles to choose from.
I appreciate having so many on-the-board buttons for things like power, reset, and even overclocking. Though my personal preference is to always do my overclocking through the bios.

The only real "defect" on my board was the plastic connector on OC Panel was really tight and it was really difficult to pull off. But other than that, it's a solid board that's beautiful and unlike anything on the market right now.

For those of you that care about color coordination, the board has several on-board lights. There's green in the display readout, red in the audio chip and separation line, blue near the power connections. There's a lot going on. My dives into the BIOS haven't revealed any way to turn any of these off. But I'll come back and edit this if I end up finding something.

If you're willing to pay more than double what you might pay for a motherboard, you'll get a motherboard unlike anything seen before. A metallic white with black style is unheard of. So if you really want a board that has that "wow factor" while still providing all the enthusiast options an overclocker would want, then this might be the board for you.

title: COMPLETELY UNUSABLE for a single ISP-connection setup. TOTAL GARBAGE!
text:
This router might be great for a dual-ISP network setup, but it is virtually unusable for a normal single-ISP setup. I have a small business. For years I had cable internet that topped out at 80 Mbps, and I ran a very similar router with dual-wan ports made by Linksys (owned by Cisco). I only had it connected to my single cable-modem and it worked like a dream. In fact it still works like a dream, but I need a new router, because...

Recently we upgraded to Verizon fios. Now we have a 750 Mbps ISP connection and the old router is a major bottleneck. This router has most of the same features, it's made by Cisco (the parent company), it was an easy sell. But then...

Setup was easy, plug it in turn it on, good to go, right? Wrong. Long story short, the thing never gave me a working connection to the Internet. I was able to log into the router itself, but no matter how much I tried to tweak the settings, it simply never recognized the ethernet connection to my cable modem. I spent hours Googling and found years of other people having the same trouble. Nobody had a solution that worked for me.

Finally, I gave in and I called Cisco tech support. When the first thing their support guy told me was that "I have tech support for 1 year under my warranty (he made me verify the router's serial # first, btw) – but I need to create a Cisco customer account so he can open a support ticket for my issue" ... well, I just about lost my mind. I was like, "Wait, this isn't a warranty issue. I can power the router and log into the admin, but it fails to recognize the network connection no matter what I do - and I've found countless others on Google with the same problem. You can't just walk me through some steps to make this work?" ..."No sir, we must first open a ticket then a technician will follow up with you."

Yeah, I told him this was complete garbage and I was returning the router to Amazon. That's what I did.

Right now my old router is still plugged into that same cable modem, with not a single configuration change mind you, and it works great. If not for the fact that it still throttles us to 100 Mbps I'd never change it - but alas, now I must continue shopping for a good gigabit router.

If you don't literally have a dual-wan ISP arrangement, DO NOT MAKE THE SAME MISTAKE I DID. This thing is garbage for most people's network setup, tech support is useless, and you'll never figure out how to get it working in the admin settings. Keep shopping. Period.

I like this monitor enough to own two of them now (bought one in 2014 and another in 2015). It is inexpensive, lightweight (for a wall-mounted multi-monitor rack; I'm a developer and I like to have coding screens open along with output screens), and good looking. I haven't had any problems with backlight color, bleed, or uneven-ness, so I'm pleased overall.

However, the monitor I bought in June 2015 has updated firmware that's has an annoying problem. I use an ultra-low power system (Rasberry Pi) on a secondary input (HDMI) for times when I want to look something up or check email without running my workstation. Normally my workstation goes to sleep and all the monitors go to sleep including the Asus VS228 monitors. The newest one, however, detects that there is still something active plugged into HDMI and instead of going to sleep, it switches input to the Pi. This means not only does the monitor stay on instead of going into low power mode, I also have to manually switch it back to DVI mode every time I wake the workstation from sleep.

Auto input switching should be an optional feature instead of something we can't change. For now I'm back to using the older Asus monitor with the secondary input, and I'm trying to get reliable power saving mode working on the Pi, but it's still annoying that the monitor doesn't respect the mode it is in. I understand it's designed as a feature so that users don't have to switch modes when a new system is turned on or plugged in, but we should be able to turn that off.

title: Good value for a short tube refractor
text:
I bought this telescope for two main reasons. One, I wanted a short tube refractor to take with me when I go camping so I can get wide-field views of the sky, as well as correct-image terrestrial viewing, while still having the ability to examine the moon and planets when they're in the sky. Two, I liked the alt-az mount with slow-motion controls, and because of the way the mount is designed, I plan on modifying my other refractor, a 70mm Orion w/ a longer focal length but crappier mount, by creating a detachable dovetail mount that can be used with this mount. I tested everything out, and it all works very well.

Of course, a short focal length this short means you're going to have some chromatic aberration if you're not spending the money on an apochromatic refractor. There's only so much that can be done about that. But, for what it is, this telescope seems like an excellent value, and it certainly works well enough for my needs.

One other point: this can be mounted on any standard photographic tripod capable of supporting its weight. The telescope is actually pretty light, so if you don't need the slow motion controls, you can carry a lightweight photo tripod with you instead.

title: More like an Android tablet with keyboard, pen, and full fledged Chrome browser
text:
HARDWARE:
- ARM CPU is fast enough.
- Full aluminum body is nice, but does not feel overly premium.
- Convertible, works as laptop, tablet, and tent.
- Screen is brilliant. 4:3 aspect ratio with 2400x1600 resolution. Bright and super sharp.
- Keyboard and touchpad are just OK. Both feel a bit cheap.
- Pen works fine, has palm rejection, but there is some input lag.
- SD card slot is a necessity since on board storage is really low.
- USB-C only (for peripherals and charging).
It's actually a brilliant package. Samsung cut costs where it did not matter too much and delivered an excellence overall experience for a low price. I thought the pen is just a nice bonus, but I use it all the time. Like it much more than the touchpad or using the finger on the screen. I also use the tablet and tent options more often than I thought. Especially when just reading though some documents (or commenting on documents with the pen). USB-C charging means that I can use my car charger, external battery and smartphone charger to charge it. It also means that I cannot simply connect a mouse or projector to it. That is just a matter of time though - USB-C makes it future proof, and you can get dongles for the old USB standard, HDMI, etc.

SOFTWARE:
- Full fledged chrome browser in the super safe Chrome OS environment.
- First Chromebook to officially support Android apps.
Basically this means that it is a super secure Android tablet with a full Chrome browser - so you can use all extensions (AdBlock!) and all web apps. (there are many web apps -- for example video conference systems -- that do not work on Android's Chrome browser)
The Play Store with all Android apps works extremely well. There are still a few rough edges, especially in tablet portrait mode, but this will be taken care of in the coming months. The Play Store is still labeled "beta".
With the addition of Android apps, you have full video playback support, professional file managers, photo editing software. This drastically changes the capabilities of Chromebooks in general.

PLUS vs PRO
The Pro version of the Samsung Chromebook has an Intel i3 CPU. This one has an ARM chip. While the i3 should be faster in normal operation in Chrome OS, the ARM chip is actually superior for Android apps since most apps are optimized for the ARM architecture. Battery lifetime on the ARM version is also extremely good.

This laptop will not replace your windows machine if you are doing professional programming, video or photo editing, ... but this small flexible thing is also way more versatile and capable than you average Chromebook.

title: No one is more surprised than me to find that I do not like this device
text:
To begin with, understand that I am very pro-Amazon. My account is decades old, I buy all of my digital media from them, I have owned every generation of Kindle Fire and one generation of the Kindel E-reader before that. And so no one is more surprised than me to find that I do not like this device. I do not like it to the extent that I am returning it, something I don't recall ever doing to ANYTHING I've purchased from Amazon.

To be clear, I am reviewing the 10.1" version of the 3rd generation Kindle Fire (Fire HD 10). A couple of my complaints probably will not apply to the smaller screens of this generation.

Here are the issues I have with the device:

1) The new interface is just terrible.
- It is clumsy, illogical and a step backwards from any previous generation of device.
- Rather than the carousel plus a home screen the user had complete control over, we now have a cluttered mess of a page with all the application icons on it. You cannot hide or delete Amazon applications or links. You CAN create groups however, and so to stop the brain hurt from looking at all that clutter I created a "junk" group and dragged all the Amazon icons in to it.
- Speaking of those Amazon icons that clutter the screen. Most of them are pointless. You access the exact same functions from the menu at the top. The exception is photos which, inexplicably, are not a menu option.
- The whole interface experience gives a "buy more stuff from us!" feeling. Now, I understand fully that Amazon sells these things at a loss with the intent to use them to sell you more stuff, and I am OK with that. But in the past Amazon has done a fairly masterful job of balancing that while avoiding throwing it in your face.

2) The most unforgivable sin in my book is that text is not sharp. It seems that the pixel density is just not sufficient to provide clear, sharp text either in the e-reader app, in the browser, or in the Facebook app. As a result, each character has a soft edge. It is minor, but noticeable. And annoying.

3) Slow app startup. It would sometimes take many seconds to switch apps or launch new ones. Facebook in particular would routinely be nothing but a white screen for 5 or six seconds.

4) It turns out there is such a thing as too large. I found the device awkward to hold. This is 100% user preference and I did not dock points from Amazon for it, but it is something I learned about myself. My 2nd Generation 8.9" Fire is the PERFECT size, it turns out.

All of that being said, there were some good things:

1) Despite text being a problem, video is PHENOMENAL. As sharp and clear as you could possibly want. And the large screen size is great for this.

2) Despite the larger size, it weighs less than my 8.9" Fire. I find that impressive.

In conclusion, this new generation of Fire (at least the 10.1") has a cheap feel and regressive interface design. I get the distinct feeling it was rushed to market. As an engineer myself, I also sense this device was designed more by the finance department than it was the engineering department.

title: So frustrating! USB 3. 1 doesn't mean USB ...
text:
So frustrating! USB 3.1 doesn't mean USB C. USB C doesn't mean USB 3.1. You can have USB 3.1 over USB Standard-A connectors. A Type-A connector can work for USB 3.1, USB 3.0, USB 2.0, USB 1.1, USB 1.0... USB Type-C is merely a connector type, no different than Mini USB, Micro USB, Type-A, or Type-B. Likewise, a device with a Type-C connector doesn't necessarily run USB 3.1.
Manufacturers aren't making things easier for consumers to navigate this by using the terms interchangeably as if they're synonymous. If you're going to make a 3.1 hub, why would you have 3.0 ports? Is that mislabeling and you mean they're Type-A USB 3.1 or are you really running multiple USB protocols?

The first month I had this in the driveway it worked very well. I had lots of visitors, and it was a big help to be alerted that they had arrived. Occasionally something else would set off the alarm, presumably some kind of wildlife; once a heavy rainstorm set off the alarm. After the first month it seemed to go off repeatedly. I could not see, from the window, what was setting it off. I tried moving it around, in case it was tree branches waving in the wind, but it didn't seem to help. I finally took it down because the false alarms were a nuisance. Now I just use it inside to frighten anyone who might break in when I'm not home. Overall, it wasn't worth the price. It was only helpful for a month, and now I can't use it outside. Maybe it isn't as weatherproof as they say it is? Who knows.
They sent me a replacement and so far it seems to work ok outdoors. However, I'm getting tired of the false alarms caused by birds and who knows what other animals at night. I may only use it indoors now, as an alarm to startle anyone who walks in the door while I'm not at home. Originally had bought it to alert me to family member getting out of bed unassisted at night. Ok for that purpose, but the need has passed so I can't speak much to that use. I had a great deal of trouble understanding their instructions, which are written in poorly translated English.

title: Sturdy, works well, would recommend
text:
The build quality on this feels pretty good. I wish it were water- and sand-proof, as it would be a great boat radio, but it's small enough to put in a sandwich-size Ziploc or a small dry box for temporary waterproofness. Fairly lightweight at half a pound, though ultralight backpackers will be disappointed. Definitely not much to add into a backpack for the school or office or in a tote bag for the beach. We wanted it to be easy to find if all we had was moonlight, so we got it in yellow, which is a nice canary yellow, not a blinding chartreuse.

You're not going to bring down the house with the quality of FM tunes from the built-in speaker, but the sound quality is plenty good enough to understand sports broadcasts and, most importantly, NOAA weather broadcasts. You could always plug in an external speaker to the headphone jack if sound quality is a concern.

The crank is easy to use, though the handle could stand to be a bit longer. The crank tucks up underneath the unit, if you were wondering where it is. Just a few cranks and it'll run for a while. The solar charger is very sensitive: I had it in the middle of a room with the blinds open and it was picking up a small charge! I'm really satisfied with the off-the-grid power backups.

Although it doesn't come with a charger, it charges off of micro-USB, and chances are good you already have a micro USB charger. Many small electronics, including Kindles and most Android devices, are powered on micro USB. If you don't have a micro USB charger, you can pick one up pretty cheaply here on Amazon or at pretty much any store.

On to the USB power out (phone charger): it doesn't work well for power-hungry smartphones. Instead of relying on the built-in battery to charge off of it, you have to use the crank, and you can't keep your phone on to check on progress (which is super slow). Don't rely on this thing to power your smartphone through week-long hiking trips or your arm might fall off. Not bad on less power-hungry devices like dumbphones or e-ink readers.

The flashlight is good and bright. Didn't expect any disappointment there.

All around a great little device, and cheap and small enough to keep one in your car, office, or wherever you might want emergency weather updates.

title: Don't be mislead by the "extra bass" label
text: For what it offers with regards to sound, I believe this speaker belongs in the sub-$50 range. It's not grossly overpriced, but I do feel like the XB10s include a small premium for brand recognition when you can get better value elsewhere. The extra bass marketing is definitely a stretch. While the bass is loud relative to the balance of mids and highs, it sounds completely flat. Above 50% volume, low tones sound are clipped and unclear. There's little resonance at the low frequencies at any decent listening range. Had Sony omitted the bass branding, I would've thought it was just an average speaker with poor bass. But the "extra bass" is ironically the worse part of the speaker sound-wise. Otherwise, the feature set is adequate, if not above average for the price. Range is decent, though not impressive by any measure. One gripe I had with range was that sometimes the connection would clip when the speaker was upright, but would suddenly reconnect if I turned the speaker on its side, or vice versa. I just felt like though the range was decent, it was inconsistent. Battery life and charge time are fine. Media / phone controls are nice to have, and NFC is an added bonus. The directional stand included is nice as a hook, but I think fails at its main goal. It's almost entirely flat, meaning the speaker is pointed at your chest or arms if placed on a normal height desk. I feel like the stand should point the speaker slightly up, although this is a minor complaint considering the stand itself is more of an added bonus than an essential component to the speaker. The build is not stellar, but I would consider it comfortable. The soft touch material is comfortable and grippy, and it feels like I can drop it without having a major scare (although I wouldn't recommend it obviously). I like that it's splash proof so I don't have to worry about stuff like shower steam ruining the device. Overall, I'd say it's a 4 star level product that's been dragged down a notch by misleading marketing as well as overall disappointing sound. Reviewers have called this the loudest small form factor speaker, but honestly if volume is an issue for you you should consider getting a slightly larger speaker. The JBL flip series is maybe 50% larger, but sound quality and volume aren't even comparable. You'd shell out $10-20 extra depending on where you get it, but the XB10 simply straddles an uncomfortable middle ground between volume and size. It's not quite a tiny portable speaker, but it's also not large enough to comfortably fill a room. Go either smaller or larger to fit your needs rather than trying this product out as a middle ground.

text:
This is all preliminary, but after my first outdoor experience with the Sonys, they only dropped sound 2-3 times for a 40-minute dog walk. That works for me. In the house, no dropouts. Connected to an iPhone 6-Plus. Very comfortable. I have asymmetrical ear canals, so using a smaller Sony tip on the right ear, medium on the left. Sound is very good. Audiophile? Don't think so, but plenty good for BT and wireless. I only rated it 4 stars for the lack of a volume control, and it seems the volume doesn't work when the phone is locked. Have to take a look at that, I mean when using the phone volume buttons. Also, volume is a bit limited, but that's fine with me, loud enough. Depends on the track too. Older rips need more of a sound boost, prior to the loudness wars!

If these continue to hold up re cutouts/dropouts, they will be a keeper. Comfort is great if you choose the right tips. I have owned plenty of deep insertion IEMs, including the Ety ER4P, and I have a pair of custom Jerry Harvey IEMs, JH5s, and so the deep insertion is not an issue for me.

As far as the Headphone Connect app, the NC feature seems to make very little difference. But since they seal very well, doesn't matter much to me.

Update: Sorry to say, the phones are going back. Took an extended walk today and several dropouts from the right phone/both earpieces. Had my phone in sweatshirt pocket, and if that's the cause, or turning my head, they don't suit my purposes. Also, after extensive listening indoors today, the dropouts were not an issue with my phone on the table, but the SQ ... meh. I think the Optoma Nuforce BE2s sound better for $50. I know, doesn't make sense. But the ears never lie, and maybe mine are defective. And just as an FYI, I also tried the Nuforce BE Free8 and returned them as well. Same wireless type, but even worse dropouts. Nuforce graciously offered a second pair as a return, but I am thinking that this technology just isn't there yet. These early models all seem to suffer a bit from that dropout issue, whatever the cause. And while I don't expect true high-end sound performance from BT phones, the $50 BE2s sound just as good for a lot less money. If I want great SQ from in-ears, I guss I will stick with the JH5 customs or even my pair of Westone W20s, both wired and both superior to the Sonys, sorry to say. I just finished a trip to France, 8-hour flight, and the Westones with custom tips were in my ears the entire time, great sound, noise isolation and comfort.

title: Pay attention to dates of reviews!
text:
From the product photos, the strap has been redesigned. Older reviews will be for the older design, and will be less reliable with respect to the newer design. For reference, I've included a photo of one of the older straps. I've included some important information below.

This review is for the older design, so is less reliable for the current model.

*** Background: ***

This was included when I purchased the Garmin Forerunner 220 with heart rate monitor (bundle). It has two parts: A chest strap, which has the electrodes (skin contact pads), and an electronics pod. The pod is removed when not in use.

*** Review: ***

I found it very comfortable. When I was running, at first, it worked well in both dry weather and in rain. But, I had the same 2 problems other reviewers have reported: The strap had a short life, and the electronics pod was difficult to open in order that the battery be changed.

****** Important information, for both old and new model ******

For longer life, be sure and follow Garmin's use and care instructions. When washing the strap, put it in a washing bag. If you don't have a washing bag, use a sock, but close the sock with a rubber band or something. To loosen the screws, use a #0 Phillips driver. It looks too big, but it is the correct one.

The strap will eventually wear out. If the electronics pod is still good, you can buy a replacement strap without the pod.

This can transmit battery status. Check your receiving device to see if it is available. It may save you from unnecessarily opening it to check the battery.

*** Probably more than you want to know: ***

After less than a year's use*, it began working poorly. The 220 showed either the wrong heart rate, or no heart rate. I suspected a weak battery in the HRM. I found the battery cover screws hard to remove, even when using what I thought was a properly sized jeweler's screwdriver. One of the screws was harder to remove than the other 3, and was damaged by my attempts to remove it. I did finally get to the battery, which tested as good.

The cause of the failure seems to be the strap.

Suggestion for Garmin: Include a bag suitable for using when this is machine washed.

*I had it for 1 & 1/3 year, running at most every other day, with a 7 month lay off before it seemed to fail.

title: A beautiful, big, tilting, pivoting, ultra-bright marvel.
text:
In moving from my old 24" LCD to this ViewSonic 27" LED monitor, I'm struck by the massive differences between the two technologies. Of course, LED is still LCD tech, but the difference in lighting has a profound effect on the visual quality. It also has an effect on the ease of calibration. The old LCD is generally darker, with a bit of a yellow hue to all colors. When I put the monitors side-by-side, the "blue" on the LCD isn't as deep and true as the blue on the LED. However, when it comes to setting contrast on the two monitors, the LCD is a bit easier, as the LED lighting of the ViewSonic is very strong, very bright, and almost unwilling to be toned down a bit. In the end, the LED looks better, but certainly blares much brighter whites. For me, with light-sensitivity issues, this is a minor problem as I end up with tired eyes after looking at all the white backgrounds on web pages, which leads me to ask: WHY do so many web pages use flat white as a background? Why not a muted off-white, light grey, or something that doesn't burn out your retinas?

All that aside, the ViewSonic XG2701 is a lot of monitor. 27" on the desktop looks quite big! Once you get the hang of calibration, the screen is gorgeous, and the monitor certainly has enough different viewing modes-- everything from the standard movie/web/plain modes to a selection of gaming modes designed for different types of games-- that you're sure to find a built-in setting that makes whatever you're looking at look the way you want it. Even so, I still encourage Windows users to go through Windows color calibration by selecting Display Settings / Advanced Display Settings / Color Calibration with a right-click on your desktop. Trust me, it will be worth it.

I was exceptionally pleased with the pedestal included with this monitor. It allows tilting, raising, and lowering. You can easily pivot the monitor to a portrait mode if you so desire, and with the LED lighting it doesn't fade out or suffer image quality problems when tilted. This is excellent for word processing, reading books, and other things that benefit from being able to see a whole page at once. The pedestal also comes with a cable management ring (separate in the box, and you have to attach it yourself) that works very well to keep all the cables managed, and a headphone hook. This latter item is a clever innovation that I wish more monitor stands would include, even though I had to use a tool to actually pry it out of the housing the first time (it was really stuck in there!) it now holds my Corsair headset handily out of the way.

This monitor has two HDMI ports, a DisplayPort, a mini DisplayPort, and an input for USB 3.0 that allows you to use the built in 2 USB 3.0 ports (on the back/bottom) and the 2 USB 2.0 ports (on the left side). It's always nice to get a bonus USB 3.0 hub out of your monitor. I mean, it's already on your desk, so it just makes sense to add this feature. I'm grateful for it.

The advanced features like black stabilization, low input lag, and AMD FreeSync Technology all have their place, as well. I'm currently using a GeForce card with this monitor, so the AMD FreeSync Technology isn't active and I'm unable to properly review that, but the black stabilization is very handy. It basically fixes black levels in games so that when you're in a dark scene, you can still distinguish different objects in the room. The effect isn't as jarring as just cranking up the gamma (You know who you are, gamma-crankers!) and it comes in handy from time to time. The high refresh rate is noticeable in fast-action games, like GTA V, Need For Speed, etc. and it serves to prevent blurring. This has a positive effect (easier to see objects in game) but also a weird sort-of-negative effect in that my eyes are just not used to it, and it makes things look a bit less realistic sometimes. I suspect as I get used to it, my eyes will adjust. Remember, I'm used to an old LCD screen!

All in all, I give this high marks. I can't say it's perfect because I find the calibration of this monitor a bit difficult with the multi-button panel you have to manipulate, and I am generally displeased with the engineers' decision to put all the input ports facing down, making them harder to connect than if they were facing back. Seriously, you either have to bring the monitor to the edge of the desk and get on your knees, or pick the monitor up and tilt it back to get at the ports. Why do monitors not take a cue from HDTVs when it comes to port access?

So I'm calling this a four-star "I like it" item. It borders on five "I love it" stars, but since Amazon doesn't allow half-stars, we'll have to leave it here at four. I recommend this monitor to anyone looking to upgrade or buy a new monitor. You'll be pleased, for sure.

UPDATE 03/2016 -- I discovered that my ASUS STRIXX GTX 970 wasn't playing nice with this monitor over DisplayPort. The monitor would choose not to wake up after sleep or shutdown sometimes. After some research I learned that the GTX 970 series of graphics cards are known for this issue sometimes, and that a firmware update to the graphics card (not the monitor) will fix the issue. If you're having similar troubles with this monitor over DisplayPort, look to the graphics card's manufacturer for a firmware update. It should take care of the problem.

title: Wi-Fi is trash - STAY AWAY
text:
There is something fundamentally broken with this router (WRT AC3200). Not sure if it’s hardware or software related. But the Wi-Fi performance on this thing was absolute GARBAGE after about 4-5 months of use. Initially it was good. But it quickly became nearly unusable. Frequent signal drops requiring reboot. And even when it was “working”, the speed was very poor. I expected something at least functional for $250.

Search the googles for Wi-Fi problems on this router and you’ll see it’s not an isolated incident. There appears to be a fundamental design problem that Linksys has not fixed. I tried every imaginable troubleshooting step and various configurations. Firmware is fully up to date as of this writing (12/30/2017).

I know the problem was with Wi-Fi on this router, because my PCs wired to the router via Ethernet cables had flawless full speed internet.

I gave up and threw it in the garbage.

I replaced this $250 Linksys paper weight with a $60 ASUS RT-ACRH13 Wi-Fi router that is now working beautifully and flawlessly, blanketing my house with strong and fast Wi-Fi signal for all of my devices.

The color choice is honestly pretty great for bargain shoppers, cause you can just pick the least popular (ahem, cheapest) color to save a few bucks.

Regarding speed: my next newest external HDD, about 6 years old now, doesn't support USB 3 like this does. The difference in backup and retrieval speed is like night and day, and is best reason I can think of to upgrade your external storage if you are still using one with old tech. I originally bought this to serve as an extra backup drive (since my oldest drives may be nearing end of life) but had I known what I was missing out on I would have picked it up sooner.

Windows 10 recognizes the capacity of this at 1.81 TB.

title: Simple, solid install for Sonos Playbar
text:
There's really not a whole lot to say about this. If you want to mount your Sonos Playbar to a wall, this is pretty much your only option. Fortunately, it's also a very good option. It provides enough mounting holes that you should be able to mount it to studs in just about any place where you have standard stud spacing. In my case, the place I needed to mount it happened to be the one place in the room where the builder opted to play fast and loose with stud spacing, making it impossible to mount to two studs in the area where I wanted the Playbar. No worries, the mount kit also includes wall anchors, so you can mount it into drywall alone if you need to.

The mount kit also includes a small level to help ensure that you get the mount plate installed correctly, but I found that the level I received was inaccurate. It would give different readings based on which side of the level you used, so there was really no way to know which side was correct. It's a nice gesture to include it, but if you already own a proper level, I'd recommend using that instead.

Finally, it's important to note that the mounting orientation is different depending on whether you're mounting the Playbar above or below your TV, and the mounting orientation is sort of the opposite of what you'd expect. Mounted below the TV, the power and optical cables from the Playbar exit from the bottom, and mounted above the TV, the cables exit from the top (i.e., in either orientation, the Playbar cables are naturally pointing away from the TV). This is to ensure that the speakers in the Playbar are firing in the correct direction (more up if below the TV, more down if above the TV). This could cause some issues with cable routing, but fortunately the Playbar and wall mount kit take steps to sufficiently address this. When wall-mounted, there is enough room behind the middle of the Playbar to route your cables; so even though the cables are naturally exiting away from the TV, you can still route them back behind the Playbar and toward your TV. I was a little worried about having to do this with the optical cable, since they don't usually handle sharp bends well, but this setup provides sufficient room to make that u-bend gently enough.

All in all, if you've got a Playbar and you want to put it on the wall, this is the thing you need.

title: Great Sounding Buds with a Quality Build at Budget-Friendly Price Point
text:
[[VIDEOID:d7629cbce533bc80e99942560c99ba95]] [[VIDEOID:5388525f96746bc9742b1d9896b15a88]] I was offered the SoundPEATS B10's [[ASIN:B016OF0IDI SoundPEATS B10 3.5mm Headphones In-ear Wired Earphones Earbuds - Black]], to perform a side-by-side comparison to the Panasonic HJE120 [[ASIN:B003EM8008 Panasonic RPHJE120K In-Ear Headphone, Black]]. Below (and, as offered in the video) is what I discovered.

Pros: Sturdy box with reserved, professional look; straight 3.5mm gold-plated connector; includes 3 sets of silicone buds (S,M--preinstalled,L); buds very comfortable and stayed in my ear when moving around; during unboxing thought the slightly longer housing might cause issues, however, it didn’t--that, and the decent-sized porthole under the silicone bud, allow for strong bass; cable has quality rubberized feel, thicker than the 120's; where wire enters housing is snug, but flexes--secure feel to it; well-built bud housing; SoundPEATS offers full-year warranty--better than other warranty lengths I’ve seen.

Cons: The box specifically calls out the B10 as the enclosed product. On one side of the box, the content listing notes a wired headphone, w/ inline mic/remote, and 3 buds; the other side of the box shows a graphic of a hand using an inline mic/control. This headset does not come w/ an inline mic/control. Packaging shouldn’t reflect something that isn’t accurate, IMHO. Please see General Comments about this issue.

General Comments: Regarding the box content list issue, it’s important to note the product description on Amazon’s site DOES NOT list the headphone as having an inline mic/remote. Therefore, while the packaging is incorrect (at least on the one I received), you are not purchasing this item thinking it has an inline remote/mic anyway. It’s just somewhat confusing to see it listed on the side of the box when the headphones arrive. This issue should not dissuade you from considering these buds. Something I do for all my buds, I ran an audio test using an audio-check site. As always, a good seal is crucial for good sound. Make sure to change buds to get the best sound. Results follow:

**Bass: Picked up at 20hz range. For little buds, it hit hard -- not make-your-eardrums-bleed hard; but hard nonetheless. The SoundPEATS did better here than the 120's.
**Treble: Picked up at 17khz-8khz. Minor distortion occurred at middle frequencies. Drivers compensated well, though, and sound cleaned up quick. This was the case for both the B10's and the 120's.
**Mids: As tested in a spectral flatness test, mids were not overly pronounced, but present--which seems to be the case in all buds I test in this price range.This was also the case for both the B10's and the 120's.
**Dynamic Range: Picked up sounds at, and slightly below, 66db below full scale. This was the case for both the B10's and the 120's.
**Quality (Bass-Shake Test): From lowest low to highest low, the B10s hit hard, clear, and consistently. They didn’t break at all through this fairly rigorous test. The 120's broke in the beginning and end of the test, but only initially. For the 120's, a break-in period might be needed.
**Driver-Matching: Sounds produced matched perfectly in both ear pieces for both earbuds.
**Wiring Test: Left and Right channel separation was perfect. Center and twisted test sounds occurred as described by the site, which is apparently good. This was the case for both the B10's and the 120's.
**Binaural Test: Both the B10's and the 120's passed this test w/ flying colors.
**Songs in General: Sound is subjective. I played a number of songs meant to test buds w/ combo of bass, mids, and highs. Both reproduced sounds well for buds in this price range--with what seems to be the v-shaped profile common to buds around this price point.

Recommended Purchase?: Yes. Five stars equates to “I Love It.” To love a set of headphones, they have to floor me. I’m not quite there; but, they are definitely way better than “It’s Okay.” I can say, without reservation, I’m feeling the four-star “I Like It” vibe for these headphones. These will be great on-the-go buds to shove in your backpack, for going to the gym (assuming wires won’t be an issue for you--if wires are a problem, check out BlueTooth buds instead), for hiking, biking, etc. The sound is good; and, for the sale price (especially if you have Prime free two-day shipping), you will not regret the purchase. Do I recommend purchasing the B10's over the 120's, the short answer is, yes, because of overall build quality and bass, where the B10's excel over the 120's.

Disclaimer: I don't work for the company for whom I wrote this product review. However, I did receive the product at a discount in exchange for a truthful review, which I strove to offer here. Stars are not bought or sold--a product receives the stars I believe it deserves. I only offer reviews for items I personally use and test. Please know I did the best I could at the time I wrote this review. I always welcome both constructive feedback (to make future reviews better) and all questions related to this review (to make it better and help where I can). I will try to address both as time allows, within a reasonable period from the date I posted the review. I'm a family man; so, my time isn't always my own. Thanks for understanding.

title: FINALLY a laptop that can handle the Adobe creative suite like a BOSS and CRUSH the competition (Yoga, XPS13 and Macbook etc)!!
text:
BUY THIS LAPTOP RIGHT NOW!!! JUST DO IT!! YOU WILL BE SO HAPPY YOU DID!! Ok if you need more of an explanation then read on...

Before I start, I want to point out that I bought this certified refurbished which made me a little nervous at first, but I'm SO GLAD I did!! It did not come in a fancy box, didn't include the pen or the leather sleeve or a big instruction manual, and it did have some very minor scratches on the HP logo (see pics), but I saved between $300-$400 and otherwise it works and looks just like new! To me it was a great decision and totally worth the money I saved. I highly recommend giving certified refurbished a try. You can always send it back if it arrives in a condition that you're unsatisfied with so what do you have to lose besides a lot of money by going straight for the new one!?

By way of background, I have not owned a laptop in nearly 10 years. I built an incredible custom workhorse PC for myself years ago and have just relied on it and on my iPad for on the go needs, but I've been wanting a laptop for years that can handle editing photo, audio and video using the Adobe suite (specifically Premiere Pro and After Effects). Anyone who has worked with Premiere or AE knows they require a beefy system and even the best laptops aren't usually built to handle the strain that these programs put on its resources. I have been keeping my eyes open for a THIN laptop that is finally up to the task and when the 8th generation (a big step up in terms of performance from the 7th gen) of this HP Spectre x360 came out, I knew it was the one for me. Two words people: QUAD CORE!!!!!! HALLELUJAH!! I have been using this laptop to edit in the Adobe suite for a couple weeks now and it is an absolute CHAMP! If you plan to use it for this purpose I do recommend setting playback to 1/2 instead of full resolution if you want completely smooth playback, and also to use an external SSD like I do to store all your project files so as not to bog down the C drive, but that being said, this machine really is a BEAST and I'm so incredibly in love with it!!

Besides the ability to edit with Adobe, the rest of the features are an absolute joy. This is my first purchase of a 2-in-1 and I have to say I will never go back!! I LOVE the touch screen!! Not only does it work incredibly well but the 4k display is just GORGEOUS!!! I've used it in all the different modes (presentation, tablet etc) and it switches back and forth automatically and flawlessly and has been SO USEFUL! I use a USB mouse with it for when I'm doing heavy editing because that's what I'm used to and work fastest with but for everything else, the track pad is huge and very sensitive/easy to use.

The backlit keyboard is spacious and beautiful and the key action is one of the best I've ever felt on a laptop. The port selection is practically perfect in my opinion. Also, it charges VERY quickly!! While it is a little heavier than some similar products, it also beats those out in the specs department by a long shot, so that's to be expected and I'd rather have the 4k display and a longer lasting battery than a slightly lighter machine. It's still so incredibly light for what it can do. It's also incredibly thin!! See my side by side comparison with a MacBook (which it also KILLS in the specs department). The battery life so far has been excellent and I know could be even better if I used battery saving mode.

Additionally, this has to be the SEXIEST laptop ever made!! I mean, it's a little thing, but every time I pull it out of my case (I bought the Tomtoc 15.6" laptop case and it's perfect for this) I feel like I'm unwrapping a dove dark chocolate. It is seriously so beautiful. Well done HP! The facial recognition unlock was a little buggy for the first week but now the moment I open the lid and look at the camera it recognizes me within a fraction of a second and unlocks. That is such a cool feature! It boots up faster than any laptop I've ever seen. It fits with plenty of room to spare in the laptop sleeve of my Thule backpack for when I don't feel like bringing my laptop bag and accessories along (see pic).

In terms of complaints, I have a few that you should know about, but for me, none of them take away from the overall amazingness that is this machine so I didn't take off any stars. You can decide what is important to you. First, I mentioned the scratches to the HP logo, which really are hardly visible but I was still a little bummed at first. WORTH the money I saved by buying refurbished for sure though! I do wish it came with the pen, but honestly I wanted to use a different pen with it anyway. The Wacom Bamboo Inksmart stylus works GREAT with this laptop and is better than the HP pen in my opinion. Also, this laptop does run pretty hot when I'm pushing it (editing), but that's to be expected. If you're a big gamer or plan to really push the system, plan to do so while sitting at a table/desk or at least with a stand over your lap. It would not be comfortable to push this laptop hard with it actually on your legs directly or even in bed with a comforter between your legs and the machine. It can be a bit of a fingerprint magnet, but I love the look and wouldn't change it, even though lame/boring silver would probably show less fingerprints than the sexy chocolate and gold finish they went with. The lid can be a little tricky to open and nearly impossible with one hand. This can be a bit annoying, but certainly isn't that big of a deal to me. Also, I wish it had an anti-glare and privacy screen, but it doesn't.

I could talk about this laptop all day, but after doing a lot of research and comparing with similar machines, trust me when I tell you that this is the best of the best and you will not find a better, beefier, sexier, more versatile machine in such a slender package anywhere right now. If you've been in the market for a new laptop, THIS IS THE ONE YOU WANT!!!! You can thank me after you buy it. And again, make sure you know which generation you're getting. The 8th gen is quad core vs dual core in the 7th, has a bigger battery, faster charge and upgraded dedicated graphics card. The one I bought is the 8th gen 15.6" with the 512 SSD and the 16GB of RAM. It is an absolute dream boat machine. I love it so much I just might marry it. Hope this helps! And yes I paid full price for it!! Worth. Every. Penny.

title: Adequate complement to a lap top if the DisplayLink driver doesn't leave you with blue screen woes
text:
I bought one of these for use while on the road so I can do work on my laptop in the same manner as for my multi-monitor system at home. It appears it will suffice for that purpose. The buying decision was prompted by it being USB powered and only slightly larger than my lap top, a Toshiba Ultrabook, enabling me to fit both in my lap top case and forgoing the need to carry yet another wall wart. Getting it operational was another story and is the reason I cannot recommend buying one of these. The problems with getting it operational for my machine were not so bad as to cause me to return it, but had I known in advance about them I would gone looking for a different option rather than risk the potential negatives associated with AOC's DisplayLink driver. Here are the major issues I encountered:
1. My laptop has 2 USB2 ports and 1 USB3 port. The monitor won't operate unless its Y-connector uses both the USB3 and one of the two USB2 ports, leaving me with just one USB2 port for anything else (such as a wireless mouse, etc). While I can plug a hub into the USB2 port, many devices won't work unless a hub is powered, in which case I might as well have gone with a secondary monitor powered from an outlet rather than USB.
2. Getting the AOC to operate required not only updating my USB3 driver, but the DataLink driver as well, which incidentally compromised Intel's igfxext display driver on my laptop, a known problem they have not fixed. While that doesn't appear to have had any negative effect for my lap top display, I have to wonder if I'm going to have trouble trying to operate a projector or some other display device should the need arise down the road.
3. In extending the primary display to the AOC, icons are scattered across both, rather than just providing me with an auxiliary work area. Also, the primary display's background is simply pasted at the primary's resolution on the AOC, nevermind the background's source image is at a resolution higher than either display.
4. Plug and play was not in the cards for my lap top, a bad sign since it is a major name brand. I convinced a friend to try the AOC on his lap top (a different Toshiba model), where it proved to be operable from a single USB3; however, installing the DisplayLink driver on his machine caused a far more serious problem in that his previously working bluetooth dongle consistently caused the machine to blue screen if plugged in. Bluetooth is integrated into my lap top, so I count myself fortunate I didn't encounter that particular woe. In any event, the DisplayLink driver is at best a work in progress, so buyer beware that you might be faced with an uninstall/return if you opt to purchase one.

Since I have the device working OK for me, I am hanging on to it, but the blue screen episode and the other issues with the DisplayLink software definitely leads to a do not buy recommendation.

title: Excellent route guidance with maps, but many other features are inferior.
text:
I create routes and lead rides for a small Southern California cycling club. I ride about 500 miles per month. I find having a GPS device with a large display that clearly shows me the pre-planned course is essential. The Garmin Edge 1000 does an excellent job at this. The reason why I rated it only 3-stars is because of everything else.

I'm happy to say that after a number of years, Garmin has made a lot of improvements to its companion website, Garmin Connect. Unfortunately, I still cannot use it for planning club rides because not every member of my club has a GPS device, so I need to create turn-by-turn cue sheets to pass out at each ride. Garmin Connect doesn't have a print option for courses that provides this. (I know that I can use other websites like Strava to do this, but I'm reviewing Garmin, okay?)

The Garmin bundle includes a heart rate monitor. In my experience, they last about 5 months and then quit working. I've tried replacing the CR2032 battery, but that doesn't help. After going through two Garmin heart rate monitors, I gave up and now use a rechargeable wrist heart rate monitor made by Mio.

Another issue is Bluetooth. I periodically have to re-pair the device to my iPhone because every couple of months they stop speaking to each other. Also, the Garmin has to be paired to the iPhone twice: Once for GPS data to be uploaded from the device to the iPhone to transfer your activity to Garmin Connect and the other pairing is for incoming call data and SMS messages to be displayed on the Garmin device while riding. These Bluetooth connections are very flaky. While riding, it is not uncommon to see the message flash across the Garmin's display saying Phone Disconnected and then some time later by Phone Connected.

Finally, there's the power button on the left side of the device. It is a microswitch under a rubberlike band that wraps around the entire perimeter of the device. This rubberlike band eventually wears out and breaks, making it impossible to operate the power button. Garmin wants $200 to repair it. I fixed mine with a few tiny pieces of rubber that I cut from an old inner tube and a piece of duct tape.

Overall, I'm not terribly impressed with Garmin, but I don't really have any viable alternatives.

title: Just Barely Passes - That's About It...
text:
I ordered and received two of these from the same vendor Premier Audio Video: I do professional graphics work and did not expect these low-cost monitors to meet mid-level graphics-intensive requirements but rather for general computer usage. My low-level expectations were met...

Shipping and Delivery:
Although I ordered two monitors from the same vendor at the same time, on the same order. For some odd reason the vendor shipped them separately, via Fedex, resulting in two separate deliveries by two separate Fedex trucks at two different times of the day ! From a shipping standpoint I think it would have been easier to ship them as a single shipment... but perhaps there's something about shipping with Fedex that I don't know.

Cables and CD:
One of the monitors came with its power cord, VGA cable, and a CD with drivers and basically marketing junk. The 2nd monitor, came with the same cables, and was missing the CD - go figure. Luckily, with one CD I could get to the drivers and utilities, etc for both monitors.

The CD contains 3 utilities that facilitate adjusting the monitor, and a set of drivers. There are no written instructions at all. The drivers on the CD include drivers for various AOC monitors and includes a folder named "2770" and another name "2770 Win 10".

Initial Setup: I installed one monitor on a Windows 7 Pro machine and the other on a Windows 10 machine. In both cases, the monitor automatically adjusted its aspect ratio to provide a full screen view, no other adjustments were necessary. And in both cases, the monitor produce pretty much the same quality level of image/presentation. Initially, even if you don't install the monitor's driver, Windows sets up the monitor with a generic PnP driver and it seems to work well enough.

I decided to use the drivers from AOC, so proceeded to update the current driver. However, after selecting the 2770 Win 10 folder to do a driver update, Windows 10 says that its current driver is better.

Just to be sure Windows was not leaving anything out on the driver side, I went to the AOC website (U.S website), looked up the monitor model and downloaded the driver package for the E2770SHE. I proceeded to install the AOC provided driver: Windows used a generic PnP driver and initially, if you try and change it Windows will report that it already has the "best driver" installed. However, you can override that and install the driver manually by looking for the driver on your machine with the "I have a disk" option. After doing so I installed the just downloaded driver from AOC - note that if you do this, if you previously set any options on the monitor they will be lost. After installing the AOC driver I saw absolutely no difference in the quality of the image produced. So for completeness you can load the AOC driver but in my case it made no difference, and it might not in your case if you do the same.

Missing Pixels: I didn't detect missing pixels, at least not so far.

Sharpness: The monitor is not the sharpest, granted it is a 27" monitor, the sharpness could be better. There is a feature accessible using the buttons on the underside called "Clear View" that acts like a sharpening filter if you've ever used one to sharpen images in a graphics program. There are three levels of sharpening and even the lowest setting there was a noticeable blooming and halo effect around text. The remaining setting are even more severe. In my opinion, the :"Clear View" feature is totally useless and I would avoid like the plague, especially for anything with text.

Brightness: The monitor is large, and is capable of high brightness (even though it uses an SDR color space) so you can be easily blinded by its brightness, particularly with text on a white background.

Adjustments: The monitor has a set of buttons on the underside that gets you into the menu for adjustments, etc. One of the three utilities also does the same thing - so you can do adjustments via software and/or using the monitors buttons. Using the buttons takes some practice and can be quite frustrating since you'll invariably make mistakes along the way and wind up changing a setting when you don't want to, or getting out of a particular setting's menu when you don't want to.

Software utilities: You can also install and use one of the utilities from the CD that can access all the same adjustment features, at least on a Windows 10 machine, with the exception of the previously mentioned "Clear View" feature - in that instance, not being able to access "Clear VIew" is no loss since it doesn't make anything better: I'd recommend using the software utility for adjustments over using the buttons on the monitor - you'll experience less trauma that way. However, on a Windows 7 machine not all of the utilities menu selections are available; on Windows 10 they are. Why they are not available on Windows 7 vs Windows 10 is not indicated in the utility.

Saving your settings: Once you've gotten the settings to what you prefer you can save them using a short 8 character file name.

I spent about 1 hour adjusting one monitor, using Windows 10, to get the contrast / brightness / color-temp and a few other areas as good as I could, after which the presentation was nothing more than "satisfactory".

Inputs: This monitor has two HDMI inputs, and a single VGA input. The VGA input makes it compatible with almost all computers. The two HDMI inputs are useful if you have a computer with an HDMI output, or you want to connect something like a streaming stick (something I did not try).

Thin Bezel: The Amazon page says "thin bezel" : Not at all. This particular model AOC has a rather typical bezel. It's rather thick. If you're planning on putting them side-by-side for a two or more monitor set up, don't ! Otherwise, I had no issue with the bezel.

Final thoughts:

The biggest issue with this model are: a) sharpness; it should be better, b) text on white background, c) washed-out colors:

In fairness to AOC I didn't try using an HDMI input with the computers I have, mainly because they don't put out an HDMI signal. But if you have a computer that does, it's possible you'll have better experience than I did with some of these issues. But even my non-HDMI monitors have better clarity and contrast using a VGA input than this AOC model does.

No matter what I did to adjust the monitor I could not get colors and contrast to what I see on some of my other (similarly low-end) monitors. Contrast seems to not really work as "contrast" but more like Gamma which affects brightness. Even after adjustments colors were somewhat washed out. Viewing text on a white background is a challenge with this monitor, add to this the fact that many websites have adopted to using very light text on a white background and you will likely have issues with the text being really hard to read. This is an area where it will take lots of effort to adjust the monitor so that you can see text well enough, has good white, yet doesn't blind you.

Now just because this is an inexpensive monitor doesn't mean it should have the issues I found with it. I have "cheap" monitors that work better with all the shortcoming this one has. So while price is a factor, in this day and age any monitor should be sharp enough and contrast should work well. If you need a monitor for any kind of graphics work, even non-professional work, I think you will be disappointed with this model. If you want a monitor for general usage this will sort of "fill-the-bill" if you have the patience to do the adjustments, and even after that you're likely to be somewhat unhappy with it in my opinion.

I would have sent my two monitors back, but the vendor charges a 20% restock fee which is pretty punitive IMO, and of course you'll have to pay return shipping as well. If I expected to do serious graphics work these would have failed miserably, but I was not expecting to do that. Aside from the issues I found they still are quite usable for average use.

But, having said that, there are better monitors in this price range, so definitely pass this one up.

And, try and purchase from a vendor that doesn't have such a punitive return policy as Premier Audio Video.

title: Failed when it was needed most due to terrible software and quality control. Stay away!
text:
I've had this dash cam for 9 months now, and after putting a trouble-free Viofo A118 (this model's predecessor) in my old car, I assumed that this model would be just as good. Boy, was I mistaken.

At first, my A119S would simply forget its saved settings every few weeks or so. Then, after several months, it would complain more and more regularly about requiring SD card formatting, even a startup or two after a fresh SD card format. I thought these were annoying quirks I could live with, but then the worst bug of all reared its ugly head. It would start up and show its video feed, seemingly without any problems, but would not respond to button presses and would not actually record any video. This was almost impossible to spot unless you waited for the camera to start up, waited for 10 additional seconds, and noticed that the "recording" icon on the camera screen's UI wasn't blinking as it normally would. Confusingly, the red "recording" LED on the front of the camera *was* still illuminated!

I learned this the hard way when someone ran into me at low speed, a case that should have been easy for me to prove their fault. However, I went to check my footage and found that the dash cam simply hadn't been recording anything for the last two weeks! So I ended up having no way to prove the other party at fault and was now on the hook for the cost of my insurance deductible because this product *failed to do the one job it was supposed to do* when I needed it to.

I RMAed the camera and got a working replacement, only to have the same unresponsiveness issue show up in my replacement after two months. I then get a *SECOND* RMA replacement, and what would you know, the unresponsiveness issue happens *YET AGAIN* within a month! After a little due diligence, I finally found out that this was actually a firmware issue that company handling my RMAs wasn't aware of. (For all of you unfortunately burdened with one of these things, search for the "Viofo A119S 2.2 firmware update"). With the firmware update, I *finally* got the camera working in normal order for the first time I could remember. That is, until last week, when it started forgetting its saved settings again.

The bottom line is that they hardware on this model may be very good, but the software leaves me with absolutely no confidence in this product. I'll be shopping around for a replacement, and it definitely won't be one of these.

This proved to be a problem when we left home shortly after the install and set the email function to notify on motion. My email goes off every few minutes with the change of light in the room, reflections in the room, birds at the windows and motion lights coming on outside. We will be gone for a few weeks and my email will have me up all night and all day because these settings can't be changed remotely. I know.. I should have tested it more thoroughly before leaving it, but with people and pets moving around while we were home, we simply ran out of time and turned the motion on when we left. Most systems have remote access to these things and I had already struggled with the software issues for 5 days before we left and decided to let it go until we arrived at our destination and finish it all up.  Because the company is in China, the support center is open during a completely different time proving difficult to connect with. While they have been somewhat helpful it took a long time to get to the point where they finally understood my problem and told me there was no way to access the settings remotely. Unfortunately, this system is nothing more than a monitoring system that can be easily viewed and modified while we are next to the actual system components at home. It does not work well if you travel often and need easy access, reliability or ease of use. We will have to add an additional system to this one that has options similar to our previous Lorex system. Having been burglarized in recent months, this is quite frustrating and a disappointment besides the fact that my email notifications will drive me crazy in the coming days with no way to modify them other than turning off my email.  If they can get their software issues resolved, I would recommend the system. If not, check your reviews before you purchase and ask specific questions that suit your needs before purchasing. The cameras seem to drop off for short periods frequently but come back up quickly. I can't speak as to the quality of the cameras placed outside just yet. title: Incredible value and nice selection of apps, including PlayStation Now
text:
I bought this in replacement of my Sony BDP-S1100 Blu-ray player, which was getting old and started freezing up and having other issues. I have not had any problems with this Blu-ray player so far.

Sony has released four Blu-ray players this year: The BDP-S1500 (this Blu-ray player), the BDP-S3500, the BDP-S5500, and the BDP-S6500. The S1500 is the cheapest and has the fewest features. The S3500 adds Wi-Fi and Miracast, as well as some other small features. The S5500 adds 3D capability and 2D to 3D upscaling. And the S6500 adds 4k upscaling. If you don't need Wi-Fi, Miracast, 3D or 4k upscaling, then this player is for you. If you need any of those things, you will have to pay more to buy a higher model.

What's new in this 2015 Blu-ray player? A couple things. First of all, there's a new interface. From the Home screen you can easily launch your favorite apps, play the disc, or browse the pictures, music, and videos on your USB. If you go to All Apps, you can see all the apps available. The interface is easy to use and navigate, and it looks nice, too. Also, there is the PlayStation Now feature, which I'll mention later.

PICTURE/AUDIO QUALITY
_____________________20/20

¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯
Picture quality is pretty awesome. Blu-ray discs look incredible on an HDTV. DVDs obviously aren't as nice, but still look great with the 1080p upscaling. The audio quality is awesome. I have tested the audio from the coaxial port and the HDMI, and they both sound great (I have 5.1 surround sound and it's working perfectly).

FEATURES

¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯
No Wi-Fi, 3D, or 4k upscaling, but at this price, it will be very hard to get these things. It does, however play Blu-rays, DVDs and Audio CDs, as well as the pictures, videos, and music on your USB flash drive, and has a decent selection of apps (including Netflix, Amazon Instant Video, Hulu Plus, Vudu, Crackle, YouTube, Pandora, Facebook, and more, plus others in the Opera TV Store app), and has the PlayStation Now feature. With PlayStation Now, you can stream PlayStation games (you can rent games or buy a supscription). I haven't tried it out yet, but I don't think it will run as fast or be as good as a PlayStation, and you will still have to buy a game controller. Still, it's a cool feature not found on other Blu-ray player brands.

DESIGN

The overall design is nice. It has a clean, simple design that's pleasing to the eye. It is very compact (1½ in. tall, 9 in. from left to right, and 7¼ in. from back to front), which is nice, but also means that there is not enough room for a display that tells you the run time of the disc. The Blu-ray player boots fast, and loads DVDs and Blu-ray Discs quickly. There is a slight bit of lag when navigating the menus, but apps open relatively fast (faster than any other Sony Blu-ray player I've tried).
