title: Amazing at everything!
text:
I'm blown away by these. There is no other way to describe it. The sound-stage and imaging are wide and detailed. Bass has amazing quality *and quantity* without killing the lower mid-range. Vocals are clear as a bell. Electric guitars have crunch and detail to them. Treble is refined and clear without being overbearing or fatiguing. The hammock style headband causes no pressure points, and is very comfortable. Once in a while I find I do reach up and readjust pressure of the headband, but only rarely during long listening or gaming sessions. The ear-pads are soft velour, but the foam is a little stiff. I predict that will soften up with use. I honestly can't find fault with anything these headphones do. If I had to pick nits, I'd say that they aren't the lightest headphones I own. Even that isn't a flaw, because the sense of build quality is superb.

I purchased these along with the Beyerdynamic DT 1770 Pro headphones. They sound much alike, except that the X2s have a much more open sound (instruments and vocals seem to come from outside the headphones vs being confined within), and they don't have the sometimes shrill treble the 1770's had. The X2 bass hit just as hard. Vocals and guitars were very present but not quite as loud. High hats and symbols were just as clear without being harsh at higher volumes. Both are exceedingly comfortable, with a few minor gripes for each. The 1770s would cause a pressure point on the top of my head, but the X2s I would have to adjust the headband from time to time over multi-hour listening periods. I would say both are very amazing headphones, but the X2's for 1/3rd of the price are the clear winners. (Full disclosure - the 1770s I tried did have a slight volume imbalance in the L and R channels, so I'm not sure I got a 100% good set. ?? Dunno.)

I also compared these to my Fostex T50RP with Shure HPAEC1540 Replacement Alcantara Ear Pads and Mr. Speakers Comfort Leather Headstrap. You can immediately tell these are headphones meant for 2 different audiences. The T50RP had no where near the quantity of bass, nor the extension into the treble that the X2s have. The T50RPs sound much more volume balanced across all frequencies than the X2. The T50RPs would probably satisfy audiophiles looking more for neutral or flat. The X2s are fun, in every category. Don't get me wrong, the T50RPs sound fantastic, but for Rock / EDM / HipHop / Rap, you won't get the visceral bass impact that make the X2 just so addicting. Comfort (without modifications / accessories) goes to the X2. With the Shure earpads and headstrap, the T50RPs win. TL;DR - for my tastes, X2 wins.

Compared to my Sennheiser HD650, the X2s just destroy them in the bass department. People have called the 650's dark, and now I get it. Compared to the X2 they most definitely are. It's much of the same in comparison between the T50RP vs the X2. The HD650 just don't have the extended fun of the low and high end, and sound more flat. The 650's have even less bass than my T50RPs, but to be kind to the 650's they are my oldest set of headphones at +10 years old. The X2 has repaced the 650's as my full-time computer headphones.

X2s as computer gaming headphones - Some of the best I've heard. Playing Overwatch with it's Dolby Atmos setting turned on, I get a very real sense of space from the sounds in the game. I've heard players coming from around corners before I could see them. I've clearly heard players come up behind me. It's uncanny. I was accused of cheating! (To be expected, I suppose.) Anyway, for spatial sense and clarity, these are as good as I've heard for gaming.

The set I received did not have glue holding the ear pads in place. I left them on a piece of paper, and no color bleed. The reviews stating these were issues just weren't issues for the set I received.

Hardware: PC running Jriver Media Center 21 connected via USB to Teac UD-503 (home) or Micca Origen+ (work).
All music files @ 16/320 MP3s or higher / FLAC.

title: It's absolutely perfect!
text:
Before I explain why I loved this tablet, I have to commend Huion for how they packaged it. Not only was it packed neatly with Styrofoam, but the front and back was guarded with plywood. That tells me that they really care about making sure their products get to the customer with as little risk of damage as possible!

Now onto the actual tablet, As someone who wants to make digital art more the actual tablet, I started off drawing on a normal tablet, I've been wanting to invest in a pen display tablet, and almost fell into the trap of thinking that the only way to go was pouring a ton of money in Wacom Cintiq. But before sealing that deal, curious me went on the hunt for Cintiq alts, and this angel showed itself!

This tablet is simply Amazing! The build of the tablet feel very sturdy and comfortable to hold, and the huge screen provides a lot of work space, which is desirable for a big person like myself. The matte-finish screen has a slightly rough feel, but not too rough where it feels really cringingly gritty. Kind of like the simulated feel of drawing on a paper canvas. The matte finish also makes the screen glare-resistant (not glare-PROOF, but resistant).

When drawing on the screen, I can certainly feel the 8000+ levels of pressure sensitivity. I really do feel I can draw as light or as heavy as I desire. And one of the greatest things about this thing is its lack of parallax! It's practically non-existent until you start going to the far edges of the screen. But otherwise, cursor placement is really spot on!

I do have one MINOR issue with the tablet, and it's more of a personal gripe than a flaw. I do love the express keys and slide bar, but it never stops bothering me that they're mirrored on both sides. I understand that they did that so it's comfortable for both left and right-handed users, but having all the buttons individually programmable wouldn't have been any less hassling for both parties. I can easily work with just 10 buttons and 1 slide bar, but I just personally feel that customizability was cut in half with this decision.

There are other things like the RPS, color gamut, etc. But I'm not that spec-tech savvy to really have an input on that. The colors look great to me after a little calibrating, and as long as the tablet, drivers, and express keys work efficiently with the art programs I'm using, that's enough for me to be satisfied.

I gladly give this product 4.75/5 stars, which may as well still be 5 stars! My personal gripe aside, I've had this tablet for a few months now, and it is simply magnificent and I don't know if I'll ever upgrade from this model! title: A Great Little Speaker For What I Need It For
text:
I received this iHome model iBT16 Portable Rechargeable Bluetooth Speaker (NIP) from my brother today. I needed an extension speaker which I could connect to my large flat screen television and set next to my bedside, so that I (and no others) will only hear the television without me having to wear headphones at home...heh...heh. Well, this little plastic speaker with a rubberized finish (just slightly smaller than a 3" cube) does that job well. The speaker simply plugs into my TV's 'headphone out' jack via an extended 25' 3.5 mm (male / male connectors) audio cable (available at any audiophile store).

Although it came with its own USB to micro USB charging cable, I went ahead and used one (with wall adapter) from one of my cell phones and it worked just fine. As matter of fact, the cell phone charging unit actually charged the speaker to (its initial) full capacity in just under two hours as compared to the eight hours if it would've been plugged into a laptop or a PC (per the owner's manual).

Although the Bluetooth (paring / auto sync) connectivity feature works great (I tried it on three of my phones), I really won't be using this speaker that way for the most part. BTW, the speaker's volume is controlled by my TV's remote, as my TV is automatically placed into 'mute mode' whenever the TV's headphone jack is occupied.

Although the owner's manual is not quite clear; i.e., the photo schematic just designates the speaker's rear Aux Jack as an Aux-out (only) Jack, it's actually dual purpose - AUX-In and AUX-Out. Just slide the power switch all the way to the right and the speaker can then be used as an external / extension speaker from that same jack for any audio source using a 3.5 mm audio-out jack. Since I like the way this speaker sounds (not distorted and not 'tinny'...even with my TV's volume set to 50% which is more than loud enough), I will be purchasing an additional one in black from Amazon.com, because I'm afraid that this color might be on its way to being discontinued; i.e., I can no longer find one in black on the iHome site?

UPDATE:

After being plugged into my television and playing overnight, so far, the battery life has exceeded well over twelve hours of continual (uninterrupted) operation with much more to go; however, I prefer not to operate the speaker until its battery life has been fully exhausted...cheers.

The double tap only lets you choose between Siri or Play pause. It would have been great to have left tap for Siri, right for play/pause or some kind of volume control gesture. Second, the whole double tap detection itself was very flaky, based on my usage for around 2 days, the earphones just failed to detect double taps 80% of the time, often I had to go to my phone screen and pause a song or start it. The other issue I had was I experience momentary disconnects while music was playing even though the phone was in my pocket when I either put my hand on the back of the phone or moved my head in a certain way. These disconnects were not very frequent but they did happen.
And now the obvious flaw that everyone mentions, the possibility of losing them. I considered getting a lanyard, but given the way these recharge, it will be impractical to remove and re-attach the lanyard every time I have to put these in their case.

In short I am not impressed with this product, its an excellent idea and I love their product design as always. But the product seems unfinished, especially the bluetooth and gesture recognition. Hopefully this is something they can fix over software patches. But for now I think I will be returning mine as I did not feel the price was worth the overall usability of this product.

title: Yet another great Fuji prime
text:
I've owned a Fujifilm X100 (sold for X100s), X100s, X-E2, 18-55mm OIS, 35mm f/1.4, 56mm f/1.2, Zeiss 12mm f/2.8 and a couple flashes. I'm biased towards my positive experiences in the system and the "look" I get from the jpegs (which are amazing btw) and RAW. With that in mind ...

I love this lens. This and the 56mm were the two I most looked forward to. I do a lot of candid shots of people and more shots of my pets than I want to admit. I used to think the 56mm is the ultimate portrait lens, but in many ways this eclipses it (both have great merits).

For starters 90mm is a great portrait focal length. ~85mm-95mm is probably the most common one for DSLR users these days, and it's much more flattering than ~50mm. Cropping helps with some things, but good ole fashioned focal lengths help with conveying depth, or in this case slightly compressing it. 90mm will start to make features more subtle (the extreme opposite effect can be seen in ultra wides which can fill a frame with a nose), and most of us look better with subtle features. That model in a magazine or catalog was probably photoshopped, but pick up old magazines. They still looked great. Yeah there were some darkroom tricks, but it's not uncommon to see 135mm-300mm used in studios to compress features. Fuji didn't invent this effect, but it's one huge leg up this lens has on the already stellar 56mm f/1.2. 90mm generally is better than 56mm for portraits (1.5x focal length crops really don't matter here, but even if you think they do, 135mm is better than 85mm).

Onto this particular lens. It's really your only option for the X system outside of adapters and manually focusing with a lens from another system, but even if you could magically put a Nikon or Canon 85mm lens on with AF and everything, this lens has them beat. It's amazingly sharp edge to edge. You will get a noticeable bump in sharpness stopping down to 2.8, but honestly it's good to go wide open. Sharpness is just one aspect, and while easy to see/measure, it's probably less important than contrast (my opinion at least). This lens excels there as well. Pictures really shine with a very crisp clear yet flattering look. It's not quite up to the best Zeiss glass (sadly neither does the Zeiss glass available for the X system), but it's quite remarkable, and better than my Nikon primes.

It is heavy, but it handles surprisingly well on my X-E2. I'd prefer a X-T1 and a grip, but It's not too bad, nor do I worry about my strap lugs pulling out. The generously sized MF barrel (no surprise, as there's no need for a zoom) is well damped, but I'm not generally a fan of MF feel on the X system. The aperture ring is a nice step up from earlier ones on the 35mm f/1.4 that seemed to lose their place a bit too easily. In both cases, my old Nikon glass does still leave me wanting here (direct manual focus and an aperture lock), but that old glass has nothing on this. Autofocus isn't a strength here again, but it's no worse than other X system glass. Plenty for portraits. Not ideal for moving subjects (unless they are parallel to focal plane).

The rest is all good. Modest but generally low distortion, flare, and CA (distortion and CA should be fixed automatically), and ghosting is all but a non issue. Compared to the 56mm f/1.2, I'd say this is a better portrait lens, and it's a bit better all around (YMMV and sometimes 56mm fits the bill better than 90mm no matter the lens). The basis for this is the overall sharpness wide open (though stop down the 56mm to f/2 and it's comparable), more flattering focal length, and better close focusing. The 56mm f/1.2 has a greater minimum focal length. It's a real tour de force and statement with the f/1.2 max aperture, but this lens is a bit more practical. Then again, I enjoy owning both. Plus the same grads, polarizers, NDs, etc... work on both.

Do I recommend this lens? For some, absolutely. If you're already using the system and and you're comfortable using primes, it's highly recommended. I'm quite delighted!

title: Great device that has been a serious longterm headache to get properly working, solution was completely illogical!
text:
I've been a Tivo user for almost ten years, and my previous unit lasted forever with no problems, but was about to become obsolete with Comcast/Xfinity. So I upgraded to a Bolt because the price was reasonable, considering that a year of service was included. The interface of the Bolt is awesome and I was really enjoying my new machine, until after about a month or so when certain HD channels slowly started becoming more and more pixelated.

The problem has continued to get worse, and I've been troubleshooting the problem with the advice of Tivo's website, forums online, and calls to both Xfinity and Tivo, to no avail. The issue according to Tivo is that my cable signal strength isn't good enough, but Xfinity sent a tech out and the signal is fine until it gets inside the Tivo unit, at which point readings are 65-70% signal strength (80-99% is ideal), with an SNR of 26 to 27db (29 to 35 is needed). What both Tivo and Xfinity suggested was removing any splitters in my line, but for some bizarre reason, removing a splitter results in NO SIGNAL AT ALL which is completely illogical.

Tivo's tech support is frustrating and they ask you the same 40 questions without really listening to you and can't offer any advice beyond what their website troubleshooting would give, and when they told me that I needed to take the issue up with Xfinity, I finally decided to ask for a "manager" (who seemed more like an actual knowledgeable tech, but who also did not seem to believe me) and I insisted that they send me a new box to try, in case mine is defective. They agreed, but it will cost me $50 and take a week to arrive.

In the meantime, since I've done everything that I can possibly think of and read all kinds of different horror stories about similar scenarios (a lot of longtime customers think Tivo has taken a big dive in quality and service in the last year or two), I decided to try something completely ridiculous. Since I can only get a signal with a splitter attached for some reason, I decided to add another splitter right before the one that is hooked up to my Tivo/modem, and SHOCKINGLY my signal instantly got stronger, not weaker. This goes against everything that Tivo and Xfinity techs will tell you, and makes me wonder if my particular Bolt is possessed or something. So since this worked, I added yet another splitter to the line and now my signal is nearly full strength, and there is no more pixelation at all. Perhaps my Xfinity signal is TOO STRONG for the Bolt, and it needs these splitters to cut it down to something it can handle?

So now my Bolt is working close to how it should, no thanks to Tivo, just due to my own hours of trial and error and some dumb luck. I'm still waiting on the replacement unit they are sending, and it will be interesting to see if it behaves similarly. If there's no difference, they said I could return it and get a refund for the $50 replacement charge... though after reading some consumer complaints elsewhere about their billing practices, I'm a little nervous about whether I'll actually be able to get a refund.

title: One of the best upgrades I ever made on my computer!
text:
My aging i7 desktop computer was purchased in 2009. After replacing the graphics adapter, I saw that the last real upgrade I can make to it (besides swapping out the motherboard, which would require a new CPU and RAM and is like basically getting a new computer) would be to move to a SSD. From the good reviews, I chose this Intel drive. The 480GB size would let it match my current 450GB drive, and I wouldn't have to uninstall software so that I could move my system over to it.

The drive came in a very small package with a SATA cable and a mini-CD. You'll need to have an available SATA power cable in your chassis. Since it's a 2.5" drive, I also purchased an adapter kit so that the drive could be mounted in the 3.5" drive bay (thankfully, the kits are cheap). I used the supplied cable to plug the drive into an existing SATA port on my motherboard, then dangled the drive from an existing SATA power cable that was available. Starting up the computer, the drive was recognized and Windows 8.1 offered to initialize it for my system. You need to do that if you want to access it with the Intel Toolbox or cloning tool (more on that later in the review). Initializing it didn't add any partitions to it, but let Windows now see it as an non-partitioned drive.

The mini-CD only contained basic operating manuals and no software. Choose the PDF for your language, and there were basic instructions and a link to the tools needed from Intel. Download the Toolbox and the Intel Data Migration Software (which is a stripped down version of Acronis software tailored for the Intel SSD), and install them. When you run the Data Migration Software, it recognizes the drive, then reboots your computer directly into the software (this must often be done as Windows is usually using the system files and they can't be accessed by programs while it's running). The tool then cloned my existing drive to the SSD (it took about an hour), told me it was done, and then let me shut down the computer. I then pulled out my existing hard drive, mounted the Intel SSD into the adapter bracket, and put the SSD into my computer where my old hard drive was. After plugging in the original cables I used for my original hard drive, I powered up my system and watched as Windows came up with blazing speed. Within seconds, I was at the login screen. After supplying my password, the Start screen popped up a second later. Normally I'd have to wait several minutes for background programs and processes to finish loading because it overtaxes my hard drive too much, but now there was no wait.

It was incredible! I rebooted several times just because it was so fun watching it boot so quickly.

Some advice..... my system came with a "recovery partition". It was a 14GB partition that would let me restore my computer to its factory settings. My system originally came with Vista, so there's no reason why I'd ever go back that far. When I cloned my hard drive, that partition was cloned too. And, this is IMPORTANT, the partition was *before* my main partition that holds Windows. Even after deleting that partition from the SSD, available space has to be *after* the partition you want to expand/extend. Since that partition is *before* my system partition, I now have a 14GB section of space that will be its own 14GB drive. Yes, I can still use the space, but it's not all that useful to have such a small partition. It'd be much better to have that space added to the main partition. So if you have a recovery partition you don't need anymore, delete it BEFORE you clone your drive.

My older motherboard means Windows is using an Intel AHCI driver. There's a feature built into the drive called "trim" that the AHCI driver doesn't support. As the OS deletes files, it tells the SSD that the file has been deleted and that the SSD shouldn't treat those areas anymore as holding data. The Intel AHCI driver doesn't do that, so you have to regularly run the Optimizer from the Toolbox. It's recommended to run it weekly, but it seems to run very quickly (within a minute), so you can do it more frequently. That's about the only drawback I can see from using the drive with the older motherboard (which must support AHCI). It's barely an inconvenience as it can be scheduled to run at regular intervals, so don't let that deter you.

Not everything is lightning fast. When loading large games or doing updates, your system still has to process information in memory, so it's not like everything is instantaneous. But it's still amazing how fast things load and how fast Windows starts up and is ready for use. What took minutes before now takes seconds. It's one of the best upgrades I ever made on my computer!

title: What a pleasant surprise!
text:
I've known Yamaha for a long time for their high quality musical equipment (and odd as it might seem for their high performance, big wheel stand motorcycles) starting with 30 year old desktop computer speakers that are still amongst the best I have. So it was no surprise that the 107BL sound bar performed beyond beyond my explanations.

Before getting the 107BL I had a couple of 55"+ sets that I equipped with Samsung true 5.1 systems that were terrific. But earlier this year I decided that one of the HDTV units actually had some picture and quality tradeoffs as it was a 3-D set. (Remember that time a few years ago when it had to be 3-D or nothing? When was the last time you saw any studio using 3-D to promote the sale of a new release?)

Being disappointed with the 3-D set I decided to replace it with a new 4K QLED 55" set that is simply spectacular. With the new 4K set inheriting the 5.1 surround sound system, what to do for audio on the 3-D set that I moved to a spare bedroom?

I didn't want to go to expense and installation hassle of a new 5.1 system so did some research on sound bars. When I saw that Yamaha was making a series I knew that I couldn't go wrong so ordered a 107BL unit as it had the features I was looking for and a size that hid it nicely behind the HDTV that sits atop a dresser.

I connected it via IR cable so that all the HDTV inputs would feed to it without having to make any switch changes. I leave the sound bar on all of time so all the time so all you need do is turn on the set and whichever input is being used.

It's good to note that with the set off and sound bar still on, there isn't a hiss, pop or hum to be heard. Also the current draw is nil without any signal input and you can actually hear a single pop when the set is turned on which I assume is the amplifiers waking up.

Switching to a sound bar was certainly easier and less expensive than installing another 5.1 system. And the surround sound effect is nearly as good at least in a rectangular room with sufficient hard wall spaces. Of particular importance is their Clear Voice feature. Both my wife and I have some hearing loss and I was worried that absent the dedicated center 5.1 voice channel speaker that we would have difficulty clearly understanding voice content. Well I don't know how they did it but voices come through clearly and strong. Finally, for its size, the bases/subwoofers do not disappoint.

title: Will NOT work with NVME M.2 SSDs!
text:
NOTE: This will NOT work with an NVME M.2 SSD. There is no mention of that fact in the product description. I discovered that the computer would not recognize the StarTech adapter, with either an Intel SSD6 or an HP Turbo Drive G2 M.2 NVME SSD that I have, both of which work perfectly fine in an Asus HyperX PCIE board.

Apparently, NVME is not compatible with SATA, unbeknownst to me.

I confirmed that the StarTech adapter will not work with NVME M.2 SSDs with StarTech (who returned my emails very quickly, I might add).

Here is what they said:

"Unfortunately, yes, the SAT32M225 is not compatible with NVMe m.2 drives. I apologize for the confusion and the inconvenience.
I apologize that this information was not available on Amazon. It is however available on our website under the knowledge base (link removed).

We do however, have 2 adapters that do allow NVMe connections (note, both are PCIE cards). PEX4M2E1 allows a singular M key NVMe M.2 drive to be connected PEXM2SAT32N1 allowed two B key SATA M.2 drives, and a M key NVMe m.2 drive to be connected."

So bottom line, if you have an NVME M.2, this StarTech adapter WILL NOT WORK.

title: Wildly overpriced and utterly useless
text:
I'm willing to pay extra to be an early adopter, but deliver a compelling product.....and bite some of the cost. Google glass is less than $100 in hardware and an utterly, completely, useless, device. I have to assume that Google R&D priced this thing to keep your typical consumer away -- knowing that people probably wouldn't find a single compelling use for it (correct!). The only reason I could imagine buying this is if you think it's going to be to smart glasses what Altair 8800 was to personal computers or maybe a niche product like the Apple Lisa......some kind of wildly speculative technology collector.

A lot is made out of privacy concerns and being a "glasshole"......but the honest truth is that people will put those concerns aside in a second if the product delivers. If this was game changing technology, like smart phones, then everybody willingly hands off their privacy. The real reason people find Google Glass annoying is because they are annoying....and do nothing.

title: Backup Camera Setup Could Be Much Better
text:
I am taking off 2 stars for a poorly designed backup camera system.

Pros: I prefer Garmin GPS software over my Tom-Tom and Magellan GPS systems. I like the idea of incorporating a backup camera function into the unit. The wireless signal is strong between the GPS and camera setup.

Cons: All of my negatives have to do with the backup camera setup:

The backup camera system displays a smeary picture. In this day and age of cheap mega-pixel cameras, it is unbelievable that Garmin charges so much for this kit and uses a poor quality camera. Three years ago, I purchased a $40 backup camera system for my pickup and it displays a much better image (check my previous review of that item).

The cable between the camera and the wireless sender is too short. They should have had at least a couple of feet more, if not 5 feet. (They want you to buy an extra 15 foot extension!)

The power supply cable for the wireless sender unit is long enough and has a tough housing but the wires used are too small and delicate. At the junction with the wireless sender, these small wires hang freely in order to incorporate an old fashioned glass fuse and fuse holder. It looks amateurish and is the weak spot in this setup. Garmin admits in their manual that this part is not waterproof.

The receiver for the wireless backup camera is not securely attached to the back of the GPS unit. It is easily released. You need to be careful with it or you lose your camera signal.

title: Excellent laptop, mine just had a small defect
text:
Over the years I've had a number of laptops from different manufacturers, all in the $4-500 range, and eventually they all had some problem or another that led me to replace them in a couple years. I read that business class laptops tend to last longer and have fewer issues, and after a lot of research I concluded that this one had all the features I want and should last longer than a consumer grade laptop. Pretty much everything about it is as good as I would expect - the touch screen, keyboard, track pad, speed, etc. There is a little but not very much bloatware which is nice. The included wacom pen works great, and although some common apps like PDF editors are not yet optimized for them, that's not really an issue with the laptop.

I took off one star because the laptop I got seemed to have a quality control issue - there was a faintly dim part of the screen near the bottom, like one of the LED lights was out. It wasn't very noticeable, but for a ~$1500 laptop I didn't want to be bothered by a manufacturer defect for years to come. Fortunately Amazon was great about troubleshooting the problem with me and giving me a full refund that it was deemed a defect rather than something I could fix on my own.

Overall I would highly recommend this laptop, just make sure your screen doesn't have an issues.
